en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
The Tantravārtika:
"Since the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that as their purpose are useless; therefore, they are said to be non-eternal."
Since the Veda has been established as a valid means of knowledge in every respect regarding dharma,
its utility in the form of explanatory passages (arthavādas) and mantras is now stated accordingly, because [otherwise] there would be an absence of result.

If, first of all, in the case of the *Garga-trirātra-brāhmaṇa* and the *Vedānumantraṇa*, the mention of the beauty of the face and the birth of a horse—which exist only at the time of the knowledge [of the mantra]—is not authoritative with respect to Dharma; and if, on the other hand, they do not exist [at that time], then it is so even with respect to their own literal meaning. Furthermore, because these are stated as present-tense descriptions (*vartamānāpadeśa*), there is a contradiction with perceptual non-apprehension (*pratyakṣānupalabdhi*). Since the refinement of knowledge (*vidyā-saṃskāra*) serves to qualify a person capable of performing the ritual—just like the initiation (*dīkṣita*) or bathing at a sacred ford (*tīrtha-snāna*)—it is self-sufficient and thus its status as an injunction for a fruit (*phala-vidhi*) will be refuted.

Because it would be redundant, one should not investigate that matter; therefore, he says: "Since it has already been refuted there by its being an injunction of a result, the investigation here concerns whether it is a meaningless *arthavāda*.

Furthermore, it is already established that even the purpose of praise (*stuti*) cannot belong to what is non-existent, because there can be no negation of something that does not participate [in the action].
All three statements concerning the earth and so forth negate an object that is not subject to negation.
First, because [the earth] has not reached the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) or the sky (*div*), it is not within the scope of negation;
and for this reason, since there is nothing to be excluded, there can be no exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

For since the piling [of the altar] is already established as being eternally present in the intermediate space, in heaven, and on earth, the injunction for it would be purposeless; and even if it were a restatement of the eternal, it would still lack the status of a prescriptive act (*akriyārthatva*).
Furthermore, both the prohibition and the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the piling on earth are impossible without subverting the injunction for piling;
and if there were such subversion, the injunction itself would be rendered purposeless.
Even in the alternative view, there is a contradiction;
moreover, because of its connection with desire, the fire-altar is indeed optional,
and the prohibition is weak.
Because, given that the earth is the primary object, it must be postulated as being piled;
this very fact constitutes its own internal inconsistency.
For immediately after the injunction, it is stated: "Having placed gold, one should pile," and "One should pile the fire-altar with bricks"—this would create a contradiction.

But the idea that it serves as an incitement (*prarocanā*) does not arise at all, because [the arthavāda] forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction; thus, they must serve the purpose of praise for the injunctions.
Why, then, is the sentence concerning Vāyu introduced when the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the previously cited sentences themselves ought to be stated?
Some say:
"Because the principle is the same, this [case] should also be seen as included there, and those [cases] should also be seen as cited here.
Even if that is so, nevertheless, a new example requires a different underlying intention.
That is now explained:
in all the previously cited examples, there is a suspicion that the literal meaning may be untrue.

In such cases, who would undertake the labor of establishing that [untruth] at the very outset? Therefore, the citation of the *vāyavya* passage is intended for the ease of understanding that—while its literal meaning is well-known to be true—it serves as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to the means of knowing Dharma (*dharmapramāṇa*) by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) through the medium of praise.
In this regard, the authors of the Bhāṣya state that [the mantra] serves the purpose of praise through its well-known status as a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatva).
However, this much must first be addressed here:
for what reason is the integrity of the form [of the mantra] not maintained, and why is syntactical unity or the human purposefulness of the Veda asserted by force?

Regarding the second quarter of the first chapter of the *Laukika*, if it should be argued that "in the case of worldly sentences, [the meaning] is perceived," to that it is replied: It is appropriate in the world to conceive of the sentence-meaning otherwise, because it is accessible through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); however, here [in the Veda], because the subject matter is entirely beyond the senses (*atyantātīndriya*), if there were any deviation from the literal sense, even if it were merely a fault, it would result in the Veda being of human origin (*pauruṣeya*).

Moreover, in the world as well, those statements whose objects are not known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) but which become authoritative for listeners solely by virtue of trust in a reliable person (*āpta*), cannot possibly be conceived of as being otherwise.
Regarding this, some say:
"And the traditional transmission is equal," and by what he will state later, it is established that the entire Veda has human purpose as its goal.
For conscious persons would not, with effort, maintain this [body] if it were of no benefit to the self.
And even if some might be ignorant, the assumption that our predecessors—the many past investigators—were negligent is without proof.
Therefore, in whatever way the body serves the purpose of the person, in that very way its nature as "food" (bhakṣya) is explained.
But this is not reasonable.
Why? Because it would entail that the validity [of the Veda] depends upon a person.
For if even an object that has not been perceived could be thus imagined by people like us, [the Veda would lose its authority].

If it is argued that because we uphold this [Veda] with great effort, its purpose is for the sake of merit (*puṇya*), then in that case, its authority would have to be admitted as being dependent upon human activity.

Alternatively, if one were to say that another person upholds it, even so, by virtue of that person, they too would depend on yet another, and so on; thus, even if there were no beginning, it would result in a "succession of the blind" (*andhaparamparā*), and since everyone would rely on the word of another, there would be no establishment of authority anywhere.
For everywhere there is the cognition "this person knows the Veda," but never the cognition "this is the meaning.
Therefore, although it may be inferred that those various students certainly consider the Veda to be for the sake of human ends,
nevertheless, because it lacks a foundation, it is not established by that alone.
Therefore, as long as the Veda itself does not present its entirety as being for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), it remains non-authoritative.
This is stated as follows:
first, regarding the entire Veda, the injunction to cultivate the act of study is established by the rule, "One's own portion of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied."

In that regard, when the expectation arises as to "what one should effect" (*bhāvayet*), although "study" (*adhyayana*) presents itself, it is excluded from the factor of the object (*karman*) because the injunctive [element], which possesses the power to impel a person toward activity, cannot impel one toward an effectuation (*bhāvanā*) whose result is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). Consequently, since there is no contradiction with "by means of study" (*adhyayanena*) and due to proximity, it enters into the factor of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
When one asks "What is the use of that?", because of the connection with "whatever is possible," the apprehension of syllables follows.

Since even that does not constitute a human goal, the question "What is the use of that? leads to the determination of words. From that comes the knowledge of word-meanings; from that, the knowledge of sentence-meanings; from that, performance; and through performance, the attainment of results such as heaven. When this much has been reached, the expectancy ceases. Thus, all injunctions remain incomplete until the attainment of a human goal.
Nor can it be assumed that heaven and the like are the result simply because they are seen in the injunctions;
for, by virtue of logical fitness (*yogyatā*), that alone is determined to be the effect of an action whose operation is observed to culminate immediately therein.
In that case, if the result is attained at some distance along the path in accordance with that very [operation], then it does not deserve to be postulated as something intermediate.

Even by means of an indirect purpose (*pāraṃparya-prayojana*), since the scriptural injunction is established, there is no occurrence of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) characterized by the impossibility of any other explanation.

However, where an immediately perceived effect is neither itself a human goal nor attains one indirectly—as, for example, the reaching of the *āhavanīya* fire or the reduction to ashes resulting from the *homa*—there, bypassing that effect, one must postulate an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) directly from the ritual act itself. This principle is to be applied in all cases.

However, where an action has been enjoined for one desiring a fruit, and there exists a series of subsequent duties not constituting that [primary] fruit, if some intermediate element is enjoined for the sake of the sacrifice or for a human purpose, then that alone is the means for achieving that [intermediate result]; the preceding injunction, however, culminates in being merely for the sake of assisting it.

As for those effects of the subsequent injunction that precede it, since they are not enjoined as having the relationship of end and means, they are to be understood as mere operations within the previously enjoined rites, occurring by way of necessity—just as the burning of wood and so forth [is necessary for cooking].

However, where nothing intermediate is enjoined that is produced through a traditional sequence (*pāraṃparya*), there all [subsidiary acts] are made one's own operations, and the enjoined [act] itself is the means to the fruit.

In that regard, those injunctive sentences which establish established or yet-to-be-established means for achieving human goals are brought forward by the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*) until their meaning is fully conveyed; since their possession of a fruit is already known thereafter, they are not [treated as the subject matter] of the second quarter of the first chapter. They are reached only subsequently.

However, those [verses] which are recited in that context likewise—proceeding through the sequence of grasping syllables and so forth until their own meaning is understood—do not directly become auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice.
Why?

Because the sacrifice, which requires an unseen means (*adṛṣṭa-upāya*) as to how [the result is achieved], does not attach itself to syllables and the like since they have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). Therefore, on that day, only the ritual action (*karma*) itself is adopted by way of its purpose, and nothing else.
Therefore, the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) are equal to the principal sentence;
however, their sentences are more external, like the rules for Vedic study and so forth.

Thus, for sentences concerning sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and the like—which terminate in the mere refinement (*saṃskāra*) of rice and other materials—their connection with the principal act is more remote, being separated by the stages of rice-grains, flour, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), the cutting of portions (*avadāna*), and so on.

In the same way, the sentences concerning the *ārādupakāraka* (indirectly contributing) and *sāmavāyika* (directly contributing) auxiliary elements, which are studied outside of any specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), are to be applied [to the primary rites].
However, there is this much distinction:
because they do not reside within a specific ritual context (*aprakaraṇasthatvāt*), they do not touch the primary rite directly, but are connected to it through their very purposes.

As for those sentences concerning the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and so forth, they too terminate in the prescription of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the *āhavanīya* fire—which are subsidiaries of fruit-bearing sacrifices—and are rendered free of expectancy by that very distant fruit.
By this, the self-sufficiency (*nairākāṅkṣya*) of the Upaniṣads, through their presentation of the object and the agent, is explained.
As for mantras and names, their application within their own respective domains will be discussed later.
Therefore, it is established that all [scriptural passages] are included within the process of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
As for the objection that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are not included because they do not fall within the three factors of cultivation,
to that it is replied:
It is true that nothing additional is apprehended;
rather, it is included within existence.
How so?

For here, in sentences containing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, two types of productive energy (*bhāvanā*) are understood: that consisting of the word (*śabdātmikā*) and that consisting of the meaning (*arthātmikā*). Among these, the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are not required by the productive energy consisting of the meaning, but they will be grasped by the productive energy consisting of the word.
For that [latter] proceeds in this manner:

By the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*), all other injunctive texts are subordinated; and the Self, denoted by the term *svādhyāya*, is enjoined [with the sense] "one should bring it about" (*bhāvayet*).

In that context, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth possess the status of the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛtva*), while the person is the one to be instigated (*prayojya*). Thus, when there arises the expectation "what [should he do]?", it is connected with "the instigation of the person.

Alternatively, if by virtue of its inherent fitness the action whose object is the optative suffix and so forth is stated as "he should instigate," then, when the expectation "what [should he do]? is raised, it is connected precisely with "the person."

Although such a state of being an instigator (*prayojakatva*) is not possible for the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth because they are insentient, nevertheless, since it is impossible for the person who is the one to be impelled (*prayojya*) to be the instigator, the instigating power of the prescriptive elements exists by means of the consciousness residing in that [person].
And if this were not postulated, these [suffixes] would not even have the designation of "prescriptive.
Now, when the question "by what? is expected, it is connected with "by the cognition of the injunction," which depends upon the experience of a prior connection.
"How so? [The answer is: "By that which is assisted by the knowledge of its excellence.
Why is this so?
For persons who act with prior reflection do not engage in an action as long as they have not understood that "this is excellent."
In that context, the injunctive suffix falters; the cognition of excellence (*prāśastya*) supports it.
And since, regarding the portion consisting of the fruit—which is the human goal—everyone naturally engages in its performance, it is well known and thus does not need to arise from the Veda.

However, because there is no impulsion for a person who has not yet begun acting toward the means (*sādhana*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the Veda itself is required to establish their excellence.

Furthermore, when there arises an expectation for a means to perform that [act], it may be established either by the word expressing the fruit— meaning "this is praiseworthy because its fruit is prosperity"—
or by the injunction itself— meaning "it is free from all suspicion of defect because it is ordained by the Veda"—
or else by its being endowed with specific materials, deities, and procedural details.

In that case, since words such as those denoting the result (*phala*) serve a different purpose, it is not logical for them to have a purpose elsewhere [in the injunction]. Furthermore, this expectancy arises after the injunction (*vidhi*), whereas the introduction of the word for the result occurs prior to it;
therefore, the injunction is not set aside by them either.
And these [results and so forth] are postulated through secondary figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) from these [words].

However, that [indication] is not appropriate when the literal meaning is possible, because it is contradictory for two meanings to function simultaneously. If the intention were merely to praise [the injunction], then the results and so forth would not exist; for it cannot be said that things mentioned in another recension as being merely means [to an end] lack absolute reality.
For this very reason, that which is understood by implication from the meaning—because words are intended for something else—does not constitute the purpose of commendation (*prāśastya*).
Indeed, whatever is perceived is not necessarily determined to be the fruit of the scripture.

Just as when it is said, "The first one runs," although a second person is implied, he is nevertheless not connected with the action; so too is the case with the incitement (*prarocanā*) that is understood [by implication]. This concludes the second quarter of the first chapter.
Nor does it remain as a scriptural meaning already employed for another purpose;

rather, this [meaning] would have to be inferred from them through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*). And the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" occurs only when all other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have been set aside.
And that absence of a means of valid cognition which occurs despite one’s striving in every possible way—that itself constitutes a means of valid cognition.

Therefore, if we do not obtain [the required rule] through some direct instruction (upadeśa) or extended application (atideśa), then, according to the principle of the *darvihoma*, we shall postulate two powers for the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) itself. However, if it can be established by something even remotely related, then one must follow that; thus the injunction remains expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*).

Likewise, in such passages as "Vāyu is indeed the most powerful deity," even though the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*) is presented by the injunction for study as being for the sake of human ends (*puruṣārtha*), and because of the connection [in the injunction] that "one should do whatever is possible," [the study] cannot suddenly be linked with that [deity]. Thus, since it does not result in a human end, as in the previous case, it extends—as far as possible—to the meaning of the sentence consisting of the narrative of the elements (*bhūtākhyāna*).

Furthermore, since that [injunction] is indeed expectant, the meaning consisting of praise—namely, that the rite which accomplishes the deity quickly will, by way of producing a result corresponding to its means, grant its fruit immediately—is accepted because it is required by the injunction (*vidhi*) that follows immediately after, and because it is capable of being understood as a means to the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
This is a conjunction like that of a man who has lost his horse and another whose chariot is burnt.
And thus, the incitement (*prarocanā*) produced by something else is not a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the ritual act.
Nor can another purpose be established by means of the words of explanatory praise (arthavāda); thus, by the force of the sacred tradition (āmnāna), there is a restriction regarding both.
By this, the connection of the words of censure with the prohibition for the sake of establishing the aversion required by that prohibition is explained.
For even in that case, one does not desist from knowledge without that aversion.

Furthermore, hatred arises dependent upon an undesirable cognition (*apraśasta-pratyaya*). Nor can such an undesirable cognition be apprehended through words such as "not" (*na*), which—by not denoting anything desirable or undesirable—are restricted solely to negation, its result, and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Therefore, blame (*nindā*), having no other purpose, is understood only through the sentence as a whole;
thus, the status of being a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*) is established.
Furthermore, in the case of injunctions and prohibitions, the supplementary portions (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the sentences serve as the means for determining praise and blame in their respective order.

For praise and blame are not fixed [by their literal form], because we observe the opposite: there are instances where what appears to be blame is actually praise, and what appears to be praise is actually blame.
As he will say: "For a deprecatory statement (*nindā*) does not function to deprecate that which is deprecated, but rather to praise that which is enjoined."

Likewise, in the sentences concerning the Traiyambaka offerings, although the non-sprinkling of ghee is praised by the statement, "If one were to sprinkle it, he would place it in the mouth of Rudra," that non-sprinkling will not be adopted as the rule. Furthermore, even though it is censured, sprinkling alone will be understood as the recommended course because a mandatory injunction is seen at the end.
Moreover, even praises and censures that are ambiguous are determined by the context itself; as the author will say: "We do not know whether the Asuras are censured or not censured.
For since this rite sometimes brings the Asuras under its control, it must surely be praiseworthy"—thus it would be a praise.
Alternatively, it is a censure because [the verse] is inauspicious due to being the cause for the arrival of the destructive Asuras;
in that context, since the Sāman is prescribed at the end, it is understood that the censure of the Ṛks is for the purpose of praising that [Sāman].
And in every case, while one particular word praises and another censures, they all attain their purpose through syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*).

Even where such a word does not exist, one must resort to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or indirect indication based on what has been indicated (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*), because it would otherwise be inexplicable.
Furthermore, since injunctions and prohibitions are invariably concomitant with praise and censure respectively, upon seeing one of these, the other should be inferred and the sentence completed.
In this manner, the sentences of the *Mahābhārata* and other such texts are to be explained.

For even for them, according to injunctions such as "one should cause the four castes to hear [this]," because one seeks the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), the result—transcending the mere syllables and so forth—is the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and the avoidance of adharma, anartha, duḥkha, and saṃsāra; it consists of the practice of adoption and rejection as the means to these ends.

Furthermore, among those [texts], regarding gifts, kingship, liberation, dharma, and so on, some are direct injunctions (*vidhi*), while others are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) in the form of accounts of what was done by others (*parakṛti*) or ancient history (*purākalpa*).

Furthermore, since the injunction "one should cause [them] to be heard" would be purposeless if there were an intentionality (*tātparya*) regarding all the narratives (*upākhyāna*), one must somehow accept that they are intended for praise or censure as understood from the context.
And because their primary aim lies elsewhere, one should not become overly attached to the factual reality of the narratives.
Indeed, through the practice of the Vedic method of exposition, Vālmīki, Dvaipāyana, and others composed their own works in precisely that same manner.
And because those to be instructed possess diverse intellectual capacities, this is indeed appropriate;
for here, some understand through mere injunction alone.
Some [explanatory passages] are brief, others are concise, and others are extensive;
the undertaking is such that the minds of all [beings] are to be captured.

Among these, some injunctions and prohibitions have their root in the Vedas (*śruti*), while some have their root in the world regarding matters such as practical utility and pleasure; likewise, some explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are purely Vedic, some are purely worldly, and some are composed by the author himself according to the principles of poetry.
And all [such passages] are authoritative by virtue of their being praise;
however, some do not function as supplements to a primary injunction (*vākyaśeṣa*). Even those, such as the descriptions of Mount Mandara and so forth, which are heard on their own, produce delight.
But those that are descriptions of battles serve the kings of both the brave and the timid, as they provide them with inspiration.
However, where nothing defective is perceived, one must postulate an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) by means of the praise of a specific deity and so forth;
this is the general direction [of the argument]. Some say: "Because it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*)."

If it is asked, "For what purpose is praise? [the answer is: so that [an action] might be pleasing and thereby performed; thus, by means of praise and censure, there is the communication of engagement and desistance, while by means of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth, there is the denotation [of the injunction]. Therefore, their purpose is the same.
And there is no combination (*samuccaya*) of those which have the same purpose.

In this regard, where the optative suffixes and so forth are devoid of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and where the explanatory passages are devoid of those [suffixes], their status as motivators or desistors established according to their respective domains is not contradictory.
But where there is a conflict between two [requirements], since the purpose is accomplished by either one, and since one must necessarily be set aside, it is proper to favor the more numerous;

the injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*) is abandoned—just as in the saying "one should sacrifice an individual for the sake of the family"—because a verbal root cannot be used alone. Thus, it functions as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the injunction already obtained through the encouragement intended to favor that [more numerous requirement].

Just as in the case of the statement, "Having concluded the Satra sacrifice, they should sacrifice with the Pṛṣṭha-śamanīya," the status of being a restatement of an activity established by the *tṛc* suffix (*ktvā*) is expressed;
therefore, only this much is intended: "The touching of the Āgneyī [cow] is white.

And that very same injunctive core (*vidhyuddeśa*), after the connection with the result and so forth has been made, is itself restricted; this is what is meant by the phrase "the injunctive core ends with 'one who desires prosperity' (*bhūtikāmaḥ*)."
Otherwise, the taking up of the summary (uddeśagrahaṇa) would indeed be purposeless.
Since syntactic unity with that which is stated in the Sūtra is not possible according to the prescribed rule, [the author] disregards it and adopts the subject matter from the Tantravārtika.
And thus he says: "This is not the connection.

By negating the connection between an injunction and that which is enjoined, he expresses the intended connection between the praise and that which is praised, namely: "Because from this [praise] comes prosperity (bhūti). And that very [connection] is the application of the cause of prosperity.
The phrase "even though they are distinct" refers back to the two previously mentioned relationships.
If it is asked, "For what purpose is the praise?"— if the suffix has been uprooted, then what is the use of praise for that which is not being enjoined?
Alternatively, thinking that "whatever is to be accomplished by this [Arthavāda] can be achieved through its very authority," he says:

"Even if there is an authoritative statement from the Teacher, since the attainment of that purpose occurs through the Arthavāda alone—and since both possibilities exist, considering the Arthavāda to be the supportive factor—he asks, 'How is it pleasing?
The other [the opponent] clarifies the intention behind the question.
"Even before the proof [is established], the statement of praise is useless"—
this is the point where the text is cut off by the words "na hi" (for it is not so).
In all cases, intermediate sentences do not constitute authority within great sentences, just as intermediate numbers do not [constitute authority] within large numbers.

However, when those very [words] are employed in isolation, they become a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because of their independence, as in the case of "the cloth exists. Nor is there a lack of expectancy in every instance simply because completion is not observed at that point; for expectancy is not seen to be absent merely by such a degree of completion.
For all sentences reach their completion through the non-utterance of other words that would be appropriate;
otherwise, however, even for those of keen insight, an expectation persists beyond the words actually heard,
and that expectation is removed by the fact of its non-perception.
And thus, wherever they are perceived, they will be understood as forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*).

Otherwise, even upon the utterance of those [words], that [unity] would not exist; therefore, he says: "when there are no words of praise," meaning that in the absence of a great sentence (*mahāvākya*), a subordinate sentence (*avāntaravākya*) is authoritative, but when it exists, it is not.
"Now, if this were so," [it is objected].

Where the fruit of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) and its subordinate sentences (*avāntaravākya*) differs—as in the case of the production of a cloth versus the production of color—there such a distinction is appropriate. But here, since the meaning is not distinct, what is the purpose of discarding the subordinate sentences? Is it not the case that the fruit of the great sentence is simply the negation of the subordinate sentences?
To this, he says:

"If there were a person who were the author of the Veda, he alone would be subject to such an objection: 'Let that not be a great sentence (mahāvākya) in which there exists a subordinate sentence (avāntaravākya) that enjoins truth; for [truth] exists even without it. Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter.
If [the goal] is already accomplished, why do you rely on the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*)?
To this, there is no objection, because they are absent [in that case].
It would be like traveling toward a village by way of a detour; it would result in nothing more than excessive fatigue, not the failure to reach the destination.
The recourse to honorific terminology is observed in cases of this kind;

for example, when a certain object is already established by the mere word "space" (*kham*), people may still designate it using terms such as "ether" (*ākāśa*) and the like, yet they do not incur any fault. Similarly, in this case, although the meaning is already established by the injunctive suffixes (*liṅ* etc.), one may still grasp it from the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

Furthermore, it can be argued here that just as an action performed while being remembered through a mantra brings about prosperity when multiple means are available, so too does an act become efficacious when it is enjoined by an injunction, even if that injunction is conveyed through an explanatory passage that establishes the rule.

Now, as for the objection: "But even though there are words of praise..."—where a heavy means is resorted to without adopting a light one, there it might be so; but here, a lighter and more capable means was already adopted previously. Therefore, just as when the word *kha* (sky) is employed, words such as *ākāśa* (ether) are not employed at that same time, so too, since the injunction is already established, praise should not be resorted to.
In that case, because they would require a further expectation [of something else], the words of praise would be meaningless.
If it is argued that [the passage] is merely for the sake of praise (*bhavana*), we reply:
no; because it possesses meaning according to the principle already stated, it is not right to claim its purpose is unintended.

For when two possibilities exist, since there is a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) with what is directly perceived, it is logical to accept the support of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
[Objection: Since the meaning has already been covered by the phrase "even when [the auxiliary] exists," it should not have been said "certainly not from that which is independent.
[Reply: It is said in response:

In that case, it was stated in order to avoid abandoning the *arthavāda*; however, even if there were a connection with praise for the whole, the connection with the injunction regarding the nature of the preceding part as it is understood must not be sublated.
If its power were to be withdrawn anywhere, then, due to the absence of a cause for its restoration, there would follow the undesirable consequence of total incapacity.
To this it is replied:
let the injunctive power of the former [text] remain; however, since this [power] has not been sublated anywhere, it cannot be sublated elsewhere either.
That which has manifested at some time manifests everywhere.
However, where it is employed through the praise of another meaning and so forth, there the manifested power initiates its effect.
But where there is the manifestation of another power that constitutes an exception, the former power is concealed due to the consequence of splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
By way of question and answer, this very previously mentioned division of sentences (*vākyabheda*) is being referred to.

Therefore, because they share a single purpose, the injunction here occurs solely through the act of incitement (*prarocanā*). Thus, it is by means of inciting those who are to perform the rite that [the injunction functions].
"Why does the status of *saṃpradāna* (recipient) not apply [to the object] by the rule 'rucy-arthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ' (Pāṇini 1.4.33)?
If it is argued that this is because *prarocayate* is a different verbal root (*prakṛti*), we say no;
for even there, the connection with the root *ruc* is not lost."
Now, if the genitive case is stated with the intention of expressing a general relationship, that too is difficult to establish when a specific [referent] has already been mentioned.
Therefore, the connection is "of the action of the performers"; and when there is an expectation as to "for whom" they are being incited, it is understood by implication that it is "for them" alone.
Alternatively, the connection is "benefiting the performers."
The word *kriyāyāḥ* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*), for it is from the action itself that these [arthavādas] are inciting.

Alternatively, the genitive sense (*ṣaṣṭhy-artha*) may be understood in the phrase *kriyārtham*. They praise some object—this being the present participle ending in *-at*—whether that object be the thing to be enjoined, something related to it, or the action itself, or something related to it; and this occurs by way of praise. Thus, the authority of the arthavāda is established through the medium of the suffix.
However, they do not accept this explanation.

For if there were an eradication of the cognition (*pratyaya*), then by what could the praise be expressed? It cannot be by the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*), because how can there be a productive operation (*bhāva*) [in that case]?

Even if one were to postulate an expectation of "from what [is it praised]?", that too would concern only the injunction (*vidhi*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), since its purpose is to assist those very things.
The difference, however, consists merely in the designation by another word;
and even that [designation] occurs only for a person who is being enjoined, not from the mere hearing of the action itself.

For when it is said, "The white animal is to be sacrificed to Vāyu," no expectation arises as to whether it is commendable or uncommendable prior to the statement of its being something to be done or not to be done.
And those [words] which express something not required [by the sentence], by means of mere hearing alone, do not constitute explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
Furthermore, no connection or requirement exists for anything with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*),
because everything is directed toward the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).
But once meditation (*bhāvanā*) has been removed by means of the exclusion of the causal factor (*pratyaya*), what would it require?

Therefore, because the three constituent parts contained therein have been eliminated, there is neither a result (*phala*), nor a sacrifice (*yāga*) as the instrument (*karaṇa*), nor any procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

Furthermore, even if the excellence (*prāśastya*) has been stated, since the reason "why" is not required, once it is determined merely that "this is excellent," the cognition of what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*) would not arise at all unless one were to state "because it is excellent."
Or rather, that [injunction] would be the final conclusion; this would be like saying, "This cloth is praiseworthy, it must be made," or "It must be dyed red.
If there were no injunction, the statement would be entirely purposeless.

Furthermore, to set aside a direct injunction and instead accept it from the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) through a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on tradition is an unprecedented mode of expression.

And there is no occasion for such a conceptual construction, because [the meaning] is established from another source. For if it were not already stated, an injunction would have to be inferred from an explanatory passage (arthavāda) only if it could not otherwise be accounted for. However, since it is established by direct cognition, there is no "otherwise-unaccountability" (anyathānupapatti). Likewise, even an explanatory passage would be carried far away [from its literal sense] only if it were purposeless for the sake of persuasion, as in the case of fictional narratives and the like. But this is not the case here.

However, according to the reasoning already stated, because it serves as a means of encouragement (*prarocanā*), one does not go elsewhere; and this encouragement must necessarily be performed. If that were established from another source, then one would not depend on the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
But since it has no other recourse, it relies upon that very passage.

And in every Vedic matter, a word would have to be postulated through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and from that, the meaning would be established; thus, by means of the incitement (*prarocanā*), the injunctive word itself would be postulated, not the meaning. At the time of that postulation, just as in the sentences concerning Indra-Vāyu and others, the presence of the statement "one should sacrifice with Soma" precludes the postulation of another sacrifice, so too here, by the word "one should immolate" (*ālabheta*), there is a blockage of the inference of anything else.
Furthermore, between two [means] having the same purpose, there occurs either sublation (*bādha*) or option (*vikalpa*).

Furthermore, because the suffix (*pratyaya*) and the verbal root (*arthavāda*) have distinct objects—namely, the object of the beneficiary (*anugrāhya*) and the object of the benefactor (*anugrāhaka*) respectively—their coexistence (*samuccaya*) constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) due to their difference in meaning. Moreover, if there were an eradication of the suffix, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the destruction of the distinctions such as the agent, number, voice (*upagraha*), the result of the action (*kriyāphala*), and whether the action is for one's own sake or for the sake of another.
This might be argued:
It might be argued that by not intending to convey the mere fact of being an injunction, the number of the agent and so forth are obtained through the desire to express everything else;
however, this is impossible because the suffix is employed for that very purpose [of expressing the injunction].
By its inherent capacity, it necessarily expresses the state of being an injunction.

Furthermore, for that which is already known, there can be either no intention to speak of it at all, or a lack of contact with an injunction; and in neither case is there a status as a restatement (*anuvādaka*), as in the case of the *aindrī* mantra used for the *homā*.

First of all, there is no such thing as "the non-injunctive nature of an injunction. Nor is it a restatement, because at that stage [of the ritual], the matter has not yet been established. For it is not possible to say: "This performance of the white animal sacrifice to Vāyu which is to be performed is praiseworthy."
However, it must indeed be performed in this way because it is praised.

As for the argument that "it is like the *avasānīya* [concluding rite]," even there, since the mere performance is enjoined by the force of the particle *ha*, and injunction (*vidhi*) and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) are disregarded, the status of being an injunction (*vidhitva*) is necessarily accepted; thus, that example is not applicable.

Furthermore, if there were no intention to enjoin, then due to proximity, the meaning of the verbal root itself would fall within the objective portion (*sādhyāṃśa*), and consequently, it would be fruitless.
Therefore, syntactic unity with the injunction exists precisely through the non-abandonment of the sūtra.
And thus the author of the Bhāṣya says: "The injunctive statement (vidhyuddeśa) ends with 'one desiring prosperity' (bhūtikāmaḥ),' for it includes the injunction itself."

Otherwise, he would have simply said "the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvartha*). In that case, it could be asserted that this [meaning of the root] constitutes the injunctive portion (*vidhyuddeśa*) merely by virtue of being an action (*kriyā*). Therefore, the suffix alone is the injunctive portion because it is the enjoiner of the injunction.
However, because it is impossible for [the injunction] to form a single syntactical unit with the injunctive sense, the mention of the subject matter (*uddeśa*) occurs outside of the sūtra.
The phrases "desiring prosperity" and "ending thus" are intended to demonstrate the occasion for praise (*stuti*) at a time subsequent to the connection with the result and so forth.

But if this were the case, since there would be no expectancy in instances of statements in the present tense (*vartamānāpadeśa*), the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) would not be connected [to the injunction].

It is exactly so; nevertheless, because there is no attainment through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), in some cases it is established by the injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*) and in others by the fifth verbal suffix (*leṭ*).

Alternatively, once the status of being an injunction (*vidhitva*) is postulated on the grounds that the heard present tense would otherwise be inexplicable, its connection with an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) follows.
Even in those cases where the status of being an injunction is seen solely from the presence of an explanatory passage, the only recourse is the fact that it would otherwise be inexplicable.

Since a grave fault is not appropriate when a minor transgression occurs, as for the objection that this interpretation involves a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to relying on two separate connections—that has been refuted by the fact that it is logically possible for there to be a single flow [of meaning] in the form "one should sacrifice because it is praiseworthy.

For it is established that the requirement for praise belongs only to that which is being enjoined; thus, the principle of a single application (*tantratva*) is justified by the absence of any inconsistency.

And if a sentence were to be split by such various types of relations, then it would likewise be split by the relations of the goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Therefore, the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "this relation is not intended" is to be understood as follows: it is not the case that the completion of the injunction for the primary rite along with its subsidiaries was intended in the previous [section], because the first section’s second quarter deals with the doorways of injunctionality and so forth, as well as the incitement to action (*prarocanā*).
Because of the excessive complexity of the conceptualization and because of the resulting split in the sentence structure, [the opponent asks] "For what purpose is the praise? [The response is:

Since there is the conceit that the incitement to action is already accomplished by the preceding [injunction] itself, the statement regarding the assistance to the injunction [is made] to explain how one might be incited to act.
The phrase "nanu prāk" (surely previously) is an explanation of the prior intention.

[The objection] "na hi" (for not) means: since there is an absence of praise, one must resort to its two powers out of necessity, even though they are possible; it is not the case that, at that time, the injunction for one desiring prosperity is completed. Thus he says.
As in the case of the word "cloth";
the meaning has already been explained.
By the word "injunction" (vidhi), it is clarified that there is an incitement [to action]; thus, the diversity of functions between the injunction and the praise is demonstrated.
"Now, if it is so"—if there is indeed the capacity even to inspire interest (*prarocanā*), why should anything else be required?
"True," [he replies]; therefore, that meaning which is understood is understood whether that [capacity] exists or does not exist.
And what is this? It means that praise is the purpose of those two [the injunction and the explanatory passage], not of the former alone;
furthermore, because it provides the object for the praise, the injunction is also designated as having praise as its purpose, for praise without an object is not possible.

But in the absence of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), one will have no choice but to accept the burden of complexity (*gaurava*) even for a solitary [word]. "Even though they exist"— this should be explained in the same manner as before.
"Therefore, from this injunction" means:
now, because of its connection with the remainder of the sentence in the genitive case, we understand its praise as originating from that [remainder] itself, and not from itself; this is the meaning.
[Objection: "But [it could be understood] even from an independent [statement]."

If, in some instances, the power of a certain injunction to impel action were independent of any *itikartavyatā* (the "how-to" procedure), why would it require anything else? Consequently, even when such procedures exist, they would be disregarded. However, the Teacher [Kumārila], speaking with a touch of irony, said: "Let it be that where this [injunction] is employed alone and is independent, there is no contradiction;
but here, that is not possible, because it is expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) and is drawn in by other words."

For a single sentence is the enjoiner of only one relationship; in that case, if it were to perform [the injunction] within the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) itself, then there would be a split (*bheda*).
For this [sentence] serves as an incentive (*prarocanā*), showing that this quality belongs precisely to those things which have been brought forward by the injunctive statement.

Therefore, because they form a single syntactical unit with the injunctions, the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) possess meaning by virtue of supporting them; thus, the previously raised objection is untenable. For contradiction would occur only in the actual performance [of the ritual], whereas the meaning of the word is not part of that performance; therefore, the refutation of the stated defect follows from this.
We consider that the incongruity mentioned regarding the formulation of rules for the sacrificial journey—which contradicts what is seen in the scriptures—applies to our own position.
Alternatively, for those who have the reading with the short vowel (*hṛsvaḥ*), this must be explained as a figurative interpretation (*stuti-vyākhyāna*) so that the incongruity does not apply;

for if these were taken literally in their performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), there would be a contradiction in enjoining such things as weeping, cutting out the omentum, moving toward the directions, stealing, and speaking untruths.
For us, however, that literal meaning of these words is not intended at all;
nor is there an injunction [to be derived] through ellipsis and other such means. Rather, mere praise is what is intended. And since that is not contradicted, it is therefore logical.

Alternatively, the phrase "but the meaning of the word" indicates that this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) exists for the purpose of supporting the injunctive word; it is not connected through the performance of its own literal meaning. Since it has not reached the stage of practical application and is not part of the performance itself, it is therefore appropriate [as an *arthavāda*].
There are three readings here:
"and the non-occurrence of what has not been established"—this is the completion of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), which we consider to be the intended sense.
Another [interpretation] is that "non-attainment" (aprāptam) and "impossibility" (anupapattiḥ) are supplied there as the explanation;
and another [interpretation] is that "non-attained" (aprāptā) and "impossible" (anupapattiḥ) are to be understood there in our position according to their form and general usage.

In this world, everything that is being done is performed after having first formed a mental intention (*saṅkalpa*) and expressed it through speech; therefore, even though these two are extremely internal, they are far inferior to gold because of their connection with theft and falsehood.

A censure that results solely in itself has the purpose of prohibition. However, when it is subordinate to an injunction, it arises for the sake of praise, since its justification serves a visible purpose.

As he will state: "If one does not postulate another [cause], then [the statement] would be a mere explanatory praise (arthavāda) regarding what has already been established. Thus, due to the transgression of the performer, the father sees his son;
while the *pravara* is being chosen, the sacrificer should say: "O gods, O ancestors," and so forth.

For the purpose of praising that [act], it was said: "Even one who is not a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Brāhmaṇa through the *pravarānumantraṇa*. In that context, since those whose Brāhmaṇahood is already well-known would find the acquisition of Brāhmaṇahood useless, it was stated for the sake of justifying that [act]: "And we do not know this. However, speaking of ignorance when something is actually known is due to its being difficult to discern.
That which is ignorance by virtue of pleasure is indeed ignorance; and that is caused by the threefold transgression.

Moreover, even if there were an offense against the truth, if the son belonged to the mother alone or to the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*), then, because their caste would be well-established, there would be no confusion regarding it.
In the same way, by tracing it back through their ancestors and so on, caste would certainly be determined according to the principle of beginninglessness.
For the view of the traditional authorities (*smṛtikāra*) is that "the mother is but a leather bag; the son belongs to the father."
Furthermore, the possibility of the progenitor belonging to various castes results in a mixture of classes (*varṇasaṅkara*).

Moreover, even in the Veda, the statement "O you who are vigilant, protect this thread" is intelligible only as referring to the interruption of a lineage caused by a son who commits a triple offense;
for otherwise, even if one did not protect it, there would be no interruption of the thread of one's own caste.
Therefore, there is room for praise:

because of the recitation of the lineage of ancestors (pravara) of one whose Brāhmaṇahood is firmly established, and because of the resulting knowledge that "this person is born from that [lineage]," he becomes a Brāhmaṇa; this is the praise, which is a glorification of sacred learning (vidyā).

Since it is supplementary to the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), it is not an injunction of a fruit; rather, it is understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the "beauty of the face" and "possession of horses," as already known. Furthermore, there is not only one kind of facial beauty—namely, its configuration, loveliness, and charm—for that refers specifically to women.
For the learned, however, the face shines by emitting words, sentences, and logic; thus, in its own nature, it shines in the primary sense of the term.
And the son shall be possessed of vigor and endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Even if this is figurative, there is no fault because it is intended as praise;
since the fruit arises from the performance of the ritual, there will be a distinction in the fruit according to its magnitude, as is seen in the world.

And this [principle] is introduced as being applicable to the Agnihotra and other rites which have the same fruits such as heaven, because the results correspond to their means. For all desires, when obtained through the Pūrṇāhuti, are acquired only in small measure; therefore, it is established that the injunction for another rite is meaningful for one who seeks an abundance of fruit. This being so, an objection is raised: it is logical in the world that the production of fruits from agriculture and the like corresponds to the means, since this is perceived through direct observation.

But in the case of the *pūrṇāhuti* and other such acts, since they are entirely dependent on their respective Vedic branches (*śākhā*), and since no distinction is heard regarding the fruit, on what basis could a distinction be imagined?
For no distinction whatsoever is heard between the heaven resulting from the *agnihotra* and that resulting from the *jyotiṣṭoma*. Nor is inference capable of establishing such a matter.
That is now stated:
this is established by the very force of the capacity [of the words] in the second quarter of the first chapter on injunctions.
How so?

For if an equal fruit were produced from both small and great actions, then, by the very principle of "if one finds honey on the ground," no one would engage in the great action when it could be accomplished by a small one. In that case, there would be a subversion of the injunction’s efficacy; however, since its efficacy is not subverted—and according to the principle that "the [injunction] exists because it is a part of the same conceptual construction"—it is the injunction itself that acknowledges the superiority of the fruit.
Therefore, just as the relationship between the *viśvajit* sacrifice and its fruit is established by valid means of knowledge, so too here is the specific [relationship] established. Furthermore,

just as there is a fixed rule for the application (*viniyoga*) of subsidiaries and the principal act according to their sequential recitation— where the first [subsidiary] belongs to the first [principal], the second to the second— likewise, in the domain of action, a small amount of fruit corresponds to a small action, based on the general principle of proportionality.
The middle [size] belongs to the middle [rite], and the large to the large; thus, the size itself is the factor that determines the application.

Recollection (smaraṇa) is likewise. Furthermore, in the Cāturmāsya and Soma sacrifices, there is an explanatory passage concerning the fruit (*phalārthavāda*) which begins: "When one offers the Agnihotra, one thereby obtains ten Gṛhamedha [offerings] in a single night," and so on. This statement—showing that by the performance of the Agnihotra for less than ten years and so forth, one obtains the result of a single Darśapūrṇamāsa performance and so on—demonstrates a distinction in the fruit based on the smallness or greatness of the ritual action.
*Tantravārtika*:
Or it may be an injunction (*vidhi*), because it conveys something not previously known; for otherwise, it would be a mere statement and thus purposeless.

Now, after the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) that stand in opposition to injunctions—such as those concerning purposelessness and legendary narratives (*upākhyāna*)—have been explained, those that stand in opposition to injunctions are now being investigated.
Whence arises this doubt?
For in the previous case, it was accepted that praise is to be understood as being remote because it serves no purpose for its own sake;
however, when that [direct utility] is possible, even praise would result in being equivalent to something meaningless.
Furthermore, the injunctive portion (*vidhyaṃśa*) is not established from anything other than [the injunction] itself.

On the other hand, it has been stated previously that the incitement (*prarocanā*) can somehow be derived even from the statement of the injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*). Moreover, since the injunction is the primary element and the praise is its subordinate member (*aṅga*), it is logical that the praise—which exists as a qualification of the primary element—should belong to that very element.

And when the statement of the injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*) is completed, the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) proceeds; however, it is precisely at that stage of its commencement that the constituent parts of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) come together.

Thinking that the result [is connected] to the *viśiṣṭa* (the qualified injunction) by virtue of its being primary and foremost, and so forth, he says "because of its unprecedented nature" (*apūrvatvāt*).
And with respect to that, he considers mere praise to be purposeless.

But surely, an injunction regarding such a fruit and the discussion concerning the explanatory passages (arthavāda) regarding that fruit will occur in the fourth [book] under the section beginning with "substances, purificatory acts, and subordinate rites";
therefore, this should not be introduced here.
Regarding this, some say:
Since the meaning has already been understood through this, it is appropriate to direct this inquiry there alone; thus, this is not a mere repetition.
This is true, provided that by waiting for that [other] occasion, some other resolution might be found, and we could seek it there.
However, if it can be explained right here, then even if it is stated now, the fault is slight.

Regarding this, others say: "In that [previous case], there was merely a refutation of its being an injunction of a result; here, however, it is for the sake of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), and thus it should be an explanatory praise. To this, he will later state that it must be understood as being solely intent upon refuting its status as an injunction. That is incorrect, because when those [passages] were displaced from being injunctions of results, their potential meaninglessness was avoided by establishing their purpose as praise through the very same previous section (*adhikaraṇa*).
And this has been demonstrated in such [passages] as "his face shines," and so forth. However, some others say:
it is appropriate that passages such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest" belong to the second quarter (pāda) of the first chapter.
Regarding the nature of praise (*stuti*):

just as [the passage] is displaced from being an injunction of a result (*phalavidhi*) because it is for the sake of attaining nourishment (*ūrj*), so too is it displaced from being a praise because of its contradiction. [The opponent might argue: "Let it be an injunction at will, by which the contradiction—due to the fact that the result occurs at a later time—is somehow removed.
This commencement [of the argument] is also untenable.
Moreover, since there is clearly no contradiction in the Veda, the reason [adduced] would indeed be redundant and not non-tautologous;
however, the very body of the formal argument (*adhikaraṇa*) remains the same.
Furthermore, by the statement that "even contradiction is a figurative description" (*guṇavāda*), nothing remains unaddressed.
Furthermore, the same response will apply to me once again.

Therefore, others maintain that because the word "rule" (*vidhi*) is used without qualification, and because the mention of a result (*phala-śruti*) occurs in the fourth [book], only those passages here that resemble injunctions of substance, quality, and action, while resembling injunctions of results there, serve as examples. Accordingly, they cite such instances as: "The rule is meaningless in some context where it is possible," and "The horse has its origin in water; the reed is water-eating; that which is burnt [is of earth]."

Otherwise, if one were to present merely the injunction regarding the fruit, it would be entirely disconnected from that [previous statement]. Furthermore, since the former has a specific scope, this [latter] would have a meaning not yet understood; however, because the latter encompasses all objects in a general sense, it would be a mere repetition. Some cite this as a settled rule (*vyavasthā*).

In this regard, one might argue that the examples cited by the author of the Bhāṣya—namely, the injunctions regarding substances (*dravya*) and the like, and the injunctions regarding results (*phala*)—should be disregarded and other examples should be provided. To this we reply: Why must two distinct topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) necessarily be commenced such that this restriction of examples is adopted? For a topical section is not divided merely because of a difference in examples.
Let it not be that, even though the *khadira* and *udumbara* [trees] are distinct, there is no lack of redundancy because they are established as such;
rather, since the topics (*adhikaraṇa*) have the nature of being objects of logical inquiry, their very distinction is the cause for the absence of redundancy.
Not all rules concerning substances and so forth have been examined here; some were discussed in the *Tatsiddhisūtra*,
while others were treated in the sections on the *nivīta* and other such topics.
In the sixth [book], others [are discussed] by way of the doctrines of other schools and ancient legends;
in the ninth, [the topic is] that "one should praise with a verse," and so forth, where there is an option (*vikalpa*) due to the unity of purpose;
and in the tenth, [there are rules] similar in form to the injunctions for *jartila* seeds and *gavīdhuka* grain.
Therefore, one must simply state that repetition is not a great fault;
or rather, the undertaking is renewed because some specific portion of the very same principle is being refined;
or else, the difference in subject matter should be clearly described in this manner.

In this context, it is established that those passages which resemble injunctions in every respect are merely *arthavādas* (explanatory or commendatory statements), by virtue of the exclusion of their status as injunctions.

As for the renewed discussion in the fourth book (*caturtha-adhyāya*), its intention is as follows: when an injunction is postulated based on an *arthavāda*, at the time of the requirement for a result (*phalākāṅkṣā*), even though [the result] is already obtained for another purpose, it is from the perspective of the ritual application-injunction (*kratuprayogavacana*) that the very same [result] is more proximate; furthermore, it is easy to establish a specific qualification for that which has an already established connection.

Otherwise, one would have to postulate both the connection and its specific qualification in the form of being a benefactor (*upakārakatva*), whereby there would be the status of an injunction for a result (*phalavidhitva*), as in the case of the "attainment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) in the *Rātrisatra*. This is the view of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Since another purpose can somehow be found, it is not logical for a single [passage] to have multiple meanings; therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is indeed an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
By this, the sections concerning the *nivīta* and others are explained.
Alternatively, those [sections] are to be understood as having been stated after first setting forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the section concerning the *udumbara*.

For, by accepting [the status of] being an injunction (*vidhi*), one must investigate whether it is a supplement to a sacrifice or to a person, and so forth; having thus deliberated, the conclusion is reached here that it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

Similarly, regarding *parakṛti* and *purākalpa*, it was considered whether they apply to those of that specific lineage or to all men. Likewise, in connection with the topics of modification (*ūha*) and sublation (*bādha*), the investigation contained in the ninth and tenth books is merely an ancillary discussion providing the basis for the statement in the *tatsiddhisūtra*.
Alternatively, this is an example where, within the injunction for a result (*phalavidhi*) itself, there are distinct words expressing both praise and the result;

for instance, in the passage "The udumbara is strength, cattle are strength," praise is expressed by these very words, while the result is expressed by the phrase "for the attainment of strength" (*ūrjāvaruddhyai*).
Furthermore, where the result or the praise must be stated by that alone, those are the fourth [type].

Alternatively, because of the designation of a reason in the phrase "because of being for the sake of another" (*parārthatvāt*), and because of the common usage of a well-known reason, those whose subservience to another is already understood are the examples; as in: "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood.
For the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood must necessarily be enjoined by restating the *juhū*, since it cannot be connected to a result independently.

For everywhere, a quality being enjoined for the sake of a result requires some substratum; and without a context (*prakaraṇa*), there is no way to obtain such a substratum. Therefore, in this case, if the *parṇa* [leaf]—[as discussed in] the second quarter of the first chapter...
When the statement "one should effect the fruit by means of the *yūpa*" is expressed, and there arises the requirement as to what it depends upon— namely, "with what should it be connected?"—
if it is argued that it is the *juhū* [ladle], that cannot be so,
because it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
Moreover, that [expectation] does not cease to be expectant until the acquisition of the action;
nor is there any means of valid cognition for its connection with the action.
Therefore, because it cannot be otherwise resolved, one must abandon this mode of expression and resort to the other.

In that context, regarding the injunction "he offers with the *juhū*," since its purpose is already known within the context (*prakaraṇa*), there exists an expectancy for a specific material that has not been prescribed. As soon as the class-property of being made of *parṇa*-wood is presented, it attains the status of an auxiliary (*aṅga*) because it is in a state where its purpose is yet unknown. Consequently, since that [expectancy] has been satisfied by that very sentence, there is no basis for postulating a fruit; thus, its status as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is logical. Here, however, the quality of being made of *udumbara* wood, which is heard in the context of a modified animal sacrifice (*vaikṛtapaśu*), is cited as an example.
Furthermore, its being for the sake of another is not established, such that it could fall within the scope of the fourth section [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra*].
How so?
For in this case, it is certainly not possible to enjoin a genus when the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) has not yet been obtained.

If its attainment is certain, then [the injunction] must necessarily become free of expectancy through the very use of the prescribed *khadira* wood and so forth, whose assistance has already been established.
Therefore, how could there be an injunction for another species to serve that purpose? Consequently, it is an injunction regarding the result (*phala*).

Furthermore, even the requirement for a substratum (*āśraya*) is satisfied by the inclusion of those things obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal transfer rule) connected to the original rite; thus, there is no obstacle.

Therefore, since the connection with a fruit would necessarily follow from the fact that [the act] is for the sake of another even prior [to this discussion], it must be refuted by means of another principle; thus begins this section (*adhikaraṇa*).
This is another view:
both the sentence concerning the *audumbara* wood and the sentence concerning the *juhū* ladle are examples in both cases.
How is there an absence of redundancy through the investigation of different parts of the cultivation?

First, the relationship between the probandum and the probans is possible only when both have been presented as being fit [for that relationship], and not otherwise. In that regard, in the fourth [chapter], there is an investigation of the probandum alone, either by disregarding or presupposing the investigation of what is fit for the part of the probans.

The inquiry is whether, by means of such a word—devoid of the attachment of a verbal suffix (*kāma*)—which expresses a connection with a present result, it is possible to convey the status of being a "result" (*phalatva*).
Here, however, the investigation concerns the factor of the means (*sādhana*) alone, either by disregarding or presupposing the factor of the end (*sādhya*). That is:
do substances, qualities, and actions, by means of such a word lacking an injunctive suffix (*vidhi-vibhakti*), come to be presented as means toward something or not?

Whatever is presented in its own essential nature becomes connected with that which is expressed by another word—provided it stands in need of a specific counter-correlate—once it has been associated with that [other term].
In that context, when "the probandum" (sādhya) is determined, the remaining element is understood as the "probans" (sādhana) by process of elimination;
likewise, when the probans is determined, both parts must be defined according to their own essential natures.

Therefore, one should understand that whatever contact with the portion consisting of the fruit occurs while the portion consisting of the means (*sādhana*) is being deliberated upon here, that is established in the fourth [book] as a reason by way of incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*).
Likewise, whatever reference to the portion consisting of the means occurs there [in the fourth book], that is established here by way of incidental discussion; thus, there is no tautology.
But if this is so, since this is a deliberation on the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), it would not be connected with the section concerning explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
This is not a fault, because the determination of the object occurs precisely by means of that [injunction].
For if it were understood from the preceding [text] as something being enjoined, then it would not be an *arthavāda*; but if it is for the purpose of praise (*stuti*), then it is an *arthavāda*.
In this regard, the intention of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows:

In every case, that which is uttered in proximity to the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*) becomes a means (*sādhana*), even if it is not explicitly stated as such, by virtue of the requirement of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Just as [the word] "by means of sacrifice" (*yāgena*) is connected even though it was not previously mentioned, so too is [the word] "by means of the *udumbara*" (*udumbareṇa*). In that context, what would the injunction (*vidhi*) do? It would cause the person to engage in action.
And since he has already engaged in action solely out of a desire for the fruit, what is the use of an injunction?
Alternatively, this [injunction] merely effects the connection with the fruit of that which has been enjoined by the *prayogavacana* (the statement of performance).
Or else, the fifth mood (*liṅ*) will enjoin it.

It has already been stated that [the passage] is either a portion of an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) or [an injunction]. Therefore, in the phrase "for the sake of securing strength" (*ūrjāvaruddhyai*), the fruit is clearly presented by means of the dative case expressing purpose (*tādarthya-caturthī*). Thus, the injunction regarding the use of *udumbara* wood applies to that [fruit].
[Objection: Should it not rather be understood as an injunction of the fruit itself? For in the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, injunctions of fruits are prohibited. [Response:
There is no contradiction, because from the words "the *udumbara* is strength," it follows that this is a statement of praise (*stuti*).
Therefore, since a primary injunction is possible, praise should not be understood through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Thus, [the opponent's argument] "because it is prior" is not a valid example; for in the world, praise is justified because it depends upon the comprehension of something through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which is possible in that context.

However, because the Veda is said to be unknown [to ordinary people], they would not have faith in it; or rather, if someone were to give something unknown in the world itself, then people would certainly not have faith in it,
as in the case of a previous statement or the like, such as a mere injunction.
Alternatively, this is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*):

people place their trust in a statement when it concerns something previously experienced, but not so when it concerns what is unknown; furthermore, these people, such as thieves and others, are not persuaded by mere words, but rather precisely because [the matter] is known.

For if the Veda were characterized by the unreality of its explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), one would lose confidence in the injunction (*vidhi*) and thus fail to engage in action. Alternatively, he who bypasses the injunction to seek out the explanatory passage surely lacks trust in the injunction; if there is no confidence in that [injunction], how could there be conviction in the explanatory passage?
Moreover, there is clearly a contradiction in the Veda with respect to present reality; this praise is not based on the current obstruction of vigor (*ūrj*), for such a thing does not exist.
In that case, it would be like the mention of abundant milk where none exists.

First of all, the identity of the *udumbara* tree with food is unestablished by any property of the animal sacrifice; and because the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is unestablished, the status of the reason (*hetu*) is also unestablished.

For it is not established in either worldly usage or the Veda that "whatever is food is a sacrificial post"; thus, [the claim] is incoherent. Therefore, because there is no correspondence, the injunction alone is sufficient; what need is there for praise? If one asks why there is a requirement for correspondence, [the answer is that] the injunction would otherwise be purposeless in some cases. Consequently, praise should be understood from those instances where such correspondence exists, and by analogy, the same applies to others. (Tantravārtika) Furthermore, if injunctions of this kind were to exist, then all the previously cited injunctions regarding substances, qualities, and actions would likewise become mere injunctions.
Vāyu, the swiftest deity, is to be fashioned; a horse not born from a womb is to be fashioned; the asuja reed, the vetasa, and the avakā plant are to be fashioned;
the waters are peaceful; the udumbara tree is vigor, and so forth.
In that regard, although some injunctions regarding actions and the like can be carried out,
these [others] are impossible to perform because they are established by their very nature (*svabhāvasiddhi*) and cannot be accomplished even through effort.
In the cases of wind, heat, water, mud, and so forth, there is establishment by nature.
The impossibility [of procuring] horses, udumbara wood, and so forth [is raised].
He shows what kind of praise it is by saying,
"with waters that pacify," and so on.

Regarding this, the commentators maintain that it is not a textual corruption because there is no inconsistency; for here, while the *avaka* grass, the connection, and the state of being a pacifier were not introduced, the reed (*vetasa*) was introduced, yet even that was not shown at the time of the praise. In this regard, the following is the explanation:
by the very example of the reed, the *avaka* and others are also understood as being included, since they are similar [in their properties].

Nor is this connection between the horse and the ass being stated; rather, it is with water. However, since no praise whatsoever has been manifested by that much alone, [the author] shows that it proceeds in dependence upon another explanatory passage (arthavāda).
"Water is indeed peaceful.

By this [statement], because it has deviated from being an injunction (*vidhi*), the excellence of water is expressed; therein, for some [things] whose connection is well-known, praise occurs through the mere mention of that [quality] alone.
For others, however, a connection is proclaimed by way of a connection with something related.

This is for the purpose of making known such praise as follows: because of the connection with waters, which are renowned for their peaceful nature, even a horse or similar animal possesses a peaceful essence; and by means of a ritual act connected to that [horse], the suffering of the sacrificer is pacified.
