Thus, once it is established that there is praise in the sense that one quickly obtains the fruit through a deity who is swift-acting, and that one obtains food through a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) made of wood, then other things following the same logic must also be understood as having this same character. Furthermore, if these were treated as injunctions (*vidhi*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

If one were to introduce an injunctive suffix (*vidhi-vibhakti*) by treating [the passage] as a praise (*stuti*), and then again conceive of a fruit (*phala*) by means of that very same [suffix], there would be a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*); therefore, it is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
Or rather, it may be a reason (*hetu*), because of its meaningfulness and logical consistency;
for those things which are here stated like reasons by means of words such as "for" (*hi*) are not, in the ultimate sense, actual reasons—this is the illustration.

In this regard, if the status of being a reason (*hetutva*) is being enjoined, then it is already covered by what was stated previously. If the reason here is intended with respect to the connection with the *śarpa* oblation, then since that [connection] has not been enjoined, for what could it be called a reason?

On the other hand, if it is merely a restatement of an existing fact (*bhūtānuvāda*), then that is already understood—just as in the case of the wind being the swiftest—and thus this [section] need not have been commenced.
It is said:

First of all, by this very sentence, neither is the status of being a reason (*hetutva*) enjoined, nor is it a mere restatement of an established fact (*bhūtānuvāda*). What then? Since a reason must be preceded by its own establishment, for as long as there is a doubt regarding its non-establishment, its establishment is obtained through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) from that which is taught as if already established. Furthermore, whatever expectation there may be for an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*)—namely, "why [is this so]?"—that too is considered to be satisfied by this very reason.

Even if it were an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), nevertheless, since its causal character is determined by that [statement], it is understood to apply to the making of all food; and thus, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the reason is indeed "because of this.
Furthermore, because the relationship is what is to be enjoined, he states that the causality belongs to the oblation itself as part of that [relationship].
[The opponent objects: "But the relation of cause and effect is not well-established."
What are the objections? Inference applies only to cause and effect;
and thus he will state later regarding the passage, "for one desiring sensory power, [curd is to be used]."
This is logically consistent;

for we observe that even among things related as cause and effect, such as the stars Kṛttikā and others, there exists the capacity to serve as a cause for the cognition of Rohiṇī and others that have recently risen.
Therefore, it is precisely the relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakatva*) that is considered to be the nature of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
[Objection: But surely that [connection] too, being posterior to inference, cannot be a constituent factor [of inference]. [Reply:
True.
However, since this connection is established only after another [prior] connection exists, he presents it as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the practical application of inference.

Alternatively, this refers to the intention of the word *śakti* (capacity). For indeed, the status of being a logical reason (*hetutā*) belongs precisely to those two things which, at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), are attended to as having the nature of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) by virtue of their capacity as the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakasāmarthya*).
Or rather, this is the definition of a logical reason with respect to the subject matter cited in the examples.

For inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is divided into many varieties, such as the relations of cause and effect, owner and property, and concomitance; among these, in the case of the oblation (*homa*), since no other relation is mentioned when it is stated to be a reason, it must be a reason by virtue of its being a cause.

And that [connection] is unestablished; therefore, it is not a statement of a reason (*hetu*). True, in worldly discourse regarding causes, one first requires the establishment of a relationship through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, in the Veda, since the status of being a reason is conveyed by the word "hi," an illustrative statement expressing the relationship must be inferred on the grounds that the status of being a reason as expressed by the word cannot otherwise be accounted for—namely, "Whatever is a means of making food, with that one should offer the oblation. And by this, the status of being a reason is established. What is the purpose? It is with the intention expressed by the words, "If it were a reason, it would remain [as such]."
When the pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding "not tasting other [food]" is established, the oblation (*homa*) which is the means for accomplishing all food becomes established. Why?
Because that alone is the intended meaning of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Alternatively, how could the ladle, the pot, and so forth possess the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*)?
However, the opponent [argues] that since they possess utility (*arthavattā*) in the act of preparing food, one might rely on that much alone;
and the meaning of the word "possibility" (*upapatti*) is that [the result] can indeed be achieved by those [implements] as well.
But by the preceding [statement], identity of purpose is understood;
through that, there is the intention to speak. This refers to the capacity [of the word].
For indeed, only that which is merely useful for it can somehow be intended as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*).

Alternatively, since "possessing a purpose" (*arthavattva*) is the basis for the mention of the instrumental case-ending, and since that [instrumentality] is established through reasoning, he states the justification for the doubt— arising from the fact that what is currently existing cannot be designated as the cause of an action because such a thing is untenable with respect to the oblation— by saying, "and it is possible by means of that."
Regarding this, an objection is raised: "Since it is said that 'this is being done,' how can it be stated that 'it has been done'? The answer is:
"Because a present action is impossible [to express as completed]."
Alternatively, he himself anticipates and dispels this objection:

"If [the opponent argues that] there is no mention of both [the pestle and the mortar] in the phrase 'neither the pestle nor the pot,' and that [the pestle] lacks the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) and the state of being present, then since these qualities are likewise absent in the case of the pestle, there would be no praise for it.
Therefore, just as you have some way of establishing the purpose of praise, so too do I have the purpose of establishing the logical reason; thus, there is no difference between us."

The phrase "and in the case of the reason, there is direct scriptural statement" (*hetau ca śrutiḥ*) and so forth should be understood at the end [of the section], as it pertains to the defect of an unrelated sentence.
Regarding the praise (*stuti*), there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*); by means of being an instrument for food—a quality esteemed by all people—the excellence (*prāśastya*) is indicated.

And in this view, the expression "with the winnowing basket" (*śūrpeṇa*) is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*) of what is already established through the general property of being an instrument for food.

Or rather, this is the method of interpreting the Sūtra: first, "possessing a purpose" (*arthavattva*) means that its utility is more effective than that of a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), and this is established through logical reasoning (*upapatti*). Furthermore, the connection [between the means and the end] is merely conceptual; therefore, the reason [for the injunction] is [the capacity for action].

If it is argued that praise is improper when the purpose is already achieved, and as for what was said—that praise would not apply even to the winnowing basket because its being an instrument for making food is impossible—what is the answer to that?
And if it is argued that the cause persists because of the general nature of the instruction, then there would be a lack of restriction regarding the injunctions;
this is merely a concessionary argument (*abhyupetyavāda*).
Even if there were an injunction for the cause, nevertheless, there would be no contingency of using a ladle, a pot, or similar items.
For how could the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) be stated as the reason for the preparation of food?
Moreover, that [reason] is not well-known in the world; it must be established by inferring a word that expresses the illustrative example.

And regarding that inference, the authority is the fact that the stated reason would otherwise be inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*). That [authority] is not capable of postulating anything beyond what is required for the reason to be logically consistent.

Since the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) has been proposed as being connected with the act of offering (*homa*), and because a property belonging to something else cannot serve as a logical reason (*hetu*), one must necessarily state that the quality of being a means of preparing food (*annakaraṇatva*) resides in that very [basket].
And due to proximity (*saṃnidhi*), that [quality] is understood precisely as it is delimited by that [basket].

Furthermore, in common worldly usage, whatever reason is taught in reference to a particular subject (*dharmin*), it is first understood precisely through its specific nature as residing in that [subject].

However, because that which consists of those [particulars] lacks conformity with the probandum-part (*sādhyāṃśa*), it is determined at the very time of employing the example that only the universal (*sāmānya*) is intended. Furthermore, for reasons, neither a connection with the probandum through the nature of a universal nor through the nature of a particular has been previously cognized; rather, that [connection] must now be postulated through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). In that case, since a particular is being introduced and a universal is not established—and since there is no possibility for abandoning [the particular]—the non-occurrence otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*) is restricted solely to the particular that has been introduced. Consequently, the statement of the example itself leads to the postulation of that very [connection].
For if that [connection] were not postulated, the scriptural statement of the reason would be contradicted;

for if the inseparable connection between the act of offering (*homa*) and its relation to the status of being an instrument for preparing food— as found in the ladle, the cooking pot, and so forth— were not postulated.

Nothing that has been heard or seen is inconsistent with this; therefore, such an illustrative statement must be supplied: "Whatever powder serves as a means of preparing food, with that one should offer the oblation.
This is an inference based on a perceived particularity.
Even in the world, upon seeing smoke from grass, it is inferred that there is specifically a fire of grass, not merely fire in general.

Just as the act of going, when adopted as the basis for the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word "cow," attains the status of a defining cause only as it inheres in the universal (*sāmānya*) characterized by the dewlap and so forth—occurring subsequent to the cognition of that universal—and not merely with respect to any individual that goes, such is the established usage (*vyavasthā*) of the word "cow"; likewise, because the reason given is the capacity to prepare food inherent in the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), there is no contingency of that causal capacity applying to other things.
In that case, the meaning would be this much:
whatever is capable of preparing food may be used to offer the oblation, and there would be no inclusion of the ladle (*darvī*), the cooking pot (*piṭhara*), and so forth.

Just as when fire is described as the cause of burning while being strongly fanned, that same fire would not burn if it were not fanned, yet conch shells and the like do not burn even when strongly fanned; therefore, there is no fixed rule [in the case of the winnowing-basket]. If, on the other hand, a "great universal" (*mahāsāmānya*) were intended over and above the specific function of making food (*annakaraṇa*) residing in the winnowing-basket, then since whatever is grasped possesses some kind of causality for food, the word "food-making" (*annakaraṇa*)—being a mere restatement of the substance already implied by the lack of a fixed rule—would be purposeless. Therefore, it is better that it be a praise (*stuti*) by virtue of being a cause of food.

Because of the restriction on the order of words, the meaning that is understood from "agnirmūrdhā" (Fire is the head) would also be understood from "mūrdhāgniḥ"; thus, what is the purpose of the restriction? However, for one for whom [the mantra] has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*), if the order were different, there would be no basis for the invisible merit produced by its recitation; therefore, since a change in order is not appropriate, the restriction is meaningful.

Now, if it were argued that an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) must be postulated because of the necessity of conveying a fixed meaning, that is already established by the mere utterance [of the words], since the fixed comprehension depends upon that very utterance.
As for the restriction observed in the case of bases, suffixes, and compounds whose meanings are perceptible—
such as *indrāgnī*, *nīlotpalam*, *rājapuruṣaḥ*, *citraguḥ*, and *niṣkāśambhiḥ*— [it is accounted for by the same principle].
In that case, the opposite would be logical, because it would entail the faults of being ungrammatical (*apaśabda*), a change in meaning, or meaninglessness.
For in those instances, a fixed preceding placement (*pūrvanipāta*) is traditionally taught based on specific conditions, such as being a word beginning with *a-* or ending in *-a*.
Consequently, in the case of *agnīndrau*, there would be grammatical incorrectness; in *puruṣarāja*, a change in meaning; and in *kauśāmbiniḥ*, meaninglessness.
As for the occasional usage "agnīndrau," that must be understood as being Vedic (chāndasa), intended to express Agni's preeminence;
however, when the meaning of the compound is perceived, it remains fixed as referring to Indra-Agni.
[Objection: But in this case as well, would it not be non-mantric (amantra) due to the alteration of the sequence?
If that very [efficacy] depends upon the purposefulness of the mantra, we do not know what the cause for its non-destruction might be;
therefore, there is also the sūtra: "Because of the restriction of the sentence in the case of the establishment of the mantra.
Or rather, let it be so because of the restriction of sentences studied outside of a specific context (*aprakaraṇa*).
There is no distinction between that which belongs to another and that which belongs to oneself in the matter of expressing a meaning.
Alternatively, since the capacity to express a meaning is equal for both mantra and human sentences, the restriction to the mantra sentence serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Or else, it is due to the restriction of the sentence when there is the possibility of various means of recollection, such as meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth.

For there is no distinction whatsoever between a mantra or meditation and so forth when the object is perceptible; thus, they have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*) because they speak of what does not exist.
Furthermore, no ritual action such as "the four horns" or anything related to it exists either in the archetype (*prakṛti*) or in the modification (*vikṛti*).

And although there might be something [to be gained] by way of figurative praise (*guṇavāda*), nevertheless, because there is no performance of that [act], there is no purpose served by its recollection.
Furthermore, it is not known in which specific context it should be employed;
in that case, since mere utterance follows the order of the mantra-text, the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is established.
"May you not harm me, may you not cause me distress," and so forth—these are examples from the second quarter of the first chapter of the *Vedadhī*.
Since they concern objects such as the *vinā* [lute] which are insentient, they serve as illustrations for the principle that "there is no binding of an insentient object.
However, in the present case, since injury (*hiṃsā*) is not even a possibility, a prohibition would be purposeless.
Because of the contradiction in meaning,
the nature of heaven and the nature of the intermediate space, as well as the oneness and multiplicity of the sacrificial pap (caru) substance, are contradictory;
yet this contradictory meaning is not impossible.
Or how could the deity Vāditṛ be the intermediate space or the sky?

Furthermore, this pair of reasons cannot be refuted even on the grounds that they serve as praise (*stuti*), for in the Brāhmaṇas, praises that function as supplements to injunctions (*vidhi*) are meaningful;
however, the praise found in a mantra (*mantra-stuti*) need not be respected because it serves no purpose.
Some categories of objects are unknowable because they cannot be known through cognition; however,
for others, the very meaning of the sentence itself is not understood.

Furthermore, the meaning of a mantra does not assist [the ritual] by its mere existence if it is not remembered at the time of performance; therefore, it is determined that the only thing which can be performed with absolute certainty is the recitation itself.

As for the sentence-meaning, it remains undifferentiated; since the recitation of the mantra has its requirements satisfied by the apprehension of the syllables, it does not directly attain the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice.
And just as the Veda is not grasped by the context because it lacks the nature of a procedure (*itikartavyatā*)— being like a mere substance (*dravya*)—
so too, the knowledge of word-meanings is not grasped [by the context], because it is satisfied by the cognition of the sentence-meaning.

However, the cognition of the sentence-meaning, while still incomplete within the context and revolving [in the mind],—because it consists of an action, is required by the injunction of performance; and since its fruit is the recollection of the object to be accomplished as inherent in the ritual act, it becomes the *itikartavyatā* (the "how-to" procedure).

In that case, there is no ground for postulating an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), for such a postulation would only be made on the basis of the otherwise inexplicability of the textual recitation, not when the meaningfulness of the text is already established.

Even if there were an occasion for such a postulation, it could at best arise from the cognition of the sentence-meaning itself, and certainly not from a sentence that has no further expectancy because its purposeful meaning has already been perceived.

Furthermore, when something is being employed for either a visible or an invisible purpose, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must necessarily be presented here; and in this case, the context (*prakaraṇa*) indicates an invisible purpose, while the indicative mark (*liṅga*) indicates a visible purpose.
Since the context cannot enjoin the employment of something for a purpose that is impossible, it follows with certainty that one should perform whatever [action] can be done by means of the mantra.
And as for its capacity to produce an invisible result—whether worldly or Vedic—no such means of valid cognition exists.
Therefore, there is syntactic unity between both the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*) through their application to a perceptible purpose.
This being the case, because the usage is well-established among ritual practitioners (*yājñika*), there will be no difficulty in postulating another basis [for its authority].
Consequently, the primacy of the meaning remains established as inherent.
It is not so;
[the purpose] is not seen in the object.
By the mere fact that [the action] has been accomplished, its being for that purpose is determined.

Because the injunction for the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*) would be rendered purposeless if it were not for the utility of its literal meaning; and because there is no utility for the meaning of mantras in the case of the Buddha’s scriptures, since they consist of words that do not exist [in the world] and whose meanings are not bound [by conventional usage].

In that regard, if we cannot escape the assumption of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) even at a distance, then, in the absence of any reason for bypassing it, it must be assumed to arise from the mere utterance itself.
Since the necessity of utterance is established for both disputants, and since the postulation of an unseen result (adṛṣṭa) arises from that [necessity],
it is stated in response: "In the sacrifice, the purpose is precisely the manifestation of the constituent parts of the sacrifice."

Even though there is no practical transaction with those [conventions] as they exist in common worldly usage, nevertheless, the mere illumination of their essential nature is beneficial to the performers. Therefore, only that which is useless, such as forms of address and the like, need not be intended to be expressed; however, it does not follow that everything seen therein must be explicitly stated. Indeed, uniformity (ekarūpya) is not determined by anyone, according to the *Tantravārttika*.
Therefore, just as in the case of "He gives a gift to the gods' abode" and so forth, the primacy of the meaning is unimpaired according to our acceptance based on observation;
we say the same regarding the verse beginning with "He takes it up with four," which is a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*).

For as long as the traditional recitation of a mantra has its purpose not yet understood and the context remains incomplete, everything that is postulated for the sake of accomplishing that [purpose] is Vedic. However, after the requirement for further information has been satisfied, even that which is imagined would be non-authoritative due to its human origin.
Furthermore, it will be stated that the authority of indicative power (*liṅga*) and the other means of proof does not exist independently without shaking the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
This is what he says: "And when there is a sentence, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is the separator, and that [sentence] does not exist for this [mantra].

For at the very moment it is intended to be inferred from the context (*prakaraṇa*) that "one should sacrifice with this" or "one should take hold of the rope," at that same moment the mantra is taken away by the phrase "of the horse's halter" (*aśvābhidhānīm*).

As for the objection that since there is no connection [between the horse and the reins], how can one say "he takes up the horse's bridle" (*aśvābhidhānīm ādatte*), the answer is that this should be understood as referring to the action alone, because a connection with the *kāraka* (the object, the horse) is impossible; it is not intended in a general sense. Therefore, it is not the mere act of taking up that is enjoined, but rather the act of taking up as qualified by the horse's bridle. Alternatively, this is the second quarter of the first chapter.
Consequently, a subsequent connection with the performer is proposed;
in every respect, there is no [conflict] with the Darśa sacrifice.
For if that which is obtained from the wording of the mantra were exactly the same as that which is stated by the direct (perceptual) injunction, then we might be subject to reproach.

[Objection: "In that case, since this has become a rule for what was previously unestablished (*aprāptavidhi*), one should not call it an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*). [Response: There is no fault, because it is designated as such by way of its result.

For in all cases, unless there is the word *parisaṃkhyā* itself or the particle *eva*, neither an exclusive specification nor a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is expressed by the direct statement (*śruti*). Rather, it is simply a rule (*vidhi*) of this kind that is designated as such by way of its result.
What, then, is the distinction between a rule (*vidhi*), a restrictive rule (*niyama*), and an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*)?
It is said:
An injunction (*vidhi*) applies when [the matter] is not established at all; a restrictive rule (*niyama*) applies when it is optionally established;
and an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) is said to apply when [the matter] is established both there and elsewhere.
For an injunction (*vidhi*) itself is differentiated in this way by a certain specific feature.

In that case, where something is absolutely unestablished and will not be established prior to the statement [of the rule], it is understood that the application (*niyoga*) there is a pure injunction (*vidhi*), such as "one sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*).

However, where an optional establishment is possible prior to the statement, the injunction that operates there—filling in the aspect of non-establishment—is called a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) because of its restrictive nature.

As in the case of the injunction "one threshes the rice," since that [threshing] is already established by the very implication of the purpose of producing rice, the result of the injunction is not merely the attainment of that [act], but rather the fulfillment of what has not yet been attained.

And while that [threshing] might otherwise be implied through other means for the sake of attaining rice, once its fulfillment is achieved, their cessation occurs by implication (*arthāt*), not from the sentence itself.
Furthermore, that exclusion (*āraṇa*) is not a restrictive rule (*niyama*);

for in that case, it would be an exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*). Having abandoned the fixed proximity of threshing, there is no occasion to conceive of a result consisting in the exclusion of other [actions].

However, since the non-restriction of the *avahanti* (threshing) arose through its connection with that [rice], the exclusion is understood by implication as being inherent within the restrictive rule itself.

Furthermore, this injunction did not operate when [the threshing] was already established, such that one might imagine its purpose to be the exclusion of other [methods]. Rather, because it operates beforehand, it blocks the power of the [general rule] that would otherwise establish the matter; thus, it effects another establishment, and since that is obtained through the sense of the text, it is not designated by that [other method] alone.

Furthermore, that which might be obtained both there and elsewhere prior to the application [of a restrictive rule], or whatever else [might be so obtained], is *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification).
As in the example cited here, and as in the *Tantravārtika*: [it is] like this.
And [this applies] in the fifth alternative regarding the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice.

Here too, this [injunction] does not operate upon something already established, because the scriptural passage that would establish it has not been inferred. How then [is it understood]? It means: "If this sentence had not existed, then one would have obtained it from that [other source]. For every perceptible (direct) statement, the result is intended to be merely the prevention of an inferential statement.

For what is the use of that recitation by which the purpose is accomplished even from another source? To that end, the exclusion of the donkey’s halter (*gaībharaśanā*) is postulated as the result. This is postulated by means of the method of a hypothetical inquiry (*kṛtvācintā*): "Even if this sentence did not exist, what kind of performance would there be?
In that case, the application of the mantra would certainly be established for the horse’s halter (*aśvābhidhānī*), but it would likewise follow [unnecessarily] for the donkey’s halter as well.

But when, by this direct statement (*pratyakṣa-vākya*), the inference of a general application-capable sentence is precluded due to the absence of expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*), then the establishment of the fact that [the mantra] refers exclusively to the horse’s bridle follows; thus, because there is no tautology, the sentence is meaningful and not contradictory.
This concludes the second quarter of the first chapter.

Even for those who maintain that the utterance has a visible purpose, another unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) must necessarily be postulated due to the restriction [on its use]; that same unseen result will also arise for me from the restriction on the communication [of meaning], so there is no contradiction.
By this, the restriction regarding the status of being a *mantra* and so forth is refuted.

Even when other means exist, because specific *mantras* with a particular sequence are traditionally taught, other means are excluded; thus, since the expression of meaning is established by merely postulating a restrictive unseen result, [the *mantra* functions as intended].
In the *abhivāna*, it is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*);

by way of a metaphor (*rūpaka*) stating "four horns," it is a praise of the sacrifice that generates enthusiasm for the performance at the proper time. In the *hautra*, however, this is employed as the *ājya* of the Hotṛ priest during the *viṣuvat* day.
And because that [Agni] belongs to Agni and because of the praise of the Sun as his deity, the praise of Agni in the form of the Sun is described there.
In that context, "four horns" refers to the watches (yāmas) of the day;
"three feet" refers to the seasons of cold, heat, and rain.
"Two heads" refers to the two solstices;
"seven hands" is a praise of the horse; "bound in three ways" refers to the three pressings of the Soma sacrifice.
"O bull"—this is a praise by virtue of being the cause of rain;
"he roars loudly" refers to the thunder, as is well known throughout the world. This is the *Tantravārtika*.
"The god entered mortals through the two gates"— this [Vedic statement] serves as an incentive for action because it describes his entry into the hearts of all persons.
Thus, by this path, there exists at least the recollection of the means for accomplishing *dharma*,
since there is no mention of knowledge (*vidyā*) in connection with it.
Although this intention was not set forth in the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position, it is nevertheless presented here because it is possible.

For if the statement of the meaning were useful at the time of Vedic study (svādhyāya), then it would be resorted to; however, this is not the case, because there is no connection with ritual acts (karma).
Furthermore, its non-repetition is due to its ease of performance, like the act of sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and so forth.
The second quarter of the first chapter:
It has been stated that there is a connection with what is non-eternal,
but that this is merely a commonality of sound.
The sacrificer is the petitioner, and Indra is the one petitioned; this has always been so.
Although the *kokaṭas* are a specific region, they are nonetheless eternal.
Alternatively, the *kīkaṭas* are the wretched people residing in all the worlds; *pramaganda* refers to one who lives by usury, for he gives [the gift] thinking, "He will bring back much more."
One who has low branches is a *ṣaṇḍha*; his wealth is called *naicāśākham*.
And all of that, not being an auxiliary to sacrifice because they do not engage in ritual action, he brings to us. The rest is self-evident.

Modification (*ūha*) refers to the observation of modification; [the phrase] "the mother does not grow" (*na mātā vardhate*) is understood as a prohibition regarding the words themselves, because growth in the sense of nourishment and the like is directly perceived and thus a prohibition is impossible, and because [the literal sense] would otherwise be purposeless, it is known to apply to their constituent parts (*tadaṅgeṣu*).

Even there, since growth in the sense of physical bulk and the like is impossible, the prohibition applies to the dual and plural numbers by virtue of their expressing an additional meaning. And that [prohibition] is possible only if the words are intent upon the meaning, when there is a desire to include all the specific attributes of the animal, such as its measure.
And as for this cognition of the existence of the increase of other words: although [the text] merely restates what is already established—

that the modification (*ūha*) of the mother and so forth is not required because they exist for the sake of another and their distinction is established solely through the difference in their relations— nevertheless, by mentioning *ūha* which has been understood through reasoning, it is made known that the meaning is intended to be expressed in the archetype (*prakṛti*), since the cognition of *ūha* occurs only when things are beneficial according to the principles of logic.
Otherwise, however, that observed [result] would have to be accomplished by means of the unmodified [mantras] themselves.

Likewise, even though the animal sacrifice belongs to another deity, the *manotā* verse addressed to Agni must still be employed; thus, the observation of the application of modification (*ūha*)—as seen in the scriptural recitation of "of the ewes," "of the rams," and so forth, which are modified according to their actual meaning—will also serve the intended purpose.
Otherwise, if one were to abandon the original words and substitute others, two observed [results] would have to be postulated.
For if they were not based on meaning, everything would be purposeless;
therefore, it is established in the Tantravārtika that mantras are words intended to convey meaning.
"Since Dharma has its root in the Word (śabda), that which is not the Word should be disregarded.

Thus far, the utility of the Veda—consisting of injunctions (vidhi), explanatory passages (arthavāda), mantras, and names—with respect to Dharma has been established. Now, consideration is given to human-authored Smṛtis, which have as their scope matters remembered from the past and are composed by Manu and others, as well as to practices (ācāras) that possess the status of Smṛti.

In this regard, an investigation should be conducted by citing specific examples; thus, the Smṛti texts concerning the Aṣṭakā and other rites found in the works of Manu and others are cited as instances where the question of their validity or invalidity is subject to inquiry. Furthermore, the cause for doubt is stated.

The statements of Manu and others depend upon Smṛti, and Smṛti itself depends upon its foundational source of authority (mūla-pramāṇa); thus, not even one of them can have its authority determined as independent, like that of the Veda. However, since those who profess the Veda maintain these [Smṛtis] with unwavering firmness through an uninterrupted tradition, it is not right to conclude their lack of authority; therefore, a doubt is appropriate here. To this, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) says: "Their very authority need not be accepted. Why?
In general, all forms of recollection arise in conformity with an object already apprehended through perception and other means of knowledge, and they serve to corroborate that object. Thus,

it has been established here that perception and the other means of knowledge do not, in the first instance, grasp the relationship between the Aṣṭakā and other rites as being the means for achieving results such as heaven.
Furthermore, just as sound is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the case of the *agnihotra* and other such rites, it is not so with mantras;
for sound, there is only one means of valid cognition, namely direct perception.

If it is asserted that [mantras] exist even though they are not apprehended by that [direct perception], then it would be better to simply accept the existence of *dharma* itself as being without any means of valid cognition.
Nor can inference be applied here to postulate a lost Vedic text;
for no such Smṛti is observed to possess the necessary invariable concomitance (*vyāpti*), nor is anything else seen that could serve as an inferential mark.

Just as no logical mark (*liṅga*) applies to Dharma because its relationship [with any perceptible sign] is not perceived, so too it does not apply to the Śruti of the Aṣṭakā and other rites. Nor can that [Dharma] be understood through scripture—whether eternal or artificial.
There is no confidence in that which is artificial, nor can it be established as eternal;
furthermore, it is not understood what kind of statement has been determined [by such means]. This concludes the third quarter of the first chapter.
For we see many people wandering due to [texts] such as *arthavādas*;
moreover, analogy (*upamāna*) is not accepted when the object is unseen or when the similarity is unestablished. Therefore, by that means as well, the root scripture (*mūla-śruti*) is not proven.

For if a Smṛti could not be established without the postulation of a Vedic text (śruti), then it would indeed be pure. However, since it is possible for it to be impure—such as in the case of a dream—there is no room for presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) or for inference based on general observation (sāmānyato dṛṣṭa), because of this lack of invariable concomitance (anaikāntyāt). Therefore, when the Vedic text is within the scope of non-perception, even though other means of purification exist, it is designated as "rootless" (nirmūla) due to the absence of its intended source.
Now, surely those who know that "this ritual act must be performed with such a procedure and such a result"—

or rather, those who know that "it must be performed in this manner"— being thus cognizant, how could they possibly deceive us by saying, "this should not be performed"? Indeed, some say it must be performed, while others say it need not be performed.

How can there be any difference [between them], when such a cognition arises even upon being told, "This is remembered by them as well"? Or alternatively, how could Manu and others— who know that this matter is not to be performed— speak so as to deceive the world without fault, saying, "This must indeed be performed"?
Regarding the phrase "due to the impossibility of recollection":
first, as for those persons who lived after Manu and others, their knowledge cannot be considered *smṛti* (recollection), because it does not concern an object previously experienced.

If even for Manu and others some prior means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is conceivable, then memory may arise; otherwise it could not. Why, then, was the example of the daughter’s son of a barren woman given, bypassing the son or daughter?
Because the position [of the case] is analogous.

For the prior cognition of Manu and others occupies the position of a son, while the memory [of the tradition] occupies the position of a daughter's son; therefore, just as one considers the recollection of a daughter's son to be an error after having concluded that the daughter herself is absent, so too should the memory of the Aṣṭakā and other rites by Manu and others be considered false upon concluding that perception and the other means of knowledge are impossible.

Just as the statement "this is the Veda" was spoken with the intention of inferring a verbal tradition based on its unbroken continuity through successive generations, the other [author], however, thinking that this [tradition] consists merely of a memory whose object is itself unbroken, asserts once more that it is without foundation.

Furthermore, the Veda is perceived with its specific details through direct perception; in that regard, just as with objects such as jars, one perceives it as residing in another person and remembers it, and others, perceiving what has been remembered by them, remember it themselves and transmit it to yet others in the same manner—thus there is beginninglessness (*anāditā*).

Moreover, since for everyone perception must necessarily precede their own remembrance, there is no lack of a foundation (*nirmūlatā*). And the mere acquisition of the relationship between word and meaning depends solely upon the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*).

For even prior to the word "Veda," other entities distinct from one another—such as the form of the Ṛgveda and so forth residing in the student, or the forms of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas which are distinct from others—are perceived.

And since the names of all these are beginningless, it has been established that those [entities] perceived at a time subsequent to the application of those names are also objects of direct perception (pratyakṣa).

Now, in the case of the Aṣṭakā and other rites, even though they reside in other persons, there exists some root in knowledge—just as in the case of a potter’s activity. For if the nature of the action alone were [the object of memory], then others, having seen someone else performing cooking or similar acts with their senses, would remember them. But since the relationship between the means and the end, such as heaven and so forth, is remembered, and this [relationship] is not seen by anyone arising in other persons, it follows that [the tradition] lacks authority according to the maxim of a "succession of the blind."

Because everyone has the conceit of establishing [the Veda] as authoritative through the presentation of beginningless usage— just like the Veda itself— the illustration of a "succession of the blind" is given;

for while the third quarter of the first chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra*] concerns the beginninglessness of authority (*prāmāṇya*) in the Veda, here it concerns the beginninglessness of non-authority (*aprāmāṇya*).
How can such a recollection of the Vāṣṭaka and other rites exist when no original injunction (*codanā*) is perceived?
Furthermore, that whose relationship [to its source] has not been experienced cannot be inferred.

If the Smṛtis had proceeded from the Veda after being understood from it, then, just like the recollection of their meaning, the fact that "this was composed by Manu and others" would also have been remembered through tradition.
This might be so.
It is argued that for those who have already achieved their purpose through the recollection of the meaning, the recollection of the root text is useless and therefore not required.
This is incorrect; for it is not reasonable to forget that very thing by which the authority [of the text] was established.
Because the memory of meaning lacks intrinsic validity (*svataḥ prāmāṇya*),
all persons indeed know that validity is not ascertained through knowledge based on the Veda and so forth;
how then could they possibly show disregard for it?

Moreover, if indeed even they [the ancient sages] understood only the mere meaning from others and did not accept the Veda as the source, then this same objection would apply to those who preceded them; thus, you cannot escape the consequence that the tradition is rootless.
If, however, it were imagined that the Vedic branches had perished, then by that same logic, the authority of all the works of the Buddha and others would also follow.
Furthermore, whoever has a particular intention may simply select those [meanings] from the lost branches and treat them as authoritative.
Even if these matters were indeed contained within the extant branches, all persons—just like Manu and others—would have perceived them from those very sources.

Moreover, since the understanding of the injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*) would be more appropriately derived directly from that [Veda] itself, the composition of the Smṛtis would be rendered useless.
And this is not understood:
from what kind of statement was this accepted by Manu and others—was it from one consisting of an injunction (*vidhi*), or rather from one in the form of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)?
Behold!
Nor can we determine that [the Smṛtis] have the Veda as their source on the basis of the words of Manu and others;
for they might, having fabricated even something rootless for the sake of deceiving the world through such causes as greed and delusion, speak in this manner.
Therefore, it is not authoritative.

Furthermore, in every case where an unseen entity (adṛṣṭa) must be postulated, one should postulate such a thing that does not contradict what is observed and does not necessitate the assumption of yet another unseen entity.
In that regard, first concerning error:
there would be the consequence of contradicting the observation of the authoritative scriptures of the wise, as well as the subversion of the firm validity accepted by the entire world.

Even by persons of the present day, the errors of Manu and others have been followed, and the presentation of their refutations has likewise been attributed to Manu and others; thus, there is the postulation of many unseen things (*adṛṣṭa*).
Even regarding direct experience, that very experience itself must first be postulated.

Furthermore, the postulation of a capacity in Manu and others that is contrary to the nature of all contemporary human beings has already been refuted in the discussion on the doctrine of omniscience.
The tradition of human speech has also been refuted as being like a succession of blind men;
for no such thing is observed to acquire the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) without a firm foundation.
Likewise, the third quarter of the first chapter [discusses] the assumption of that [authorship] even in the case of a deceptive work;
for one must rely on such factors as the purpose of the deception, the world's delusion regarding it, and the persistence of that delusion for such a long time.
Furthermore, because the validity of a firm cognition that has already arisen is being rejected, there is a contradiction with what is perceived.
Therefore, among all [theories], the postulation of *codanā* alone is superior;
for in that case, the acceptance of the unseen [result] follows from that [cognition] alone.
But all the remaining factors, such as acceptance by the great multitude and so forth, are merely followed along.
Furthermore, it is possible that Manu and others possessed prior knowledge of the Vedic injunctions as its cause;
for this very reason, he said: "Therefore, the connection with the Veda is established for the members of the three castes."

Furthermore, regarding those such as the Mlecchas, for whom there is no possibility of the Veda having been produced, their recollections of supersensuous matters do not even reach the stage of being considered possible at the very time one postulates their source; thus, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), since the four possible sources of error remain, they lack authority.

However, once the Veda is considered a possible source and other causes have been ruled out, it is established by elimination that its basis is indeed the Vedic injunction (*codanā*), since a sourceless origin is impossible.
As for the question, "Why are these injunctions not perceived?"—[the answer follows].
Regarding this, some say:
"They are eternally inferable and are never actually uttered,
just like those [words] postulated on the basis of grammatical markers (*liṅga*) and so forth."
If it is asked how those [Vedic texts] that have not been recited can be established as the root source, this is not a fault.

For their establishment occurs through tradition, just like the uninterrupted transmission of a text; for just as a book maintains its existence through an unbroken lineage of transmission (*saṃpradāya*), so too is the continuity of the tradition of the eternally inferable revelation (*śruti*) established by means of the [traditional] assertion (*pratijñā*).
That is logically consistent,
for it follows the maxim of a succession of the blind.

For that injunction which is never uttered at any time— its existence being more difficult to establish because it lacks the manifestation of perception and other means of knowledge for all persons— is exceedingly rare.
And thus, for Smṛti as well, that same status of being equal to the grandson of a barren woman applies.
However, because the *liṅga* (indicative marks) and so forth are eternal, it is not contradictory for them to be the cause of an inference of an eternally accompanying Śruti;
therefore, it is better to simply infer a lost Śruti.
Nor is dissolution impossible;
for it is observed that through negligence, laziness, and so forth, as well as due to the decline of human beings, the scope [of knowledge] becomes limited.
And this being the case, it does not follow that there is any arbitrary lack of valid means of cognition.

Furthermore, the inference of a Vedic text (*śruti*) is obtained through the necessity of accounting for the otherwise inexplicable firmness of the tradition of the learned members of the three [upper] castes;
or rather, let it be that the text is rooted in a Vedic revelation existing within currently extant recensions (*śākhā*).
If it is asked how there is non-apprehension, it is replied:
as for the question, "For what reason were the Vedic sentences themselves not included?
it is because of the fear of breaking the tradition.
For it is heard in scripture that the Veda must be studied as established in its specific sequence;
furthermore, certain Smṛti practices pertain to particular branches (śākhās) of the Veda,
and even among those, some are prescribed specifically with reference to a particular person.

Those [injunctions] which are recited in the context of the *ṛtu* (seasonal sacrifices) but, due to some specific cause, are displaced [from that context], attain the status of being duties for all persons (*puruṣadharma*).
For example: "One should not converse with a woman in her menses," "Therefore, one should not strike a Brāhmaṇa," and so forth.

In that regard, if they were to extract only those very sentences and teach them [independently], then, because of the alteration of the sequence, there would be a contradiction with the injunction regarding the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyavidhi*).
And by this explanation, others too might study merely the injunctions or merely what is useful through the medium of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*);
in that case, the disappearance of the Veda would follow as a consequence.
Furthermore, Manu and the others were not necessarily students of all the Vedic branches (*sarvaśākhādhyāyin*).
For they, having heard the mere meaning from students of other recensions through diligent effort, would compose it in their own words for the sake of not forgetting;
yet no specific wording [of the original] would be known.
Just as, due to the firmness of the tradition, there is no basis in error for the Smṛti, so too there is no basis in explanatory passages (arthavāda).
For they are indeed capable of distinguishing between an injunction (*vidhi*) and an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

In that context, since the Smṛti consists of injunctions, its being preceded by an *arthavāda*—which would require a basis for inference through identity with the original Vedic source (*prakṛti*)—is without proof.
Moreover:

"The entire Veda is the root of Dharma"—since this has been stated by the Smṛti-authors themselves, they have effectively bound their own selves by this [assertion]. Furthermore, this was perceived by the authors of those times through the application of their intellect; therefore, the validity [of the Smṛtis] is established as being mediated by the Veda. As for one who, on the basis of the identity of the author, seeks to prove either the independent authority of the Smṛtis or their rootedness in the Veda through inference, his argument is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of practices observed among those who follow the pursuit of wealth and pleasure, which are seen to be based on perceptible motives.
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction because its validity would depend upon a heard revelation (*śruti*).

Therefore, it is precisely presumption (*arthāpatti*)—which, due to its non-deviation, is figuratively called inference (*anumāna*) as a subsequent means of knowledge—that is intended by the firmness of this very recollection (*smṛti*).
Alternatively, it refers to the inference of a cause based on the firmness [of the recollection].

It is not said that [the connection] is impossible because, as is the case with humans, death—which severs all residual impressions (*saṃskāra*)—intervenes, making it impossible to reconnect with the results of karma.

Rather, since there is a commonality of agents regarding both memory and Vedic matters, the connection of the three social classes (*traivarṇika*) with the Veda is established; thus, for the sake of attaining the status of being rooted in the Vedic injunction (*codanā*), even forgetfulness is possible.
Indeed, even today one observes the forgetting of the meaning while the text itself is lost.

Even if those [passages] do indeed exist in other Vedic branches (*śākhā*), there may still be a forgetting of which specific passages are found in which branch; however, they preserve the mere fact of their being Vedic for the sake of establishing their authority. Furthermore, knowledge of those specific details is to be disregarded altogether, as it is of no practical utility.

Likewise, regarding those rules established "for each occasion" (*pratyupasthita-niyama*), such as rising from one's seat for elders and so forth—those which are regulated in response to each specific circumstance that arises—their authority is derived solely from their having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*).
This is correct.
Why?
For not every single practice of his is accepted as authoritative as if it were the root [of all knowledge],
because this is the section concerning the inquiry into Dharma (*dharma-jijñāsā*).

Furthermore, if following the teacher and so forth had only a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), then they should not have been cited, as they would lack authority regarding Dharma— just like the case of the sages (*ṛṣi*) and others.
It might be argued that these are presented as being non-authoritative;
but this is not so,
for if that were the case, they would have been cited under the rule "and because a reason is seen" (hetudarśanāt).
Therefore, the view that [the injunction] "one should seek what is better" is fruitless is incorrect;

nor is attainment necessarily achieved through the scripture alone. For it is possible to cause a teacher to perform teaching and other such duties by other means as well, such as conciliation or bribery.
Thus, there is scope for a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) in this regard.

And in all cases, some visible purpose—such as gaining the favor of the world, securing protection, or engendering affection—can be stated for whatever action is performed, just as the author of the Bhāṣya has described.
Nor is it the case that acts with visible purposes, such as threshing and the like, or sacrifices intended for rain and so forth, are non-Vedic.

Therefore, even though a visible purpose exists, the Vedic character of these acts is possible because the transcendental result (*adṛṣṭa*) arising from the restrictive rule (*niyama*) cannot be established by any other means of knowledge. Consequently, since following the teacher and similar acts are occasional (*naimittika*), there is sin in their omission, but not in their performance.
And it is observed that [the student thinks], "The teacher, being pleased, will teach me," and so forth;
furthermore, by virtue of the restrictive rule (*niyama*), there is the attainment of a transcendental merit (*apūrva*) for the sake of completing the rite without obstacles.

Thus, when practices are being undertaken according to traditional conduct (*ācāra*), it is appropriate to investigate whether such [practices] should be performed once or repeatedly, as in the case of the statement, "it should be so."
Otherwise, however, there would be a restriction [on the authority of Smṛti] based solely on the fact that its purpose is visible (dṛṣṭārthatva), just as in the case of drinking water and so forth.

As for the statement made by the author of the Bhāṣya that "its authority arises precisely because its purpose is visible," this was said for the sake of excelling the opponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin).

He means: "If you might somehow render those Smṛtis lacking authority which have invisible purposes (adṛṣṭārtha), how then could these, which concern matters such as following one's teacher, possibly lack authority?"

Although the specific details of the assembly hall (*sabhā*), water-stations (*prapā*), and so forth are indeed inferred from the scriptural mention [of the general category], nevertheless, their authority is established because they are all included by the very scriptural mention of "benefiting others.

Therefore, in the context of the injunction "one should follow one who is superior," the fact that those who are superior follow [others] is shown as an established reality, just as it is with the donkey.

Just as water-stations established in a waterless desert benefit others, so too are you—such is the statement devoted to the praise of the deity; in this sentence, the existence of the water-stations is treated as an established fact, and its ultimate purpose is observed.

The practice of wearing a tuft of hair (*śikhā*) serves as a mark of one's lineage (*gotra*); yet, since even that rule of conduct has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), its mere maintenance is not the sole objective.
It is possible to remember one’s lineage through other means as well; therefore, there must be another underlying intention.

To begin with, the lineage must necessarily be remembered for the sake of establishing the divisions of the four-fold or five-fold portions (*caturavatta-pañcāvatta*) which constitute parts of the ritual action.

And for this reason, even for the sake of that indicative mark (*liṅga*), the third quarter of the first chapter establishes the authority of the *Śikhākalpa-smṛti*. However, because the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from that restrictive rule has no other possible application, its status as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) will be established by necessity.

Thus, the validity of all Smṛtis is established as being purposeful. In this regard, it must be distinguished that whatever is connected with liberation originates from the Veda, whereas that which concerns worldly objects and pleasure is preceded by worldly usage.
This same principle applies to the instructional statements found even in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
As for the narrative episodes (upākhyānas), they have been explained as being among the arthavādas.

However, that which concerns the description of the divisions of the earth is intended to distinguish the regions where the fruits of dharma and adharma are experienced; some of it is based on observation, while some is rooted in the Veda.

The genealogical succession (*vaṃśānukramaṇam*) is also rooted in direct perception and tradition for the purpose of knowing the lineages and clans (*gotra*) of the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya castes. The measurement of space and time is also for the sake of establishing worldly and astronomical practice; it is a future exposition based on inference from the tradition of observation and calculation. Furthermore, the description of the diversity in the ripening of the fruits of the performance of *dharma* and *adharma* according to the nature of the ages (*yuga*) that have proceeded since beginningless time is rooted in the Veda, by way of providing knowledge [of these matters]. As for the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgavidyā*), their exposition of what is beneficial for the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what is beneficial for the person (*puruṣārtha*) must be distinguished as being preceded by both worldly experience and the Veda.

In that regard, concerning the training (*śikṣā*), first, the exposition of the distinctions of phonemes, articulation, vowels, and timing is based on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, the recollection of specific results arising from practice through such knowledge—
such as the traditional teaching that "a mantra is deficient if [wrong] in accent or phoneme," and the traditional teaching regarding transgression— is rooted in the Veda.

Thus, in the *Kalpasūtras*, the determination of meaning—which results in the integration of injunctions obtained through reasoning scattered across different recensions (*śākhās*) mixed with explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) and the like—is accepted as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, certain usages of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others, which are preceded by worldly usage, are adopted as causes for the attainment of happiness. In grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) as well, the knowledge of the distinction between correct words (*sādhuśabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*) is a cause for the formation of linguistic cognition, just like the distinction between the suffixes *sākṣāt* and so forth. According to the Vedic tradition, the accomplishment of the fruit [of the ritual] arises from the use of correct words, whereas the use of a corrupt word results in a deficiency of the fruit.
Even in the *Chandoviciti*, the distinction between the *gāyatrī* and other meters in both worldly and Vedic usage is as evident as before.

However, it is stated in the Śruti that the fruit [of ritual action] arises from its performance preceded by knowledge of those [meters]: "He who, indeed, performs a sacrifice or officiates at a sacrifice with a mantra whose seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), deity (*devatā*), and explanatory passage (*brāhmaṇa*) are unknown," and so forth; thus, an undesirable result is heard [in the scripture].

In the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) as well, the knowledge of lunar days (*tithi*) and constellations (*nakṣatra*)—derived through the measurement of planetary revolutions and the division of the movements of the moon, sun, and other bodies—is rooted in calculation based on an unbroken tradition. It indicates the ripening of the fruits of previously performed auspicious and inauspicious actions by means of the stability or instability of the planets, and it is rooted in the Veda by way of prescribing rites for pacification (*śānti*) and so forth regarding those [planetary states]. By this, the sciences of physiognomy (*sāmudra*) and architecture (*vāstuvidyā*) are also explained.
Such methods are to be inferred everywhere.
When such an arrangement of the house, the body, and so forth exists, it must be understood that "this and that" is to be accepted.
However, *mīmāṃsā* has proceeded from the world itself through perception, inference, and the like, via the scholarly practices of an uninterrupted tradition;
for no one at all is capable of first devising such a collection of logical arguments.

By this [method], one should explain the Nyāya-vistara; for by means of perception and the other [means of knowledge]— which are distinguished by their own specific characteristics and have been thoroughly examined— it is possible to discern [the truth], but not by themselves.
And likewise it has been stated in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]:
"Direct perception, inference, and verbal testimony consisting of various traditions— these three, when well-understood, should be employed by one desiring purity in dharma."
By such statements as these, the purity of reasoning (*tarka*) is relied upon.

Generally, because human beings are preponderantly characterized by unrighteousness (*adharma*), their intuitive insights (*pratibhā*), being obstructed by that [unrighteousness], proceed toward various evil paths.

In this regard, the third quarter of the first chapter of the *Sarvavipra* [text] concerns the treatises on reasoning (*tarka-śāstra*) which proceed from the Upaniṣads and the explanatory passages concerning worldly purposes (*lokārthavāda*).
The demonstration of the gateway of right faith,
its logical justifications, and the gateway of certainty preceded by reasoning are thus explained;
otherwise, however—
But in case of contradiction, it should be disregarded; for while the authority of Smṛti was established as being inferential and applicable to all objects when no contradiction existed,
that very authority is now set aside whenever there is a conflict with the Veda.
Having cited every instance of Smṛti that contradicts the perceptible words of the Veda,
it is now deliberated: is even such [Smṛti] determined to be an authority for Dharma,
or is it set aside?
If it is asked, "Whence arises this doubt? it is replied:

two cognitions that bring forward contradictory meanings regarding a single object are in conflict; and through the determination of their relative strength and weakness, they enter into a relationship of sublation and sublated. Therefore, if even for Śruti and Smṛti, whose contradiction has been suspected, a settlement could be established by some means through having different objects, [the doubt would be resolved].

Alternatively, because there is no contradiction between that which is to be enjoined and that which is to be prohibited, and because their coexistence is possible even within a single subject—given that they cannot both reside in a single application—it may be that by accepting the authority of both, both will be accommodated in different applications. Thus, even if one resorts to an option (vikalpa), since there is no absolute contradiction and since the cognitions produced by the directly perceived Vedic text and the inferred Vedic text are equally strong due to the lack of distinction in their being Vedic, the authority of both is established.
Therefore, even regarding the subject matter as it has been presented, the authority of Smṛti must be acknowledged. This concludes the third quarter of the first chapter.

Now, even if one searches with effort, there is no settled distinction based on different objects, nor is there a combination (samuccaya) because there is no contradiction with other objects of knowledge (prameya), nor is there an acceptance of both by way of option (vikalpa). Rather, because both are undermined, there is indeed absolute contradiction. Since there is a great difference in strength between direct perception (pratyakṣa) and inference (anumāna)—just as between worldly perception and inference—and since there is no other recourse when it is impossible to accept both, the authority of the Smṛti will have to be disregarded in favor of the superior strength of Śruti.

For those Smṛtis that are free from the suspicion of deception, error, and the like, and whose status as being rooted in the Veda is established without obstruction, can be established as having genuine authority as constituent parts of the practice of Dharma.

However, when their lack of authority is postulated on account of any reason—such as the perception of a cause for contradiction with the Veda, or mutual inconsistency among them—then they cannot be so established.

At that time, among the Vedas—which are divided into many branches and all their various sections—and which consist of diverse means of knowledge such as direct instruction (upadeśa) through the doors of direct Vedic statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), and so forth, as well as extension (atideśa) through names and the like—who could know which Smṛti, being contradicted by some portion of the Veda, would ever be inferred [to be authoritative]?
Consequently, no one would have confidence at all; and due to this lack of confidence, the authority [of Smṛti] would be utterly destroyed.
For instance:

When a single basis [for a Smṛti] is established, the rejection of any other basis is possible for the purpose of removing its lack of authority; however, this cannot be done by ignoring it. Therefore, for a Smṛti that contradicts Śruti, there must be another basis.
Therefore, let it be understood that just as there is validity for those [texts] being recited even when there is a contradiction,
so it is exactly the same for those that are recited and those that are remembered; and furthermore, any other source has already been refuted in general terms previously.

Furthermore, it is subsequently animated by that [scripture]; thus, there is no over-extension [of the principle of sublation] to cases where it does not exist. Moreover, this position regarding sublation—which relies on the possibility or impossibility of [the Smṛtis] being rooted in error and so forth—is untenable with respect to the Smṛtis.

Those who remember [the Smṛtis] know their contradictory nature; since they remember them while abandoning the authority rooted in the Veda, what other cause could there be for this than passion, hatred, pride, madness, negligence, laziness, and greed?
Where could the reasons for the non-authoritativeness of Smṛti not be set forth? Or what religious act (dharmakriyā) is there in which a perceived reason is not applicable?
Furthermore, how could there be contradiction with the Śrutis?
They consider even Vedic rituals to have only visible purposes,
and they invent contradictions based on even the slightest pretext;
indeed, those who cannot find any scope whatsoever are like monkeys.
Piśācas do not attack them so long as they remain within their own domain;
therefore, the Mīmāṃsakas, who abide in the Lokāyata position and are characterized by the destruction of the Dharma,
should not fulfill their desires in this manner.
That [Vedic injunction] must be accepted exactly as it is and should not be relaxed in the interim;
for one who relaxes it would suffer, like a poorly hitched cart.
And if the Veda were to have a perceptible purpose, or if it were contradicted by what is being perceived, [it would not be authoritative].

Therefore, one should not perform such [acts], and one should abandon the Smṛti rules based upon them, such as the giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the *tānūnaptra* rite and others;
for all these are held to serve a visible purpose for the priests and the sacrificer.
In that case, how could a non-Vedic matter with a perceptible purpose ever be established by the intellect?

Therefore, the fact that the Smṛtis have their root in the Veda was established from the very beginning; thus, [the authority of those Smṛtis] which are not contradicted by the Veda and possess perceptible purposes is established through reasoning.
The authority of the Smṛtis must not be impaired even in the slightest;
for in case of contradiction, their authority—though rooted in the Smṛtis—would become unreliable.
Indeed, it is only when there is no contradiction with the Veda that its source is inferred to be the Veda itself.
First of all, the independent validity of memory is not accepted;

furthermore, the inference that the Veda is its source is contradicted by direct perception. Indeed, while the [Vedic] text is being heard through direct perception, there can be no inferential knowledge [of it].
For even when an elephant has been seen,
inferential objects do not continue to manifest before one by means of its footprint as long as their foundation is not cut away by the direct perception of the scripture.
For it is not possible for memories to possess direct validity,
since they cannot have another source, and that source is not found;
for whatever object of knowledge is to be determined by some means of cognition [must be apprehended directly].
Its nature as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) would consist in its delimitation of that [object];

yet even if it has reached a distant point, it has not attained even a single step. When the other [means of cognition] has already proceeded, it is defeated by that very one alone, for that by which validity was never previously obtained cannot [now] prevail.
Therefore, the Lord ordains that such a person shall always obtain it;
however, for one whose root is cut away as soon as it arises,
or whose mouth is blocked, there is never any self-luminosity.
Nor is the self always established merely by the absence of sublation;
for even when there is contradiction, it must be established because of the prior perception of a general rule, since a general rule is sometimes set aside by an exception.
Therefore, it is also not accepted that this [inference] is sublated everywhere;
for if one were to seek worldly activity based on what is seen through generalization (*sāmānyadṛṣṭa*),
even the waters of a mirage would suffice for him to sever his thirst.
Or, having seen a mirage that has been sublated, even if it appears before one's eyes,
one would not perform bathing or other such acts out of fear of deception;
likewise, inference arises as a means of valid cognition regarding those objects.
As long as an object is not obstructed by [a cognition] born of direct perception,
there would be no partial mutilation for those who establish validity in some cases and invalidity in others according to reason.
Therefore, one should not say either that all [cognitions] are valid,
or that none of them is so if it is independent; for why is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) not accepted as being [valid] along with the Vedic scriptures?

Since conceptual construction possesses eight defects, it cannot for that reason be accepted [as a means of valid cognition]. Furthermore, if subsequent [cognition] were invalid, memories would be utterly refuted; for as long as memory does not ascend to the status of a means of valid cognition, it remains unestablished.
First of all, it is utterly sublated by the Śruti, which is independent of anything else;

for [the Smṛti], being dependent on another source of knowledge, does not stand as an authority in its own right. And once it has been sublated by that [Śruti], it is no longer capable of being revived.
That which is recognized as being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is itself extraordinary;

first, there would be this one fault due to the contradiction with what is commonly recognized, and that too would be another fault due to the contradiction with the actual object of the means of valid cognition.
Even having previously accepted those two faults for some reason, one fault indeed arises now for him who denies them; namely,
that which was refuted before as being of a firm form through direct perception.
These same [faults] would also follow if a second [alternative] were postulated; thus,
although this listener proceeds even with respect to the two statements regarding *vrīhi* and *yava*, he is nevertheless constrained by the *vrīhi* injunction.
Like the two ears of a horse's face, the third quarter (pāda) of the first chapter [is situated] equally on both sides;
for both would result in being non-authoritative due to mutual contradiction.
In that case, the assumption of invalidity for what is fit to be valid,
or the inability to determine the validity of one [of two cognitions], does not imply the invalidity of both merely because of that single instance of invalidity.
And this destruction of both [the rice and the barley] occurs because the purpose of neither is accepted;
or rather, because no rule is seen for mixing them for the sacrificer, for it is understood that the rice alone, independent [of anything else], is the means of accomplishing the sacrifice.
Furthermore, a mixture of those two—barley and rice—is not possible;
it would neither be desired as rice nor as barley according to the scriptural injunctions.
If one were to sacrifice with a mixture, there would be a subversion of both.
It is utterly unreasonable for both to lack a fixed status;
for a lack of fixed status is not tenable when a fixed status can be established.
Therefore, that which possesses the nature of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) must always remain a means of valid cognition.
But as for that [cognition] which is itself non-authoritative, let it be called non-authoritative;
for in that case, no fixed characteristic exists that would establish authoritativeness in one instance and non-authoritativeness in another.
Furthermore, there are two clear grounds for the distinction between Śruti and Smṛti,
by which the authority of Śruti is established while the lack of authority of Smṛti is demonstrated:
that which has attained its own inherent status may, through some other cause, undergo a reversal of that status.
It is understood that the Vedic (śrauta) [text] sublates the Smṛti because of its superior strength;
this has already been established regarding both perception and inference.
As long as it is cognized by the Smṛti, so long is it validated by the Śruti.
A single entity does not admit of contradictory properties;

and having remembered and reflected upon an object, just as one would proceed to infer it based on the scripture concerning that object, by that time the object has already passed away through other [means of cognition].
If the Śruti and the Smṛti were to measure their object simultaneously,
then, because they would have grasped the same specific [object], they would be of equal force. (From the third quarter of the first chapter.)

Therefore, even though there is a distance in terms of the object, there would indeed be equality in terms of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) between Śruti and Smṛti; for the meaning of Smṛti arises from its being embraced by Śruti through an established [connection]. Consequently, the unstable [Smṛti] should be sublated by the [Śruti].
Indeed, a [contrary] Smṛti that is independent of its source is discarded simply because it is a Smṛti;
however, one that depends upon such a source is sublated by Śruti, being devoid of a [valid] basis, and thus falls into the category of an option (vikalpa) according to the second mode.
Although wisdom (prajñā) completely sublates a conflict belonging to the side of [Smṛti],
the authority of that [Smṛti] is nevertheless caused by its being rooted in Śruti;
therefore, at that time, it is determined to be without such a root.
If, setting aside the Veda, some other source for the Smṛti is postulated,
then its status as a valid means of knowledge is completely undermined by that very act;
it is not possible for the authority of the Smṛti to be revived again.
Because its root in the revealed scripture (śruti) has been severed and it is swallowed up by causes such as delusion,
that [Smṛti] would always be refuted by the path you have described; however,
there is no possibility for this [refutation] in the case of a Smṛti that was previously accepted.
Even if heard later, the scriptural statement would not be an obstacle;
