for a horse, having overtaken a donkey, does not take away what the donkey has already carried.
Thus, in the first section, by means of which the teaching regarding rice (*vrīhi*) is understood.
In the second [case], the scriptural injunction is not weak with respect to each of those;
for the authors of the ritual manuals (kalpakāras) bind together the injunctions found in other branches, even those prescribed in their own branch, as all being optional alternatives.
What wise person would dogmatically assert that what was previously attained possesses validity while that which follows lacks it?
For [otherwise] every sacred scripture (*śruti*) would be tainted by impurity, or else everything would be rooted in delusion.
In this way, memory may be defined, yet there would be no confusion regarding its source;
consequently, reflecting that "this [subsequent] cognition is false because of the prior cognition," one determines that memory is indeed non-authoritative.
Because they have the same object, there is also a sublation of the earlier ones;
for if those were not false, the present one could not be false.
This is not so.
This is because each individual performance requires a fresh consideration of the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For if one were to carry out subsequent performances based solely on the consideration made during the first performance, then a person who, disregarding the scriptural injunction regarding rice (*vrīhi*), had adopted barley (*yava*), would have to sacrifice with those barleys alone for as long as he lived; thus, the practical application of the ritual by means of both options, which are held to be optional for each individual, would never be established.

Therefore, by the force of the observation of the means of knowledge that arises during the preliminary application (*prayoga*), even if one does not hear any Vedic text previously inferred, one again relies upon the Smṛti itself and infers a Vedic text solely on the basis of the commonality of the author. Then, with the mind captivated by the directly perceived Vedic text, and by means of its authority—which cannot otherwise be accounted for—one postulates the lack of authority of the Smṛti; thus, one arrives at a reversal of the very source as previously determined, rather than merely superimposing a lack of authority upon what was previously established as valid. This is because, by the very fact of being currently experienced, this [Vedic text] is easily known.
And as for this objection regarding non-finality (*anavasthāna*) that you raise against me, it applies equally to you; therefore, from one perspective, it is not a valid objection.
Furthermore, even at another time, that sublation which is apprehended with clarity—
That lack of authority which was established by that [reasoning] is not thereby set aside.
But surely, in that case, even the *yava* (barley) scriptural passage, when accepted as authoritative, would suffer sublation by other persons;
thus, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its falsity.
However, since memory can never exist for as many persons as it would first become the object of perception for, it cannot escape invalidity; thus,
falsity might be superimposed upon the luminous Śruti.

If that [Smṛti] has already been established as being based on the Veda through memory, for what purpose is it postulated [again]? Indeed, how could the certainty that a Smṛti contradicted by Śruti is rooted in Śruti be obtained even through inference? It would be obstructed by someone [who points out the contradiction].

Consequently, there is an avoidance of the contingency of such a slaughter. For example, although the total wrapping of the Audumbarī post is established by a direct Vedic text (śruti) that is consistent with its meaning— despite being recorded in a manner distinct from the Smṛtis of those who study the branches of Dharma— it is nevertheless cited as if it were a Smṛti, both because of the intention to express its extreme internal connection [with the Veda] as will be explained later, and because there is no difference in its being taught in a harsh (authoritative) manner.

Although the statement regarding the food of one whose king has been purchased exists in the Atharvaveda, nevertheless—because it lacks connection with the sacrificial acts related to the *āhavanīya* fire, and because it would contradict the prohibition against eating until the completion of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice as prescribed by the three Vedas (*trayī*) to which one is entitled—it would be contradictory in the specific context of the *iṣṭi*. According to this principle, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) cites the Smṛti rule concerning the non-disposal of the sacrificial animal, intending to show the distinction between the relative strength and weakness of those who are entitled [to the Vedic rites] and those who are not.

Although the state of having black hair is ambiguous as to its specific temporal occurrence because it depends on an unstable stage of life and its presence is doubtful in the case of one who has already fathered a son, nevertheless—given that the Smṛti texts such as "one should seek Dharma while still young" indicate its intended meaning by referring to the stage of youth, or at least by relying on not exceeding the [proper] age—the contradiction is clearly perceived. This is because the period of forty-eight years of studentship, together with the time prior to initiation, necessarily results in an unavoidable lapse of age amounting to fifty-two or fifty-four years, thereby inevitably exceeding the prescribed age limit.
But surely there is no contradiction, since touching is possible only for that which has been covered after the prior act of covering all around has been performed?
How can there be no contradiction when "touching" (sparśana) is defined as the perception of the object of touch through the medium of the sense of touch (tvag-indriya),
and the touch of the *udumbara* post is not perceived when it is separated by a cloth?
And when a garment is touched, the *audumbarī* tree is not touched,
because there is an absolute difference between the touch of a garment and the touch of an individual instance (*vyakti*) of the *audumbara* species.

[Objection: Is it not the case that there is a disparity between the two examples? For on the ground, there is an absence of the cognition of an udumbara fruit, whereas when [the fruit] is separated by a cloth, that cognition is observed to persist.
[Reply: True; however, in that case, bathing is indeed intended, as it is caused by the contact with that [fruit].
And that cause is considered to be like the touch of a *caṇḍāla*.
But how is it determined that this defect—arising from touching something touched by a *caṇḍāla*—occurs even though it is not recorded in the treatises on Dharma?
Or why is such a defect not admitted in the case of wood, clods of earth, grass, and so forth?
Logical arguments do not apply here regarding those things touched by what was touched, just as the purification of wood and the like occurs through wind alone;
it is not remembered that the purification of cloth occurs in this same way through washing with water and so forth.
For they recite thus regarding impurity:
"Since there is indeed impurity in a garment touched by a Caṇḍāla,
therefore there must be purification by water and so forth."

Now, since the prescription of penance caused by the touch of a *caṇḍāla* is enjoined specifically for a human being, it is understood that impurity consists in uncleanness (*amedhyatva*) belonging to the person, not to other substances such as cows or horses.

Therefore, when there is a doubt as to whether a garment is as unblemished as a cow or a horse, or whether it is as blemished as a human being, it is more appropriate to determine it as being equal to a cow or a horse; for [otherwise] bathing with one's clothes on would have been prescribed for the human being.
Therefore, the person is not considered to be like cattle, horses, and so forth;
by the very path previously described, one should abandon all extremist assertions which necessarily fall into conceptual construction, and instead restrict oneself to memory alone.
It is not possible to imagine that the sacred scripture (*śruti*) is the result of a careless recitation;
for memory (*smṛti*) arises from faulty hearing, dreams, or cognition, whereas the two [scripture and memory] are mutually contradictory, like a contradiction and its non-deviation.
Where two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) appear to conflict, a definitive conclusion is reached through another [means], because a means of valid cognition reaches its source, the Śruti.

Therefore, Smṛti is called a "means of valid cognition" because it is derived from [the root] √mā in the sense of measuring. Furthermore, the elision of the letter *ya* will not fail to occur simply on the grounds that [the word *pramāṇa*] depends upon a vowel.
For the elision of *y* by the rule *vyor vali* depends upon suffixes such as *van*; once that *y*-elision has been performed, there remains a pure vowel *a*.
From that which ends in this [vowel], the feminine suffix *ṣṭrī* is subsequently applied.
Thus it has been stated that this results in a circular dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Alternatively, the authority of the Smṛti is desired because the Śruti lacks authoritative status;
yet, from the established authority of that [Smṛti], the lack of authority of the Śruti is inferred.
Thus, for the proponent of conceptual construction (*vikalpavādin*), this mutual dependence— wherein the basis of perception is established and that of memory is to be postulated—
is avoided; for since the Veda possesses intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), its basis would be already established.
Since the authority of Smṛti consists in its being an indicator of Śruti, it must be assumed that its basis is the Śruti;
nor can there be a lack of authority for the Śruti even when it is being superimposed [upon the Smṛti].
Furthermore, as long as that Śruti is not established, the authority of the Smṛti cannot possibly exist.

Thus, one who merely assumes the authority of Smṛti is defeated at the very outset. However, when the mutual dependence regarding the authority of Śruti is considered, even there, because the determination of its unassailable authority depends upon the prior non-authority of the Smṛti which serves as its counter-position, it remains dependent on that previously established non-authority of the Smṛti.

Therefore, since the lack of authority seen in the memory at the very first moment—while it has not yet been inferred—is sufficient for the Veda to attain the status of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and thus remain forever possessed of unimpeachable authority, the determination [of its validity] is established by another means; having made that the single limit, it is firmly established in the first moment.
It should proceed in sequence until another [subsequent] cognition clearly arises.
Furthermore, because a cause is observed,
there is no validity [of perception] here, since the root cause perishes in an instant;
for if there were deviation, there would be no arising of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or inference (*anumāna*).
Whether it be doubt, or both [doubt and certainty], or the conceptualization of logical reasoning,
it cannot be rejected as a cause for intuitive insight (*pratibhā*), just as its being rooted in the Veda cannot be established due to the lack of exclusivity (*anekānta*).

Because of that, it is stated here with the intention [of showing] that there may also be another root source, or that it may be a separate legal case (*adhikaraṇa*); however, since the sublation is already established by the first reason— the powerful contradiction with scripture— there is no great purpose in the reason for the cumulative conjunction (*anvācaya*).

In another section (*adhikaraṇa*), it is demonstrated that the previously mentioned reason is sufficient by itself to sublate a single recollection (*smṛti*) without depending on other factors; thus, it is shown as being independent. Furthermore, when a recollection pervaded by contradiction is rendered invalid, there arises no further exception (*apavāda*). Regarding the rule "the Adhvaryu takes the cloth used at the *visarjana-homa*," this refers to the cloth covering the sacrificer connected to the time of the *visarjana-homa* for the purpose of carrying forward the *Agnīṣoma*; the Adhvaryu takes that cloth which has been set aside. This is inferred from the context of the first chapter, third quarter (*pāda*).
Recollection (*smaraṇa*):

In this way, they establish through a Smṛti—inferred solely from the practice of performing the gift of the "Yūpahastin" (the one with the sacrificial post in hand)—that the cloth used for wrapping the sacrificial post (*yūpaparivyāṇaśāṭaka*) is to be taken by the Adhvaryu priest, having designated it by the term "Yūpacasti."

For the officiating priests (ṛtvij), knowing that the sacrificer has fallen into the midst of the performance and is bound by the necessity of completing the rite once begun, and knowing his freedom of will regarding the time after completion, rise up of their own accord at the very moment when he is occupied with his duties—just like hired laborers—and having set aside the distinction of their own primary status, they beg for various things to be received, preceded by explanatory passages (arthavāda) intended to inspire faith.

Furthermore, a sacrificer, deluded by the illustration of other gifts prescribed in direct Vedic revelation (*pratyaśruti*), might—out of faith—accept [the Smṛti] as such and bestow gifts upon those [recipients]; thus, there might be the suspicion that this Smṛti was promulgated by them [the reciters]. In such a case, its basis in the Veda is not inferred.
As before, the conclusion is reached that the assumption of it being preceded by greed is more appropriate; thus, through this determination, doubt is removed.
And this point, which has been demonstrated by the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), should be understood as having already been shown in the previous case as well, since the cause is the same.
This much must be stated regarding both of these sections:

indeed, those Vedic sentences which are scattered across different recensions (*śākhā*) and are directly perceived by other persons, but which have not been recited in the sequence of the performance of human duties, are—out of fear of destroying the traditional transmission of the Veda—not presented in their original form; rather, they are made into a single whole and composed by means of that very [work], which serves as a substitute for specific sounds, being manifested through it even though they remain indirect (*parokṣa*), by way of a connection to the meaning.

In this regard, just as students comprehend a statement— whether it has been uttered or not— as "this is taught thus" based on the authority of a trustworthy person, so too the words of the author of the Sūtras, which stand in the place of the words of a teacher,

cease their function after merely presenting the Vedic sentences in their own form; therefore, they are not to be disparaged as being of human origin like the impelling of sounds from the palate and other organs, for at the time when they are not being uttered, they exist solely through mental impressions (saṃskāras).
Or else, this Veda persists among the students through recollections produced by that [Veda]; and if the state of being a Smṛti were a single entity, then the whole would be non-Vedic.
Consequently, one [Smṛti] would be excluded, while the others would merely become auxiliary to worldly transaction.
Then, when some single sentence falling within that [collection] is heard to have originated from another source, our tongue does not proceed to speak it;
at that time, O you who pride yourself on being a Naiyāyika, what would the expression on your face be?
In this way, an inevitable instability regarding what is sublated and what is not sublated arises;
therefore, because it lacks a foundational basis, that [example] is not a valid illustration for the third quarter of the first chapter.
Indeed, it is only logical that there be an option, since the measurements are equal;
for if the udumbara post were wrapped from the upper part, leaving two or three finger-breadths in the middle, what indeed would not have been accomplished?
Even the word "pari" (around), which might otherwise denote encircling on all sides,
becomes meaningful there only when it signifies being excluded from the immediate vicinity,
just as the lower and upper garments of women [are distinguished by their position].
One should not remember [the rule] regarding silk garments as being without qualities,
nor is there any visible reason for the statement concerning the encircling with *kuśa* grass;
even if it were a restrictive injunction (*niyama*), such a thing is not observed in the case of one whose garment has its fringe pointing upwards.
If it is argued that the Atharva Veda is not mentioned here because it is not useful for sacrifices,
by what means is its status as a valid authority for other matters (arthāntara) refuted?
Furthermore, this [Atharva] is not a rule concerning sacrificial accessories (yajñāṅga), just like the branches dealing with pacification (śānti) and so forth.
The validity of this [text] is also precluded by its human purpose, since the eating of food seen at a sacrifice is prohibited by other sentences;
subsequently, however, two specific limits for permission regarding that very act are heard.
Furthermore, even the period of impurity (āśauca) depends upon considerations such as the impairment of dharma;
indeed, therefore, equality [of status] is not at all appropriate for that [impurity] either, whether it be one night or three nights for both the king and the Brāhmaṇa.
How could impurity continue for ten nights? Furthermore,
this would be so because whatever time is previously determined for that specific *homa*, it remains exactly as it was before the rising of the sun.
And the statement regarding the *uditahoma* (the sacrifice after sunrise) is not purposeless merely because of the mention of the *anudita-homa* (the sacrifice before sunrise).
This concludes the third quarter of the first chapter;
there is no excess whatsoever here concerning [the rules for] *keśava*, *vaya*, *vyaya*, and so forth.
Moreover, no one accepts that fortnit [of the month] as being primarily characterized by hair;
if that were not admitted, his statement would be meaningless.
Furthermore, [the rules apply] respectively to those whose teeth have grown, to those whose teeth have grown out [after falling], and to those who have not yet had their tonsure ceremony performed.
The cremation rite is the single occasion for the increase of the period of impurity;
or rather, when some cause for impurity arises during the interval,
the purification that occurs there by means of the remainder shall be this "remaining" [period].
The period of impurity beginning from ten days and so forth is set in motion and remains unremoved; it pervades any intervening impurity according to its own duration,
for the purification by the lapse of time is understood from scripture, as it is not perceived otherwise.
But surely, in this way, there is a restriction regarding the object of eating;
even in this case, if that [object] is impossible or if it is offered elsewhere, they give it away—
so says the Tantravārtika.
When the purchase of Soma has been made, food provided by those appointed for that purpose may be eaten;
thus, another kind of invalidity has been stated.
For Viśvāmitra, being distressed in times of calamity, ate the haunch of a dog.
One [act] is performed even without permission because there is no other way to proceed;
however, another is performed with permission, and there is a great difference between the two.
Thus it has also been stated by Manu regarding one who has fallen into calamity:
At the end of the remaining sins therein, purification will occur;
first, however, there must be that which consists of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Then, for one purified by that, there will be another [means] for the sake of the fruit.

It has been deliberated that the Lord [declares] that he who follows a secondary rule (anukalpa) instead of the primary rule (prathamakalpa) does not obtain its fruit, both in this world and in the next;
or rather, it is due to a discrepancy in time between the true and the deficient [rules].
The absence of contradiction is determined by establishing the distinction between different meanings;
for example, abstaining from food at a funeral feast (*aśrāddha-bhojitva*) or the eating of meat (*māṃsa-bhakṣaṇa*),
which are prescribed as righteous (*dharmya*) for the sake of spiritual welfare (*śreyas*), are not prohibited in all circumstances.
In that regard, it is understood that the rule against eating the food of those lacking faith is for the sake of attaining heaven (*svarga*).

Likewise, since the consumption of meat, sexual intercourse, and similar acts are prohibited on the sixth, eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth lunar days, a rule is established for the householder to refrain from them, as he would otherwise be subject to acting according to his own will. As it has been said:

"Indeed, because two distinct sentences are observed there, a separation of connection (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*) is appropriate; but here, since there is only one sentence prohibiting the eating of the food of the initiated (*dīkṣita*), how can it prohibit [eating] prior to the purchase [of the Soma], and yet enjoin [abstinence] for the subsequent period until the completion of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice for the sake of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*)?"
These two sentences might indeed be conceived as having two limits:
the first negation established here [in the context of] "when the king has been purchased" (krītarājaka) is the prior limit;
however, a further limit for that [negation] is not possible because of its unity.

Because we observe the permission to eat the second [portion] of food, it is understood that when the offering has already been permitted by the act of choosing (*varaṇa*), what further need is there for permission?
Furthermore, a prohibition followed by a permission is seen as a mere option; therefore, the permission regarding what was excluded is accepted as being established by a specific rule (*vyavasthā*).
Because it would entail [the pursuit of] an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha), this is not accepted as an injunction (vidhi).
Thus, due to the diversity of their objects, there is no contradiction and no sublation.
Having studied the Vedas, or both Vedas, or even one Veda, respectively—

This is stated with the qualification that [the person] possesses the capacity, the stage of life, and the fitness; for in that regard, it can be said: "For those men who are blind, lame, or otherwise disabled, and who are unable to perform the duties of a householder, this rule is intended."
Therefore, one who is still a student (*upakurvāṇaka*) should spend a long time [in study];
having attained an abundance of knowledge, with his impurities destroyed by purifying acts,
Dvaipāyana and others have declared:

Furthermore, those fruits which arise from the *brahmayajña*—consisting of the daily application of the *ṛk*, *sāman*, *yajus*, *brāhmaṇas*, *kalpas*, and commentaries—which, because they would otherwise result in meaninglessness for persons qualified for ritual sacrifices (*kratvadhikṛta*), are excluded from them and instead pertain to the domain of celibate students (*brahmacārin*) and wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) who are qualified only for recitation and meditation; these too will become most abundant through the abundance of one's knowledge of the Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vijñāna*). Thus, there is the instruction regarding *brahmacarya* for each Veda.

Or, if someone, by virtue of his intelligence, having quickly studied even the four Vedas, does not abandon his application toward understanding their meaning at the appropriate time, and becomes a householder after completing his studies according to this sequence—that person is covered by the very same Smṛti rule of twelve or forty-eight years as previously established; thus, these two cases should not be cited as being excessively contrary to Śruti.
Therefore, no excessive contradiction between Śruti and Smṛti is observed;
for such a contradiction is seen only between two Śruti texts, and it is not found anywhere in the case of Smṛti.
This very point is thoroughly established by Jaimini, the teacher of what is most beneficial, for those desiring to know:
as long as one ritual action is perceived in the Śruti and another in the Smṛti,
when there is a conflict between the two, the performance of the Śruti injunction is desired.
Even if memory were indeed of equal status to the existent [scriptural tradition],
there would still be no fault for those who act according to the meaning of the revealed scripture (śruti); for as long as it remains merely a report, it will not be accepted at all.
But when [a teaching] has reached the stage of being heard, it does not differ from this [Vedic tradition].

For instance, there are those systems embraced by those outside the three Vedas (*trayī*), which fall under the shadow of a semblance of dharma mixed with something else, which are intent on the purposes of worldly association, gain, honor, and fame, which are composed based primarily on reasoning such as perception, inference, analogy, and presumption regarding visible beauty and so forth that are contrary to and unconnected with the three Vedas—namely, the systems of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, Pāśupata, Śākya, and Nirgrantha, which are treatises on dharma and adharma embraced by these [sects]. This is the third quarter of the first chapter.

By means of the demonstration of occasional success based on a few mantras and medicinal herbs capable of subjugation (*avaśīkaraṇa*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), and bewilderment (*unmādana*), it is established that those teachings which consist primarily of livelihoods scented only with the faint fragrance of a few meanings consistent with the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*—such as non-violence, truthful speech, self-restraint, charity, and compassion—and those even more external ones which are rooted in the practice of eating mixed food according to the customs of barbarians (*mleccha*), are not to be respected, because they are shown to contradict the *Śruti* and because reasons [for their rejection] are perceived.

Nor has this been determined in any other legal treatise (*adhikaraṇa*), nor is it something that cannot be stated; for, like the cognition of the expressive power of words such as *gāvī* [for "cow"], it is extremely well-known, or else [it is known] due to beauty, ease, or the influence of the Kali age.
Otherwise, people might fall into the delusion that one should abandon the animal sacrifice prescribed for the *yajña*.
Therefore, even if some contradictory Smṛti were to be found that was previously cited, nevertheless, in this context, only this [Smṛti] is applicable—
namely, that which is accepted by the great multitude of people and followed by one's ancestors and others.
They too, with respect to other continents, say that one should avoid from afar a person who, while professing their own view, acts in contradiction to the next world;
for how could one who deceives himself be beneficial to another?

Therefore, when there is a contradiction with a directly perceived Vedic revelation (śruti), the authority of the texts composed by authors— whether they be reciters (grahotṛ) or performers (ācaritr)— is sublated. Furthermore,
the destruction of another Vedic branch (śākhā) never occurs at any time.
Because these [faults] have been previously stated to be eternal, they do not possess a visible root; furthermore, greed and other such causes are perceived here as being quite different.
When that [eternal cause] is present and observed, there is no experience of any other root.
Nor do they assert that their [teachings] are rooted in the Vedas, as is the case with Gautama and others; rather, reasons are stated for why those dharmas remain far removed [from them].
Furthermore, Manu and others have declared that the very texts of these [heterodox teachers] are to be avoided.

"Whatever Smṛtis are outside the Vedas, and whatever false doctrines there may be—all of them are fruitless after death, for they are declared to have darkness as their ultimate goal. (Tantravārttika).
If it is argued that [the Smṛti] is contradicted when there is no conflict with the learned (śiṣṭa)...

Thus, having first determined the validity or invalidity of the Smṛtis concerning human goals—both in cases of non-contradiction and contradiction—we now consider only the presence or absence of contradiction regarding those Smṛtis concerning ritual purposes, such as the wearing of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), sipping water (*ācamana*), and using the right hand, which fall within the scope of many Vedic texts.
Once that determination is made, the establishment of their validity or invalidity follows from the two preceding sections.

If the *yajñopavīta* (sacred thread) and other such items, being introduced into the sacrifice, are neither embraced by the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) nor the *prayogavacana* (performative injunction), or are rather excluded, then there is a contradiction.

On the other hand, if—due to their compatibility—they enter into the sacrifice through a connection with a text inferred from Smṛti, just like those items mentioned in the context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, and do not subvert anything previously accepted, then they are not contradictory.

However, another view holds that even when a contradiction exists, doubt arises due to a discrepancy between the strength and weakness of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*).
For it is thus:
when there is a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, their relative strength and weakness is already known;
and when there is a conflict between a property (dharma) and its substratum (dharmī), the substrata are more powerful.
Is it logical that there is no contradiction even with a Smṛti that prescribes an auxiliary for the sake of the sacrifice?

For its purposeful action is not contradicted by what is heard in the Śruti, nor is it abandoned by the Smṛti; likewise, it is established by the locative case-ending as well as by the conduct of the learned.

"Just as the factors of the means [of action] are grasped by the unprecedented results (*apūrva*) produced through cultivation, so too [the agent] is not [excluded]; for it is said, 'Because the Vedic branches are of limited extent,' the meaning of the word would otherwise be over-extended."

For who is able to transgress the established limit [of the sacrifice] as delineated by the two sets of six— namely, the six means of knowledge beginning with direct audition (śruti) and the sequence of time?
For if the categories of meaning belonging to Smṛti and worldly usage were to enter [the ritual], they would indeed cause sublation.
The entire duration of the performance—including the forenoon, midday, and so forth—would be transgressed.

Furthermore, the sequence understood through the six criteria of direct statement (*śruti*), meaning (*artha*), textual order (*pāṭha*), position (*sthāna*), primary function (*mukhya*), and procedure (*pravṛtti*)—as established in the *Tantravārtika*—has its locus, authority, and extent determined by its being rooted in Vedic matters; yet, that very sequence would be rendered otherwise by the interruption caused by sipping water (*ācamana*) due to such occasions as spitting (*chuta*).
In this same manner, it should be applied even when there is an interruption caused by the seat, the sacred thread, or the re-performance [of a rite].

No other measure for the sequence of the prescribed dimensions is conceivable; likewise, the dimension of the items established as a cumulative whole, as understood from the Vedic texts and other sources, must necessarily be determined by the Adhvaryu and others for the purpose of performing all the items without expansion.
Consequently, that which was first conceived [as the sequence] later—

Furthermore, in the performance of the ritual acts whose meanings have been understood, because of the failure of the prior determination [of the procedure], there arises an inability to discern what has been fully performed and what remains unperformed. For one who thus harbors doubts regarding defects in the performance, there is an absence of proficiency in the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) caused by the correct knowledge of reality; consequently, due to the weakness of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), the result obtained would necessarily be deficient.

Alternatively, since the extent of the auxiliary branches (*aṅga-śākhā*) consists of the limited injunctions, indications, and extended applications (*atideśa*), there is no room for auxiliary branches beyond those.

Furthermore, when the constituent elements that must be performed together have passed away, the injunction regarding the performance allows for only as much extension of time as occurs due to absolute incapacity, even for one who is hurrying with all his might.
However, if a capable person were to cause a delay of even a single moment, he would not be in accordance with the injunction of the performance.
Therefore, because it does not alter the threefold measure of the Vedic branches (śākhā-parimāṇa), [the practice of] sipping water (ācamana) is not contradictory [to the ritual rules].
It is said:
moreover, since no reason is perceived for why these [acts] are not included,
there is no contradiction with the Vedic injunctions regarding the sacrifice for acts such as sipping water (ācamana).
But where no other cause can be apprehended even through poetic fancy (utprekṣā),
its status as authoritative scripture arises because it has no root other than itself; and when the root is determined to be scripture that has no other root, [the derivative work is established].
Even in the case of contradiction, the authority of Smṛti is not precluded by Śruti;
for, because it occurs first, the strength of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) appears superior to the strength or weakness of the object of knowledge (prameya).
Indeed, it is only after observing the contradiction residing in the objects of knowledge that the cognition of a contradiction between the means of knowledge arises.
Thus, at that very moment when a contradiction is observed between those two objects of cognition (*prameya*), their relative strength or weakness resides in their own essential nature;
and for those things whose greater strength has been determined by virtue of being the primary meaning of a word (*padārtha*).
It is not removed again by the strength of memory,
nor is it based on the relative weakness or strength of the object of cognition;
the status of memory as a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) that has been established is not sublated by that which stands as a [different] means of valid knowledge.
This very point is stated by Bādarāyaṇa from the perspective of Śruti:
"Where Smṛti is useless, even a great Smṛti cannot sublate Śruti; for it is accepted that the application of all sequential rules occurs at the very end [of the procedure]."

Even an object of the smallest possible measure is not apprehended by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) prior to [the perception of] the object itself; the extent of an object is determined by no means of knowledge.

In that regard, if there were no other causes for the recollection of all objects apart from that [measure], then this too would be a single cause, and thus even measurement (*parimāṇa*) would be established.

Even in that state, just as in the third quarter of the first chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*], one does not stop at the measure consisting merely of the [textual] extent, but rather relies on the determination of the measure pertaining to the ritual elements (padārtha) as reached by means of the name (samākhyā); likewise, it will rely on the measure understood as far as the [traditions of] death and custom (mṛtyācāra). Thus, there is no fault.

For this is indeed the time for the primary act together with all its constituent parts; it is precisely such proximity of the parts that is enjoined here. The purity, the sacred thread, and so forth do not constitute independent ritual items.
For everything is for the sake of both the subsidiary and the primary; therefore, it does not constitute an interruption.
When one sips water after having prepared the altar, but before having prepared the altar, it can then be said that "he prepares the altar itself."
With this very point in mind, the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "And such matters do not become obstacles to the meanings of words.
For otherwise, if the status of being for the sake of both the subsidiary and the primary were not accepted, this would indeed be the speech of one with an empty heart.

[Objection: But surely the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) should be cited here as an example, because it is directly enjoined as a subsidiary of the sacrifice in the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites by the text: "He wears it over the left shoulder; he thereby makes it the mark of the gods."

Likewise, in the *Kaṭhaka*, through a rule not connected to a specific context (*anārabhyavāda*), there is heard a connection with performing sacrifices and officiating at sacrifices for all sacrifices, as well as a connection with teaching and studying:

"By means of the extended sacrifice (*prasṛta-yajña*), the gods went to the heavenly world; by means of the non-extended sacrifice, they caused the Asuras to perish. The sacrifice of one who wears the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavītin*) is indeed extended; that of one who does not wear it is non-extended. Whatever a Brāhmaṇa studies while wearing the sacrificial thread, he truly performs a sacrifice thereby. Therefore, one should study, officiate at sacrifices, or perform sacrifices only while wearing the sacrificial thread, for the sake of extending the sacrifice."

Likewise, the rule for sipping water (*ācamana*) is stated: "Having girt the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder, having sat down, having washed both hands, having sipped water three times, having wiped [the mouth] twice, having spread out a large quantity of *darbha* grass, having assumed the lap-posture (*upastha*), and having sat facing east, one should study the Veda. Although this is heard in the context of the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), nevertheless, because it is connected with the utterance of the Vedas, it is understood as a subsidiary part of that; and since all sacrifices are performed with the recitation of mantras, it consequently becomes a subsidiary part of them as well.
And thus, the statement "they do not become defiled by Soma" is determined solely for the purpose of prohibiting the [otherwise] established practice of sipping water (ācamana).

As for the quality of being "right-handed" (dakṣiṇācāra), in a sentence intended to enjoin that the sacrificial ground (devayajana) should slope toward the east and north—such as "just as the right hand is, so is the sacrificial ground"—it is understood as a point of comparison because it shares the status of being an auxiliary to the sacrifice, like the sacrificial ground itself; therefore, there is not even a single instance here that is subject to the suspicion of contradiction or sublation, and thus these are not [valid] examples.
Therefore, this is not a separate section (*adhikaraṇa*).

Rather, the sūtras should be explained solely as sūtras that provide refutations and resolutions to the objections raised against the preceding section. Thus, that which is ordained by the Veda and does not contradict it—such as the construction of sacrificial altars (*vihāra*) and pleasure groves (*ārāma*), detachment, the practice of meditation, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), truthfulness, self-restraint, charity, purity, and so forth—which learned people (*śiṣṭas*) who know the Veda do not find offensive, [is authoritative]. (The Third Pāda of the First Adhyāya).
If it is argued that [the scripture] is established as being non-contradictory by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we say no;
because its extent is limited,
it has as its object the meaning of the previous scriptures in the form of a mere reflection (*pratibimba*).
Whatever else is performed, its lack of authority with respect to Dharma has been authorized by the Veda itself for those very [beings] who are the original creators,
regarding the eternal subjects [of law] during the intervals between Manvantaras and at the beginnings of Yugas.
And likewise, in the supplementary portion (vākyaśeṣa) of the injunction, "The *ṛc* verses of Manu become the *sāmidhenīs*," it is heard:
"Whatever Manu said was indeed medicine, for the sake of its medicinal quality. This statement regarding the instruction on expiations and so forth is the medicine for the disease of sin;
and in every Manvantara, a different Smṛti is thus ordained.
Furthermore, fourteen Manus are eternally established in every Kalpa, and for each sacrifice there are always sixteen other officiating priests (ṛtvij). [As stated in the] Tantravārtika:
"Nor does the Veda possess a beginning [in the sense of being newly created], because it is not bound to the specific deeds of those [Manus]."
Even though the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* are determined to be artificial compositions,
they are nevertheless accepted as being based on that [Veda] which is uncreated;
therefore, those very branches (*śākhās*) do not transgress their foundation in the Veda.
Dharma, which bestows its fruit, is known through those very [means] that remain established;
likewise, for those who act by transgressing the boundaries prescribed in the Vedas,
it is not accepted as a cause of Dharma even when their words are consistent with the truth.
Just as in the case of artificial camphor, gold, and the like,
whatever seed is imparted also clearly dissolves because it cannot be perceived,
once that matter is clearly determined by means of another branch [of the Veda].
In that case, since [the practice] would be established by that very [scripture], the other [scriptural injunction] would be redundant.

As for those who are "cultured" (*śiṣṭas*), they are those whose conduct is virtuous; and virtuous conduct is that which is performed by them. Thus, because the determination [of what is virtuous conduct] is mutually dependent, there is no definitive conclusion.
Indeed, satisfaction arises for some even in regard to an inauspicious action,

just as the Śākya feels satisfaction in the statement of fallacious reasons that reviles the Vedas and Brāhmaṇas; for the twice-born are satisfied with sacrifices involving the slaughter of animals and the like.
For it is from these very sacrifices that the Śākyas cry out when oppressed;
yet other twice-born ones are satisfied even by eating the food of Śūdras,
while a man from the South is satisfied upon obtaining his own maternal uncle’s daughter as a wife.

Even those authors of the Smṛtis, who claim that the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is a source of authority while remaining ignorant of its own root, do not shine; for no Vedic revelation (*śruti*) is seen to be the basis for their legal procedure (*vyavahāra*).
And if it were [otherwise], even that which is beyond the senses would certainly be remembered;

for [the Sūtra states]: "Or rather, when the cause is not perceived, those [acts] employed should be understood [as Dharma]. Thus, those actions which are devoid of perceptible causes but are performed by the virtuous (sādhu)—those too should be understood here as having the nature of Dharma. (Tantravārtika)
Whatever practices have been adopted as dharma by the learned, even if they are not found in the Veda,
their status as dharma is accepted because of the commonality of the agents; likewise,
for all young girls, there are fasts on the fourth lunar day and others.

The scripture, like a lamp, is capable of making known the connection with a fruit that has not yet been attained for those virtuous persons who are being instructed by the learned— just as the *godohana* vessel [is connected to a specific result]— through the joy of giving lamps, foot-stools, food, incense, and milk-rice.

When the status of being an *āpta* (an authoritative person) is understood from the fact that one acts in accordance with the meaning of the scriptures (*śāstra*), and the mention of the scriptures is based on that status of being an *āpta*, there would be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*). For those who have acquired the designation of being *āpta*s through the performance of duties prescribed for each respective Veda, whatever else they perform according to tradition with the thought that it is dharma— since it leads to heaven— that too is indeed of the nature of dharma.
Therefore, just as there is no beginning to the sequence of days and nights, there is no risk of circularity regarding the relationship between the causes and their effects.
Furthermore, since the Smṛti also proceeds solely for the purpose of sanctioning conduct or Vedic statements upon having perceived them, there is no fault.
For even in the Veda, many injunctions are indeed seen that are touched by the scent of perceptible purposes; yet, this does not entail an absence of Vedic foundation.

Whatever worship of gods, Brahmins, and so forth they perform— even that possesses the nature of dharma, for it is considered the conduct of the cultured (śiṣṭa). In this regard, he who follows only the cultured in the form of what ought to be done [is truly wise].
That alone is the true dharma, and not anything else belonging to mere living beings.

Likewise, it is said with the understanding that for those who have cultivated impressions (*saṃskāra*) through long-term study of the Vedas and their meanings, and whose intuitive flashes (*pratibhāna*) follow the path prescribed by the Vedas, no such flash of intuition could possibly arise on a wrong path.
Thus it is stated: "Whatever an *anūcāna* (one who has studied the Vedas) conjectures, that becomes the word of the Ṛṣis."
Because it is produced from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the Veda, that very [satisfaction] becomes the Veda itself;
just as in Rumā, in salt-mines, on Mount Meru, or in a field of *vāñcancaru* plants,
whatever is born there would consist of that very substance, so too should the satisfaction of the self of one who knows the Veda be understood.
For one whose self has been permeated by dharma practiced over many days, satisfaction of the self in the form of performing dharma is not possible anywhere else; thus it is authorized as dharma,
just as in the case of that which arises from the propitiation of a deity through the granting of a boon.
Whatever you shall say, "This mantra of yours is a poison-destroyer," once it has been thus consecrated,
people will remember that mantra for the removal of poisons and the like;
or just as, according to the Sarpasiddhānta, the mongoose [remembers] whichever medicinal herb [it finds].

Or, just as a certain land where a meritorious person dwells is accepted as a cause of merit because it is purified by that association; so too, for those who observe transgressions of dharma in the conduct of the learned— such as the historical accounts showing that Prajāpati had sexual intercourse with his own daughter Uṣas, and that Indra was the paramour of Ahalyā Maitreyī— the authority of the conduct of the learned is difficult to establish.

To this it is replied: we shall demonstrate how there is no contradiction. For that conduct which is performed with the intention of merit (puṇya) attains the status of being a mirror of Dharma; however, that which is perceived as being caused by desire, anger, greed, delusion, grief, and so forth, will proceed according to the injunctions and prohibitions [of the scriptures].

Therefore, by the maxim that "even for one who has ascended the forest of austerity, whatever conduct is preceded by passion and hatred is all wholesome for one who is bound," it follows that even for one who has performed great austerities and brings them to exhaustion, or who later remedies them through purificatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) to achieve purification from sin, [the transgression] may be digested.
However, for those of weak austerity, such acts would lead only to self-destruction, like an elephant's consumption of large pieces of wood from a banyan tree.

Even for Dvaipāyana, by the command of his preceptor, the birth of a son from his brother’s wife—though he was without a husband—was not excessively difficult, for according to the scriptures, a woman in her season may approach her brother-in-law when urged by her preceptor; furthermore, such an act involving a maternal relative, the wife of a brother, or the procreation of a son, is not too hard to accomplish through the power of asceticism performed either previously or subsequently.
Anyone else who possesses such power of asceticism and could carry it out would certainly do so.
As for Rāma and Bhīma, however, it was due to the influence of affection and filial devotion.

The accomplishment of the sacrifice occurs only when there is a direct connection between the father and the son, provided that the object of the act is merely the existing dharma and the purpose is the removal of the father's debt; likewise, the making of Sītā out of gold was for the sake of livelihood, intended to dispel the suspicion of a lack of compassion toward Sītā who had been abandoned due to fear of public scandal.

Thus, by the principle of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), it is understood— even though not explicitly stated— that Dhṛtarāṣṭra also had a connection with his wife solely for the purpose of sacrifice, having thereby discharged his debt to his father through Vicitravīrya’s son born of that wife;
furthermore, by the grace of Vyāsa, he indeed beheld his sons during the time of the *Aśvamedha* sacrifice, even though their time [of birth] had passed.
Great seers are known to be capable of both cursing and bestowing grace.

Just as it is well understood that he became blind by virtue of their word, so too, from the statement regarding the performance of sacrifice, it is easily known through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) that he saw [the sun] during that period.
Alternatively, since the root *yaj*—in the sense of "worship of the gods," "forming a connection," and "giving"—can here have the meaning of "giving" alone, this will be the case.

Furthermore, it is heard that acts such as giving gifts and performing austerities are equal to the fruits of sacrifices; therefore, there is a figurative application of the term "sacrifice" to those acts.
And as for the contradiction regarding the single wife of the sons of Pāṇḍu, that too was explained and established by Dvaipāyana himself.
And for this very reason it was said:
"And regarding that, the brahmin-seer, who transcended the human condition, spoke of this supreme and wondrous form:
'O lady of great majesty, why did she not remain a maiden even as day after day passed?'"
Alternatively, this will not pertain to Arjuna alone; rather,
it is shown as a common renown in order to demonstrate its flawlessness.

Likewise, regarding the expiation for lying—which was a constituent part of the slaughter of Droṇa—it is held by some that this applies even to an intentional act; thus, the Aśvamedha sacrifice was indeed performed at the end as an expiation, and therefore its status as a practice of the virtuous (sadācāra) cannot be accepted.

As for the instance cited where the drinking of liquor and the marriage to one's maternal uncle’s daughter by Vāsudeva and Arjuna were presented as being contrary to the Smṛtis: therein, the prohibition of liquor restricted to the three higher castes (traivarṇika) refers only to *surā* as a derivative of grain (*annavikāra*);

however, there is no prohibition whatsoever against *madhu* (honey-liquor) and *sīdhu* (molasses-liquor) for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, because the statement "Liquor is [forbidden] eternally for the Brāhmaṇa" has as its sole scope the Brāhmaṇa.

This [objection] is also refuted because the term *brahmavādin* is based on the grounds of habitually performing that [action], possessing that disposition, or being skilled in it; and because, by resorting to the rule of verbal derivation (*pravr̥tti-nimitta*), the roots *brū* (to speak) and *vad* (to speak) have the same meaning. Furthermore, due to the restrictive rule "A Brāhmaṇa, however, should proclaim these," only he whose [duty] is proclamation becomes habitually so, possesses that quality, or is skilled in it. Therefore, only Brāhmaṇas are *brahmavādins*. And thus, it has been stated in the deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) which serves as a limb for the general prohibition of liquor: [The text continues with the cited verse: "Even if one were to pour out the ocean, or were to eat the entire earth, one would not reach the end of the sin of drinking liquor. Thus, the prohibition of liquor is established through this deprecatory passage. Therefore, the conclusion is that liquor is prohibited for all castes. As for the statement regarding the *Śūdra*, that refers to a specific occasion (*naimittika*). For example, when a *Śūdra* is about to die, his funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*) must be performed; at that time, the *Śūdra* may drink liquor. This is because the *Śūdra* is permitted to drink liquor in such circumstances, whereas for others, it is prohibited except in cases of extreme distress (*āpad-dharma*). Therefore, this is what is meant: just as even a single instance of liquor made from grain is undrinkable for all three [classes], so too is every [kind of liquor] undrinkable by those who discourse on Brahman (*brahmavādin*).
Otherwise, both the words "just as a single [instance]" and "by those who discourse on Brahman" would be entirely redundant;
for the connection with the three castes is already obtained through the specification in the subsequent verse.

Therefore, it is not contradictory that both are honey-liquors (*madhv-āsava*). Likewise, there is a scriptural passage showing another meaning, which is a statement of permission: "That which was the flower-garland (*mālya*) was later transformed into wine (*surā*); from that [wine] he produced the Kṣatriya. Therefore, the elder brother, the daughter-in-law, and the mother-in-law, having drunk wine, sit lamenting. The flower-garland is indeed evil; therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not drink wine, lest he be united with evil. Now, a Kṣatriya might say to a Brāhmaṇa: 'Wine does not harm one who drinks it knowing this.'"
This [practice] is rendered indifferent by the presence of honey and *sīdhu* [wine].

As for the marriage with the daughter of a maternal uncle (*mātula-duhitṛ*), even though there is an intervention by the relationship of being the sister of one's mother’s brother (*mātṛ-svasrīya*) and so forth, it is not contradictory because of the exclusion of [marrying] a sister or similar [close kin].

Although Subhadrā is described as the sister of Vāsudeva, nevertheless, since Baladeva and Vāsudeva—as well as Ekānaṃśā—were declared to be his own [uterine] siblings at birth, it is understood from the authorization of the marriage that Subhadrā was either the sister of his mother’s brother or the daughter of his mother’s father’s sister.
But this is not the *Tantravārttika*, for it has been stated elsewhere:
"Whatever a superior person practices, that very thing other people also do."
"Whatever standard he sets, the world follows that"— based on such statements as these,
Āpastamba has established the status of being defective or non-defective for all [these practices] according to their regional distribution.

Likewise, Manu has also stated: "But those who do not practice a livelihood that was indeed practiced by their fathers and ancestors, yet is not prohibited by other Smṛtis— they either continue to follow it, or, if they avoid it, they are shunned by their kinsmen and others."
Now, it might be argued that Gautama stated in the third quarter of the first chapter that practices contrary to the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) lack authority;
however, even this is not correct, because the word *āmnāya* is also employed in the context of the Smṛti texts.

For in the section concerning the Dharma of the Smṛtis, Śaṅkha and Likhita have stated: "The tradition (āmnāya) is the upholder of the Smṛti. Thus, the tradition consisting of the works composed by the authors of the Smṛtis is said to exist for the purpose of maintaining the Smṛti among those who study the Smṛti texts. Consequently, it is impossible to accept the authority of practices that are prohibited by the statements of Manu and others.
However, the statement of Āpastamba has been refuted by Baudhāyana, who provides examples of corrupt practices that contradict the Smṛti.
Since other clear motives such as lust and so forth are observed, it is not possible for either these contradictory practices or the statement of Āpastamba to have their root in Śruti.
He says:
By whom was the drinking of *surā* prohibited for Brāhmaṇas?
Therefore, it is stated by this [text]: "A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink *surā*."
If one were to kill not even a single individual, then one would have achieved the purpose [of the prohibition];

and if the drinking of liquor were avoided by even one person, it would be as before. For the prohibition applies to the consumption of *vaṣa* and *pāna* as they occur in relation to each individual Brahmin.

Even that which is intended to be expressed cannot be an adverbial qualifier because it is being restated; how much less so when this is understood as a mere restatement of the singularity inherent in the genus? For in the prohibition of killing, the Brāhmaṇa is the object (*karman*) of the act, whereas in the drinking of *surā*, he is taken up as the agent (*kartṛ*), as in the case of one who desires heaven.
There is a disparity between this example and the case of the *udumbara* post, because there is no possibility of intending both the sacrificer’s effort and the equality [of the post] simultaneously.
To explain:

an injunctive statement (*vidhāyaka*) intent upon a prohibition of an injunction—having enjoined the prohibition of killing specifically qualified by the mere caste of "Brāhmaṇa" due to the impossibility of prohibiting killing in general—and having thereby ceased its operation, would have to enjoin either a further mark (*liṅga*) or another prohibition regarding the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. In that case, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) due to the repetition of the suffix (*pratyaya*).
For those for whom injunctions and prohibitions are absolutely distinct meanings of Vedic sentences.

The negative particle (*nañ*), whose power is assisted by its connection with those [other] words, acquires a function exceeding the mere denotation of non-existence; having fulfilled its purpose by negating—after restating—the killing qualified by a Brāhmaṇa (as previously established by the aforementioned logic) which was already prompted by hatred and other motives for the sake of the injunctive meaning (*vidhyartha*), it is unable to negate another injunctive suffix (*liṅga*) that occurs without repetition in the injunctions regarding the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. Thus, even though it is heard, the injunctive suffix is not intended to be negated, as it is of no use for the negation of the injunction.

For in this case, the explicit syntactical meaning (*vacanavyakti*) is as follows: "That one should kill a Brahmin under the influence of anger and so forth, or that a Brahmin should be killed—that is not [to be done]. However, in the view that there is a single injunction (*vidhyekatva*), the construction of the sentence is as follows: "One should not perform the killing of a Brahmin," or "He who is a Brahmin, him one should not kill. Thus, it is either an injunction prohibiting killing qualified by the status of being a Brahmin, or an injunction prohibiting the killing of a Brahmin who is the object specified by the Śūdra [as the agent].

"A Brāhmaṇa shall not drink *surā*; it is not to be drunk by those who expound the Veda"—this [prohibition] must be shown to prohibit only that which possesses the masculine gender (*liṅga*), because in one case (the drinking of *surā*) there is an inclusion as a qualification of a specific factor of the means (*sādhana*) capable of being delimited by a number being taken up as a subordinate element (*guṇa*) conveyed by a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-pratyaya*), which is distinct from the five non-adoptables (*anupādeya*)—namely, cause, place, time, result, and the object of refinement (*saṃskārya*)—and because in the other case (the rule for Vedic teachers) there is the explicit mention of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-vibhakti*). Furthermore, even here, this masculinity is certainly not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*).

Because the Brahmin is the subject of the restatement (anuvādya), just like the prohibition of his killing, everything that is being restated is restated exactly as it has been previously established; in that case,
nothing other than what is required [by the context] is enjoined, apart from the things to be enjoined.

Since the drinking of liquor by a Brāhmaṇa and others arises from passion and delusion, there can be no possibility of an injunction regarding it. Therefore, in this case as well, the statement is expressed either as "that which a Brāhmaṇa might drink, he should not [drink]" or as "the Brāhmaṇa who [exists], he should not drink liquor. Whether by means of a prohibitive injunction through the negation of drinking qualified by liquor, or by the removal of sin (pratyavāya), the Brāhmaṇa is favored; thus, for him, there is no logical possibility of being subject to an injunction, whether it be a prohibition or otherwise. (Tantravārtika)

Furthermore, when it is restated that "the Brāhmaṇa who should drink," that [Brāhmaṇa] is a male; thus, by means of the operation of the injunction (*vidhi*), the non-restriction of gender (*liṅga*) is established. Consequently, it is proven that in both cases, the gender and number are not intended to be restrictive.

Now, if this were so, then since there would be the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā*) even upon the killing of a female Brāhmaṇa—just as there is for the killing of a male Brāhmaṇa—the prescription of the penance for killing an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā-prāyaścitta*) solely in the case of an Ātreyī would be untenable.
Who indeed would deny that the killing of a Brahmin woman constitutes the sin of *brahmahatyā*?
That her mere status as a woman serves as the basis for a different expiation is a conduct observed among the noble ones when they act with a sense of righteousness (*dharma*).
Is that [scripture] authoritative in the same way [as the Vedas], or is it without authority?
This is the third section of the first chapter.
It is said in reply:

But is it not the case that this authority has already been accepted by the authors of the Smṛtis themselves? For they state: "The tradition and conduct of those who know the Veda, as well as the practice of virtuous men—in whatever region a certain practice exists, that is called 'good conduct' (sadācāra).
Therefore, its authority is established precisely from that;
it is not without a basis, nor is there any perception of a motive for its composition.

Indeed, those Smṛti compositions which are based on the observation of Vedic passages found in other recensions (śākhās) have been accepted as authoritative. Now, it may be argued that since the Smṛtis proceed solely from the observation of the conduct of the virtuous (sadācāra), there is a possibility of inferring another source for them. For if they had heard the original sources themselves, then these would have been composed in the very same manner as the other Smṛti texts that were actually compiled; however, because they did not record them according to what they themselves perceived, but rather declared the conduct of the virtuous to be authoritative solely on the basis of others' conviction, [it follows that their authority is derivative].
Therefore, it is considered that [the Smṛti] cannot be determined as having its basis in direct perception;

therein, its authority is asserted on the strength of the two preceding sections, because it lacks contradiction with the injunctions and established states due to the identity of the agents, and because the authorization by the authors of the Smṛtis is a further and great cause.

In the *Tantravārtika*, it is stated that for those whose source is unknown, no authorization (to be a source of dharma) is possible. To begin with, the term "limited" (*parimāṇa*) denotes the state of being measurable by scripture; this [limitation] is established for dharma and adharma. Furthermore, the scriptures—consisting of the Vedas, Upavedas, and so forth—are themselves limited. Among these, there is no specific scripture concerning the conduct of the virtuous (*sadācāra*).

Nor is the conduct of the virtuous itself a scripture, nor is its observation or performance [the scripture], because they are entirely dependent [on other factors] and are themselves objects of knowledge (*prameya*).
However, it has already been stated that this tradition (*smṛti*) lacks a foundation;
for it cannot possibly have as its foundation the infinite variety of distinctions among countries, castes, and families.
For those who would postulate Vedic sentences for every single practice (*ācāra*), the Veda alone must be postulated [as the source].

However, it is not possible for a single sentence to enjoin an infinite number of practices such that those practices might proceed from it; nor did the authors of the *Dharmasūtras*, having observed this very fact, establish the authority of practices [on the basis of such a source].

Furthermore, there is no possibility of establishing a connection with the remaining sentences of the *Dharma-smṛtis* [as the source], because the *Smṛti* (the written tradition) only comes into existence after the observation of the practices. It cannot be the root of those practices, as that would lead to the absurdity of the root being posterior to the sprout.

Nor can scripture, even in the form of memory, be inferred here; for that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence, since scripture is the source of memory, whereas memory is not the source of scripture. Furthermore, it would follow that custom is rootless, as such scripture does not exist.
The third quarter of the first chapter:

[The objection] "Because the scripture has a limited scope," for the scripture applies only to a limited subject matter; since customs (*ācāra*) are unlimited, they would be of human origin (*pauruṣeya*).
Because the scripture has a limited subject matter, the scripture is meaningful only with respect to what is not already established by other means.

Just as for merchants, servants, physicians, or citizens in the cities, their conduct leads to wealth and becomes a limb of happiness, so let it be here; or rather, this very subject should be explained by means of these three sūtras.

Here, having cited the practices of the learned (śiṣṭa) residing in Āryāvarta, and when there arises a doubt regarding their authority or lack thereof as before, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is first introduced: "In the absence of contradiction by the learned, [the practice] is not opposed.
For it is thus:
if there were contradiction by the learned, its status as authoritative would be subverted.
However, because that [Vedic word] is not subject to anger, its status as an authoritative means of conduct is not contradicted.
When a single word is practiced by the learned with multiple meanings, then, due to such disagreement,
which meaning therein could be considered ultimate?
In this regard, not even the slightest doubt should be entertained;
for with respect to its application, it is common to all people in the world.
Its universal applicability is established by the fact that it is dependent upon that [commonality].
For that [convention] belongs only to some and does not exist for others;
nevertheless, it must be accepted by them as well, since it is identical to what is established for oneself.
Indeed, although the word "aśa" (non-existence) is used by them with respect to the *bibhītaka* fruit, [it functions through convention].
Nevertheless, its denotative power is known, as in the case of the axle of a cart;
for the cognition [of the meaning] is more powerful because it is based on that [denotative power], as in the third quarter of the first chapter.
For worldly practice is understood even as secondary;

yet, although both are equally worldly, that [scriptural practice] is superior because of the scripture. If those persons who abide in common speech, or their practice upon which it relies, were to differ even slightly from the scriptural meaning, it would become fruitless.
However, in the case of worldly usage, even if there is a difference, the meaning is not significantly contradicted; therefore,
those meanings which have been determined for words by the ritualists (yājñikas) or by physicians (vaidyas)—
those alone are the primary meanings of these words, and no others.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of words that is not well-known but is found in the Vedas, the determination of its meaning arises from the [Vedic] decision; therefore, O Phālguna, just as the falling of leaves occurs for other plants, so too does the determination [of meaning] arise from that [Vedic source]. (Tantravārtika)
The barley stalks remain rejoicing, adorned with their ears;
there is never any withering of other plants, because all of them rejoice.
Now, these examples are appropriate because they are established solely through worldly renown.
In no place whatsoever are priyaṅgu grains ever called barley; nor are they called jambu, vetasa, prācīnāmla, or kāyasa.
Since they are never so designated, there is no need for further deliberation on this point.

Although [the author] will provide an explanation of the means for resolving doubts regarding the material cause (*upādāna*) without first citing an example of doubt regarding the subject matter (*abhidheya*), and since that resolution extends only as far as the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) and not elsewhere—whereas this resolution of the subject matter is established in one place and thereby becomes established everywhere—it follows that there is no redundancy;

furthermore, because the grounds for figurative application (*gauṇavṛtti*), such as similarity (*sārūpya*) and so forth, are enumerated in the *Tatsiddhisūtra*, it is understood that the cognition of a "jambu" tree similar to the original is established even if it is not the literal meaning of the word; thus, there is no need for an example here.
In this regard, what is appropriate: is there equality, or is one alone more powerful?
[This is] the third quarter of the first chapter.
There would be an equal conflict among those who engage in worldly transactions for perceptible purposes.
For every word is employed for the purpose of conveying a meaning, and a meaning is expressed for the sake of establishing conventional usage.
Just as the understanding of the beginninglessness of the relationship [between word and meaning] applies to meanings accessible to the Āryas,
it would be exactly the same for those accessible to Mlecchas, for the reason is no different.
And just as smoke is an indicator of fire even in a barbarian land,
so too is a word intended by them to be expressive through its usage in its own meaning; this being the position reached, it is replied:
The entire explanation of the sūtra, "Or [it is] according to the treatise," should be applied as before. Furthermore:
"Just as [the forms] *sādhu*, *anaru*, and *ātman* [are established], even in those produced by *pramāda*, *aśakti*, and so forth..."
In the *Tantravārtika*, it is stated that a similar confusion regarding the denotative power of words arises even in the case of Mleccha languages.
Therefore, because the inhabitants of Āryāvarta are experts in [Sanskrit] speech,
their understanding alone is considered the authoritative means for determining the relationship between word and meaning as a constituent of Dharma.
Or, when there is a conflict between Smṛti and Ācāra, or when there is doubt regarding their equality or inequality,

the disagreement shall be equal, because the basis for both is the same. As for the fact that Ācāra is perceived as more powerful because it resides in the result— that is, since the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which is connected to the result is weaker [than that which is not].
First, conduct rooted in the *sāyaka* (the Vedic arrow/text) is established;
once established, how can its sublation be conceived?
Furthermore, the status of both Smṛti and conduct as being rooted in Śruti is not equal.
For a Smṛti that is composed with confidence and possesses a formal basis has its authority mediated by that [Smṛti], and thus it is kept at a distance;
for there is no Śruti whatsoever that serves as the originator of these practices.
In some context, a certain [statement] is found in a particular manner;

for example, in the section concerning fire: "That he places the brick with the formula *yat saptadaśa bhavatīm upadadhāti*, he places food on both sides; therefore, having grasped it with both hands, a person eats food. Although this has the form of a statement providing a reason (*hetuvannigada*), a reason is impossible here because it lacks any established basis in reality.

However, by the principle that "it shall be enjoined in the Veda through a direct statement," there is an inference of an injunction; and this is not something obtained necessarily by the force of the matter (*arthataḥ*), such that it could be treated as a mere restatement—as in the cases "therefore offspring, having held the embryo for ten months, are born in the eleventh," or "therefore mules do not procreate," or "therefore in later life the father lives off his sons"—which would imply it was already established by nature or by the force of the matter. Rather, it is an injunction regarding a human duty intended for another purpose.

Thus, he places that very food on the right; therefore, a man eats with his right hand. Likewise, the consecrated one first anoints his right eye, for men anoint the left first as a rule. Similarly, in the case of the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), there are two ropes for each post; therefore, women are in excess of men, and thus one man finds many wives, but one woman does not find many husbands.

Similarly, in the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), by transcending the connection with the injunction for the *āgneyī* [verse], there is the determination that the rules concerning women—such as sleeping on the ground, not bathing, not eating meat, not anointing the body, not applying collyrium, not combing the hair, not cutting the hair, not cleaning the teeth, not clipping the nails, and not handling ropes—which occur in the introduction to the acceptance of the fourth part of the sin of Brahman-slaughter incurred by Indra due to the killing of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son, and which pertain to a three-night period, belong to the duties of women outside the ritual context (*prakaraṇātirikta*).
Therefore, established practice (*ācāra*) proceeds to infer a corresponding Smṛti text.
First, based on tradition and scripture, one should determine that dharma alone is the intended meaning;

however, in common worldly usage, a different meaning is perceived for words such as *nivṛt*, *caru*, and *aśvavāla*, whereas according to those who are experts in the Veda, the meaning in the Veda is distinct and different from that.

In common worldly usage, the word *trivṛt* denotes the state of having three strands; in the Veda, however, it is established as referring to a group of nine. Likewise, this word *caru*, in common usage, is based on a cooking vessel (*sthālī*).
And regarding the well-known *svodana* (boiled rice) among the ritualists and in the Veda, those two *vidhṛti* (separating blades) made of *ikṣu* grass are composed of parts of the *ikṣu*;
likewise, in common worldly usage as well as in the Veda, they are established as being simply the roots of *kāśa* grass.
Now, since worldly consensus is not an authoritative factor regarding Dharma, the consensus of the Veda alone is superior; therefore, both of these understandings should be equal,
or rather, because it occurs first, the Vedic understanding alone is stronger.
For worldly convention attains its own status independently of the Veda;
however, the Vedic [usage] is established through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with other words well-known in the world.

This is because no contradiction is observed among those [worldly objects], and since the Arthavādas—being intent on another purpose—are for the most part figurative descriptions (*guṇavāda*), they do not contradict those worldly entities.

The meaning is as follows: because [terms such as] *ādi*, *vyaya*, *yūpa*, *yajamāna*, *prastara*, *svarga*, and *āhavanīya*—like the mention of these—are merely supplementary to an incitement (*prarocanā*), and because they lack the function of establishing a relationship between a name and the named or of explaining a grammatical derivation (*karaṇavyutpādana*), they are not determined to be auxiliary to the comprehension of the meaning of the words; furthermore, by relying on them, there would arise a contradiction with the injunction (*vidhi*), for contradiction is observed only in those very cases.
Likewise, the well-known usage of *mantra* and so forth found in the scriptures is entirely consistent with our position.
As it has been said:
When it is argued that "therefore, let this [application] be mine as well," it is replied:

the understanding established in the Vedic branch (śākhā) is itself superior in this case, because Dharma— consisting of the means of accomplishment and its fruits— is based upon that [understanding].
In the Tantravārtika:
"Whether it be secondary (gauṇa) or primary (mukhya), whatever entity is indeed resorted to by the Veda is determined to be a means for accomplishing dharma."
Moreover, even if the word is used in a figurative sense, it is nonetheless more powerful;
for when the independent Veda is observed [to be so], it cannot be set aside.

Nor is there here an equivalence with the principle "in cases of doubt, [the meaning is determined] by the remainder of the sentence" (*vākyaśeṣāt*), because both modes of understanding are themselves free from doubt.
Therefore, the practice established solely within the scriptures is more powerful;
it is not equal to isolated customs that are remote and subject to confusion.
Thus it is said.
Even though the usage based on the conventions of the Mlecchas is weak, it appears superior due to the strength of its conventional status as a whole, which resides in its own form;
thus,
