since there is doubt because of these various arguments, this much is stated for now.

Understanding through the medium of etymological analysis (*nirukta*) and grammatical derivation (*vyākriyā*) is more powerful; for even that which is established [as true] is corrupted if its foundation is unreal.
How, then, can the meaning of words contained in the Veda be understood by a barbarian (*mleccha*)?
In that case, how could an object well-known among those [ordinary people] be understood by the Noble Ones?
And this being so, who would fail to perceive the infinite lands of the barbarians, even though they themselves are not perceived?

If that very [practice] were not investigated, doubt would arise therein; it might be sublated within two or three days by a usage enjoined by the desire for profit. Furthermore, the lack of authority of the conduct of the Mlecchas would then be firmly established.
Therefore, the third quarter of the first chapter is well understood as having its own specific subject matter within the Vedas and related texts;
consequently, for the sake of their meaningfulness, the practices of the Mlecchas are not authoritative.
For that language, which resembles Sanskrit, exists with meanings different from those [of Sanskrit];
yet it does not possess the expressive power of forms that are non-expressive [in Sanskrit], and how could it ever omit a syllable or insert an extra syllable?

For example, even within the Dravidian and other languages, one observes that when words ending in consonants are used, people understand meanings corresponding to their own language by imagining vowel endings, case-terminations, feminine suffixes, and so forth.
For instance, when "odanaṃ cori" (rice, thief) is said, the ignorant imagine it refers to what is expressed by the word "cora" (thief);
or when "panthānam atari" (the path, across) is said, they imagine "atara" and thus fail to understand.
"It is true that the path is indeed difficult to cross; therefore, it is 'atara' (uncrossable).
Likewise, having imagined the word *pāpa* ending in *pa*—which denotes a snake—to end in *a*, they say, "It is true, this is indeed *pāpa* (sinful).
Similarly, having imagined the word *mālā*, which denotes a woman (*sī*), to be *māla*, they say, "It is true."
They claim that the word *vairi*, ending in the letter *r*, is a substitute for the word *udara* (belly),
because the belly functions in the same way as an enemy (*vairin*) in causing all that is deposited [within it] to be discharged.

But if such arbitrary conceptualizations exist in the Dravidian and other languages, we do not know what they will imagine or how they will understand in the languages of the Persians, Barbaras, Yavanas, Romans, and so forth.

It follows that whatever meaning is understood through the medium of etymological analysis (*nirukta*) and grammatical derivation (*vyākriyā*) shall be the very meaning of words such as *pika* and *nemi*;
for words belonging to regional dialects (*deśabhāṣā*) and corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) are so full of obscurity that they cannot be distinguished [by etymology alone].
That [word-meaning] should be accepted as such precisely because it is not contradicted by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For the *pika*, *nemi*, and so forth have been determined in this way by experts;
it is certain that such a thing should be accepted as being established by valid cognition.
That [Vedic injunction] is not contradicted by the authority known as the Veda,
because it functions in dependence upon the knowledge of the relationship between words and their referents;
wherever there is established usage, the meaning of the sentence is understood accordingly.
Or rather, its connection with the term "feeling" (vedanā) is established by valid cognition;
for it is not in contradiction with the Noble Ones, as they too acknowledge it.
Since it is well-known to exist, it is accepted as being associated with that [feeling].
But when [the latter] is non-existent, the former possesses superior force; that which is established through conceptual construction is stronger than the [merely] conventional,
for while the former exists, the other cannot establish itself.

Therefore, just as there is greater skill among the Mlecchas in matters such as service and domestic architecture (*Tantravārtika*), so too is there [greater skill] in determining the meaning of what is expressed.
And as for that which is called *patravāravāda* (the "leaf-ear-whisper") originating from that region,
who indeed would be able to know it, since it was not even mentioned by them?
In the *Nirukta*, words that are already well-established in worldly usage are not etymologically explained merely on the basis of their connection to specific actions or causes.

Even in grammar, there is performed merely the formal description (*anvākhyāna*) of those words whose meanings are already well-established and whose forms are uncorrupted; therein, the determination of meaning is only incidental. Those [grammatical rules] do not subvert anything other than their own specific domain, even if they are weak. That which is scattered, multiform, and productive of doubt will be accepted only in certain instances where there is no other means.
As stated by Dvaipāyana in the narrative of the *Nirvāṇa-vacana* in the third quarter of the first chapter of the *Mahābhārata*:
"Because of its greatness and because it is the Bhārata, it is called the *Mahābhārata*."
"He who knows its etymology is liberated from all sins.
If it is argued that [the Kalpasūtras] are "treatises on ritual application" (*prayogaśāstra*),
then, having cited the Kalpasūtras, this is now considered.
Is the authority of these [texts] independent, like that of the Vedas?
What, then, are the *kalpas* and what are the *sūtras*? It is said:
The *prayoga* (ritual application) is established in its form by those who follow the ritual actions;
however, the *sūtra* merely indicates them, as its own *prayogas* must be inferred.
For the *kalpas* are indeed established through recitation as the *prayogas* for each sacrifice.
A sūtra that possesses both reason and illustration is a characteristic that pervades the entire body of the tantra;
likewise, the Āśvalāyana-sūtra was composed by Baijavāpi.
Furthermore, as for the claim that the Smṛtis lack authority because they are not based on direct Vedic revelation (aśabda), [that is refuted].
In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), it is not possible to state that [the Kalpasūtras] are authoritative;
or, even if they were so designated, there would still be an investigation of them,
and thus their authority is excluded here as well for all of them.

Alternatively, since the status of being a *prayoga-śāstra* (treatise on ritual application) is attributed to the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*), or else the status of being Veda is [attributed] even to the six auxiliaries— for indeed there is a traditional recollection (*smṛti*) of their being Veda—
therefore they too are either the Veda itself or are intrinsically authoritative (*pramāṇa*).
One must state "they appear" in order to avoid a different mode of presentation; for even the Śākyas and others speak in this very way:
"Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this permanence of phenomena remains constant."
Granted that one might not enter a village when forbidden by those bearing staffs;
yet now he clearly enters by the very main road—
when such a doubt arises as to what the status of the *Kalpasūtras* is?
First, it is clear beyond doubt that the status of the *prayoga-śākhās* as branches [of the Veda] has been authorized by the Veda itself; thus, their authority regarding *dharma* is established.
Or rather, their very status as Veda is proven through such means of valid cognition as corroboration (*saṃvāda*).

Just as the branches (śākhās) proclaimed by Kaṭha and others are designated by the names "Kaṭhaka" and so forth and are established as being non-artificial (akṛtrima), so too must the fixed nature of those texts recited in the Veda that are designated by names such as "Aśvaka" and so on be understood.

Just as in the case of the Sāmavedic recensions, although there are designations based on their origin—such as "this is the ṛṣi of this"—there is no contradiction to their eternity; the same applies to the treatises on the well-known ṛṣis, the Kalpas, and the Sūtras.
For instance:

Just as in the passage, "As childhood belongs to a child, so the Aṅgirasas are the givers of mantras among the makers of mantras," the term *mantrakṛt* (maker of mantras) is applied to the user; likewise, those who employ various forms or sūtras shall be designated as their "makers" by virtue of being their users. Furthermore, in the injunction for the *brahmayajña*, after it has been stated, "Thus knowing, one should study one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*)," its elaboration specifies: "Whatever Ṛks he studies, whatever Yajus, whatever Sāmans, whatever Brāhmaṇas, whatever Itihāsas and Purāṇas, and whatever Kalpas"—since these are prescribed here as objects to be recited (*japyamāna*), they are understood to possess the status of being composed by seers (*ārṣatva*).

Since those [mantras] composed by humans cannot be the subject of a mandatory injunction (*nityavidhi*) because they serve as causes for dharma only through the occasion of recitation (*japanimitta*),

and since the *Aruṇaparāśara-śākhā-brāhmaṇa* is of the nature of a ritual manual (*kalpa*), and since all ritualists determine that it possesses no authority equal to the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) set forth by other branches (*śākhā*) apart from their own, there is equality between these [mantras found in the *kalpa*] and those mantras studied in other recensions (*samāmnāya*), because both rely upon the application (*viniyoga*) of the mantras to the sacrifice.

Even by Lāṭyāyana and Drāhyāyaṇa, with respect to the authority of the *Arṣakalpa*, this [rule] was stated—having considered the Māśaka [Kalpa] and having accepted that what is prescribed by the *Arṣakalpa* is more authoritative than even that which is prescribed in the Brāhmaṇas, since no inference [of such authority] exists there:

"In the context of the carrying forth of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*), as stated by Kātyāyana, regarding the supplementary portions of the injunctions for the *stotra*s found in the Brāhmaṇas concerning the sacrifice, it shall be performed according to the Māśaka [Kalpa], because of its authority, and not from the authority of the pure Brāhmaṇa alone independent of that."

And likewise, although it is stated in the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa that the Jarābodhīya Agniṣṭoma-sāman should be performed as an optional alternative to the Yajñāyajñīya at the Prāyaṇīya Agniṣṭoma-sāman, Kātyāyana—following the tradition of Māśaka—has determined that the Jarābodhīya is to be used as the third Gāyatrī verse of the Ārbhava-stotra. This concludes the third quarter of the first chapter.

For the name *sam* was applied by him to the *sāman* immediately following the *gāyatra* contained within the *ārbhavīya-gāyatrī*; and because it follows that [sāman], the *jarābodhīya* is mentioned using a part of the word (*padaikadeśa*), while the *yajñāyajñīya*—which is the established *agniṣṭoma-sāman* of the Jyotiṣṭoma—is designated by the term *ḍha*. If Kātyāyana had considered the Brāhmaṇa to be supplementary to the Kalpa, he would have stated the option as seen directly in the Brāhmaṇa; moreover, the authority of the Teacher’s words is established in the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
The sages who composed the constituent parts [of the Vedas] are considered to be teachers;

even those statements of untrustworthy persons that accord with the meaning established by other means of valid cognition are determined to be true—how much more so, then, the words of those whose speech is truth?
Furthermore, [the Vedic texts are authoritative].

Furthermore, the scriptural injunction for the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*), which was previously shown in the *Tantravārttika* regarding the inclusion of the ritual manuals (*kalpa-grahaṇa*), is equally traditional;
[it applies] to the inquiries into the Vedas and to those who follow the path of the *Mārgavṛtti*.
The status of being a complete Veda cannot be attained by those [texts] that lack the Kalpasūtras and the like;
therefore, this treatise on the performance of rituals is undoubtedly either the Veda itself or equal to the Veda, such as the Kalpasūtras and so forth.
Who that knows the Veda will deny the status of a *prayoga-śāstra* (manual of ritual application) to those works in which the term *dharmaśāstra* is employed at all times? And furthermore:
Likewise, how could practices such as the *avakīrṇi-yajña* or penances like the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, which are clearly revealed by Vedic mantras, be considered non-Vedic?
And in this way, on what basis is it inferred that these [practices] lack a foundation in the Vedas?
Since their status as Veda and their eternity are indeed equal,
for the perfected ones (siddhas), either their eternity alone or their status as Veda is easily understood;
this is established because their subject matter consists of the meaning of the Vedas without any doubt.

It is better to assume that those very foundational statements of the Dharmaśāstras which you consider to be [the source] are themselves what are being recited; by this, it is understood that those [foundational statements] were indeed transmitted by them [the authors of the Dharmaśāstras].
For if those [original works] were found, who would accept mere imitations?
Moreover, due to the destruction of the tradition, the transmission of that [knowledge] has ceased;
thus, the composition of their own treatises by Manu and others must be inferred in that manner.

Only from the Veda itself is the meaning of the Veda known, and that alone can accomplish the fruit; not from any other human composition, such as a mere semblance of a mantra, just as it is traditionally taught. Therefore, one must not compose works that wear the cloak of the Brāhmaṇas.

It is indeed certain that an action not ordained by the Veda does not bear fruit; for such is this sequence, and such is the nature of the Vedic text. It is therefore appropriate to form this understanding, rather than postulating another source.
Since it has already been determined that Dharma is characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*),
the authority of even a Brāhmaṇa text that is not Veda is not accepted.
These [Brāhmaṇas] speak of Dharma and lead one to understand the injunctions.
It is impossible to state such a thing as long as [the matter] is measured by what has been explicitly stated;
therefore, for a direct application of Dharma that has been explicitly taught,
the Dharma-śāstra itself would be the authority, not the Veda through the intervention [of the śāstra].
For by the very same reasoning through which the authorlessness of the Veda is established,
the same will apply to the scriptures of the Śākyas and others;
thus, they are not corrupted either by the absence of an author or by the defects of an author.
Whatever has been stated for the sake of establishing the authority of the Veda— namely, that it is devoid of any recollection of an author—
understands by way of extension (atideśa) to apply to the words of the Buddha as well.
This being the case, we reply here: "Because there is no fixed rule regarding that.
For all that was previously stated by the opponent—who, while engaged in debate with others, prattles on with various words—is indeed without foundation.
Illusory arguments arise from the words of others,
just as the Śākyas, Vaiśeṣikas, and others, terrified by the Mīmāṃsakas, declare:
"Our scripture is indeed eternal," while their minds are empty [of truth].
Those who rely on mere reasoning claim that even non-violence and other virtues were not preceded by that [Veda];
consequently, because they are of human origin, they lack authority regarding matters beyond the senses.

Even those Mīmāṃsakas—who, by refuting the authority of the words of a person regarding supersensible objects, believe they have rendered impossible the establishment of an unimpeachable authority whose suspicion of causal defects has been removed by the determination of its being authorless—find themselves unable to counter this [our argument]. Having become speechless, their hearts torn by self-protective utterances resembling the mimicry of children, and their nets of arguments for the validity of the Veda utterly exhausted, they are, when challenged with "This statement of ours belongs to you," like foolish suitors who have come to choose a bride and are asked to answer the questions of a cowherd.

Having heard this, the Mīmāṃsakas say: "This has been taken away by us alone; even though it is well-established among the Śākyas, their doctrine of universal momentariness is abandoned because it contradicts the established tenets of the Veda. Thus they constantly speak with scriptural authority.
For instance:
he who, disregarding the threads, intends to produce a cloth merely by grasping the shuttle, would be attempting to strike the sky with his fists.

Furthermore, the term "permanence of linguistic usage" (*vyavahāra-nityatā*) is a synonym for the permanence of activity. Therefore, for one who holds that the relationship between word and meaning is impermanent, upon what basis could there be permanence of usage dependent upon those [words]? This is extremely difficult to establish.
While words and so forth are perishing, where could linguistic usage reside?
Thus, the statement "this is the nature of things" (*sthitaiṣā dharmatā*) is devoid of meaning.

Therefore, for those who maintain that words are impermanent, the eternity of the Veda is untenable. Furthermore, since a sentence whose subject matter pertains to each individual sense-object cannot constitute a treatise on ritual application (*prayoga-śāstra*), it is said [in the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra] "not because of the absence of restriction" (*na saṃniyamāt*).
For those [Vedic texts] are based upon correct words (*sādhu-śabda*) that are interspersed with Magadhan, Southern dialects, and their corruptions.
O sages, all ritual actions and formal procedures are for me like a vessel placed upon a slope;
there is a cause for its being set up, but there is no cause for its falling.
These narrow dharmas arise with a cause, and they perish without a cause.
Consequently, since words are unreal, how could there be reality in their objects?
Furthermore, when their forms are seen to be corrupted, how could they possibly possess beginninglessness?
For that form which is fit to persist as the essence of the word is not observed.

"But when one's own nature is perceived as it truly is, error ceases" (Tantravārttika). In worldly transactions concerning perceptible objects, people compose poems using sentences that follow common usage and words of the very same kind.
"I praise Agni, the domestic priest, the god of sacrifice, the officiating priest, the invoker,
the bestower of jewels"— how is this nine-verse hymn [to be understood], and where has the priesthood of Agni been observed such that it is here celebrated?
Furthermore, where has the usage of the word [for a deity] been observed as being the object of a hymn?
For divinity is never established by way of genus (jāti).
Moreover, its status as a *hotṛ* priest is caused by the invocation of the deity.
And let it be considered by men: from what source could there be any utility in cutting off branches?
Likewise, by what person acting with deliberate intelligence could this mantra, "ūrg," be said to have a purpose, or be employed, for the sprinkling of branches?

Regarding the mantra "vāyavaḥ stha" (Ye are the winds), what man acting with conscious intent would alter the letter *a* of the word *agna*— which is among the Ṛgvedic verses whose meanings are well-known and have never before been understood through the sounds of the three worlds— into a protracted *o* (*au*) for the purpose of driving away the calf?
What fool, or even one acting with conscious intent, would so prescribe it as a rule?
Therefore, the independence of the Veda is indeed understood from its very form.

And thus, when students, teachers, or bystanders examine the forms of the Vedic words, sentences, and their meanings, they determine its authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) through their own direct experience.

In the works of the Śākyas and others, however, even if something is employed with the intention of using correct words and with an undisturbed intellect, because the usage consists mostly of terms such as *prajñapti*, *vijñapti*, *paśyata*, and *tiṣṭhata*, only a very small portion of the correct form is found there.

The Vedas are perceived in such a manner as they are found [to be], whereas it is not so with that spoken by the Śākyas and others; because of the absence of a fixed rule of application (*prayoga-niyama*), its status as a scripture is not established.

Furthermore, the statement "due to the lack of restriction" (*asaṃniyamāt*) was said either with the intention of refuting the momentariness of this [scripture]—since permanence is not proven—or else with the intention of pointing out the non-existence of any restrictive rule regarding the text, given that [the Buddhists] do not accept a fixed textual tradition.
Furthermore, because the memory of their authors is firm, these [Kalpasūtras] are not considered to be unauthored.
Therefore, since they lack independence regarding matters known through non-human (unauthored) sources, they do not possess the status of an independent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By this, the independence of the Kalpasūtras is refuted.

The authorship of these [Kalpasūtras] is firmly known through tradition; their ritual procedures are considered authoritative just like those of other Smṛti texts based on the Vedāṅgas. Indeed, just as teachers who study and teach them remember Āśvalāyana, Baudhāyana, Āpastamba, Kātyāyana, and others as their authors, it is not merely on the strength of their names that their authorship is asserted.
The reply, "Because of its designation [as Veda]," would likewise establish the non-Vedic status of those mantras studied in the Kalpas,
as well as those taught in the Gṛhyasūtras and the Chāndogya Brāhmaṇas.
Consequently, it follows that even those [Vedic texts] would lack the status of being Veda due to the absence of accents;
therefore, the reason here is the absence of that self-evident nature which has been described.
For there are many supplementary passages whose non-existence in common worldly usage is well known.
In the *Tantravārtika*:
"By that [reasoning], the lack of prior intentionality of the Veda is established even by them;
for, even though it is eternal, they [the Mīmāṃsakas] apply injunctions to it with great effort."

Having composed them, the author, while teaching them, would have manifested his own proficiency through the absence of errors; furthermore, due to their lack of formal rules, they possess the character of being prescribed and explained, yet they are not understood as having the capacity to convey a previously unknown meaning.
Even a present-tense designation, when incited by an explanatory passage (arthavāda), acquires the status of an injunction;
however, this does not occur in the case of the Kalpasūtras.
Although the Vedic character of the Kalpasūtras might be established by the statement "the Veda has six limbs," [this is not the case].
Nevertheless, their status as *chandas* (Vedic scripture) is not established in the same way as that of the *Tarka* [logic] texts;
for the rules governing *chandas* are fixed exclusively for the *Mantra* and *Brāhmaṇa* portions.
Through the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*, however, the practice of the *Sātvata* [Pāñcarātra] tradition is considered to be consistently authoritative.

As for the fact that their necessity is declared even in the context of the *brahmayajña* (Vedic recitation sacrifice) because the compendium of the meaning of the Vedas cannot be accomplished by those who do not rely on the *kalpasūtras*, and because there must necessarily exist some *kalpasūtras*— even while [the Veda] is being practiced as far as the Veda extends and as far as the performance of rituals extends— in order that the fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) not remain empty; and since the purpose of the injunction here is understood to be the intent toward the practice of ritual action, and that purpose is indeed eternal, it does not follow that the text is non-eternal.

The status of being denotable by the word "Veda" does not apply to these [auxiliaries] even among those who study them; nor is it stated in the established doctrine that "the Veda with its six auxiliaries is one. Since they have attained the status of restatements (anuvāda) in the *Kālpasūtras* and other texts, by process of elimination, [they are not part of the Veda].

Nor does the logic of different recensions (śākhāntara) apply here, because they share the same student-body; due to this commonality of students, they are never capable of being injunctions [of distinct rites]. Furthermore, they are seen to explain [their contents] by means of reasons arising from the Brāhmaṇas.
Therefore, even for this reason, the independence of the Kalpas is not tenable;
[as stated] in the Tantravārtika:
"Because some [Kalpas] share the same purpose and because of the similarity of others."
Because it possesses the same commonality of scriptural authority, its purpose is also stated to be something else.
The meaning of the word "Ācārya" has been explained by Manu and others as follows for one who explains the meaning of the Vedas and speaks the Vedas themselves.

Furthermore, at the time of the transmission of the Vedas, it was stated that "the word of the teacher is authoritative" for the purpose of ensuring that students might indeed have faith in what he says; this does not concern the words of the authors of the Kalpa-sūtras.
Likewise, it has been stated elsewhere:
"Therefore, this speech speaks both truth and falsehood, for it is pierced by evil."
And by the statement "because it is applied everywhere," this is demonstrated:
because of the proximity of the Vedic branch (*śākhā*), any contradiction is quite evident;
yet, due to the establishment of inference, that which is connected to it would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Having cited the laws of various regions, this [matter] is now considered; for all [such matters] are to be cited and examined individually—
those which the virtuous of the East practice and those which they avoid.
All the practices of the northerners (Udīcyas) are likewise to be examined;
this should also be considered here up to the first two Sūtras,
for the systematic arrangement of the Gṛhya-sūtras, the Gautama-sūtra, and others applies universally.
What, then, should be understood? That the rule is indeed established by the textual reading;

for a mark (*liṅga*) situated elsewhere does not allow one to infer the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) elsewhere. Having observed that [the rule] is fixed, let the possessor of the mark be understood as being located right there.

Whether it be an affirmation or a negation, that [fire] is not indeed inferred elsewhere than from smoke located in another house; for it is certain that fire in a different house is not cognized by those who have not seen the smoke.
And just as the laws of castes, their subdivisions, and families are established,

so too shall the establishment of the laws of countries and so forth come to pass; for the conduct prescribed by the treatises on all subjects would be practiced by capable men throughout all lands, just like the *agnihotra* sacrifice.
Furthermore, the Vedic text is understood through the principle of "presumption based on the impossibility otherwise" (anyathānupapatti);
and because that [text] is impossible without it, it is restricted to that very context.
This is so if the instrument for preparing food is enjoined as the reason for the *śūrpa* (winnowing-basket) oblation.
One should likewise postulate even an illustrative example that pertains only to those [specific cases];
for, having observed local customs established in this manner everywhere,
it is logical to postulate a Vedic source that has those [customs] alone as its object and which is rooted in them.
Alternatively, regarding the objection that [the injunction] might apply to all dharmas, the following answer is stated:
Because the injunction is logical for one who possesses the mere capacity as the qualified agent, it is understood that the agent is specifically determined for each individual action.
[The word *dharma*] is connected with the qualifiers of "fitness," "non-prohibition," and "particularity"; however, there is no accompanying term (*upapada*) here that follows established usage,
which could be inferred as a qualification of the specific agent observed in a particular region.

Although the qualification (*adhikāra*) applies without distinction by virtue of general eligibility, it may be restricted by some specific word qualifying the agent—just as in cases such as "the king [performs] the Rājasūya," "the two kings [perform]," or "the Vaiśya [performs] the Vaiśyastoma. However, in this case, it is not possible to conceive of either one or many [agents] who possess the quality of being seen practicing [the ritual]. Why? [Because...]

First of all, no such universal as "being an Easterner" (*prācyatva*) or "being a Southerner" (*dākṣiṇātyatva*), which is excluded from those who are Westerners, Northerners, and so forth, and yet is concomitant with all individual instances of Easterners and the like, is logically possible; for if such a term were possible, it could qualify the application of the *Holākā* and other rites. As for the universals such as "humanity" (*manuṣyatva*) or "Brahminhood" (*brāhmaṇatva*), these do exist in those [individuals], but since they are indistinct across all individuals residing in every region, they are not known to have the capacity to serve as qualifiers corresponding to specific local customs.

For it is not possible for a single denotation to be established for the individual persons of the east and so forth, who are infinite in variety, because it is impossible to experience the relationship [of a word] with them either individually or collectively.
By this, the view that [the word] denotes individual persons qualified by qualities, actions, or universals is refuted;
for no qualities, actions, or universals can possibly be conceived as being capable of delimiting individual persons situated in every location.
In all cases, even there, [the application] proceeds by way of exclusion based on specific distinctions. Furthermore,
no category of object exists that is entirely devoid of both individual manifestation (*vyakti*) and generic form (*ākṛti*),
such that it could serve as the basis for the qualification of a particular qualified person (*adhikārin*).
Likewise, because of the understanding of both the desire for results and the capacity of the agent,
human birth alone is qualified for all duties pertaining to place.

Furthermore, a certain person, describing the meaning of verbal roots (*ākhyāta-śabda*), while refuting this reading of the text and attempting to establish a novel position, fails to perceive the distinction between the injunction (*vidhi*) and the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) arising from the delusion caused by the word *vidhāna* as it occurs in the Sūtra. Ignoring the inquiry into the essential nature of both, and thereby destroying the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the section concerning non-existential objects (*abhāvārtha-adhikaraṇa*), he says: "The 'being' (*bhāva*) is indeed inexpressible by its own characteristic; it is other than the cognition of the word, like a causal factor (*kāraka*);
for when one is told 'one should do,' one understands 'I am doing.'"

Whether it be the efficient force (*vidhi*) or the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), this treatise is intended for the purpose of investigating the validity of all dharmas through the customs of regions and the nature of universals and individuals. If it is explained as a commentary on the *Pāṇinian* aphorisms, by way of resolving objections through the aforementioned logical path, then it remains connected with the exposition of this very sūtra. However, if one were to abandon that [approach] and describe the meanings of verbal suffixes as being "inexpressible" because they lack the nature of individuals and actions, then—being utterly disconnected, useless, and devoid of justification—it would simply have to be rejected.

Since a verbal form does not denote an individual through its generic form, it is therefore a matter of wonder that the action prescribed by it applies to all [individuals]. Furthermore, having stated that [the universal] is inexpressible, [the opponent] has done so by means of synonyms imagined by himself.

That which has been stated as an alternative explanation contradicts what was previously said; for there, the application [of the term] would be seen through the systematic distinction of genus (*jāti*) and so forth denoted by a single word,
just like the ritual property of the five-fold cutting (*pañcāvatta*).

Furthermore, since there is no grammatical indicator (*liṅga*) for an eternal entity, when the meanings [of words]— namely the individual (*vyakti*) and the form (*ākṛti*)— are rejected as the denotable objects,
the qualifiers such as "red" and so forth are also now refuted by another [argument].
Furthermore, because there is no gender for that which is eternal, there can be no qualification of the agent by it.
For an eternal agent is characterized by a fixed gender;

however, for one who considers the word "eternal" (nitya) to be a qualifier of the gender, there would result the fault of an improper compound (*asamartha-samāsa*), since [the term] would depend on a gender that has become subordinate.

Now, one might object: since the word *liṅga* is always dependent [on another], there can be no loss of semantic capacity (*sāmarthyavighāta*) because it implies another related term; therefore, a compound must indeed occur here, as in "Devadatta’s teacher’s family" (*devadattasya gurukulam*). For the word *guru* (teacher) derives its very existence only through dependence on a student (*śiṣya*); thus, because its own meaning is already internally contained within the relation to the student expressed by the word *devadatta*, there is no contingency of an obstruction to semantic capacity caused by an additional requirement.

Although this word *liṅga* functions when there is a relationship between the signifier (*gamaka*) and the signified (*gamya*), nevertheless—unlike relationships such as those between teacher and pupil or father and son—it is not well-known as a "relational term" (*saṃbandhiśabda*) whose basis for application depends upon that [relationship].

For although the word *liṅga* is said to be based on its connection with the action in the sense that "it is marked by this," it is not thereby called a relational term; yet, even so, it does not abandon its dependence on other factors of action (*kāraka*) inherent in the action. Thus, in cases such as "the perception of the mark (*liṅga*) of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*)," the lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*) may indeed be avoided.

Furthermore, eternality (*nityatva*) depends upon its own meaning as a grammatical indicator (*liṅga*); since it is presented by the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) as a property of that [eternality], there arises an unavoidable consequence of incapacity when there is a requirement for a relationship with it.

Therefore, the term "of the eternal" (*nityasya*) is merely a qualification of a specific agent indicated by a fixed mark, or a qualification of the entitlement (*adhikāra*). Since there exists no mark whatsoever that establishes either a fixed agent or an eternal entitlement, it is not possible to justify the injunction regarding the *dolākā* and other such items through a specific accompanying word (*upapada*) denoting that [agent or entitlement].

For all regional customs (*deśācāra*) are performed by persons designated as Easterners (*prācya*), Southerners (*dākṣiṇātya*), and so forth; they are not observed among those who lack such designations. Therefore, because the injunction (*vidhi*) is inferred as qualified by these designations, the fivefold means of knowledge (*pramāṇapañcaka*) connected with them is indeed superior. To this, the following rebuttal is offered:
If it is argued that a country must be distinguished by its direction, and the nature of direction is unstable,
and that improper conduct does not persist because of its connection with that specific place—
meaning it would not exist in other countries— then [the following response follows].
If you have refuted the name [of the Veda] on the grounds that it is based on place,
then I can again state that its basis is something else; or let it be entirely without a basis, for even so it will still distinguish [the texts].
For those who have already acquired the conduct regarding signs, what further sign would be required for us?
Indeed, the designation "Yoga" [is established] through many connections, just as the name of a region is applied [to a city], like Mathurā.
Because it arises from the state of being a place of residence, by means of the causes for its arrival, or through the nature of karma— just like a slope;
as in the case of a land sloping toward the east or north, or even one sloping toward the southeast.
Place becomes a constituent part of the ritual action; it should be understood as "the eastern region" and so forth.
For that which is the eastern region for some is the southern region for others (as stated in the *Tantravārtika*).
Furthermore, whatever variety exists in clay and other materials is the same in one place as it is in another.
Therefore, the injunction regarding the *holākā* and other such rites is not qualified by that [Vedic word] either, because there is no scripture for its application or origin.

Since multiple applications are observed from a single word, when multiple meanings present themselves, the determination of the meaning of words such as "cow" (*go*)—which are unsettled due to the fear of the fault of optionality (*vikalpa*) and the consequence of postulating multiple unseen potencies (*adṛṣṭa-śakti*)—is established by relying on the distinction between the primary and secondary senses. This is achieved through the force of settled Vedic usage, which sublates unsettled worldly usage, as has been demonstrated.

Furthermore, regarding a single object such as a cow (*go*), many words like *go*, *gāvī*, and so forth are employed. In this regard, since it is logical that each word possesses a distinct expressive power (*śakti*) inherent in its connection to the object—as understood through the linguistic usage of elders—and since there is no contradiction between the application of all words found in the scriptures and worldly words, and because the operation of the Vedic branches (scriptures) consisting of sentences is established as being preceded by words, the function [of grammar] does not lie in establishing the correctness and incorrectness residing in individual words. This is because it would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). To explain: [The text continues: For instance...

For in the case of sentence-meanings, a lack of authority was determined by the successive observation of contradictions with Śruti, Smṛti, and custom; but here, because the order is reversed, it is merely a resonance (dhvani). [The word] consists either of correct phonemes in their own right, or a collection independent of meaning, like the instruction regarding the māṭṛkā and so forth.
Furthermore, if it is argued that a word is incorrect because it is non-expressive,
its unacceptability is not established, as this contradicts common worldly usage;
for by direct perception, the phonemes are first perceived as pure and indistinguishable in both cases.
Correctness or incorrectness does not reside in those [individual phonemes] nor in their collection;
nor can they be inferred from a relationship that has not been experienced.

By refuting that [inference], the refutation of human speech—which is preceded by such [inference]—is also established. Furthermore, the Vedic word, which aims merely at describing the nature of things and the qualities or defects residing therein, and which is independent of injunctions and prohibitions, cannot in any way function as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that because correctness (*sādhutva*) and incorrectness (*asādhutva*) do not consist in performance or non-performance, they cannot be the objects of injunctions or prohibitions,

and that it is possible for them to be enjoined or prohibited as the instruments of the *abhidhā-bhāvanā* (the efficient force of expression), we say no; for it is untenable to postulate, for every single word, an infinite number of inferred injunctive and prohibitive sentences.
Corrupt words (apaśabda) are established as being more numerous than correct words (śabda);
however, they cannot be subject to prohibition in the same manner as musical notes (kalā) and the like,
for the genus "word-ness" (śabdatva-jāti) is undivided between correct words and corrupt words.
Indeed, when two views exist regarding a particular intermediate generality, that which is already established by the expressive words need not be enjoined;
furthermore, the prohibition of what is non-expressive is not possible because it has not been established.
Furthermore, that object which has already been attained is not within the scope of the scripture;
for the application of words and the definition of their meaning are established from worldly usage alone.
Moreover, that which is absolutely unattainable cannot be restricted by anything other than that [worldly usage].
And for you, there is an absolute non-attainment [of the result], whereas for me, there is attainment;

for if the virtuous and the non-virtuous were one and the same object, they might be attained through conceptual alternation, and only then would there be scope for the restriction that "the virtuous [alone] attain it.
But in your view, however:
However, because it is absolutely non-expressive, it does not follow that it is incorrect;
for in this case, the restriction regarding the correctness of words—which yields its fruit through their application—becomes meaningful.
If it is argued that the usage of corrupt forms is observed in the expression of meaning:
It is said:
Even other [gestures] such as the contraction of the eyebrows are seen to be employed toward objects;
yet no restriction is observed whose fruit is the exclusion of those [other gestures].
Furthermore, the purpose of a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) is not the removal of an opposing alternative;

since its purpose is that of an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), it is not appropriate for this to be the subject of an exclusive specification, because there is no possibility of simultaneous application (*yugapatprāpti*). (Śābarabhāṣya-tantravārttika)
Furthermore, its purpose cannot be established as being merely visible;
for even an invisible result is not understood from that which has no expectancy toward a visible one,
and since this is not based on a restrictive unseen merit (*niyamāpūrva*), it is not understood where it might reside.
The word, its meaning, the hearer, the cognition, the speaker, and the act of utterance do not constitute the primary subject here, as in the case of "one who desires heaven.
This concludes the third quarter of the first chapter.
Nor does its primacy follow from its being connected with the genitive case;
nor is its utterance for the sake of the utterer, whereby it might be considered equal to food and the like.
Rather, because it is perishable by its very nature, it is subject to refinement just like a vessel.
Regarding this, it has been said: "If it is argued that [the auxiliary sciences] are *prayoga-śāstra* (treatises on application), we say no, because there is no fixed rule.
For grammar and the other sciences do not possess independence by virtue of being Veda;
and because their operation depends upon human agency, they lack the status of independent authority (*apramāṇatā*).
Furthermore, no other death is observed that falls within the scope of its effects;
thus, there would be no firm scriptural authority or inference—such as exists for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and so forth—by which [the necessity of this rite] could be established.
To begin with, the author of the Sūtras has not stated any purpose whatsoever.
And how could there be such a lapse of memory regarding the purpose within such an extensive treatise?
For it is described therein that dharma consists of actions such as sacrifices connected to their results;
yet, nothing of the sort is taught in grammar.
For the meaning of a treatise becomes clearly defined through investigation.

In this context, having introduced the idea that knowledge is the inherent nature of dharma, the author of the Vārttika stated that "prosperity results from the prior application of the treatise" for one who fears the consequence of non-dharma.
To this, the author of the Bhāṣya says:
Alternatively, let it be that "dharma" resides in the cognition; yet, such an unrestricted determination of its nature as dharma has not been stated.

Therefore, if in this case cognition itself is determined to be the dharma, then—even though the fulfillment of assistance occurs through the production [of the result] from cognition—the cognition lacks the status of being the *prayojaka* (the instigator), just like the *vājina* and other [subsidiary offerings], because the ritual application (*prayoga*) is already established by worldly convention.

But in the case of an application preceded by the sacred scriptures (*śāstra*), since knowledge is an integral part of that [application] and thus becomes devoid of further expectancy, there is no expectancy for another purpose. Even if there were some scriptural mention of a fruit, it would be understood as a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) according to the principle stated in the sūtra *dravyasaṃskārakarmasu* (JS 4.3.1).
For it has been explained that when two things traveling the same path are known, and the latter is known to possess a fruit, the former is not thereby known to possess a fruit as well.
“He who performs the horse sacrifice, and he who knows it thus.
Furthermore,
this is the third quarter of the first chapter.
Furthermore, because they have a beginning in time, the status of being *dharma* cannot belong to grammar or its application;
for the Vedic revelation does not depend upon grammar,
nor is grammar understood to be eternal in any way whatsoever.
For the death of the author indeed refutes the position that [the treatise] is eternal.

Even if one were to postulate an infinite succession of human grammatical treatises based on the principle of the eternity of worldly practice (*vyavahāra-nityatā*), nevertheless, because the principle that "it must have been preceded by the word of a teacher" (*ukta-tu-śabda-pūrvatva*) remains established,
grammar— even if composed by many persons— cannot attain the status of being rooted in the Veda.

Now, [it might be argued that] even though the aspect of the *lakṣaṇa* (the rule) in the statement "grammar is the *lakṣaṇa*" is artificial (*kṛtrima*), the injunction would be established as eternal because of its eternal aspect, the *lakṣya* (the thing to be characterized).
That is untenable.
Why?

It has been stated that because words are of an entirely distinct nature, there is no single basis for them through their definitions and so forth; thus, no such basis exists for a positive injunction (*vidhi*). For it is said that Vedic speech is "defined" by worldly speech that is itself undefined, when its form is determined through the relationship between teacher and pupil by means of accents, phonemes, and measures whose forms are not lost.

And in that [Veda] consisting of mantra and brāhmaṇa, dharma certainly exists in its ritual applications, its knowledge, and its practice. As for the statement, "A single word, correctly understood, well-employed, and in accordance with the scriptures, becomes a cow of plenty in the heavenly world," that too is merely a supplementary praise of the study of one's own Vedic recitation (svādhyāya).

Regarding the statement, "Every day one should study one's own Veda," this was said for the purpose of establishing a rule of necessary performance, meaning that even a single Ṛg-verse, Yajus-formula, or Sāman-chant must necessarily be studied. For even he who, due to incapacity, cannot study the entire collection of mantras—
even a single word endowed with scriptural authority yields heaven for him who desires it.
For generally, among the learned whose minds are intent upon righteous conduct, only some minor lapse in conduct occurs due to negligence;
however, regarding the employment of words such as *gāvī* and the like, no one perceives them as improper conduct.
Nor is any aversion or censure observed toward them, as there is toward the consumption of *kalāja* and other such [forbidden] things.
Nor is even one person seen among a thousand who maintain the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) who conducts his discourse using only those "correct words" favored by you;

for instance, in the neuter nominative singular forms ending in *t* such as *samānam itaraccyena* and so forth, Maśaka employed them here and there, saying, “*samānam itaraṃ jyotiṣṭomena*” and “*samānam itaraṃ gavā aikācikeneti*,” and the author of the Sūtras has likewise stated this.

Regarding the statement, "They should praise with the Bahiṣpavamāna chants in the Sadas," although the result of the action does not accrue to the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*) and the praise is performed by officiating priests (*vyutvikartṛka*), the Ātmanepada ending was employed despite the fact that, according to grammar, the Parasmaipada should have been used—as in the expression "the sacrificers sacrifice" (*yajanti yājakāḥ*).
Similarly, Āśvalāyana uses the suffix *lyap* even in a compound in the rule, "Having sat down facing [the fire], they should offer the expiation oblation" (*pratyasitvā prāyaścittaṃ juhuyuḥ*);
yet he uses it even in a non-compound in the phrase, "having anointed the eyes with clarified butter" (*ājyenākṣiṇī ājya*).
Likewise, in the *Śikṣā*, Nārada employs the expression "one should contemplate Brahman at dawn" (*pratyūṣe brahma cintayet*) in a manner identical to the colloquial word *gāvī* and others;

similarly, Manu also, in the passage "there are knowers of me" (*jñātāraḥ santi me*), formed the *saṃhitā* compound even though one ought to have said *santi ma ity ukte*, thereby disregarding grammar.

Likewise, in the *Mīmāṃsā*, in the rule *gavyasya ca tadādiṣu*, the word *gavya*—which is suitable for correct usage as a derivative or a part of a cow—is employed elsewhere in reference to the *Gavāmayana* sacrifice.

Likewise, where one ought to say "of heaven and earth" (*dyāvāpṛthivyoḥ*), the form *dyāvostatheti cet* was used, which is deficient in its grammatical characteristics; thus, many usages lacking the proper rules have been employed.

Similarly, while the author of the *Gṛhya-sūtra* should have said "smelling on the head" (*mūrdhanyabhighrāṇam*), he used the form *mūrdhanyabhijighrāṇam*, applying the substitute *jighra* in an inappropriate context.
Even regarding the application of grammar and etymology (*nirukta*), there are many instances of usage that fall short of the prescribed rules, such as the expression *yadvad brāhmaṇo bravaṇāt*.

When providing the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) for the word *maṇḍūka* as it occurs in the mantra "Those who sleep for a year," [the author]—demonstrating that the term is based on the quality of speaking—employed the form *bravaṇāt* rather than applying the substitution of *vac* for *brū*, according to the rule *bruvo vaciḥ*. Furthermore, the usage *ubhābhyām* (meaning "that which proceeds from both tusks") has been employed by all commentators, such as Pālakāpya and Rājaputra, independently of grammar; for these forms are not established through the transposition of case endings, verbal suffixes, or voices, nor by the application of the limited scope of the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*.

For example, it occurs as *madhyam āpaḥ tiṣṭhanti* and *nīcīnavāraṃ varuṇaḥ kabandham*. Indeed, the form *āpaḥ* is seen to conform to the grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇānugata*), because it is explained as being the genitive plural of the prātipadika *āp*, which ends in a consonant and has "ām" as its feminine suffix (*liṅga*) in its constant state.
Furthermore, the word *vāra* cannot possibly occur in place of the word *ḍāra* except in the Lāṭa dialect;
therefore, this [treatment] was undertaken without a specific starting point because it is impossible for it to cover the entire scope of the subject matter.
Grammar has been composed there where the meaning consists of following the sequence of words.
Even those who are established on the further shore of grammar themselves employ words such as *gāvī* and the like all the more;
moreover, the use of incorrect words (*apaśabda*) is observed even within the *Sūtra*, *Vārttika*, and *Bhāṣya*.
How could conscious people, mounted on horses, forget their horses? Those who have no following would succeed through [the use of] traps.
(Tantravārtika)
However, in the case of words that follow a different [grammatical] pattern, tradition (smṛti) sublates the application [of a rule].

When there is a conflict between direct perception (pratyakṣa) and tradition, even for a word lacking a formal definition, its correctness (sādhutva) is established through the derivation (nipātana) based on the inference of a tradition regarding the conformity of its constituent parts, arising from the practice of the learned (śiṣṭācāra).

Nor is the conformity with a definition to be disregarded simply because of the contradiction of an action directed toward itself, or because the words of a definition lack self-referential utility; rather, such a word is brought into conformity by means of a definition established in another location.

A word existing in another region is the object to be defined just like any other word; since [the meaning] is already established in common usage, a definition for agriculture and such things is useless.

In the same way, a definition for words established in the Veda is useless. Furthermore, as for the purpose of grammatical exposition (*anvākhyāna*) that was mentioned here—namely, protection (*rakṣā*) and so forth—[it is likewise unnecessary].
Even that [grammar] is not established from another source, nor is it of little importance because it is established from that [source];
for even though the Sāmaveda is well-known through traditional recitation, there exists no [independent] definition for it.
That [grammar] is appropriate, because it establishes everything and is purposeful by means of its content regarding what is to be performed.
He who perceives the many sequences of words and sentences from the sacred tradition would perceive even more clearly the sequence of roots and suffixes;
provided that the proponents of the Veda would accept [the authority] of grammar.
In the houses of grammarians, they shall sever their doubts regarding the Vedas; whatever has a specific meaning in the world, or wherever certain authorities are held to be experts,
let that [meaning] be correctly understood by them from those [authorities].
The third quarter of the first chapter:

However, for those who study the Veda, grammar or grammarians are never of use—aside from more proficient fellow students—in removing ignorance, doubt, or error regarding the letters, words, and sentences of the Veda; therefore, [the knowledge of the Veda arises] from preceptors who are pleased, compassionate, and so forth.
The Veda cannot be destroyed; rather, it is by means of grammar that meanings are established in the world through all languages.
Without grammar, these meanings are accomplished through common usage, even in works such as poetry, without any doubt.
Moreover, this [knowledge of grammar] is not at all useful even for the beautification of poetry;
for due to the fault of grammarians, people employ difficult meters,
yet there is no rule that one must employ what is non-worldly (alaukika).
But if the usage is already established in the world, then a grammatical definition would be useless;
therefore, even in the world, there is never any preservation of words by means of grammar.
And so it is.

How could one whose understanding of these [words] arises from other sources, even without formal grammatical instruction, not obtain a suitable footing in their usage? Or rather, even that which is employed in the sense of an object by means of [corrupt forms] such as *gāvī* and so forth—
Who can prevent one who has acquired proficiency through the mastery of meaning from [attaining it]?
This concludes the third quarter of the first chapter.
Therefore, by means of skill in modification (ūha), in the ritual action, in the auxiliary parts of the ritual, and in the knowledge of the meaning of sentences—
Since [correct forms] are established through usage in common speech and the Vedas, what is the use of grammar?
[The following are exceptions: the limbs (*aṅga*), kinship names (*jñāti*), names of comparison (*upamā*), and the sense organs (*indriya*);
these do not undergo *vṛddhi*, for that [grammar] is indeed difficult to master.
For indeed, the sacred tradition (*āgama*) is declared to be the root of everything that is to be performed, not its purpose;
by the presentation of the study of the six-limbed Veda as being without cause, the uselessness of grammar is stated all the more clearly.

Therefore, the injunction for the mere study of the Veda—namely, "one's own portion of the Veda is to be studied"—is seen in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* and other texts, and it is logical because it has the obligatory duty (*nitya-artha*) as its objective.
Furthermore, the injunction for the study of the auxiliary sciences such as grammar is not heard in any Vedic branch (śākhā).

Moreover, being concerned with a subject matter that has a beginning, it cannot attain the status of being a Veda or the status of being a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), which depends on beginninglessness.
To begin with, its purposefulness is not understood through direct Vedic statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), and so forth.
Or how could there be any artificial constituent part in that which is uncreated?
It has been stated that the Veda is "six-limbed" (ṣaḍaṅga) in dependence upon direct revelation (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), and so forth;
for when divided by those six, it indeed brings about the awakening of the wise.
A qualification can exist through the principles of possibility and deviation;
however, since the Śruti and other means do not deviate [from their respective objects], what could be qualified by those auxiliary parts (*aṅga*)?
That which has been divided into those [means] separately according to cause, form, and fruit—[it is that which is qualified].
Having understood this, he alone fulfills for us the purpose of this injunction;
or rather, the form of the root *dhyai* (to meditate) is based on the idea that "he is to be meditated upon.
He, who is the object of all the meanings of the Vedas and other scriptures, must always be meditated upon by the twice-born.
Within the Veda itself, there exist internal [auxiliaries] such as grammar and the rest;
or perhaps the traditional injunction to study the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) refers to those very things;
or else it may refer to the *Prātiśākhyas*, which are studied just like one's own personal recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*).
Since they are grasped as having that [Veda] as their object, their status as auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) is established therein;

however, for you, there is no connection with what was previously stated, nor is there any traditional scripture (*āgama*). Scripture consists primarily of Vedic study, whereas the instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*) has been proclaimed [as a separate treatise].
Or, if it is argued that "lightness" is merely attributed to "heaviness" through a figurative description of its opposite— just as the word *kātara* [is used for one who is actually brave]—
then it must have been stated that there is no comprehension of the true nature of words without grammar; this same point should have been asserted regarding color, taste, smell, and touch as well.
For this very reason, the second half of the verse must be stated;
no one disputes it, since such [a process] is not observed among the deaf:
"When a name is derived from verbal roots, its connection with action is perceived."
Furthermore, at the time of denotation, there is not even the slightest cognition of that [specific individual],
as long as one remains engaged in the apprehension of the word "wife" (*dāra*) and so forth;
the established meaning of a word does not remain restricted to only that much.
In compounds such as *śvakarṇa* and *ajakarṇa*, when the formation of the compound is understood,
the meaning is seen to be one in which the meanings of the constituent parts have departed, just like the word *vṛtta*.
Similarly, the grammatical instruction (*śabdānuśāsana*) is observed to have a meaning that contradicts the Veda.
If it were understood in that way, its status as an auxiliary to the Vedas (*vedāṅga*) would be contradicted;

for according to the rule *kaneḍhak* and *vāmadevāḍ yaḍ-yaau*, there is the understanding by a grammarian that [the suffixes] refer to the Sāmans seen by Kali and Vāmadeva. This concludes the third quarter of the first chapter.

In the Veda, however, we observe the derivation of meanings in passages such as, “From that, desirable wealth arose; therefore it is called *āmādevyam*,” and “Because he brought it forth (*akālayat*), that is the *kāleyatva* of the *kāleya*. Such instances contradict the understanding that follows strictly from grammar. Likewise, the authors of the *Kalpasūtras* explain meanings—such as the description of a “black-fringed cloth” (*kṛṣṇadaśa*) or a “black-spotted antelope skin” (*kṛṣṇavalaja*)—which cannot be understood even by a hundred grammatical analyses, but which have been handed down through the tradition of those who know the meaning of the Veda. Furthermore, they provide explanations for words like *yūpa* (sacrificial post), whose meanings are understood from the context of preceding and following Vedic sentences.

Just as in these and similar cases, the comprehension of the meaning free from doubt occurs for those who do not depend on grammar, so too in the case of words such as *sthūlapṛṣatī*, the determination of the meaning is established solely through the tradition of successive commentators; thus, grammar need not be relied upon.
Furthermore:

If grammar were intended for the purpose of removing doubt regarding the meaning of the Vedas, then it would resolve such doubts as: do the *arthavādas* convey some independent meaning, or are they subordinate to an injunction (*vidhi*)? Likewise, does the use of *audumbara* wood result in the attainment of strength (*ūrj*), or is it mentioned merely for the sake of praise? Furthermore, it would resolve uncertainties concerning whether a statement is a reason, an injunction, a *hetvarthavāda*, or a mantra; whether its application has a visible or invisible purpose; and whether there is an intention to express the singularity of the cup (*graha-ekatva*), and so forth.

Now, since such matters as these are established by Mīmāṃsā and thus do not require presentation here, the utility of restricting the meaning of certain terms— such as *pṛṣatī*— based on the statements of the authors of the Kalpasūtras is all the more not to be relied upon.
Furthermore, by this very maxim,

"the specific meaning is understood from the commentary" (*vyākhyānato viśeṣapratipattiḥ*), one cannot say, "it is not Veda because of doubt," any more than one can say, "it is not a definition because of doubt."
Just as the Veda exists eternally in its established state, so too does its interpretation always exist;
therefore, interpretations such as *sthāṇu-pṛṣatī* and the like cannot be understood without grammar. Furthermore, the accentuation of words as they are used in common worldly speech is not observed.
Because worldly usage is subject to error, no certain determination of meaning can be derived from it;
however, where there is the well-known knowledge of accents (*svara*) in Vedic sentences,
there is simply no possibility of definitively ascertaining the meanings of the words.

Even in that case, whatever determination may arise from the meaning, context, and so forth, it is established by those very factors; thus, accentuation does not serve as a means of expression. Furthermore, even if its conformity with grammar should somehow be useful for that [determination], it is not for the purpose of worldly usage.
Because it is utterly unused,
grammar should not be studied even for the sake of removing doubt;
for it is not a science that produces the application of specific accents which serve as a factor for determining the meaning of words.

Furthermore, regarding these additional purposes of the instruction of grammar (*śabdānuśāsana*) that have been presented in this manner: some among them are simply incapable of being considered purposes; some are mere semblances of purposes; and some are devoid of any authoritative basis (*apramāṇaka*).

Moreover, as for the prohibition of the word *spa* which was presented as a purpose in the context of the mythological narrative (*purākalpa*) concerning the Asuras, beginning with "those were the Asuras," its status as it actually stands has already been explained previously.

In the case of the statement "the word is defective" (*duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ*), the author reveals his partiality for his own position by inserting the term "word" (*śabdapada*) through the medium of a mantra-passage recited by the *Śikṣākāra* and well-known among many people.
Indeed, when a defective mantra is employed, a transgression (*pratyavāya*) for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is certainly accepted;

for, as seen in such passages as "That which the Hotṛ utters, speech indeed abandons that sacrificer," a fault resulting in harm to the sacrificer is observed whenever mantras used by any officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) are corrupted.
Likewise, the fault of destroying the application of a mantra is illustrated by the example: "O Indra, let your enemy prosper" (*indraśatru vardhasva*).

As for what is stated in the *Nirukta*—"That which is studied without being understood [is mastered] merely through recitation"—we have already addressed that while explaining the word *artha* in the very first sūtra, as the reason for transgressing the traditional rule regarding ritual bathing (*snāna-smṛti*). For if we did not transgress it, we would be rendering the Veda—which actually possesses meaning—meaningless; indeed, its purpose is observed to be the comprehension of ritual action (*karma-avabodhana*).
If it is argued that the Veda does not shine forth because its meaning is not elucidated by grammar, then [the response is]:
this is indeed true;
however, grammar has no utility in that regard.
Because [grammar] is not an authoritative source regarding the production of ritual applications (*karmaprayoga*).
If it is argued that this is a science of words (*śabdaśāstra*), then even in those cases, there would be no established authority due to the lack of a foundation as previously stated.

Therefore, it is appropriate that the purpose belongs to the *Kalpasūtras*, *Nirukta*, and *Mīmāṃsā* alone, since they are capable of serving the understanding of the meaning of the studied Mantras and Brāhmaṇas; but this does not apply to grammar. Furthermore, the statement "he who employs [it correctly]" is understood to have the correct employment of the words of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas as its very purpose.
"Because it deviates from what has been traditionally handed down and because of the use of corrupt words (*apaśabda*), it becomes defective.

From this statement, it is understood that there is also a restatement of the defect known from the scriptural injunction: "If the Vedic word is corrupted during the study, teaching, or performance of sacrifices, the sacrifice shall suffer ruin. Thus, the defect is recognized through this very declaration.

The *Tantravārttika* states that one who is "conversant with the application of speech" (*vāgyogavid*) is a person who, through observing extensive worldly usage and so forth, has mastered the relationship between words and their meanings on a daily basis; who, in Vedic prose (*brāhmaṇa-vākya*), has discerned the specific syntactical structures (*vacana-vyakti*) by determining the status of what is being referred to (*uddiśyamāna*), what is being enjoined (*upādīyamāna*), and the distinction between subordinate and principal elements; and who, in the case of mantras, knows whether a word is directly enjoined or not, and whether it is capable of manifesting its own meaning or the meaning of another. Such a person alone is called "conversant with the application of speech," and not a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*), because for a grammarian, the science of grammar does not provide instruction on the production of such [Vedic] applications.

Furthermore, as for the statement "even those who are ignorant," which is a reproach directed at those unaware of the protracted vowel (*pluta*) at the end of a name during a return greeting—that reproach applies because the *pluta* (the three-mora vowel) is not commonly known in that context. Since the application of the final syllable of the name has been established through the teachings of Manu and others, this [prose passage] lacks the status of being a scripture (*śāstra*) for the production of that specific usage.

Nor, on that account, is it assumed by Manu and others—through this cited verse—that the knowledge of the distinction between correct words (*śabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*) is achieved, nor is its utility established, by means of analyzing the division of stems (*prakṛti*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), and so forth.

As for the claim that the *prayāja* offerings must be performed with their case-endings (*savibhaktika*), this is established by the instruction of the ritualists (*yājñika*). Furthermore, since the case-endings are observed in the Brāhmaṇa texts within the context of the six-day sacrifice (*ṣaḍaha*)—such as "Agni shall slay the Vṛtras," "Agni, the greatest slayer of Vṛtra, for you," and "Agni is kindled by Agni"—the performance of the *prayāja* offerings with their case-endings is accomplished even without grammar, simply by observing the various case-forms. Therefore, grammar is not a necessary science (*śāstra*) for this purpose.
"He who arranges this speech word by word or syllable by syllable becomes a *śrāvijña*"; thus it is said that one who has studied the *Sāmaveda* correctly is so designated.

Likewise, regarding the statement "Speech is measured in four quarters," those [four quarters] have been explained by the etymologists (*nairukta*) as following the abundance of purposes such as the syllable *oṃ* and the great invocations (*mahāvyāhṛti*), even though they are analyzed based on the similarity of phonemes and letters; in that regard, grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) has no authority whatsoever.

As for the reliance on the grammarians' doctrine consisting of the fourfold division of nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles— that too does not depend significantly on grammar, precisely because that fourfold division is established in common worldly usage.
Furthermore, if this were the subject matter [of the Vedānta], the third quarter of the first chapter, stating "Humans speak only a fourth part of speech," would become entirely incoherent.

Since all four classes of words are spoken by humans, the meaning of this mantra is therefore explained here as being consistent with its preceding and following context: "There are indeed four immeasurable steps. Those by which speech proceeds—that is, by which it is understood—are these four means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) known as perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), comparison (*upamāna*), and postulation (*arthāpatti*).

In that context, those portions which are understood through the three means of knowledge known as inference, comparison, and presumptive testimony—arising from the observation of similarity between archetypal and modified ritual injunctions, or from the impossibility [of otherwise accounting for a fact]—do not move nor are they uttered, precisely because they are established by those [means].

However, that portion which cannot be conveyed by them, the fourth part, which is to be apprehended through direct perception, human students speak of and recite; this is the meaning. And from among the six means of knowledge, two have been excluded because they consist of words.
First of all, non-existence (*abhāva*) cannot be a word because its very nature consists in being an object of non-existence.
Furthermore, since speech itself is the essence of *gama*, it is untenable to rely on the status of being a "word" for that which is dependent upon speech as it is being uttered.
And because it is already included within perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is not mentioned separately.

However, the meaning of the mantra "catvāri śṛṅgā" (four horns), which is employed by the Hotṛ priest during the *viṣuvat* sacrifice in connection with the clarified butter (*ājya*), has already been explained in the section on Mantras (*Mantrādhikaraṇa*).
Nor is there any dependence upon grammar here.

As for the description of a different meaning—based merely on a commonality of number, such as "the four classes of words are the horns"—without regard for the application to the ritual act, that is nothing more than a display of verbal skill produced by grammar.
Since such [arguments] could also be applied to the Vaiśeṣika and other systems by those proficient in them, they are not to be respected.

Furthermore, when the mantra “uta tvaḥ paśyan” is understood as being intended solely to praise the knowledge of word-meanings and sentence-meanings arising from reliance upon the Lokāyata, Nirukta, Kalpasūtra, and Mīmāṃsā, it does not show regard for grammar.

Likewise, this mantra “saktumiva titaunā” should also be described, as before, as being intended to praise the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedic syllables purified by the study of one's own recitation (svādhyāya) without interruption.
“An āhitāgni who employs an incorrect word”—this has already been explained.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that in the naming of a child (nāmakaraṇa), a name beginning with a sonant letter and ending in a suffix consisting of two or four syllables is to be adopted while excluding secondary derivatives (taddhita)—this is because even in grammar, the designations of "primary" (kṛt) and "secondary" (taddhita) are employed only as they were previously established; because the measurement of syllables depends upon perception and subsequent memory; and because the properties such as being sonant are enumerated in the Śikṣās and Prātiśākhyas. Therefore, all Vedic scholars can easily form names without depending on grammar, for grammar is required only as a science for the derivation of word-usage (prayoga).

In the verse "sudevo 'si varuṇa," although the seven case-endings (*vibhakti*) themselves are explained as the "seven rivers" (*saptasindhu*), nevertheless, their designation as "case-endings" is either established by grammar or accepted as already well-known. As for their actual forms of usage, these are directly perceived in both common parlance and the Veda according to their respective divisions; thus, they are not described in this way solely in dependence upon grammar.

Furthermore, when the seven *sindhus* are understood as being merely rivers—either in the context of praising the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and the priests, or as the seven types of speech belonging to the *hotṛ* priests, or as the seven musical tones belonging to the *sāman* chants, or as the divisions thereof—then, because they fall within the domain of historians and ritualists, they are indeed the subject matter of grammar. Now, once the correctness (*sādhutva*) of refined (*saṃskṛta*) words has been established, it must be stated: for what [word] is there refinement, and how is it performed?
First of all, there is no such thing as the embellishment (saṃskriyā) of the universal "sound-ness" (śabdatva), the universal "letter-ness" (varṇatva), or the individual manifestation (vyakti);
for, due to the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) [of such an embellishment] to all things, no fixed determination (vyavasthā) can be established.
By this, the theory of the embellishment of the individual manifestation of letters is also refuted.
Thus, each individual conditioned factor (*saṃskāra*) is not unwholesome for anyone;
yet there is no such thing as a "collection" of them, because they do not exist simultaneously.
Even when present, the momentary conditioned factor does not endure at all.

It would perish at that very moment before it could be consecrated; just as in the case of groats consecrated by a *homa* sacrifice, once they have been reduced to ashes, it is impossible for them to be seen again or employed [elsewhere]. If one were to accept that the groats are the objects to be consecrated—as indicated by the accusative case—then the *homa*, its performance, and the injunction would all result in futility. Therefore, one does not rely on such a consecration. In the same way, if one holds the view that the individual sound (*śabda-vyakti*) is momentary and undergoes consecration, there follows the consequence of total futility.

Furthermore, as for this "lack of restriction" (aniyama) which was stated—that whether sound is eternal or produced, the grammatical rules (*lakṣaṇa*) must be applied in both cases—that is intended solely to reveal a fear of logical analysis, or perhaps for the purpose of confusing the students; it is not fit to be accepted.

Moreover, on the view that [sound] is produced, this would be a "refinement" (*saṃskāra*) rather than a true production (*utpāda*). Consequently, the rule would even more clearly result in being a non-authoritative branch of usage (*prayoga-utpatti-aśākhata*). Or, if the Veda itself were composed of words produced by grammar...
Consequently, like grammar, even the Veda would lack authority;
therefore, if it were eternally refined while abandoning its lack of fixed order,
then even that refinement called "modification" could not possibly apply to it.
Furthermore, regarding words whose meanings are already perceived, there is no purpose served by something unseen (adṛṣṭa).

For it is not accepted that a result arises from the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of rice grains intended for consumption; nor is an injunction for grammatical analysis (*vyākriyā-vidhi*) possible, as it would be like an injunction for [the sprinkling of] sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and so forth.
