In the world, that which expresses [meaning] directly is called the *vācaka* (denotative word), while that which indicates it through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) is clearly the *vācaka*. Furthermore, it has been stated that remembrance [of the connection] is understood more easily through established usage (*ācāra*).

Just as, even among Brahmins and others who possess the same physical form of head, hands, and so forth, and who are perceived by worldly view as being intermingled, the determination of their specific caste (*varṇa*) occurs solely through the remembrance of their relationship with their mother and father; in the same way, the determination of correct words (*sādhuśabda*) also occurs. Thus, there is no contradiction with worldly experience.

This distinction between correct and incorrect words is established from the very beginning through tradition and is also apprehended by direct perception, just as experts distinguish between different colors;
therefore, one who would attempt to establish a confusion of words through mere reasoning [is mistaken].
Its contradiction by perception is also like the contradiction regarding the mixing of phonemes (*varṇasaṃkara*).

Just as in the case of the mixing of phonemes, [the existence of sphoṭa] is contradicted by auditory cognition whose object is the form of the expressive [phonemes]—which are remembered, which have not perished, and whose sequence is determined—which are manifested at specific times such as those of *hasva* (short) and so on, and which are free from defects such as being swallowed, suppressed, or nasalized (*ambūkṛta*); thus, like the high-pitched accent (*udātta*) and so forth, they are perceived by the sense organ.

Furthermore, there exists an infallible mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the analysis of roots, suffixes, augments, modifications, substitutes, and so forth, as found in the study of grammar, which facilitates the comprehension of meanings encountered in linguistic usage occurring at a time subsequent to that [acquisition].

Moreover, this very same subject matter—and others like it—pertains to both types of scripture, namely those in the form of *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, whose purposes are: (1) to establish the means for achieving the accomplishment of heaven and the assistance of sacrifices, and (2) to provide knowledge of the nature of what is beneficial and what is harmful.
For one who speaks using uncorrupted words, the benefits of heaven and sacrifice are attained.

Furthermore, in the case of one who speaks with corrupt words (*apaśabda*) during a sacrificial rite—as if speaking a falsehood—there arises the contingency of a deficiency in the ritual (*ṛtuvaiguṇya*), caused by the performance of what is prohibited.
As it has been stated: "One who knows the proper application of speech is defiled by corrupt words."

Furthermore, since these two [correct words and correct meanings] cannot be established by anything other than the treatise (*śāstra*), they are the exclusive domain of the treatise. Moreover, because one should speak with uncorrupted words—desiring to assist in the attainment of heaven and sacrifice—by means of both injunctions and prohibitions, and not with corrupted ones, there is no consequence of having to postulate infinite injunctions and prohibitions for every single word and corrupt form (*apaśabda*).

Nor is it the case that a treatise must consist solely of injunctions and prohibitions rather than serving to inform one of the nature of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*); this is established by the command of the Lord (*Īśvara*).

Furthermore, the purpose of the scriptural passages such as "This Self, O Maitreyī, is indeed imperishable and of an indestructible nature," along with the four sections of the *Daśvīnas* and the supplementary statements such as "At the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the Vinaśana," is not found to be the mere exposition of the reality of objects;
nor is there any contradiction in their being designated by the term "scripture" (*śāstra*) even if they do not establish that [reality].

Even if there were some convention that a scripture must consist exclusively of injunctions and prohibitions, nevertheless, an injunction of this kind is certainly possible: namely, "Such correct words are to be understood."

When one who desires an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa-phala*) known from another statement wishes to speak using words that have not perished, he would employ these very forms and their respective sequences of phonemes (*varṇa*), neither more nor less; for as long as it is possible to demonstrate injunctions and prohibitions through such forms, the status of the scripture (*śāstra*) as its subject matter is established.

Furthermore, by analogy with words such as "Devadatta" or "that-ness" (*tattā*), which are used by both elders and children without doubt, it can be understood that all words must necessarily exist in both perished and unperished forms.
In this way, by analogy with the non-destruction of Vedic words that conform to grammar, one should also demonstrate the comparison of such worldly words to being destroyed.
Likewise, there is first a determination of correctness obtained through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), based on the expressive power (*vācakatva*) evoked by the cognition of worldly meaning.
Following that, there is the exclusive exposition of correct forms, excluding corrupted forms caused by negligence, laziness, or defects in the organs of articulation.
Since it cannot be explained otherwise, the knowledge of grammatical correctness is indeed established by another *arthāpatti* (presumption);
thus,
although there is usage by those who are unlearned, it is characterized by confusion.
Even so, those who are diligent will discern [the correct forms] just as [one discerns] Brahmins and others;
just as in the examination of gems there is the definition of what is genuine and what is spurious,
so too is the determination of the correct word established through grammar.
Neither a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) nor an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) is intended here with regard to the exclusion [of improper speech] and so forth;
rather, why is it not accepted that the restrictive injunction effects only its own permanence?
In this context, for one seeking the highest good, the use of correct speech is necessarily enjoined.
For by performing that [action] through a mandatory injunction (*niyoga*), one will accomplish the *apūrva*.

Alternatively, corrupt words (*apaśabda*) do not at all attain denotative power as distinct from correct ones—unlike multiple substances, qualities, and so forth, which share a single action as their object; rather, it is those [correct words] that would be excluded by the restriction to correct forms.
However,...
For example,
it is prescribed that one who is "burnt" (vidagdha) must first be censured for such faults as being "belonging to the Nairṛtas," and so forth, before being subjected to the heat [of the ordeal].
Likewise, a defective word is censured on account of its harshness, its phonemes, and so on.

Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa must not speak like a barbarian (*mleccha*), nor should he use corrupt speech; for that which is a corrupt word (*apaśabda*) is indeed a barbarian. This person is a "barbarian" because he has strayed from the accomplishment of meaning—which is the function of words—due to the destruction [of correct usage] caused by negligence and other factors. According to the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*), "one becomes a *mleccha* in indistinct speech," it follows that such [corrupt speech] must not be employed; thus there is a prohibition. Furthermore, the injunction, "Therefore, this articulated speech (*vyākṛtā vāk*) is uttered," is intended to establish the rule of unimpaired usage. Others say: [these rules are stated] so that others may easily ascend to the path of correctness and not be forced into distress.
Those who are capable and vigilant may employ [these forms] without being hindered;
others too, though they be ordinary people, when engaged in business with devotees,
employ them as well upon approaching those [devotees].

As for the claim that "it is not a scripture because it lacks the production of an application for an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha), since it is satisfied by making known a seen purpose (dṛṣṭārtha)," it is replied: when one [thing] serves two purposes, the cause is the principle of "separateness of connection" (saṃyogapṛthaktva); and this is understood from both the context (prakaraṇa) and the detached statements (anārabhyavāda). In that case—

For that which is for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*), because its means have not yet been established, is capable of encompassing all unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*); thus, while it assimilates the transcendental result of the restriction (*niyamāpūrva*) to itself, it renders the mention of a fruit in the text a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). However, since a restriction for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) must necessarily have a purpose, and since the attainment of that [fruit] is already more than sufficiently established even through yawning, falling asleep, or other such acts, it lacks the capacity to subsist upon an unrequested transcendental result of restriction. Therefore, one must necessarily resort to the very fruits mentioned in the explanatory praise—such as "the cow of plenty in the heavenly world" (*svargaloke kāmadhuk*)—as the actual result.

As for the objection that it is not known which apūrva of the injunction depends upon this [speech], it is stated here: "On account of the specific context, the refinement of that which is connected with it is like that of the substance" (PMS 3.1.12). For, since the word *brāhmaṇa* occurring within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma refers to the sacrificer who is the means (*sādhana*) for that apūrva, the apūrva of the rule regarding correct speech consists in the refinement of the sacrificer who is the means for that [sacrificial] apūrva.

The duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), however, are understood to be based on that [knowledge] alone, for the purpose of establishing the fitness to receive the fruit, according to the maxim: "Because it is the primary factor, they are like the ritual acts" (*tatpradhānatvāt karmavat*).

Even in the case of a statement concerning the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), because the properly known and correctly employed [knowledge] brings to mind both the knower and the agent who employs it, and because the fruit of the action belongs to them, it results as being based on the knower and the agent, just like the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the primary sacrifice and so forth.

Just as in the case of the rule "one sprinkles the oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja*," even though the remnant is indicated by the third case (*tṛtīyā*), it is determined to be the object of refinement (*saṃskārya*) because it is useful for the ritual action; so too is it for the Brāhmaṇa—therefore, there is no fault. Furthermore, that which is a subordinate state (*guṇabhāva*) in the sacrifice is actually a state of primacy (*pradhānatā*) in terms of refinement.
For being a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāritva*) does not constitute the utility of that which is directly connected [to the primary act].

Even though the prohibition of [acts such as] resorting to women, eating meat, and so forth— which serve human purposes— is intended as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice due to its dependence on the context (*prakaraṇa*), nevertheless, when both the restrictive rule (*niyama*) and the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) depend upon an utterance for the sake of another, they are understood to have the person present as their primary referent, because they require a purpose for themselves.

Furthermore, the objection that its status as a scripture (*śāstra*) is inherently subverted by its artificiality would contradict common consensus, like the statement "the moon is not the moon. For one who would attempt to negate its established status as a scripture through mere reasoning—
The third quarter of the first chapter will also prevent the eternality of the Veda, just as iron [prevents fire].
A son who behaves improperly toward others is restrained by his parents.
Of those two, who would be the restrainer of the undisciplined one?
Indeed, he who is angry and kills another cuts off that person's limbs;
when his limbs have been cut, how much destruction could there be for him thereafter?

Since it has been established through reasoning that the Śruti and Smṛti possess the status of authoritative means of knowledge, who could claim that the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) lack authority or do not constitute part of the Veda?
Nevertheless, the term "Smṛti" does not denote the auxiliary sciences.
Nevertheless, there is no refutation of their status as scripture (*śāstra*) or their validity (*prāmāṇya*);
for it has been previously demonstrated that they possess equal authority according to traditional recollection (*smaraṇa*), and that they are rooted in the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, because its fruits are both seen and unseen, the status of the Veda as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not undermined;
for that which is said to be of human origin has an impossible foundation,
and its lack of stability at the root is like the word of a person blind from birth regarding colors.
Disagreement is not at all a reason for the invalidity of Smṛtis;
for indeed, a great deal of disagreement is observed even among the Śrutis themselves.
Indeed, the authority of Smṛtis depends upon their conformity with the source (the Veda), and that [conformity] is established through the absence of such disagreement.
And regarding the aspect of being a means for establishing the Dharma, there is no disagreement whatsoever.
However, as for the disagreement concerning the grammatical explanations (*anvākhyāna*), it does not constitute a fault because the illustrative examples (*lakṣya*) differ.
As for the phrase "or rather, its status as a valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇatva*): [the rest follows].
Since it is rooted in the Veda, nothing at all is faulty; and as for those who advocate the addition of further rules, they rely on other Smṛtis,
as follows:
Since the Ādhvaryava [ritual] is found in the Vājasaneyi-śākhā and the Bahvṛca [ritual] in the Caraka-śākhās, one does not disregard it as having a limited scope merely on that account;
therefore, this too is not a defect. As for the criticism that the author of the Sūtra failed to state the purpose:
And truthful speech is established in all the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* texts as a means for attaining heaven and as a means for performing sacrifice.
Truth is of two kinds: verbal truth (*śabda-satya*) and objective truth (*artha-satya*).

In this regard, just as speaking words whose meaning is consistent with reality and uncorrupted is a means to the highest good (*śreyas*), so too is speaking words that are verbally true to reality; and just as the opposite of objective truth leads to sin (*pratyavāya*), so too does the speaking of words contrary to what was intended at the time of their application.

And it has been stated that the knowledge of the correctness of words arises from a specific application to grammar; nor do some object against the intended purpose of grammar. Rather, the question is whether that very purpose is logically tenable or not—this is a different point—and grammar is employed for two restrictive purposes (niyama).

The attainment of the results of sacrifice and heaven through the prior employment [of words] based on the knowledge of correct words is indeed rooted in the Veda, since it has no other source of authority. Therefore, this regulation of *dharma* is established everywhere by the scripture known as the Veda; for knowledge is understood to function as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*).
And because of the restrictive statement that it is a subordinate limb (*parāṅga*) elsewhere than in the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavijñāna*), [it applies only to ritual acts].

Nor does the injunction of knowledge serve to exclude the connection with ritual action; for even the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, which are prescribed for each specific stage of life (*āśrama*) and caste (*varṇa*), must be performed for the purpose of exhausting the accumulation of previously committed evil and for the purpose of avoiding future transgressions caused by non-performance. Since these rites have distinct purposes and follow distinct paths, it is impossible for them to stand in a relationship of sublation (*bādha*), optionality (*vikalpa*), or mutual subsidiarity (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*).

However, because the knowledge of words is invariably an auxiliary to usage and occurs even earlier [than the usage], it is impossible for it to have a separate connection with a fruit; thus, it is determined that its fruit consists solely in being preceded by knowledge prior to usage.

As for the objection that a connection between the fruit of usage and the knowledge of grammar—which begins with the first grammarian—and the knowledge preceding it cannot be based on an eternal injunction (*anādividhi*), that is not a valid criticism, because, like the series of sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) and so forth, the tradition of grammar is beginningless.
Therefore, the expression "this has been analyzed" (*eṣā vyākṛtā*) declares the eternality of the practice of grammar.

Furthermore, that which was stated by Manu among the "purifiers of the assembly" (*paṅktipāvana*) as being derived from the Veda itself—"He who explains speech and he who investigates the sacrifice"—must necessarily rely upon this very knowledge of grammar, since it concerns a subject distinct from the study of the Vedas and the investigation of sacrifices mentioned earlier and later; thus, its eternity is established.
Having set aside this point pertaining to the Sannyāsins, what follows shall now be discussed.
For the sake of establishing the fruit of the means [of knowledge], this is first investigated:

it is said that if there were non-difference between the words and their meanings in both common worldly usage (*loka*) and the Veda, then, by means of following the numerous usages found in the linguistic practice of the elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), one would be able to determine, within this inquiry into the denotation of individuals (*vyakti*) and forms (*ākṛti*), whether something is denotable or not denotable.

For when a word is employed in the presence of many conflated meanings, it produces a cognition regarding only a certain portion of those meanings; thus, even by that part of the denotation which is understood as undifferentiated,
when the accomplishment of the ritual act is being performed through that which is endowed with all its properties,
everything— such as the offering of curd— is indeed characterized by purpose in the world.
But when [the inquiry] is undertaken under its influence, it is not to be considered as having the nature of a scriptural injunction;
therefore, this investigation arises in the world as being purposeless.
It would be purposeful in the Veda, yet the means for such knowledge is difficult to obtain.

Therefore, since the word and its meaning are non-different, the investigation into the individual (*vyakti*) and the form (*ākṛti*) need not be undertaken in any way for the sake of distinguishing between what is denotable and what is not denotable.

Consequently, having determined that the section on form (*ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*) must be commenced because it is both logical and purposeful when the worldly and Vedic word-meanings are identical, whereas it would be unnecessary under the theory of difference, the theory of difference is first set forth.

If there were a difference between the word and its meaning in the world and in the Veda—due to differences in form caused by fixed and unfixed accents, the rules of *chandas*, the elision or addition of stems and suffixes, and the modification or presence of phonemes; or due to differences regarding times of study and non-study (*adhyāya*/*anadhyāya*), the initiated and the uninitiated, the three or four castes, their eligibility or ineligibility for use, the oral tradition received from a teacher propitiated through service, the specific application of words, or the difference in the meanings of those words—then, because worldly usage would prevail over the Veda, the Veda would be devoid of meaning, and thus Dharma would not be characterized by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*).

One might think there is a difference in form due to the accent, based on whether it is a time for study or not, and through its connection with meanings such as the slaying of Vṛtra; however, like an unintelligent sentence, this results in a breakdown of the sentence structure, as in the case of the "upside-down carriage" (uttānavahana) statement.

Furthermore, since all Vedic passages are distinct from one another, no comprehension of meaning can arise from them even through their sequential order. This applies to the *tantravārtika* concerning the properties of *yājyā* and other mantras.

It might be argued that there is a distinction between words and their meanings—whether worldly or Vedic—due to two types of differentiation: first, through the fixed arrangement of specific words and sentences (*niyatapada-vākya-racanā*), and second, through the differentiation of conventional designations (*vyapadeśa*). To this, it is replied: if such a distinction were real, all Vedic words would be devoid of meaning because their relationship [to objects] would be unestablished; consequently, there would be an absolute absence of injunctions for performance, which consist of the connection between actions and their factors (*kriyā-kāraka-saṃsarga*).

While one ought to say "the oneness of word and meaning" (*śabdārtha-ekatva*), the expression "oneness of object" (*arthaikatva*) was used with the thought that the statement of the oneness of the word is established by the very result [of the argument].

Alternatively, because "object" (*vastu*) and "thing-in-itself" (*mātra*) are synonyms, the statement regarding their identity of meaning is made with the intention that both are common [to the two positions].

The consequence of the absence of injunctions for practice (*prayoga-codanā*) applies only when debating with a proponent of the establishment of that [object] within the framework of either the opponent's position (*parapakṣa*) or one's own position (*svapakṣa*), and not with anyone else; therefore, he says: "Let this purpose be stated as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
That is now being explained.

The various alternative reasons [for the identity of words] are as follows: because of the non-differentiation of the cognition in the form of recognition; or because of the non-differentiation of the forms of both objects of knowledge as they are being known; or because of the non-differentiation in the designation of the subject matter—namely the words and phonemes—which have become the basis for the collection of sentences and their constituent parts; or because of the non-differentiation of the places of articulation, the instruments, and the efforts of those who utter them in that manner; or because of the non-differentiation in the conformity with the greater number [of grammatical rules] by those who know the technical definitions (*lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, even when there is a hearing of a different word-form (*vācyāntara*), it is merely a difference in secondary qualities (*guṇamātra*) so long as it does not contradict the unity of the meaning, as stated in the *Yathāśruta-vāda* and other such works.
Even if this were so, if a property distinct from "cowness" and the like exists [in the word],

there is no difference in the object [denoted] by virtue of this alone, because no specific distinction is expressed. Likewise, if the status of being a "gold coin" belongs to a tree on Mount Meru, then why would the word [for it] in the world of the gods not denote a different object?
Furthermore, if everything were unestablished, not even a single thing could be understood as such;
therefore, for those things that are unestablished, there can be no determination of their difference from other unestablished things.
Although the author of the Bhāṣya has presented two [reasons] later on, [the same logic applies].

Nevertheless, commentators may here propose other alternative positions as well. These positions, moreover, should be applied by interweaving them with one another—through gender, case-role, and number, both in their combined and uncombined forms. Thus, is it the action (*kṛti*) that is qualified by the relation alone, or by the aggregate [of the two], or by the two alternatives, or by the two combined?
Likewise, regarding this [entity] as qualified, is it the form (*ākṛti*) alone, or the individual (*vyakti*) alone; or, if they are conceptualized, are they combined?
Similarly, is it the individual alone qualified by the form, or the form alone qualified by the relationship; or is it a conceptual alternative, or a combination?
This same logic should be applied to the aggregate as well.

Likewise, one must consider the following alternative views regarding the qualified aggregate: is it the individual qualified by the relation and qualified by the form (*ākṛti*), or is it the individual qualified by the form and qualified by the relation? Or is it a case of option (*vikalpa*), or is it a case of conjunction (*samuccaya*)? In this manner, the various positions concerning the qualified aggregate should be postulated.

Similarly, is it the individual qualified by the relation which is itself qualified by the genus (*jāti*), or is it the genus qualified by the relation which is itself qualified by the individual? This concludes the third quarter of the first chapter.
Is it a genus qualified by a relation, or an alternative, or a combination?

Thus, by way of summary, the state of being qualified should likewise be applied: is the individual qualified by a genus qualified by a relation alone, or is the genus qualified by such an individual alone, or is it an alternative, or a combination?
In this same manner, [the analysis] applies again to the nature of the word itself in relation to the genus and so forth.
Conceptual construction occurs with one, two, three, four, five, or six [factors]; in all cases, a slight difference is perceived through the sense organ and its indicative mark (liṅga).
However, by means of a word, even the most subtle portion of a real entity (vastu) is distinguished.
In this regard, the position that "it is the form alone" is firmly established on one side;
however, all others follow the view that the individual instance is primary.
It is not because of this [position] that [the other views] are untrue, nor are they without purpose.
For these [explanations] are conceptual constructs intended to expand the wisdom of one who desires to know;
therefore,
since the nature of the *ākṛti* has already been determined in the very first chapter (*pāda*), the present question and answer serve little purpose.

The generic form (*ākṛti*) is merely the commonality among substances, qualities, and actions; furthermore, it consists of the distinctions such as air-ness, fire-ness, water-ness, self-ness, earth-ness, and jar-ness, which are fully realized in their respective individual instances (*vyakti*).
Just as [the discussion of] the Brāhmaṇa, Kauṇḍinya, Kaṭha, and so forth is concluded,
so too are the qualities, the nature of action, the state of being a form, birth, and so on, which constitute the third quarter (pāda) of the first chapter.
It has been stated that [the sacrifice] is divided by means of the elements (dhātu) which are not synonymous;
furthermore, there is the enumeration of the various forms, the qualities, and the different sections. However, other teachers consider this distinction to belong to the ritual actions themselves.
Alternatively, due to the difference [in the materials], there may be a single form despite the diversity of locations.
And because of the non-distinction between color and sound, Jaimini will indeed say this:
"Thus, everything that is a universal of objects is the *ākṛti*";
or else, if the commonality of configuration is taken as the *ākṛti*.

Since this would apply equally to horses and other animals, there would be a confusion of forms (*ākṛti-saṃkara*). Upon close examination, that [form] is found to be nothing other than the universal (*jāti*); and by the principle that "that which is a universal is indeed the commonality," it follows that [the form is the universal]. Therefore, the suspicion that the first pāda refers to shape as the denotation of *ākṛti*—based on the examples of the *rucaka*, *svastika*, and *vardhamānaka*—is set aside by the question and answer beginning with "it was like something unseen" (*adarśanavat*).
Therefore, whatever commonality exists among substances, qualities, and actions prior to their individual manifestations, all that is intended by the term *ākṛti*;
it is with this in mind that the word "mere" (*mātra*) is employed.
An individual manifestation (*vyakti*), on the other hand, consists of specific, non-common characteristics.
Some say:
the unique particulars (*viśeṣa*) themselves are the individual (*vyakti*),
because there is no individual apart from the particular.
And these [distinctions] are seen elsewhere as well, even among other species;
for although distinctions such as the *śāvaleyā* (the brindled cow) and others exist among the various offspring, those which were seen as divided are seen again as united.
The universal (piṇḍa) is indicated by them through its commonality with the individual; thus,
there is a refutation of the view that "there is a referent for all words," as in the case of [words for] the unseen force (apūrva),
deities, heaven, and the path.
However, because universals are defined through their division into classes (*kacyā*),
that [term "existence"] is not applied to cows and the like; for those who say "these are existence," they do not mean pure existence, but rather existence as qualified by its adjuncts.
Indeed, it is impossible to say that they "speak" in either of two ways, because neither is possible.
First, if they were pure expressions [of existence], then since all of them would convey the same single meaning, it would follow that they are synonyms;
furthermore, because of this tautology, the employment of the word *asti* (is) would be untenable.
Even when considering factors such as place and time, it is not proper to assert non-existence regarding existence (*sattā*),
because, by virtue of its omnipresence and eternity, it pervades all places and times;
for that which is expressed by the word "exists" (*asti*) is the second transformation of being (*bhāvavikāra*).
In all things, from the states of arising and transformation up to the point of destruction, the apprehension of the form of the thing is observed.

Therefore, even if it is asserted that the "Great Universal" (mahāsāmānya) is the denotable object, then since the meaning of all words is the thing itself, one must certainly say that the definition of what is to be communicated is "the thing," and not "non-existence."

Furthermore, the words *sat* and *sattā* do not function by abandoning their constituent meanings; rather, as with the word *bhavat*, "being" (*sadbhāva*) is *sattā*. It is not according to the Vaiśeṣika technical definition—that *sattā* is that universal which is the cause of the cognition "existent" (*sat*) with respect to substances, qualities, and actions—by which such a genus (*jāti*) is to be understood.
This is because the two cognitions "existence" (*astitva*) and "is-ness" (*astitā*) are observed [to occur].

That word expressing the entity "existent" (sat), which resembles a verb—such as in the case of *asti-tīrā gauḥ*—cannot be classified as a compound ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) because such a formation has not been specifically enumerated. Therefore, it must be accepted that the term *kṣīra* forms a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the indeclinable (*avyaya*) *sad*, which is capable of being a nominal stem (*subanta*) through the suffix *-dāṇ* (as in *sad-dāṇ*), in order to convey the meaning of another word. In that context, this word expresses the sense of "existent," as evidenced by the production of the cognition: "a cow possessing milk" (*sat-kṣīrā gauḥ*).

Furthermore, since the entity exists, the logicians—disregarding the word *asti* (is) which is actually employed, and instead adopting the word *sat* (being) as being closely proximate to its meaning, and [ignoring] the suffix *-tal* in *devatvam* as a *svārthika* suffix (denoting the same base meaning) just as in *devane-tal*—and failing to accept that the cognition of an agent qualified by the meaning expressed by the root *as* is intended here, they take the words *sat* and *sattā* as denoting merely the bare meaning of the root. Thus, they postulate that "Being" (*sattā*), which is the denotation of the word *sat*, is the "Great Universal" (*mahāsāmānya*).

Furthermore, due to a lack of regard for the aforementioned deliberations, even those learned in words and sentences have neglected this [term], so that it has reached a state as if it were well-established, whereby the word *vastu* (entity) can even be imagined to be denotable by words such as "cow" (*go*).
For the word *vastu*, being a conventional term (*rūḍhi*), refers to a universal (*sāmānya*) based on neither individuals nor classes; this is understood from its meaning through words such as "cow."

Whatever reason was given for rejecting the position that the word denotes the individual qualified by the form, or the position that it denotes the form qualified by the individual, that same reason is easily applicable here as well;
for in those cases, it would follow that the qualifier must necessarily be denoted first.

Since it is impossible to denote a qualified object without first denoting its qualifier, and because the qualifier is intrinsically connected with the qualified object, the cognition of "Being" (sattā) is established simply through its connection with "cowness" (gotva), which is the previously denoted qualifier.
Therefore, the postulation of a denotative power for that [Being] does not proceed, as the claim that its result is otherwise established by presumptive implication (arthāpatti) is refuted.
This same reason serves to refute the view that the word denotes "Being" as qualified by the individual (vyakti).

Furthermore, the hypothesis that a single *sattā* (Being) is denoted—preceded by the denotation of individuals and the infinite expressive powers of words based on knowledge of their impermanent relations—is untenable, just like the position that only the individual is denoted.
As for the statement, "It is equal to the *apūrva*, the deity, and heaven," [it refers to the same].

Some [words] imply existence through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), while others, being expressive only of specific meanings presented by the remainder of a sentence or by another sentence, lead to the cognition of existence by means of their own invariably concomitant meanings; thus they are determined to be non-denotative [of existence itself]. Since the category of existence (*sattā*) is not subject to deviation, the cognition of existence from those words occurs solely through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Just as all things possess potencies that are to be understood through the presumption of their effects (*kāryārthāpatti*), so too there exists in persons a potency for the attainment of results produced by sacrifices and the like, which is denoted by the term *apūrva*. Because it did not exist prior to the performance of the sacrifice and arises after the performance has taken place, it is designated by the word *apūrva* (the "new" or "unprecedented") precisely due to its etymological derivation; this designation is applicable in all such cases. Similarly, they are called *devas* because they "play" (*divyanti*) or "shine" (*dyotante*) in the form of the moon, sun, fire, planets, constellations, and stars, and because they are praised by all mantras through their constant movement. Since they are connected with well-known words in their specific forms, they do not fall within the scope of [pure] Being (*sattā*).

Likewise, by the word "heaven" (*svarga*), neither the region of the stars nor Mount Meru is meant according to Vedic tradition, Puranic lore, and the systems of ritualists; for as it is said in the Veda: "For those people who are doers of merit go to the heavenly world (*svarga-loka*); these luminaries, the constellations, belong to them," and likewise, "He wins that luminous, meritorious world. Or else, [it refers to] the summit of Meru as established in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.

Alternatively, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), there exists a distinct, pure pleasure that is experienced for a year or more, which—though never previously seen as such—is established by implication (*arthāpatti*) as being devoid of all means of suffering such as cold, heat, and thirst, and is to be experienced in another region. Even though it has not been seen before in that manner, it is nonetheless extracted through discrimination from mixed experience and, being known as the referent of the word "heaven" (*svarga*), establishes its own existence; therefore, it does not require a direct denotation [of that specific pleasure]. Consequently, the word "cow" (*go*) likewise does not denote the existence of a cow.
However, because there is doubt as to whether the denotatum is the form (ākṛti) called "cowness," it is investigated;
it is said that the denotatum is the individual (vyakti), since it is understood through its connection with action.
Yet, in accordance with the expressive power of the word, it does not differ from the form.

What, then, is the prima facie view? That [the Veda] is eternal, just as in the case of words that have been handed down, because they are intended for the purpose of conveying meaning; therefore, its [eternality] is determined by that very fact.

If the meaning of words such as "cow" were the form (ākṛti), for whom would there be rites such as sprinkling? And by what could one sacrifice? For the abandonment [of the offering] is not possible with respect to a form;
indeed, the form is incorporeal and eternal, and thus it cannot be the object of acts such as threshing.

Therefore, neither an injunction nor a prohibition is applicable to it [the universal]. Such is the case with actions like "he threshes the rice," "he immolates the animal," "he presses the Soma," "he purifies the Soma," and "he sacrifices with Soma, an animal, and rice. All such preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) which concern perishable, corporeal objects, or those intended for the accomplishment of a purpose, are enjoined for their practical application because they do not exist in the universal (*ākṛti*), but do exist in the individual (*vyakti*). Furthermore, since the cognition of the word-meaning is primarily concerned with the task at hand, and since all human activity is dependent upon an injunction, one must necessarily accept the postulation of word-meanings capable of fulfilling the sentence-meaning as being within the scope of the injunction.

Likewise, even regarding the injunctions of prohibition such as "A Brahmin must not be killed" or "Meat from a village pig must not be eaten," these too would be purposeless if there were no prior possibility of occurrence, since they depend on the existence of that possibility; furthermore, because individuals cannot be the subject of such rules, if there were no possibility of occurrence, the prohibitions would be meaningless.

Therefore, it is logical to accept only that meaning of words by which the application of the injunctions becomes effective; it is not proper to postulate word-meanings merely for the sake of establishing the realization of ultimate reality.

It might be argued that in injunctions (*codanā*) where the application arises from the individual (*vyakti*), the word refers to the individual; but elsewhere, it will refer only to the form (*ākṛti*).
That is incorrect.

For, by logical principle, it is established that a single word cannot have multiple unstable relationships, as this would entail the fault of postulating multiple unseen expressive powers (*vācaka-śakti*) and the resulting dilemma of optionality (*vikalpa*).
Since, among related objects, the understanding of one is established by the mention of the other alone, [the opponent asks:
"How then is there the cognition of the universal (jāti)?
To this, he says: "Because of the distinction."

Since there is, however, always an inseparable connection between the individual (vyakti) and the form (ākṛti), the individual, once it has been denoted, is indeed capable of causing the form to be understood.
This has been stated in the *Tadbhūtādhikaraṇa*:

"For whatever meaning is accepted as the primary denotation of a word, since it is impossible for that [word] to abandon that [meaning], another meaning residing therein must necessarily be admitted as being indicated by secondary implication (lakṣaṇā). (First Adhyāya, Third Pāda).

Furthermore, for one who holds that the *ākṛti* (form) is the word-meaning, there would be no determination [of the object] because it is common to and indeterminate among the individuals (*vyakti*). However, for one who holds that the individual is the word-meaning, since the determination of the form—which is entirely included within the individual—is established, the postulation of a separate operation of the word is not tenable. Therefore, the individual alone is the word-meaning, not the form. Nor are the alternatives of denoting the relation, the collection, the aggregate, or one qualified by the other possible; for all these cognitions are established precisely through non-distinction (*avibhāga*).

If words such as *go* (cow) were denotative of the *ākṛti* (form), then in usages such as "the cow is white," "one buys [the Soma] with a red, tawny-eyed, one-year-old cow," "six cows are to be given," or "one should give one cow as the sacrificial fee," grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would not be possible, because all such words would denote merely the genus (*jāti*) or the quality (*guṇa*). For the form of "cowness" (*gotvākṛti*) is neither white, nor red, nor possessed of six qualities; rather, it is the individual (*vyakti*) that possesses such qualities. Therefore, the individual alone is the denoted meaning.

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) occurs in perception either because a word denotes an individual qualified by genus and quality, or because it denotes a pure individual; and in that case, it is indeed a substance (*dravya*). [The author] shows the undesirable consequence of its absence under your view by means of the negative particle (*nañ*), stating: "In your position, even such a state of being a word for the same substance would not exist. As for what the Commentator said—accepting an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound) with the negative particle and using the word "substance" (*dravya*) in its opposite sense—he says: "For one who maintains the theory of the form (*ākṛti*), there would be no word denoting that which resides in a substance."

Therefore, it must be disregarded as being excessively strained and unfit for the application of qualities specified in a different grammatical case. Furthermore, do not entertain the following interpretation as being the intended meaning:

"A word denoting a quality that resides in a substance (*dravyāśraya*) is a non-substance-word (*adravyaśabda*); because a generic form (*ākṛti*) is devoid of qualities, such a word cannot enter into a syntactic connection within a single sentence [with the substance], just as in the case of expressions like 'cowness' (*gotva*) or 'white' (*śukla*)."

As for the objection regarding grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it is equally untenable even within our own position because there is no distinction [between the two cases]; therefore, the previous explanation must be maintained. Furthermore, it is not accepted that the form (*ākṛti*) is produced by bricks, such that there could be a censure based on its being a substance composed of sinews and so forth by its very nature; rather, in both positions, the purpose of the injunction is the accomplishment of a resemblance, like a lion made from a lump of flour. That resemblance, however, should consist in the form of a hawk (*śyena-ākṛti*) distinct from other forms, and not in a specific individual hawk distinct from other individuals or through some unique characteristic.
Because it is devoid of form, similarity as a mere individual, independent of universals and particulars, cannot be the object of an injunction, since it is equal across all substances.
Furthermore, because only one individual is grasped, similarity with another individual could not be effected.
Therefore, the performance of an action by means of a word is possible only when the word's referent is the individual.

"It is not the most effective means" [is the objection]. For the Smṛti rule "In the case of the word *śyena*, when it is used in the sense of the act of piling (*cayana*), it is applied to the fire-altar" does not intend for the *śyena* to accomplish the piling as its primary or most effective means; rather, since the primary meaning is impossible in that context, it adopts a secondary (figurative) sense.

Because it is impossible for a word to apply to a unique particular (*asādhāraṇa*), and because [the particular] is everywhere indistinguishable in its state of being indefinable, when a thing is determined through a universal form, the universal that is the pervader (*vyāpaka*)—in relation to the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—does not have such a nature as the other form, namely the particular which is the pervaded (*vyāpya*).

In that regard, if the position of the particular were adopted, there would be faults such as the impossibility of explaining the relationship [between word and object], deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the absence of a cognition of the universal, and the postulation of a power in each individual object.
Furthermore, since that which is subject to doubt cannot be what is signified by a word, the word would be rendered devoid of an object.
By this, the view that both [the universal and the individual] are denoted independently is refuted.

Furthermore, the view that the form (prakṛti) qualified by the individual is denoted is also untenable, because of the logical principle that "a qualifier cannot be apprehended unless it has been apprehended itself," which would entail the necessity of apprehending it first.

Moreover, since there is no cognition of the intrinsic nature of either the relation or the aggregate, and since these would apply without distinction in all cases, one must necessarily admit that they function as qualifiers of the relata and the members of the aggregate.
In that case as well, there would be the postulation of three powers; furthermore, the aforementioned defects would result regarding the aspect of the individual instance (*vyakti*).
Nor [does this apply] to the third quarter of the first chapter.

It is logical that the two—the individual (*vyakti*) and the form (*ākṛti*)—which have distinct functions, and which exist in various states as subordinate or primary, should approach each other as a composite whole; for since they are not absolutely different, it is not tenable that there be a composite consisting of two distinct properties related to separate substrata. Nor is it the case that even when qualified by the form, a specific individual is not perceived; for if one argues that "it is merely the individual" because there is no cognition of a specific individual, we say no, because at that time it cannot be defined as something other than the form.
For the word *mātra* denotes a universal (*sāmānya*), and thus it refers precisely to the form (*ākṛti*).

Since capacities (*śakti*) follow those distinctions among entities that possess various forms, it is understood—through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—that the capacity for being denoted by the word "cow" is based solely on the form of cowness (*gotva*).
Therefore, the cognition of another universal residing in the same substratum, or the desire for a specific form, occurs through the pervasion and non-pervasion of the object.
Furthermore, because the *ākṛti* (form) is not absolutely distinct [from the individual], there is no occurrence of defects such as its being incorporeal;

for it is perceived as having a fixed form, yet when connected with action, it indeed becomes endowed with the individual (*vyakti*). Thus, acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and entering (*āveśana*) are by no means impossible.
Even acts such as slaughter (*viśasana*) are certainly possible, insofar as they are considered in relation to the non-distinction from the individual.

For instance, in the case of animals whose limbs have been removed, since there is no cognition of specific differences, the cognition characterized by dismemberment and so forth is observed to be purely in the form of a universal.

Now, one might object that in this way the *ākṛti* (form) would be impermanent; however, it is indeed accepted as such in that respect. But because it is not destroyed when other substrates perish, its indestructibility must necessarily be accepted by everyone.

Therefore, its destruction would consist only in that much; however, for that which occupies multiple locations, there could be no destruction whatsoever. Thus, the conventional usage [of "destruction"] occurs in both ways. But if there were absolute difference [between the substance and its properties], this injunction of a property would not find its application.
Furthermore, "cowness" (paśutva) is not [the property in question] here, because it is formless (amūrtatva).

However, that substance which is qualified by that [quality] cannot be understood in its specific form apart from "substanceness" (*dravyatva*); therefore, because it does not pervade inherence (*samavāya*), the substance must be understood through a single referent. Even in that case, there is the fault of [the quality] being incorporeal (*amūrtatva*).
Furthermore, because it depends on a substratum, there is the undesirable consequence of it being merely a substance.
Moreover, the particularity (*viśeṣa*)—whether it be "cowness" (*paśutva*) or "substanceness"—is ungraspable because it does not pervade [the whole].
Nor is that which is already understood connected with an injunction; nor is that which is subject to doubt "already understood.

Furthermore, since a property stated in one place cannot possibly apply elsewhere, it cannot be applied elsewhere; therefore, what is established for a universal is not logically applicable to its particulars. Moreover, because they are designated [by the same term], the particulars are themselves the universal, and thus [the universal] possesses incorporeality (*amūrtatā*).

However, no linguistic usage occurs through the uncommon [form]; therefore, the object of the injunction regarding dharma is indefinable. Furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth, which contradict common worldly understanding, must be postulated through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). But the Commentator, by accepting the distinction [between the word and its referent], stated that the cognition of the substratum alone [is obtained], for the individual (*vyakti*) is never perceived in its specific form.
Even that state of nourishment is merely figurative;

furthermore, one should not rely on a specific definition there when a general one suffices, because it exists merely by implication. Alternatively, this entire elaboration pertains precisely to that subject.
Is it by means of the word or by means of the form (ākṛti)?
Through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), the determination is that it is by means of the form.
For one who understands the nature of fire from smoke, the expectation for its particularity (naicitya) is already established.
Regarding the phrase "due to a mental error":

for one who, setting aside the fact that the word denotes the universal (*jāti*), considers only some particular instance—wherein a relation has been experienced—to be the denotable object, there is no dependence on other particulars because the universal is not being perceived. Alternatively, just as one understands the form (*ākṛti*) from the word as something independent, it is never the case that one understands the individual (*vyakti*) without first understanding the form.
What, then, is the difference between the word *gotva* (cowness) and the word *go* (cow)?
The aspect of exclusion (*vyatirekāṃśa*) is intended for a specific purpose in one context;
however, the clear cognition "possessing cowness" (*gotvavān*) denotes that which possesses the universal (*jātimad*), as the distinction [between the two] is logically established.
Furthermore, because the universal serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), there is no fault regarding the loss of the particular (*bheda*).
And this [term] denotes each and every one of the individual divisions;
as for the doubt that arises when they are being mentioned, it concerns the substratum of the number,
whereas when they are being pointed out as subjects, there is indeed certainty.
The inclusion of words such as "cow" (gavādi) is for the purpose of subsuming all nouns and verbs.

The purpose [of this discussion] is that, because general and particular terms share a single object, there would be no sublation of the general by the particular qualified [term] according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Or rather, it is thus:
In this [work], regarding the fourfold categories of words, the determination of the meaning of two types is carried out here in the third quarter (pāda) of the first chapter;
it is undertaken because doubt arises concerning prefixes (upasarga) and particles (nipāta).
Even when [the word] functions as a denoter, in cases such as "he goes after" (anuyāti),
that specific distinction which is perceived is not obtained through doubt;
for surely, even in this case, an investigation into the meaning of the verb is not appropriate.

Since this [topic] will be treated in detail from the second [chapter] onwards, the fact that the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*)— namely, the state of being (*bhāva*)— is the expressed meaning has already been established;
now, an investigation is undertaken for the purpose of distinguishing it from the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*).

Furthermore, that which was stated by the Commentator—that sacrifice and so forth are denotable—is established here for the sake of distinction; in that context, it was spoken of as the "bhāva" (action/state). Therefore, between the noun and the verb, which word is the denoter of what meaning?
Does [the denotation] consist of the form (ākṛti) or of the individual (vyakti)? This inquiry proceeds. Furthermore, how is the connection of this inquiry with the subject at hand established?
This must first be stated by means of an investigation based on the root of the traditional teaching (smṛti).
If the meaning were to be stated first, it would be prior to the determination of the form of the word;

for indeed, the correctness (*sādhutva*) of a word cannot be ascertained without knowing its denoted object (*vācya*), since correctness is not apprehended when the mere denoted object remains unknown.

Neither without the form (ākṛti) nor without the individual instance (vyakti) is that [denotation] possible; thus, the cognition that "the individual instance is the denotable object" lacks a valid foundation because it is impossible. Therefore, such a tradition (smṛti) regarding grammar is not considered authoritative.

But surely, even on the view that the word denotes the form (ākṛti), both action and non-action occur only with respect to the individual (vyakti), since that is the actual referent of the word; why, then, is this investigation undertaken?
On the view that the word denotes the individual, there would be an option regarding the curd and the buttermilk for Kauṇḍinya.
Because the general statement is weaker, sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) must indeed be performed in the other case as well; even in the prima facie view, it should be performed for worldly objects too.
Just as in the case of rice-grains (*brīhi*), the force of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) sets aside both proximity (*sannidhi*) and order (*krama*),

so too in the case of the oblation (*homa*) involving curd and other such substances— whether in their original form or otherwise— the nature of being an oblation (*homatva*), which is denoted by the direct scriptural statement, is indeed possible in the original form.
But surely all this has already been examined in the discussion on the word "cow" (*gaur*) and so forth;
since its purpose has been fulfilled by those [previous] arguments, it is not appropriate to consider it again.
This was also pointed out by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) in the passage beginning with "and as in the case of the form" (*yathā cākṛtiḥ*).
Furthermore, the reason for this proposition will also be stated; or, even though the expressibility [of the universal] has been mentioned,
the question of whether the individual is denotable or not is now investigated in order to establish the existence of the universal.
If there were identity between the word and its denoted object, an investigation into them would have to be undertaken;
however, since there is no doubt [of their identity], there is no occasion for such reflection.
Furthermore, regarding the non-worldly nature of the word and its meaning in their respective capacities as signifier and signified—
No doubt regarding the object to be expressed can arise for those two who do not recognize it;
and in this matter, for you, recognition alone is the cause of non-difference.
Any other [reason] would be merely a cumulative addition; therefore, further deliberation on that point is not appropriate.
And since there are differences such as designations and so forth, how could difference not arise?

This investigation has been undertaken to state what was left unsaid therein; and this reflection applies even when there is non-difference in meaning, despite the existence of non-difference in the words.
To whom does the status of being the denotable belong? Since both the individual (vyakti) and the universal (ākṛti) are present, doubt arises from the two grounds of difference and non-difference.
What is the conclusion? It is said that the word and its object are distinct.
Because of the difference in designation between the world and the Veda, as well as in their names and definitions,
and because of the difference in the pronunciation of accents and the observation of elision and transposition.
That is incorrect, for a difference in agents is not admitted when there is a difference in actions;
moreover, the agency of fire in burning is understood from the objects themselves.
How, then, can a difference from the action be perceived through something that is non-existent?

Since the meaning of the word *vṛtra* is unprecedented (*apūrva*), and even though it is a word denoting an action (*kriyāśabda*), it is non-worldly (*alaukika*) and lacks the nature of an action; therefore, as will be explained by the statements in the Bhāṣya,
it is only for the aforementioned word— such as *trivṛt* and so on— that [the application] occurs in the sense of "nine" and so forth.
In this regard, it is true that the difference in a word is not caused by the qualities of its meaning;
therefore, the distinction in form must be stated through differences such as accent (*svara*) and so forth.
It is said that those very same words and meanings which exist in the Veda are also present in common worldly usage.
In the *Tantravārtika*, it is argued that the entire Veda would consequently fall into the state of being non-authoritative,
because the existence of the meaning of the suffix— that is, the injunction—
would not be established; furthermore, the application of a word to any other meaning is not enjoined.
Even regarding Vedic words, when they are uttered repeatedly through perception by means of distinct sounds,
it is in every way impossible to assert a difference between the word and its denoted object.
If [the Veda] were one, the established consensus of the ritualists would be upheld; yet,
in the case of the Vedic word perceived through direct recognition, there is a difference in form,
as well as a distinction in designations and so forth, caused by differences in accent and the like.

Difference [of the Veda] is not tenable because it is contradicted by direct perception and recognition; nor is there any difference in its verbal form, nor even its exclusion from Śūdras. Furthermore, distinctness among other well-known objects is not tenable.
And for certain [beings] that are lying on their backs and are unslain, the third quarter of the first chapter is not prescribed;
therefore, no distinction is perceived from the passage beginning with "lying on their backs" (uttāna).
Therefore, regarding those two— the word and its meaning— which were previously examined in the world as to whether the category of the object is the form (ākṛti), the individual (vyakti), or both;
many positions appear here, which [arise] at every step.

Genus (*jāti*), individual (*vyakti*), relation (*saṃbandha*), aggregate (*samūha*), gender (*liṅga*), case-role (*kāraka*), and number (*saṃkhyā*)—these are the seven [factors]; for these two [categories], there is an eightfold alternative (*aṣṭapakṣī*).
Alternatively, the genus is qualified by the individual, or the individual is qualified by the genus.

In this same manner, eight [variations] should subsequently be applied to both genus and relation, as well as to generality and collection, by means of six [factors] for each, as previously stated. In this way, the infinity of these five categories is understood.

Furthermore, by means of the presentation of these [views]—whether they be contrary to the individual as qualified by the genus or otherwise—all of them are to be understood as having been elaborated [previously].
Therefore, for now, only two positions shall be examined: is the meaning of a word the *ākṛti* (form), or is it the *vyakti* (individual)?

Furthermore, the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that the cause of doubt is "because action is possible in both the universal (sāmānya) and the individual (vyakti). This is incorrect; since the individual is also being perceived, how can it be asserted that only the universal is being perceived?
Moreover, if the individual were indeed being perceived, then there would be no doubt at all—what, then, would be expressed by this [word]?
Nor is the possibility of action a valid reason for denotability, as it would follow that other individuals [of the same class] would also be denoted.
Therefore, one should consider the cause of doubt to be exactly as previously stated.

Doubt arises because [the word] is common to both the application (*prayoga*) and the cognition (*pratīti*), and because in other treatises, both the individual (*vyakti*) and the form (*ākṛti*) are accepted.

Alternatively, it has been stated that when a word is uttered, there is a cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*); since the cognition of the universal is identical for both the individual and the form, and because actions such as touching, seizing, and building a fire-altar like a hawk (*śyena-cayana*) are possible in the case of the individual, whereas such cognitions and actions are impossible in the case of the universal; and because [the word] is used for both the universal and the individual.
What, then, is *ākṛti* (form) and what is *vyakti* (individual)?
Furthermore, how can this question arise when, in the inquiry "What is the meaning of this word 'cow'?", the universal (*jāti*) has already been determined?
This is not a fault.

He who has understood this [system] asks: "What, then, is the form (ākṛti) and what is the individual (vyakti)? Or, because of doubt regarding both being perceived here, he asks: "Which is the individual, and how much is the genus (jāti)?"

Or, someone might ask by way of contradiction: "When no distinct, manifest entity other than the individual cows such as Śābaleya is perceived, then from what source does this distinction arise—'this is an individual' and 'this is a universal'? Or rather, all this deliberation is undertaken for the sake of linguistic usage; yet even if the universal were the referent of a word, since action is possible only with respect to the individual, such deliberation would be useless. Since he nevertheless investigates this with such effort, the implication is that he must surely intend some universal that is absolutely distinct from the individual and capable of being the object of linguistic usage.
In this context, "form" (*ākṛti*) is simply the commonality among substances, qualities, and actions.
First, as for those who maintain that [form] is either non-existent or a matter of doubt, their refutation must be stated merely by explaining its true nature.
However, the refutation of the one who maintains the contrary view is now set forth.

Although a universal (*jāti*) is not perceived as being absolutely distinct from the individual (*vyakti*), nevertheless, when that variegated form is not perceived, the basis for the cognition of the commonality (*sāmānya-buddhi*)—according to the principle stated in the first chapter—is the "form" (*ākṛti*), while the other is the individual. Nor is the existence or the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) of the universal established by this passage; rather, it merely describes the distinction between the universal and the individual.
It is for that very reason that the word *mātra* (mere) is employed; otherwise, its meaning would already be implied.
As for what was said—that a certain absolutely distinct genus must surely be intended—the reply to that is:
what is intended as the "form" (*ākṛti*) is merely the commonality (*sāmānyamātra*) of substances, qualities, and actions, not something absolutely separate from them.

And by this, that universal which consists of existence (*sattā*)—the commonality of all things such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth—is indicated; through the indication of that, the indication of the intermediate universals is also established.

Alternatively, because the word "universal" is connected to each [term], the three universals beginning with substantiality (*dravyatva*) are indicated, since there is no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) for existence itself.
Alternatively,

due to the use of the word *mātra*, everything from the intermediate generalities (*avāntarasāmānya*) up to the highest generality (*mahāsāmānya*) found in [categories such as] cow and so forth is denoted.
The term *vyakti* (individual) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which possesses uncommon particulars."

That individual in which there are uncommon particulars is "that which has uncommon particulars"; however, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not possible in the sense that "those [particulars] are uncommon and they are particulars," because it will be stated later that the substratum of the particulars is the individual (*vyakti*),
and because of the evidence of traditional memory (*smṛti*).
Therefore, it has been correctly stated: "What is the nature of the individual (vyakti)?

What is established? Since injunctions regarding ritual performance—such as seizing, sprinkling, and immolating—are possible only in the case of an individual and impossible in the case of a form (ākṛti), and since prohibitory injunctions—such as "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed" or "Liquor must not be drunk"—are possible only in the case of an individual, and since worldly linguistic usage—instructions such as "Devadatta, bring the cow"—is thus explained, it is determined that the individual is the meaning of the word.
Furthermore, this is because number and grammatical case-role (kāraka) are logically consistent [only with an individual].

For if the individual (vyakti) were the meaning of a word, then in expressions such as *vṛkṣau* ("two trees") and *vṛkṣābhyām* ("by two trees"), both [number and case-role] would be appropriate: the number such as duality denoted by the suffix, and the case-role (*kāraka*) such as the instrument, would apply to the individuals already expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). In the other view, however, neither is possible because the universal (*jāti*) is not subject to number and lacks the status of a *kāraka*. Furthermore, one would have to resort to a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the individual; and if that were so, all Vedic sentence-meanings would become merely figurative.

Furthermore, in the view that the individual is the meaning of the word, the primary grammatical coreferentiality (*mukhya-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the term "person" with "Devadatta" is logically established.

In the view that the universal (*jāti*) is the meaning, one would have to assume a coreferentiality based on metaphorical indication (*lākṣaṇika*); by this very fact, it is understood that the individual is the referent of the word.
Moreover, following the scriptural injunction "one should sacrifice the animal," subsequent usage is observed through the limbs of the individual, such as the heart and the tongue.

The individual (vyakti) is the meaning of the word because it is required for both genus (jāti) and action (karma); since the denotation of the universal is desired only when the individual is present, and it is logical that the individual—whose nature is already established—is the thing to be denoted, whereas the genus is not yet established, therefore the individual is the word-meaning. If it is asked: "Why is it not accepted that both [genus and individual] are the expressed meaning, since the application [of the word], the cognition, and the accomplishment of the action are all possible?
[the answer is: No.

Because it would entail the postulation of multiple powers (*śakti*), and because the cognition of the other [the universal] is adequately accounted for through its relation to the single denoted [individual], it is the individual (*vyakti*) alone that is the denotable object. If it is asked how the cognition of the universal arises, it will be accounted for through its connection with the individual. If it is argued that it is logical for a word to denote the individual only where the application of an action is impossible—thereby necessitating it by implication (*arthāpatti*)—but elsewhere, since the universal is first cognized, it is more reasonable that the word denotes the universal; [we reply: [This argument is not tenable. For even in cases where an action is possible, such as "bring the cow," the word is observed to denote the individual. Furthermore, if the universal were the primary denotation, one would have to assume a secondary figurative usage (*lakṣaṇā*) for the individual, whereas the reverse is more parsimonious. Moreover, since the universal is not perceived apart from the individual, it cannot be established as the primary denotation. Therefore, the individual is the denotable object. As for the cognition of the universal, it arises through the relation to the individual, just as the cognition of "forest" arises from the trees. Thus, the view that the individual is the denotable object is the correct one.
No;

for according to the stated path, there would follow the faults of postulating multiple powers [for a single word], the contingency of an unstable relationship between word and meaning, and the occurrence of doubt. If it is asked, "How can a word apply to another individual without a cause, according to the proponent of the individual (vyaktivādin)?"—the answer is that there is no contradiction in its application to another individual because the sign of the generic form (ākṛti) serves as the cause.
The author of the Bhāṣya, however, having raised the question "How is there a cognition of the universal?", provides the answer that "the *ākṛti* (form) will be the indicator. That is irrelevant;
for when asked about the cause of the non-cognition of the universal, why is the reason for the application [of the word] to other individuals being stated?
Therefore, this must be explained by supplying an ellipsis.
If it is asked how there is an understanding of the universal, [the answer is] through its connection with individuals.
If it is asked how there is application to another individual, [the answer is] because the configuration (*ākṛti*) serves as the mark, and so forth.

If it is asked, "How is there an understanding of the universal?"—when this objection has been raised, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin), being unable to dispel the understanding of the universal, accepts the position that the word denotes the individual qualified by the form (ākṛti). [He argues: "The form will serve as the signifier, the qualifier, and the denoted object; therefore, the cognition of it is not to be questioned. Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter.
Therefore, the word-meaning is either the individual alone or the individual as qualified [by a universal].
And thus, in cases such as "six [cows] are to be given," the number six and so forth will be logically applicable.
Furthermore, in the case of another individual, the use of the word "other" (*anya*) and the cognition of it as "other" will likewise be possible.

Otherwise, even if another individual were brought in, both [alternatives] would be untenable because the genus (*jāti*) is non-different [from itself] and because it is not a quality (*guṇa*). Therefore, when the position has been reached that the individual (*vyakti*) is the meaning of the word, it is stated in reply: this is not the case; the individual is not denoted by the word, but rather the form (*ākṛti*) is understood to be the word-meaning (*padārtha*). For from the scriptural hearing, "One should pile the *śyena-cit*," the meaning of the sentence must be either that one should produce the individual *śyena* by means of piling, or that one should produce the form. [The former is impossible. Thus, the form is the word-meaning. Furthermore, since the sacrifice is enjoined as something to be accomplished, it cannot be performed by means of the individual, because the individual is perishable. On the other hand, the form is eternal and can be produced by piling. Therefore, the form is the word-meaning. Moreover, because the forms of various animals such as the hawk (*śyena*), the curlew (*krauñca*), and the francolin (*tittiri*) are mentioned, the word-meaning must be the genus (*jāti*). If the individual were the word-meaning, there would be no mention of those [other] forms. Furthermore, because the forms of various animals are mentioned, the word-meaning must be the genus. [The two] may be [the names of sacrifices].

For as long as the *iṣṭakāciti* (brick-altar) and so forth are not clearly manifest—as they cannot be performed [as such] due to the impossibility of their construction, because they are not constituted by sinews and the like, and because the *iṣṭakāciti* would be sublated—the *cyenaciti* (falcon-altar) is clearly manifest. This is because the purpose [of the sacrifice] must be postulated, since the root *ci* (to pile) does not have its primary meaning [restricted to bricks], and because it would entail the abandonment of the traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating, "In the case of the name *agni*, [it applies] when it refers to an action."

First of all, it is not tenable that one should "construct the individual hawk (śyenavyakti) by means of piling (cayana)," because the form (ākṛti) cannot be constructed with bricks, as it is created by the gods; furthermore, this would lead to the word *cinoti* ("he piles") being used in a non-literal sense and would contradict traditional scripture (smṛti). Nor is it tenable that one should "construct the form," for the same reasons.
By process of elimination, the meaning of the sentence is: "One should bring about the state of fire situated within the altar, which is piled like a hawk, by means of piling."

Therefore, since it is impossible to fetch fire that is similar to any particular individual hawk (*śyena-vyakti*), because similarity to every individual is unattainable, and because similarity to past or future individuals is untenable, whereas the attainment of similarity to the form (*ākṛti*) of the hawk is possible, it is determined that the word’s referent is the form. This is because one previously experiences a variegated cognition based on the knowledge of the universal (*sāmānya*), and because from a sentence such as "Bring a cow," one adopts [the meaning] according to one's inclination.

Therefore, since the existence of generic form (*ākṛti*), substance (*dravya*), action (*karman*), and so forth is possible, it is established in the *Tantravārtika* that the generic form alone is the meaning of a word. It has been stated: "The Vedic collection has this as its purpose; therefore, everything therein should be for that purpose.

Now, once the authority of the Veda—along with the Smṛtis—is thus established, and at this juncture of explaining the meaning of sentences, the introduction to the inquiry into names (*nāmadheya*) is undertaken by means of a connection that does not conclude the section on the definition of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Are words such as *cit* and *avadā*,
as well as *kimuḥ* and *nihnida*, the means of knowing a quality (*guṇa*), or are they merely names (*nāmadheya*) for actions?
That [position] is incorrect.
If this were so, the entire treatise would be non-distinct from the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa*.
For in every case, this is investigated: "Is this sentence the authority (*pramāṇa*) for this meaning, or for another?

Furthermore, even those who explain these two sūtras as belonging to the same section by imagining them as the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*uttarapakṣa*), must state which intended final conclusion, consistent with the prima facie position, is enjoined by this sūtra: "The Veda has that [dharma] as its sole purpose" (*samāmnāyaidamarthyam*).
It is not undesirable that words such as *udbhid* are included within the category of those whose meaning is not [inherently] connected [to an action].

Therefore, this pair of sūtras should be explained as the two subsequent positions (*uttarapakṣa*) regarding the two preceding sections (*adhikaraṇa*), both of which have had their prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) inferred.
In that regard, first, taking *udbhid* and others as examples, a doubt is raised: do these serve a purpose toward some action, or not?
What, then, is the prima facie position? That [the Upaniṣads] are purposeless, because [the Veda] has action as its purpose;
and it has been said:

They are not included within injunctions (*vidhi*) and the like, because they do not express the goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), or the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
