To that extent, they are outside the scope of *codanā* (Vedic injunction). Furthermore, due to the absence of the cognition of praise, they are distinct from *arthavāda*.
Since there is no object to be manifested by them as a constituent part of a ritual action—such as being designated by a specific name—their function as *mantras* ceases.

And since there is no other purpose for the Veda, those [texts] of such a kind are indeed not authoritative. To this, it is replied: when it has been established that [the Veda] has one of those three purposes, then what is the point of this inquiry?
First of all, it cannot be an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) because it lacks the status of being a supplementary part of a sentence (vākyaśeṣa).
But how is it not a supplementary part, when a syntactic unity is perceived just as in the case of "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest," and so forth?
This is not so.
For that which remains after what is to be enjoined is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise);
however, since this [statement] does not exceed the scope of the injunctive portion (*vidhyuddeśa*) itself, it is not a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*).
Furthermore, it has been stated in the *Audumbara-adhikaraṇa* that it is not logical for something possible under those circumstances to serve the purpose of praise.

Furthermore, praise is never seen to be expressed by a single word, nor do we apprehend such praise here. Even if one were to imagine this as a commendation— namely, that "by this [act], the separation of the animals is performed"— that too is set aside by the well-established fact of instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), which is more powerful because it relies on the entire group of words ending in the instrumental case.

Otherwise, due to the predominance of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the nominative case-ending alone would have been employed, as in the expression "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest" (*vāyur vai kṣepiṣṭhaḥ*).
Furthermore, this [word] does not possess the status of a mantra, because it is not perceived as having that form,
and because there is no recollection of its being studied [as such].
Nor does it possess expectancy merely because it consists of a single word, nor does it serve as a reminder through the cognition of an instrument.

Furthermore, no meaning denoted by this [word] is observed to be an element inherent in the performance [of the rite]. And there can be no status as a subsidiary to the ritual action (*karmāṅgatva*) in the manifestation of something that is not inherently connected [to the rite].
Even in the case of postulating a substance based on the wording of a mantra (*māntravarṇika*), there is the burden of complexity;
moreover, there is no direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*) enjoining this [rite] as there is for the *sūktavāka*, by which a substance based on the wording of a mantra might be postulated.
Furthermore, its form is not suitable for performance.
Therefore, because it is not enjoined, it cannot be employed by supplying missing words—as in the case of "iṣe tvā" and so on—to render it self-sufficient;
moreover, its status as a single syntactical unit with the Brāhmaṇa is clear, and thus it lacks the character of a mantra.

Consequently, that which is included within the statement of the injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*) alone is what is investigated in the subsequent section as being either an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) or a name (*nāmadheya*).
In that regard, first of all,
the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) applies to an object such as a spade that possesses the capacity for digging, based on the conventional meaning of its constituent parts;
nor is a collective whole denoting a distinct meaning established in common worldly usage.
Furthermore, an object not already known from the world cannot be understood from the Veda, because the relationship [between word and meaning] is not caused by the scripture (*śāstra*).

Moreover, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) expresses the instrument (*karaṇa*); and since the instrument of an action is either a substance possessing power or the power itself residing in that substance, it follows that a sacrifice having "the *udbhid*" as its means is what is understood.
Yet, neither the "udbhid-ness" nor the instrumentality of the sacrifice is established anywhere [else].

Because it possesses meaning, it effects a specific activity; for there is a distinction in the activity of the injunction, the word, and the person [involved], otherwise their activity would be no different from that of words which have not been uttered. Alternatively, "possessing meaning" (*arthavattva*) refers to being meaningful in the sense of having a denotable content (*abhidheyavattva*), as a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*); whereas in the case of a name (*nāmadheya*), the meaning is not understood—this is how the argument is to be applied.

Or else, "possessing meaning" is the reason by way of distinction, because the word *udbhid* has a different result than the root *yaj* (to sacrifice); and consequently, it should be stated that there is a distinction in the activity of both the injunction and the person.
But surely even a name, by qualifying the sacrifice, would be meaningful and serve to produce a specific activity?
This is not so.
Why?

When, first of all, a specific sacrifice is conveyed by the verbal root itself through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) as being fit to be the object of an injunction, then what else could a name do there? If, on the other hand, it is argued that only the mere status of being a name is expressed, then that would be undesirable for it; thus he will state that a name cannot be enjoined because the qualified object is already established and therefore [the name] is irrelevant.

And when, by some means, words such as *udbhid* are shown to be denotative of specific [sacrifices], then, because they would denote a universal that is absolutely inseparable from that [specific], the word *yaji* (to sacrifice) would become redundant. Furthermore, there will be parsimony (*lāghava*) in the injunction of the accessory (*guṇavidhi*),
since it would be an injunction based on the restatement (*anuvāda*) of the sacrifice.

If this is so, then because the capacity for injunction has already been accumulated by the qualities, the ritual act (*karman*) is not enjoined; and since the ritual act is thus [already] enjoined, for what would the quality be enjoined? Therefore, there would be pointlessness (*ānarthakya*).
Consequently, [the rule applies] to the archetype (*prakṛti*), namely the Jyotiṣṭoma.

Now, [an objection may be raised]: "In the case where these are injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*), since even the phrase *jyotiṣṭomena* would be directed toward that [accessory], the ritual action itself would remain unenjoined. Since there is no other way out, this [sentence] must be an injunction of a single ritual action. Furthermore, once the injunctive force has been diverted elsewhere, it is impossible to enjoin an accessory; therefore, the word *jyotiṣṭoma* alone must be the name [of the sacrifice]. Alternatively, that one [sentence] is the injunction of a ritual action qualified by an accessory, while the others are injunctions of accessories by way of restating (*anuvāda*) the ritual actions."

Now, if this were the case, all injunctions for one-day (*ekāha*), multi-day (*ahīna*), and sessional (*satra*) sacrifices would not exceed the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself by way of being injunctions of its qualities; thus, since there would be no other ritual acts, the Jyotiṣṭoma would not be the archetype (*prakṛti*) of anything, and therefore it should not be designated by that word [“archetype”].
Some hold this view according to the intention of the Siddhāntin.
Alternatively, it is called an “archetype” (*prakṛti*) because it is the model (*prakriyate*); the meaning is that the Jyotiṣṭoma is the model.

Alternatively, since terms such as "atha eṣa jyotiḥ" lack contact with instrumental case endings or verbal suffixes, it is impossible for them to be injunctions of accessory qualities (guṇavidhi); therefore, they must unilaterally function as names of rituals (karmanāmadheya). In relation to these, the Jyotiṣṭoma is the archetype (prakṛti). [Objection: But surely, because the Jyotiṣṭoma is already occupied by the Soma enjoined in its originative statement (utpattivākya), it is improper to enjoin other accessories within that same sacrifice.
[Response: Because they are optional (kāmya), the Udbhid and others will serve as superseding factors (bādhaka).
In the case of a permanent rite (*nitya*), there is purposefulness for the previously mentioned quality.

Alternatively, even though an action is enjoined with specific qualifications, when its essential nature alone is extracted and it is enjoined with another quality, it does not differ from its original form;
otherwise, because no other recourse is possible, it is considered an option (*vikalpa*).

First, regarding the injunction [of *dadhi*] with respect to the fruit (*phala*), there are the following defects: the injunction of a connection with another word (*parapada-sambandha*), the assumption of an intervention (*vyavahita-kalpanā*), the subordination of the verbal root (*dhātu-pārārthya*), the sublation of the original *soma* (*autpattika-soma-bādha*), and the performance of a sacrifice by means of something entirely unestablished such as a spade—a non-edible substance (*anadanīya*). Likewise, if it were an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇa-vidhi*) with respect to the sacrifice (*yāga*), the word for the fruit would be meaningless;
or, if it were a qualification of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* already established through the principle of "all desires" (*sārvakāmya*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

The remoteness from the operation of the causal factor (*pratyaya*), the subordination of the verbal root (*dhātu*) to another, the sacrifice of inedible substances, and the [logical] alternatives regarding the Soma-sacrifice are all utterly untenable. Likewise, there are the following defects: the prescription of a qualified entity, the subordination of everything to another, the postulation of multiple injunctive potencies, the abandonment of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) understood through the possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), and the sacrifice of inedible substances.

Therefore, this does not indicate an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). Otherwise, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) would express "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," or "one should obtain [heaven] by means of the *vayaṃtī*," as the text reads.

Having set aside the capacity of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), he shows by means of the phrase "one should perform by means of sacrifice" (*yāgena kuryāt*) and so forth that this very [meaning] is understood through its connection with the case-ending (*vibhakti*). Furthermore:

Since it is accepted that in such cases as "by the third case-ending denoting the instrument" (*yatkaraṇābhidhāyinyā tṛtīyayā*), the kārakas are the meanings of the case-endings, how can it be said that [the suffix *ṭhañ*] is applied "from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) expressing the instrument"?
This is not a fault; for the intended meaning is "from a nominal stem expressing that which is the substratum of the instrument."
Alternatively, whatever meaning the word "instrument" (*karaṇa*) expresses, that very meaning is denoted by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

For it is the substance itself, qualified by its functional capacity (*kāraka*), that is expressed by a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, and not a power (*śakti*) abstracted from it as is the case with case-endings.
Thus, we observe the connection of other functional capacities (*kāraka*) with it, as in the expressions "the instrument," "by the instrument," and "for the instrument."
Otherwise, since the substance would be subsumed by that single *kāraka* already expressed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*), it could not enter into a connection with another *kāraka*;
for a capacity (*śakti*) simply cannot possess another capacity.

Therefore, because verbal derivatives (*kṛdanta*) denote a substance qualified by a capacity, it is established that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) expresses the meaning of the word "instrument" (*karaṇa*).
Therefore, this is what is meant:

in this sentence, a third case ending must arise from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the action; and it will be stated later that in this context, the sacrifice (*yāga*) is the instrument for the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) of the result, not the substance (*dravya*).

Consequently, if that second word is indeed expressive of the sacrifice, then being in the third case, it would form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*); however, if it were expressive of a different meaning, it would be incoherent.
But surely,

just as in cases such as "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*) or "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), where there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with the instrument (*karaṇa*), the use of the third case ending is not contradictory even when there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), so it is here as well.
This is the point.

Just as water that has long covered the substances at the edge of an ancient pond continues to cover them again and again of its own accord even when being baled out, so too is one who acts according to their own whims known as "chaṭha.
This is what is said.

For words such as *śrīhi* (rice) and others are so deeply conventionalized (*atyantarūḍha*) that, without abandoning their own primary meanings and failing to attain grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), they are understood as referring to qualities (*guṇa*) due to the absence of any other alternative.

However, as for those like *udbhid* which are etymological (*yaugika*), in the very same manner and by the same effort through which their denotation of a substance is established, their denotation of an action is also logically possible. Thus, when direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) remains indifferent [to the specific meaning], there is no fault in employing inference (*anumāna*) to eliminate ignorance and doubt. Indeed, this is the means for determining the meaning of all words: namely, well-established coreferentiality.
Furthermore, the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), having acquired its own nature within the sacrifice, is capable of causing the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) to refer to itself.
Moreover, according to your position, one would necessarily have to postulate some injunctive power (*vidhi-śakti*) for the suffix even with respect to the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*).
Therefore, there is also well-established usage for "action" (karman) by way of its constituent parts.
If it is argued that this name would also apply to the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites because they too bring about the manifestation of their own fruits, we say:
no.
This is because the specific object determined through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is explained as being a constituent part [of that sacrifice].
Furthermore, there is no co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of this [term] with the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other such sacrifices.

Alternatively, by the force of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the act of "breaking open" (*udbhedana*) is established as the occasioning cause (*nimitta*) specifically for this particular [sacrifice], and since it does not exist elsewhere, the restriction is maintained.
Just as the status of being the cause for a specific movement residing in that which possesses a dewlap and so forth will be enjoined;

[in this case], there is no formal injunction in the form of a relationship between a name and the named—such as in "vṛddhir ādaic" and so on—because that is established through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the well-known meaning of the constituent parts.
Now, [this concludes] the fourth quarter of the first chapter of the *Nāma*.
The meaning to be enjoined is not [independently] prescribed, because the establishment of the specific sacrifice depends upon it.

For here, although there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the name and the named, nevertheless, the name conveys an object that is already delimited by its own form; thus, it does not differ from the relation of qualifier and qualified.
[Objection: But in this way, would it not follow that the word denotes its own phonetic form?
There is no such contingency, because [the word] denotes an object qualified by a nature that has been apprehended through perception.

For in all cases, a cognition of a qualified object is never observed when its qualifier has not been grasped, but it is not the case that it cannot occur when the qualifier has not been expressed by a word.
Nor does this entail the contingency of superimposing the very form of the word [onto the object].
It was stated previously that this is because, in accordance with those [names], existing or future specificities are extracted.

Furthermore, by their very names, these [actions] are distinct from the archetype (*prakṛti*); otherwise, the sacrifice (*yajati*), being unqualified, would not differentiate the ritual action even when heard again for the sake of a quality or a result, as it would simply revert to the archetype.

Alternatively, in all names there exists some qualifying attribute inherent in the object itself; thus, as in the case of "red" (*aruṇā*) or "one-year-old female cow" (*ekahāyanī*), there is a relationship between qualifier and qualified.
Furthermore, since this [term] cannot function as the name of a specific sacrifice without the utterance of the *yajati* (he sacrifices), it is not the case that the general term is meaningless.

For, through mutual proximity, it is understood that the name refers to a sacrifice, and the sacrifice is delimited by this [name]; thus, it is neither a mere generality nor merely the subject matter at hand (*prakṛta*).

Therefore, both [the root and the suffix] possess purposefulness; and because there is an injunction of a qualified *bhāvanā* (efficient force), there is an injunction of both as well, so they do not constitute a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). This being the case, the status of being a name (*nāmatva*) is not merely the counter-correlative of being an injunction (*vidhitva*); thus, the view of those who—having established the inclusion of names within the injunction in the *pūrvapakṣa*—describe names as being distinct from injunctions, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras, is indeed improper. Furthermore, because they serve as a factor in specific linguistic usage, they do not fail to produce a specific engagement in action. For instance, in the selection of priests (*ṛtvij-varaṇa*) and similar contexts, this would serve as a concise means of communication, such as "I shall sacrifice with this [name]."

For one about to commence the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there would not otherwise be the connection with a quality in the statement "May these two Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices be mine," nor the connection with a fruit in the statement "One desiring heaven [should sacrifice] by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
Therefore, it is established that such terms are indeed names;
thus, whether it is a name or a quality, it is determined at the time of the original injunction (utpatti).
That very [quality] becomes a constituent of legal procedure when it is capable of being cited as an example;
for the connection with variegatedness (*citratva*) and thinness (*lītvatva*) belongs naturally to the class of living beings.
Therefore, these two are parts of the sacrifice involving living beings, whether they depend on the original form (*prakṛti*) or on a modified form (*vikṛti*). — Vārtika.
Whenever another word is heard connected with a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the injunctive power (*vidhi-śakti*) is transferred [to that word], and the verbal root becomes a restatement (*anuvāda*).

To the extent that further things to be enjoined (*vidheya*) are introduced, to that same extent there arises a requirement for the preceding [root] to be a restatement, out of fear of postulating multiple injunctive powers; however, when there is no other way, one must accept an injunction even there.

And here, the Agniṣomīya sacrifice—which possesses the characteristics of being feminine and variegated—is restated. Since the fruit is assigned to the group [of sacrifices], why is the view that the gender is not intended (avivakṣā) rejected even while the alternative position—that it is an injunction of an accessory (guṇavidhi)—is still present?
Some maintain that this portion of the Siddhānta text was written by mistake.
Others, however, say:
"In connection with the fruit, because it is the primary element, there would be an obstruction to the statement of its subordinate qualities.
That is incorrect.

In every respect, the rule concerning a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is the opposite of a name (*nāmadheya*), and that [quality-rule] remains applicable even when there is a connection with a result (*phala*).
And so he will say later: "While this topic (*adhikaraṇa*) remains, there is an inquiry as to whether it is a rule concerning a quality or a name.

For in the case of a connection with a result, because there is an absolute absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the sacrifice, it must necessarily be a rule concerning a quality; therefore, it should be stated thus.
Three positions appear plausible:

[the word is] either an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), or it refers to the fruit, or it is a name (*nāmadheya*) for the sacrifice; and for each of these, two [other] alternatives must be refuted.
Among them, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) himself, because it is the weakest position, refutes the third alternative.
Because it would entail the consequence that the constituent elements (dhātu) would be for the sake of another;
and therefore, as in the case of "one should sacrifice with rice grains" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*), there is an injunction of a subordinate element (*guṇavidhāna*) regarding the sacrifice.

Furthermore, when a subordinate element is enjoined by way of restating the objective portion—which, although the sacrifice is the instrument, is implied by the sense of the action understood from the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*)—there is no indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).
Or rather, it is precisely because the proponent of the quality (guṇavādī) is unable to overcome [the objection] that he resorts to the injunction of a quality within the sacrifice;
for if one were to postulate an injunction of a quality with respect to the result, the defects mentioned in the previous section would follow.

Likewise, in the case of "The *ājya* offerings are fifteen," there is the assumption of existence (*sattā*) based on the rule "the verb 'to be' is understood after 'asti' and 'bhavanti'," and the injunction arises from the statement of performance (*prayogavacana*).

But is it not the case that words such as "fifteen" (*pañcadaśāni*) and "seventeen" (*saptadaśāni*) do not denote mere number, because of the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) that the suffix *ḍa* is prescribed for the word *stoma* in the sense of "fifteen" and so forth?
For the term *stoma* is not prescribed as anything other than the number of verses (*stotrīya*) in a hymn.
(Jaiminisūtra 1.4.1)
There is no fault here;

for by the mere determination of the means of praise (*stotra-sādhana*), the *stoma*—which consists essentially of the measure of praise—is established. Thus, when there is a determination of similar verses (*ṛc*) or a determination of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), the word *stoma* denotes that which has the measure of praise as its cause.
Furthermore, in this case, there is no indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).
For what reason?
Because an injunction brings about some specific purpose through its own meaning;
however, an injunction regarding a qualifier does not take up another qualifier.

Indeed, every action that is understood from its originative injunction is restated; and it is not possible for another quality that contradicts it to be applied to an action already dependent on qualities.
For an action first connects with the qualities residing in its own sentence;
it does not attain those qualities belonging to another sentence until later, when it is [otherwise] isolated.
For the human goal (puruṣārtha) is desired by everyone spontaneously; however,
activity toward its means and their subsidiaries does not occur without a desire [for them], nor without the connection to intermediate actions provided by the sentence.
The primary actions grasp their qualities and substances through the requirements of "how" (kathaṃbhāva); and for the sake of establishing the subordinate sentences regarding qualities,
as well as by virtue of co-occurrence and explanatory passages (arthavāda), the status of being a name (nāmadheya) is resorted to.
The Fourth Pāda of the First Adhyāya:
"And there is another scriptural authority that makes [the meaning] known" (Tatprakyam cānyaśāstram).

Now, is it not the case that everywhere a nominal term is of only two kinds—technical (*sāṃvijñāyika*) and etymological (*yaugika*)—and both have been established by means of two preceding sections? What, then, remains for which this must be investigated again?
It is said:

here the inquiry concerns only derivative (*yaugika*) terms, avoiding the figurative indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*); however, in the subsequent section, such a [possessive] indication is impossible for conventional (*sāṃvijñāyika*) terms because it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

In that case, even according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), since it is accepted that "it belongs to Agni" (*agnaye hotram asmin*), and because no other compound meaning is perceived, the possessive sense is already internally contained.

The *bahuvrīhi* compound, without difficulty, prescribes a quality; and those very factors—such as conventional usage (*prasiddhi*) and so forth—are the grounds for this. Furthermore, even though Agni is obtained through the evening oblation, because the morning oblation merely restates the act of offering (*homamātra-anuvāda*), the injunction applies by the power of the sentence to all *darvihoma* offerings that do not have a specifically mentioned deity.
Likewise, in the expression "that which is poured out (*āghāryate*) is the *āghāra*," substances capable of being poured, such as clarified butter (*ājya*), milk (*payas*), and so forth, are denoted.

And that [act of utterance], being determined by the second mention as the object to be refined by the act of utterance (*cāraṇa-kriyā*), requires a purpose, since a refinement for which there is no utility is untenable. Its only refuge is the property (*dharma*) itself, because it terminates solely with the meaning of the word; it does not effect the utterance of the entire [word]. Thus, there remains an expectation as to what should be done with the portion already uttered. Furthermore, even in common worldly practice, they perform a slight refinement through utterance regarding liquid substances that are intended to be used for drinking or similar purposes.

Therefore, like the *pūtīka* plant used in place of Soma for the pressing, or like the fruit-cups (*phalacamasa*) used in place of the Soma-drink, the substance to be consecrated requires only an action;

by virtue of the context, it approaches the principal rites of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Furthermore, since the offerings to Agni and others consist of various substances, the *upāṃśuyāja* alone remains expectant [of a substance]; thus, it attains the status of being for that purpose.
And it is said:

"Alternatively, [the phrase] *yatkaroni* (that which one does) serves merely to indicate the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), precisely because it is expectant (*sākāṅkṣatvāt*). Thus, in the *Upāṃśu-tantravārtika*, having referred back (*anūdya*) the efficient-force of the sacrifice (*yāga-bhāvanā*), when the substance for the *āghāra* offering is enjoined by the sentence, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—being already established as the means to that [offering]—is merely restated."

Or rather, once its perishable nature is understood through the very act of hearing, one considers the injunction regarding milk and other substances to be merely for the purpose of that which is perishable.
Furthermore, there is no need for a nominal stem (*nāman*) since [the meaning] is already established by the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone;
nor are any purificatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*) ever seen to possess nominal stems.

The statement that "the quality is enjoined by the direct scriptural statement (śruti) itself" intends to convey that, because it is to be refined (saṃskārya) by the very force of the accusative case-ending, its status as a quality must necessarily be understood in some context.
To this, we reply: here we say—
But when a rule regarding the deity is stated for a *homa* that has no deity, and [the material] for the *upāṃśuyāja*, then how can there be the designation "named after that" (*tatprakhyatā*)?
If it were a rule, then the *agnihotra* would be the subject sought by this [designation].

The application [of the injunction] may pertain either to the subject at hand or even to that which is not the subject; furthermore, every accessory (guṇa) is enjoined as following upon the meaning of the verbal root.

Nor is there a mere restatement (anuvāda) of an action already under discussion; for if something not under discussion were being restated, then this accessory would be enjoined with respect to the oblation (homa).
In that case, its renown elsewhere does not constitute an injunction because it is already encompassed by another;
furthermore, a restatement (*anuvāda*) of something situated at a distance is not tenable due to the intervention [of other elements],
as it fails to enter the mind, just like the *kauṇḍapāyina* sacrifice.
Furthermore, the defining characteristic of a fourth-case (caturthī) compound is not found here;
nor can the postulation of a rule for the deity be possible without it,
and yet that relationship between the meanings of two subsequent words must be established.

Even in the case of *prātaḥ*, this co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established by that very fire alone, as is the case with the object (*karman*) in relation to the element to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Furthermore,
the status of being a name for a substance (*dravyanāmatva*) is clearly not perceived in the case of *āghāra*, nor is there any designation of it as such.
Now, this is an illustration with the exception of "atha eṣa jyotiḥ" and so forth;
for since there is no mention of them in the instrumental case, it is impossible for them to be injunctions of subordinate qualities (guṇavidhi).
Furthermore, those [mantras] are only subject to such investigation when they are encountered in other sentences where they are mentioned in the instrumental case.

Alternatively, since it is possible to introduce even a substance by means of a nominative designation and subsequently present that which is to be accomplished by it, these cases are also indeed examples [of guṇavidhi].
In those instances, there is an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) based on those very factors such as renown (prasiddhi) and so forth;
nor is there any basis for the application of the term to the ritual action itself.

If one were to proceed toward the object [of the sacrifice] by adopting the meaning of the possessive suffix (*matup*), there would be an extreme remoteness from the primary sense; in that case, it is better to assume the presence of the possessive suffix (*matup*). For when the means (*sādhana*) is understood, it conveys the action to be accomplished (*sādhya*) without difficulty due to their absolute non-separation, even without the elision of the possessive suffix.
Furthermore,

under the view that it is an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi), the word *śyena* at the time of its own utterance enjoins its own primary meaning alone; subsequently, however, it indicates that which possesses that [quality] without abandoning its own meaning.

For you, however, since it is accepted that the word was employed from the very beginning with the intention of excluding similarity because of its lack of utility for the purpose [of the injunction], there arises the consequence of contradicting the Vedic revelation (*śrutibādha*). To this it is said:

indeed, in the passages concerning the *śyena* sacrifice and others, no praise is observed, because it is accepted that "just as a hawk swoops down and seizes [its prey], so too does this [sacrifice]."
And that which is being enjoined by it must necessarily exist;
furthermore, when a quality is enjoined, a substance is generally also enjoined, and thus that very substance is what ought to be praised.
Nor is it logical for a thing to be compared with itself.
Now, it might be argued that praise is even greater by way of non-difference, because its conduct is impossible for anyone other [than the deity];
likewise, since qualities are heard in the name, there must be an injunction [of those qualities]. If this is said:

Through the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application), the meaning of the verbal root expressed by a word does not contradict its status as both the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the result and the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*) with respect to the subordinate quality (*guṇa*). Therefore, by the simultaneous operation of the injunction—namely, "one should effect the sacrifice by means of the *udbhid*, and one should effect cattle by means of the sacrifice"—the relationship is established without even the need for the *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (indication of possession).
Likewise, through *tantra*, the word *ājya* (clarified butter) and others are connected simultaneously with the hymns (*stotra*), the numbers, and so forth.

Therefore, since in every case regarding a name imagined by you, the cognition of a quality does not cease because of the hearing of a quality [in the word] due to its well-known meaning and so forth, let there simply be an injunction of that [quality]; enough with treating it as a name. This [discussion] is commenced by challenging all the previous topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) as far as possible, so that this sentence too may remain pure; the mention of the *vājapeya* is for that purpose, though in fact all [such examples] should have been cited here.
And because the two actions are equal, there is no single-wordness [of the agent], as in the case of something for the sake of another.
The status of being a *tantra* (a single performance for multiple purposes) arises from uniformity due to equal benefit;
however, when there is a difference in benefit, it is characterized by repetition (*āvṛtti*). This would not be the case unless the sacrifices were enjoined by some other word.
Those qualities would indeed be taught by way of an injunction without distinction;
however, the requirement for a mantra on the part of the substance is not possible in its own form,
nor is a connection with that [substance] perceived through a word denoting something else.

For if the nature of sacrifice (*yāgatva*) were first ascertained, then—given the resulting expectancy for a deity—the mantras expressive of deities would be connected [to it]; however, that is not what is expressed by the word *bhavati*.
Furthermore, prior to the connection with the sacrifice, the universal character (*viṣvatva*) of the *puroḍāśa* and other materials is not ascertained;
for this is a relative term (*saṃbandhiśabda*), not one applied solely by virtue of the intrinsic nature of the substance.
For indeed, substances such as milk and the like, when connected with a material sacrifice (*dravyayāga*), are not denoted by the word *havis* in common worldly usage.
By this, the argument that [the term *havis*] is a name for the ritual action (*karmanāman*) based on the injunction regarding the fourfold portioning (*caturavatta*) is refuted.

In the case of the *āghāra* libations and others, however, because they consist of action, there arises an expectancy for a mantra; and due to the application [of mantras] by direct statement (*vacana*), there occurs the postulation of a deity based on the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇikadevatā*).

Furthermore, this rule regarding deities is the very last resort; since it is possible within the rule regarding deities expressed by *taddhita* suffixes—which are the most senior—why is it resorted to?
Otherwise, as stated in the *Tantravārtika*, its basis would be the impossibility [of another explanation], yet such impossibility does not exist in the case of the *taddhita*.

Therefore, once the connection between the substance (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*) has been established by this very [injunction] preceded by an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and the action has been enjoined by means of the verb *bhavati*, the recitation of the mantras follows in sequence for the purpose of providing specific details.
And because there is no other way, the injunction of multiple meanings is accepted;
this is with the intention that the word ending in a *taddhita* suffix serves the purpose of an injunction.
Therefore, all of this is understood as being inseparable.

First, the deity is expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); the substance qualified by that [deity] is expressed by the secondary suffix (*taddhita*); and even the relationship [between them] is grasped within that very [suffix] through the force of the meaning. Furthermore, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that, the word *aṣṭākapāla*—which includes all its own subordinate elements—is included therein as a qualifier. And since the coming-into-being of a substance cannot occur unless it is characterized by being "for Agni" (*āgneyatva*), the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) implied by that [substance] is also contained right there.
And since it is not possible to bring about the state of being dedicated to Agni (*āgneyatva*) without a sacrifice, the sacrifice—which is a specific human activity—is also included therein.
Consequently, everything else that is implied by implication (*arthāt*) through the injunction contained in the word ending in the *taddhita* suffix does not split the sentence.

Furthermore, since in all cases the injunction regarding the meaning of the verbal root and its factors (*kāraka*) is preceded by an injunction regarding the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), that very [efficient force], though not explicitly heard, is first enjoined as qualified [by the other elements].

Therefore, because the qualifying attributes would otherwise be inexplicable (*viśeṣaṇānyathānupapatti*) and because it consists of the connection of all [factors], one denotes that very [connection] by the word "relation" (*saṃbandha*); however, a relation between substance and deity cannot be enjoined because it is not of the nature of an operation (*avyāpārātmakatva*).
The phrase "due to non-separation" (*avibhāgāt*) is the reason for the implication of the object.
And the statement "not by another" (*na ced anyena*) is an expression based on the resort to inexplicability otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*).
In the world, linguistic usage is not observed with reference to sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and the like;
therefore, like the word *yava* (barley), their status as causes of refinement (*saṃskāra*) is established by the Veda.
Furthermore, even when a word is seen to be based on a genus (*jāti*) in one particular instance, [it may apply elsewhere].
Because that [word] is not abandoned, there is no postulation of another cause for it;

for it is established that "the very words that are worldly are the same as those that are Vedic, and their meanings are the same. Since this is settled, where a word's status as being based on a genus (*jāti*) is obtained even in a single portion of the Veda according to worldly convention, it is impossible to postulate a further power of another cause there. Furthermore, because the genus does not depart even in the case of refined (*saṃskṛta*) words, one cannot claim a departure from its being based on that [genus]; and therefore, since there is no contradiction with what is established in the various branches of the Veda (*śākhā*), there is no sublation.
Furthermore,
these [characteristics] do not deviate from birth;
however, they do deviate from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), because at the time of conventional worldly usage, conditioned phenomena are absent due to their not being so designated.

For if, at the time of the injunction for cutting or the injunction for tying, some worldly object were found [to be fit], then why would one imagine a reversal of the established syntactical expression such that "that which is cut is surely the sacrificial post" (yūpa)?
Since there is an application for the *barhis* grass and so forth, therefore, in the case of well-known conventional meanings of wholes (*samudāya-prasiddhi*), people perceive a lack of parity.
Because it brings together the constituent parts of the meaning, the other [meaning] is set aside;
when a word whose individual parts have no meaning is employed for another meaning,
the collective whole is established there by virtue of having no other recourse.
If the horse-ear [leaf] were somehow present in trees,
who would ever imagine an unseen power for the whole [of the tree], as is the case with the fire-drill?

Even in the case of *nirmanthya* (to be produced by friction), its etymological nature (*yaugikatva*) must be established—just as in the previous section—by means of the genus (*jāti*), refinement (*saṃskāra*), and the immediate proximity (*paścādvāda*) of the cause (*nimitta*).

If it were a conventional term (*rūḍha*) characterized solely by its function (*karma-artha-lakṣaṇa*) in common usage, there would be no cognition of "freshly churned ghee" (*aciranirdagdha-ghṛta*) through a meaning not conveyed by the word itself.
Furthermore, since all ghee is a modification of butter (*navanīta-vikāra*), the repetition of the term would have to signify "freshly churned butter."

But here, in a case where verbal testimony (*śabda*) is the means of knowledge, the word *nirmanthya*—which has fulfilled its purpose merely by excluding what is produced by other actions—is incapable of taking on the qualification of "long" or "short" [duration]. How then can it be assumed to have as its object that which was churned recently? Furthermore, "recentness" (*aciratva*) is not included within the etymological derivation (*yoga*), because the derivation is based solely on connection with the action. Therefore, this [objection] is invalid.
This is not a fault;

for just as in injunctions such as "wearing a red turban" (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*), because the subjects are already established, the purpose is solely to enjoin the qualification, so too here, by way of restating the subject, the action itself—which serves as the qualification—is enjoined as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the cooking (*pāka*). And it is stated that subsidiaries share the same place, time, and agent as the primary act.
Since this *Tantravārttika* was composed by him not long ago, not far in the past, and by no other author,
the term "not long ago" (*acira*) should be understood as being used for the sake of illustration;
there is no purpose whatsoever in restating the entire compound.
The Viśvedevas have not been established [as recipients] either individually or collectively; yet,
although there is no distinction in their being the subject under discussion, where such establishment does not exist,
there will be no inconsistency (vairūpya) because of the restrictive application (upasaṃhāra) of the injunction.

Because it is already occupied by another quality, there is no room for a further quality; nor is there an option, because of the resulting inequality. Therefore, it is only appropriate that they be mere names, as there is no mutual connection of meaning between them.
Having taken up the Vaiśvadeva [offering], no separate deity is taught; for a single word cannot simultaneously function as both an injunction and a restatement.
Because the qualities are for the sake of another,
it is also possible that this [sūtra] forms a single sūtra with the preceding one.
If they were offered together with one another, there would be a connection to futility due to the absence of the attainment of thirty.
Why, then, should a simultaneous abandonment be performed by him? When the capacity for simultaneous offering exists, a sequential performance is not appropriate.
Furthermore, because the deities are agreed upon as being common, simultaneous offering is both possible and uncontradicted. (End of the fourth quarter of the first chapter.)
Consequently, there is no contradiction with the number thirty;

and for some, the completion of the thirty is as follows: nine *prayāja* offerings, nine *anuyāja* offerings, two *āghāra* libations, two *ājyabhāga* portions, and eight principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*).
For others, however, because the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the *ājinejyā* are included [in the count], the two *āghāra* libations are not counted.
In every respect, however, the establishment of the distinction between the primary [rite] and the subsidiary [rites] is achieved when the name denotes a previously known object;
for otherwise, these [faults], such as the lack of applicability, would arise, just as in the case of the option regarding the Vaiśvadeva.

Even though intermediate numbers exist within the great numbers by virtue of their objective nature, they cannot serve as qualifiers for the ritual action because they lack the capacity for delimitation.

Furthermore, if the purpose were the injunction of a quality (guṇa), then the other qualities would be rendered useless in the performance [of the rite]; for [in that case], with respect to that [quality], there would be no [need for] the first word denoting the object. (First Chapter, Fourth Pāda)
In this way, whether it be an accessory (guṇa) in a sacrifice that is either primary or secondary, or even a substance (dravya),
a substance— being likewise possessed of an accessory— is not in any way enjoined [as the primary object].

Nor is the word *vaiśvānara* connected to the sacrifice; because it is joined with a different case-ending, it would otherwise be meaningless. If it is argued that its status as a supplement (*śeṣa*) is not possible, [we reply] that since there is no separation [from the injunction], they may be consistent with the purpose of praise within the context of the injunction.
The fourth quarter of the first chapter:
This [statement regarding] the number eight and so forth is for the purpose of enjoining [the twelve]; it is a commendation (*prarocanā*) of that.
Therefore, the number twelve is commended by means of its constituent parts.

For everywhere, praises are seen to consist of either few or many syllables; and because there are various types of praise, some of them may be meaningful in certain contexts. Just as in some cases, when an action is accomplished merely by the mention of a number, a praise with a different purpose is resorted to, so too, even when the task could be accomplished by a brief praise, a great praise may be employed.
Thus, it has been argued that the injunction of numbers such as eight and the like, as well as the act of praising itself, are useless because they are subsumed within the number twelve.
Therefore, it is not purposeless;
for the state of having twelve potsherds is constant.

However, for one who seeks specific qualities as fruits—such as the *brahmavarcasa* (brilliance of sacred knowledge) and so forth—the numbers eight and others are prescribed by way of superseding the number twelve.
For indeed, every effort is for the sake of accomplishing the human goal (puruṣārtha); therefore, that which is proximate to it becomes more powerful.

The number twelve is remote from the human goal, since it serves only to delimit the potsherds used for the refinement of the sacrificial materials employed in the sacrifice that achieves that goal. On the other hand, numbers such as eight and so forth, being dependent on those [potsherds], directly accomplish results such as spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) and the like; thus, due to their proximity, they are more powerful and are therefore meaningful.
Now, some there say:
"The objection here is based on the logic of the *pūrva-pakṣa* and *uttara-pakṣa* regarding the *audumbara* [wood] and the *rādhika* [offering]"; that, however, is not tenable.
Because the answer has already been given in that very place,
the intended meaning here is as follows:
by the words "he is indeed purified, he is radiant," and so forth, the fruit [of the action] is being stated.
The passage beginning with "By the Gāyatrī itself [he purifies him]" is the individual injunction for the offering.

Through the sentences beginning with "When [the cake] on eight potsherds," etc., together with their explanatory passages (arthavādas), the connection with the results—such as "he becomes purified"—is made for each of the offerings prescribed individually according to their respective order.

We observe that what was introduced at the beginning—"When a son is born, [he should offer] a cake on twelve potsherds"—is concluded at the end by the mention of the twelve potsherds among the eight and so forth, in the phrases "that which is on twelve potsherds" and "when he is born, this [offering]."
And to that extent, qualities such as non-perishing and so forth cannot exist as separate [entities] in the fourth quarter of the first chapter;
furthermore, their syntactical unity with that [subject] is not possible without being a praise,
because if they were intended to convey a different meaning, they would be purposeless.
For if these were connected to the agent, then they would be the causes or motivators for him;
however, these are connected to Vaiśvānara.
Therefore, since no other purpose is possible, they serve the purpose of praise.
It is enjoined;

and because phrases such as "he indeed becomes purified," which contain the word *tat* (he), are required by the phrase "on whose birth [the son is born]," they do not have a connection with the preceding [results] as their fruit.
Nor is there any lack of utility here, whereby they would be detached from the context and taken elsewhere.
Furthermore, there is no connection between the "not being lame" and so forth with the "brahmanic luster" and so forth by way of these [latter] being its divisions.
However, in cases where a division exists, such as in the passage beginning "By means of the Gāyatrī he [obtains] this," the status of being a praise (*stuti*) is indeed accepted.
Therefore, the attribution of results to those [passages] beginning with "He who is named Pūta" pertains only to the sacrifice, and not to the "not being lame" and so forth.

However, at the initial occurrence, even what appears to be praise is indeed praise; for, being devoid of independent volition (*kāmakāra*), it lacks the formal characteristics of an injunction regarding a result (*phalavidhi*).

Since these very [passages] serve as the basis for the logical consistency of statements such as "when [the cake] on eight potsherds," it is established that they are not injunctions of subordinate qualities (*guṇavidhi*).

The operation of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is held to occur when [the word] is connected with that which is inseparably related (*avinābhūta*) to the primary meaning. However, figurative usage (*gauṇatā*) is accepted as occurring through connection with the qualities (*guṇa*) of the object being indicated;
for instance, from the object indicated by "fire-ness" (*vahnitva*), such things as "hotness" (*auṣṇya*) and "sharpness" (*taiikṣṇya*) are understood.

Therefore, the cognition of "boy" arises [in the case of the boy] due to similarity; for it is not possible for any single entity to possess the capacity for both [the primary action and the secondary action]. Because of contradiction, since there is no injunction for the sacrificer to act as the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*), and because of the perception of various attributes such as being the father and acting with force, the cognition of Devadatta arises. Thus, the previously established power alone is the cause. One should not resort to abandoning what is well-known and imagining what is unknown—which would result in the destruction of linguistic usage by serving as a cause for doubt.

Others, however, hold the view that all words such as "lion" and the like denote a collection of genus, quality, and action; and when the full range of these meanings is not present, they are applied figuratively to individuals like Devadatta due to the presence of only a few qualities and actions. To this, it is replied: indeed, even when only the genus is perceived and all actions and qualities have ceased, the word is still employed.
Furthermore, the cognition [of the word] occurs through its primary sense alone, and is not metaphorical—as in the case of the word "lion" applied to Devadatta and others.
Moreover, the fact that [the word] denotes a universal (sāmānya), which was established in the *Akṛtyadhikaraṇa*, would be contradicted [if it were metaphorical]. As stated in the *Tantravārtika*:
"Because actions and qualities are infinite, it is impossible to experience their relationship with every individual instance."

Nor can a universal be postulated on the basis of what is not a universal, because even in a different genus, some [qualities] may exist in certain things; for a "lion-ness" that has not been expressed cannot serve as a delimiter for qualities and actions, since it is not perceived. But if it were expressed, then by the very fact of cognition, all qualities and actions would be understood, and thus there would be no determination of a specific denotative power. Therefore, it is impossible for words denoting a whole to be applied figuratively to its parts.

Someone else, however, says that a secondary (gauṇa) term is one to which the nature [of another] has been superimposed. His view is this: in no way can a word for something else function with respect to another object—except by means of the mere action or quality that serves as its own basis—without that genus which constitutes its own basis.
Furthermore, if the word "lion" were not functioning [therein], the application of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "Devadatta is a lion" would not be possible.

How, then, is it that Devadatta and others attain a state of similarity through the perception of actions and qualities similar to those of lions and the like, by means of a conventional mental construction?
Consequently, the word is employed in its own primary sense; yet there is no consequence of it being a primary [denotation] in this case, because the object is merely superimposed.
But where that very object is not superimposed, there it is primary; thus there is no fault. To this it is said: this is not so, because such a conceptual construction is impossible.
For instance:

When, first of all, one superimposes water upon a mirage through delusion and employs a word [for it], then because both [speaker and hearer] apprehend the water by way of determining the primary meaning, the delusion constitutes primacy.

Furthermore, even if the speaker is discerning and employs the word for the sake of another’s speech, but the hearer does not discern [the distinction], then since one lacks superimposition due to discernment while the other possesses determination based on delusion, the status of being secondary (gauṇatva) is not possible with respect to either.
However, when both are free from delusion, there is an absence of superimposition because both determine the object present [in the mirage] as something else, based on causes such as similarity.
For instance,

just as there can be no superimposition of one thing upon another— such as between dissimilar objects like the bitter and the sweet— because there is no cognition [of them as such], so too the discernment of even similar things is not possible. Indeed,
no cognition of a name other than the determination of the object can serve as a factor for linguistic convention.
Furthermore,
it has been stated in the *Śūnyavāda* that cognition does not arise devoid of an object, merely experiencing its own form alone.
Moreover:

In every respect, this distinction between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*) functions to enable listeners to determine a specific meaning. At the time of hearing the words, they apprehend the word "lion" and so forth as functioning with its own primary sense unimposed; yet, because the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as "Devadatta" would otherwise be inexplicable, they postulate a secondary sense. In that case, according to the *Tantravārtika*, the perception of similarity to that [lion] arises for them even without their themselves superimposing the quality of being a lion.

And for those who investigate whether that [cognition] arises from the word or from the object, the conclusion—by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*—is reached that it arises from the object.
How so? When there is no superimposition (*adhyāropa*) on the part of the listeners themselves, then they do not form such a conception regarding the speaker as "surely he has superimposed lionhood."

How, then, is it that [the word "lion"] expresses the collection of various activities and qualities inseparable from lionhood? It is because one does not speak by means of individual denotations out of fear of excessive effort and prolixity. Furthermore, there is no single word that denotes this entire collection; therefore, how could the cognition of those [qualities] arise from "lionhood" alone through their inseparability? To this, it is first stated: human linguistic usage proceeds by virtue of the established power of words; it does not produce a new power based on that [usage].
Furthermore, for this reason, the definition that "the secondary (gauṇa) is that which functions for the sake of the manifestation of qualities" is alone logical, and not otherwise. [Objection:

If this were so, there would be the undesirable consequence that terms such as "sky-flower" could never be employed, because they lack qualities invariably concomitant with their own referents; likewise, when negating the *pradhāna* and other categories imagined by the Sāṃkhya and others, Buddhists and others would be unable to employ such terms without resorting to superimposition (*adhyāropa*). For if the [imagined entity] is not admitted, its negation is purposeless; if it is admitted, there is a contradiction. However, there is no fault if the negation is directed toward what has been superimposed.
And it is further stated:
"This fault belongs to you alone.
Why?"
How could the nature of a sky-flower, which is non-existent, be superimposed upon a non-entity?
Or rather, would it not be superimposed [if it were possible]?
For an object whose existence is known elsewhere is never transferred to another place.
However, a single entity is not understood to possess both the nature of existence and the nature of non-existence—
that very action which negations such as "he does not go" express;
rather, by means of [affirmative expressions] such as "he stands," that same action is perceived as having the nature of a real thing.
The genus (*jāti*) is described as being of the nature of the cause of bodies and so forth, consisting of atoms and the like; it is said that there is no other form of the primal matter (*pradhāna*).

In this regard, the words *āgneya* and so forth apply primarily (*mukhyatvam*) to the Brāhmaṇas and others because the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is produced through some connection [between them and Agni].

Alternatively, there is indeed a connection with the deity; for it is not only that which is offered which has a connection with the deity, since by that very same connection, the deity belongs to the sacrificer as well.
As he will state: "That deity also belongs to the person who sacrifices."
Therefore, that [example] is not an illustration.

Consequently, one should cite as examples those usages such as "Agni, indeed, is the Brāhmaṇa," for the well-known Agni, by virtue of the commonality of being born from the mouth, brings to mind the Brāhmaṇas and others.

And here, by the term "birth" (jāti), the acquisition of birth is intended; and although such a thing does not exist as a factual reality, nevertheless, because it has been stated so in another explanatory passage (arthavāda), its status as the basis for that word will be understood here as a praise.
But surely, it has been stated everywhere that the purpose of a figurative statement (guṇavāda) is to serve as a basis for praise?

True; elsewhere, the mention of "fruit" (*phala*) is merely a figurative praise (*guṇavāda*), but here it serves as the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) due to its similarity to the actual quality.
If one asks how this is so:

first of all, it cannot be said that buffaloes and the like lack the essential nature of being "animals" (*paśu*), because that would contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). One might then suppose it refers to the prohibition of their specific functions (*kārya*); however, even that is impossible, since those functions are prescribed in various places by scriptural injunctions.

Nor can there be an option (vikalpa) because of the inequality [of the two cases]. For in this case, the injunction (*vidhi*) is yet to be established, whereas in the other case, it is already established; or rather, [the latter] possesses purpose through praise (*stuti*), and thus one resorts to that [established injunction] as a last resort. Furthermore, the abandonment of the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*) is equal in both instances. Moreover, the repeated mention "animals such as cows" would be meaningless; nor is it possible to distinguish the actions and qualities that are inherent in the single referent of "animal-ness" (*paśutva*).
Furthermore, if the specific qualities inherent in cows and horses were to be negated, even then the result would be meager;
moreover, since the intended meaning is already established by the word "other" (*anya*) alone, [the use of the negative particle] would be redundant.

Furthermore, one must necessarily follow the meaning of the negandum as it was first presented by the subsequent member of the compound, because a negation directed toward an object not so specified is impossible.
Furthermore, nothing other than excellence (*praśastatva*) is required when something is being adopted.
And because they are connected with cows, horses, and so forth, these [words] are capable of conveying that excellence.
Although they are also capable of conveying non-excellence (*apraśastatva*), nevertheless, in view of the context (*prakrama*), that is not what is intended here; thus, only excellence is negated.
Moreover, even that mere negation is not itself purposeful; rather, by means of it, the superior excellence of others is indicated.
This is what is meant:
without regard for cows, horses, and so forth, no other [animal] possesses excellence—this is the fourth quarter of the first chapter.

The prohibition [of the suffix *niṣṭhā*] is based on the praise of another [suffix], namely that [the action] "exists" (*vidyate*). Since that [praise] is resorted to here first of all, it is understood later as having no other purpose.
In other cases, however, this [praise] occurs only at a subsequent time and is stated as the cause; furthermore, such an action must be mentioned even if it is already applicable.
For the narrative concerning the *dhvargyava* is understood in that way; since the middle layer (*madhyamā citiḥ*) mentioned in the direct Brāhmaṇa text is the locus [of those rites],
a connection must also be established for that purpose between the mantra and the act of placing the bricks (*upadhāna*).
The author of the Bhāṣya, however, avoiding figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case of an injunction, has resorted to the status of a restatement (*anuvāda*).

For in the passage "They praise with one," since the beginning of the section itself possesses the characteristic mark of creation, there would be the abandonment of its own primary sense for the sake of indicating another; and having indicated that, its own self would also have to be established again—this would be excessive complexity. But since it is a restatement for the purpose of praising the placing (*upadhāna*), the figurative indication is not faulty.
And it has been said: "Where, having aimed at the indicator, the action is enjoined upon the indicated object..."
The mention of "only that" (tanmātra) applies to both [the agent and the object] when they serve as the substratum (upādāna).
But what, then, is the cause for doubt here? Some say it is the mention of the general form (sāmānyagrahaṇa) in the injunction (vidhi); that is incorrect.
In that case, it is because there is a determination of just that much.
One might ask: "How can a universal exist without particularity? We reply: "Like clarified butter."

Furthermore, even there, the doubt regarding whether the substance is fresh or old cow’s ghee, buffalo ghee, and so forth, remains; yet, just as there is no doubt through the determination of "ghee" alone, and the purpose is accomplished by all [of them] despite the non-specification of particulars, so too here, there is no doubt because of the inclusion of any substance capable of providing lubrication (*snehana*).
Therefore, others claim that there is uncertainty because of the mention of "ghee" (*ghṛta*) in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
Nevertheless, this is not correct, because the matter has been determined through the understanding of the specific [context].
"For indeed, no one doubts in the case of [the sentence] 'Let the white cow be brought' that it is a cow;
this is an unequal comparison.
How so?"

For if it were the case that [the injunction] were "one places the pebbles smeared with ghee," then one would have no reason for doubt at all; but if, as in the case of the sentence "bring the cow, the white one is excellent," it were heard thus, then there would indeed be a cause for doubt. This too would merely be an illustration.
Therefore, the doubt arises from this: that the general [form] is in one place and the specific [quality] is in another.
Some, indeed, declare that injunctions and eulogies constitute separate sentences merely because they appear as distinct;
however, when there is a division of sentences, it is reasonable to have a doubt, since one sentence is complete in its general sense while the other is directed toward a particular detail.

As for the statement, "But [it is so] because of being a single sentence with the injunction," that is intended to show that a connection exists subsequently, just as in the case of sentences concerning subsidiary and principal elements.
Since praises are dependent upon injunctions and are merely restatements, they are understood through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).

However, because the injunction possesses primacy and there is no contradiction, that [figurative sense] is not assumed; rather, let that explanatory passage (arthavāda) be taken as it is, while the injunction regarding ghee remains general.
The Fourth Pāda of the First Adhyāya:
Without a eulogy (stuti), however, an injunction would apply only to its own specific substance; for no injunction is ever completed unless it has been made attractive (aprarocita).
Having observed an incentive regarding clarified butter (*ghṛta*), a rule (*vidhi*) is inferred therein;
or rather, it is a conceptual construction based on the sense of the matter, because it is a part of the same [instruction].
Now, in a case where there is doubt and no remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) exists, [the meaning must be determined otherwise].

In that regard, the determination is made solely by the injunctive element established through functional capacity (*sāmarthya*). Just as the verbal recitation (*pāṭha*) is a means of comprehension, so too is the functional capacity of the Vedic texts.
For this very reason, these [texts] do not record [the full details]; they would only record a thousandth part of what is actually there.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the Mīmāṃsā-vārttika composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Kumārila; [this is] the Tantravārttika.
Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
Here, the meaning of the definition is, in its true nature, the distinction [of the word] from other words and so forth.

Even though the distinction of *tantra* (commonality) and *āvāpa* (repetition) was discussed previously, the first quarter (*pāda*) of the second chapter is primarily intended for the establishment of that [distinction].
All matters such as the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*) are based upon the distinction of ritual acts (*karmabheda*).
When the subject matter (*kārya*) is known, there arises the authority for instruction and extension (*upadeśātideśadhī*).

First of all, prior to the examination of the meaning of the divisions (*bheda*) through the definitions of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇalakṣaṇa*), there is no introduction of any definition of division (*bhedalakṣaṇa*) and so forth; therefore, its commencement occurs at a later time.

Even therein, since the relationship of subsidiary and principal (*śeṣaśeṣitva*), the relationship of motivator and non-motivator (*prayojakāprayojakatva*), and the sequence (*krama*) pertain to distinct entities, the definition of division is not commenced before [the definition of] subsidiarity.

Likewise, since the qualification (*adhikāra*) can only be determined once the nature of the ritual action (*karmasvarūpa*) has been ascertained—and because it can be defined through its suitability for that action—it awaits all five characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Similarly, the latter six chapters, because they are the subject matter of extended application (*atideśa*), achieve their establishment only by depending on the knowledge of the primary injunctions (*upadeśa*); thus, they depend entirely upon the entire preceding six chapters.
Therefore, this connection of the section on difference (*bhedalakṣaṇa*) being established by process of elimination is commenced here.

Regarding the phrase "of which kind is the differentiation of action" (*yadvidhaḥ karmabheda*): although the term "name" (*nāmadheya*) should have been recited immediately after "number" (*saṃkhyā*)—because it is a metaphorical designation for the differentiation of the means (*sādhana*) and because it follows the sequence of the sūtras to be explained—it is recited at the end out of disregard [for that order]. The particle *iti* has the sense of a reason; that is to say, the sixfold differentiation of action is due to these causes. Alternatively, having derived the word "differentiation" (*bheda*) in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), the terms beginning with "different words" (*śabdāntara*) may be explained as being in grammatical apposition [to "differentiation"]. We shall explain later, in their proper place, how there is no redundancy between the two types of terms—namely, proper names and different words—and between number and quality.

And since these [means] have distinct objects in every case, there will be an investigation into whether they are [to be used] through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and so forth; thus, the primary intent (*tātparya*) is merely to establish their distinction. Other matters follow as incidental corollaries (*upodghāta-prasaktānuprasakti*), such as how this very section (adhikaraṇa) serves as an incidental introduction for the purpose of establishing the distinction of the unseen potency (*apūrva*) that is produced as a consequence of the subject matter. From whichever [means] the fruit is connected, one must understand the distinction or non-distinction of all [the other means].

If both the sentence and the sentence-meaning were partless (*niravayava*), then the investigation into whether dharma resides in each individual word and so forth would be entirely irrelevant; therefore, [the author] says: "And in the sentence, there is the meaning of the words. To this, an objection is raised:

For if the essential nature of *dharma* itself were being denoted, then the inquiry as to whether it is expressed by each individual word would be appropriate; however, this is not the case in a figurative (lakṣaṇika) context. Moreover, the inquiry here is not "Is that which is *dharma* expressed by each individual word? Rather, the question is: "Is that which is expressed by each individual word a *dharma* understood as the meaning of the sentence after its connection with the result has been established, or is it a single word-meaning assisted by the meanings of the other words? In this way, it is established by all [the authorities] that the status of *dharma* belongs to the whole.
This is because they accept that only that which is a means to the fruit is *dharma*.

There is no single object common to all [words] such that it could be relied upon as being one and the same for everyone. Furthermore, they consider the meaning of that which is connected with the word "fruit" (*phala*) to be *dharma*, namely, the means to the *apūrva*.
Therefore, the inquiry is whether all the words are connected with the result, or whether only one is. What is the prima facie view? That it is so for each word individually.
Why? Because a uniform connection with the principal [result] is not established.
Therefore, every word is connected with the word denoting the fruit;
from that which has a connection with the fruit, the *apūrva* (transcendental potency) is postulated.
For if the sentence were to terminate merely in the connection with the fruit, then all [words] might perhaps be connected with the fruit at some time.

Since the [result] is not established by that much alone, another *apūrva* (unseen potency) must be postulated; however, that [postulation] lacks a basis in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). In that case, since the matter is already established by the postulation of a single *apūrva*, there is no evidence for postulating another unseen entity.

For he who postulates multiple *apūrvas* would have to postulate at least one; and once that one has been postulated, the "presumption from the otherwise inexplicability" (*arthāpatti*) of the sentence is exhausted by its meaningfulness, and thus does not serve as a means of knowledge for another *apūrva*. Therefore, there is only one [apūrva] connected with the result, and from that, the other is determined to be an auxiliary factor, like the result itself.

And there will be no contradiction here, because the objection is resolved by [the name] being a mere designation (*nāmadheya*). Alternatively, in the absence of another way, one may resort to the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), as in the case of the statement "one should wipe the cup with the *daśāpavitra*. Or rather, since the instrumentality belonging to the verbal roots is established through the medium of the two parts of the meaning to be accomplished (*arthātiprasādhyāṃśa*), [the name applies]. This being the case, when it is uncertain which single [name] should be connected—since, in every way, one would have to resort to the assumption of multiple unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*) and thus a state of non-restriction (*aniyama*) would result—it is said in the *Tantravārtika*: [text follows].

That which is connected to the fruit is the primary [act], and that which is connected to it is held to be its subsidiary (*aṅga*). It is not possible for one and the same thing to be both a primary act and a subsidiary act.
For whatever meaning is understood from a word that cannot be obtained from any other source—that alone constitutes the entire meaning of the word.
In every verbal expression (ākhyāta), both the meaning of the root (dhātvartha) and the productive operation (bhāvanā) colored by it are understood;
therefore, they are designated as having "the sense of becoming" (bhāvārtha).
However, words denoting substance (dravya) and quality (guṇa) are understood to be distinct from those. [This concludes] the first quarter of the second chapter.

Thus, they were not questioned [regarding this]. In that context, since words such as *dravya* (substance) and so forth denote accomplished entities (*niṣpannārtha*), they possess the capacity to function as instruments (*karaṇa*); therefore, it follows that they are connected with the result (*phala*).

For everywhere, a result—being by nature something to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—requires a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), but not another thing to be accomplished. Furthermore, the meaning of a noun (*nāmārtha*), being already established (*siddha*), is capable of fulfilling that requirement; whereas the meanings of verbal suffixes (*ākhyātārtha*) are themselves things to be accomplished and thus cannot [serve as the instrument]. Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the result arises from substances and the like. To this, the answer is given by the Sūtra:
The cause for the connection with the fruit is the understanding of the *apūrva*.
And that connection is preceded by a requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*).
That [requirement] is observed to extend from words denoting action (*bhāva*), but not from words denoting substance (*dravya*) or quality (*guṇa*).

Therefore, from verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*), the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) and the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) are understood; and therein, due to proximity, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is apprehended as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Consequently, it is determined that by that very [root-meaning], which serves as the instrument for the fruit, the *apūrva* is brought about through the principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (*anyathānupapatti*).

But how is the meaning of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*)—expressed solely by the suffix as "one should bring about" (*bhāvayet*)—obtained by isolating the roots such as *yaj* (to sacrifice) and others?
Why?
Because verbal roots such as *yaj* (to sacrifice) do not convey the meaning of another root, since they are occupied solely with their own respective meanings.
Therefore, this [meaning] is superimposed even though it is devoid of a word, namely, "one should bring about" (*bhāvayet*).

Furthermore, for example, when it is said, "Bring the *pika*," one who does not understand the meaning employs only the word "kokila" (cuckoo) for that person, and not the expression "the *kokila* is the *pika*.
