Similarly, in this case, if the root *karoti* or the causative *bhāvayati* were synonyms for the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), then in explaining its meaning, only that [root] alone should be employed, and not even the verbal suffix; for at that time, it would not be specifically known by which part the action is conveyed.
However, in this context, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is indeed used again in such forms as "one should bring into being" (*bhāvayet*) or "one should do" (*kuryāt*).

And therefore, whatever meaning is conveyed by this [suffix] after the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is conveyed by that very same suffix after the root *bhū* (to bring into being); thus, the root *bhāvaya* is merely an addition (*adhikāvāpa*).
Consequently, it is not Vedic.
To this, it is replied:

In every instance, the meaning of "to do" is understood through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); indeed, there is no agent of the act of doing that exists without an object being done.
The agent of the sense of "becoming" (bhavati) becomes the object of the verb "to do" (karoti). That which has no constant becoming, or that which is eternally existent,
cannot be something currently being produced, just like a sky-flower or space.
He who is the agent of the action of "causing" is the instigator (*prayojaka*);

then, in relation to him, the one who is to become [the agent] attains the status of the "instigated" (*prayojya*). Verbs that express the exclusive activity of the instigated agent [are used in the causative].

Only those [verbal roots] ending in -eyat are employed in the sense of the actions that instigate them; for the capacities of all entities are not to be questioned, being inherent by their very nature.
Therefore, bases, suffixes, and so forth, express various meanings.
As for the claim that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth do not express an object other than their nature as injunctions (*vidhi*),
that is incorrect.
Why?
Because the root alone is not employed [in speech], because it includes the agent, number, and so forth,

and because its form is established as being indestructible, the suffix (*pratyaya*) is also employed. Furthermore, when the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is understood in the proximity of both the root and the suffix, it is never clearly perceived to which of the two it belongs as its denotation.
The base and the suffix always express their respective meanings together;
however, because of its predominance, the meaning of the suffix is determined to be *bhāvanā*.
Thus, it is always the case for both the base and the suffix, which possess a fixed sequence, that [the suffix's meaning prevails].
At the time of hearing the suffix (pratyaya), that which consists of the efficient force (bhāvanā) is understood;
even in cases such as the verb root *as* (to be), when something is to be brought into being, the efficient force certainly exists.

It is not manifested in that way elsewhere because it exists in its entirety [only there]. Although, in cases such as "he causes to be" (*bhāvayati*), the operation of the instigator is not very clearly perceived—since the agent is not yet accomplished and there is no separate object to be brought into being—nevertheless, by the power of the verbal suffix, it is understood that "he brings into being. When the question "what? arises, since nothing else can be conceived while the agent is unaccomplished, it is connected with "himself" (*ātmānam*). As for the questions "by what bringing into being? and "in what manner?", they refer to the manner of generating parts and so forth.

All three components there are fulfilled by the very act of becoming (*bhavana*), since no other operation is possible. Among them, some parts are engaged in the activity of becoming (*bhāvanā-vyāpṛta*), while others are already established as the instigators of that becoming (*siddha-bhavana-prayojaka*).
And the commonality (*sāmānya*) existing in both that which is already established and that which is yet to be established is called "becoming" (*bhāvanā*) due to its connection with both.
By this, [terms such as] *jāyate* (is born), *niṣpadyate* (is produced), and *sidhyati* (is accomplished) are explained.

Furthermore, the root *asti* (to be), having the same meaning as *jan* (to be born), receives a verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*) in the sense of "bringing about one's own existence" (*ātma-bhavana*) through its subsequent state of being (*bhaviṣyat-sattā*).

Even in that case, however, just as before, one must follow the conceptualization of the operations of the prompted and the prompter (*prayojya-prayojaka-vyāpāra*) by way of the forms of general existence (*sāmānya-sattā*) distinguished as prior and posterior by time.

Nevertheless, even when such a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) exists, injunctions (*vidhi*) and prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) are impossible, because their object is an agent who is already accomplished and conscious (*niṣpanna-cetana-kartṛ*).
It might be argued:
since it is observed that the *rathantara* [sāman] is used, therefore the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) of the *prāyaṇīya* day must be the same.
The *rathantara* occurs.
"In this case, there should be an Adhvaryu;
here there should be Ukthya offerings.
True, it is so seen, but the meaning here is not the same as that of the preceding [passage].

For it is said that a person who is drowsy (*middha*) should bring about his status as a priest (*ṛtvij*), which is the cause for connection with ritual action, by means of other activities of speech, body, and mind.

Likewise, in the case of the *rathantara* and other [Sāmans], even though there is a connection with the injunction of bringing into being (*bhāvanā*) through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), since that is possible there, it is the inferred *bhāvanā* itself that is enjoined.

However, where the usage is "one should become such-and-such" (*āmuko bhavet*), since the root *bhū* there signifies the sense of "standing" or "existing," it is understood that something distinct must indeed be brought into being.

"One should cause something else to exist by means of its locus"—this being the principle, it follows that the status of *bhāvanā* (the act of causing to be) belongs only to the non-ultimate activity of the agent (*bhavitṛ-vyāpāra*) as expressed through the mere designations of past, future, and present, and not to [the meanings of] injunctions (*vidhi*) and the like.

Even when describing the past and so forth, when the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself takes up the entire operation (*vyāpāra*) without resorting to distinctions created by parts such as the beginning [of the action], then—due to the clear contradiction—the mere meaning of the root and the number of the agent (*kartṛ-saṃkhyā*) etc. are determined as the referents (*padārtha*) of the finite verb (*ākhyāta*), and not the *bhāvanā*.
And it has already been stated that there is no fault in the deviation of the verbal root from the abstract action (*bhāvanā*).

As for the claim that even in the case of words ending in *kṛt* suffixes, the roots do not deviate from the actions: it is true that the meanings of the roots do not deviate; however, because those very [roots] convey the meaning [of the action], it is also possible to say that [the action] is not directly expressed (*anabhidheya*).

For instance, just as in a verb (ākhyāta), because the action (bhāva) is the primary meaning, the cognition of the factors of action (kāraka) as subordinate is established through their connection to that very action—and thus there is no direct denotation of the agent or the object—so too, since the efficient force (bhāvanā) is established through the very denotation of the agent and so forth (as it could not otherwise be accounted for), there is no direct denotation [of the action itself]. Furthermore, the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the word "karoti" (he does) depends solely on what is implied, just as the word "pacati" (he cooks) is coreferential with the word "Devadatta. And in this very manner, its connection with the factors of action will also be logically consistent.

Alternatively, since the factors of action (*kāraka*) exist for the purpose of accomplishing the meaning of the verbal root—which is itself subordinate to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*)—their connection is established with the meaning of the verbal root alone.
For it is that [meaning of the root] which requires them for its own accomplishment, and the *bhāvanā* likewise takes up those very factors as they are; thus, the connection is not contradictory.

However, in the case of gerunds (*kṛtya*), because they express an injunction (*praiṣa*), even though the *bhāvanā* is not explicitly denoted, their own meaning does not reach completion until a *bhāvanā* complete in its three constituent parts has been obtained.
Why?

Because a person is not capable of performing anything other than his own activity once that [activity] has been set aside; and it is the injunctions (*praiṣas*) that cause this [activity] to be performed.
If they could not somehow bring about that activity, they would be unable to enjoin it; thus, even in this way, the implication of *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) is established.

Furthermore, whatever injunction (*praiṣa*) pertains to a Brāhmaṇa, all of it becomes an injunction (*vidhi*) precisely because there is no prior acquisition [of the act]; therefore, even without the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*), the *kṛtya* suffixes possess injunctive power.
This alone is the distinction between an injunction (*vidhi*) and an exhortation (*praiṣa*).
Therefore, it is established that *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) is the meaning of the suffix.

Now, an objection may be raised: if *bhāvanā* is held to be the operation of an instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*), then in the case of the root *pac* (to cook), there would be the action of heating and so forth, and in the case of *yaj* (to sacrifice), there would be the mental resolve and so forth; since these are themselves the meanings of the verbal roots (*dhātvartha*), it would follow that *bhāvanā* is expressed by the verbal root itself.
This is not a fault.
Even though this [apūrva] is not found apart from the meaning of the verbal root,
it is nevertheless understood as something distinct by way of its nature as a universal common to all [actions].
For indeed, in the case of sacrifice and the like, the universal is of the nature of an instrument (karaṇa).

Furthermore, that which is established as the object to be accomplished is called *bhāvanā*. Neither the *bhāvanā* as it exists in the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) nor the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is ever expressed by other words in its very same form.

And it has been stated that the mere relation is the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) as the bhāvanā. When [the word] is directed toward one part [of that relation] by direct denotation (śruti), its operation regarding that [other part] does not exist.
Once the direct denotation has ceased its operation after establishing the mere relation, the application to the other part must be resorted to on the basis of suitability (yogyatva).

Thus, if it is excluded from the part to be accomplished (sādhya) by means of its being more proximate as an injunction (vidhi) grasped by a single cognition, then it is understood that it will certainly be accomplished through another factor.
Furthermore,
how could the agency of that which [is established] in the act of coming into being be determined in any way?
Whether in its own sentence or in another's, that [efficient force, *bhāvanā*] attains the status of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Consequently, once the objective portion (*sādhyāṃśa*) such as heaven has been determined, the *bhāvanā* requires an instrument (*karaṇa*), asking "by what should one bring this about?

In that regard, since its operation is dependent upon scripture, when proximity to it is resorted to—and because the suitability or unsuitability [of other elements] cannot be known through any other means of knowledge, because there is no contradiction with the injunction, and because there is no reason to bypass the meaning of the verbal root which is presented through extreme proximity—it is understood that [the instrument] is "by means of sacrifice" (*yāgena*), for all *bhāvanās* of results are untenable without some specific verbal root-meaning.
And although the sacrifice itself is not yet accomplished at the outset, it will nevertheless be accomplished once it has been brought to completion by its own means.
Indeed, everything is at some time accomplished and at other times unaccomplished.

Furthermore, prior to the operation of the branches [of the ritual], accomplishment serves no purpose, because the accomplishment of the instrument is useful only at the time when the fruit is being realized.
And by virtue of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no contradiction in things existing in the three periods of time also being instrumental causes (*sādhana*).
Therefore, sacrifice and the like possess the status of instruments, and that [instrumentality] occurs through the medium of the *apūrva*; thus, the *apūrva* is understood from those words.
Consequently, the meaning of the Sūtra is possible even in this way.

"From those verbal roots such as *yaj* (to sacrifice) and others, which denote an action (*bhāvārtha*) and have the purpose of productive activity (*bhāvanā*), the efficient force (*kriyā*) should be understood.

But has it not already been stated that, according to the principle regarding the relationship between the object and the instrument, the understanding of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) must arise from a verb associated with a transitive root?
For it is thus:
Either all verbal roots would incur the status of being transitive, or else there could be no productive activity (*bhāvanā*) from intransitive roots.
This is not a fault. Why?

In the expressions "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*) and "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), one object (*karman*) is obtained as the completion of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha-apavarga*), while another is the object of the productive activity (*bhāvanā-karman*). In this regard, sometimes the very object of the verbal root also functions as the object of the productive activity, as in "he brings about the cooking by means of the rice. At other times, however, the productive activity—conjoined with the meaning of the root as qualified by its own object—is connected with a further object, as in "he should bring about his own purpose by means of going to the village" and "by means of cooking the rice."

And this [result], being understood as merely that which is to be attained subsequent to the meaning of the verbal root, is determined everywhere as the object of the productive operation (bhāvanā), its distinctness from the root-meaning being obscured.
And that [result] generally enters into a connection with the word "desire" (kāma) itself, as in:
"one desiring happiness should sit," "one desiring health should lie down."

Even though the roots *ās* (to sit) and *śī* (to lie down) are intransitive, when the meaning of "doing" (*karoti*) is expressed by a suffix, the objects such as "sweetness" (*svādu*) are determined to be the objects of that [action].

Therefore, since the root *kṛ* is always transitive, and because we observe coreferentiality even with intransitive verbal forms—as in "What is he doing? He sits" (*kiṃ karoty āste*) or "What is he doing? He lies down" (*kiṃ karoti śete*)—the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) in these cases is also transitive.
Abandoning that [activity], the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is then attributed to the sons, which is based upon that very productive activity.

In cases such as sitting or lying down, when an action is defined by a rule for a specific day or by immediate succession—such that it is understood as "this is the Veda" or "this is the ritual"—those are designated as intransitive (*akarmaka*).

However, for verbs such as *pac* (to cook) and *gam* (to go), their status as transitive (*sakarmaka*) arises from the fact that they are invariably connected to an object that is either produced (*vikṛti*) or directly related to them; there is no difference, however, regarding the qualification of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*).
This very productive activity is [discussed] in the *Tantravārtika* under the section on the three parts (*aṃśatraya*).

Since it is impossible for all the instruments [of action] to function as instruments unless they are assisted by means (*upāya*), the perfected [cognition] requires the "manner of performance" (*itikartavyatā*)—asking, "How should one bring about [the result]? And since perception and the other [means of knowledge] lack the power to assist in this regard, that manner of performance is to be understood entirely through scripture. Being established in some way according to proximity—or, in its absence, in whatever way possible—it is postulated through the authority of scripture, via direct injunction (*śruti*), instruction (*upadeśa*), or extended application (*atideśa*) based on similarity of the impulsion (*codanā*), by means of an entirely unseen assistance (*adṛṣṭopakāra*), as otherwise it would be inexplicable.

Therefore, because it is complete, it is enjoined as something fit to be performed. And from the injunction of that [root-meaning], the injunction of sacrifices and so forth follows by implication; thus, the status of the verbal root as the meaning of the action is established. There are certain words denoting action (*karma-śabda*), such as "sacrifice" (*yāga*), "offering" (*yajana*), and "worship" (*ijyā*). Although these should have been cited as examples, the citation of *naicikī* is intended to establish their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with those. Furthermore, since they denote the instrumentality of sacrifice and so forth, their status as words for action—which arises subsequent to the injunction—is understood through their dependence on another [the root].
For independent [words] cannot possibly have the sense of "being" (bhāva) in any way whatsoever.
Indeed, even independently, sacrifices and the like might at some time be subjects of doubt regarding the sense of "being" based on inference;

however, certain words that do not denote action (*karmaśabda*)—such as *bhāvayet* or *kuryāt*, which are cited as examples—are not truly words denoting "being" as previously described, because they express the operation of the person to be prompted (*prayojya*). Thus, words such as *bhūti* and the like are not valid examples.
In this regard, although by some means of etymological derivation from the causative suffix (*ṇic*) one might lead the word *bhāva* alone [to denote the action],
the other two [the root and the suffix] are also cited as having the sense of "being" (*bhāva*) insofar as they involve a portion of the agent's activity.

Alternatively, according to the explanation of the meaning of the second sūtra, since the purpose of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) does not reside in the denotation of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), the terms are "denotators of being" (*bhāvārtha*) even without expressing the entire meaning [of the productive operation].

But how is it that these are not *karma-śabda*s (words denoting the ritual action), given that the verbal root alone has been stated to be the *karma-śabda*? Since a root in its undifferentiated, generic form cannot be performed, it lacks the status of a *karma-śabda*. Therefore, because the term *karma-śabda* is understood to apply only to those roots that express specific actions, this objection is not valid. For if words such as *citrayā*, *darśa*, and *paurṇamāsa* were generally connected with the results [rather than the actions], then, due to the absence of the sacrifice being the instrument (*karaṇa*), there would be no basis for their being names (*nāmadheya*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This concludes the first quarter of the second chapter.

Since [the alternative] is untenable due to the lack of logical consistency, it must be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) by virtue of its well-known status and so forth; therefore, he says that this point is established in this section. But why was this not brought under that very same [section]? Because of the lack of connection with the end of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And why is the status of being a name (*nāmadheya*) not brought here? Because of the lack of connection with the section defining difference (*bhedalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, as they stand in their respective positions, the sequence of priority and posteriority is established by implication.
Nor is there a desire for these [results], which refers to the word denoting the fruit (*phalapada*).

"Because of the absence of case-endings" means either the disappearance of the verbal endings that express the causal relation (*saṃbandha*), or else "absence of case-endings" refers to the connection with specific nominal endings (*sub-vibhakti*) that denote an already accomplished entity (*niṣpannārtha*).
Therefore, words such as "substance" (*dravya*) and so forth do not have a connection with the result (*phala*).
And it has been said:
The relationship between the goal and the means is always dependent upon *bhāvanā* (efficient force).
Therefore, its establishment would not be possible if it were devoid of the cognition of *bhāvanā*.

For if it were maintained that only the word expressing *bhāvanā* conveys the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), or if the verbal root alone, independent of the suffix, were held to do so, then the position of the nominal stem (*nāman*) would be weak. However, in our view, just as the verbal root—supported by its connection with the suffix—possesses the capacity to denote the instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of being colored by *bhāvanā*, so too does the nominal word; thus there is no distinction.

Those things whose form is perceived when they arise in their own application are called *nāman* (names); therefore, there is no further expectation for them, because they have already become manifest in their own application. As for what was said—that when the unseen merit (*apūrva*) arises from one [action], then the other will be for its sake—that group first demonstrates a distinction by means of the nature of the thing itself. How so?
When the unseen merit is postulated from one [action], if the other partakes of that same purpose by virtue of having a visible purpose, then parsimony (*lāghava*) is obtained.

However, in order to establish that [the name] has that purpose, one must again postulate an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) even beyond that; therefore, it is better that all [elements] are connected directly with the fruit itself.

Nor is there any need to resort to a distinction in the relationship [of the name], for if the name is connected to the fruit, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) must necessarily be admitted as being for the sake of assisting it. And since that [verbal meaning] is something to be accomplished, it cannot assist the name—which is already established in its form—through any visible means.

Indeed, the object does not depend [on anything else] at the very moment of the employment of the word, because it is understood as already accomplished; nor is there a possibility of dependence on something yet to be established, since that which is required must already be established. Furthermore, the term *prayoga* (employment) refers precisely to the denoted object, in the sense of "that in which [the word] is employed. For the perception of an accomplished form has that very [object] as its substratum. If one were to speak of the non-arising of an action, the demonstration of perishability would follow; for even that which is accomplished, being momentary, logically requires repeated accomplishment. Thus, the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) is supplied: "there is no further expectation," meaning "no other expectation," or "no expectation of a primary [result] by way of being produced."
Alternatively, the meaning is that it "desires" what is beyond or far from them.
Why? Because of its very existence (*bhūtatvāt*).
This is stated for the purpose of describing its essential nature (*svarūpa*): because it is already accomplished (*niṣpannatvāt*).
Furthermore, at the end, the author of the Sūtras has indicated that very same point as the reason:

"But those verbal roots for which no usage is found in their own primary meaning are [called] *ākhyāta*s; therefore, because they are understood from them, there is no need for further application. (This concludes the first quarter of the second chapter.)
The meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), residing in the verb, is perceived as having the nature of that which is to be accomplished (sādhya).
When that [meaning] is desired as possessing a result, it is accepted that the name (nāman) has a visible purpose;
for even though the meaning of the verbal root consists of that which is to be accomplished, [it is still designated by a noun].
When it is designated by name,
then it is understood as having a completed nature, just like a substance;
the injunction, moreover, is the commencement.
Having established that [the Veda] is authoritative, an investigation was previously conducted regarding the specific words that serve as the means for its comprehension.
Since its very authoritativeness (*siddhatva*) remains unestablished, that alone must first be demonstrated; thus, the *Tantravārtika* states:
"An action enjoined for the sake of a fruit, though momentary, [produces a result] occurring after a long time."
Thus, because the accomplishment of that [result] cannot be otherwise, one understands the *apūrva* (the unseen force);
since it is not known through the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the *apūrva* is the object of the sixth [means, namely, inference].
Therefore, this is understood as having a name according to its actual meaning, and not as a [perceptible] entity.
Nowhere do we hear of a word or a sentence that denotes this [universal];
therefore, its being cognizable through words is not at all tenable.
As for the argument from perceived facts (arthāpatti), it must be rejected here just as it was in the case of existence.
Since the diversity of conditions such as being wealthy or poor can be accounted for even by means of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth,
what kind of presumption based on scripture (*śrutārthāpatti*) could there be where the inconsistency is seen through direct perception itself,
and where the postulated object is not contradicted by anything?
For example, when it is said "one should cut with a knife," it is because it is perceptually evident that meat, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), and the like cannot be cut by it in any way whatsoever.
Furthermore, even in that case, the assumption is made that [the rule applies] to liquids;
and this assumption is not contradicted by anything, as there is no conceptualization of what is heard versus what is not heard.
But the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is never conceived as being a means to the fruit;
for when other causes are negated, the status of the *apūrva* as the remaining alternative is established.
However, the status of the *apūrva* as the cause is not understood merely by the negation of other causes, because that would lead to an over-extension (*anaikāntika*) such as the horns of a hare.
Moreover, if the apūrva (the unseen potency) is intended as the goal to be accomplished by the sacrifice, then the heaven mentioned in the scripture would be rendered superfluous.
This is the conclusion in the Tantravārtika;
otherwise, if the sacrifice itself were the means toward the fruit, that same [conclusion] would follow.
And it cannot be determined by means of any other mode;
therefore, on the basis of the authority of scripture (*āgama-prāmāṇya*), the fruit must arise from the sacrifice itself.
If it is asked, "How can that which has perished bring about [the result]?"

If it is understood from the scripture itself in this way, what contradiction does that pose for you? Furthermore, what is the proof for the claim that the result must be accomplished by one who is being killed?
Moreover, why do eternal and ever-present entities such as space (*ākāśa*) not accomplish a result?

If it is assumed that the fruit is accomplished by the former [element] because permanence is possible for what exceeds what is heard, then it would be better to assume it from space itself; for its existence and permanence are at least well-known. One need only assume that it is the cause of the fruit. In the case of the former [element], however, everything from its existence onwards must be assumed without any basis of proof.

Now, if the intention is that some [entity] persisting through its connection with the sacrifice must bestow the fruit, even so, it is better to establish the status of the sacrificer himself as the cause—provided he remains conjoined with the sacrifices and persists; for in that case there is simplicity (*lāghava*). When this destruction of the action itself will accomplish the fruit for us, [the postulation of an intermediate entity is unnecessary].
If, on account of the injunction for bodily sacrifice, that [result] were to be postulated without effort, and if you were to state categorically that words denote a result at a later time,
then some other objective cause would have to be postulated by that very [injunction].
Having first ascertained the meaning of the scriptural branch (*śākhā*), one indeed proceeds to the performance;
however, the meaning of the scriptural branch is not determined at a time subsequent to the performance.

For it is not the case that an ignorant person is entitled to perform what is enjoined; therefore, everything that is to be understood from the scripture must necessarily be comprehended prior to the execution of the rite.
Furthermore, at that time, there exists no cause for knowledge of the separation from the fruit of karma.
And as for the claim that what was not ascertained as being included within the scope of the scripture at the time of its engagement is ascertained only at a later time—how can this be so? Moreover:
Since births are alike in their nature of consisting of both pleasure and pain,
heaven and hell exist here immediately following action; furthermore,
in the case of prohibitions, no *apūrva* (unseen potency) is produced as the purpose of the Vedic injunction.
But that which arises from their transgression would not be preceded by an *apūrva*,
for if the subsidiaries were to produce an *apūrva* while remaining at a distance,
there could be no benefit to the primary rites due to the lack of connection.
It cannot first be produced simultaneously by actions that occur sequentially;
nor can it be perceived sequentially because it lacks parts.

Since all manifestations must proceed through one or another formative impression (*saṃskāra*), another formative impression would necessarily have to be postulated. Consequently, the same fault remains; thus, [the theory] lacks validity.
If the *apūrva* were perceived immediately after the ritual action, then we might say that it is manifested;
and if there were a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its prior existence.

But since neither of these two conditions exists, the *apūrva* does not exist in any way whatsoever. Furthermore, this sūtra is not clear in establishing that [concept]; therefore, this is not a valid interpretation.
To this it is replied:
that which you have refuted as being a corporeal entity previously non-existent, conceived by your own imagination—that does not contradict us in the least.

For such a thing is not accepted by anyone; rather, what is intended is that "apūrva" (the unseen potency) is the supreme capacity—accessible through the scriptures—of either the action or the person, who prior to the performance of the action was incapable [of its result].
Prior to the performance of the primary rites or the subsidiary rites, persons are unfit for attaining heaven and the like, and sacrifices are unfit for their own effects.
Both of these types of unfitness must be set aside by the production of fitness through the primary and subsidiary rites; this is a point that everyone must accept.
For if that fitness did not exist, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of everything remaining as it was when unperformed.
And that very capacity, residing either in the person or in the ritual act, is designated as *apūrva* (the unprecedented) in this treatise.

As for the claim that it cannot be known through perception and other means of knowledge—that is true; it is not known by means other than scriptural presumption (*śrutārthāpatti*), but that is no fault. Why?
Because presumption alone is not accepted as its sole means of proof.
Furthermore, because it is a part of the word [itself], for us the scripture (āgama) alone establishes its own meaning:
since no single action whatsoever can ever function toward its result simultaneously due to momentariness, how much less so could many [actions] do so?
All entities possess causal potencies that conform to worldly transactional usage;
therefore, even at another time and place, that [result] is established through those potencies in its form.
Indeed, the fruit arises from the sacrifice itself by means of these potencies.
Or rather, that very result arises in the form of a subtle power;
when it is said, "The wood is to be cooked," the act of burning is thereby indicated.
And when a sprout is being born, the tree is also held to have arisen.
How can it be urged that permanence— which possesses a proven capacity— is required for a means of accomplishment (sādhana) known in both worldly and Vedic contexts to be perishable? Furthermore,
the emergence of a fruit does not arise from persons who have already passed away after performing the sacrifice.

There is indeed no distinction for you between what has been transcended and what has not been transcended; for if there were some specific factor among the constituent parts (*aṅga*) that would constitute the performance [of the rite], then,
because the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) is established, there would be a non-attainment of the constituent parts in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
Whether one disease is removed or ten diseases are removed,
no difference whatsoever is seen between those two in their state of health;
nor is it heard in scripture that heaven and other such fruits result from the destruction of karma.
And because of the contrary [evidence], that which is born from these [parents] cannot belong to the sacrifice;
for even worldly results such as sons and the like possess the nature of arising in a sequence.
No one determines that a result is obtained immediately after the ritual act.

Since desire and the like have as their nature the fruit of enjoyment over a long period of time, it is impossible for them to be identical [with the action] immediately after the performance of the rite. Consequently, if there were no intermediate cause, the result would necessarily follow at that very moment; therefore, something must certainly persist until the completion of the entire enjoyment.

Thus, because the restriction "prior to the performance" is established, the argument based on presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) regarding the absence of any deficiency in the agent is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); this [objection] is incorrect. As for the claim that in prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) the *apūrva* is not understood from the text: just as the *apūrva* is understood from prescriptive injunctions (*vidhi-śāstra*) in relation to the things enjoined, [so it is here].
In the same way, through negations, that [agent] is expressed by negations; it is indeed the agent and its locus, and action also resides in this very [locus].
For this agency in all actions is established within the doctrine of the self (ātman).
If the potency of actions were held to reside only in their own substratum,

then upon the destruction of those actions, that potency would cease to exist; however, the potency residing in the agent does not perish, because it is inferred from its effect and is employed as residing precisely where that effect occurs.
That [subservience] must be accepted as residing either in that [principal] itself or in something else which supports it;
for subservience (śeṣatva) exists by virtue of being for the sake of that [principal], not because of a relationship between a support and its supported.
A man seeking saffron always carries the fragrant powder on his shoulder even though it belongs to the king.

In this case, through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), one *apūrva* is first cognized; then, for the sake of establishing that, there would be further valid cognition of other *apūrvas*. Even very many unseen things are postulated when they are supported by means of knowledge.
Indeed, not even a hundredth part of what is unperceived should be postulated if it lacks a means of valid cognition;
just as a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) arises gradually through repetitions in the study of a chapter,
so too will the *apūrva* (transcendental result) come into being through the form of the constituent parts of the sentence.
The manifestation of entities is not perceived as being of only one form;
rather, its manifestation will consist in the unfolding of what resides within itself.
Therefore, there exists something unprecedented, and we see no other meaning for the Sūtra that is not already contained within this [principle].
Therefore, the very meaning is that the injunction regarding the commencement [of the action] is itself the injunction for the *apūrva* (the unseen potency).

If, however, one thinks that because of the force of the statement regarding the fruit, even that [action] has perished and thus the postulation of an *apūrva* lacks a basis of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: "This is better.

For it is not correct to say, "We do not perceive the form of actions," because in the passage beginning with "due to the non-distinction of the word 'form' (*rūpaśabda*)," there is a mention of perception by direct observation (*pratyakṣa*).
And since the context is the commencement of a sacrifice, it is incoherent to say that [the substance] reaches another location by means of its substratum, given that it is immovable by nature.
To this, the *Tantravārtika* replies:

"Even though the essential form of the action (*karmasvarūpa*) is perceived, nevertheless, because it lacks persistence until another time, it is not of service [to the result]; thus we say it is 'not perceived'."

For the production of a result does not occur through mere intention alone, since the scripture declares that the fruit arises from an action that possesses its entire essence and its complete procedure. In that context, because acts such as the throwing of two portions [of the offering] and acts such as taking up and placing down have conjunction and disjunction as their results, there must necessarily be a stable substratum for them.
Yet such a substratum does not exist;
nor is any manifested form perceived.
Since even volitions (*saṅkalpa*) and the like are obscured by subsequent volitions and so forth, it is not possible for them to abide in their own essential nature (*svarūpa*) here.
Furthermore, such abiding would have to occur either as inherent in the self (*ātman*) or as inherent in the substance to be offered (*pradeyadravya*).

First of all, motion does not inhere in the self; because the self is all-pervading, there is no possibility of a location being joined with or separated from it, and thus it lacks the capacity to move.
If it is asked how this [Self] possesses all-pervasiveness, it is because its effects are perceived everywhere.
For, through inference, the mere existence of the Self whose nature is consciousness is understood, but it is not qualified by [specific] place or time.
And therefore:
They maintain that an entity which is not delimited by space and time is eternal and all-pervading; thus, the all-pervasiveness of the self is asserted [by them].
However, one who holds the doctrine that the self is contained within the body alone [does not accept this].
But surely, O King, the arrival from another country is a mark [of such a person];
therefore, this is a contradictory reason.
Why?

For if we were to perceive any effect of the self outside of the body—such as pleasure, pain, and so forth—in another body, then we might conclude its omnipresence. However, since the effect is observed only within one's own body, and wherever that body goes, it is perceived there in succession, it follows that this [self] exists only where the body is, just like the body itself.

Otherwise, the body too would have to be omnipresent; therefore, because it would necessarily follow that the self moves from place to place just like the body, the consequence of its being subject to action (sakriyatva) is all the more certain.
Or let there be doubt, because [the reason] is inconclusive due to being common to both sides;
and it has been said that the rebuttal to that is: "For when there is no arrival, nothing at all is contradicted."

However, for those who read the text as *na tu tadeva*, the interpretation of the passage is as follows: the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) himself, having raised the objection that the observation of the effects of the self (*ātmakāryopalambhana*) occurs everywhere in turn and thus remains indistinguishable as a mark of its coming (*āgamana*), states the following reply. But how is this a reply? [The opponent asks: "For it is not the case that there is no coming. To explain: [The text continues: *tathā hi*... [and so forth].
For indeed, another might say that there is nothing contradictory in the existence of going;

to this it is replied: by way of an exhaustive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*), there is nothing contradictory in the non-existence of coming, but when going exists, there is much that is contradictory—thus he says.

Regarding that which is being discussed: when even subtle elements such as the light of the moon and sun do not admit of a state of mixture with lumps of clay and the like, then how can there be a mixing of the self—which by its very nature is absolutely formless—or of the continuum of consciousness, with material elements? From where could this be established? Furthermore, if a proponent of the *syādvāda* were to argue that because the selves are not entirely distinct from the body, the soul indeed possesses corporeality, for him too there would follow the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): corporeality [would follow] from the state of being mixed, and the state of being mixed from corporeality.
Therefore, because its formlessness is established by the illustration of its state of liberation, its corporeality cannot be proven to be caused by contact with a body.

Consequently, being distinct from the body, unassociated with it, and—due to its incorporeality—not drawn along with it, the self moves toward the body; like the space-portion occupied by that [body], the self remains right there once it has subsequently emerged, for it has no propulsion by air, earth, or other elements, by which it might move either independently or impelled by another.
However, in the case of flames and the like, because they possess tangibility, it is logical that they move when impelled by the wind or carried away by a torch or similar object.

Consequently, if only the body were to move, it would be insentient. But if [the self] is omnipresent, then wherever one goes, there the self’s continuity exists; thus, the persistence of sentience is logical.
Just as when a previous spatial point is vacated, the provision of space by the subsequent [point] is established precisely because of its omnipresence;
furthermore,
the position that knowledge exists as a continuum has already been refuted.

In that case, if the eternal self were to exist within the body as something of atomic dimension, then perception would occur only of those pleasures, pains, and so forth located in the specific region occupied by it; furthermore, there would be no simultaneous experience of sensations in both the head and the feet at a single moment.

Now, it might be argued that [the self] is perceived here and there because of its subtle mobility; however, there is no evidence for this. Furthermore, no difference in time is perceived; since it is impossible for something unstable to be perceived at a specific time, it would not be perceived anywhere at all. Therefore, this is merely a conceptual construction. Moreover, the lack of desiccation and the presence of nourishment and so forth in the limbs of the body occur only when they are presided over by the self, as the opposite is observed in the state of death. In that case, whichever limb is abandoned by the self, that very limb would wither like a corpse. If, on the other hand, the self is admitted to be co-extensive with the body, then even in that view, many things would have to be postulated that are not observed.

For all these [factors], such as the existence of constituent parts, being beyond the scope of perception and other means of knowledge, are merely imagined; they are to be rejected just like the [doctrine of] sound.

Furthermore, it is impossible even to imagine an infinity of these [parts] limited only by the body; nor does there exist any cause for their cohesion apart from fluidity and the like. And those that are not cohered lack the capacity to initiate a single living being.
Furthermore, because all conjunctions are invariably followed by disjunction, the soul (jīva) might at some point undergo total destruction, just like a jar or other objects.
Moreover, the claim that when a limb is severed, the parts of the soul residing in that limb exit from it and re-enter the remaining portion of the body is without proof.

As for the observed throbbing of hands and other limbs immediately after being severed, that is caused by the wind impelled by the impact; one cannot conclude from this that there is a migration of parts of the soul.
That being the case, we see no evidence whatsoever in the *Tantravārtika* for the claim that contraction and expansion occur in these [atoms]. However,
in the case of things such as the light of a lamp, such [phenomena] are possible because they are perceptible.

Nor does the light of a lamp undergo contraction when a jar or similar object is placed nearby, because the remaining light is not destroyed; for the flame, being unobstructed, is capable of producing a circle of light around itself, and it is not covered.
By this very argument, expansion is also refuted; for it is entirely different parts that accumulate there and produce extension, rather than an expansion of those same [original] parts.

Furthermore, for things possessing tangibility, expansion through the occupation of other locations is possible due to the mutual obstruction of their spatial positions; however, since the constituent parts of the soul (*jīva*) are formless, there would be no impediment to all of them occupying the same location, leading to the undesirable consequence that the soul would eternally remain the size of an atom.
Moreover, how could contraction and expansion—measured by the bodies of a tiny insect or an elephant—be logically attributed to a single soul?

Furthermore, the transition of the soul into the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) at the time of death, the claim that this exists yet is not perceived due to some obstruction, and the assertion that the soul departs entirely from one body to enter another, are all without any basis in valid cognition.
Therefore, it is omnipresent.

As for the demonstration in the Upaniṣads that [the self] is the size of a grain of millet or rice, this is because that which is actually all-pervasive—as shown by other scriptural passages—is within the range of perception as something subtle.
Furthermore, as was stated by Dvaipāyana:

The statement, "Yama dragged forth a man the size of a thumb from the forest," should likewise be understood as being intended for the poetic embellishment of the verse and for the purpose of praising the conduct of death, occurring within a discourse primarily devoted to extolling the devoted wife; it is to be viewed as similar to [the stories of] Prajāpati cutting out his own omentum and so forth.
For indeed, in the Gītā and other works, he has described the omnipresence of the Self in many ways.
But surely, if the Self is omnipresent like space, it follows that there is only one single Self in all bodies.
This is not a fault;
for there is a multiplicity of bodies, and because we observe a fixed distribution of the experience of pleasure and pain in each individual body.
Otherwise, since the purpose would be fulfilled by a single body alone, the existence of multiple bodies would be rendered useless.
If it is argued that there is no fault because [the body] is like a body in another birth, we say no.

In that case, since there would be repeated initiations for the sake of various experiences under the influence of other karmas, there would be the perception of everything contained within all bodies for each individual body.

Furthermore, one would perceive through the sense organs belonging to others, because [those organs] would belong to oneself as they reside within another body, just like the perception of a hole [in a wall]. This concludes the first quarter of the second chapter.
There would be an absence of the distinctions between the social classes (varṇas) and so forth;
furthermore, there would be no differentiation in the injunctions for ritual action based on the established order of specific castes,
because a single self, when connected with various bodies, could arise as any caste whatsoever.
However, there is no fault in the case of the plurality of selves (*ātmanānātva*).
Furthermore, since all [selves] are omnipresent and devoid of material form (*mūrti*), there is no contradiction in their occupying the same location.

It is precisely with reference to this, and because they are non-distinct in their nature as consciousness (*caitanya*), that the practice of designating "oneness" (*aikātmya*) occurs in the Upaniṣads.

But how is it that, even though [the self] is of the nature of cognition, there is no perception of the pleasure, pain, and so forth belonging to another, since all [selves] are connected with all bodies?

First, some who maintain the theory of the transformation of the body say: "Furthermore, this same fault applies to that [theory] as well; because the [new] self in the womb occupies the same location as the previous self, the mother would perceive the pleasure and so forth residing therein."
In that regard, the rebuttal to this is that it will apply to all selves in all bodies; thus there is no fault.

If a logical justification (*upapatti*) were to be stated here, it would not be a mere concession to the opponent's position, because both you and he would be subject to further questioning by another.
Furthermore, that [self] has the dimension of the sense of touch (*tvagindriya*).

Since the self is not admitted to exist within the space of the body in the same manner as it exists externally, there is no contact between the mother’s body and the *kṣetrajña* (the conscious self) in the womb; therefore, that [alleged] fault does not stand.
Consequently, it should be answered as follows:
if the cause of experience were held to be a relationship characterized by the self and its qualities, such as pleasure, occupying the same location, then this fault would indeed arise.

In this case, however, the relationship [of the self] with the eyes and other senses is characterized by its fitness as the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field). Just as color and other objects, though occupying the same location as the sense of touch, are not perceived by it, so too another self does not perceive the pleasure, pain, and so forth acquired through the merit and demerit of another.
Therefore, there is no fault, because the distinction between one's own and another's is established as stated in the doctrine of the self (*ātmavāda*).
Thus, due to its omnipresence, the immobility of the self is established.
Then, regarding that which was present as the portion taken for the offering, he says:
"That has perished. And its non-destruction is not the case, because a different substance, contrary to it, is perceived.
Furthermore, there is no cause for the obstruction of its perception by which it would not be perceived.

If, on the other hand, an obstruction to perception and so forth were to be postulated through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*), even so, one would have to postulate many unseen things that did not exist before and are contrary to what is observed:
namely, that [the action] remains undestroyed, that it is not seen [in that state], and likewise, that there is a cause for its obstruction.
Furthermore, there would be an infinite regress, as one would have to postulate yet another cause for the non-perception of that [non-perception], and so on for each subsequent one.

Likewise, it would involve excessive complexity to postulate both the persistence of a momentary action and a cause for its non-perception. This is the case when one assumes the persistence of an action that is not dependent [on anything else].

If it were argued that [the substance] remained performing conjunctions and disjunctions while residing in the self, even in that case, one would have to resort to the assumption of an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) contrary to what is observed; therefore, it is better to assume the *apūrva* (transcendental result). Thus, the purpose of this initial section is established. Since substances and other factors are connected with the fruit [of the action], they lack a substitute (*pratinidhi*), because their purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*), just like ritual acts themselves.

However, regarding the connection between the action and its fruit, since substances and the like serve an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) through the production of the ritual act, there is a substitute (*pratinidhi*) because they are known to have an identical function.

How then, for the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*), is there an absence of the fault of leaving an commenced rite unfinished? [The answer is: the rite must indeed be completed by means of whatever substance is available.

However, one need not strive to obtain a similar substance, because even from a simultaneous [substitution], the fruit is not attained; and because an action whose specific means were not prescribed does not require similarity, it is established by whatever is available. Furthermore, that which was previously used is called a "substitute" (*pratinidhi*) for the original substance because it serves a different purpose and lacks similarity. For the original substance had not yet begun to yield its fruit, whereas the substance now being brought in is intended either to avoid the transgression (*pratyavāya*) or to ensure the completion of an action already undertaken for the sake of a conditional fruit (*naimittika-phala*). This concludes the first quarter of the second chapter.
The establishment of the name is also indeed a purpose;
however, it was not demonstrated because it has already been stated previously,
since there is no difference in their being verbal suffixes (ākhyātatva) [in that] the accomplished (bhūta) brings about the purpose of the to-be-accomplished (bhavya).

And since the capacity for being an object-to-be-accomplished (sādhya) resides in what is already established [as the primary], the predominance of all verbal forms [is established] in the relationship between the meanings of nouns and verbs;
it is logical that whatever lacks an established purpose therein has an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha), whereas for the other [which has an established purpose], such a claim lacks authoritative basis.

However, those substances which are not intended to be produced [by the ritual acts] are primary, because the substance is subordinate to them—those acts by which the substance is not desired to be produced either in its essential form or in its properties, such as the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. Since they are primary with respect to their own means of accomplishment, they serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
For a substance mentioned in connection with the primary act does not set aside the substance of a subsidiary act.
In the *prayāja* sacrifice, because it possesses clarified butter (*ājya*), there should be no sublation of the rice (*vrīhi*) when [the *caru*] is made of meat.

But is it not the case that even the first member [of the compound *prayāja*], being prompted by the primary rite, does not serve as a motivator (*prayojaka*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*) since it is merely a substratum for the rice? Therefore, in the *prayaṅgava-caru*, the pounding would not obtain for the rice grains that are not grasped by the primary rite.
This is not so.
The first quarter of the second chapter:
For the connection with the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) is equal in the case of the branch-offering (*śākhā-yāga*) and the threshing (*avaghāta*);
likewise, the offering of the whey (*vājina-yāga*) and so forth are equal, and thus do not possess the characteristic of being non-efficient causes (*aprayojaka*).
But [if it were] merely a property (*dharmamātra*), the action would apply [to all], because there is no completion [of the purpose], as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings.

The separate examples given for the cleansing of the ladle (*sruk*), the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the fire (*agni*), and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) are due to the difference in the degree of proximity to the primary act in each successive case.
This is what is meant:

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) argues that by the very definition of a primary action previously stated— namely, "that which is not intended for the sake of a substance"— it is observed that no action produced by a substance is seen to confer any benefit upon that substance.
Therefore, actions such as sweeping and sprinkling are primary actions,
because they provide a visible benefit to substances already established through other means.
Since there is nothing new [in the case] of those [verbs] such as *hanti* and so forth, their citation is for that purpose.
That alone is a valid means of proof which is conclusive (*ekāntika*).

However, the accusative case is inconclusive (*anaikāntikī*) regarding predominance (*prādhānya*), because it is observed even when a substance is taught as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*), as in "he offers the groats" (*saktūn juhoti*).

Likewise, in the case of the injunction "he sprinkles the sacrificial oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja*," the predominance of the clarified butter (*ājya*) is observed even in the absence of the accusative case-ending.

Therefore, in the phrase "they swell" (*srīṇanti*), although both [the accusative ending and the context] are possible, the predominance of the substance is established solely by the observation of its utility (*upakāra*),
not by the accusative case-ending.

And since that [purpose] does not exist in cases such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth, one might argue: "In this case as well, let the substance itself be taught by means of the accusative case.
To this we reply: No, because it exists for the sake of that [action], as in common worldly usage, and because it is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*).
Let the matter of the actual performance (*prayoga*) rest for now.
What is the reason?
For if conduct were of a single uniform nature, the *smṛtis* would certainly not need to be maintained with such effort;
rather, because it is muddled, that very conduct is clarified by means of the *smṛti*.

Furthermore, it is traditionally taught that the meaning of the accusative case is predominance, as stated in the rules: "The second [case-ending] is used for the object" and "The object is that which is most desired by the agent.
Accordingly, it is employed in both common usage and the Veda, as in the examples: *ghaṭaṃ karoti* ("he makes a jar") and *vrīhīn avahanti* ("he threshes the rice-grains").
And he cites those instances which are grounds for suspicion of worldly deviation:
"Cook rice-grains into boiled rice; make balbaja grass into crests; offer parched grains today," as stated in the *Tantravārtika*.

When the second case is employed where "with rice" (*taṇḍulaiḥ*) and "with balvaja grass" (*balvajaiḥ*) ought to have been used, it is understood that this [second case] must indeed have the same meaning as the third case. To this it is replied:

when rice and balvaja grass are intended to be expressed as the means for producing a specific type of cooked rice (*odana-śikhaṇḍaka*) which is a distinct entity, then they take the form of words ending in the third case.

When, however, the rice grains are seen in the form of sprouts (*śikhaṇḍaka*) for the sake of producing softness, having reached the state of being fit for food through the process of transformation—just as *balvaja* grass is used [for mats]—so too, those grains whose status as subordinate factors (*guṇabhāva*) is understood from Vedic statements remain well-cut for the *agnihotra* sacrifice which has substances as its means; because of their beauty, they are intended by some Brahmin woman for the purpose of displaying the excellence of her own work as being connected to the oblation (*homa*).

She sends him thus, either because she desires his virtues or because she says to the sacrificer, "Offer the oblation with rice grains for prosperity"; in that case, it partakes of the sense of the accusative. For in the world, there are many varieties of intention (*vivakṣā*): sometimes a certain aspect of primacy is intended even when an object is subordinate, and likewise, an aspect of subordination is intended even among things that are primary;
sometimes both are intended, and sometimes neither.

Furthermore, there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to the effect that whatever one intends to express must necessarily be denoted by that very word; rather, for the sake of fulfilling the speaker's intention, one may resort to other means such as metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), but this does not constitute an abandonment of the word’s own primary meaning.
Therefore, predominance (*prādhānya*) alone is the meaning of the accusative case.
But how is it that in cases such as *saktūn* (barley meal), there is subserviency (*guṇatva*)?
That is explained as follows:

first of all, the accusative case expresses "object-ness" (*karmatva*) as its primary form through its own power; however, because that [primary object-ness] is contradicted by another cause, it is not accepted here. Rather, since it consists of a specific *kāraka*, that which is expressed as the general category of *kāraka* that is invariably concomitant with it is what is intended by the accusative case. This concludes the first quarter of the second chapter.
It is distinguished because of its contradiction [with other meanings].
In this context, the meaning understood is that the groats (*saktu*) are the instrument (*kāraka*) of the oblation (*homa*).
And since a general category is not capable of functioning in linguistic usage without a specific instance, when a specific instance is required, they will function as the instrument.

"Of substances, [there is] connection with action," according to the principle of the simultaneous enunciation of the past and the future. But how, then, is the intention to express the predominance of the barley meal (*saktu*) not contradicted?
To this, he says:

For when it is determined that a certain substance will have some utility—either already accomplished or yet to be accomplished—it attains primacy with respect to the ritual action because it is fit for refinement (*saṃskāra*).

However, as for that which has not been used nor will be used, its refinement would be purposeless; thus, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the injunctions prescribing such refinement being rendered meaningless.

Furthermore, these parched grains (*saktu*) are not used prior to the oblation (*homa*), nor are they used subsequently, because they do not exist after the state of ash, and because there is no scriptural statement regarding their application (*viniyoga*) as ash.

Otherwise, that entire statement would be meaningless, or else the definition [of the word] must be understood as "the secondary sense (lakṣaṇā) has occurred. Since the authority of the Veda is established, the secondary sense must be accepted;
for the application of the primary meaning, being the general rule, comes to be recognized as erroneous upon seeing an exception.
In every case, the recourse to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is caused by the contingency of meaninglessness;

otherwise, the primary sense would be applicable. Therefore, because of the contradiction [otherwise], the injunction for the oblation as a means of accomplishment is understood as being connected to the context.

[The opponent objects: "But surely even the groats [would be meaningful]"—meaning that even the groats, by being associated with the oblation, will become purposeful by assisting the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
However, the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) concedes, by way of a concession, that those very things which have become the means for the oblation possess meaning; for who would say "no"?
And this is true in every case.

Just as a fire-oblation (homa), being of the nature of an action, requires the answer "for what purpose? and is thus grasped as an auxiliary to the "manner of performance" (kathaṃbhāva) of the principal rite, so it is not with a substance. Nor, therefore, can there be an assumption of an unseen result (adṛṣṭa) from it, because transcendental results (apūrvas) are brought about by actions.

Even in cases where a substance is enjoined for the sake of a visible result— such as "one desiring cattle [should sacrifice] with a milk-pail"— there too, no *apūrva* (transcendental merit) will arise without the mediation of an action having another purpose.
How much more so when the flour-grains (*saktu*) are not heard of as being subsidiary to anything at all,
and there is no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for such a postulation?
If it is argued that [the accusative case] is the second [case], the answer is "no.

For the second case, by expressing the predominance (*prādhānya*) of the barley flour, would make the oblation (*homa*) for its sake, rather than producing a transcendental result (*apūrva*) from the barley flour; such is the established understanding.
Therefore, because of the second [textual] statement, the oblation (*homa*) would have *saktu* (barley meal) as its material;
for how else could the *saktu* be pervaded by the act of oblation?
There is no hearing of it being for any other purpose.

And these [grains] become flour when used in a *homa*; since the flour is connected to the *homa*, the accusative case-ending is already established even before the purpose is attained, even in the case of things that have no further utility, because the status of being an object (*karman*) is accomplished simply by its primacy (*prādhānya*) with respect to the *homa*.

Once the meaning of the sentence is thus established, one subsequently realizes that they are of no use either to the person or to the sacrifice; therefore, based on that statement, either an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) must be postulated, or the cognition of primacy must be considered an error.
To this, he says:
It is not possible to assume anything else based on that statement;
rather, it is logical to understand it as expressing predominance (*prādhānya*).
Consequently, considering that the sense of the instrumental case is thereby established, the author of the *Mahābhāṣya* stated that the second case occurs in place of the third.

Thus, there is indeed a disparity between the oblation (*homa*) and the cleansing (*saṃmārga*): because the groats (*saktu*) serve no visible purpose, they exist for the sake of that [oblation], whereas the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and other items, being subsidiary to something else, are fit for purificatory rites such as carrying fire around them (*paryagnikaraṇa*).
Once the meaning of the scripture is firmly established, even in the absence of a visible benefit, an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) result will be postulated.

Even in common worldly practice, purificatory rites with invisible purposes are understood from custom, such as the circling of fire, salt, curd, and clarified butter over the heads of those arriving from another village for the sake of pacification, and their placement in a pure location.
Nor is there any impossibility for this [subordinate status], because of the authority of established practice (*ācāra*).
Therefore, even for those [actions] whose purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*), there exists a state of being subordinate due to their having an identical scriptural basis (*tulya-śrutitva*).

But if this is so, since everything would everywhere possess a purpose, the primacy of the substance (*dravya-prādhānya*) would already be established; thus, it need not be stated in the first quarter of the second chapter.

Regarding the phrase "because it is based on the direct statement" (*mūlya-śrutitvāt*): when something must be demonstrated, there are cases where primacy is established solely by the accusative case-ending, independent of any practical purpose, or where subsidiarity is established solely by the instrumental case-ending.
This is explained as follows:

first, regarding primacy, in the case of the injunction "one worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī verse," since the primary purpose of the verse is understood to be Indra through its indicative mark (*liṅga*), and because it forms a single syntactical unit with the word "Gārhapatya," there arises the contingency that the worship of Indra would be the means for attaining that [primacy]; thus, the primacy of the Gārhapatya fire is established solely by the accusative case-ending.

Likewise, in the case of the statement "the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*," since there is no difference between the two in terms of having a purpose, the *sūktavāka* alone—by virtue of the instrumental case-ending—is subordinate to the throwing of the *prastara*. Thus, when the relationship of principal and subordinate is expressed by the case-endings themselves, the absence of a purpose serves as an exception; however, the distinction is that subordination is not determined by the mere presence or absence of a purpose. As for the purpose of this section (*adhikaraṇa*), they do not fully agree; for instance: [The text continues: "In this way... (as follows).

It is logical that originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*), being understood as pertaining solely to the primary act (*pradhāna*), do not apply to the subsidiaries (*aṅga*). However, in the case of [the rule] regarding "being made of *śamī* wood" and so forth, which is enjoined by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the ladles (*sruc*) and other implements alone, it is understood to pertain to both the subsidiaries and the primary acts. This is because, according to the principle "or [it applies] to all, since the subsidiariness is not prompted by that [primary act]," the strength of the syntactical connection (*vākya-saṃyoga*) overrides the status of pertaining to the primary act derived from the context (*prakaraṇa*). Furthermore, no qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) has been mentioned here by which there could be a cognition of the ladles and so forth belonging exclusively to the primary act; even if such a qualification existed, it would not be intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*) because it serves merely as a qualification of that which is being referred to (*uddiśyamāna-viśeṣaṇatva*).

Therefore, even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), those items such as the sacrificial ladles (*sruk*) which are connected to the primary acts, and those such as the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) which are connected to the auxiliary acts that provide indirect assistance (*ārādupakāraka*), are all endowed with the quality of being made of *śamī* wood; thus, the separate cutting and cleansing of various types of wood is improper.

It might be argued: "The primary meaning [of the rule] applies because the subsidiary is not enjoined," since the specific modifications (*vaikṛta*) pertain solely to the primary act, and therefore here there will be no application to both subsidiary and primary acts.
That is incorrect.
Why?

Because in the case of the *yajñātharvaṇa*, it is said that "the optional sacrifices (*kāmyā iṣṭayaḥ*) are indeed to be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*)," for it will be stated that the quality of being low-voiced, being connected only with the principal acts denoted by the word "optional," is not enjoined for the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*). And there is no such connection with the principal acts here; thus, there is a difference [between this case and the previous one]. Now, an objection might be raised: since the subsidiaries have not yet attained their status at the stage when they are unestablished, the instruction regarding [materials] such as the *śamī* wood, being imparted while they are in that state, would pertain only to the principal acts.
It cannot be so;

for it must remain as it is, since it is impossible to enjoin multiple matters [simultaneously]. Therefore, the *sruc* and other implements must be restated (as *anuvāda*). Even though this is a direct instruction (*pratyakṣopadeśa*), it awaits the extension of application (*atideśa*) first.

In this regard, there is no distinction, for the same amount of time required for the primary ladles (*sruk*) and so forth to reach [the cleansing agent] is exactly the same for the subsidiary ladles as well.

Furthermore, by the very same means used to avoid the cleansing of the needles (*sūci*), one would also incur the avoidance of the *prayāja* ladles and so forth; however, this is not desired, as there is no logical justification for it.

Even if there were some cause for a connection with the primary [element] alone, nevertheless, according to the principle of the Soma-altar and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it is appropriate to include the generic form of the archetypal rite through incidental accomplishment (*prasaṅga*).
Furthermore,
the term *paridhi* refers to a substance intended for the purpose of encircling the fire.

Likewise, since the *juhv* and other implements serve the purpose of the *homa* (oblation) and so forth, it can be argued that the act of cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) is not the primary motive for their use, as it merely serves to denote the object. Consequently, when the *paridhi* (enclosing sticks) are prescribed to be made of reeds (*bāṇa*),
if they were not already familiar [as such], then even if they were made of *palāśa* wood and the like, they would simply be objects of cleansing and would not function as true *paridhis*.
If one were to wrap those [additional sticks] as well, then once the wrapping has been performed, they would not serve the original purpose;
moreover, the simultaneous employment (samuccaya) of items serving the same purpose is not observed.
Therefore, another enclosing stick (paridhi) need not be produced.

Since the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) is an original act (*apūrva*), it culminates solely in what is expressly stated; and since it is enjoined to be performed with its subsidiaries in the waters, by what means could fire be obtained for the purpose of cleansing, such that it would have to be produced?
Therefore, these [details regarding fire] serve no purpose.
However, there is one true example of this.

For in that context, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that "the meat belongs to the *savanīya* [offerings]," the meat— which is not connected with the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) alone— is not connected with the cake used for the *pariyagnikaraṇa* rite, because it is not a *savanīya*. Indeed, the term *savanīya* is not applied to a subsidiary of the *savanīya* offerings, since its scope is restricted to those things directly related to the *savana* (pressing) itself.

Furthermore, since the subsidiary of the *savanīya* sacrifice does not serve the purpose of being offered (*asavanārthatvāt*), even in that case it is difficult to obtain the quality of being made of rice (*vrīhimayatva*).
This is because their connection with the phrase "one should sacrifice with rice" (*brīhibhir yajeta*) pertains only to the principal sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
Therefore, the practical application (*prayojana*) is that the sacrificial cake for the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite may consist of any material.
That too is incorrect;

for if that were the case, then by the logic of "one who eats from a bronze vessel" (*kāṃsyabhojin*), the purpose of the scripture would be fulfilled merely by the *pari-agni-karaṇa* (circumambulatory fire-purification) performed with the flour-offering, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of the ritual being identical to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Therefore, it must be stated that, in some way, the status of being a means [to the sacrifice] accrues to the rice-flour cake (*puroḍāśa*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*) because it is enjoined by scripture.

Even in that case, however, because it would lack a specific purpose according to the principle of "being perceived as one" (*ekacāyanī-nyāya*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its elision in its absence;
therefore, one must accept that this very [purpose] is the motive,
or else that its occurrence is indefinite (*aniyata-vyakatva*).
And the maxim of "eating from a bronze vessel" (kāṃsyabhojinyāya) does not apply here, because the nature of being a *puroḍāśa* is not manifested by means of meat.
If it is asked, "How is this so in the case of the *savanīya-puroḍāśa*? [the answer follows].

In this case, the status of being a *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake) is not intended at all; rather, by virtue of the scriptural injunction, meat—which is essentially not a *puroḍāśa*—is prescribed in place of the *puroḍāśa*, just as [barley] grains (*dhānā*) and so forth are.
For in no way can grains and the like be produced from meat.
Consequently, according to the principle of the *praiyaṅgava* sacrifice, the *puroḍāśa* is replaced by meat only with respect to the primary element itself.
However, in the *Tantravārtika*, it is established that the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire) has the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) as its means;
furthermore, since its substance is restricted to a living being, or alternatively, by observing the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is established that its substance consists of rice or barley.
