And these are the purposes [of the discussion]: because the cleaning of the *sruk* ladles serves multiple functions in the archetype, and because the number three is scripturally mandated according to the *kapiñjala-nyāya*, even when the vessels are increased in number—as in the animal sacrifices and the *Cāturmāsya* rites—only three [ladles] are to be cleaned according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, all [the enclosing sticks] are to be wiped, because a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) must be repeated for each primary object.

Likewise, according to the logic of the animal sacrifice (*paśunyāya*), since a singular number is intended, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) only one enclosing stick (*paridhi*) is to be wiped;
but in the final conclusion, all are.
And where there is an increase in the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), there is a specific rule;
likewise, the carrying of fire around (*paryagnikaraṇa*) must be stated for both a single sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and for all the cakes.
Nevertheless, in that context, it would be according to worldly practice, as in the case of the statement, "having placed the fire nearby, they chant praises."
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the sweeping of the fire-altars (*agnisaṃmārga*) is the purpose;

however, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), because that [sweeping] lacks a specific purpose, it is not a purificatory rite (*asaṃskāryatvāt*) for them, whereas for all [fires] such as the Āhavanīya and others, it is so—this is the distinction.
But in the case of the *stotra* and *śastra*, there is a purificatory rite, because, like the *yājyā*, they consist in the naming of the deity.

The presentation of the *stotra* and *śastra* is as an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule that "those by which a substance is intended to be prepared [are subordinate]. A *stotra* is indeed praise (*stuti*), and a *śastra* is also that same praise; it is established that praise is accomplished by means of mantras not set to song (*apragīta*). Furthermore, praise consists in the proclamation of the relationship between a quality (*guṇa*) and its possessor (*guṇin*).
And that praise is first brought about by means of the quality and the possessor of the quality.
In the absence of that [connection with a specific action], mere utterance of words cannot be designated as "praise" (*stuti*).

Among these, since qualities (*guṇa*) have no purpose when they are not auxiliary to an action, they are exclusively for the sake of praise. As for the praise produced by them, does it become a subordinate element (*śeṣin*) by way of reminding the object of praise, or does it exist for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*) through its own primacy?
What follows?

If a mantra whose meaning is non-existent here is employed for the purpose of praise, then because its meaning has been set aside, the consequence is that it would sublate what has already been established.

For Indra alone who is praised by the *abhivatī* verses is the very same one worshipped with the *māhendra* cup; since the referent is indeed present there, why should there be a displacement [of the mantra]?
Nor is it the case that everything existing as a constituent of the ritual action must be denoted by the mantra; rather, whether less or more, the mantra denotes whatever it is capable of denoting.

Therefore, the manifestation of Indra without qualities occurs because the qualities are not essential (*atantratvāt*) or because they are obtainable from the context (*prakaraṇalabhyatvāt*), just like the manifestation of a substance without qualities.
It is not so, because it is inherent in the Vedic revelation;
this claim that there is no displacement because of the mention of Indra as being devoid of qualities does not hold.
Displacement indeed follows as a necessary consequence.
Why?

If the word "Mahendra" were explained through the etymological derivation of its parts as "he who is great (mahān) and he who is Indra," and if the application of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) were made accordingly, then it would be understood that Indra himself, as qualified by the attribute of greatness, is the deity of this cup.

However, this is not the case; for, because the conventional meaning of the whole word (*samudāyaprasiddhi*) is more powerful, there arises the cognition of Mahendra as a distinct entity denoted by a conventional term separate from Indra.
For instance:
if Mahendra is analyzed [as a compound], the oneness of the word and so forth is impaired;
if there is no analysis, the referent "Mahendra" would clearly be a distinct entity.

The rule "a grammatical operation concerning words applies when they are semantically connected" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*), as well as "of those that are semantically connected, the first [is compounded]" (*samarthānāṃ prathamād dha*), serve as qualifiers for both compound formation (*samāsa*) and secondary derivation (*taddhitavṛtti*).
Therefore, in the absence of such semantic connection, neither of these two should occur.
If the compound (*samāsa*) and the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) were both explained simultaneously, then no semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) would be obtained even in a single case.
Why?

Because semantic capacity—whether characterized by the unification of a single meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) or characterized by mutual dependence (*vyapekṣā*)—is in neither case possible for that which is dependent on something else.
How so?
For it is held that there is no single purpose (*ekārthatā*) when things are independent of other entities;
however, that which is dependent and distracted by others does not attain a single purpose.
Furthermore, "mutual expectancy" (vyapekṣā) is explicitly stated to be the absence of expectancy;
for if there were expectancy, that [expectancy] would be remote, and thus there would be a lack of semantic competency (asamarthatā).
Moreover, if the meanings were being conveyed in succession, there would be a split in the sentence (vākyabheda), because of the impossibility of such a thing.
If one were to form a compound by combining [the two words], there would again be two words, namely "Mahendra"; for in that case, "mahat" (greatness) would not be an attribute of Indra.

Indeed, a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) whose own meaning has been subsumed does not connect with other qualifiers, nor does it do so when it functions as part of a compound meaning; this is stated merely to avoid a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

Having thus established that there is no sequential occurrence [of the two meanings], the *Tantravārtika* introduces the simultaneous occurrence once again with the intention of pointing out another defect:
"By the principle that 'when a single word has multiple meanings, it is like [the meaning] for the sake of another,' the word *indra* [is connected] with the suffix *mahat*."
There is the consequence of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*) due to the presence of contradictory characteristics as the cause;
furthermore, there is another type of sentence-splitting consisting of multiple operations for a single injunction. To explain:
And because of designation,
and because of the difference in designation, there is a distinction; and in this way, the arrangement of the two mantras will be established.
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction in the alternative view;
and if there were no difference in meaning, a difference in the mantra would result in its purpose being merely transcendental (adṛṣṭārtha).
However, when explained in this way, the secondary derivative suffix (taddhita) exists by virtue of conventional usage (rūḍhi).
Agni, Soma, and all others are not dual deities by virtue of being conventional designations (*rūḍhi*).
First of all, one must necessarily postulate that the words *mahat* and *indra* possess the capacity to denote distinct meanings;
and since those two denote a quality and a qualified entity respectively, they are determined to have the nature of qualifier and qualified.
In that case, as soon as they are uttered in combination, there arises a cognition of a qualified object by virtue of its connection with an object previously experienced;
and there is nothing to subvert this.
Nor is there any means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for postulating a new, distinct power (*śakti*) in the aggregate, as stated in the Tantravārtika.
Once established, the conventional designation of a whole subverts the designation of its parts;
nor can there be an appearance as that [whole] without the clear employment of a distinct meaning devoid of the meanings of the parts.

Furthermore, even regarding an object that is directly perceived, the postulation of multiple word-powers is without proof; how much more so where the very existence of the object itself must be postulated?

Thus, here, because the use of the word "Indra" would otherwise be inexplicable, Indra is postulated even though he is not perceived. If, moreover, the use of the word "Mahendra" were likewise inexplicable, then another entity named Mahendra would have to be postulated.

But when the usage is established by the very same powers of the words *mahat* and *indra* as previously conceived, and that same object is recognized as being qualified in some particular way, who then would be able to postulate a different meaning?
Therefore, it is established that Mahendra is none other than Indra himself as qualified by greatness.

Furthermore, there is no incapacity in forming the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) after having formed the compound, because at the time of compounding and at the time of the derivative, no other required meaning is introduced.

Nor does there arise the contingency of a syntactical split (vākya-bheda) caused by double utterance, because multiple meanings are expressed by a single word uttered only once. For the term *māhendra* consists of two constituent elements (*vṛtti*), and each constituent element functions toward the meaning of the sentence.
In this regard, those two meanings of the two sentences which were introduced [previously] are now explained by breaking them down from those [compounds].
Furthermore, the repeated utterance seen here does not belong to the Vedic text itself;
for there is no such Vedic text at all. [For instance: "He is great and he is Indra, thus Mahendra"; that which has him as its deity is "Māhendra."
Nor is it the case that this Vedic word itself is divided in this manner, for since such a division would be of human origin, it would result in its being non-Vedic;
rather, [this refers to] the first quarter (pāda) of the second chapter.
For words possess diverse powers (*vicitra-śakti*), since they bring about the cognition of one or many word-meanings.

Thus, the expression of their meaning is sometimes performed by another single word and sometimes by a sentence; and even by that [sentence], it may be by one or many, or by two words or many words—such is the diversity.
For example: "What is a *pika*? "A *kokila*. "Who is an *aupagava*? "The offspring of Upagu."
Or, it is like [the son] Upagu produced by his own beloved wife.

Similarly, when "he cooks" (*pacati*) is said, it is stated that a single agent brings about, during the present time, an action of cooking (*pāka*) that extends over a sequence of prior and posterior stages and culminates in another.
And for those who speak in this manner, no fragmentation of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) follows.
Nor is it determined that [the meaning] is the literal sense of the word itself.

In this very way, if the object denoted by the term *māhendra* is explained—whether by one or more persons who understand the power of words—by means of their own sentences, what "splitting of the sentence" (*vākyabheda*) is there? For even if one's own sentence is uttered a hundred times, it does not vitiate the Veda;
nor does the meaning expressed therein incur the status of being human-authored (*pauruṣeya*).
Furthermore, when a manifold meaning is expressed by persons, it must necessarily be spoken sequentially; and that too is spoken by means of the prior and posterior order of roots and suffixes,
as in "this is Māndhātṛ" and "this is Indra," and so forth.
And thus there is no such state of dependence.

Alternatively, a compound does indeed occur even when the principal member is dependent; for although the word *indra* is dependent on a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), it nevertheless receives the compound because of its predominance with respect to "greatness" (*mahattva*).
Consequently, there is no contradiction in the simultaneous dependence, yet the formation of the word (*vṛtti*) occurs only sequentially.
Why?
Because wherever the principal element is dependent, it must first function in that very manner; thus, the compound itself occurs first.

Alternatively, if one were to accept a simultaneous application (tantra) after the compound has already been formed, then since "Śacīndra" would be connected to the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix, and "Indra" alone would be part of the compound, Indra—being devoid of the qualifying attribute—would result in being the deity by himself, leading to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the attribute being purposeless.

Furthermore, when "Indra" and "greatness" fall simultaneously upon the referent of the dvandva compound— as in the case of "aruṇā" (red) and "ekahāyanī" (one-year-old)— no restriction is obtained through mutual dependence (*sampravārtika*).
For there is no simultaneous application to an action, nor is there the capacity to bring about a specific qualification.
Furthermore, there would be the consequence that [the compound] would have a dual deity.

Moreover, since the words *mahat* and *indra* would not form a compound, they would be plural; consequently, there would be the undesirable result of an absence of connection with the secondary suffix (*taddhita*), which is conditioned by a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) intended to express the singular number.
Furthermore:
Therefore, there is no simultaneous occurrence; thus, by means of sequential occurrence, the deityhood belongs to the very meaning of the compound itself.

Consequently, Indra alone, when joined with the attribute [mahat], is Mahendra and not a different entity; thus, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position alone is sound, and another answer must be stated.

Even though the object is non-different, nevertheless, because of the principle that "the state [of being a deity] should exist in the mantra according to the word of the injunction," the deityhood in this cup-offering (grahayāga) belongs to that which is expressed by the word *Mahendra* itself, and not otherwise.

In that case, even when denoted by a word such as *buddhīndra* (the Indra of the intellect) through its full etymological derivation (*sakalaparyāya*), it does not possess the status of a deity; how much less so by the deficient term *indra* alone?
For why is this so?
It is observed that even when the substance is one, there is a conventional usage of distinctness based on a difference in causes, as in the case of "the teacher of the mother"; furthermore,
[if this were not so,] a quality would be rendered purposeless.

If a quality—whether beginningless or having a beginning—is mentioned solely for the purpose of praising Indra and does not enter into the nature of the deity, then its mention would be entirely useless.
For every deity is either denoted or enjoined for this very purpose: namely, so that the ritual act may be performed by means of that [deity]. This is the intent of the Tantravārtika.
Furthermore, if Indra were designated by the word "Indra" alone regardless of whether a quality was prescribed or not, then there would be no purpose in mentioning the quality.
Moreover,

the connection of Indra with the cup (graha) is not already established [by another injunction], such that "greatness" could be mentioned solely for the sake of praise by way of restating (anuvāda) Indra as it pertains to that cup.
Furthermore, since Mahendra is not already established [as the deity] by virtue of his qualities, he would have to be enjoined as such;
therefore, because it is an injunction of what is not otherwise established, there is a difference in the deity.
The same applies to the *yājyā* and *puroruc* verses.

Or rather, as in the previous case, there is a distinction in the designation of the mantra; since it possesses meaning, the position of [the mantra being] a preparatory act (*saṃskāra*) would be abandoned only if there were a contradiction with a stronger means of knowledge, but such a contradiction does not exist. Because the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is more powerful, the displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the mantra is established; thus, there is no exclusion of the position that it is a preparatory act.

Alternatively, even without being displaced (*anutkṛṣyamāṇa*), the *pragātha*— by virtue of its proximity (*sannidhi*) and through its constituent parts (*avayava-dvāreṇa*)— will manifest Mahendra for the sake of non-contradiction and for the purpose of the *hara*, just as in the *manotā* hymn of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, the word "Agni," though perceived as residing in the whole (*samastha*) by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*),
is understood to refer to the entire compound meaning by expressing Soma as well due to its function (*icaryāt*).
Therefore, there is no fault even if there is no displacement.
For Yama and the others do not possess divinity even in other [sacrificial] extractions (*graha*) such that they could be celebrated by superior mantras like Indra;
therefore, since their [mantras] would otherwise result in the futility of the injunctions, one must necessarily admit that they have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Consequently, because of the similarity with them, the same applies to the others; thus, they do not constitute preparatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*).

The application of the *maṇḍūka-sūkta* is in the fire-ritual (*agni*), because it is traditionally taught there that the fire is dragged out by means of a frog. The application of the *akṣa-vākya* is at the Royal Consecration (*rājasūya*), because it is prescribed therein that one "plays with dice" (*akṣair dīvyati*). The application of the *mūṣika-vākya* is in the set of eleven sacrificial animals (*ekādaśinī*); when the connection is mentioned in the phrase "the rat is the victim for the Upaśaya," the praise is directed toward the Upaśaya itself by way of that [mention].
As for the *Kuṣumbhaka-sūkta* and others, if their meaning is not found in any specific form [in the ritual], then they will possess purpose through general application,
because all mantras are prescribed for the *Vācastoma*,
and likewise because all *ṛcs* are prescribed for the *Āśvina* [śastra] when completion until sunrise is impossible.

In that case, because there is no other way [to explain] the capacity of the injunction to prescribe mantras whose meanings are not integrated [with the ritual action], one must resort to an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). However, it is not proper to assume an invisible purpose everywhere simply because of an invisible purpose in some instances; for otherwise, even when a visible meaning is perceived, one would have to assume an invisible purpose. Thus, indeed, according to the principle "Or rather, because of the connection with the Vedic text, the two verbs *stauti* and *śaṃsati* should enjoin the production of the ritual acts within the context."
As for the claim that, just as in the case of the *manotā* mantra, the word "Agni" indicates the meaning of the compound through the word "Indra," that is incorrect.
Why?
Precisely because of this fault:
there is no contradiction whatsoever for the word "candra" while it expresses its own primary meaning, such that the direct audition (śruti) would abandon its function.
Furthermore, since it is possible to somehow establish a visible purpose for all things whose purposes are otherwise unseen through figurative application (macāyā), this [objection] is untenable.

As for what was said—that it should indeed be displaced—that is incorrect; for its status as a supplement to the hymn under discussion is established by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) through proximity (*sannidhi*).
Furthermore, an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not a means of application (*aviniyojaka*) without a general relationship (*sāmānyasambandha*).
And thus, the seventh, sixth, and second [case endings] will be applied to the roots *stu* and *śaṃs*;
in your view, they will function with other meanings.
Furthermore, manifestation, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), has the self as its substrate.
Furthermore, after the status of being an object (*karmmatva*) has been established, [the *kavatīs*] serve as the substratum for the deity because they are that which is pervaded (*vyāpyatva*).
In that case, the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) belongs exclusively to the *kavatīs*; thus, there is a disparity.

Moreover, in the expressions "he praises" (*stauti*) and "he recites" (*śaṃsati*), a process of producing praise (*stutibhāvanā*) consisting of a sequence of prior and posterior stages is heard in the scripture.

In that context, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the remaining factors of action (*kāraka*) are invariably connected to and productive of the meaning of the verbal root.
Therefore, if the mantras serve the purpose of accomplishing the hymn of praise (*stotra*), they would have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) because they perform a required function;
however, if they were to perform mere illumination (*prakāśana*), they would have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) because they would be performing what was not enjoined.
And therefore, it is better that the three [means of knowledge] alone have perceptible objects;
moreover,
because of the distinctness of the words.
The number twelve, which resides in distinct individuals, is not expressed by the word when there is no distinction in manifestation;
or, when the universal is not intended to be expressed, it remains as twelve because that [number] is accomplished for each individual instance in perception.
But is this not equally true even in the case of praise?

For instance, if the praises (*stutayaḥ*)—which consist of collections of verses according to the requirements of the *stoma*—are counted as such, then the illuminations (*prakāśanāni*) are likewise [to be counted]; thus there is no distinction.
Actions terminate with their results; therefore, the counting of them is always by that number.
Furthermore, because they are not previously established as being twelve, their status as twelve must be defined; yet that statement is purposeless,

because the ṛks cannot be modified (anūhya), and since their status as means for praise belonging to Agni is already established by the injunction regarding the Āgneya cups themselves, the statement "they praise with those verses addressed to Agni" (āgneyīṣu stuvate) is redundant.
And the naming [of the action] is like the action itself; that is to say, this naming, which is presented as having an accusative object, is another reason for its primacy.

For the primary action is understood through some means, as in "he performs the *agnihotra* oblation" or "he pours the *āghāra* libation," whereas a preparatory (*saṃskāra*) action is not so understood because it is entirely subordinate.
Alternatively, the designation of the *stotra* and *śastra* as "recitation" (*abhidhāna*) is for the purpose of making known their predominance;
otherwise, the designation would simply be "illumination" (*prakāśana*),
and there would be no distinction such as [the difference between] threshing and the *āghāra* offering.
Since the deity is the primary factor, it is the deity that should be petitioned for the fruit, just as in the case of a ritual act;
while the master is present, no one petitions the servant for the result.
Furthermore, there is no distinctness of action here, because of the recognition [of the same act] as being like a bond.
No subordinate quality (*guṇa*) is mentioned here, nor is there praise in another sentence (the first quarter of the second chapter). Indeed,

there is no specific reason present here to determine whether the mantra— its injunctive power having been superseded by the *āmnāya* prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa— serves as a reminder (*smāraka*), or whether the opposite is the case.
In this case, since it is impossible for both to be mere restatements (anuvāda) and because their specific characteristics are being grasped, both must be injunctive (vidhāyaka).
Furthermore, due to repetition (abhyāsa), there would be a difference in the ritual acts (karmabheda).
As for the recognition (pratyabhijñā) similar to that of the *vaṣaṭ*-call, the answer will be provided in the section concerning repetition (abhyāsādhikaraṇa).
Therefore, the status of being an expressive [word] is not established in this way;
even those who argue thus have merely asserted it in a general sense.
Why?
Because the power of the injunction is not removed from the mantra by the act of enjoining;
even while being injunctive, the Brāhmaṇa will serve to remind one of its meaning.
"But in case of conflict, it should be by means of the mantra"— this is what will be stated hereafter; or rather, according to the *Tantravārtika*, because of the capacity of the application,
the mantra should be understood as denoting the name.

There is a third category, namely that which is called "denotative" (*abhidhāyakatva*). This refers to the denotative power of verbal roots found in the *Mantras* and the *Brāhmaṇas*, whose injunctive capacity is set aside by another word; such is their denotative function.

In that regard, in the phrase "the dancers perish" (*natā naśanti*), the injunctive element introduced by the word *nāvadyat* does not seek to be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). Likewise, [injunctions are present] through the vocative case in "O Ahi Budhnya, protect my mantra," and through the first-person verb form in "I give" (*dāmi*) and "I take" (*gṛhṇāmi*).
"Should they consume the Soma," by means of the word "yadi" (if).
And since these and similar [expressions] generally occur in mantras, mantras are the illustrative examples;
furthermore, it is well known that "mantras are non-injunctive."
In the case of the Brāhmaṇa, however, there are many more injunctive elements; therefore, it is well known as "that which contains injunctions.
Since those that lack such form are non-injunctive, they are not cited here [as examples].
As for being injunctive or non-injunctive, the cause is exactly as stated; thus, the functions of being a Mantra or being a Brāhmaṇa are not operative [in this distinction].
In this regard, however, the following function is observed:
once the status of being an injunction (*vidhi*) has ceased for those [words] such as *rūpa* that have arrived from the Veda, they serve the purpose of conveying the cause (*nimitta*) and so forth;
for their form is not suitable for employment in ritual acts (*karman*).

In the case of those [mantras] contained within the *mantra* category, however, having perceived their very form, there arises the cognition of application (*viniyoga-buddhi*)—namely, that "I cut," "I take," "I strew," "I do this and that," "dispense the fires," "spread the grass," and "do this"—thinking, "these [mantras] are capable of remembering these actions.
This is the first quarter of the second chapter.

Since no ritual item can be performed without being remembered, and since memory necessarily arises, one begins to employ whatever means are appropriate for that purpose—whether it be the recollection of some Brāhmaṇa passage, a review of a preceding item, a manual of aphorisms (*sūtra*), one's own notes, or the presence of an observer and so forth.

In that regard, having perceived that the mantras—which have no other purpose—are being recited within a specific context and are grasped by the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance) in a general sense as "something must be done with these," one understands their nature by recognizing that they are of such a kind as to be required for the formation of a mental recollection (*smṛti*) through a particular sentence. Once their application is established by means of a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) inferred from their indicative power (*liṅga*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), it is understood that their purpose is to convey meaning. Consequently, other means [of recollection] are excluded because they lack authoritative basis. Furthermore, it is determined that the accomplishment of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rule (*niyama*) occurs when the action is performed after having recollected it specifically by means of the mantras alone.
The commentary (*bhāṣya*) on this point should also be applied as follows:
the statement "because that cognition [of the action] arises even when the name is uttered" is not intended to mean that [the action] is already established [by other means].

Rather, it is because of the connection with the word *yat* (in the phrase *yad... karoti*), which gives rise to a cognition of the form: "I am stating the very meaning of this mantra-verb as something already obtained from elsewhere."

For even when such [words] as these are uttered a hundred times, they do not produce a cognition of something previously unknown (*apūrva*) by their own inherent power alone; for that very reason, because the cognition of what has already been apprehended arises, even the seers (*ṛṣi*) do not reach the end of individual linguistic forms (*lakṣya*). However, through the grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*), the wise reach the end of those forms that have been established.

The extensive application of mantras is generally considered to consist of: commands (praiṣa), searching (anveṣaṇa), questioning (pṛṣṭa), narration (ākhyāna), supplementary connection (anuṣaṅga), and ritual performance (prayoga), as well as their inherent capacity (sāmarthya).
The term "Brāhmaṇa" applies to what remains.
It may appear that this sūtra is unnecessary, since the definition of a Brāhmaṇa is already established by elimination (*pariśeṣasiddhatva*) and thus need not be stated.

However, because of the use of the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) therein and because no definition has yet been explicitly set forth, it should be understood that this is indeed an exposition of the sūtra.
For what purpose, then, is the sūtra commenced?
If it were universally established that the Veda consists solely of Mantra and Brāhmaṇa, this [discussion] would not have been commenced. However,

for those for whom this is not established, the author says "the remainder is called Brāhmaṇa" (in the first pāda of the second adhyāya) in order to demonstrate that the Veda has only two divisions, thereby refuting a third category and so forth.
A narrative concerning the deeds of a single individual is *parakṛti*;
one concerning many individuals is *purākalpa*.
Where a meaning appears to be otherwise, but through an examination of the sequence of preceding and following passages it is determined to be different, that is *vyavadhāraṇakalpanā*.

For example, one might hear "he should accept" and then conceive of it as "he should cause [another] to accept. In this context, the word *vidhi* denotes a Brāhmaṇa; it refers to those mantra passages that are recorded within the Brāhmaṇas when they are being recited during Vedic study (*svādhyāya*).
It is established that the characteristic of mantras is indeed their non-alteration (*anabhidhāna*).
Now, when a word is being modified (*ūhyamāna*), does the status of being a mantra belong to the entire [formula], or only to the modified word itself?
The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it belongs to the entire [formula].
How so?
If there is a difference in form recognized at the time of the tradition, and even a single part has been altered, it is impossible to recognize its status as a mantra.

If, on the other hand, one were to admit the existence of that [mantra-status] even when only a portion is present, then it would follow that all words are mantras without distinction, because they are all equally [mere] words.
Therefore, since the status of being a *mantra* ceases even upon the loss of a single syllable, there is a cessation of all its ritual functions.

Consequently, just as there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) when such a [Vedic] text is destroyed—since it resides in all its constituent parts—likewise, regarding the subject of *mantras* and Vedic meters, one must not employ those specific words which are traditionally remembered as belonging to that category. Thus, when there is a substitution of a single word or its part, and all the Vedic (*chāndasa*) forms contained within that *mantra* are set aside, one should employ worldly (*laukika*) words.
The designation [of a thing] is precisely that much.
Why?
Because when a dewlap is produced on a cow, or when its horns are broken, the nature of "cowness" (gotva) is not concealed, since other parts capable of manifesting it continue to exist.
Even when a certain portion of its structure is lost, it is recognized in its entirety;
and we observe that this very form of the mantra, manifested through its specific sequence of accents, phonemes, and so forth, does not perish upon the sight of some modification.
For instance:

In cases such as "having made it *aira*, one should sing," where the application occurs after performing a deletion or modification of a syllable based on an explicit injunction, and in cases where a single tone (*ekaśruti*) is prescribed by abandoning the accents and other qualities observed during Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), the cognition that the text is a mantra does not depart there.
It might be argued that it does not depart here due to the force of the injunction;
however, wherever there is a difference from the Vedic [text], there the status of being a mantra is intended.
But when it is postulated through reasoning (*nyāya*), its specific determination is not possible;
yet even a true *ūha* (adaptation) is not non-Vedic.

For this very reason it is said that what is not explicitly recited is "non-mantra" (*amantra*); for while some portion of the Veda is heard directly (*pratyakṣa*), some is to be understood through inference (*anumāna*) and other means.

That which is directly heard in scripture (*śruta*) is called *anāmnāta* (not explicitly mentioned elsewhere). In that regard, while the application (*viniyoga*) of words such as *irāpada* is heard [in the text], it is not so for words such as *sūrya*.

[Objection: But surely, in the case of "the *caru* for Sūrya" (*saurthaṃ carum*), this very phrase—because of its connection with the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*)—is heard as the applicator of the word *sūrya* as the deity.

This does not state that the word "sūrya" is to be inserted into the mantra, because it merely prescribes its utterance at the time of the offering of the oblation (*havis*). As for the insertion of that word into the mantras, that will occur by way of extension (*atideśa*); moreover, it is not recorded in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) because the principle of extension is not explicitly stated.
Therefore, because they lack an enjoined application that is explicitly recited (*anāmnāta-viniyojakatva*), the words "Sūrya" and so forth do not possess the status of *mantra*.

[Objection: If this were the case, it would follow that the *pravara* (ancestral invocation) and the names (*nāmadheya*)—since they are directly recited—would also have the status of *mantra*. [Response:

This would indeed be so if their specific forms (*svarūpa*) were being taught; however, since one employs the *pravara* and the names only after knowing their meaning from the injunctions, they are not included within the definition of *mantra*, as they are not themselves recited in the text.

If that were so, then even in cases where there is a traditional recitation of a mantra containing a pronoun (*sarvanāma*), and another word is substituted in its place, that [substituted portion] would also lack the status of being a mantra.
Some maintain that it should indeed be so.

Alternatively, since it is impossible to recite all specific instances due to their infinity and because they do not occur simultaneously, there is indeed a recitation of the essential form by way of a pronoun; thus, because the mantra is established in this manner, one can define it as follows: "That word which is inserted here is the mantra."

Otherwise, since pronouns are unfit for independent use, if the specific names were not understood as being included therein by that very means, then—due to the deficiency of that constituent part—the inclusion of the pronoun in the mantra-text would be entirely purposeless.
However, because they are enjoined just like the *pravara* and the name, the employment of words occupying those positions is inferred.
Therefore, these and similar items, being explicitly recited, should be connected with the properties of mantras.
However, at the time of reciting the *pravara* and other such formulas, there is no contact whatsoever with the Brahmins.

Nor has any form been shown by the Brahmin by which one could determine that it is a mantra because it possesses the characteristics of the sacred teaching (*pravacana*). Consequently, when a mantra is employed in modified rituals (*vikṛti*) through the force of the name, the seer’s injunction, or the requirement, whatever portion is added merely for the sake of the meaning—being devoid of [Vedic] significance—is purely worldly (*laukika*).

As for the remainder, it is established that since it is obtained in that same manner and its status as a mantra is recognized through its function within the ritual (*kratv-ākāṅkṣā*), it is not to be excluded by means of expiations or Vedic linguistic usages (*chāndasa-prayoga*).

Regarding those [mantras], the definition of the *ṛc* and so forth— which was introduced incidentally because the arrangement into quarters (*pāda-vyavasthā*) follows from the requirement of meaning— is now stated.

Since the meaning of a word is understood through the usage of elders, even though a definition has been provided, [the author] demonstrates that its very foundation is the instruction of those who are proficient [in the tradition].
Because no verb is employed in the phrase "Agni by the ancients," the sense remains incomplete; nevertheless, the division into quarters (pādas) is established by virtue of the meter (vṛtta).

But surely, even in the case of "agnim īḷe," since it is a complete *ṛc*, it does not terminate its meaning with each quarter-verse (*pāda*); thus, this division into quarters is not determined by the force of the meaning.
Why should it not be stated that in "agnim īḷe purohitam," a completed meaning is directly perceived?
As for the two subsequent quarters, it was previously stated here that [the division] is according to the force of the meaning.
Since this [statement] is for the purpose of illustration, there is no exclusion of those [names] that have already occurred; thus, it was stated as not being prohibited.
The phrase "the designation 'Sāman' applies to them" is understood to carry over from the previous context.
Where a qualified object is understood through a single, indivisible word,
the status of being the expressed meaning belongs there to the qualifier; in all other cases, the term "Yajus" applies.
The word "in the remainder" (śeṣe) should be explained as forming a compound, just as in the case of the expression "the word *brāhmaṇa* [is used] in the remainder.

Alternatively, the word *nigada* may be the fourth [category], because of its specific characteristic (*dharma-viśeṣāt*). The word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of excluding the notion that the word *yajus* applies to the remainder.
The fourth type of mantra-group would be *nigada* because of its difference in properties (*dharma*).
If it were an injunction (*vidhi*) stating "one should recite loudly as a *nigada*," then, so that the properties of a *yajus* are not sublated, there must be a difference in meaning.
Alternatively, if it were a restatement (*anuvāda*), it could not be established at all without such a distinction; thus, there is a difference [between the two].

It has been explained that there is no distinction in the nature of the dharma because it is obtained through reasoning; it is not due to an injunction, since it is known to be a restatement (*anuvāda*).
However, as for the meaning they express, it is said "because of the statement" that they would be able to speak it with a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
The designation is for the sake of a quality;
there is a distinction in designation by the King, as in the case of "the Brahmins and the wandering mendicants.
If it is argued that this applies to all [of them]:
By means of the door of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), [the author] refutes the notion that a quality (*guṇa*) is the cause for designation.

For in the world, a sentence functions only when the meaning has already been understood from another source. In that regard, because the unity of meaning is recognized, there is the easy comprehension of a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*). — *Tantravārttika* (Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a portion of the *Tantravārttika*, specifically discussing the conditions for syntactical unity and the role of qualities in linguistic expression.)
Since it is to be understood from eternal sentences, the Vedic meaning proceeds according to the sentence;
because that [eternity] is not established, the sentence does not have subordination to the meaning.
For Jaimini, who is engaged in the exposition of the Veda, what occasion is there for stating a definition of worldly sentences?
Furthermore, what occasion is there for the definition of Vedic sentences within the context of the definition of difference?
Why was it not stated in the very definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
Moreover, the word "single" (*eka*) need not be mentioned, since it is established by the mere statement that "a sentence consists in the unity of meaning" (*arthakatvād vākyam*).
And how can a subject irrelevant to the topic of mantras be discussed here?
Furthermore, the author of the Bhāṣya’s introduction—“in the case of Yajus verses recited in close conjunction”—though well-founded, has been bypassed without any justification.
Moreover:

In the case of the *ṛc* and *sāman*, since their extent is well known as being sufficient for performance, no assistance is rendered by the definition of a sentence (*vākya-lakṣaṇa*) or the definition of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).

Likewise, when persons are enjoined toward an efficient force (*bhāvanā*) consisting of the end, the means, and the procedure by means of sentences such as those concerning the *agnihotra* in the *Brāhmaṇa*, the knowledge of one or many sentences is of no use.
But surely there is this utility: the definition of syntactic unity will serve to delimit the division of sentences (*vākya-bheda*).
The first quarter of the second chapter:
This is not applicable.
Why?

Whether defined as the occurrence of a single word or a part thereof, or as consisting of the consequence of repetition (*āvṛtti*), or characterized by the division [of the sentence], these are determined to be defects precisely without depending on the cognition of the unity or plurality of the sentence.

In the case where no division is heard, the abandonment of the understood connection and the postulation of multiple unseen factors (*adṛṣṭa*) constitute a defect; in the other case, there is a lack of authority because repetition is not perceived. Thus, there is no need for a definition of a single sentence.
However, in the case of human sentences, since worldly usage is established independently of such definitions, they are of absolutely no necessity.

Furthermore, if the unity of a sentence is determined by the unity of its meaning—since a sentence exists for the purpose of communicating meaning—then what is the use of a cognition of the unity of the sentence that occurs subsequent to the cognition of the unity of its nature? Moreover, since speakers employ sentences for the purpose of communicating to others, they have no need to rely on a knowledge of the definition [of a sentence] for their own sake. As for listeners, however, even the speech of a person, when it functions toward a meaning that was previously entirely unknown, does not differ from a Vedic sentence.
However, since that which has already had its meaning understood is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), it is to be disregarded; thus, neither a single nor multiple cognitions are required.
Furthermore, for what purpose was the definition of Vedic [words] not stated?
If you argue that it was already stated by implication (*arthāpatti*), that is not so.

Having thus stated that [the definition of a Vedic sentence], one might argue that the establishment of the definition of worldly sentences must be understood through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*).
However, such presumptive implication is not possible;
for this knowledge of the characteristics of worldly sentences is not inexplicable without such a definition of Vedic sentences.

Furthermore, its status as a single sentence is not established, because the definition of a single sentence— namely, the unity of meaning— is dependent on the presentation of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), as stated in the *Tantravārtika*. Moreover, it is possible that even among Vedic texts there may be some that are studied [in this manner].
Nor can there be an *arthāpatti* (presumption) based on necessity, because it is not certain that something extremely remote might be indicated by the mark.
Nor is it a case of *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification), since no distinction between a general rule and a particular exception is established.

For if, after first expressing this [mark] in a general sense, it were then stated specifically as connected only with the *parigraha* (acceptance), then by virtue of that *parisaṃkhyā*, one would only understand that the [mark] does not belong to Vedic matters; however, that is not the case here.
But there is no specific rule regarding the number [of words], because of the possibility of multiple interpretations.
For even in this way, the postulation of objects is possible: "If a single sentence, being independent, were to exist upon division due to the multiplicity of meanings";
or alternatively, "Due to the unity of meaning, there is the status of multiple sentences."
Therefore, this [theory] is non-conceptual. Furthermore, how can the unity of a sentence be established if it is independent of the meaning?
For this [cognition] is not determined by the knowledge of the phonemes in their own form;
for it is observed that it occurs while as many words as are being heard from that [source] are being perceived.
The unity of meaning is perfectly clear through that much; there is syntactical unity when the word-meanings are understood from the words.
The meaning of the sentence is established by those word-meanings;
in this regard, there is no distinctiveness from the world [of common usage] as a cause for the unity of the sentence.
And the meaning of a sentence is indeed the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) as qualified by its own factors (*kārakas*);
and its distinction [from other sentences] is always produced through differences such as the use of different words,
according to the *Tantravārtika*.

To the extent that a collection of words causes the means of sacrifice to be remembered, to that extent it is designated as both a *yajus* and a *vākya*. A single word cannot possess the quality of having a single meaning if it lacks internal expectancy; therefore, such a word is not [considered a sentence].
The Saṃgha consists of parts that are mutually expectant; however, a single member of it does not exist as a second.
Separation (bheda) is the mutual delimitation of entities.

And because it is the meaning of the individual word (*pratipadārtha*), that [sentence-meaning] does not attain oneness; for when the two—whiteness and cowness—are denoted by their own forms as the meanings of the words *śukla* (white) and *go* (cow), their mutual connection (*itaretarānurajjana*) constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
And this connection of whiteness with cowness, or of cowness with whiteness, is perceived as manifold because it applies in its entirety to each individual instance.

Even if, in some way, unity were understood because there is a single connection between two words in both cases, nevertheless, in the case of many words, there is multiplicity because they are perceived in various forms of connection according to whichever specific portion each pair of words connects with.
Furthermore, as long as the unity of purpose is not resorted to, the independent word-meanings cannot be brought to a state of oneness; thus, they experience difference and connection separately.
Therefore, it is also not manifold.

And although, for us, because the word’s referent is the form (ākṛti), difference itself is not intended as the sentence-meaning, nevertheless it was presented by the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin) merely as an alternative possibility. The explanation of the intention of the final position (siddhānta) is appropriate, since the word *artha* signifies purpose (*prayojana*).

Thus, it can also be said that each individual object is primarily a qualifier and is mentioned for the sake of others; and because of the distinction and the conjunction of all those [objects], there is a single distinction or a single conjunction. Therefore, since they are perceived as being in a state of inherence (*samavāya*) and serve a visible purpose, the manifestation of the offering (*nirvāpa*) qualified by all the objects such as the *avitrī* mantra and so forth constitutes the single purpose of the entire collection of words. Thus, the example is established. But the opponent, not understanding the primacy of the act of offering, asks:
"But here, regarding 'of the god'..."

And if it is argued that the phrase "if I offer" (*yadi nirvapāmi*) is connected [to both] by way of ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*), then that ellipsis would exist as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*); yet it cannot be subordinate because it possesses its own purpose.
Furthermore, since [the words] *mavica*, etc., do not inhere in the action (*akarmasamavāya*), they have a single meaning.
Now, for what purpose are both [the word and the ellipsis] indicated?

It must be stated that for those things which, when combined, have a single purpose, there is an absolute expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) on the part of those same things when separated, due to their incapacity [to function individually] in that regard.

Alternatively, expectancy upon being divided does not exist without the state of having a single purpose when combined, because there is the possibility of independent activity toward individual effects.
Therefore, since the remainder is understood precisely through the division of what is expectant, it shows a counter-example that this very [expectancy] must be expressed.
It is said: one observed purpose for those [mantras] taken independently is the manifestation of the manner of dividing the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

Furthermore, even though it was stated later regarding the offering (*nirvāpa*), the objection concerning the plurality of divisions is raised here; for, since no specific qualifiers are employed collectively, there is no fault of "attachment" (*anuṣaṅga*) when they are used again and again.

To this, the reply is as follows: first of all, we shall explain that there is no multiplicity of actions even due to a difference in the means (*sādhana*), for the primacy of the means has already been refuted. This distinction [of action] does not constitute a limb of the ritual act (*karma-aṅga*), and thus it belongs to the first quarter of the second chapter.
Because it is a general declaration that [the fire] is to be honored through the act of giving, there is a single meaning.
Even though the phrase "in that [fire] he sits" depends upon what precedes it, the sentences constitute distinct units because their purposes differ.
Therefore, they possess the status of separate sentences.

In the case of those [mantras] for which no ritual action is perceived—because they lack an inherent connection to a purpose and thus lack application based on indicative power (*liṅga*)—their application is determined by direct statement (*vacana*). For such mantras, there is a single-mantra status prior to the limit of the mantra whose purpose is already seen;
for it is as follows:

For when the assumption of multiple unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) is without proof, and only a single unseen force is postulated for all [the acts], then, because each individual act lacks the power to accomplish that [single] result, they lose their distinctness and thus achieve syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).
But how, then, can there be an application (*viniyoga*) through such divisions of formulas as "With *iṣe* thee" [he cuts the branch] and "With *ūrje* thee" [he touches it]?
And how is there the plural designation in the rule "He causes [them] to recite the *klṛptī*s"?
This is explained as follows:
by mentioning the beginning, middle, and end, even a single mantra, though employed in various contexts, is not impaired;
for it will recur in its entirety according to each specific application, since a fragment has no independent utility.

Furthermore, because of the repeated application of the expressions "let it be prepared" (*kalpatām*) and "let it be prepared" (*kalpatām*), there is no contradiction in using the plural number even when there is a single sentence; this is said [by the opponent].
To this, we reply: it is not so.
Let alone the postulation of a purpose or an injunctive statement; for it is not logical to determine the essential nature [of a mantra] at a time subsequent to that.
This is because one cannot employ what is of unknown form, and it is impossible to postulate a purpose for that which has not been employed.
Rather, its specific form is ascertained from the very text itself, independent of those [other factors].
However, at that time, the conformity to difference and non-difference is disregarded regarding the purpose and the application.
It has been stated that even if there are many [factors], they may be postulated just like the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, at the moment of perceiving the form, the *iṣetvā* and other [mantras] are not considered to have mutual expectancy or a single common purpose.
Furthermore, once the difference has been determined without opposition, no reason subsequently exists for establishing unity.

Nor can it be assumed that there was a state of expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) not previously perceived; and even if there were a single purpose despite the absence of such expectancy, there would still be a lack of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) due to the deficiency of a single constituent part. How much more so when, due to the difference in form, there is a difference in application (*viniyoga*), and because of that difference, there is a difference in purpose (*prayojana*), even if the purpose is transcendental (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Moreover, in your own view as well, there must necessarily be a distinct application for each respective [instance].
However, this is the distinction: for you [the Mīmāṃsakas], the mantras are taken as a whole, whereas for me [the Vedāntin], they are taken individually.
Nor is there a lack of purpose in these mantras, because, as taught in the Brāhmaṇas, they serve as means for an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha).

And by virtue of that [inherent capacity], whatever is necessary for them to possess the power to perform the enjoined action—even if it is not explicitly mentioned—must be supplied, such as the act of "cutting" and so forth.

Alternatively, just as in the case of the statement, "He begins the Māhendra-stotra with the sound of a chariot," where even though the sound is not expressive of the meaning, it serves as a sign directing one toward the stotra through the mere consideration of its application, so too do words like *iṣe tvā* serve as the cause for the recollection of cutting and other acts. Both of these cases are authoritative, and thus the author of the Sūtras has accepted them in some way or another.
In every respect, it must be concluded as follows:
since the employment of an incomplete sentence is impossible and the use of non-expressive words is untenable, there must be an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).

Alternatively, in accordance with the application (*viniyoga*) as traditionally handed down, one must strive to instill the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) in the memory by means of that very [text] as it has been transmitted.
In this regard, since the adoption of one or the other depends upon the intention of the performer,
the split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is established even from the difference in visible purposes;
furthermore:

If there were necessarily different effects for those [mantras] that are independent of one another, then each would individually be a cause of the sacrifice, and thus the status of being a *yajus* would not be possible.

For it is not the case that perception alone is the sole means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding Vedic sentences; rather, inference and the other means of valid cognition are equally authoritative.
And when all other means of valid cognition have ceased to apply, non-existence is determined by the sixth [means], namely, non-apprehension (*abhāva*).
Therefore, in this case, when there is no perception of a remainder of the sentence through direct observation, one should not stop at that point alone.
If inference and the other means of knowledge also cease to function, we shall conclude that "this mantra is exactly this much.
However, if something is understood by them, then we determine that "this mantra is complete up to that point; prior to that, it was deficient."
Therefore, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), one must first determine in a general sense that "there exists some remainder.

Consequently, this statement—which would otherwise provide no occasion for non-existence—is not fit for formal application. When there arises a desire for a specific detail, a doubt occurs as to whether a worldly [remainder] should be supplied, or whether it should be the Vedic one found in the preceding mantra, such as "the sixteenth year" and so forth; in response to this doubt, he says: "It is the worldly one."
For indeed,
a Vedic composition cannot be applied elsewhere;
however, a worldly object may be employed for any purpose as one desires.

If, however, because there is no difference in their immediate proximity, it were admitted that this [word *rajāśaya*] is also connected with [the preceding word], then its application would necessarily occur right before it, according to the order of placement in the recitation.
Therefore, since it is not a Vedic supplement (*vaidika-śeṣa*), the following is stated:
"In the Veda, where there is freedom from constraint, there is room for worldly [usage]."
When its own operation has ceased and all searching has come to an end,
the meaning that was sought in the suffix is then sought again in the base; but if it is not found within its own word, it must be sought in another word.

Therefore, in this case, since the remainder (*śeṣa*) of the two sentences containing "rājāśaya" and "aharāśaya" is not produced within their own words or sentences, it is necessarily supplied from another sentence.
And that [remainder], in whatever form it is conceived, is perceived immediately after it [in the sequence], whereas for another [sentence] it is separated by an interval.

Even though that [remainder] does not require those two because its purpose is fulfilled in the first mantra, those two—being untenable without it—impel the person [to supply it] into their own proximity, precisely because it is not recited elsewhere.

Since it is impossible to recite [the entire text] at once in the proximity of everything, and because it has not been heard again and again due to the absence of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), this supplementary portion (*śeṣa*) was indeed recorded for the sake of both of us; it must not be assumed to belong to one alone based on the error caused by the specific proximity. Even if it is examined from the preceding part, nevertheless, those [verses] which are connected to a particular location are applied by them to that very place. Why?

For since it is recited only once, it cannot be recited in all the desired locations; thus, it is recited in its proper sequence for one [verse], and for the other two, it reaches the range of the intellect. Having been grasped there, it is itself incapable of remaining in another location, nor is it desired by those two as occurring elsewhere. Since its capacity has been observed previously in the subsequent position, it is placed at the very end.

The Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), however, having stated that because it is recited between the first and second [sections], the "remainder" (śeṣa) lacks any distinguishing feature and thus relates to both by immediate sequence, raised the objection that it cannot relate to the third due to the intervention [of the second]. Having then established that there is no intervention by forming a collective whole of both since their need [for the remainder] is identical, he further raised the doubt that it would consequently follow that it belongs to the remainder of the collective whole itself; this is addressed in the *Asadhyavārtika*.

Because it is fit for application (*prayogārhatvāt*), the connection belongs to the composite whole (*samudāyi*); even there, since those two [the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*] are primary, and because otherwise mutual expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*) would be untenable, it is determined that the connection with all the subsidiary elements (*śeṣa*) is established for each one individually. Having thus concluded, another explanation is then commenced: "Moreover, [it applies] when there is proximity to that which possesses expectancy. Regarding this, some have maintained that there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*) in the interpretation.
Others, however, say that the latter [position] was formulated because of dissatisfaction with the former:
for "being a collection" (samudāyatva) would have to arise either from performing a single function or from being designated by a single word; yet neither of these exists here.
But is this not the very state of having a single function, namely, the inclusion of a single supplementary portion of the sentence?
Ah! Indeed, the function of mantras has been understood.
For in that regard, there would be a mutual dependence between the two.
How is that function described? It is said as follows:
Furthermore, since that [remainder] belongs to those two, it is not logical for it to attain the status of a collective by virtue of them;

or rather, if its connection with the two members of the collection is desired only later, then the status of being a collective cannot be established from the very beginning. If they have already attained the status of a collective and then subsequently connect with each individual member, one falls into the "king's only-son" fallacy.
Furthermore, the application [of the mantra] would necessarily occur only before [the action], because it is immediately preceded by that specific collection [of words].
Nor is there a distinction in the mantras based on a difference in location, since no such distinction is perceived;
for while the first [mantra] remains in the location as previously conceived, the other two do not.
Therefore, this alone is the correct explanation:

when something is mentioned once as being related to many, it must necessarily have proximity to at least one of them; however, that [proximity] alone is not then relied upon as the cause of the relationship.
For even in the case of the *mantra*, the relationship is established from this very same triad of causes.
However, due to the proximity of the second chapter’s first section, there arises a misconception regarding the inheritance [of the fruit].

That misconception is removed by observing other related factors that are proximate, capable, and in need of connection—just as the notion of an injunction regarding the meaning of verbal roots and so forth is set aside by the capacity for the adoption of qualities and the like; for it is understood in that manner there.

Since this [subject] being recited has all things as its object, and because there is no possibility of a common immediate sequence (ānantarya) for all [subjects], and because the sentence is a single unit, it is understood in proximity to some one [particular subject].
Therefore, immediate sequence is not the cause [of connection].
"Proximity" (sannidhi), on the other hand, is the mental presence (viparivṛtti).

And that [sandhi] occurs both in immediate succession (*ānantarya*) and when there is an intervention by a connected word (*saṃbaddhapadavyavāya*). An intervention by a connected word is also simply a type of immediate succession.
How so?

The remainder required by the verse "O Agni, that [body] of yours which dwells in the dust" (*yā te agne rajāśaya*), though not recited immediately thereafter, is obtained by looking back from what follows; it is "the body most excellent" (*tanūr varṣiṣṭhā*). And when that [verse] has been supplied, it becomes contiguous with "that which dwells in the flame" (*harāśaya*) and likewise connects with the third [verse] as well. Beyond that, however, since no other [verse] is recited, the connection extends only that far.
In all such cases, the expectation (ākāṅkṣā) extends both before and after; it remains active until it is satisfied by something appropriate, or until an inappropriate element is perceived.
Once everything has been examined and withdrawn, the expectation ceases.

Although proximity and distance are perceived due to sequential utterance, nevertheless, because the Veda is eternal, the expectation and the connection exist simultaneously with respect to what is proximate and what is distant. Since these are understood subsequently, there is no difference in their authority.

Thus, the connection between words within a sentence and the connection between sentences within a context occurs through non-intervention [of other words], provided that there is expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and the capacity to bring about the subsequent connection. Even in the absence of intervention, there must be no separation;
the meaning is that the connection takes place when there is no intervention by a contradictory word, even if there is some distance.
Therefore, *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation) is completion (*samāpti*).
It is called *anuṣaṅga* because it is attached (*anuṣajyate*), and it is called *samāpti* because that very [sentence] is completed by means of it; thus says the *Tantravārtika*.

In cases where the principal elements (*śeṣin*) are themselves expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*), it is as described above. However, where there is no mutual expectancy among all the principals, yet a single subsidiary element (*śeṣa*) is found to be expectant—such as in the case of "May Citpati purify you," at the end of which "with an unbroken [strainer]" and so forth occurs—how is that to be understood?
What is stated first?
This [phrase] "may he purify" is connected with the specific qualification of "immediacy."
And that [mantra] is indeed one and the same in all three sentences; because of its oneness, the meaning is also one.
Nor does it become divided by the difference in the grammatical cases (kārakas), such that its non-difference from what is connected with Citpati and so forth would not be recognized.
Nor is the ritual action one whose purpose is merely "to be without flaw" (achidra), such that one would be satisfied by a single connection;
for the arrangement of the recitations is based on their application to distinct transcendental results (apūrva).
Furthermore, because other officiants are assigned [to specific parts], there is no confusion regarding the roles of Citpati and the others.

Therefore, although this word *punātu* occurs within all mantras, it is seen that all [the words] are repeated immediately; however, due to an interruption (*vyavāya*), it is not supplied by transference (*anuṣajyate*). (Tantravārtika)
This is stated as a counter-example on account of proximity:
because of the disparity caused by the concealment of the connection, it is not to be supplied;
for that which is being recited and is being supplied is included within the determination of the mantra.
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the *Mīmāṃsā-tantravārttika* composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Kumārila.

Among those [means of differentiation], "difference of words" (*śabdāntara*) is cited first because it is the most evident. All verbal roots connected with one or more verbal suffixes—such as *yajati*, *dadāti*, *juhoti*, *nirvapati*, *gṛhṇāti*, *stṛṇāti*, *śaṃsati*, *stauti*, and so forth—are the examples.
The second quarter of the second chapter.

However, the Commentator has cited [the three roots] *yajati* and so forth as being even more clearly non-different because they are proximate in meaning through the factor of the renunciation of ownership (*svatva-parityāga*). In that regard, since three types of prima facie views (*pūrvapakṣa*) are observed, the presentation of the doubt (*saṃśaya*) also appears to be consistent with them.
For example:

do the three *bhāvanās* (efficient forces) produce one unprecedented result (*apūrva*), or three? Likewise, do the three meanings of the verbal roots (*dhātvartha*) qualify one *bhāvanā*, or three? Similarly, do the three verbal roots express one meaning of a verbal root, or three?

Since the *kārya* (the effect), the word, the *apūrva*, and the *bhāvanā* are employed without distinction as that which is assisted within the meanings of the verbal roots, these—the *bhāvanā*, the meanings of the verbal roots, and the verbal roots—are designated as the means (*sādhana*) because they function as the assistance through the production, qualification, and communication [of the result].
Whence arises this doubt?

Or rather, there is here this one ultimate doubt: is the single efficient force (*bhāvanā*) colored by the collection of the meanings of the verbal roots, or is there a distinction of efficient forces for each meaning of the verbal root? It is the single efficient force, colored by the meanings of the verbal roots, that is expressed by the word "action" (*karman*).

For that very [action], the difference will be established by means of different words and so forth; since the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is not itself denoted, it follows as a consequence of the distinction between actions and thus does not merit a separate investigation.

As for the incidental mention of the unity of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), since it is in any case not universal—being applicable only to sacrifices (*yajyādi*) and the like—it need not be emphasized too much in this context.

Furthermore, this also appears as a ground for doubt to the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*): Is the *bhāvanā* (efficient force), being undertaken with respect to each of the root-meanings (*dhātvartha*), completed individually, or are those root-meanings, being undertaken with respect to it, collectively qualify it?

What, then, is the initial position? It is that they qualify it collectively. In that regard, since the collective whole (*samudāya*) is what is intended to be performed, and because there is a single *apūrva* (transcendental result) from the collective whole—as seen in the repeated mention of the word "collective whole" in passages such as "there is no [single] *apūrva* from a collective whole"—and because of the statement regarding the unity of the *apūrva*, the prima facie view is that a single *apūrva* arises from the three *bhāvanās*.
Or this is the logical justification: when there is a contradiction with what is seen or heard, one postulates something unseen;
and once consistency is established by means of a single [postulation], there is no [need for] a multiplicity of assumptions.
And for that very reason,
because the meaning of the suffix is predominant, it does not differ with each verbal root; furthermore,
because it is presented there, the meaning of the roots is combined.
When there is a difference in the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), a difference in the object to be cultivated (*bhāvya*) follows as a matter of necessity.
Nor is this [object] accepted as being a mere aggregate, because it is designated by a single word and so forth; thus it is said.

Just as when a crystal is covered by a red substrate, another crystal—associated with the designation of black and so forth—is perceived; for, since both the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya) are traditionally and conventionally understood to express their own respective meanings with a fixed sequence always intended, the suffix, falling upon perceivers who are already occupied with the meaning of the base expressed first, expresses its own meaning only as something accompanied by that [base]. Therefore, the meaning of the suffix is never obtained in its pure form.

As it has been stated: "The second case-ending (dvitīyā vibhakti) arising from the nominal stem (prātipadika)—as taught in the second quarter of the second chapter—is a qualifier of the meaning of the nominal stem. For the connection with existence belongs to the whole [the word] by virtue of its being a subordinate element within the sentence of usage.

The assumption of a single *apūrva* is based on the conception of a productive operation (*bhāvanā*) colored by the aggregate [of actions]. Alternatively, the assumption of an *apūrva* is caused by the connection with the fruit.

Furthermore, the connection with the fruit occurs for the originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*) by virtue of their being supplementary to the performance injunction (*prayogavākya*), not by their own intrinsic forms.

And since actions whose forms have not yet been established are grasped by the performance injunction, once their distinctness is understood, they cannot be unified. Nor do we observe that the acts of giving (*dadāti*) and offering (*juhoti*) function as supplements to the performance injunction, because in the statement "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*), only the sacrifice (*yāga*) is heard; and by that [injunction], neither giving nor offering is obtained.

If both [meanings] were resorted to, there would be the fault of simultaneously requiring both direct denotation (*śakti*) and metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), which entails the undesirable consequence of abandoning one's own primary meaning.
Therefore, no assumption of a collective whole exists.
Consequently, because it is a different word due to its difference from the verbal root, its distinction as qualified by the suffix *keva* is understood.
Nor is it set aside by another cognition;
nor does it consist merely in the unity of the root-meaning, because there is the addition of pouring out and the transfer of ownership.
Nor is there a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) based on mere relinquishment, since the syntactical connection of the sentence is established even by the word functioning in its own primary sense.

Since no quality known as "giving" (*dāna*) is established [as a distinct ritual act], it is logical that [the term *dadāti*] is a name [for the sacrifice] due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Therefore, so that the sentence does not become meaningless, the oblation (*homa*) is enjoined. However, if the sacrifice were restated by means of the verb *dadāti* and a quality were then enjoined, there would be the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) due to the connection between the gold and Ātreya; thus, a distinction [of acts] can also arise from a quality. In this case, since there is a single quality, the repetition of the same [act] would be purposeless unless there is a specific distinction. Therefore, [the act] is distinct.

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument regarding repetition is easily stated by way of a counter-example to the section on "different words" (śabdāntarādhikaraṇa); therefore, its commencement follows immediately after that. In this regard, having extracted the words *samid* and so forth from such passages as "He offers the *samidhs*" (*samidho yajati*) and "He offers the *tanūnapāt*" (*tanūnapātaṃ yajati*), it is cited whether the word *yajati* ("he offers"), which is uttered five times, denotes a single action or multiple actions; that [prima facie view] is now being refuted.

All six causes of differentiation must be shown to exist separately, with their respective capacities and functions as their results. Therefore, as long as the differentiating power of the quality (*guṇa*) and the name (*nāmadheya*) has not been removed from this context, there is no possibility for repetition (*abhyāsa*) to attain its own distinct status; thus, another example must be cited. And that is not possible here, because all [sentences] such as "He takes the Aindravāyava cup" are differentiated by their connection with inherent qualities (*utpattika-guṇa-yoga*) through mutual association.

Passages such as "He offers when [the vessel] has broken" and "He offers when it has spilled" are distinct acts because they are undertaken with respect to specific conditions (*nimitta*), according to the principle that "or [a result occurs] when there is proximity to an action. Furthermore, because their purpose is to establish a connection with a condition, the repetition is not meaningless; thus, they do not constitute a single act.

As for those who cite the repetition in the *Pañcaśāradīya* sacrifice—namely, "those [animals] over which the fire has been carried," "those [animals] over which the fire has been carried"—for them, that repetition serves the purpose of reminding one of the original (*prakṛta*) rite of carrying the fire around the animals.

Alternatively, since no *yajati* (sacrificial act) is heard here whose repetition might cause a distinction [in the ritual], there is no example at all; rather, the resolution lies precisely in the examples already cited. This concludes the second quarter of the second chapter.

Those noun-words which have a meaning to be adopted (as a primary object) are, for their part, dependent upon the verb; therefore, following its lead, they await its mode of operation. If that [verb] is already established in the context, then the noun-word is either a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*) or a name (*nāmadheya*) for that very [action]. If, however, a new [action] (*apūrva*) is postulated by it, then the noun-word is understood as pertaining to that [new action]. Thus, when the distinction or non-distinction [between the two] has been understood, the word *samit* and so forth, arriving later, remains indifferent because it contributes nothing further; therefore, setting that aside, only the verb is investigated. [Objection:
