But if this is the case, it would follow that names and subordinate qualities (*guṇa*) are not distinct [from the action].
In that case, differentiation occurs where a verbal form (*ākhyāta-pada*) is operative, as he will illustrate with the example:
"Now this [is] *jyotis*; [there is] *vājina* for the *vājins*.

In the case of *vājina*, no verbal form is heard at all; and since even in the case of *jyotis* and the others, it is possible for the verbal form to enter into the context through its operation in connecting the quality with the fruit, differentiation will therefore arise from the name itself, which functions prior to that.

Even in cases where the verb, by its own inherent force, would naturally apply to the action under discussion, if that application is obstructed and a quality is enjoined because it cannot otherwise be established, even there this [quality] serves as a differentiator. As he will state in the section on *abhyupetyavāda*: "This connection between the deity and the sacrifice being enjoined," and so forth. And since that occurs when the power of the verb to differentiate is neutralized, that very point is first examined:

whether there is one *apūrva*—this is the presentation of the difference or non-difference of actions from the perspective of the result—namely, whether one action and one *apūrva* are enjoined, or whether all five actions have their own respective *apūrvas*.
What follows is that there is a single *apūrva*.
Why?

Just as the word *yajati* (he sacrifices), having been perceived once through direct perception, is not considered different when uttered again because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is that very same [word]," so too is it here.

Likewise, its meaning is also [the same]; and just as in this very case, the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that effects the awakening of the Buddha, even though it is purposeless, cannot bring about a difference in the word itself, so too repetition does not bring about a difference in the meaning. Indeed, what is called "purposelessness" (*ānarthakya*) is not included anywhere within the category of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And whatever the Veda makes known, that alone must be accepted by those who maintain its authority as a means of knowledge.
Therefore, when non-difference has been understood here by the Veda through the word "one" (*eka*), whoever imagines otherwise would be rendering the Veda itself invalid.
Nor does the futility of what is understood through a valid means of knowledge constitute a defect;
for there is also this alternative interpretation.

A word touched by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), while establishing its own meaning, is itself grasped as being subject to that performance; or rather, repetition (*abhyāsa*) will serve the purpose of indicating frequency (*abhīkṣṇya*) and so forth, for in common usage, even beyond mere reduplication, there is repetition for as many times as is required to manifest the intended meaning. And thus, in the narrative of Pañcendra, when the old maiden requested a boon, the repetition "Give me a husband" is heard five times.

And it is not as in that case where there is a deceptive intent on the part of the deity; here, there is no such thing for anyone by which one might imagine five sacrifices like the "five husbands" (patipañcaka). Alternatively, when the injunction is relied upon in all the recitations, the unity of the ritual action (*karmaikatva*) is understood, just as in the sentences concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites found in different Vedic branches (*śākhā*).

Therefore, since those having the same purpose are optional (*vaikalpika*), that very same ritual action will at one time be denoted by the *samidh* formula and at another time by the *tanūnapāt* formula.
For it is not understood that because rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*) have the same purpose, one of them would be rendered useless while the other accomplishes a different purpose.

Alternatively, [the passage] is not meaningless because it serves to enjoin deities such as Tanūnapāt; for if there were an injunction of an action (*karman*), it would be a name (*nāmadheya*), but since this is a restatement (*anuvāda*), an injunction of a name is impossible, and thus it must be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). Therefore, this is also not a separate action.
Furthermore, in other places as well, the word and its meaning are the very same.

For even there, they are recognized; indeed, when one has emerged from the house, it is impossible to assert that there is a different object [in the case] of the recognition of the people in the house, just as in the previous instance. How much more so when the cognition is firmly established by an immediate succession of recollection?

Furthermore, if there were a difference in the meaning with each utterance, it would follow that the word denotes an impermanent individual instance; yet, as in the case of "g-ness" (gatva) and so forth, the nature of sacrifice (yāgatva) is not distinct from these [individual acts]. Moreover, since the unity of the individual is firmly established, how could this be a different ritual action?

The verbal suffix first enjoins [an action] by virtue of its capacity for action; however, when its capacity is projected by another [suffix], it requires that which is restated. This status as a restatement (anuvāda) arises from the suffix belonging to the present context.

The application of that [injunction] to the general case is obtained from its own sentence itself; for the injunctive *śruti*, being uncontradicted by anything else, is firmly established only in the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Producing the nature of an injunction (*vidhitva*) regarding that very object which has not yet been established, it suppresses the cognition of establishment produced by the authority known as the "fifth position" (*pañcamasthāna*), and thus conceives of another action (*karmāntara*) as the object to be enjoined. If that injunction were to follow the *śruti*, it would determine another action; however, because of proximity (*sannidhi*), there is no status as a separate action.
Furthermore, where the scriptural injunction (*vidhiśruti*) is occupied elsewhere, there arises—due to the absence of contradiction—the cognition of oneness based on proximity (*saṃnidhi*).

Therefore, in this case, the delusion of recognition is caused solely by the oneness of the universal (*sāmānya*) as it is presented through the result of the specific sacrifice (*yāgavyakti*) to be enjoined. Indeed, there is no basis whatsoever for the recognition of an individual (*vyakti*).
And when something is recognized as being the same in its ultimate sense, there is no dispute regarding its unity.

Thus, one might object: "In this case, since the oneness of the ritual action is understood through the direct statement (*śruti*) itself, it should not be said that this unity is established merely by proximity (*sannidhi*).
This is not so.
For individual instances are enjoined as qualified by a universal;
therefore, the determination of difference and non-difference here pertains only to that [universal], insofar as it is ascertained in its own nature as "the single action."
Beyond that, there is no further difference; therefore, the determination of difference occurs prior to that.
Furthermore, it is not the case that only that which is apprehended as distinct by perception alone is differentiated.

Since verbal testimony (*śabda*) possesses no lesser authority [than perception], the difference in this context must be determined by means of the six criteria beginning with "difference in words" (*śabdāntara*).

For in the case of the *iṣṭi*, *paśu*, and *soma* sacrifices, as well as the *ekāha*, *ahīna*, and *satra* rites, the cognition of difference—which is based on external conditions—never undergoes sublation.
Therefore, it is precisely within those individual instances (*vyakti*) that constitute the objects of injunction that the eternal [forms] are manifested;

and from these, the accomplishment of the nature of the result follows. Indeed, there is only one internal universal (*avāntara-sāmānya*), namely *yāgatva* (the nature of sacrifice), and nothing else.

But surely, "oneness of day" (*ekāhatva*) and so forth are also accepted as intermediate universals (*avāntarasāmānya*)? No; for the application of a single, undifferentiated word and cognition is established simply through connection with a specific time, just as in the case of "one who possesses a staff" (*daṇḍin*) and the like. For "oneness of day" (*ekāhatva*) results from connection with a single day; "multiday-ness" (*yāḍhitva*) results from not being deficient in [days] such as the *yājuṣa*; and that which consists of less than twelve days is of both natures. Furthermore, it is established that "satra-ness" (the nature of a sacrificial session) is based on connection with a period of years numbering up to one thousand, while "iṣṭi-ness" (the nature of an offering sacrifice) and so forth result from connection with specific oblations. Thus it is proven.
Furthermore, even if intermediate generalities (*avāntarasāmānya*) are again postulated, there is still no contradiction with our position.
Likewise, if [the sacrifices] such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* become extremely distinct due to differences in place, time, and so forth, there is still no fault.

Similarly, although all [sacrifices] might be considered a single sacrifice because they consist of the renunciation of a substance intended for a deity, the practical application (*vyavahāra*) is established through the various means of knowledge for their distinction and the understanding of the diversity in their performance.

If this is so, then by parity with the repetition of the cups (*graha*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the repetitions of the *samit* and other sacrificial offerings constitute distinct acts (*karmāntara*).

In any case, distinctions such as those between the *parvan* sacrifices are established; nevertheless, it is well-known here that there is a cognition of a distinction between acts in the case of the cups, and a distinction of repetition in the case of the sacrifices. (This concludes the second section of the second chapter.)

This very reason is the injunction for the differentiation of the performance of all forms of sacrifice; furthermore, although each individual repetition possesses the nature of a sacrifice (*yāgatva*), it does not possess the nature of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* because the name *Jyotiṣṭoma* applies to the whole consisting of those repetitions. Thus, the notion of a "part" (*avayava*) applies to the repetition, but not to the other [the whole], because no distinct composite entity (*avayavin*) is produced there—this is the distinction.
We shall explain the purpose of this knowledge in the section concerning animals and Soma.
It is precisely with this in view that the *Bhāṣya* states: "Therefore, the sacrifice is to be repeated."
Alternatively, the term "repetition" (abhyāsa) refers to the requirement of a commonality among distinct individual acts.

Now, you might argue that since it was stated that [the injunction] cannot enjoin a different meaning, there is no contradiction because the injunctive power, having recourse to the mention of deities such as Tanūnapāt and others, turns back [from its primary function].

In this regard, concerning the principle "and another scriptural text is like that," since words such as *samit* and so forth function as names by means of a connection with deities established through the indicative power (*liṅga*) and the wording of mantras applied in their respective order, they are not themselves objects of injunction; thus, it must be stated that there is no implication of injunctive power. The presentation of the injunction of the connection between deity and sacrifice is made as a concession (*abhyupetyavāda*). As for your view that the first [sentence] is an injunction of sacrifice because it is not otherwise established, that is incorrect, because even that is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the primary sacrifice.
In that context, neither a substance nor a deity is enjoined by the words *samit* and so forth.
Furthermore, both [theories] contradict the substance and deity enjoined by the originative injunctions, such as "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni.

Moreover, the connection with a sacrifice produced by this sentence must necessarily be established; and since that is not possible without another sacrifice, once the status of being an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) has been refuted, the result is that it becomes a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).

Thus, because subsequent injunctions of qualities cannot apply to the previously mentioned ritual action, all would become distinct actions; consequently, the effort expended in proposing them as injunctions of qualities is futile.
The *Tantravārttika* also explains that it cannot be a prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).
It has already been explained in the section on *saktu* that it is not possible for a substance to be denoted by the word [‘saktu’].

Furthermore, specifically, a connection with a substance that is the object of the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) is not tenable; nor is this a prescription of a deity (*devatāvidhi*), as will be stated in the ninth book.
Therefore, the establishment of difference [between rites] occurs solely through the injunctions regarding ritual actions (*karmavidhi*).
This investigation into the relationship between subsidiary and principal elements (*aṅga-pradhāna*) belongs to the scope of the fourth chapter;
by what occasion, indeed, has it been introduced here under the definition of difference?
And since no capacity is observed in the case of differentiation for the sake of establishing equal primacy,
how can the repetition of another word be cited as a reason? [The view is that] the deity is the common substance derived from the words of the mantra.
Therefore, two sacrifices possessing form are enjoined; their separate placement occurs only in those cases where there is a separate denotation of the two,
and the fruit [accrues] from those qualified by them— thus, parity is not tenable.
It is always accepted that the well-known serves as the qualifier for the unknown;
therefore, the name is determined in accordance with the sacrifice.

There are certain sacrifices under discussion that are connected with the time of speech and are associated with the number two; moreover, they possess established usage. Even though the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) occurs in connection with its own denotation in the case of the *Āgneya* and other offerings, nevertheless, because those [offerings] are plural, the number two is impossible, and thus the word is incapable [of expressing it]. Even where the number two exists—as in the case of the two *āghāra* libations or the two *ājyabhāga* portions—there too the nominal stem is utterly incapable [of expressing it].

Furthermore, there is no clear grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words "meaning" (*artha*), "context" (*prakaraṇa*), or "other words" (*śabdāntara*), by virtue of which one might determine that these two refer to those [meanings] either through some commonality of phonemes, according to the principle of modification of verbal roots (*ākhyāvikāra*), or as a figurative usage (*gauṇatva*). Why, then, are these two unprecedented sacrifices— the Full Moon and the New Moon— not enjoined for the sake of the fruit?
For it is said in the Tantravārtika:
"Even in the established conclusion (siddhānta), those two groups are indeed referred to by those two words [denoting the sacrifices]."
They will bring about the fruit;

for when there is a connection with time among the eight [factors], there is no reason for a restrictive determination by which the connection with the fruit would belong to these two alone. This might be so.
Among these, it is incorrect to claim that a relationship with the fruit exists for any two [of them] alone;

for, since there is no specific reason and the equality of their connection to the sacrifice and the time remains the same, if only those two were selected, it would result in a contradiction by relegating the others—who possess primacy and authoritative status—to the position of being mere subsidiaries (*aṅga*).

Alternatively, if one were to assume a sequential favor for all of them through option (*vikalpa*), even then it would be contradictory for that very same [element] to be primary at one time and a subsidiary at another.

Furthermore, since those things possessing a dual nature proceed as subordinate members (*aṅga*) and cease as primary ones (*pradhāna*), there would arise the contingency of doubt regarding the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices when they enter into a modified form (*vikṛti*) throughout one's entire life.
Moreover, all numbers function toward their objects of enumeration by means of some intermediate commonality (*avāntara-sāmānya*).
[End of] the second quarter of the second chapter.

Furthermore, no intermediate commonality whatsoever is observed between the two previously mentioned [sacrifices], or among the Agni and other sacrifices taken collectively, or even in part, by which a duality could be determined.

For when a certain [sacrifice] is grasped, its very self—considered in relation to another sacrifice—is sublated by the plurality [of those others], while its own individual nature is sublated by its unity;
consequently, the application of the dual number is not established.

In the Siddhānta, however, because two groups are established by the two words, there arises a connection with duality through the application of intermediate attributes due to the distinctness of the sacrifices constituting those groups; and by virtue of that [duality], a connection with time [also arises]. Thus, the application of the nominal stems *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* is somehow established, and their status as qualifiers of the sacrifice is justified. This is not the case in the Pūrvapakṣa, where—due to the absence of the establishment of two groups—the number cannot function [as a qualifier]; consequently, the connection with the fruit would apply only to the sacrifices under discussion in general. Now, why are not exactly eight sacrifices enjoined, having acquired their specific qualifiers in view of the duality residing in the times of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)?
Just as in the Siddhānta, six [offerings] are prescribed with reference to the duality residing in the aggregate,

it is not possible here to set aside what has been explained by relying solely on the context of the sacrifice, even though the vision [of the text] is not explicit. Furthermore, because there is an absolute distinction [between time and the sacrifice], a number belonging to time cannot be designated in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the sacrifice.
In our final position (siddhānta), the connection with number is not contradictory because there is no distinction between the aggregate and that which constitutes the aggregate.

Therefore, according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), since the application of the name-word occurs solely by virtue of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) without distinction, all sacrifices are equally primary.
This being the case, the following is stated [in response].
The context (*prakaraṇa*) would be the basis for those [rites] connected with the full moon and the new moon;
for "context" means that which is being set forth (*prakriyate*).
Alternatively, the context serves as a cooperative factor for those two, and therefore the meaning to be understood must be accepted as consisting of that alone.
Why?
Because by this word "yajati" (he sacrifices), no cognition of sacrifice in general is produced through the words "paurṇamāsī" or "amāvāsyā";
nor is there, according to your view, a reference to the actions under discussion.
In that case, since the form is unknown in a previously unheard-of ritual action (*apūrva karma*), one could not be prompted to act in any way whatsoever;

consequently, the entire scriptural statement would become meaningless. However, if the [sacrifices] mentioned in the context are taken up, their form is known through the connection with specific substances and deities, as well as through their occurrence at this particular time; thus, they possess purposefulness.
But was it not already stated that even in the modified sacrifice (*matyaya*) there is a substance and a deity?
True; however,
even if some common substance were somehow established,
one is still not liberated because there is no deity, due to the absence of form.

For if time, which is well-known to the entire world, were not applicable here, then the two actions might be understood by transgressing that [restriction]. Moreover, it is more appropriate for the word *sa* to denote time, because time is everywhere the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), whereas it is untenable for an action to be the locus; thus, as in the case of the second foot of the teacher [Pāṇini], it would have to be interpreted in some way or another.

As for the question, "What is the connection with time?"—if there were only the relationship of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) as the single connection, and if that were what we were asserting here, then it would be appropriate to speak thus: once the relationship of being for that purpose with respect to the two *ājyabhāga* offerings is established, and when a confusion [of usage] has arisen, a mere restriction is made regarding the two mantras employed at different times, such that the *vārcaghna* mantras apply to the *ājyabhāgas* performed on the full moon day, and the *vṛdhanvatī* mantras to those performed on the new moon day.
Furthermore, what else?

In every case, a connection is established only through expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Furthermore, since the two *ājyabhāga* offerings have Agni and Soma as their well-known deities, they require mantras capable of denoting those deities; thus, they accept the mantras without effort. In your view, however, because the two new rites have unknown deities, there is no requirement for mantras. Consequently, by postulating mantras and their specific dual nature and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of enjoining many unintended matters. Moreover, one would have to postulate multiple deities based on the wording of the mantras; yet, a single ritual action has no need for multiple deities or multiple invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*).
Furthermore, there would be the assumption of unmentioned *jyā* verses for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, and the assumption of unmentioned *puronuvākyā*s;
and as for the claim that there will be one *yājyā* and one *anuvākyā*,
that is not so, because it would contradict the designation (*samākhyā*) "anuvākyā."

Furthermore, in your view, because the indicative mark (*liṅga*) lacks the power to assign application (*viniyojakatva*), and because the sentence (*vākya*) is relied upon as the instrument [of application], the mantras such as "vaiṣṇavīm anūcya" and so forth would result in the production of many unseen effects (*adṛṣṭārtha*), since they would not serve as illuminators (*prakāśaka*)—for that which is to be illuminated does not require them. Moreover, it is better for them to be remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*) based on the deity indicated by the words of the mantra itself. In the case of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, however, because they are dual and their deities are already known, the mantras that illuminate the deities, being assigned by both indicative mark and order (*krama*), attain exclusively the status of having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*).

And in that case, since [the deities] such as Mantra-taviśeṣa and others are already established, there is conciseness of the sentence due to the prescription of a mere restriction by way of time; nor is it purposeless, as stated in the Tantravārtika.
For the state of proximity is not established [by the sentence itself].
Therefore, this is not an injunction of a deity, because of the lack of connection.

And thus, because it possesses form, it is not a separate action; what, then, is the purpose of this collective restatement? Behold, it is said: just as the originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*) serve as constituent parts of the performance injunction (*prayogavacana*).
In the same way, by taking up those [two] as a basis, the cognition of duality arises for these two as well;

because they are conjoined at a single time, it is possible to present them as a composite whole even though their constituent actions are distinct, just like a tree standing upon a single spot of ground.

From the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) in the expression "one should sacrifice the Paurṇamāsī," it is understood that this is the name of a sacrifice. Furthermore, the nature of being a sacrifice (*yāgatva*) does not reside inherently in the collection (*samudāya*) of the Āgneya and other offerings; rather, it resides in each individual offering, such as the Āgneya. Therefore, just as the act of sacrificing itself applies to each of these individually, so too does this name.

Moreover, it is not logical for the origin of a collection to occur at a single time, because at the conclusion of the origin of the Āgneya and others, since they are independent of one another, the status of a "collection" is not yet produced.

Consequently, it could be argued that each [act] has its own name by virtue of its connection with the desired result (*kānta*). Furthermore, if these two names belonged to the two groups independently of the individual members, then the group itself would be enjoined toward the fruit by the ritual injunction (*prayoga-vākya*); consequently, since the individual parts would not be the means, a single *apūrva* would arise from the group.

And thus, because there would be no separate *apūrvas* for each [part], the distinction between the acts would be rendered meaningless. Moreover, since all the ritual properties (*dharma*) would be based on a single *apūrva*, they would result in a confused application (*saṃkīrṇavṛttitva*).

Furthermore, the Āgneya and other sacrifices would not be connected to the *itikartavyatā* (the procedure) individually; consequently, discussions regarding the *tantra* (commonality), *āvṛtti* (repetition), and *prayoga* (performance) pertaining to them would become irrelevant. Nor could there be an extension (*atideśa*) of the entire procedure to individual modifications such as the Saurya sacrifice, because—as in the case of words like "army" (*senā*)—there is no application [of the term] to its parts. This would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of destroying linguistic conventions such as: "The Full Moon sacrifice has one sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)," and "The New Moon sacrifice is prepared with the *sānnāyya*."

In such cases as "because the collection (*saṃghāta*) is not enjoined" and "because the collection is a subordinate quality (*guṇa*)," it is clearly accepted that words of this kind denote the members of the collection (*samudāyin*). For otherwise, that very collection would be enjoined because it is expressed by the word, and it would become the primary element due to its connection with the result. Therefore, it is the members of the collection themselves that are denoted, while the collection has become subordinate. Since those members are many, there would follow the use of the plural; however, intending that the singular number is applied through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), he says that [the word] will be treated as a term for the collection.

And so it is stated in the *Tantravārtika*: "The singular number of many [is used] with reference to the aggregate. This refers merely to the aggregate as a basis for the suffix, not to its being the primary denotation (*abhidheya*). Even the words *yūtha* (herd) and *vana* (forest), when they denote the individuals that constitute the aggregate while subordinating the aggregate itself, serve as examples in their entirety; however, when they denote the aggregate alone, they serve as examples by virtue of the singular number being applied on account of that [aggregate].
By this, the two words *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* are explained as synonyms for this [sacrifice];
for otherwise, this [word] would be connected with the instrumental aspect of the action.
Otherwise, for that which exists as a continuous stream of arising, which is mutually independent, whose temporal duration is not known, and whose intrinsic nature does not perish—
there is no fault in saying that its time is conditioned by something else.
If it is argued that this [time] exists even through the primary part of the limbs, such as the head, by means of the day and so forth, and thus these [limbs] do not serve as its cause—[we reply:

is it not true that those situated at a distance cannot provide assistance? Must it not be assisted by those in close proximity? To this we say: this is not so in all cases; rather, whether assistance is rendered or not depends upon the specific scriptural injunction.

In that regard, in the absence of a statement concerning proximity (*sannikarṣa*), there is no proof whatsoever for the claim that what is remote does not assist [the rite]. Now, one might argue: "This simultaneous performance (*tantra-prayoga*) is established by another very sentence itself—namely, those such as 'with the iṣṭi, with the animal sacrifice, with the Soma'—because even there, due to the use of the instrumental case-ending, the iṣṭi is presented in relation to time together with its own constituent parts (*svāṅga*); thus, the intended meaning is obtained here. True, it is obtained, but the simultaneous performance is not thereby established as desired.
For instance, it is not established that the word "iṣṭi" (sacrifice) denotes the triad [of sacrifices];

since the term "iṣṭi" applies to each one individually as a distinct sacrifice, the performance would occur on either the new moon day or the full moon day for each one separately, and thus the correct performance of the whole is not achieved.

Now, if it is argued that the entire set of sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya is grasped [as a whole] because its application has somehow already commenced—just as the application of the iṣṭi commences at the Soma sacrifice—even so, due to the unity of the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), the two groups would have to be performed either on the full moon day or on the new moon day.

In that case, there would be the same contradiction with the time prescribed by the originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭakāla*); and if it is then suggested that one should resort to an option fixed according to those [circumstances], [we reply: no.
Even so, following the order of their origination would entail the performance of each [rite] individually; likewise,
because the full-moon and new-moon sacrifices are not prescribed as being performed separately from their constituent parts (*aṅga*), they would have to be performed in some single location.

Therefore, this sentence does not have the same meaning as those two [previous rules]; since it would be ineffective regarding the archetype (*prakṛti*), it applies only to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) for the sake of establishing the immediate timing (*sadyaḥkālatā*).
[Objection: But surely by this, the performance of the ritual as a single unit (*tantra*) would be established;

for in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices on level ground," since the location is not something to be specifically undertaken (*anupādeya*), the requirement of simultaneity (*sāhitya*) is logically justified.
To this it is replied: even when [the subsidiaries] are performed separately, their status as *tantra* (common/shared) is established simply by the fact that they do not go to different locations.

Alternatively, *tantratva* is said to mean that by virtue of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), at the very moment one sacrifice is joined with a particular [subsidiary], the others are joined with it as well.

If that were the case, since all six [offerings] would be taken up simultaneously, the same aforementioned contradiction regarding the performance (*prayoga*) would arise, provided one proceeds in accordance with the injunctions for their production (*utpattivākya*). Consequently, because each is connected to its own specific time, a simultaneous conjunction (*sāhitya*) must be achieved; thus, the performance would have to be completed on exactly six full-moon and new-moon days.
Furthermore, the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) must be performed without being displaced from that duration; therefore, they would have to be performed at some point within the interval between them.
If the connection with time for sacrifices were not established at their origin,
then the status of being a restatement of a collective (*samudāyānuvāda*) would be untenable due to a lack of basis;
furthermore, because a distinction is observed, there would be no application [of the injunction] to the preceding [sacrifices], as they are equal [in that regard].

And if these two were separate acts, then the *āghāra* offerings and so forth would be equally primary; consequently, because an act does not proceed [as a subordinate], there would be no connection between the fruit, the restriction, and the collection of performers, according to the principle that "because it is bound to those [primary acts]. Thus, just as with the *āgneya* sacrifice, since the *prayāja*s and other elements would fall under the category of instruments, they would not be grasped by the modified (*vikṛti*) productive operation (*bhāvanā*), which requires the "how" (*kathaṃbhāva*) and seeks out what is suitable for its fulfillment. Therefore, the injunction of the *kṛṣṇala* grain in reference to the already-established *prayāja*s would be untenable.

Therefore, how could the *prayāja* and other such rites possess the quality of being related to Agni? [The answer is: It must be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the aggregate, or else it is an injunction (*codanā*) regarding the qualities, because they are taught simultaneously. For if they were enjoined separately, each would be taught for its own sake;
thus, these [elements] such as the potsherds (*kapāla*) and so forth are not the objects of the qualities.
For why is this so?

In a sentence expressing the origin of an action (*karmotpatti-vākya*), the suffix (*pratyaya*) begins by intending to enjoin the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), because that activity has not yet been established. As long as that activity is not fulfilled by the meaning of the verbal root and its factors (*kāraka*), it is unfit for performance; thus, the injunction does not reach its final completion. In that context, since the general factors understood as being subsumed within the nature of the productive activity cannot otherwise be accounted for, there arises a requirement for their specific details. These details are supplied from the sentence itself through the specific terms ending in case-terminations uttered in the same sentence, which, while seeking only the productive activity, serve to qualify it.

And at every step, whatever substance-based attributes such as genus, gender, number, and so forth exist, all of them— having attained the relationship of qualifier and qualified through the hearing (*śruti*) characterized by their being conveyed by a single word, yet not having reached a state of mutual subservience (*śeṣa-śeṣitva*) toward one another— attain their status as being for the sake of the *bhāvanā* in the form of a *kāraka* solely through the power of case-inflection (*vibhakti-śruti*).
Thus, however many words stand in proximity or distance, they all simultaneously converge, disregarding proximity and distance according to the path explained in the section on *anvaya-anuṣaṅga*.
The injunction reaches its conclusion by taking up a productive urge (*bhāvanā*) that is qualified by all its attributes and is fit for performance;
and since it enjoins that which is thus qualified through a single effort alone, there is no fault of falling into the error of postulating multiple potencies.
For instance:

If, after having invested the status of an injunction (*vidhitva*)—which is heard [in the Veda]—into a qualified [action], it were to operate again elsewhere by means of direct audition (*śruti*) itself, then it would incur the fault of redundant utterance (*punaruccāraṇa*), resulting in its own non-Vedic character (*avaidiktvāpatti*). This [injunction], however, having enjoined once and ceased its operation, brings forth other distinct injunctions residing in each of the qualifiers through the impossibility of its own purpose otherwise being fulfilled; thus, without abandoning the single form understood from the traditional collection (*samāmnāya*), it functions toward the fruit of that which has not been repeatedly uttered.

Although presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) arises subsequently because it depends on a specific cause and thus makes known the injunctions of the qualifiers at a later time, nevertheless—according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*—since a qualified operation is impossible without first apprehending the qualifiers, those [injunctions] regarding the qualifiers must certainly have been established previously; for we observe that the cognition of the qualified is seen to be dependent upon them. Therefore, these are indeed many injunctions obtained through direct perception and presumptive testimony; they function either simultaneously or sequentially. Thus, by the grace of a single qualified injunction capable of generating many other injunctions, the prescription of multiple qualities is easily accomplished in the case of an injunction for a new productive activity (*apūrvabhāvanā*), but not otherwise.

How so? For when a meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) has already been obtained from another [source], then the injunctive [element], its power being neutralized like the grinding of what has already been ground, does not enjoin it; consequently, it does not become the cause for generating the operation of multiple injunctions whose objects are connected with that [cultivation].
When there is an injunction of something qualified (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*), other injunctions are postulated through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*).

And since that [simultaneous injunction] is not possible here, the suffix (pratyaya), while still in its state of unutilized function, descends from the efficient force (bhāvanā) due to its own lack of purpose, according to the maxim "that which is purposeless attaches itself to the subsidiaries. Therein, all qualifiers of a single *kāraka*—whether they be genus (*jāti*), gender (*liṅga*), substance (*dravya*), number (*saṃkhyā*), or quality (*guṇa*)—are enjoined by the very same principle of the injunction of a qualified efficient force, because they are implied by that *kāraka*. Thus, even when the efficient force has been reached, the injunction of multiple objects is established.

However, when there is a convergence of multiple factors (kārakas) expressed by multiple words, because there is no mutual relationship between those factors, even though they are connected to their respective individual words, if an injunction (vidhi) applies to one, it does not thereby apply to the other; likewise, if it applies to the other, its application to the first is untenable precisely due to that lack of connection. And thus, unlike the case of *bhāvanā*, one [factor] cannot, by being enjoined, cause the other to be understood through implication (*arthāt*).

In that case, since there is no production of another injunction for a different purpose, the Vedic injunction (*śrauta-vidhi*), which is unitary in nature, being exhausted in one place, must—if it is assumed to exist elsewhere as well—be accepted as being established only through the repeated utterance of its name; thus, there follows the contingency of multiple human utterances.

This is what [the author] demonstrates: for when a ritual action has been enjoined and is already established, the suffix (the injunctive element) would have to be taught and uttered again and again for the sake of enjoining each respective accessory (*guṇa*), because its purpose is to serve those accessories. This is the meaning.

In that regard, for the purpose of establishing the connection with the eight potsherds (*aṣṭakapāla*), when the word *āgneya* is restated, it is not known what the deity is for that which pertains to the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*). Alternatively, if one were to simultaneously assume both a reference (*anuvāda*) and an injunction (*vidhi*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Following this very path, the endlessness of syntactical splits must be elaborated through the modes of verbal expression shown at the beginning of the *Kṛtya-adhikaraṇa*. Therefore, the connection between the material and the deity must necessarily be enjoined here; and since that [connection] is not possible within an action already previously established, there is a distinct action (*karmāntaratva*) according to the principle: "And because of the connection with something new (*apūrva-saṃyoga*). This is from the *Gubanna-vārtika*.

And if it were a separate action (*karmāntara*), then the non-mention of "form" (*rūpa*) would remain as it was, resulting in a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). Furthermore, one would necessarily have to resort to secondary indicators (*lakṣaṇā*) such as the singular number for the sake of the *baḍabaḍa* [or *bajādika*]. Moreover, this sentence is not completed by being connected with another action; nor does it require another sentence because it is complete in its own meaning.
And so it has been said:
"The designation is likewise [applicable] to some; if there is a desire for the New Moon sacrifice, then [it applies to] the Sānnāyya and the plants."

For when there is a distinction between the two rites, because their objects are distinct, the combination of the *mānna* and the *puroḍāśa* occurs; thus, the collective gathering (*saṃbharaṇa*) and the designation as "first" and "subsequent" are appropriate, but not otherwise. Furthermore, in the first case, since there is yet another [offering] following the fourth, the term "subsequent ones" (*uttarāṇi*) would apply, whereas in the Full Moon sacrifice, when there are three, and in the context of the New Moon sacrifice, when there are two, it is established that these are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) of the two groups.
And furthermore:
since the primary object is established by the power of the word,
the previously mentioned principle— that "one sacrifices the Upāṃśuyāja between [the two offerings]"— applies here as well.
Why, first of all, is the injunction in those [passages] not certain because of the suffix *tavya*?

In that case, if another sacrifice were to be postulated here, it would follow that there is an ignorance of the ritual form (*rūpa*) and the assumption of another unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, is the production of offspring understood as the fruit for each of these individually?
And the mention of the *upāṃśuyāja* is made by way of the fault of *jāmi* (monotony/redundancy).

Just as in the case of the *vaiśvānara* passage, where the offerings on twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*)—through the opening and concluding statements—attain syntactic unity with the eight-potsherd and other offerings and thus do not constitute separate injunctions; so too, in the opening of the injunction "This indeed is *jāmi*," the mention of a fault is understood to be for the purpose of praising that which is being enjoined, by means of removing that fault. This concludes the second quarter of the second chapter.

Since "jāmitā" (monotony) occurs when nothing is prescribed between the two *puroḍāśa* cakes, it is determined that the praise of "producing non-monotony" (*ajāmirakatva*) applies to whatever will be prescribed as connected with the intermediate time; thus, because the phrase "between [the two]" (*antareṇa*) is understood as being for the purpose of praise, and because the mention of the praise in the form of "non-monotony" is required by the context of the *iṣvādi* and other such sacrifices, its status as an injunction is disregarded as unnecessary, and it is accepted as having the purpose of praise.

Nor is there a connection with an intermediate time in the case of those [sacrifices] associated with Viṣṇu and others, such that the injunction for them or the defect of redundancy (*jāmitva*) inherent in them would be required as a basis for praise through the mention of the beginning of that [intermediate period]. Since, however, there is an explicit injunction in the passage beginning with the mention of "redundancy" regarding the intermediate time associated with Punarvasu, and since that is seen to serve as a basis for praising the others, it is not proper to accept an injunction that entails the assumption of multiple unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*).
For it is not said that one who praises deities becomes a sacrificer even by engaging in their worship.
And because it is an inherent material cause (*samavāyin*), the deity does not become the object of worship in the same manner as a guest;
furthermore, it will be stated in the ninth [book] that the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) has that [deity] as its primary referent.
Therefore, wherever there is an indication of the status of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*), this is what is meant: [the deity is the recipient].
"One should renounce the substance with that [deity] as the objective in order to bring about the ownership of another.
Even where there is an instruction regarding the ritual action (*karman*), the meaning there is this: "one should designate the deity for the substance already renounced.

And thus, in those cases involving the mere act of designation—lacking the element of renunciation—the injunction *yajeta* ("one should sacrifice") occurs; both of these [interpretations] are therefore figurative (*lākṣaṇika*).

In that case as well, although the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*)—because it is invariably concomitant with the constituent part of relinquishment (*tyāga*) and because it does not consist of the whole [action]—is also flawed, it is nonetheless more proximate to the nature of a deity (*devatātva*).

On the other hand, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is more remote from the nature of a deity, because it is subject to deviation, since the state of being pervaded (*vyāpyamānatva*) can occur even in other actions;
for it is not determined that everything is the object in relation to the sacrifice (*yajña*) in the same way that [everything] possesses the nature of a deity.
Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), divinity is denoted by the word "deity" (*devatā*) or by the suffix *-taddhita*, and not by any kāraka case-ending.
And so it is said:
"Pāṇini did not [intend] for the production of a *taddhita* suffix that [the deity] be [expressed] in such a way."

This [statement] "idam agnaye" (this for Agni) is declared by him as if it were already purchased; for the kind of *bhāvanā* (efficient force) which is primarily expressed by a verbal root (*ākhyāta*)—being a sequence of prior and posterior stages and directed toward something not to be taken up (*anupādeya*)—is not the same kind that is presented by statements such as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to" (*viṣṇur yaṣṭavyaḥ*). Thus, there is no collapse of the assumption of an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*). Considering that even though the others possess the status of injunctions regarding ritual acts (*karmavidhi*), they would constitute separate rituals and not a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the one under discussion, he says:
It might be argued that [the word] would be expressive of a different action;

however, since the deity is to be taken up as an object of attainment (*upādeya*), an injunction (*vidhi*) with respect to the action is possible, and thus the notion of it being a restatement (*anuvāda*) does not depart.

The intention is that if an injunction regarding the action is accepted, even though there is the existence of a subject matter under discussion (*prakṛta*), there is an absence of those forms belonging to the subject matter under discussion.

Alternatively, if this [sentence] enjoins a ritual action distinct from the Āgneya and others, then the word *upāṃśuyājaṃ yajati* would be the expressive term for that [action], and not for the others. Therefore, since its status as an injunction of a distinct ritual action is certain by virtue of the fact that the interval (*antarā*) is not something to be prescribed (*anupādeyatva*), the other words must necessarily be explanatory supplements (*arthavāda*). Furthermore, when the suffix prescribes the meaning of the verbal root elsewhere, it will function in close proximity [to that root].
However, since that [connection] with qualities such as *upāṃśutva* (whispering) is enjoined, he considers the word *upāṃśu* to be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).
As for the objection raised at the end—that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of non-expressiveness—it is said in reply: this is equal in your view as well.
Why?
Because the relationship between signifier and signified is first established between word and meaning;
only afterwards can there be the status of injunction and restatement, both resting upon that common basis.
Nor is this name tenable in its literal sense;
for animalhood has not been enjoined by any other scripture whatsoever.
It cannot first be enjoined by one associated with Viṣṇu and others, because that [passage] is merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).
Because the injunction regarding the *kāna* [low-voiced] quality, by the statement "not low-voiced on the *parṇamāsī*," precludes multiple injunctions;
therefore, it is enjoined precisely by its originative injunction. And thus the author of the Sūtras will state.
Regarding the phrase "due to the connection with qualities":

the removal of monotony (*jāmitva*) is understood in every respect—from the substance, the meter, and the deity—as in the case where a sacrifice is enjoined with the instruction "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to, or Prajāpati, or Agni-Soma. When a deity is necessarily required for such a rite, and there is a contingency of no fixed rule, certain deities such as Viṣṇu and others are established by their preeminence.

It has been mentioned for the purpose of demonstrating variety; although they are not to be sacrificed to in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), nevertheless, because the intent is praise, their inclusion is stated in some way by way of figurative description (*guṇavāda*). Since they are obtained through injunctions in other recensional branches (*śākhāntara*), they are not explicitly cited here. Having clearly stated this, [the author] will consider that nothing would be impossible to accomplish, and that in that context, as discussed in the tenth book, the mantra-textual nature (*māntravarṇikatva*) of the deity would be established by Jaimini in such passages as "Or Viṣṇu should be [the deity], because of being traditionally taught in the *Ṛgveda*," and so forth.
Even if it is argued that there is no attainment [of the quality], this very doubt has been shown by the author himself.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that because it is a property of the *upāṃśu* (whispered) recitation, it is attained [in all *prājāpatya* offerings], and therefore "whatever is *prājāpatya*"—that too is incorrect.

This is because of a reversal in the formulation of the statement; for the statement is not "that which is *upāṃśu* is *prājāpatya*," but rather "that which is *prājāpatya* is *upāṃśu*. Therefore, the *prājāpatya* offerings do not become [restricted] by virtue of being *upāṃśu*.

As for the injunction regarding Agni and Soma, [the phrase] "udbhidā yajeta" (one should sacrifice with the udbhid) is not an injunction because it consists of a nominal suffix (taddhita) and a mantra-text;
for if Agni and Soma were to say, "We two are here," then the sacrificers, understanding "What would happen to us?", would conclude, "We have not been directed toward a deity.

Furthermore, because its primary purpose is to enjoin time, a deity cannot be enjoined by this [phrase]; or, if it were intended to enjoin a deity, there would be an abandonment of the injunction of time.

Furthermore, it would not even be referred to by the term *pūrṇamāsa*; thus, because it is not grasped by the word *pūrṇamāsa*, if it lacks the status of a primary act (*pradhāna*), the consequence would be that it is merely a subsidiary (*aṅga*).

Moreover, the author of the *Bhāṣya*, while not desiring an *upāṃśuyāja* on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) in the tenth [book], presented this very point as being intended for the injunction of the *paurṇamāsī* offerings.

The resolution here is as follows: it is established that the deity is enjoined through the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*). For, in the sequence of the *upāṃśuyāja*, the pairs of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras dedicated to Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, and Agnīṣoma are recited.
And by those who imagine [the deity] to have multiple meanings and so forth, the deities are obtained only through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Furthermore, they say that this very *chattram* is another branch (*śākhāntara*), yet even in the *Adhvaryu* [Veda], there is indeed the recitation of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras in the form of *tvarūpa*; thus, the mention of "another branch" is intended for that purpose, or it is for the sake of highlighting its status as having the *upāṃśu* (whispered) quality.
For if another deity were introduced here, it would abandon its own duty of loudness (*uccais*) and incur the duty of another, namely *upāṃśutva* (whispering), which would be contradictory.

Because Viṣṇu and Prajāpati possess attributes closely associated with [the full moon], there is no contradiction; likewise, because it is impossible for Agni and Soma to be the deities of the injunction, the mention of Agni and Soma in the injunction regarding the time of the full moon is made as far as possible. Furthermore, from the statement "he offers near the heart" (*hṛdayam upaśuyājaḥ*), and because of the praise of the sacrifice-person (*yajñapuruṣa*) by means of its principal part, it is understood that the *Upāṃśuyāja* is a primary rite.
But how does the consequence of non-priority arise in the prima facie view?
It is said:

[In the phrase] "Let Agni and Soma [be the deities]," that single sacrifice which has Agni and Soma as its deity is enjoined with respect to the fruit by means of the mention of the *Paurṇamāsī* (Full Moon), being connected with a specific time.

In that case, because the Vaiṣṇava and Prājāpatya offerings lack specific qualities (guṇas), it would be impossible to state that the Upāṃśuyāja is the primary sacrifice. [Objection: But even for you, since the deities are optional, the Upāṃśuyāja is primary only when it has Agni-Soma as its deity; therefore, the proclamation of its primacy as if it were permanent (nityavat) is not tenable.
[Reply: This is not a fault.

For if the connection with the Full Moon sacrifice were made only with Agni and Soma, then it would not apply to the five [deities] including Viṣṇu and Prajāpati. This, however, is a connection of the sacrifice as characterized by its deities. And everywhere, even when the indicator (upalakṣaṇa) is absent, that which is indicated (upalakṣya) is still grasped; as he will say: "And there is no loss of the time, for the two cakes are merely indicators."

Furthermore, it is not logically tenable for a single action to be both primary at one time and subsidiary at another; such would be possible only if there were multiple actions, but that is not the case here. Thus, it is impossible.
Therefore, according to the *Tantravārtika*, the injunction "one performs the *upāṃśuyāja* in between" is itself the rule for establishing the unity of the ritual action;
the *agnihotra* is not [the model], because it lacks a specific form (*arūpatvāt*).
By such injunctions as "He pours the libation upwards" and "He offers oblations with rice-grains," these very *āghāra* pourings and *homa* offerings are prescribed and recur [in the ritual context].

For there is no subordination of the productive operations (*bhāvanā*) of sacrifice and offering due to the predominance of the material—as is the case in passages such as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a whisper.
Nor do these [sentences] form a single syntactical unit with others, nor is the Vedic revelation intended merely for praise.

Therefore, an injunction is exclusively concerned with an action possessing qualities; the nature of being an injunction is acquired through the optative suffix (*liṅ*), and it does not belong to a nominal stem.
If that injunction arises from the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), then the [action] itself must be enjoined first.
Furthermore, because it is connected with a specific designation, this should be understood as a general term; since it is already known, it is not a separate action.
Because that [substance] is not something to be known [as an object], its prescription elsewhere is appropriate;
the use of the accusative case in the expressions "the *āghāra*" and "the *agnihotra*" is fitting for an instrument (*kāraka*) governed by an action.
Furthermore, the self itself cannot be the object of the verbs *juhoti* (he offers) and *āghārayati* (he pours).

There is a contradiction in an action being directed toward itself; however, a collection (*samudāya*), when extracted and expressed by a word as having the nature of a distinct entity, can be designated as the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*). This is just as in the expression "he cooks the cooking of rice," where the specific instance is expressed as the object (*karman*) by means of the general term. [Objection: But since the collection is not distinct [from its parts], its status as an object of accomplishment cannot be established in any way. [Reply: This objection is incorrect, for the collection is established as an object of accomplishment because it consists of the accumulation of the actions of its constituent parts.

For if [the whole] were not distinct from all its parts taken together, there would be no such grasping [of it as a whole]; yet the nature of the whole is intended to be something different from the individual forms of the parts, and since the production of the nature of the whole does not occur without the individual forms, its status as the most excellent is established.

Now, one might object: "Since words such as these are determined to denote a collection (*samudāya*), the contradiction of an action occurring within the self of the members of that collection remains exactly as it was.
This is not a fault.
Even by means of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), which denotes the aggregate, the aggregate itself is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, just as its singularity is accepted, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) will be attributed to the aggregate.

Furthermore, for you, the states of being an action (*kriyātva*) and being an object (*karmatva*) cannot exist even through the distinction between the general and the particular, as in the case of "cooking" (*pāka*); for there is no employment of distinct words for the general and the particular.

And this [argument] should also be applied to the conclusion regarding the phrase "the full moon [sacrifice]" (*paurṇamāsīm*); therefore, just like that, it must be stated that these are restatements of the composite [acts], because the meaning of the word [in the injunction] pertains to the performance [of the act]. Consequently, due to their proximity, the repeated mention is for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), and thus there would be two injunctions of ritual acts (*karma-codanā*). The inclusion of the term "internal" (*antara*) is to be understood as in the section concerning the *upāṃśuyāja*.
Since the injunctive power is not already implied by other factors for the acts of *ācarati* and *juhoti*, it is understood that the very injunction of their performance is the meaning of the words.

Furthermore, there is no existence of the *āghāra* and *homa* acts as part of the archetype (*prakṛti*), because when the injunctive power is implied by the curd and other substances mentioned in the archetypal sentences, the cognition of them as mere references to existing rites (*karmānuvāda*) does not disappear.
Nor can the principle of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*) be established here, as it is precluded by the exception stating "if they have been enjoined by another" (*na ced anyena śiṣṭāḥ*).
He demonstrates this: for when this injunction of the relationship exists, perception cannot infer the [other] meanings; such is the meaning.
Alternatively, when this injunction of the relationship exists, only the relationship itself is resorted to by means of the other injunction of qualities.

Therefore, it is not possible for the *homā* and *āghāra* offerings to be inferred from the meaning by means of injunctions of relationship that are independent of this sentence, such that these two would be mere restatements (*anuvāda*).

If it is argued that [the injunction] is not connected with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) or the meaning of the verbal root because it is separated from them by the optative suffix and so forth, this is true; however, the injunctive character is not removed from the efficient force. Rather, the quality (*guṇa*) is brought into contact with it precisely through that [efficient force], since the quality is introduced into the midst of the efficient force by means of a case-ending denoting a factor of action (*kāraka-vibhakti*).

Therefore, this is what is taught: in every instance, after the prescription of a qualified [action] has occurred, when one investigates what is already established and what is not, the injunction is said to be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the efficient force and the meaning of the verbal root, because its application is restricted solely to that which is not already established.
However, there is never any manifestation of the meaning of the scripture in which a quality or a substance is enjoined by first restating [something already known].

In that regard, when the subsequent operation is being explained through a coarse method for the sake of comprehension by those of dull intellect, some—thinking that these very modes of expression were created by the author of the scripture itself—display various types of scriptural readings that possess a weakness toward others, thereby creating delusion even in others as if they were their own.

The first mode of verbal expression (*śrutiprakāra*) is the injunction of the root-meaning (*dhātvarthavidhāna*); the second is the injunction of the root-meaning along with its qualifiers (*saguṇa-dhātvarthavidhāna*); the third is the injunction of the root-meaning with reference to something else; the fourth is the injunction of a qualified entity in that very context; the fifth, however, is the injunction of another thing with reference to the root-meaning; the sixth is the connection between two things by means of the root-meaning; the seventh is the connection between two things by means of the suffix (*pratyaya*) as qualified by the root-meaning; and the eighth is the connection between two things alone, setting aside the root-meaning.
In this regard, first of all, the claim that "one performs the Agnihotra sacrifice" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*) is an injunction regarding the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is incorrect.
For an injunction does not descend upon the meaning of the verbal root while abandoning the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), nor does a person engage in anything other than the productive activity.
Indeed, the productive activity is the person's own operation, whereas the meaning of the verbal root sometimes even becomes dependent upon an object (*karman*).

Just as this very question relies on the two types of purification (*vyavadāna*), and since one person cannot perform the activity of another, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) must necessarily be enjoined as a qualification of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), just like curds and so forth.
And this was stated in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*: that the meaning of the verbal root is not enjoined as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

For if it were not of the nature of an instrument (*karaṇa*), it could not be enjoined toward a result even by means of a different sentence, because it would require something else to be accomplished.

In the case of "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*) as well, according to the method explained in the *tadbhūta* section (PMS 1.4.27–30), the meaning of the verbal root and the factors (*kārakas*), such as the *aruṇā* (red) quality and the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow), do not relate to one another directly; rather, they first connect with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), and only subsequently do they provide mutual assistance.
Thus, as will be stated in the seventh and ninth chapters, there is no injunction of a qualified verbal meaning.

Furthermore, since the sacrifice is the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the *bhāvanā*, it cannot simultaneously be the object (*karman*) with respect to the substance; therefore, the principle that "when there is a single word, [the subordinate] is for the sake of another" would apply, making this [position of yours] untenable.

Likewise, in the case of the statement "one sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), there is no connection between the act of sprinkling and the rice-grains other than through their connection with the meaning of the verb; therefore, the verbal root-meaning is not enjoined with respect to the rice-grains.
If, however, it is argued that the injunction elsewhere is made with reference to the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), that is indistinguishable in all cases.
Furthermore, this [injunction] does not possess any inherent weakness due to being a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*).
Placement in the third category is also untenable.

Furthermore, the refutation stated for both positions applies here as well to the case of "he cleanses the cup with the *daśāpavitra*"; thus, it is incorrect to enjoin a qualified verbal root-meaning elsewhere.
Even in the case of "he offers with curd," the meaning "he performs an offering that is not already enjoined" is never expressed by the word.

For the status of the oblation as a locus (adhikaraṇatva) is established neither by the word nor by actual fact in the Tantravārtika; nor is there an inherent "thing-to-be-done" (kartavyatā) in the curd, because it always exists as an instrument (karaṇa).

Moreover, this scriptural statement (*śruti*) is stronger than even the two-fold qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), because when a single injunction is possible, it is illogical for there to be multiple potencies; and because an injunction of a remote object (*viprakṛṣṭārtha-vidhi*), which arises in both cases, cannot be questioned. Furthermore, the adoption of this remote [meaning] is caused solely by the impossibility of the proximate one. In that case, if both were resorted to simultaneously, there would result the occurrence of both the possible and the impossible, which are mutually contradictory; yet this is accepted only as a last resort (*agatyā*). Since it does not involve an injunction of a qualified verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) elsewhere, nor is it excessively burdensome, it should not be placed in the fifth category.

Alternatively, it may be performed immediately after the injunction of that [other] because of the prescription of the meaning of the pure verbal root (*dhātu*), or because of its injunction elsewhere.

As for the claim that by the statement "he gives two mirrors to the Adhvaryu," the connection between the mirrors and the Adhvaryu is enjoined within the meaning of the verbal root *dadāti* (to give), that is incorrect.

This is because of the distinction in the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*); for in every case, having connected the thing being restated by means of the word *yat*, the thing to be enjoined expressed by the word *tat* is brought forward.

Therefore, if it were enjoined that "having passed over this day" establishes a connection between the *adhvaryu* and the *prākāśa*, then, because it would be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the entire act of giving, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of all the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) being modified.
Furthermore, when an injunction is already present, assuming multiple injunctive powers for a single suffix is unavoidable.

For a relationship being enjoined must first imply its relata; however, the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) must itself be enjoined as a relatum. Otherwise, the relatum would be subordinate to the relationship itself rather than to the action.

In that case, since a suffix colored by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) will necessarily enjoin [the connection] there—just as in the case of *viḍ* and *adhaḍha*—then the separate mention of the two subsequent scriptural texts would be useless, as they too would be included within this very same category. For a suffix uncolored by the meaning of the verbal root does not establish a relationship, as in the cases: "One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu" (*vāyavyaṃ śvetam ālabheta*) or "One desiring sensory power should offer curd" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya juhuyāt*).

Furthermore, the root *bhakṣ*, when uttered merely for the sake of its own form or as a characteristic of the base (*prakṛtiliṅga*), does nothing at all by coloring itself toward an injunction of the relationship between the substance and the deity.
Furthermore, this relationship cannot be accomplished by the verbal root (*dhātu*), because the substance and the deity have the sacrifice as their objective domain.

And if the root were to perform anything other than what is already established by the utterance of the suffix in forming the relationship— were it to do something else— it would be a second [agent] in that process.

Therefore, when the connection with curd and the sense-faculty (*indriya*) is being enjoined, why should the *homa* (oblation) be abandoned, or why should it be accepted as belonging to a different context?
Consequently, there is no injunction of a connection with something else regarding the meaning of the verbal root.
And as before, the status of the meaning of the verbal root as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and its nature as that which must be performed by the factors of action (*kāraka*) must be refuted.

Furthermore, it has been stated that even in the case of a relationship [between two factors], there can be no injunction if that relationship is not already connected with a productive operation (*bhāvanā*) prior to it.

Thus, first of all, there is no injunction regarding the relationship in the mere act of giving. Now, suppose it is argued that the giving qualified by the *adhvaryu* is being restated, or conversely, that the *adhvaryu* qualified by that [giving] is being restated—even so, because it would be a restatement of what is already established, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

In the restatement of the *śuddhādhvara* (pure sacrifice), although the literal meaning of the dative case (*saṃpradāna-śruti*) is set aside, nevertheless, because the relationship between the recipient and the gift is untenable without the act of giving (*dadāti*), an inference of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) occurs—just as [it does] from the relationship between the substance and the deity. Thus, the syntactical interpretation that "there is a connection with something else in the meaning of the verbal root" is not possible.

Furthermore, since the act of taking (*ādāna*) and the office of the *adhvaryu* are already established by the *codaka* (archetypal injunction), it is only the two *prākāśas* (mirrors/lamps) that must be enjoined;
and even though the injunction resides in the productive energy (*bhāvanā*), its purpose (*tādārthya*) is divided accordingly.
Furthermore, if this were a qualification, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*); no fruit for the restatement of the aggregate (*samudāyānuvāda*) is seen here.
However, it will attain unity of the injunction of performance (*prayogavacanaikatva*), as in the case of the Rājasūya.

The accomplishment of the apūrva [unseen potency] would result from the fires, as characterized by their status as substrates; however, because they are already encompassed by one [substrate], there is no possibility of another substrate. As for the claim that the evening and morning injunctions enjoin ritual actions because they possess multiple meanings—
To this we reply:
the time already established by other sentences such as "he offers in the evening" and "he offers in the morning" is merely restricted in the sentence concerned with the determination of the deities.
[Objection: Even so, because there is a reference (anuvāda) to a ritual act qualified by time, there would still be a syntactical split (vākyabheda).

No, because the deity is enjoined merely with respect to the time [already] obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*) regarding the ritual action. That time, however, does not connect with the deity in its own essential form; rather, it connects as colored by the ritual action inherent in the context. Alternatively, since the presentation of the relevant oblation (*homaparyupasthāpana*) is required by the deity who is being enjoined as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), there is no utility for the time [in that regard].
And a *homa* being indicated by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) does not split the sentence.

Nor is it the case that the evening time, being located elsewhere, indicates [the *homa*]; rather, by means of that [time], Agni and Prajāpati will belong to the evening *homa*, and similarly, Sūrya and Prajāpati will belong to the morning [homa]. Thus it is established.
But even so, would not the sentences be split by enjoining two deities each expressed by distinct words?
To this some reply: "No, because they possess a single kāraka (grammatical factor)."

For when there is a difference in the *kārakas*, there is a difference in the operation of the injunction (*vidhi*); however, it has been stated that even a thousand objects based on a single *kāraka* can be accomplished by a single effort. To this, it is replied: for the *kāraka* is signified by the case-ending (*vibhakti*).
And where there is a single [deity], such as Agni-Soma, the operation of the suffix occurs only once.

However, where even a single *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is expressed by multiple words connected with different case-endings—as in "to Agni and to Prajāpati"—since there is no simultaneous presentation there, Agni and Prajāpati must necessarily be denoted separately by the suffix. Now, what is called a "case-ending of a *kāraka*" is employed for the purpose of apprehending the word-meaning; and since it does not employ itself for meanings that are not uttered together, the consequence is that it would have to be repeated.
Therefore, this is not a valid solution; thus it is stated:
in both of these sentences, Prajāpati alone is enjoined.
As for Agni and Sūrya, however, their attainment occurs through the wording of the mantra itself, while the mantra having them as its deities is enjoined by another sentence.
The performance of the optional rite, complete with all its constituent parts, should be carried out by one seeking a result;
it may be performed either in the evening or in the morning as an alternative.

For in the context of the animal and Soma sacrifices, the injunction regarding the connection with specific materials would otherwise be purposeless; for that connection with materials is not intended merely for the sake of a subordinate quality.
The animal (*paśu*) is mentioned first because it is more difficult to establish [its application].
Here, two words are intended as the restatement of an accompaniment: the word "animal" and the sacrifice (*yajati*), which is inferred from its connection with Agni-Soma.
For such is this sentence—composed of both directly heard and inferred parts—that one should sacrifice with an animal dedicated to Agni-Soma (*agnīṣomīya*).

Just as the sentences concerning the Āgneya and other offerings do not terminate in their own literal meaning prior to the inference of the sacrifice, so too should it be understood in the case of the Soma sacrifice; moreover, this applies here to your view regarding the sentences concerning the Aindravāyava and other cups.
In my view, however, the distinction is that [the injunction applies] to those [subsidiaries] alone.
Furthermore,
it has been stated in the section on the Agnihotra that when a single quality is heard in relation to the primary act, the injunctive power transfers [to the subsidiaries].
Therefore, the cognition that [the sentence] is a restatement (anuvāda) of an action does not depart; thus, the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) functions as a restatement.
In that context, the word *soma* serves to restrict the substance—already implied by the general term *gṛhṇāti* (he takes)—which is the object of the injunction.

Alternatively, since the Soma juice has already been established by the subsidiary sentences within the context, such as "He buys Soma," "He presses Soma," and "He purifies Soma," the injunctions regarding *gṛhṇāti* proceed with reference to that juice; therefore, Soma itself is not being enjoined here.

Consequently, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the sacrifice— which is characterized by having an inherent instrumentality— the term becomes a name (*nāmadheya*) according to the principle "and another scriptural passage [establishes] that which is already known" (*tatprakhyaṃ cānyaśāstram*).
But is there not indeed another name, namely *jyotiṣṭoma*, [found] in the second quarter of the second chapter?
If even this is understood, what is there that is contradicted for us?
And thus, we maintain that the dual number [of the name] arises in the ritual practices of the sacrificers.
However, the sole purpose of restating the entire sentence is indeed the production of the singular number pertaining to the performance-injunction (*prayoga-vākya*).

Therefore, it is a restatement (anuvāda). It might be argued that here [in the case of the *paśu* sacrifice], because of the connection between the substance and the deity, there is indeed [a sacrifice]. But how can there be an injunction of a sacrifice by means of the act of "cutting off" (*avadyati*)—which, like the statement "one should immolate the calf," is connected merely to substances such as the heart and so forth and is devoid of a deity?
