Or how can there be a restatement of the heart and other parts by means of the mention of the "animal" (*paśu*)? This must be explained.
It is said:
when the heart and other organs are required as the primary substance and a goat is obtained from the wording of the mantra, the quality of "animal-ness" (paśutva) inherent therein is first restated;
once the deity has been enjoined there, let the sacrifice itself be enjoined.

Alternatively, by the very same principle stated in the rule "or it is the *sāṃnāyya*, because it originates from that," this act of cutting (*avadyati*)—being of the same form as the *sāṃnāyya*—is the archetype for the act of cutting; and it is well known to be for the purpose of consecrating the sacrificial materials of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-yāga*).
In that case, if the heart and other organs are the sacrificial materials, then they partake in that connection [with the archetype], and not otherwise.

Therefore, just as in the case of the pressing of fermented liquids (*pūtika*), where the connection with the sacrifice is understood—even though it is not explicitly stated—because the capacity to intoxicate would otherwise be inexplicable; and just as when one considers [the word] *anaḥ*, having inferred the act of carrying, the sacrifice is also understood because that [carrying] would otherwise be inexplicable; so too, the aggregate of those [grains] which have not been compared and which reside in each individual substance is restated.
Furthermore, this acceptance of an inferred sacrifice is common even to you; thus, this does not cause any embarrassment.

If the *somayāga* were one single sacrifice, then since the deities such as Indra and Varuṇa would be optional alternatives (*vikalpa*), the observation of both sequential order (*krama*) and simultaneous performance (*samuccaya*) would be untenable.

In my view, however, because the deities and the sacrifices— which have unseen results (*adṛṣṭārtha*)— pertain to distinct sacrifices, it will be consistent that they are enjoined toward a single result by a single word simultaneously.

Even in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the observation of sequence—namely, "first he cuts from the heart, then from the tongue"—and the observation of conjunction—namely, "there are indeed eleven portions of the animal"—have not been cited [as a reason for the unity of the act].
This is because even if there were a single act, those [portions] would be justified as being the means for accomplishing the entire animal sacrifice.
For if the heart and other parts were not conjoined, the sacrifice could not be accomplished by the "entire animal" as heard in the injunctive sentence.

The principle is that whatever portion is removed from there by an internal exclusion, the sacrifice must be performed with everything except for that specific portion. However, in the case of the Soma sacrifice, this is not so, because it arises from a single, comprehensive injunction; thus, the example is cited.
Therefore, when it is argued that these two are merely restatements (anuvāda) of the aggregate, the following is stated in reply:
If there were a recognition of the entire form as in the case of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*), then it could be considered a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Or, if the intention were that it is a restatement of the mere act of sacrifice (*yajati*), then it would be determined to be a restatement that has abandoned its specific qualifications.
However, in this case, the sacrifices under discussion are those having substances such as the heart (*hṛdaya*) and others, as well as those having no substance (*aramadravyaka*).

Moreover, these two [sacrifices] have the animal and Soma as their respective materials; since this is the case, there is no recognition [of the original sacrifice], and thus it is impossible for [the text] to be a mere restatement (anuvāda).

To this, one might object: "In the case of modifications, because of figurative treatment (upacāra) according to the model of the archetype, the words 'animal' and 'Soma' are applied precisely to the heart and other parts, and to the juice.
That is not so.
Because there is no reason to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
For a word undergoes a secondary or figurative function (*jaghanyavṛtti*) only when there is a clear coreferentiality with another word and when no other possibility exists;
however, neither of these two conditions is present here.
For it is possible to enjoin another sacrifice having as its substance the primary animal and soma; however,
these two words would not be appropriate if they were not included within those [sacrifices] belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Therefore, even though the sacrifices are enjoined by the verbal roots *avadyati* ("cuts off") and *gṛhṇāti* ("takes"), there still follows the undesirable consequence of these being distinct rituals.
Why? Because in those very same sacrifices which require their own respective materials as their source, the animal (*paśu*) and the soma-juice (*soma*) are not prescribed;
for it is the juice (*rasa*) that is designated as "for Indra and Vāyu" (*aindravāyava*).

First of all, since the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) is subordinate to the injunction regarding the deity, it cannot possibly be enjoined in a sentence that does not establish its origin; thus, it is not even brought forward for discussion.
Furthermore, the *soma* creeper, though enjoined by a sentence, is not connected [to the rite] when there is a conflict with the directly stated (*śruta*) juice.

But how can the juice be considered directly stated (*śrauta*) when no specific substance has been mentioned in the injunctions for Indra-Vāyu and the others? For that [juice] is obtained through the context (*adhikāra*).
And consequently, the attainment of the word would belong to that which is more closely related to it.
It is said in reply:
the connection with the substance is established by the words themselves through the deity-indicating suffixes (*devatātaddhita*).

Just as, when the connection with a deity has been established for this very specific object denoted by the word—which is obtained through direct audition (śruti) along with syntactical connection (vākya), context (prakaraṇa), and so forth—then, upon the inquiry "What is that specific substance?", its acquisition occurs through syntactical connection, context, and the rest; however, the connection with the deity does not occur through those alone.
Furthermore, from that, a distinction [of the ritual] would also result from the accessory (guṇa).
But this [objection] can be avoided: just as the eight-step path is established through syntactical connection even though it is already known from the Śruti,
so too Soma will be enjoined.

For example, even when the eight-potherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) is prescribed by the Vedic injunction "the cake for Agni is [to be] eight-potherd," the subsequent prescriptions of rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*) are not contradictory; this is because they constitute the material substance required for the cake. For one who takes rice does not fail to make the eight-potherd cake.
And because of that, there is no separate action here.

Since the juice is not abandoned when the *soma* is being taken up therein, there is no contradiction; thus, as the quality is possible within the very same previous [action], it cannot be a differentiator.
In that regard, just as for you the juice constitutes the essential nature (*prakṛti*) of the rite, so too will it be in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Moreover, an even greater contradiction would arise for you:

since rasa cannot be produced without its constituent essence (prakṛti), how could its connection with that essence— which is required— remain uncontradicted even when it is established by means of another sentence?

Since it is by the inherent power of the original material (*prakṛti*) itself that the occurrence of a modification (*vikāra*) is not required, it is improper for other sentences to effect that which contradicts the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*). Therefore, because the sentence concerning rice and barley is sealed by this principle, its status as an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) must be rejected merely as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the whole; for even by that much alone, the purpose regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) is accomplished. However, in the case of Soma, there is a further suspicion of its being equivalent to the sentence concerning rice; to refute this, the subsequent Sūtra must be introduced.
Alternatively, let there be a determination of the previous birth by means of the subsequent [sūtra] alone;

or, having adopted the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of the preceding sūtra, the subsequent sūtra—with the word "but" (*tu*) occupying the place of the word "however"—should be applied to the counter-argument (*uttarapakṣa*).
But how, then, is the prima facie position expressed by this phrase, "due to connection with substances" (*dravyasaṃyogāt*)?
This is explained as follows:

[In the injunctions] "He cuts off from the front of the heart" and "He draws the cup for Indra and Vāyu," are these scriptural statements intended for the purpose of preparation (*guṇārtha*), like the case of curd and so forth? And consequently, do the two subsequent [injunctions] serve the purpose of original prescriptive rules (*utpatticodanā*)?

Or rather, these are indeed injunctions of action (*karmacodanā*). What is the prima facie view? These are not repetitions for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇārtha*) as in the previous case; they are original injunctions (*utpatticodanā*). This is from the second quarter of the second chapter.
What then? They are original injunctions.

How [can there be] an injunction for the animal and the soma-sacrifice through the connection with substances—that is, through the connection with substances such as the heart—by means of those very sentences? What is the reason? For otherwise, the connection with the heart and other parts would, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), result in their being understood as sacrifices; yet that is not possible for them in the sense of being subordinate (*guṇa*) to another, because it would contradict the animal and the creeper-juice (*soma-latā*) already enjoined in the originative injunction (*utpatti-vākya*). Alternatively, according to the principle stated previously, since the animal and soma-sacrifices are established from elsewhere, the connection with substances in this context would be purposeless in your view.
For me, however, the word "Soma" is a proper name, and the sentence concerning the Agni-Soma sacrifice is for the purpose of enjoining a deity; thus, nothing is purposeless.
Therefore, the injunction for the origin of the sacrifice must be that which is connected with the acts of cutting (*avadyati*) and taking (*gṛhṇāti*).

At the very moment one begins to postulate a sacrifice because it cannot otherwise be accounted for, the directly perceived root *yaj* (to sacrifice), being present and unrestricted, stands ready to establish all the connections between substances and deities, thereby blocking any authority for postulating a separate sacrifice.
And since that [sacrifice] is not yet established, of what could there be a restatement of the aggregate?
Regarding what was said—that as in the case of the *āgneya* and others, there is no dependence on another sentence when the sacrifice (*yajña*) has not been conceptualized—we reply:

in the statement "the *āgneya* cake on eight potsherds comes into being," no human activity other than the sacrifice is perceived; therefore, prior to the inference of that [sacrifice], the sentence is incomplete.
In this case, however, in the injunction "one takes the draught for Indra and Vāyu," the person is enjoined toward the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) of taking;

therein, even prior to the inference of a sacrifice (*yajati*), there exists an object for the injunction, and thus the sentence is completed. But this is another matter: that something further is required beyond that.
For every sentence, having reached its conclusion in its own primary meaning, does not require another meaning; nor, by that much, does it remain incomplete.
One must consider the relative strength and weakness [of the means] with respect to a substance that is absolutely distinct [from the action].
The heart and other internal organs constitute the auxiliary status (*aṅgatva*) for the animal and the Soma sacrifice respectively.
For the animal and the Soma, being enjoined as the means of accomplishing the sacrifice, require a procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

In that regard, the requirement for "how" (*kathaṃbhāva*) is fulfilled by way of the production of the juice, the heart, and so forth; therefore, because they are auxiliary factors, there is no contradiction in postulating them [as the objects of the injunction] in the second quarter of the second chapter.

As for the argument that the connection with a substance is purposeless because it is already established by the contextual sentences concerning purchase and so forth, the answer to that is precisely: "And the preparatory rites are not enjoiners [of the substance]. For those [sentences] are not enjoiners of the Soma or the animal; rather, they are merely the preparatories for those two. Therefore, when it follows that the sacrifice may be accomplished by employing a substance enjoined [by the archetype] in any way whatsoever, it is ordained that it must be accomplished specifically by that which has been acquired through purchase and prepared by such rites as pressing.

Furthermore, the wording of the mantra lacks the capacity to bring about the procurement of a goat in an absolute sense; rather, it serves merely to remove doubt regarding that which is enjoined as a sacrificial animal (*paśu*). Nor does the act of cutting (*avadyati*) necessarily imply a sacrifice (*yāga*), for it is established both in common worldly usage and in the Veda that such cutting occurs even without a sacrifice, as a mere act of slicing. However, the connection between the substance and the deity cannot be established in any way without a sacrifice; thus, there is a disparity in the nature of the inference.

Nor can there be an extension of the properties [of the Sānnāyya] from the model sacrifice (prakṛti) on account of the act of cutting (avadyati), because that [act] is already included by the purpose [it serves], and thus its properties would also be obtained [by implication].
Furthermore, this [act of cutting] does not have the status of being the sacrificial substance or the procedure (itikartavyatā) such that it could be extended [to other sacrifices].
Nor does the inference based on general observation (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa) apply to such a matter.

However, in the case of the *pūtika* pressing and the fruit-cup consumption, there is a recognition of identity through both syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*); thus, they are not equal.
Even in the Soma-sentence, since a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) involves a directly perceived [element], an inferred one is impossible; therefore, it is unequal.

Furthermore, even if the sentences concerning the Aindravāyava cups and others were merely statements of accessory qualities (*guṇavākya*), as in the case of the sentences regarding the eight-potherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth, there would be no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

For how could an injunction be relied upon that prescribes the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of grasping [the soma] as qualified by Indra, Vāyu, and so forth? Alternatively, since the act of grasping is already established by the sense of the context, it is not contradictory to enjoin merely the single deity mentioned within the compound.

Furthermore, since the connection with the principal rite takes precedence over the context (*prakaraṇa*), there is no fault even if these are statements of subordinate qualities (*guṇavākya*). (Tantravārtika) Therefore, because these are purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*) that require a sacrifice from elsewhere, their injunction by another sacrifice is not contradictory.
And this being the case, the singular number in "by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma" remains primary;
nor will the word *soma* undergo the trouble of assuming a secondary sense that is otherwise purposeless;
nor will one have recourse to a useless restatement of the entire sentence, which would resemble the prima facie view regarding the Āghāra and Agnihotra offerings.
By this, it is established that there is an injunction regarding the animal and the soma.

Now, a question arises: should the portion be cut from the whole, or from each limb, or from a single one, or rather from the enumerated parts such as the heart and so forth? Regarding the soma, however, the refutation of the objection is now stated.
Where a relationship is determined by a sentence to be independent,
there a conjunction (samuccaya) is not possible because they function toward the same purpose.

If it were heard that "one should sacrifice with the Aindravāyava" or "one should accomplish the sacrifice for Indra and Vāyu," then, being understood as having the same purpose through sentences that are mutually independent, they would be subject to option (vikalpa).
These [passages], moreover, being heard in connection with the taking up [of the cups],
come to establish a connection with the sacrifice by virtue of the context (prakaraṇa) in the second quarter of the second chapter.

Furthermore, the function of the context (*prakaraṇa*) is not synonymous with an alternative (*paryāya*), such that [the deities] would be connected independently of one another. For when all [the offerings] are grasped simultaneously as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the deities belonging to them—failing to find completion through those [offerings] alone and being required by the sacrifice through the context—are connected simultaneously. In that case, an option (*vikalpa*) is indeed appropriate where things are employed for the same purpose independently of one another.
What is the reason?

It is because here the capacity of the [cups] dedicated to Indra-Vāyu and others to individually accomplish the Jyotiṣṭoma is not understood, due to the absence of any such injunctive application (viniyojaka).

Even if there were a capacity to accomplish a sacrifice individually, the accomplishment of that specific Jyotiṣṭoma would be understood according to the scriptural statement; thus, they do not have an equal purpose individually.

Furthermore, the *śrī*, *dyava*, and so forth, each having an identical purpose, are subject to option (*vikalpa*), for they are connected to the sentence and are enjoined by their respective individual sentences independently of one another.
Now, it might be argued that the sentence "He takes the cup for Indra and Vāyu" (*aindravāyavaṃ gṛhṇāti*) is itself perceived as the enjoining authority;
therefore, the capacity of the injunction regarding the deity in the phrase "for Mitra and Varuṇa" (*maitrāvaruṇam*) is understood to be independent of what precedes it.
If, in the case of an *uccana* (elevating), it is heard that [the action] was previously connected to the primary rite within the preparatory ritual (*saṃskāra*),
then that [action] serves a visible purpose; for without it, the [primary rite] would not be accomplished.

For if the deities, already connected with the sacrifice through the primary [text], were mentioned again in the acts of drawing [the cups]— as they are in the acts of pouring out, invoking, and so forth—
or if the drawing itself could not be accomplished without them,
then that mention there would be considered to have a visible purpose, serving as a reminder of what has not yet been brought to mind.
However, Indra, Vāyu, and the others are not heard of for the first time in the Jyotiṣṭoma;
nor is their inclusion established by the absence of [any other] means, as stated in the Tantravārtika.

Why is this so? Because these acts of taking up [the substances] possess deities and consist of the commencement of a sacrifice; they cannot effect the consecration of a substance for the sake of a deity without a sacrifice. Thus, there will be an expectation: "What sacrifice is there that will bring about the connection of these substances with the deities? This concludes the second quarter of the second chapter.

Furthermore, a sacrifice whose deity has not been omitted, being unable to disregard the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), cannot—due to the absence of any operation by the context (*prakaraṇa*) toward such a thing which is non-active in nature—be an allocator even with respect to the cups (*graha*).

And since those [cups] are enjoined simultaneously and are connected to distinct unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*), they are performed together; by virtue of that, the combination (*samuccaya*) of the deities is also established, according to the *Tantravārtika*.
When a substance is being taken up, there is an injunction for its dedication to a deity;
and it is not possible to perform that dedication while omitting a single deity. Furthermore:

Since the substance intended to be given to Indra and Vāyu has already been virtually manifested [as belonging to them], how could the sacrificer, having no longer mastery over it, say, "Let this be for Mitra and Varuṇa"?
Therefore, a separate drawing of the cup (graha-bheda) must necessarily be performed for each deity.
Furthermore:
For sacrifice (*yāga*) consists essentially in the relinquishment of one's own ownership for the sake of a deity.

And it can be accomplished by means of *soma* even while it is in the state of being purified, or at a time subsequent to its purchase, or even when it is divested of all its intermediate states; thus, the prescription of all the subsequent refinements (*saṃskāra*) serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

However, where a substance such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is enjoined, there every prescription of threshing and so forth is for the sake of producing that substance, and therefore it possesses a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).

Furthermore, there is no original injunction stating that one must sacrifice with Soma residing in the *graha* and *camasa* vessels, because the injunction regarding the plant itself concludes with the mere substance [of Soma]. Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing the distinct unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*) pertaining to each, the acts of drawing [the Soma] must be combined. Moreover, since that [Soma], when pressed with a fixed quantity of water, cannot be contained within the small and divided *graha* and *camasa* vessels without a distinction between the acts of drawing, it is drawn separately.

Furthermore, the sacrifice must be accomplished by one who is in such a state; yet, being unpracticed, he would be unable to bring all the requirements to completion while remaining in that state. Therefore, it is practiced for the sake of the purpose, and for that reason there is also a scriptural rule (sūtra) in this regard.

Since that [practice] consists of distinct repetitions, the repetition of the sacrificial act—such as the various Soma offerings—is accepted because of the distinctness of the substances employed; otherwise, if the entirety were not abandoned [through repetition], it would be purposeless.

Therefore, even though [the substance] is mentioned only once at the time of its origin, there is a difference in performance because one observes that it possesses the status of being a substance and a quality whose state is established by another sentence.

That substance must necessarily be given exactly as it was taken; otherwise, if it were combined again [with others], there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the previously performed distinction in taking it becoming useless.
Furthermore, the deities would not be connected with their respective portions as they were originally intended.

Furthermore, at the time of relinquishment, it is not possible to form all the mental intentions (saṃkalpa) such that those who fear the labor [of the rite] would mix all the substances together once and give them with reference to all [the deities] at once; for in that case, a confusion of portions (bhāga-saṃkara) would inevitably result.
And once a plurality of portions has been determined, the occurrence of such confusion must necessarily be avoided except by means of a scriptural injunction (vacana).
Therefore, since the offering is made according to what was intended, this [distinction] is established when there is a conjunction of all the deities.

The Adhvaryu priest draws these ten cups at the morning pressing; the Āśvina cup is drawn as the tenth, and it is said that he offers it third. By this, the fact that they constitute a single ritual action (*ekakarmatva*) is established.
According to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), in modifications of the Soma sacrifice (*somavikāra*), there should be a single performance of the ritual details (*dharma*) for only one cup.
However, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the performance must be exactly like that of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Is this a case where the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) has been performed first for those ending in a *taddhita* suffix,
or is it that the *taddhita* connection occurs later for those whose *ekaśeṣa* has not yet been made?

If the *taddhita* is formed by referring to them with a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) after the *ekaśeṣa* has been made— on the grounds that Prajāpati is their deity— then [the compound would be *prājāpatya*].

Therefore, since there is only one connection between seventeen substances and a single deity, there is a single action. However, if one were to utter "prājāpatyaḥ" (belonging to Prajāpati) seventeen times—thinking "this belongs to Prajāpati as its deity, and this belongs to Prajāpati as its deity"—and then apply the rule of *sarūpa-ekaśeṣa* (retention of one form for identical words), resulting in "prājāpatyāḥ," then seventeen distinct connections between substance and deity would be presented. Consequently, because sacrifices are inferred from each individual connection, there would be a difference in the actions.
What, then, is the prima facie conclusion?
Regarding the term *ekakarma* (single action): why?

Because when one forms a *ekaśeṣa* compound as "the Prājāpatya [offering] and the Prājāpatya [offering]," that person thereby accepts that it applies to both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). And the reason for this is the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the plural number.

Furthermore, no plural form is observed for that nominal stem (prātipadika) by which an *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) could be made for it; nor is it impossible to demonstrate the meaning of the suffix without such an *ekaśeṣa*,
because [the meaning] is expressed by a pronoun at the time of analysis (*vigraha*).
Therefore, Prajāpati is connected with many substances precisely because he is heard [in the text] only once.
Furthermore,

even if one were to apply the *ekaśeṣa* (the grammatical retention of a single term) by means of that very extended [compound], one is not thereby released from the necessity of postulating unseen and unheard-of actions and new transcendental potencies (*apūrva*), and it has been stated in the section on "Different Words" (*śabdāntarādhikaraṇa*) that such things cannot be postulated at will.

Since the connection with the deity cannot be established for the enjoined substance without that [apūrva] alone, it is possible to postulate through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) only that much which is unseen, and nothing else.
Therefore, nothing additional is obtained.
For one must necessarily postulate seventeen rites and seventeen apūrvas in a sequence beginning with one.

In this regard, by the very first conceptualization, since the performance is based on the principle of a single procedure (*tantra*) and because no distinction is perceived, all the substances become associated with the sacrifice; thus, it is not possible to arrive at a different conclusion later.

Furthermore, if there were a difference in actions due to a difference in substances, then there would have to be a difference [in the sacrifice] due to the difference between the heart and other parts, or even due to the difference between the two portions (*dvyavadāna*).
Furthermore, it cannot be so, for [the author] will indeed say: "because of the distinction [of the word], because of the word 'form' (rūpa), and because of the division.

And when the entire animal is enjoined as the means of accomplishing the sacrifice in the archetype, and it would thus follow that it must be offered in its entirety, it is understood—by virtue of another scriptural statement—that the sacrifice is to be accomplished by means of the animal through the eleven portions beginning with the heart.
Therefore, this is a property of the animal, not of the sacrifice.

Even though it is understood that seventeen [animals] serve as the means for the sacrifice, all the ritual details (dharmas) are obtained for each one by extension (atideśa); thus, even a single sacrifice, by taking up seventeen sets of portions (avadāna-gaṇa) through extension, is not frustrated.
Therefore, when the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is reached that "it is a single rite," it is replied:

this sentence does not conclude merely with "the animals dedicated to Prajāpati" (prājāpatyān paśūn); rather, there is a further supplementary portion of the sentence: "as in the archetype" (prakṛtivat).
And since there is a single action here, the archetype (prakṛti) must be applied;
and because there was only one set of portions for the sacrifice,
even in this case [of the modified sacrifice], only one such [set] would be obtained, and that too, having been accomplished as it was, must be performed in exactly that same way.

Furthermore, if one were to perform the sacrifice with this very animal alone, other animals would not be connected with Prajāpati; consequently, both the plurality expressed by its own word and the number seventeen obtained from the sentence would fail to be implemented.

However, when the understanding is formed that there are seventeen sacrifices, then by means of the extended applications (codakas) which terminate with each individual act, exactly that many sets of portions (avadāna-gaṇas) are obtained. To accomplish that, even unmentioned seventeen animals are brought in through textual supplementation (āgama); how much more so, then, for those that are explicitly mentioned?
But surely, it is not proper to abandon the oneness of the sacrifice established by perception and, in accordance with the inferential *codaka* (extended application), assume its multiplicity;
for the determination of oneness or multiplicity occurs at the time of the instruction regarding the sacrifice,
whereas the extended application (*atideśa*) does not depend upon that [instruction].
It has been previously established that when there is doubt, a definitive conclusion is reached through the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*).
Here, such a conclusion is reached through functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), which is the cause for this determination.

For it is expected [by the agent]: "How should one effect [the result] by means of the animal sacrifice to Prajāpati? and not "How [should one act] with the animal?", because the substance, by virtue of being what is being relinquished, serves as a mode of cognition.
Furthermore, even in the archetype (prakṛti), the property of the sacrifice is that it must be accomplished by a group of eleven cuttings produced from a single animal;

it does not belong to the animal itself, because the animal lacks a fruit [of its own]. For, according to the view that the property belongs to the animal, the animal would be consecrated by the cuttings. (This concludes the second quarter of the second chapter.)
And there is no purpose served by that [sacrifice] once it has perished;

rather, the purpose is served by the sacrifice when it has been accomplished, either through its own inherent connection or through the *apūrva* (unseen potency). Therefore, all of this is accepted as being a mode of its accomplishment. Consequently, a single sacrifice is not capable of producing multiple groups [of results].
And if that [single animal] were not grasped, there would be no grasping of the multiple animals.

Even if one might think that because the singularity of the source-substance (*avadāna-prakṛti*) is sublated by the number seventeen, therefore a single group produced from various animals should be grasped, nevertheless, only eleven animals would be employed, not seventeen.

However, one does not sacrifice with seventeen groups of cuttings even in a single sacrifice; rather, fearing the postulation of multiple unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*), it is thought that the word "animal" (*paśu*)—by virtue of its proximity to the sacrifice—indicates the group of cuttings, and the number seventeen will be prescribed for the purpose of delimiting that group. This is not so, because there is no reason for such an indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*).
For when there is no contradiction, figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is not appropriate; therefore, one falls into this dilemma:
seventeen animals are to be prepared, yet by means of a single set of cuttings (avadānagaṇa) derived from one animal, a single sacrifice is to be accomplished.
And this cannot be performed in any way whatsoever.
Furthermore, when a number heard in one context is applied elsewhere, it is best to assume it applies specifically to the *vara* sacrifices, which are more closely connected to the *apūrva*.
Moreover, it has been stated that as long as no contradiction arises, nothing at all should be set aside by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer).
And by the force of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*), even the postulation of multiple unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*) is faultless.
The mention of the horns and so forth is for the purpose of conveying the meaning of the entire sentence.
This is what is meant:
among those animals which are divided into seventeen species according to their color and other characteristics, one belonging to Prajāpati must be sacrificed; regarding this, he says:
For they are heard of as being distinct from the *śyāmā* [sacrifices]; therefore, there are seventeen sacrifices.

Although this practical purpose (*prayojana*) is not intended by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*), nevertheless, since only one [sacrifice] is the means for accomplishing the *sāṅgrahaṇī* sacrifice while the others are employed merely to fulfill that number, [the result] must be extracted from a single one.
If that one is destroyed, then the others would have to be repeated.
Alternatively, when the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) have been partially performed, there is a repetition of all of them precisely where that which was lost occurred.

Now, one might argue that just as in the case of seventeen sacrifices being performed together, if one is destroyed, then by the principle "in a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), however many [sacrifices] are interrupted," while the others are being observed, that very same [sacrifice] is repeated; so too it should be in the case of the collective nature of the substance (*dravyasāhitya*).

This is not so. For instance, the status of being a means to the sacrifice (*yāgasādhanatva*) inheres in the number seventeen as a single entity and is distributed [over all]; therefore, it is precisely such [an entity] that must be attended to by the rites of dedication (*upākaraṇa*) and so forth.

In that case, since the destruction of the means has occurred precisely through the loss of that very substance, all the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*)—even though the substances remain—have fallen away from their basis; therefore, they must be performed once again from the very beginning. Likewise, for one for whom these rites are being performed with newly brought materials, those rites are also heard as having the substances as their basis.
And since there can be no status as a "means" (*sādhana*) for this [new material] without its being seventeen-fold, the others must necessarily be required for the accomplishment of that number.

In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, since those [mantras] possess the capacity for being means of accomplishment independently of one another, only their simultaneous employment is performed; thus, the repetition of that [mantra] alone is logically justified.

[Objection: If this is so, then according to the logic of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), in the case of the *stotras* and *śastras*, as well as in instances such as "he takes [the cup] with four [mantras]," a repetition of the entire set would result upon the failure of even a single mantra.

[Reply: No, because in those cases, while each [mantra] possesses the status of a means of accomplishment individually, a combination (*samuccaya*) is resorted to by virtue of a specific scriptural injunction.
For when those mantras perform their respective functions—such as the recitation of hymns (*stotra*) and so forth—they possess the capacity to fulfill each individual requirement.

Otherwise, there would be only a single mantra. Furthermore, a distinct further effect is initiated through the combination of the individual functions of the mantras; thus, the efficacy (*sādhakatva*) does not reside in the mantras collectively as a whole.
As for animals, it has been stated that they possess two fathoms (vyāma) of limbs.
In that case, since mantra-activities function through collective effort, would there not be a repetition of the entire rite upon the destruction of even one?
This is not so; for there is no destruction of the effect apart from the destruction of the means of accomplishment.
The distinction is this: since human activity pertains only to the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), the performance [of the rite] must conform to their destruction;
thus, when the word "action" (*karman*) has not been explicitly stated, whatever designation is first applied cannot be removed by any means through the cognition of it as a different entity.

A sacrifice that is interrupted by the river Saṃjñāna does not proceed to the former [location], nor does the former [sacrifice] go to it; thus, having moved to another object due to the absence of connection,
the word "siñcat" (sprinkler) is observed in some cases to be used figuratively, as in the case of a young boy (*māṇava*).
Even when it is resorted to in the *Nājambha*, that meaning is not accepted;

for in the case of a connection with a new transcendental result (*apūrva*), the two sentences are equal in status, as stated in the *Tantravārtika*. Furthermore, there is parity between the two sentences regarding the subordinate quality (*guṇa*).
Henceforth, prior to the division of the sections, there will follow an investigation into difference and non-difference based on secondary qualities (guṇa).

In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, at the Vaiśvadeva parvan, after enjoining a sacrifice inferred from the connection between the material and the deity through the statement "vaiśvadevyāmikṣā," it is further stated: "vājibhyo vājinam" (the whey for the Vājins).
Regarding this, there is a doubt.

Is this an injunction of accessory details (*guṇavidhi*) regarding that very same ritual action, or is a distinct sacrifice (*yāgāntara*) postulated by means of this conjunction of substance and deity?
In that regard, the position that both the substance and the deity are enjoined in the preceding [text] is possible, yet it has not been set forth;
for the injunction of multiple accessories in a ritual action already established by another means of knowledge was refuted in the *Paurṇamāsī* section.

Therefore, does the *vājina* (the whey) relate only to that same deity in the preceding ritual action, or does it relate to a different deity and a different sacrifice, thereby constituting a new transcendental result (*apūrva*)? What is the prima facie view? That the *vājina* is merely an accessory (*guṇa*) prescribed for the preceding [action]. Why? Because [the term] *vājinaḥ* [is derived from] *vāja*, meaning food, which was taught immediately [beforehand].
The Viśvedevas are recognized [as the deity], and that action here is the *vājina* (the whey);
because it is restricted by another quality (*guṇa*), and because it is impossible [to perform] that same previous action [with that quality],
the quality, for the sake of its own connection, should produce the cognition of a different action.

The connection with the deity is intended there either by the word ending in a nominal suffix, by the fourfold meditative state (*caturdhyā*), or by the wording of the mantra; and among these, each subsequent means is weaker than the preceding one.
Furthermore, the connection with the deity is understood through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) rather than through the nominal suffix.

However, in the case of the word ending in the dative case (caturthyanta), the connection with the deity is understood through direct scriptural statement (śruti) itself in the phrase "vaiśvadevī," due to the proximity of the two words;
whereas in the other instance, "vājibhyo vājinam," it is understood only from the proximity of the two words.

If it is argued that even here the connection between the substance and the deity is understood solely through the proximity of the word "āmikṣā," then the status of being cognizable by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*) would be the same.

On the other hand, if the status of being a deity is established by the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) "vaiśvadevī" (belonging to the Viśvedevas), while the connection with the substance is established by syntactical connection, then this is no different in the present case as well.
When the status of being a deity has been expressed by the fourth case-ending (*caturthī*), the syntactical connection (*vākya*) merely effects the association with a substance.

Now, if it is argued that once the mere relationship with a substance has been established by the word ending in a taddhita suffix, the specific detail will arise from the proximity of the word *āmikṣā*,
that too is no different in the other case as well.

By stating the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) with the single word "to the Vājins" (*vājibhyaḥ*), since that [recipient] would be untenable without something to be given (*saṃpradeya*) and so forth, there arises an implication of a general category; then, through the proximity of the word *vājina*, only a specific instance is understood.
Furthermore, let it be granted that the derivative suffix (*taddhita*) expresses a mere connection with a substance (*dravyamātra*);
yet, that mere substance is not distinct even in the case of *vājina*, and thus there is no contradiction.
As for the specific distinction regarding the contradiction between the *svāmikṣā* and the *vājina*,
there is no distinction because the sentence connects with both of them equally;
therefore, an option (*vikalpa*) indeed follows.
Regarding that, it is said:
"The Viśvedevas are its deity. Here, the pronoun does not denote a mere generality of substance;
rather, it denotes the specific entity present [in the context], for only that is capable of being designated, not an unqualified substance-in-general.
Therefore, the meaning taken up individually constitutes the second quarter (pāda) of the second chapter.
By means of the *taddhita* suffix itself, through direct denotation (*śruti*), the deity of a specific substance cognizable by other means of knowledge is expressed.

Consequently, when a cognition of a specific substance qualified by a deity—whose relationship is already internalized—is produced by a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix that is independent of any other word, and when there arises an inquiry as to "what is this specific substance whose deity has been stated by the *taddhita*? it is brought forward by the demonstrative pronoun "this" (*ayam*).
In this regard, first of all, when the relationship has already been expressed prior to the specific cognition (*viśiṣṭapratyaya*), it is not something being indicated (*lakṣyamāṇa*).

Alternatively, even if the relationship is understood in the interval between the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), which function solely with their own respective meanings due to their contiguity, nevertheless, because it resides within a single word and is understood through the proximity of two words, it is called "expressed by the word" (*śrauta*). Of those relationships, one is the relationship between the substance and the deity, and the other is the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).
In this regard, the distinction is that the former [type of compound] is based on the *śruti* (direct audition), while the latter is characterized by the sentence (*vākya*).

Here, as in the case of "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*) and the like, there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified between the words *vaiśvadevī* and *āmikṣā* mediated by their meaning; rather, in this instance, a single unified meaning is not expressed by the word ending in the *taddhita* suffix.

In the word *āmikṣā*, there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified between the two [words *āmikṣā* and *vaiśvadevī*] such that the latter would qualify the former; for that which is denoted by the *taddhita*-suffix is perceived first. Rather, while the *taddhita*-suffixed form itself awaits the completion of its expressive function, the adjacent word (*upapada*) merely provides it with its specific object.
Therefore, by virtue of the proximity of the word *āmikṣā*, it is the word *vaiśvadevī* itself that denotes that [curd-mixture].

Nor, however, is this [word] now a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of the compound, because without it, the referent of that which ends in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) would not be understood.
Nor is it the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), because the meaning of the word ending in that secondary derivative suffix is not established independently. For indeed...

The meaning of a sentence is understood by grasping its constituent word-meanings as independent entities; therefore, because it merely brings forward what has already been denoted, no remoteness of meaning is created by a word mixed with a *taddhita* suffix. Thus it is said in the *Tantravārtika*: "By the primary word itself (*śruti*), the meaning of the secondary member (*upapada*) is expressed through the pronoun."
For that purpose, by means of that very secondary derivative (*taddhita*), there is thus a single denotation for the three [elements].

However, in the case of the word "vājibhyaḥ," neither the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), nor the case-ending (*vibhakti*), nor both together, denote any one of the following: the general substance, the particular, or the relation between them.
What then? It has been stated that it denotes merely this much: that the meaning of the nominal stem is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).

In that case, a connection with a substance is not in any way included within the word; therefore, it must necessarily be conveyed by the sentence itself through its proximity to the word *vājina*. Furthermore, just as here the meaning of this word is also traditionally held to be included within the *taddhita* suffix.
The dative case is not prescribed for this [word *vājibhyaḥ*] in such a way;
rather, the status of being directly stated (*śrautatva*) consists in the perception of the connection with *āmikṣā* in every respect due to its proximity (*sannikarṣa*).
And in the case of the connection with *vājina*, there is the status of being derived from syntactical context (*vākyīyatva*) because of the remoteness (*viprakarṣa*), as follows:

Even if the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix does not express the divinity of a specific substance, it nevertheless expresses that of the general category; however, this is the distinction: the general category is not expressed by the dative case-ending.
As for the claim that the general category is not contradicted even in the case of *vājina*, that is incorrect.
For in the word *vaiśvadevī*, the feminine suffix, occurring within the same compound, determines that some feminine substance has been gathered together.
Furthermore, since the horse has neither the state of being the recipient (*khītva*) nor proximity (*sannidhi*), it cannot be the substratum [of the offering].
Moreover,
there is no syntactic connection in the statement "one should prepare the *vājina* for the *vājins*."

In that case, one would necessarily have to assume the supplying of the word "giving" (dāna) [to complete the sense]; furthermore, we do not perceive grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) here, nor do we perceive the genitive case ending.

Moreover, the instrumental case ending in "vājibhyaḥ," which denotes a factor of action (*kāraka*), cannot be connected with anything other than a verbal root, and no such verbal root has been mentioned here.
In that case, there is one remoteness due to the conceptualization of a substrate (*adhyāhāra*),
and another due to the complexity of connecting three words.
If it is argued that there is no difference because the verbal root *yaji* (to sacrifice) is also conceptualized in the other instance, [we reply:]...

No, because that [connection] is to be inferred at a later time after the connection has been established; for it is only when the connection in "The *āmikṣā* belongs to Viśvedevas" has been established that the sacrifice (*yajati*) is inferred, and the cognition of the connection is not dependent upon that [sacrifice]. In your view, however, since the transfer of ownership to another is impossible, the root *dadāti* (to give) must exist for the sake of connecting with a future object, and from the very beginning, for the sake of establishing the syntactic unity of the substance and the deity—this is the distinction.
Once *dadāti* is postulated, there is no mutual connection between the two factors [substance and deity] through it; therefore, the connection is first established by that [root *dadāti*].
Therefore, because they share a single purpose, there is a mutual restriction; this constitutes remoteness (*viprakṛṣṭatā*).
However, in the case of the *āmikṣā*, there is no such thing [as a separate purpose], which constitutes proximity (*sannikarṣa*).
Furthermore, even though there is a direct connection between the horse (*vājin*) and the whey (*vājina*), there is remoteness due to their being in different grammatical cases (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).
In the case of "vaiśvadevyāmikṣā," there is proximity due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
And so it will be stated: "For those [words] with identical case-endings are more powerful, while those with different case-endings are weak.
Furthermore:

The dative case ending (*caturthī*) would merely express the state of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) for the *vājina* offering; however, when the deity is indicated as the secondary referent (*lakṣyamāṇā*), the *vājina* is again [understood as] a supplement (*pūraṇa*).
(From the second quarter of the second chapter).

While it might initially occur to one that the word *vājibhyaḥ* [is a dative] due to the similarity of its form, as long as the status of being a fifth case (ablative) is set aside and its status as a fourth case (dative) is established, there is a distraction of the mind.

But is this not the same [difficulty], since even in the case of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), there is an equal uncertainty regarding various meanings such as "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth?
This comparison is unequal.
I have presented a doubt regarding the word (*śabda*), while you have presented a doubt regarding the meaning (*artha*).
In any case, its status as a *taddhita* suffix is beyond doubt.

Furthermore, the meaning is determined to consist of a deity through the principle of semantic fitness (*yogyatva*) and the impossibility of any other [interpretation]; however, for you, even when the word has been determined, because there are multiple meanings, there remains a remoteness [from the conclusion] due to the doubt concerning the specific gender and number of the accompanying term (*upapada*).
There is no doubt regarding the meaning because both [options] are equal; nor is one alone challenged on that account. However, a doubt concerning the word is raised because it is common to both.

Furthermore, just as that which is taught at the time of origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*) is stronger, and it is impossible to extract the mere action and enjoin another quality, so it has been stated in the *Citrā-adhikaraṇa* and the *Vaiśvadeva-adhikaraṇa*.
And by the principle of the Vaiśvadeva section, the context must be expected for the other sentence concerning the *vājina* offering;
why?
Because the connection between the substance and the deity requires only a sacrifice in general.
It is indeed the *āmikṣā* sacrifice [that is intended], because there is no context for it there;

for by the well-known meaning of the constituent parts (*avayava-prasiddhi*), the Viśvedevas are indicated by the term *vājina*. And since that [indication] occurs by combining the meanings of the parts and postulating a connection, it is weaker than the "well-known meaning of the whole" (*samudāya-prasiddhi*) which is obtained through the immediate presentation of the direct Vedic word (*śruti*). Thus, the connection of the *vājina* is even more weak.
Alternatively, the word *vājin* may naturally mean "horse" (*aśva*).
It applies to the Viśvedevas even without [the performance of] a ritual action;

for all [the gods], beginning with Agni, are understood to be *vājins* (possessors of food) by means of sacrificial offerings such as the *puroḍāśa*. In that regard, there is one difficulty: the word "food" (*anna*) is applied to the clarified butter (*ājya*) alone, and not to the *puroḍāśa* and other offerings.
Furthermore, if there were a grasping of the *āmikṣā* alone, then by that very *āmikṣā* dedicated to the Viśvedevas, those things possessing it would be grasped; this is another [view].

Consequently, the scriptural statement (*śruti*), which by its own natural force applies elsewhere as well, must be restricted to a specific [meaning] by the context (*prakaraṇa*) alone, and there is no reason for it to do so there, because the deity is mentioned only as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*).

Furthermore, if it were something to be modified (*saṃskārya*), its mention would have to occur through some kind of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being a means to the *apūrva*, as in the case of "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*) and so forth;
however, that is not the case here.
For even without such a connection, the action is established as having a purpose.

Granted, the preparation (*saṃskāra*) might indeed be an act of disposal (*pratipatti*) for the horse itself, but not for the deity. Furthermore, if one were to accept the context of the original rite (*prakṛta*), there would be no definite determination because Agni and the others are also present.
Alternatively, they are included [in the term "Viśvedevas"] so that all [deities] may be comprehended within them.
This is incorrect, because there is no authoritative evidence for such a comprehensive inclusion.
If it is argued that the term "all" is understood through the hearing of the plural number, [we reply: no.

It is not so, because its purpose is fulfilled by those three alone. If it is argued that there is a cognition of restriction (avadhāraṇa-jñāna) regarding the three, we say no; for the cause of restriction exists in the primary sense, as in the injunction of the *apūrva* (the unprecedented).
Therefore, there is no authority whatsoever for the inclusion of the Viśvedevas.

Furthermore, a deity that possesses expectancy would be connected with a substance; however, in this case, since the word *vājī* (steed) conveys the deity as being already associated with a substance, it is understood as having no further expectancy and thus cannot admit of a connection with another substance. Therefore, there is an inequality [between the two cases]. Moreover: "For where a quality is enjoined in a place not already occupied by another..."
In that case, the injunction of an accessory is possible, and thus the action is not split;
for the sacrifice is established as pure by its own sentence as the subject under discussion,
and it is understood here precisely through its distinction by means of the two-fold injunction.
Those [qualities and so forth] depend upon their origination, and that [origination] is immediate;
however, for qualities and the rest, there would be no mutual connection because of the intervention [of the substance].
(From the second quarter of the second chapter)

Just as that action is qualified by curd through one sentence, so too is it [qualified] by rice and other materials; thus, it would not be of a single nature. Here, in the tenth position, curd is the qualifier of that *bhūmā* sacrifice.
Furthermore, for one who desires sense-pleasures, that [result] is not determined by that [action] either;
for when a substance is not recognized as being the same, it cannot be the cause for a difference in the action.
Therefore, it is that very same action which is enjoined with respect to the fruit, increased merely by the addition of an accessory.
This is not so.
Why?
Because the injunction of multiple purposes for an action that has already been established was previously refuted.

Furthermore, there would result the injunction of many relationships beyond your [view]; even here, where the word denotes an action and no quality is present, the action itself is enjoined repeatedly.
For a fruit is indeed heard in connection with this, and that is logically consistent with the action.

No supreme similarity is observed between agriculture and the fire-oblation (*homa*). As for the observation of some slight similarity, that exists even in the case of material substances; thus, there is no certainty [in such a comparison].

If something is seen to be the cause of a thing in a proven instance (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), and if it is understood to be the cause of that same thing in the subject (*pakṣa*) under discussion, then that [cause] becomes the means of establishing it.

From this statement, it follows that the relationship of the signified (*gamya*) and the signifier (*gamaka*) exists only between cause and effect; some consider this to be the intention of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*),
but that is incorrect.

It should be understood that even for things that are not related as cause and effect—such as the seasons and so forth—the relationship between the signifier (*gamaka*) and the signified (*gamya*) is well-established on the basis of their impermanence.
Furthermore, even between cause and effect, the cause does not function as a signifier in the same way as the effect does, because the cause is subject to many instances of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Therefore, it should be seen that only the logical mark (*liṅga*), when observed as being pervaded (*vyāpya*) in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and apprehended through the possibility of signifying the pervader (*vyāpaka*) which exists elsewhere as the probandum (*sādhya*), is called an "agent" (*kāraka*).
And thus it has been explained in the section on the reason (*hetu*).
He clarifies it accordingly:
"Therefore, even similarity (*sādṛśya*) must be examined as to whether it is a means of proof or not."

If, then, this effect is stated by means of a cause that has been examined and asserted—namely, that in the sentence "for one desiring sense organs," that which is the ritual action possesses a fruit because it is a ritual action, like a plow and so forth;

and that this fruit is achieved through the ritual action because it is a fruit, like rice and so forth—then [the opponent] renders this inference inconclusive by stating a counter-probans (*pratisādhana*): "whatever is a ritual action, that does not possess a fruit."
When an action has ceased, another substance such as a cloth is observed to arise from substances like threads and their conjunctions;
the inclusion of the term "ceased" is for the purpose of demonstrating the distinction from action.
For otherwise, one might occasionally claim here as well that the result is caused solely by action.
Therefore, he says:
in the statement regarding the desire for sensory power (*indriyakāma*), curd possesses the result [of the sacrifice] because it is a substance, like thread;
or rather, the sensory power is produced by the substance because it is a result, like a cloth and so forth.
Moreover, he asserts that the reason "because agriculture is not seen [to yield results immediately]" is contradictory (*viruddhatva*).

For just as this reason establishes that action possesses a fruit or that a fruit is produced by action, it likewise establishes that the fruit is visible, that the fruit is accessible through verbal testimony, or that the fruit is any one of [the crops] such as rice and so forth.
Therefore, regarding such a relationship between cause and effect, because all the faults of the reason would apply, this [reasoning] does not hold.
In some places, the *Tantravārtika* states that even for one who has not seen [the result] elsewhere, its accomplishment is established.
If this inference has been refuted by you yourself, how then can it be said that "the fruit is rightly obtained from the *homa*"?
Alternatively, the question ends precisely with the particle *iti*.

The answer is stated as follows: "This result is to be understood through the word [itself]"; this reply is given by introducing the section concerning the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*).

Therefore, it is logical that the fruit [arises] from the *bīja* (seed), whereas it is illogical that the fruit arises from the *dadhi* (curd); this is established by implication. That which is stated here is for the purpose of refuting the claim that they are equal in terms of their capacity as causes (*vīryavat-tva*).
At some point, even this [claim regarding curd] might become logical.
Moreover, curd is incapable of performing both functions.
First of all, there can be no status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) for curd that is independent of the ritual action (*karman*),
by which it would be connected solely with the fruit.
Therefore, it must be prescribed in both cases, yet that is not possible.

[The objection] "like the washing of a woolen blanket" (*kambala-nirṇejana-vat*) is intended either to refer to a connection with a secondary action (*prāsaṅgika-karma-sambandha*) or to refute the inherent incapacity of the thing itself.
For it is thus:
From the opponent's statement, "curd is incapable of both," it appears that the incapacity of the substance itself is being asserted according to the literal meaning.

We do not say that it is illogical for one thing to serve two purposes; nor do we deny the inherent capacity of the substance. Rather, even though the substance is capable, because its performance is not observed [to be so], it must necessarily be enjoined as having the dual purpose of curd and ghee.
And this is not the case, because establishing multiple relationships would entail the fallacy of sentence-splitting (*vākya-bheda*).
When a remote object is enjoined due to the impossibility of a proximate one, here—

where the relationship between curd and the oblation is proximate and the relationship between curd and the fruit is remote— if both were enjoined simultaneously, one would have to accept both possibility and impossibility at once.

Therefore, since one of the two must be abandoned, by virtue of proximity, both [the material and the action] are connected with the *homa*, and that [action] is also connected with the result; thus, when the action is joined with the result, the distinctness of the ritual act (*karmāntaratva*) is established.

As for the mention of a result in an injunction that is enveloped by a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), that [result], being touched by the injunction pertaining to that [quality], enters into syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with it.
Question:

But the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) [objects that] it is untenable for [the word *juhuyāt*] to be an injunction regarding the meaning of the suffix and a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the meaning of the verbal root; for since the suffix must necessarily be uttered immediately after the verbal root, one would perceive it as being separated [from the root] and thus say, "one should sacrifice with the word *juhuyāt*."

But surely, since the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) connects this [meat] with the oblation (*homa*), when any substrate (*dhātu*) might otherwise be adopted, it is stated in the *abhāvanā* that the oblation obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*) is to be adopted.
True; by the logic of the section on the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*), because the direct statement is more powerful, that which was not previously established will be restated.
And just as it has been established elsewhere that the purpose of a case-ending is not merely its denotation, so it is here.

Moreover, those who here rely upon your position would be even more severely contradicted by the fact that [the verbal root] is uttered as a necessary concomitant for the purpose of conveying merely the grammatical factor (*kāraka*) in cases such as *śrūyate* and *mriyate*.

For how can a verbal root, when uttered even for the sake of favoring [another element], convey its own meaning— which is not intended to be expressed— merely because of its connection [with that other element]?
For it cannot be said that its sole purpose is merely the communication of meaning.

Indeed, even when [the root] is being uttered, since it is possible to enjoin a small number of meanings for a verbal root by means of the favor of the suffix (*pratyaya*), the injunctive [suffix] disregards the injunction of a greater number of meanings.

And because the *homa* (oblation) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the production of the result, when it is enjoined in the sense "one should effect the sense-faculty by means of the *homa*," it communicates its own meaning.

Furthermore, since this [sacrifice], being established as the object of dispute, stands on equal footing with curd as an instrument—just as it does with the agent who grasps—it is impossible for there to be any connection [between them] that lacks an instrumental cause.

Therefore, since the intended meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do) alone is unattainable, one must necessarily accept a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), namely, "by means of an oblation possessing curd. This is what is capable of resolving the dispute.
This is not a fault;
for even though there is a connection with the oblation (*homa*), there is no evidence whatsoever for that [connection] in the word *karoti*.
Nor is the purpose accomplished merely by the fact that the meaning of the word *dadhi* does not depart when it is absent [from the context].

As for the distinction made regarding the connection with the oblation (*homa*) which allows for the status of being a name of the action based on the occasioning cause (*pravṛttinimitta*), that distinction falls away from both sides; it does not contradict anything at all.
Or else, by another way of looking at it, the word *dadhi* would result in being entirely meaningless with respect to the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).
And consequently, it would qualify [the word] according to the properties of the sound (*śabda*).
But if this were the case, the same fault would persist.

By grasping the property-bearer (*dharmin*)—the sound itself—without abandoning it, or rather, by abandoning it, the substratum is sublated; thus, the direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*) would be even more thoroughly sublated.
It is held that even pride becomes a form of forceful compulsion.
However, according to the position of the Siddhāntin regarding the co-occurrence with qualities, there is no fault whatsoever for anyone.
To this, it is said:
Jaimini says:

Since the word "one should offer" (*juhuyāt*) is practiced in other sentences, this word [in the present context] is set aside by the word "he offers" (*juhoti*). To avoid that objection, he says: "This delusion of yours—that the act of offering (*homa*) itself is the instrument—is necessarily to be abandoned.
However, in a precise sense, it should be stated as "one should offer" (*juhuyāt*).
How so?

Just as one who pursues the object to be accomplished (sādhya) due to proximity is displaced because of its unfitness [to be the means], so here, by following the word "curd" (dadhi), the absence of a means [is indicated]. And just as there, the connection between the curd and the sense organ is understood through the efficient force (bhāvanā) and the suffix;

for the suffix must necessarily be uttered to enjoin an efficient force qualified by the curd and the sense organ. And since it cannot function in isolation, it is accepted that a verbal root distinct from the suffix is required.

Furthermore, its connection with the *dadhi* (curd) will be established from the context itself; it will be stated that even though the number is not intended [to be significant], it conveys its own substrate. Likewise, in this case, the means of proof (*pramāṇa*)—which resides in another portion as a qualification of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*)—will similarly reside here as the substrate for the accessory (*guṇa*).
As the author of the *Vṛtti* has said:
"The accessory, residing in the oblation (*homa*), will accomplish the fruit."
Furthermore, what indeed is this so-called relationship between the support and the supported? Is it distinct from the "what," the "by what," and the "how," or is it non-distinct?
On this point, some say:
"This [relationship] is indeed distinct."
How so?
Just as elsewhere cultivation (bhāvanā) is understood to depend upon three factors, so too in the case of the remainder of the Guru, some say that a fourth factor is also required.
The claim that the *agnihotra* itself is the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is incorrect,
because the procedure is distinct from the instrument (*karaṇa*).

And because the sacrifice, according to the reasoning already stated, is not distinct from its instrumental factors, it is said that the procedure for the Agnihotra consists precisely of the bringing forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) and so forth. Why is this so?
Because of the misconception as to how there can be a connection with the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for something that is not the meaning of a verbal root (*adhātvartha*).
Regarding the phrase "of the curd which is the means to the fruit":
just as the oblation, by virtue of being the instrument (*karaṇa*), is assisted by the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), so too is the curd for that very same reason.
This is because of the proximity of this procedure.
Because it would result in the acceptance of an equal injunction for that which is contradicted by the context and the locus, and because of the mark of the injunction (*codanāliṅga*),
there is a lack of connection due to the introduction of the principle of extension (*atideśanyāya*).
If, first of all, it were connected by virtue of proximity (*saṃnidhāna*), what would be the use of the existence of the mark of the injunction?

Furthermore, since the existence of the indicative mark of the injunction (*codanā-liṅga*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that is no different even for something situated at a distance, the verbal expression regarding "proximity" (*sannidhāna*) is useless.

Therefore, it should be stated as follows: because the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is proximate through the sequence of providing assistance by means of the *homa* (oblation) presented by its substratum, and because the meaning of the root *juhoti*—which serves as the indicative mark of the injunction—is observed;

and because this meaning of *juhoti* is obtained from the context (*prakaraṇa*) as an indicative mark of the injunction and is thus restated (*anūdyate*), the suffix (*pratyaya*) is not injunctive with respect to either its origination (*utpatti*) or its result (*phala*).

If it is asked, "By what [means] is this a restatement (*anuvāda*) of something already established?"—to this he says: "And there is no other originative statement (*utpattivākya*) that enjoins the *bhū* sacrifice.
Some, however, describe the meaning of this statement differently.

Nor is it the case that there is no fruit such as heaven for the Agnihotra oblation other than its dominant fruit (*adhiphala*) from the sense-faculties (*indriya*), because it is obtained through its own scriptural statement (*svavākya*). Since this is not even suspected [to be the case], the introduction of an irrelevant topic makes it incoherent; therefore, what was stated previously is indeed superior.
Therefore, it is not a separate action; rather, within that very same action, the curd is the means to the result and the oblation (*homa*) is its auxiliary.

Alternatively, for the reason stated in the *Tantravārtika*—namely, because the word "curd" is read without error and because the result cannot be accomplished by curd alone—the result arises from the connection itself upon setting aside both [the individual substances], and thus both the curd and the oblation are for the sake of that [result].

In this case, however, according to the reasoning previously stated, because there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) between this sentence and the one that establishes the connection with the curd-offering (*dadhi-homa*), the contextual connection with the offering does not exist prior to the establishment of the connection with the result. Thus, if one were to assume an injunction toward the result after first establishing the connection with the offering by means of this very sentence, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) due to the injunction of multiple matters. Therefore, the interpretation that "the result belongs to the curd itself" is the only appropriate one. And so it has been concluded at the end of the section: "Therefore, the result arises from the curd as it is being connected with the offering."
Therefore, the phrase "or whatever" should be understood as intended to demonstrate mere conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*).
Others, however, say:
this single position, supported by reasoning, is concluded here having been introduced from the very beginning.
Therefore, the reading is "ta smāinaḥ phannam" (from that, this is the fruit), and "ato dadhiśabdasya vivakṣitatvāt" (because the word *dadhi* is intended to be expressed) is also a reading;
however, the phrase "atha vā" (or else) has been written down through error.
But this [objection] can be avoided.
How?

At the very moment that [the sentence] "one should effect [the result] for one desiring sense-power by means of curd" (*dadhnā indriyakāmasya bhāvayet*) is connected, it is understood that the curd is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the result; and because such instrumentality would otherwise be impossible, a connection with some action in general is understood. Furthermore, since the relationship between an action and its factors (*kāraka*) consists precisely in their capacity (*śakti*), and because the meaning of the suffix is predominant as it is contained within the instrumental case-ending, it is the relationship itself—subordinated to the meaning of the nominal stem—that is enjoined for the sake of the result.

When that [injunction] is established, as before, a specific action—namely, the oblation—is obtained from the context (*prakaraṇa*). In that case, however, once the relationship between the action and its factors has occurred through the relationship between the substance and the deity according to the established rule, there arises the expectation, "What is this specific action? In order to establish the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified, the oblation is brought forward by the context.
Therefore, it is said: "The connection of the curd with the oblation is enjoined for the sake of the fruit."
Then, the second quarter (pāda) of the second chapter begins with "tataśca" or "atha vā";
this is indeed the correct reading.
However, the concluding summary should be understood as belonging to the first position (pakṣa).
Alternatively, there is no fault because the mention of the term *saṃbadhyamāna* (being connected) serves as an indication of its connection with the subordinate element (*upasarjana*). Furthermore,
the objection that the sentence would be split due to the dual operation of the two words *nandadhna* and *indriyakāmasya* is not a valid fault.
Why?
Because a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) does not necessarily follow from multiple connections;
for a split occurs due to multiple injunctive powers (*vidhiśakti*), and such [a power] does not exist here for us.
For it is thus:

since the injunction is occupied with the connection between the Revatī verses and the Vāravantīya chant, the fruit is heard [as the result] here as well; therefore, the sacrifice is not enjoined [again].

As for the objection that there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) characterized by the repetition of the suffix—due to the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) of the connection between the *revatī* verses and the *vāravantīya* chant, and the subsequent injunction of that connection with respect to the fruit—that too should not be suspected; for the Veda itself has already provided that fruit. Once the connection is established by the phrase "having performed the *vāravantīya* on the *revatī* verses," only the connection with the fruit remains to be made by the optative suffix following the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).
Therefore, there will be no fault of repetition (*anāvṛtti*).

In that case as well, because of the mention of the substratum (*ādhāra*), the *r̥c* verses of the Revatīs are enjoined for the sake of another; or rather, due to their predominance, the *vāravantīya* chant is enjoined with respect to the fruit.

By virtue of the inclusion of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), the injunctive force is diverted from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) to enjoin the subordinate quality for the sake of the fruit; thus, it enjoins that which has not been known elsewhere as a subsidiary (*śeṣatva*).

Furthermore, because of the mention of the seventh case (*saptamī*) and because they are subordinate to the *vāravantīya* chant, the *revatī* verses do not connect with a fruit without depending on some other purpose. However, the *vāravantīya*, characterized by those [verses], is understood through the mention of the second case (*dvitīyā*) to possess primacy; being perceived as standing in the place of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) toward the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the verb *karoti*, it attains the status of having a fruit because it requires a purpose.
Or rather, even by setting aside both [the verses and the chant], it must be stated that the fruit arises simply from their connection.
