This being the case, the sacrifice (*yajati*) undergoes a transformation; the word *etat* (this) refers back to the subject matter under discussion. Consequently, the genitive case following that which is in grammatical apposition with the sacrifice expresses—by virtue of the context—the relationship between the substratum and the superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) with the result-bearing quality (*guṇa*). Furthermore, because there is no evidence for any other connection, the particle *eva* (only/just) functions to exclude such [other] relations. And the *vāravantīya* chant, as qualified by its connection to the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*, is obtained through another previously uttered statement. (End of the second quarter of the second chapter.)

Since it is like [the injunction] "one should sacrifice with the *āmikṣā*," and because it is already established as being part of every other ritual action (*karmāntara*), its mention as something already established will not give rise to a new cognition [of an independent rite].
However, in the view that it is a separate ritual action, everything would have to be enjoined because nothing has been previously established;
yet that is not possible.
Why?
Because that which possesses a single capacity by its very nature is always a prescriber of only one thing;
it is satisfied by the prescription of a minor matter and is incapable of prescribing multiple matters.
When one perceives qualities, primordial materiality (prakṛti), and action as being the substratum,
no distinction is perceived therein because of the persistence of their mutual relationship;
for it is thus.
The sacrifice does not require anything additional beyond the deity, the material, and the agent; it is established by the mantra itself that "the sacrifice is the means. And so it has been said:
The Sāman exists by its very fitness as something that serves as the means for a Stotra;
yet, since no Stotra is present in the context, no substratum is perceived.
The Sāman prescribed for the sake of a result is independent in form alone.
The Vedic study itself requires only its own production; it does not require the state of being accomplished through a single effort as a qualification for another action.
Therefore, having enjoined the action, a further injunction must be made regarding that [study].
Having performed the meaning of the word *kṛtvā* (having done), the subsequent *bhāvanā* (efficient force) takes hold [of it].
That too will take hold of the qualification that has come within its own sphere of operation.

Having established the connection between the *revatī* verses and the *vāravantīya* chant, and remaining in expectation of the subsequent *bhāvanā*, the meaning of the word *kṛtvā*—qualified by its own qualification—is grasped by the sacrifice (*kratu*).

And for this reason, the qualification of the sacrifice itself belongs to the *agniṣṭoma* [sacrifice]. However, since that [qualification] does not directly depend on its connection with it, and because it is subordinate, it casts it upon the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*). By virtue of the *vāravantīya* chant, whose position is known through extended application (*atideśa*), it further postulates that the *revatī* verses also fall within its scope. Therefore, even though the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* is not enjoined in this particular sentence, there is no fault, as the qualification of the sacrifice also transfers to that [auxiliary rite].
And for this reason, in your view, there is no connection of the *vāravantīya* with the sacrifice under discussion;
see:
for an action is supported by qualities that are non-action in their own nature.
What is the purpose of the action consisting of the *vāravantīya* chant?

In every case where it is heard in scripture that "having done this, one should do that," if the action expressed by the verbal root ending in *-tvā* is already obtained from another source, then the mention [of the *tvā*-suffix] serves the purpose of indicating a condition (*nimitta*).

However, if it is not so obtained, then the performance of the subsequent action is enjoined as occurring at a time subsequent to the completion of the prior one; since it cannot be performed without having executed that [prior action], it must necessarily be performed for that reason, and thus it will be understood as if it were directly enjoined.

Furthermore, in this case, the connection between the Revatī verses and the Vāravantīya chant is not established from any source prior to the injunction, such that it could be adopted as a mere occasion (nimitta).
Therefore, it is understood as something to be performed (anuṣṭheya) itself.
If, then, the connection is established as being with something to be performed, how is it connected with the subsequent [chant], which is already obtained as something to be performed?
To that end, he says:
"The word 'having made these two [meanings] thus' is capable of expressing this.
If it is asked, "How can multiple meanings be understood from a single [word]?", he replies: "For this mode of understanding is indeed observed in some cases."

Just as in the case of the command "bring the red horse," even though "bringing" is already established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the fact that "red" and "horse" are enjoined does not produce a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), as if they were expressed by two separate words;
likewise, here, the accomplishment (*nirvṛtti*) and the state of being prior in time are both conveyed by the word *klā*.
Or alternatively:
In that very case, there would be no qualification of a qualification;
for where [the Revatīs] are subordinate members of the substance (dravya), they are not understood to be subordinate members of the ritual action (karman).
But surely, the Revatīs are also enjoined?
If multiplicity of meaning followed merely from what is heard, then this would indeed be a valid rebuttal:
"All these are purposeful because they are being enjoined; therefore, multiplicity of meaning certainly exists.
To this, it is replied:
It is stated here that even a mere subordinate element (vidheya) is not the primary meaning;

rather, the meaning connected with the principal injunction is what is enjoined here, and that is singular. For the suffix, while enjoining the sacrifice toward the result, does not become inconsistent.
And one who is intent on non-origination will not even conceptualize origination.
Just as in the injunction regarding origination, the purpose of enjoining the ritual action is obtained, so too in the injunction regarding the fruit;
for the ritual action is enjoined with reference to the fruit. Thinking thus, he says [the following] in the second quarter of the second chapter.
Now, [the text] says: "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Vāravantīya chanted over the Revatī verses.
This is an injunction because it is logical that the chant serves as the means to the sacrifice by way of being its constituent element (*stotra*).
Alternatively, by means of this very [use of the] *itthambhūtalakṣaṇa* (instrumental denoting a characteristic), it means: "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with such [a Vāravantīya] as this."
To this, the reply is:
it cannot be so; for there would be a deficiency due to the offering of a different specific verse (*ṛgantara*).

If this were indeed that same ritual act, then since the *vāyavya* *agniṣṭomasāman* was prescribed for that [original] rite, its being sung upon a different verse named *revatī* would result in a deficiency because of the loss of the knowledge of the specific [verse] named *vāyavya* previously prescribed.
"Now, was it not just now that you yourself, regarding your own position, were questioned as to how other *sāmans* would also apply to the *revatī* verses? To this, you replied: 'This is not a fault;
for by the word "having performed" (*kṛtvā*), a completed relationship with the sacrifice is expressed.
This term "having performed" is capable of signifying these two meanings.'"

The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin), however, thinking that the prescription of multiple elements is possible only in the case of a previously unestablished ritual action (*apūrva-karma*) and not otherwise, says:

"In my position, where there is an explicit scriptural statement, it is possible; but in your position, since such a statement is absent, it would be impossible because one would have to rely merely on the mention of the *vāravantīya* chant while the *revatī* verses are being sung.
The opponent, with that same intention, replies: "In that case, there will indeed be such a scriptural statement."

[The opponent argues: "Because a specific ritual action (*karman*) is enjoined by the word *phalaja* (producing fruit), and because the word *kṛtvā* is not injunctive, the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). This is said with the intention that, although there is an injunction regarding the result, there is no injunction for the origination (*utpatti*) of the action itself. The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) states the consequence of his own intended position: that the injunction of multiple meanings cannot otherwise be justified. [He says: "If this statement is established, then it must be a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*)."
It is not the case that this is an injunction of a quality for the very same previously mentioned [sacrifice].
[Objection: But surely it is because of the reference (anuvāda) to the sacrifice in the phrase "one should sacrifice with that. [Response:
Because it has not been refuted by the scriptural statement, even now one considers one's own animal to be more powerful.
"It cannot be thus" is the explanation of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

For if the *vāravantīya* song, characterized by the *revatī* verses, were enjoined as a subordinate element (*guṇa*) with respect to the sacrifice, then that sacrifice would necessarily have to be the object of reference (*uddeśya*).

Consequently, because it is the object being referred to, the word expressing the result could not be connected either to that sacrifice or to that subordinate element; thus, [the mention of the result] would be entirely meaningless, or else, if it were so connected, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Or, if it were an injunction of an action qualified by its attributes, the action would necessarily be distinct because of its being recognized as such.
Furthermore, the statement "one desiring cattle should sacrifice" cannot be a mere restatement (anuvāda), since [the specific result] has not been previously established.
By this, the claim that this [sacrifice] serves as the occasion for the injunction of the *revatī* verses and the *vāravantīya* chant is refuted.

And for this reason, the Vāravantīya is not connected with the Revatīs by any more authoritative means of knowledge; thus, it would possess the quality of "loss of distinction" (*viśeṣahāni*) and so forth.

Alternatively, if it is an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding its connection with the sacrifice—meaning that since the result arises from the accessory itself, this sentence merely restates the status as a subsidiary of the sacrifice which was already understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*)—then [the objection stands].
But what is the distinction between this [case] and the previously refuted relationship of substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayi-sambandha*), such that it is put forward again?
That is stated:

for in that previous case, [the principle] "because of the lack of purpose, [it applies] to its subsidiaries" was refuted; however, since that [principle] is possible once the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅgatva*) is known, the connection with the *agniṣṭomasāman* is easily established—this is the intention.
He refutes that [objection] by stating that "the syntactical connection (vākya) is stronger than the context (prakaraṇa).
For it has been said that a connection with a person is accepted only when it is possible— because it is conducive to a connection with the result— but not when it is impossible.
The relationship between the subordinate and the principal, however, would arise from the apprehension of the ritual's "how-to" nature (kathaṃbhāva);
but that is not the case here, for it will be stated that [the rite] is unconnected because it belongs to the general context (prakaraṇa).
Moreover, this [rite] is connected with the fruit.
Therefore, because there is no contradiction, this is an injunction for a distinct ritual action qualified by a quality that yields a specific fruit.
This might be argued:
even though it is a distinct ritual action, the fruit arises from the very quality itself as supported by that [action].

Having analyzed that [objection], he refutes it by means of the principle of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, through which the connection between the sacrifice and its fruit is understood via the proximity of the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*).
Therefore, this is an injunction of an action (*karmavidhi*).
But if a specific sacrifice is being enjoined here, how can there be a connection with another action—the *agniṣṭomasāman*—by way of a qualifier?
The answer to that is:
"Because of the scriptural statement.
By the principle previously stated, this scriptural statement should be understood as an extended application (*atideśika*).
[The opponent argues: "It must be performed as the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*. [We reply:
There exists no such thing called the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* established as a fixed entity for which it could be assumed that the *vāravantīya* has taken over its function.
Therefore, [this belongs to] the second quarter of the second chapter concerning the archetypal [rites].
This was stated with the intention that the *jaya* hymns take over the function [of the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*].
Alternatively, the meaning is that it will serve for the sake of the *stotra* itself, namely the function of the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*.
Therefore, it is established that the fruit is connected to the ritual action (*karman*) in the same [sacrificial] sessions.

Furthermore, due to the force of the re-enactment (punarvidhāna), because the declaration of the fruit (phalaśruti) pertains to its own context, and because there is no attainment of another fruit for the *hīṣ* and other [syllables], there is no other fruit [for them]. Moreover, since everything has already been mentioned as being desired (*kāma*), the mention of desire (*kāmaśruti*) regarding that [result] would be for the purpose of the *nidhana*. Thus, the repetition is for the sake of the *nidhana*.
It is said:

[If one were to argue that] "one should effect a rain of faults, and that by means of the *nidhana*," there would be a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Furthermore, if there were no connection between them, it would be purposeless. However, according to our view, nothing is purposeless; for since the entire *saubhara* has its desire for rain and so forth stated by other scriptural injunctions, and since those specific words are already established, when only the connection with the *ṛṣabha* and others is enjoined, there is no split in the sentence. Nor is the scriptural statement purposeless, because it serves to restrict the specific *nidhana*.

Furthermore, even in the absence of a desire for specific qualities (*guṇakāmatva*), there is indeed a sublation here characterized by the general and the particular. This is because the word *saubhara* denotes the generality of all its constituent parts (*bhakti*); for while another *nidhana* would apply to it through the scriptural mention of *saubhara* by means of an indirect function (*parokṣavṛtti*), this [present rule] is direct (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, it is stronger. Just as that which is implied by the sense (*arthāt*) is set aside by what is directly stated in scripture (*śrauta*), so too is it set aside by that which functions indirectly. Alternatively, nothing at all is sublated by the song denoted by the word *saubhara*, since the injunction of the *ṛc* (verse) only sublates other non-verse elements (*aśarāntara*).

For if another part of the song were being enjoined, then even a part of the *saubhara* would be sublated; however, since this sublation of the *stobhas* pertains specifically to the *nidhana*, there is no fault. Therefore, the repetition is for the purpose of restricting the *nidhana*.
But when explained in this way, there is something that must be addressed.
Regarding that, it is said:
"The *hīṣ* [syllable] is the *nidhana*"; such a connection is undesirable because of the fault of postulating an intervention. This is likewise the case for the subsequent position as well.
If the injunction were located in the *nidhana* (concluding chant) without being specified as being for one desiring rain,
there would clearly be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because it would be a restatement of a qualified object.
Since the connection is made with the word "one desiring rain" itself, doubt arises.

By the phrase "by means of the fruit as the instrument," there is meaningfulness [of the injunction] because of the reliance on the syntactical force of the sentence; for if the connection were with the fruit alone, the injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*) would not be capable [of enjoining the action].
Furthermore:
Otherwise, by this [statement], the *saubhara*—though already understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*)—would have to be indicated as being endowed with the power to produce rain;
yet there is no purpose whatsoever in resorting to such an indication.

Furthermore, it is understood that this very same interpretation was intended by the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) when he stated, "and thus, in a matter concerning both direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*)."

The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is that this connection with desire regarding the entire Saubhara is merely being restated as previously mentioned; thus, there is no cognition of a new result. To the question, "For what purpose, then, is there a repetition of what has already been obtained? he says: "The repetition is for the sake of the *nidhana*."
But why are *hīṣ* and the others not connected with the very fruit mentioned in the Vedic text? To this it is replied:
just as the *vāravantīya* does not obtain the *iṣṭi* sacrifice as its substrate.
In the same way, in the case of the fruit, one does not obtain that which is appropriate for its substratum;
for the *saubhara* as a whole is not thereby established by means of a *nidhana* that has been established as a mere part, because the part is not perceived as being the *saubhara* itself.
Nor is there any such assumption that "one should resort to it in whatever way one is able," as has already been stated.

Even if one approaches you, since there are many *prastāva* and other *bhaktis* within the *saubhara*, it does not arise at all as to which specific *bhakti* the defects and so forth should be applied.
Or rather, according to the principle "the primary [element] [prevails] because of the prior injunction," as in the case of the *śloka*, they would apply to the *prastāva*.
In that case, the reference "therein [is] the *nidhana*" would not be tenable.

Now, it might be argued: "Just as the *ukthya* and other [sacrificial elements], though enjoined for a specific result and taking the *Jyotiṣṭoma* as their substrate by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), come to be inserted at the end by the force of another sentence (*vākya*)—despite not pervading the whole and consisting of multiple parts—in the same way, here too, the *nidhana* status will be restated for the *doṣa* and other [elements] enjoined for a result which approach the *saubhara* as their substrate and have obtained their position by virtue of the traditional recitation (*samāmnāya*). This concludes the second quarter of the second chapter.
Because there is no other scope [for them], the position is established in the case of the *ukthya* and others.
It is not understood how [the word] could have many locations such as defects (doṣa) and so forth;
for even though the word is a single entity, there is a diversity of capacities (śakti-bheda) according to its purpose.
In that case, it would not have a location in one effect while simultaneously existing in other effects.
Out of fear of the destruction of its own form, it does not attain a transition involving the application of another genus;
therefore, being restricted by all its conceptual variations according to its own traditional scripture, it cannot be subject to the rule of another's final dissolution.
If the intention were a partial restriction, then by the maxim of "eating from a bronze vessel," there would be a restriction regarding the whole;
however, this too is a possible meaning of the sentence here:
when both [factors] are already established, only their relationship is enjoined.
Since the Saubhara chant intended for one who desires vision must have the *hoṣit* as its *nidhana*, these two must be brought together in a single performance.
Therefore, it is established that there is a restrictive rule regarding the entire melody;
may it be auspicious. (Tantravārtika)

Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. But a quality, due to its connection with a specific season, should enjoin a separate ritual action, because that connection is not a subordinate part of the whole. In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* sāmans are first enjoined as optional alternatives, each serving as the basis for the *pṛṣṭha* stotra. Thereafter, it is heard again: "If the Soma sacrifice has the *rathaṃtara* as its *sāman*, one should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu; if it has the *bṛhat* as its *sāman*, [one should draw] those beginning with the *śukra* cup."

In this regard, the action accompanied by a quality (*saguṇa-karman*) being heard in the text gives rise to doubt: is it a different action from the Jyotiṣṭoma, or is it merely a scriptural mention for the sake of a condition (*nimitta*) regarding a specific precedence of the cups (*grahāgratā*) for that very same [Jyotiṣṭoma] as delimited by the *Rathantara* [Sāman]? Therefore, for the purpose of establishing this, the following must be deliberated: is this *Rathantara* connected with the entire sacrifice (*kṛtsna-kratu-saṃyoga*), or is it connected merely in its existence (*sattāmātra-saṃyoga*)? For the sake of establishing that as well, this must be considered: is the *Rathantara* qualified by the sacrifice, or is the sacrifice qualified by the *Rathantara* that is relied upon here?

Now, if it is argued that because of the connection with the word "yadi" (if), a condition (*nimitta*) is understood here, and since that [condition] is being indicated as the subject of the injunction, the relationship between qualifier and qualified would not be possible; [we reply:
this [word] may indeed have the sense of a condition, provided that such a thing as it is perceived to be is known to be obtained from some source.
However, in the absence of such prior attainment, it results in the prescription of something previously unestablished (*apūrva-vidhi*).
The third quarter of the second chapter.

Furthermore, if it is intended here that the *nimitta* (condition) must be of a specific kind, then if the Jyotiṣṭoma is of such a kind, its mention as being for the sake of the group (*gaṇa*) is established. But if it is not so, then it must be brought to that state and made the condition.

And that with which the condition is connected, such that the status of being a condition would otherwise not arise, becomes a qualification of that very condition; as will be stated in the section on the *Ārbhava*, "We admit the qualification by the oblation" (*haviṣā*), and thus there is no fault of restating something already qualified (*viśiṣṭānuvāda*).

What, then, is the prima facie view? From the context, since the possession of the *rathantara* sāman and the possession of the *bṛhat* sāman are already established by other scriptural statements, and since the use of the conditional particle "if" (*yadi*) indicates that these are conditions dependent on such prior attainment, and since the specific precedence of the cups (*grahāgratā*) is included within the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vacana*), and because it is not obstructed by any other stronger conflicting quality, the repetition of the text for the sake of those qualities—due to their proximity—is merely a restatement; thus, there is no separate ritual action (*akarmāntaratva*). Having set aside this established conclusion with the word "but" (*tu*), the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is adopted: it is a separate ritual action (*karmāntaram*).
Conciseness depends on the capacity of the intellect, and that [capacity] is desired in the case of a qualifier (*viśe�ṣaṇa*).
A qualifier serves to exclude [others], and such exclusion does not exist in the case of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
Thus, because another word-meaning is being enjoined, the *bahuvrīhi* compound is accepted as having that [other meaning] as its primary referent.
Otherwise, the sentence would have to be understood as being subordinate in purpose—like the sentence regarding the "red-turbaned" priests—by way of some indirect interpretation.

Furthermore, if the sentence were a large one containing the injunction of the precedence of the cups (*grahāgratā*), then both that injunction and the injunction of the *rathantara* chant would have to be accomplished by a single prior injunctive operation of the productive energy (*bhāvanā*), because they are multiple.

Moreover, due to the immediate proximity [of the words], it is understood that "the Soma should be" refers specifically to its performance; whereas the performance of the *rathantara* chant as the melody would only occur through a mediated construction.
However, by virtue of the word *soma*, which possesses the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the archetype, this [rite] will have the Jyotiṣṭoma as its archetype.
Therefore, it is an injunction of a ritual action; the author of the Bhāṣya demonstrates this very point with the words, "If [it is said] 'that which has the Rathantara-sāman'... and so forth.

Furthermore, the specific priority of the cups (*grahāgratā*) for this very sacrifice will be established either by the direct statement (*vākya*) or by the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).

Although the intermediate sentences within great statements (*mahāvākya*) are not authoritative, nevertheless, because the meaning [of the whole] would otherwise be impossible, and since the great statement is not intended [as primary], there is no sublation of the injunctive power by resorting to the intermediate sentences.
Thinking that [the injunction] is fulfilled by disregarding [the literal sense] and supplying [an ellipsis], the opponent shows "if it pleases you" (*yadi rocate*);
however, the other [author] asks "how then? regarding the very point of the illustration.
The relationship is established through transposition; the explanation of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) indicates a desire for the pouring of the soma.
In this context, the meaning of the sentence is as follows:
"If one should desire to draw the cups for Indra and Vāyu, one should perform the *Rathantara* Sāman at the sacrifice."

And therefore, if the two words "somaḥ syāt" (there should be Soma) are the prescriptive element, then although the phrase "he should take up the cups" (*grahān gṛhṇīyāt*) is not itself prescriptive, it will nevertheless obtain the force of an injunction because it expresses desire—according to the principle that "whatever one desires, one does. Alternatively, since the priority of the cups (*grahāgratva*) is presented as being connected with mere desire, this very optative suffix (*liṅ*) will enjoin it. Thinking that this position is more powerful even without the assumption of an interrupted connection, he introduces [the alternative] by citing the rule: "The optative suffix is used in the sense of cause and effect" (*hetuhetumator liṅ*).
In this context, the optative suffix in "syāt" (should be) denotes a reason (*hetu*), whereas in "gṛhṇīyāt" (one should take), it denotes an injunction (*vidhi*). By this, the following is stated:
"One should take the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu, having the *rathaṃtara* Sāman as their cause.
And since that [Sāman] cannot function as a cause unless it is performed, it will effectively be enjoined by implication.

Alternatively, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the phrase "one should take" (*gṛhṇīyāt*) may signify a cause (*hetu*), as in "there should be Soma. Although the causality of the Soma is not explicitly stated, it will be established through the implication of that which possesses the cause (*hetumat*) and through proximity (*saṃnidhi*). In that case as well, the meaning is this: "The Soma sacrifice, which serves as the specific cause for the precedence of the cups (*grahāgratā*), must be performed.
This is the summary verse regarding the alternative views.
All of this will be utilized specifically within the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion of a topic), as has been explained here at length.
Furthermore,
that which is to be accomplished is guaranteed by a cause that has already been established.
Nor is the existence of the *rathaṃtara* established [at that time], just as the possession of the sacrifice is not; this is stated in the *Vārttika*.

For the precedence of the cups occurs at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), while the *rathaṃtara* occurs at the midday pressing (*mādhyandina*); and it is not logical for that which is unestablished to serve as a causal condition (*nimitta*), since the word "condition" is a synonym for "cause. According to my view, however, there is no condition whatsoever.

Alternatively, it may be argued that the *kratu* (sacrifice) and the *jagatsāman* exist from the very beginning, but not the *jyotiṣṭoma*; thus, because of the absence of the *jagatsāman* in the *jyotiṣṭoma*, and because other sacrifices are established as being similar to it, they must be distinct rites (*karmāntara*).

Or else, since the *rathantara* and other *sāmans* are prescribed, the *jyotiṣṭoma* itself is enjoined by the group-injunctions (*gaṇavākya*) as having such a nature; therefore, no distinctness is perceived.
And from that follows the oneness of the ritual action.
As for the objection that the compound *rathantarasāma* is not tenable— either because of the absence of a qualifier or because it would have a qualifier that is itself dependent on another—
we reply as follows:

For if the *rathantara* were invariably present in the Jyotiṣṭoma, either alone or accompanied by another, then it would not even need to be excluded. However, since there is indeed a performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma that lacks the *rathantara*, it serves the purpose of qualification by means of such exclusion. Furthermore, if the cognition of a qualification does not arise without the particle *eva*, then it should be demonstrated in this way: "If the *rathantara* Sāman is indeed present in this [Jyotiṣṭoma]."

Regarding the statement, "When the *rathaṃtara* is indeed the *sāman* for it," what is the meaning of the word "indeed" (*eva*)? It means that although the *rathaṃtara* is always a *sāman*, nevertheless, when those two [the *bṛhat* and the *rathaṃtara*] are not present, it is said to be "the *sāman*" with respect to that [rite], because it does not possess the function of a *sāman* toward it; whereas in the case of its existence, it is called "the *rathaṃtara* is the *sāman*.

Furthermore, this status of being a *sāman* must necessarily be stated as dependent upon the ritual (*kratu*), because the status of being a *sāman* is eternally redundant in the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the *rathaṃtara*.

Furthermore, the *rathantara* does not possess the status of being a means (*sādhana*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice such that a compound could not be formed. For this [rule regarding non-compounding] applies only to those things designated by a *dvandva* compound that function as the means for a single stotra; however, in the case of individual [sāmans] which serve as the means for different stotras, their status as means is independent of one another, and thus no such semantic incapacity (*asāmarthya*) is found.

Alternatively, because of the tautology [otherwise], the word *sāman* signifies the *stotra* (hymn) accomplished by it; this, in turn, indicates the *pṛṣṭha* [laud] brought to mind by the *rathantara*.

Or rather, since the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* have distinct intermediate contexts and are connected to distinct intermediate functions, these two contradictory and competing elements—being mere restatements of what already exists—establish their status as qualifiers through mutual exclusion alone, without depending on other *sāmans*. Thus, it is established that the sacrifice qualified by the *rathantara* serves as the occasion (*nimitta*).
Alternatively, let it be that the Rathantara-sāman qualified by the sacrifice is the occasion.
But surely, that very thing is not perceived. It is said in reply:

It is not that truth is not perceived; rather, when—due to the absence of connection with all sacrifices—a sacrifice qualified by the *rathantara* is not grasped, then, in the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound, that reversed relationship of qualifier and qualified which is perceived—namely, "the *rathantara* is its *sāman*"—will not be accepted.
Furthermore, because the sacrifice is expressed in the genitive case, it will be intended as the qualifier itself, since the status of being the qualificand is manifested by the compound.

Although the *rathantara* exists by way of its own nature even in other sacrifices, it nevertheless exists here [in this specific context]; and on that basis alone, its status as a qualifier is established.

Furthermore, the cause for being a qualifier is uniqueness within one's own sentence, not actual non-existence elsewhere; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the loss of the qualifier-status of such expressions as "the blue lotus" or "Devadatta’s cow.
Moreover, if uniqueness were established by the thing itself in reality, the word would never have been employed as a qualifier.
For in this case, there is no result arising from a specific distinction, as in the statement "fire is hot.
Therefore, one must necessarily rely on the substratumhood being inherent within the sentence itself;
and this is indeed present here as well, because it is intended that the *rathantara* chant, as belonging specifically to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, serves as the condition (*nimitta*).
By virtue of that [recitation], there is proficiency in the performance, beginning from the first *sāman*.

Furthermore, the cause (*nimitta*) does not assist the effect (*naimittika*) by means of the physical proximity of its form; rather, it assists by way of being known. Therefore, even when it is not being performed, the *rathantara* is the cause because it has been intended. However, when the sacrifice is specifically characterized as the cause by that [recitation] even while it occupies only one part [of the rite], then it certainly exists [as the cause]; thus, there is no contradiction.
In the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice, because of its connection with a ritual (*yajña*), it would be said that the *Kutu* is the primary element.

In the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the injunction, "A king desiring sovereign rule (*sārājya*) should sacrifice with the *Rājasūya*," having prescribed the sacrifice known as the *Aveṣṭi* through the association of substances and deities such as "a cake on eight potsherds for Agni; gold is the sacrificial fee" (*āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālo hiraṇyaṃ dakṣiṇā*), it further enjoins:
"If a Brāhmaṇa sacrifices, he should place the *Bārhaspatya* in the middle and pour the oblation over each offering; if a Rājanya, the *Aindra*; if a Vaiśya, the *Vaiśvadeva*."

In this regard, as before, there arises a doubt: does the text enjoin a contingent ritual (naimittika) with reference to the *aveṣṭi* sacrifice—which has already attained a connection with specific castes within the *rājasūya*—as its occasion; or does it enjoin a different performance altogether, connected with Brāhmaṇas and others, which was not previously established? To resolve this, it must be investigated whether the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the *rājasūya* belongs to all three castes or to the Kṣatriya alone.

For the sake of establishing that [qualification], the word "king" (*rājan*), which serves as a qualification for the person entitled to perform the rite, must be investigated in the same manner; therefore, this too must be examined:

is the word "king" based on the fact of being a Kṣatriya, or is it based on the performance of royal sovereignty? Now, one might argue: "Since there is a separate injunction for the performance of the Rājasūya—namely, 'One desiring food should cause him to sacrifice with the Āveṣṭi'—which is unrelated to specific castes, the mention [of the king] in the context of the Āveṣṭi would merely serve to indicate the occasion [for its performance] for all three castes who are already eligible. This is not so.

For then, since it is already known to have a Kṣatriya as its performer, and since no other performer is enjoined by another statement, and because there is no reason for a separate performance, it belongs only to that which stands within the Rājasūya—according to the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*) as stated in the Tantravārtika.
Furthermore, it is understood that the fruit of sovereignty (*pārājya*) is common [to all], while the fruit of food (*annādya*) is individual;
or else, it is performed separately by the Kṣatriya alone who seeks the fruit, and has no connection with other castes.

For example, just as in the case of Vedic study (*adhyayana*) and the depositing of sacred fires (*ādhāna*), because these are performed by the three twice-born castes (*traivarṇika*), the rites dependent upon them—though their connection to a mere purpose is understood—remain restricted solely to those six [castes].

And just as in this very context, although there is no distinction in the desire for sovereignty (*khārājya-kāma*), a distinction among the performers (*bhoktṛ*) arises by virtue of the king being the agent;
therefore, the attainment [of the result] occurs through the statements of power (*vaibhava-vacana*) under the heading of the Rājasūya sacrifice. Thus, there are only two positions.
"The king is the ruler of the kingdom"—thus it is sung in all the worlds.

And in this way, the scope of the treatise will also be vast; furthermore, the Vedic injunction regarding the eligibility for the Rājasūya sacrifice, proceeding naturally with its extensive scope, will not be obstructed.
Therefore, all those of the three higher castes who exercise sovereignty are "kings," and that sovereignty is universally recognized as consisting in the protection of the realm (*janapada*).

Furthermore, even within the context of sovereignty, "uprooting" is intended to mean the removal of thorns (criminals). The phrase "residents of Āryāvarta" is used to demonstrate that they are established in the scriptures, because [the status of being a king] is contingent upon that [residence].

By stating that those who are proficient teach that "the king's action is the kingdom" (*rājyam*), you have indeed admitted the independence (*svātantrya*) of the word *rāj* itself as the base form (*prakṛti*). For instance, one does not become known as "Udamegha" merely through a connection with Udamegha;
rather, it is Udamegha himself, as an independent entity, who is understood [as the basis].
The king has indeed been recognized here as independent by the ancients;
our kingdom, however, is conceived through association with him.
This is not a fault.

In every respect, since they both exercise sovereignty, they have indeed attained the status of kingship; and by that much, the purpose of the injunction for the Rājasūya is fulfilled. As for justice and injustice, however, because those are attributes of the person, neither is grasped by the sacrifice; thus there is no distinction. For it has been stated regarding words such as *barhis* and *ājya*: even when a commonality based on a genus (*jāti*) is obtainable in a single part, another ground [for the application] should not be postulated. The opponent, however, demonstrates that the word is taken in its etymological sense merely to serve as an aid, on account of the context and the association with the word "if" (*yadi*).
"It will not enjoin another action" is said with the intention of referring to a different performance; or else, as in the *Tantravārtika*: "If one should eat at the time of peace (*śānti*)."

Words such as "tyādi" (and so forth) include various types of expressions; in that case, since it would be impossible to perform both the connection with the Brāhmaṇa and the sprinkling with clarified butter (*vāīspratya-abhighāraṇa*) by means of a single sentence, the status of being a distinct ritual action (*karmāntaratva*) is indeed primary.
Thus, having first accepted the consensus of both [parties] as authoritative, it is now introduced that the performance [of the rite] for one devoid of sovereignty is not an authority at all;
rather, this is prescribed as a connection with a specific sacrifice (*ṛtu*) for the Brāhmaṇa and others.
Indeed, one is not recognized as a king merely by virtue of having attained [the status], nor by connection with kingship (*rājyayoga*).

This word "king" (*rāja*) is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*) denoting the Kṣatriya caste; it is not etymological (*yaugika*). For it would have to be either based on connection with kingship—according to the inferred root meaning—or based on connection with radiance (*dīpti*); yet it is untenable in both ways.

Since we observe that this is a conventional word formed for that purpose, even though it is a single part [of a compound], its conventional meaning overrides the established meaning of its constituent parts.

Nor is there any inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) even regarding the well-known usage of the term *avagraha*; for the word "king" (*rāja*) is not applied to fire and other such things that are merely hot. Nor is it applied to an unappointed official (*ayuktaka*), even if he is occupied with protecting the countryside.
[Objection: But surely, because an unappointed official acts on behalf of another, like a priest (*ṛtvij*), he will have the status of a sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and not the status of a king.
Even consecration is prescribed by those who know the Dharma for the Kṣatriya alone;
therefore, that great title of "King" is not intended to apply to one who is not a Kṣatriya.
The relationship between word and meaning is eternal, following the state of things as they truly exist.
They do not rely on an unstable cause imagined according to one's own whim;

and that permanence is defined either with reference to the substance or with reference to the rule. Furthermore, there is no application of this term among the Dravidians to anything else of a different kind. For this reason as well, a king is not necessarily of the three [upper] castes. Thus, they explain that the word *rājanya*—which unambiguously denotes the Kṣatriya caste—is derived from the word *rājan* (king), as in the expression "the offspring of a king (*rājāpatyam*) is a *rājanya*."

Otherwise, since kingship belongs to those of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), the term *rājanya* would have to be applied to the offspring of all members of the three castes. Why? Because if everyone were indeed a king (*rājan*), then the term *rājanya* would be conventionally established (*ruḍha*) for the Kṣatriya caste.
If the relationship between offspring and their progeny is indeed the same [as that between a person and his own offspring], tell me, what kind of disparity exists?
For the word *jāti* is identical in its application to both the primary source (*prakṛti*) and its offspring.
Therefore, let the term *rājanya* be used everywhere as a synonym for *rājan*.

For, in this manner, the word *rājanya* is explained as a synonym (*paryāya*) of the word *rājan*; however, it is only appropriate to explain it thus when both refer to a single caste (*ekajāti*), and not otherwise.
To begin with, neither of these two words is established through independent usage.
For when there is a doubt regarding the connection between two practices, it is better that the determination be made based on the etymological meaning rather than the conventional one.
Because of its stronger connection with the root *mṛ* (to die), this very etymological derivation—that "kingship" (*rājyam*) is the action of the king—is obtained;

thus, the entire word "king" (*rājā*) is entered by "kingship," and it is appropriate that it be etymological (*yaugika*). It is not the case that the word "kingship" is entirely permeated by the "king" and therefore non-etymological (*ayaugika*).
It is indeed true that the word "rājya" (kingdom) possesses an etymological validity;
for a qualifier is desired everywhere in its uncommon sense.
Therefore, only his own actions—such as reflection and so forth—are intended, and not those of others.

For the application [of the *svāra*] in the middle of the season is already fulfilled by the *svāra-rājya* itself; the other, however, remains expectant. Therefore, the connection with the fruit belongs to that [former] alone.
Otherwise, because of the contradiction, the assumptions of either option or repetition would result.

Therefore, he must accept that [the general term] is sublated; however, in the case of the established rule (*vyavasthā*), it is not so for you, because the word "rājasūya" is a general term—like the word "paurṇamāsī"—since it denotes the individual members as qualified by the contextually relevant collection. For this very reason, it does not incur weakness even when [the specific] is performed.
This, however, is the distinction: by one [term], many are included, while by the other, few.
And yet, there is no excellence [of result] by that much alone.
[Objection: But surely there is a distinction because of the direct statement [in the text], "by this very [formula]," which is a perceptible expression.
[Reply: There would be a distinction if the word *etad* were connected with the fruit.

Or, if it were to speak of what is being introduced—as in the case of "Now this is the Jyotis" and so on—then, due to the proximity of the suffix, even there the Aveṣṭi sacrifice, as grasped by the word *yajati*, would be connected with the food-eating (*annādya*).
And since this much [proximity] exists even in the Rājasūya sacrifice, there is no distinction; thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter.

Moreover, even when speaking of what is under discussion, this root [the verbal root *brū*] does not truly denote anything at all without the consideration of sentences such as those concerning the Āgneya sacrifice.
Consequently, the *rājasūya* sacrifice itself can also be grasped with that much effort; thus, they possess equal status.
Now, one might object: "But there is indeed a distinction regarding the intermediate qualification (*avāntarādhikāra*)."

This alone is the distinction: that in one case there is the apprehension of many [factors], while in the other there is the apprehension of none; however, the status as an apprehension (*grahaṇa*) is indeed the same. And if internal difference were here an absolute [criterion], then it would be stated thus; furthermore, it has been shown that even a different action (*karmāntara*) constitutes such a distinction.
Consequently, because they have different subject matters (*viṣayāntara*), there is no contradiction between *svārājya* (sovereignty) and *annāda* (eating food).

Furthermore, even if these are distinct rites, since indicative marks such as the *bāīspatya* cup are observed, it must be understood that they are based on the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice as their archetype (*prakṛti*).

Since the *rājanya* (kingly caste) is also engaged in the same manner and the word "fruit" (*phala*) is syntactically connected [to him], his connection is likewise with a distinct rite or a distinct performance, just as in the case of the *brāhmaṇa* and the *vaiśya*.
And thus, even in that case, the statement regarding the depositing [of the fire] will be applicable when the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is performed,
because it is a subsidiary to the entire *Ādhāna* (Fire-laying).
Since there is a doubt regarding the attainment of what has not yet been attained in such injunctions as "A Brāhmaṇa should lay the fires in spring," the doubt remains exactly as before.
The laying [of the fires] is implied by the force of the context, or it is expressed by the general statement;
therefore, the repetition of the specific colors is for the purpose of providing a causal sign,
which is the reason for the final conclusion.

The capacity of a word to convey its meaning is not eternal, because even by other means such as purchase and the like, things acquired from another person are not necessarily denoted by the ātmanepada suffix;
furthermore, when there is a direct statement, and when no other possibility is perceived, one does not resort to presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) or scriptural inference (śruti).

Even the expression "one who knows thus" (*ya evaṃ vidyāt*) is a statement in the present tense; it does not acquire injunctive power (*vidhiśakti*) when a direct indicative mark (*liṅ*) is available, as in the case of sentences concerning Brāhmaṇas and the like.

And this presentation has the purpose of prescribing the collection of materials such as water and secondary items (upasarjana) joined with the direct injunction; thus, the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna), qualified by [the status of] Brāhmaṇas and so forth, is indeed enjoined as something not previously established.

As for the question "What is the cause of the connection?", it refers to the intention that there is no connection with words such as "if" (yadi). Furthermore, since there is a co-utterance of Brāhmaṇas and others with the injunctions regarding spring (vasanta) and so forth, when the injunctive power is transferred through its connection with another word, it results in being both a condition (nimitta) and a fruit.
It is not that the connection of these [rites] with the fire-consecration (āghāna) is unknown;
this being the case, we reply:
indeed, the fire-consecration is merely the means for obtaining the sacred fires (agni).

In that regard, only those things consisting of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are grasped which can be accomplished by worldly means, such as clothing, carts, and so forth; however, the *āhavanīya* fire and others are not worldly means. Therefore, it must necessarily be accepted that for these [sacrificial fires], the Veda alone is the means.
Since there is no other means apart from the formal installation (*ādhāna*), that [installation] too is included [within the scope of the Veda].
It is said:
This is not so, because [the means] are non-exclusive (*anaikāntikatvāt*).

For there exist other means, such as begging, purchasing, and so forth; and by all of these, the scriptural injunctions regarding desires—which seek only the *āhavanīya* fire and other such fires—are rendered complete.
Therefore, since the installation (*ādhāna*) is not established as an absolute necessity, there is room for a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*).
In the case of the *hastya* sacrifice, the three fires arise from the first performance of the *ādhāna*;
thereafter, however, they belong to him like his own wealth (*śrīdivat*), and there is no prohibition against other means [of obtaining them].

Consequently, just as a potter produces and sells jars and the like again and again, so too might someone, having performed the *ādhāna* of the fires repeatedly, give them to others. Therefore, since the performance of the *ādhāna* would otherwise result in its application to every individual, it is not so; thus, there is a scope for the injunction.

Alternatively, we shall explain that there is no such attainment even in the case of the [other] view; for if it were the latter view, then because the scriptural authority based on inference lacks a distinction between the ātmanepada and parasmaipada endings, there would be no contradiction even regarding the agent, and thus other means would not be excluded. Therefore, this must necessarily be enjoined.
Moreover:
By stating "even when the scriptural injunctions for the establishment of the fires (ādhāna) exist," he refutes even the possibility of such an application [of the rule].

For it has already been explained that rules such as the restrictive injunctions (niyama) are not injunctions of what is otherwise unestablished (aprāptavidhi), because there is no room for the postulation of what is not heard when what is heard is possible; indeed, a single syntactical unity with the act of establishing the fires is not possible for words such as *anupasarjana*.

In this case, there would be a plurality of sentences if the installation (*ādhāna*) were being enjoined here with a different meaning. However, since that [installation] has already been established by texts connected with the Brāhmaṇas and others, it is mentioned here again only for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).
Indeed, how can a determination be made as to which of these two is the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*)?
This is explained as follows:
if both of these two sentences were injunctive, then, being directed toward the same object, they would compete; which one of them, then, would enjoin?
But here, one is injunctive and the other is laudatory.

Nor is the injunctive character of [the passage] connected with the Brahmins and so forth precluded by the eulogizer, because it is consistent with that; for if even "he who knows thus" were of the nature of an injunction, then, since what has already been enjoined cannot be enjoined again, it would subvert our position. However, because it is enjoined by the optative suffix (*liṅ*), the repeated hearing of that which is accompanied by praise is for the purpose of enjoining the collection of related materials and for the sake of incitement; thus, it is not injunctive.

Furthermore, since the injunction of the root-meaning by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is based on what is directly expressed by its own word (*svapada*), it is "verbal" (*śrauta*); however, the excellence (*prāśastya*) is not [directly expressed] in the sentence (*vākya*). Consequently, the injunction would have to be inferred (*anumānika*), which is highly objectionable.
Now, the argument that "this too is a sentence" intends to show that there is no abandonment of the referents of words such as "Brāhmaṇa. This is the view of the Siddhāntin in the *Mantravārttika*.

First, the *ādhāna* (fire-laying) is enjoined by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), while the remainder [the purpose] is understood through syntactical connection (*vākya*). Let it be so; for there is no praise expressed by its own word.
Thus, the praise—namely, "he overcomes his hateful rival"—is established through the very connection with words such as "overcomes" (*avatti*) and "greatly" (*mahat*).

Furthermore, because the primary act of *ādhāna* is enjoined as qualified by the agent and the time, and because this avoids the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*), its status as an injunction that brings about the performance of the rite is established.

However, in the case of the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña* and others, because of their grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) and because they are not employed in the previously mentioned sacrifice, it is not contradictory for them to be presented as distinct sacrifices delimited by their own specific forms. Nor is there any well-known accessory (*guṇa*) such as curd (*dadhi*) that possesses this very name. Therefore, according to the principle of the section on the meaning of verbal roots (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*), since an injunction regarding the connection with a fruit is established, a distinct sacrifice is concluded;
thus, the sentence is complete with respect to the fruit.

Since *phañ* is not something to be adopted [as a result], an injunction directed toward an action—such as "one should sacrifice with *vrīhi* grains"—is not possible; therefore, an action must necessarily be enjoined therein.

Consequently, the distinction [of the ritual] is established, and here too, as in the case of the curd (*dadhi*) and other examples, the relationship is one of grammatical non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

Therefore, the result arises from a modification consisting of a different state of the very Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices themselves, and not from a separate ritual; furthermore, the observation of indicative marks—
such as the completion of thirty [days] or the mention of the full moon and new moon days— does not indicate a difference [between the rites].

For the thirty-year period pertaining to the Darśapūrṇamāsa cannot be completed by means of another ritual action. Nor is there an extension (atideśa) of the rule [to that other action], whereby this prescription of a fifteen-year period would apply to that other action as well. Furthermore, the fifteen-year period does not arise for the Darśapūrṇamāsa itself on the ground of the occasion of "sacrificing during the southern course of the sun," because there is no connection [between that occasion and the sacrifice].
Moreover, the expressions "two full-moon sacrifices" and "two new-moon sacrifices" would be untenable [under such an interpretation].

Even though the completion [of the action] is not distinct and no fruit is enjoined by means of the specification of the ritual act (*karman*), nevertheless, because there is an absence of a relationship between the ritual act and the fruit, it does not constitute a different ritual act.

For just as it was established in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* that "the fruit belongs to the ritual act," so too in the section beginning with "But because the two sentences are unequal" (*atulyatvāt tu vākyayoḥ*), it was stated that the sentence does not terminate in a connection between a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) and the fruit. Thus, when a doubt arises, it is established—on the basis of favoring the other word—that the fruit results from the quality itself, and not from the ritual act.
How so?

If, first of all, Nirvāṇa were heard of as being connected with the context (*prakaraṇa*), then only the application of the contextual auxiliary would follow, and there would be no suspicion of it being a separate action (*karmāntara*). However, since this is an isolated statement (*anārabhyavāda*), because qualities such as "white" are things to be adopted, a doubt arises: sometimes a quality is enjoined by way of restating something already remote, and sometimes, due to the absence of a mental transition (*viparivṛtti*), it is a separate action. Furthermore, the removal of that doubt will occur in this way: because there is no context and because there is no mention of anything specific [to the ritual], there is no cognition of the two forms—the archetypal (*prākṛta*) and the worldly (*laukika*)—as distinct from one another. Thus it shall be.
Because they are the objects of an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), the two terms "offering" (*ālambha*) and "pouring out" (*nirvāpa*) are designated by the term "injunction of a quality.
What, then, is the prima facie view?

Just as in the case of the *ayana* sacrifices, where there is no word enjoining a ritual action (*karmavidhi*) in a sentence primarily concerned with the connection of a quality, so too will it be here; this is indicated by the word "and" (*ca*).
And what is this injunction of qualities? The mention of "not being in a specific context" (aprakaraṇa) is for the purpose of determining its scope.

Alternatively, even if this much is heard outside of the context (*aprakaraṇe*) with the same prior distinction, nevertheless, because the action is not subsumed under an injunctive word (*vidhi-śabda*), this repetition is for the sake of a specific purpose (*gārthā*). Thus, at the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, that sacrificial post (*iṣā*) is to be made white and brought forward, and the *caru* offering is to be prepared; or rather, it is measured by the *caru*. Furthermore, since the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are prescribed for one desiring prosperity and Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*), as well as for all [desires], this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already established. Likewise, regarding the phrase "dedicated to Vāyu" (*vāyavyam*), since Vāyu is the deity of all forest-produce (*vanaspati*), it is somehow a restatement of the sacrificial post itself.

Furthermore, the term "sauryam" (belonging to Sūrya) is merely a reiteration of the *āgneya* (belonging to Agni), due to the commonality of having a deity characterized by light; therefore, it is prescribed as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).
Thus, disregarding the word "vāyavya" as before, one objects first by adopting the word expressing the result (*phalapada*).
For if, having reiterated the acts of touching (*ālambhana*) and offering (*nirvāpa*), "white" (*śveta*) were prescribed, then the word for the result would indeed be purposeless.
Even if it were a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the attainment of all desires, the inclusion of the word "as if permanent" would be contradictory because [attainment] is only occasional.
Alternatively, if it were a qualifier, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
However, if it is an injunction (*vidhāna*) of an animal sacrifice qualified by a specific quality, there is no fault whatsoever.
Therefore, it is said: "Because the action is the primary object.
Here, the action is the basis for the scriptural injunction as that which is to be performed, not the accessory; for the latter would not be subject to the injunction at all.
Alternatively, it would be exactly as stated [in the text], and not involving a sacrifice (*yajimat*).
Why [are these] actions? Because they are rooted in the Śruti;
for the act of sacrificing (yajati) involves a connection with substances, fruits, and enjoyers, and thus these are connected to ritual action.
Just as the position regarding subordinate qualities (guṇa) was rejected upon observing the word "fruit" (phala).
Having observed the word *devatā* (deity), its nature as being nothing more than a mere name is likewise established;

and because of the observation of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the statement "saumāraudram" (belonging to Soma and Rudra), even though the word *yajati* (he sacrifices) is absent, it is understood that in a sentence intended to enjoin the act of enclosing (*pariśrayaṇa*), such passages possess the character of enjoining a ritual action characterized by sacrifice (*yajati*), even while the root *yaj* is not being directly restated.
The Agniṣomīya [sacrifice] also possesses the quality of being a sacrifice (yajimat) by this very same [reasoning].
Previously, only this much was deliberated: whether it is a restatement of what is already established (anuvāda) or an injunction (vidhi).
But once its status as an injunction is established, the question of what constitutes its ritual action (karma) depends entirely upon this present section; thus, it must be understood here.
To those who speak thus, it is replied: no means of proof (*sādhana*) establishes its own object without having its scope demonstrated;
and by the author of the Sūtras, only the reason (*hetu*) has been set forth in this third quarter of the second chapter.
Furthermore, even by means of context, subject matter, and so forth, not one of the [required elements]—the example, the proposition, the doubt, or the reason—is perceived here.

Therefore, since this is a *gamaka-sūtra* (a rule intended to produce understanding), the authors of the commentaries (*vṛttikāra*) and others must necessarily strive to provide a remedy for the defect.
Even though it is possible [to find them], the exclusion of [elements such as] conduct (*ācāra*) and the like has been stated.

In every respect, when commentators and others proceed with the refinement of their disciples' understanding, one should accept whatever they have composed that is consistent with that [subject matter], and not insist on citing the name [of the original author].

They state this for the purpose of demonstrating that "this word was not included by the author of the Sūtra, but rather by the author of the Vṛtti. Thus, here the venerable Aparārka has cited this sentence—"One should touch the calf"—which is heard in the section concerning the milking of the bow (*dhanu-doha*) in the context of the Agnihotra; and there, as before, he has presented a threefold doubt.
Is the calf prescribed here as being exactly like the original [animal], such that both the mere touching and the fact that it is a sacrifice are identical to that action?

In this regard, since there is no qualifying characteristic, the notion that it is the original [action] does not exist; this was already established in the preceding section and thus was not introduced again. Therefore, once the idea that it denotes a sacrifice has arisen in that very sequence, this present [section] serves as a refutation of that.

In this regard, although the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) has essentially been dealt with by way of its counter-example—the conjunction with the enjoyer—it is nevertheless presented here due to the diversity of the listeners' intellects. For it is impossible to effect the removal of that misconception for one who, through the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of a logician, seeks to infer the meaning of the Veda by means of general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*); thus, it is demonstrated [here]. In this matter, some consider the root *labh* (to obtain) to be synonymous with *yaj* (to sacrifice), as established in the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), while others consider it to be a synonym for *yajvan* (the sacrificer). Both of these views are held here in exactly the same manner.

In this regard, there is a twofold prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): either it is an injunction for an entirely new sacrifice (*apūrva-yāga-vidhāna*), or it is an injunction for the calf already established [in the context].

The final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: previously, we postulated a sacrifice because the relationship between the substance and the deity could not otherwise be accounted for; this was not established by some previously unseen potency, nor by a fallacious inference based on a non-conclusive [reason], nor is such a thing present here. Therefore, the principle of "stating only what is necessary" (*yāvad-uktatā*) applies. Consequently, its inclusion among purificatory acts (*saṃskāra-karma*) such as milking becomes logical, and it possesses a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) because it serves as the cause for the cow's grazing.
However, that which is connected with the word "artha" (purpose) has that as its meaning because of its connection with the direct Vedic text (*śruti*);

this serves as a counter-example to the previously mentioned case of *āmnambhas*. But this present case concerns the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) by way of the *caru* (rice-oblation). Furthermore, the doubt regarding the deity here is an additional internal factor, which is why the discussion begins. In that regard, the status of the *caru*, the *puroḍāśa* (cake), and so forth as auxiliary elements of the sacrifice is inherent (*autpattika*). In every respect, the relinquishment of one's own ownership over these must be performed.
And because of the use of the accusative case in the expression "he places the *caru*" (*carum upadadhāti*), the act of placing it down is a secondary consecration (*pratipatti*).

Furthermore, it is not logical to perform a ritual application for something that is otherwise useless; thus, when there is an expectation [of purpose], its utility for the sacrifice is understood due to its fitness.

Moreover, if Bṛhaspati, who is mentioned in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), were connected with the injunctive portion, it would result in meaninglessness. Therefore, the conclusion reached is that one should offer the cooked rice (*caru*) dedicated to Bṛhaspati—which has the Āgneya as its archetype—without performing the other subsequent rites, and then place it upon the fire.
This being the case, we reply: the *caru* and other items do not possess an inherent purpose by their very nature;
rather, their application is understood solely according to the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, this [application] is not a mere disposal (*pratipatti*), because at the outset, no purposefulness is perceived.

Furthermore, even in the case of a purposeful ritual act (*arthakarma*), there is primacy with respect to the preparatory offering (*upadhāna*); therefore, because it does not bring about [the result] while remaining unrefined, there is no contradiction in the use of the accusative case.
Nor should Bṛhaspati be inferred as being connected with the *novāra* grains;
likewise, the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) must be interpreted so that its connection with a deity—which was not required by the injunctive core (*vidhyuddeśa*)—is established.

And as for those [who hold] that "it belongs to Bṛhaspati" (*bārhaspatyaḥ*)—whereby, through the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the *caru* offering, a deity is established in the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*)—for them too, it is impossible to enjoin a deity because the requirement is already satisfied by what is established from the injunctive portion regarding the initial placing (*upadhāna*). Consequently, in accordance with the descriptive statement (*vartamānāpadeśa*), one understands that this is merely a praise proclaimed regarding whatever nature of its belonging to Bṛhaspati we perceive as currently existing. Therefore, the very meaning of the statement from another recensional branch, "This is indeed the food of Bṛhaspati," is determined to be the same as the Taittirīya statement, "It belongs to Bṛhaspati."
Therefore, even the word *deṣa* does not denote a sacrifice; thus, the principle of "stating only what is required" (*yāvaduktatva*) is established.
Furthermore, that [animal] is not recognized as being identical to the one previously mentioned due to the absence of Tvaṣṭṛ;
and because of the connection with the term *paryagnikṛta*, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would result.

Nor is he the speaker of time, by which one might assume that [the animal] is released at the very time of the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire); by this, the view regarding the distinction of states is refuted. This concludes the third quarter of the second chapter.
First, it was established by the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) that [the animal] is released at the stage of the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire).
Now, an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) regarding the subsequent stages is stated; in that regard, the absence of fault has already been explained.

Therefore, since there is nothing to be enjoined in this sentence concerning the previous ritual action, this must be a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*) connected with its own material and deity. And since it shares a commonality of deity as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), it is established—given the prima facie view—that it is either modeled after the *Agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, which serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*), or indeed modeled after that very archetype. To this, the following is stated in reply:

The word *pātnīvata*, like the word "fire" (*agni*) in the context of the *manotā* hymn, is able to denote the sacrifice under discussion even though it is qualified by both [attributes], because the injunction regarding its specific accessory is understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*) through the statement, "One should release the animal after it has been carried around the fire. Consequently, since there is a restriction that "only these many are its limbs," and since the attainment of the essential form is already established even by the general rule (*codaka*), this sentence serves solely to exclude subsequent limbs; thus, by its result, it effects the exclusion of the state of being "unbound" (*avyadapūtvā*). And this being the case, there is no need for the labor of inferring another sacrifice or another transcendental result (*apūrva*).
Nor is there a remoteness in the injunction of the connection with the subsequent step;

for although the nature of the disposal (*utsarga*) is already established when that disposal is enjoined as qualified by everything up to the *paryagnikaraṇa*, nevertheless, because the collection of subsidiaries is enjoined with reference to it, it is stated as the very thing to be enjoined, since there is no extreme remoteness. This is the *Tantravārtika*.

In your view, however, there would be an absolute separation from the root meaning, as in the case of such injunctions as "for one desiring sensory power, [one should offer] with curd" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya*). Therefore, for this reason also, it is not a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*). Furthermore, because the inclusion of the subsidiaries ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation) is established through the context (*prakaraṇa*), the mention of the *patnīvata* cup is independent due to its being a restatement (*anuvāda*); thus, the designation [of it as a separate act] is refuted as being merely a partial reference within a qualified restatement. Consequently, it is established that this is an injunction regarding the [already existing] animal sacrifice (*paśuvidhi*). Moreover, the fact that the name [establishes a distinction] from the original rite is firmly settled.
How much more so, then, in this case where there is no cognition of non-difference from the archetypal rites?
That name is not well-known among the archetypes for anything such that a repetition would be made by the force of its being heard again.
Therefore, we consider that by the commonality of the injunction to "take" (gṛhṇāti), this one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) is enjoined as having the Jyotiṣṭoma as its archetype.
Nor is there equality with the *vatsānāṃ bhakṣa* (eating of calves) example;

for in one case, the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) is directly perceived, while in the other, although distinctness is assumed through an unerring name, the acquisition of all *jyotiṣṭoma* properties occurs via the verb *gṛhṇāti* (he takes), thereby establishing a connection between the substance and the deity.
Thus, when it is argued that this is a different sacrifice (*yāgāntara*), the following is stated in reply:
First of all, the deity is utterly remote; furthermore, even if the substance were being grasped, it would not have been appropriated by anyone.
Indeed, a substance cannot be perceived without its genus and quality.
Moreover, since the sacrifice has not yet been determined, there is no basis for inferring it to be like the Jyotiṣṭoma, by which it could be understood that "this is the taking of Soma."

Nor does the term *grahāti* (he takes) denote the Jyotiṣṭoma, for it does not deviate from its meaning as a mere expression of the act of taking (*upādāna*). Nor are these two [terms] names of the sacrifice such that they would divide it; rather, their status as names of the sacrifice arises from their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the act of taking. Indeed, we ourselves admit here that there is a distinction between the acts of taking.
However, by that much alone, there is no occurrence of a different sacrifice.

Furthermore, even in the case of a connection between a substance and a deity, the sacrificial nature (*yajimatva*) of such [acts] has been refuted by the principle that "preparatory acts (*saṃskāra*) are not injunctions" (*acodakāśca saṃskārāḥ*). Moreover, even that [sacrificial nature] does not exist here;
however, because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*), the word *agni* should be understood as denoting a ritual (*kratu*).
In the *Sampravr̥ttivārtika*, regarding the injunction "one should pile the fire" (*agniṃ cinute*), there is likewise this very doubt:

when it is stated that "one sacrifices with the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrificial terminuses to the fire," if the fire itself were the sacrifice, then it could not be sacrificed to as a subordinate element (*anuyajati*).
For in all cases, when there is a division between things that possess identical forms and identical properties, there exists a sequence of priority and posteriority.
For example, in the expression "he follows Devadatta," such following is only possible if Devadatta himself is also going; the same applies to "following-sacrifice" (*anuyajana*).

Therefore, since the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is heard [directly] while the sacrifice itself is inferred, this is an injunction for the sacrifice (*kratu-vidhāna*); however, in the latter case, being performed after the *Agniṣoma* and other rites, it would merely be a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to them, and thus the mention of a fruit would be a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

In the previous case, however, because of its independence, Ātreya [held that] the mention of the fruit constitutes an injunction of the fruit; thus, the distinction is that it serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) due to being an injunction of a fruit. The word *agni* is not etymological (*yaugika*) like *udbhid* and other such terms, nor is it joined with the characteristics of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), "being known from that" (*tat-prakhyatva*), or "mentioning that" (*tad-vidhāna*) by which it would be understood as the name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*).

As for what was said—that there is a "designation by that" (tatprakhya)—it would be so if Agni were enjoined as a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice; however, he is heard of in scripture precisely because his status as a subsidiary of the sacrifice is already established, being the object of the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) of piling (*cayana*).

The question—"Which substance?"—is asked with the intention of avoiding a contradiction in the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "piling. The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*), however, considering that there is no contradiction because the relationship between the object to be purified and the purifier is possible even through grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*)—just as in the case of "they thresh the rice"—states: "This [Agni] is fire... and so forth.

Therefore, since the word *agni* denotes its well-known meaning and the root *ci* (to pile) lacks the power to denote a sacrifice, and because there is no relationship between a substance and a deity [in this context], it is determined that the injunction means only this: "one prepares the fire by piling.
For if this word *agni* were in grammatical apposition [with the verb], then it would lead to difficulty, as if this accusative case were used in the sense of the object of the action.
