But this [usage] is an irregularity (*vyabhikaraṇa*) according to the *Mantravārttika*.

Here, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used in connection with a *karmapravacanīya* [particle]. The meaning here is that "the fire-altar construction (*agnicayana*) should be performed following (*anv-*) the *Agniṣṭoma* and other [sacrifices].
Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that sequential order (*paurvāparya*) occurs only between things of the same kind.
Sequence occurs even between things of unequal nature;
for instance, the expression "he enjoys the cooked [food]" is logically consistent.
Therefore, through that conjunction, the season would be designated by that name, and by means of it, the injunctions regarding religious duties (dharma) are established.

In cases such as "the praise of Agni" (*agneḥ stotraṃ*), one must resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) due to the lack of any other way; for what is expressed is a praise connected with fire, nor is the sacrifice itself possessed of that [fire].
Furthermore, since figurative indication cannot be resorted to in only one instance, it would have to be resorted to everywhere.
Therefore, when a direct denotation is possible, it is more appropriate that the word denotes the substance itself.

As for the discussion regarding whether the fire (*agni*) is fruitful or fruitless, archetypal or modified, permanent or non-permanent, and whether it is a modification of the *uttaravedi* or not—which was conducted by another commentator in this very section—that [discussion], although established in other sections concerning different examples and thus irrelevant here, has been inserted merely out of pride in one's memory; therefore, it should be disregarded.
This concludes the third quarter of the second chapter:
"In a different context, there is a difference of purpose."

The discussion concerning the distinctions between the characteristics of the qualities (*guṇa*), including their incidental ramifications—namely, what kind of quality, being previously non-existent, differentiates [the object], or what kind of quality exists therein—is now concluded. Since the five causes of differentiation have been established, the differentiation characterized by a change in context (*prakaraṇāntara*) is now introduced.
In that regard, first:
Just as the word *agnihotra* and others, when uttered in Pāṭaliputra or elsewhere, do not convey a different meaning, so it is even in another context (*prakaraṇāntara*).
For a different context does not manifest its power to denote a [different] meaning;

nor is it necessary that a different sacrifice (*kratvantara*) must be reached by means of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) alone, since the principal act (*pradhāna*) is also complete in its instrumental aspect (*karaṇāṃśa*), according to the *Tantravārtika*.

That which is being enjoined by its own word is contradicted; therefore, even in this case, it follows that those very [acts] such as the Agnidhra-initiation and so forth are intended. To this, it is replied:
for if the month were enjoined as something pure (independent), then there might indeed be an understanding of it as a reference to a previously mentioned action.
But this is not the case, because [the time] is heard as being subsequent to the *upasad*s; the time can be indicated by the *upasad*s that are already present.
Nor do those obligatory *upasad*s exist for their own sake or for the sake of another.
If, however, they were enjoined as having that subsequent time and the month, then there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) due to the injunction of multiple matters.
Even though this [quality] might apply to that specific Agnihotra under discussion,
nevertheless, because it is impossible there, one should state that the quality belongs to another ritual action.
In this regard, it might be argued that its equality to the Agnihotra follows from the syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*) with the phrase "having performed the Upasads."
That is correct.
Why?
Because it is logical that there should be no further attachment to that [statement], since nothing at all has been said without it.

Just as in this very context, in passages such as "for a month [one should sacrifice] with the Vaiśvadeva," until the word "yajate" (he sacrifices) is supplied, nothing has been stated and it must necessarily be supplied; here, however, the sentences concerning the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are already complete in themselves by their own words. Furthermore, the phrase "having cooked five times" (*pañcāvattya*) also has its purpose fulfilled within the preceding context and thus requires nothing else. Therefore, there is no reason whatsoever for it to be supplied.
If one were to desire *anvaya-anuṣaṅga* (the carrying over of a word) merely to avoid the fault of splitting the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), he might indeed do so;

however, because it is prescribed there that "having performed [the rite] again and again," it would follow that the performance of the *upasads* must continue for as long as that *anuṣaṅga* lasts. And this is undesirable, as it lacks the authorization of the Veda.

Now, if it were argued that the accomplishment of all the *anuṣaṅgas* (supplementary phrases) occurs simply by means of those [phrases] already placed before the *agnihotra*, then the utterance of the words would likewise remain in that state and assist the *agnihotra* and other rites in accordance with the order of recitation; thus, there would be no need for *anuṣaṅga*.
Therefore, the explanation [of the opponent] is not tenable, and it should be described in this way:
first of all, a distinction is not understood here merely because of the existence of a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*), but rather because of the interruption of the previous context.
And in all cases, regarding an action whose context has been interrupted, two types are heard in the *Tantravārttika* and other texts:
that which is to be adopted (*upādeya*) and that which is not to be adopted (*anupādeya*).
In that regard, that which is to be performed (upādeya)—such as the *āghāra* libation, the *pratipad*, and so forth—can be enjoined even when mentioned in another location.

However, that which is not to be performed (anupādeya)—consisting of place, time, cause, fruit, and the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*)—cannot serve as a counter-injunction for an action situated in another location; therefore, this mode of expression occurs:
"The action must be performed in that very [place]."
Now, if it does not enjoin [the month], then it is determined that it must itself bring about [the action].

In this case, the month cannot be enjoined by way of reference to a distant *homa* (oblation), for no one is capable of accomplishing a month on this very day merely by following a *homa* or similar act. Therefore, when the *pratihoma* and other rites are being enjoined with respect to the month—which is entirely independent and non-adoptable (*anupādeya*)—and since its power to bring about [the action] would otherwise be sublated by the originative injunctions (*utpattividhi*) located at a distance, the production [of the action] is effected right now. Furthermore, since a re-production of what has already been produced is impossible, it is understood as an original injunction (*apūrvavidhāna*).

Now, it might be argued that since terms such as *agnihotra* and so forth are co-occurrent with the original injunction (*utpatti*), they bring about the cognition of that very rite; thus, this injunction—which is occupied solely with the connection to the month—would not be a producer [of the rite], and therefore [it would not be a distinct action]. To this, [the author] replies:
"And therefore... [and so on].

If it is argued that where [a rite] is recognized as non-different even when occurring in another sentence merely through proximity, how can it be said that it will not be recognized when brought forward by a name occurring within its own sentence? It is replied:
for by means of proximity, the rite is presented exactly as it is understood in the sentences concerning place and so forth; thus, it is not different.
Furthermore, the name (nāmadheya) has already been explained as being dependent [on the verb], and thus it does not operate with respect to either difference or non-difference.

When the cognition of the operation of the verb is established—such as in "He offers oblations for a month" (*māsaṃ juhoti*) or "He sacrifices for a month" (*māsaṃ yajate*)—and one considers only the connection between the words *juhoti* and *yajati*, there is no recognition (*apratyabhijñāna*) of another instance such as *juhoti* because it does not recur within its own sentence or context.
Moreover:
By its name alone, the mere meaning of the verbal root is brought into proximity through its inherent power;
however, because the productive operation (bhāvanā) is not present [in the noun], it is determined to be distinct.
Just as in the case of a verb, even when referring to the meaning of the root, that which has become a substantive entity (sattvabhūta) is perceived.
By means of a name denoting a sentient being (*sattva*), exactly that [action] is presented;

yet, it is not the case that such an action is expressed by words like *agnihotra*, which denote objects possessing gender and number as real substances (*dravya*). Thus, due to this lack of recognition, the self is distinct, and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is merely a productive impulse (*bhāvanā*), since there is no hearing of the word *yajati* (to sacrifice).
For when that [action] is enjoined by means of its name as something to be undertaken by the self,

there occurs a difference in its meaning upon hearing a verbal root (*dhātu*) that is distinct from the name. However, in the case of the *sattra*, since the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is not heard, there is only a difference in the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) due to the recognition of the original sacrifice presented merely by the name.
Therefore, it is correctly stated that there is a difference in purpose in another context.

It should be understood that the author of the Bhāṣya, by saying "having performed the Upasads," shows that even a specified time, being of an impermissible (anupādeya) nature, serves as a cause for differentiation.
Now, if it be argued that "the Upasads are also enjoined," and so forth, this should be supported as a concessive argument (abhyupetyavāda), similar to the previous section.
In that context, the fruit has indeed been illustrated, and the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*) must also be illustrated.
[The phrase] "the *dīrghasoma* is to be performed" is employed for the purpose of refining the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

The expression "without reference to anything specific" (*anārabhya kiṃ cit*) is intended to indicate the absence of restriction by another context (*prakaraṇāntara*). In that case, the fruit should be enjoined with reference to the sacrifice, just as the *āhavanīya* fire and so forth are; for it is possible for that [fruit] to be desired even by one performing the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. However, he [the opponent] says: "There is an injunction of the fruit regarding the archetypal (*prākṛta*) rites."

The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin), however, considering that the status of the fruit as the objective of the injunction has been established in the *svargakāmādhikaraṇa* by the principle "and because of the connection with each object," says: "It is not possible to enjoin the fruit.

For if it were being enjoined, it would result in being fruitless precisely because it would become a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the action. Alternatively, even the action, if it were being enjoined, would be devoid of fruit, since it would be directed toward that [fruit].

The mention of "the fruit" (phala) is merely illustrative; however, all factors such as place (*deśa*) and so forth must also be cited as examples. Thus: "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices on level ground"; "One should sacrifice on the full moon day"; "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices for as long as one lives"; "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices"; and "From the remnant, one sacrifices to Sviṣṭakṛt. In all these cases, since [the action] is enjoined with respect to place and the other factors by means of the previous *adhikaraṇa*, it follows that they constitute distinct rites (*karmāntara*). And furthermore:

However, for actions being enjoined with reference to a specific place and so forth, it is improper to assume a restatement of their essential nature (*svarūpānuvāda*), due to the fault of simultaneous injunction and restatement (*yugapad-vidhy-anuvāda-doṣa*).
Therefore, when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that these are distinct actions (*karmāntara*), it is replied:
"Moreover, being the object of a reference (*uddiśyamānatva*) is not the cause of being a restatement (*anuvādatva*)."

There is no need for a further material offering (*upādāna*) because of the state of being subject to the injunction; for those two [the original and the modified offerings] exist by virtue of their attainment or non-attainment.

Furthermore, it is precisely this "reversal" (*viparivṛtti*) that is expressed here by the word "indivisibility" (*avibhāga*), because the cognition of the word "this" (*etacchabda*) arises from its specific nature as a distinct entity. Regarding the purpose, they raise an objection: since there is a cognition of similarity due to the use of the word "this" even in other ritual acts, just as in the case of the *Āgneya* and others, how can it be said that this is a sacrifice with a different material offering (*anyaviṣka*)?
This is a refutation of the [opponent's] position.
Just as in the case of "light" (*jyotis*) and other such terms, since the primary meaning of this word is established by its context, it is impossible for it to denote something else;
therefore, it is correctly stated that in another rite there is a sacrifice with a different oblation.
Thus have been stated the six causes of division (*bhedakāraṇa*) consisting of repetition (*māna*) and so forth.
However, in another commentary (*vṛttyantara*), only four causes of division are cited: difference of word (*śabdāntara*), name (*saṃjñā*), quality (*guṇa*), and result (*phala*).

This is because repetition (*punarśruti*) and number (*saṃkhyā*) are included within "difference of word," and because a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*) serves merely to introduce a result or other such factors.
This appears to be consistent with reality, and he will indeed state such things as: "There is also oneness because there is no difference," or "because of the non-differentiation of the word *go*.

Therefore, while the word is actually one, for one who does not perceive its difference due to some other cause, the postulation of it being a different word occurs; this is what you have stated in your *Bhāṣyamantravārtika*.

Furthermore, because it constitutes a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*), it has been stated that even in the absence of a difference in result and so forth, there is no non-distinction; this is seen in such passages as: "But in the case of proximity, there is no division," and "The repetition is for the sake of a subordinate element due to that proximity. Therefore, since it serves as the basis for recognition, a different context alone—supported by the result and other factors—should indeed be accepted as the cause of distinction.
Furthermore, the fruit [of the action] has not been determined because it is included within another section.
As for what was stated— that the fourfold reversal of the reason for unity, namely "because there is no distinction in conjunction, form, injunction, or name," serves as its indicator—
that too is not inappropriate, since in the present section, those other [reasons] are impossible.

Therefore, there are exactly six causes of differentiation as previously stated. Even so, within that established doctrine (siddhānta), it must be explained that the differentiation between names and different words, as well as between qualities and numbers, has not yet been mentioned; thus it is said: "Number also, when arising simultaneously and inhering in many [substances], is differentiated from other categories (guṇāntara) that were previously impossible."
Furthermore, it has been established that a scriptural repetition which serves no other purpose is a differentiator;
this is the third quarter of the second chapter.
And since this [passage] is of such a nature, let the Āgneya sacrifice be performed twice.
In this regard, another alternative is stated:
"Or rather, the repetition is for another purpose.

For when all possible purposes for a repetition have been investigated here and none are found—since no quality (*guṇa*) is heard [to be enjoined] and since exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) involves three defects—if it is accepted that the purpose is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), then why is there a discussion regarding the explanatory praise?

Having thus distinguished [the passage] by its explicit mention, one might think that it refers exclusively to the Āgneya [offering]; therefore, he asks: "What is the purpose of an explanatory passage (arthavāda) that is enjoined along with the injunction itself, rather than one located in another section that does not form a single syntactical unit with it? It is established that explanatory passages are supplementary to the injunctions.

However, this objection was raised from the perspective of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa); for there, since it is not specified whether it is praised or not praised, it is not understood what its specific object is—[the thought being] that "that very deity [is intended], regardless of whether it is praised or not."

However, this is not [the case] when viewed with absolute certainty; for it is seen that what was stated in the sūtra, "And the quality would be purposeless in the case of Mahendra," has been set aside by the praise determined from another sentence as referring solely to the deity.
Thus, the repetition is properly resorted to here in order to perform the praise together with Indra.

One should not be overly insistent on the claim that lifelong practice is a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*), because it is heard [only] in the context of the *Bahvṛca-brāhmaṇa* or the *Adhvaryu-brāhmaṇa*. Furthermore,

the distinction between "a property of the agent" (*kartṛdharma*) and "a property of the ritual action" (*karmadharma*) does not apply here, as it pertains to the subject matter of the *śeṣalakṣaṇa* (the section defining subsidiary elements).
Some say:
"Once the meaning of the momentary nature (*kṣaṇika*) has been concluded, an investigation regarding the river is also not contradictory, as it is being made due to proximity. That is incorrect.

Since the investigation into the differentiation of rituals (*karmabheda*) in other Vedic branches remains even now incomplete, if in that context the lifelong duration were enjoined as a property of the ritual itself, then the Agnihotra—being completed at evening and morning according to those specific injunctions—would be unable to fulfill such a long period. Consequently, by implication, it would have to be performed in a repeated form, like the Jyotiṣṭoma; for the requirement of "how" (*kathaṃbhāva*), being situated within the ritual, expects its constituent parts (*aṅga*).
And that [instruction] is established exactly in that way;
or rather, repetition will be enjoined by means of the time delimited by one's lifespan,
and since that can indeed be prescribed through the instruction regarding action, it is taught in this manner.
Furthermore, on the view that repetition is a property of the agent (*kartṛdharma*), there can in no way be a reference to the ritual action (*karman*).
And thus, since there is a single performance, the established practice of a long sacrificial session (*satra*) will be logically consistent.
Otherwise, however, because [the rite] would conclude every day, there could in no way be a resemblance to a *satra*; therefore, repetition is a property of the action (*karmadharma*).
In my view, the possibility of the word *yāvajjīvam* functioning as a direct denotation (*śrutivṛttitva*) exists;

for you, however, there would have to be a figurative application (*lakṣaṇāvṛttatā*) in that case. Furthermore, where the injunction is completed by both *juhoti* and *yajati*, that constitutes the meaning of the *codanā* (the original impulsion).
And for you, by abandoning the meaning of the verbal root "to live" (*jīv*), the two actions [of giving and sacrificing] are enjoined;
consequently, the injunction results in a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*).
To this, it might be argued that the word "as long as" (*yāvat*) in the phrase "as long as one lives" expresses time directly through its own primary denotation (*śruti*).

For example, in the case of the injunction "he should sleep until the milking," the mention of time (*kāla*) here is appropriate because this is a statement of a present fact (*vartamāna-apadeśa*); it does not depend on any causal motive (*nimitta*). Therefore, having set aside the milking as a mere matter of scriptural report (*śruti-vṛtta*), one grasps the time. However, if even here it were enjoined that "he should sleep or sit until the milking," then by what means would the milking be made the motive?
Furthermore, the word *yāvat* is not known anywhere as denoting time; rather, it qualifies the action itself by extending it up to its completion.
Since there is no difference between the action and its duration, one might object that [the word does not denote time].
However, when it is asked, "In how much time is the cow milked? specific units such as *muhūrta*s and so forth are indeed taken up as the delimiters of that time.
However, by virtue of repeated practice, even for ordinary people, there arises a capacity for delimitation based on the most common measure of time.

Furthermore, what is called "living" does not have a fixed measure like a *nimeṣa* or similar units, such that it could be accepted as time itself on the strength of its power to delimit; for the duration of one's life is not encompassed by a single ritual performance. (Tantravārtika)
If, due to a lack of full comprehension or otherwise, one performs [the rite] in vain, or if one employs it without prior practice—

supposing that one has indeed commenced the performance and, while performing some part of the ritual for a lifespan-limited sacrifice at some point in time, death occurs because its time is not fixed— if one should somehow complete it in the final state and yet not die, then because it was completed at a deficient time, there is the fault of acting contrary to what was enjoined. Or, if one were to die without completing it, even then there would be the fault of failing to complete what was begun.
Furthermore, there is no scriptural statement regarding the *sarvasvāra* sacrifice by which it could be completed even when [the sacrificer] has died.

Moreover, the injunctions for morning and evening [offerings], being recited in proximity to the lifelong and optional injunctions, would have to be assumed—without any authoritative basis—to apply solely to the optional domain under this view. However, if one were to think that both [the obligatory and optional] are intended to be accomplished by performing [the rite] only once in accordance with those [injunctions], then, just as when it is enjoined, "One should sacrifice with the *Paurṇamāsī* on the full moon day," the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled even by performing only a portion of it, the Vedic text—which results in the exclusion of other days—is not rendered superfluous.
Even if there were pervasion (*vyāpti*) in that case, it is not perceived here in this same way;

for, having passed over the interval between days until the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), the action is performed only to that extent, and the scripture has enjoined only that much—it does not establish pervasion. Furthermore, in the other case, since there is no possibility of a crow’s nest other than during life, there is nothing to be excluded; thus, in the absence of pervasion, the entire sentence would be meaningless.

Since the evening and morning injunctions are already established as occurring within the span of one's lifetime, the word "as long as" (*yāvat*) must be understood as encompassing the entire duration of life; otherwise, its performance in only a single part would be contradicted by the fourth quarter of the second chapter.
Therefore, these evening and morning injunctions, if they did not imply repeated performance (*abhyāsa*), would be unable to enjoin the person; thus, the indication [of repetition] is unavoidable.
For instance:
"Now, this fault of mine is indeed a fault of yours as well; or rather, you must state the distinction that my [resources] are exhausted every day for the purpose of feeding everyone."

And like the optional rites (*kāmya*), [the lifelong rite] is distinct; however, it is completed at your end, because your life is limited by its own duration. Since the performance of the ritual is completed only when the action is finished, the performance of the *aindravāyava* and other cups becomes unequal [to the lifelong rite]; thus, it follows that the injunction for lifelong performance entails a rule of repetition (*abhyāsa*). As for the claim that "repetition occurs by implication" (*arthāt*):

And because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*): for if it were a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*), it would be restricted by the initial commencement; and in that case, since another [action] would be purposeless, its non-occurrence would be called a "transgression of one's own duty" (*svadharmātikrama*).
For by the initial commencement, the contact with the constituent parts of the ritual action is said to be "not transgressed."

Furthermore, no one who is a performer of the Full Moon sacrifice (*pūrṇamāsa-yājī*) ever passes away without having commenced it; nor would anyone be a performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-yājī*) without performing them.

If, on the other hand, "transgression" (*atipāta*) were defined as the non-completion of the rite at its own proper time, then since such a state occurs for everyone who dies, the prescription of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) would be entirely purposeless.

For the *mātrī* [sacrificer] indeed, since the commencement and completion of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* are prescribed as the occasion for the *ujavana* [re-initiation] every month, a transgression is possible, as is the subsequent time, which falls within the scope of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*).
[Objection: But even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the monthly repetition is admitted, there will be a prescription of expiatory rites occasioned by that transgression.
[Reply: It is not possible to say this.

For when a specific cause is enjoined, the result must follow from that very cause and not according to one's whim; and here, the passing over (*atipatti*) of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and new moon (*amāvāsyā*) sacrifices is heard as the cause. Furthermore, the term [denoting the sacrifice] does not signify a mere repetition (*abhyāsa*), and the text demonstrates a distinct completion (*vyapavarga*).

If there were no distinction regarding time, the rule "having performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa" would mean, by the same logic as before, that the Soma sacrifice could only take place after all the repetitions of the Darśapūrṇamāsa have been completed.
Furthermore, it cannot be performed by one who is dead;
however, because of impermanence, this would not be the case.
Thus, he now places upon the framework of the Sūtra that which was previously stated in a detached manner.
For if it were a restrictive rule (*niyama*), this would indeed be so;

however, because of its impermanence (*anityatva*), it is not so in this case. Alternatively, having already stated that there is the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā-doṣa*) when the word "as long as life" (*yāvajjīva*) is taken to denote time, it is now asserted: even if such a metaphorical indication were accepted, it would still not be so because of its impermanence.

It is appropriate that a name be indicative of time when it is eternal and invariably concomitant with some duration of time, such as in the case of: "One should know that day on which the moon is not seen to be the new moon (amāvāsyā)," and so forth. However, the completion of the life of all living beings is not established in any fixed form from which time could be indicated by it; thus, it follows that this [name] occurs only when this [event] happens, and therefore, because it is non-eternal, it is established that this is merely a *nimitta* (an occasional cause). How then can it be called "eternal" (*nitya*) because its occasion is fixed? There is no fault here, for this is intended to mean that it exists as long as the body exists.

If the agent were the primary factor, then this rule of time (*kāla-śāstra*)—namely, "as long as one lives" (*yāvaj-jīvam*), which is your accepted view—would be merely a conditional cause (*nimitta*). This much is the meaning of the Sūtra.

As for what the Commentator stated regarding the "observation of completion" (*vyapavarga-darśana*), if that was intended to refer specifically to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, then it is redundant; if it refers to something else, that too is not understood due to its obscurity.
Therefore, it should be applied in this way according to the method of the immediate [preceding] verse:
"In your view, there would be no final cessation of the transformations; however, in our view, the established doctrine (siddhānta) that their cessation is observed will be logically consistent.
Alternatively, this may be explained as being equivalent to the conclusion (nigamana).
Alternatively, the author of the Sūtra has stated that this restriction is a property of the agent;
however, he has not explained what the status of the word "as long as one lives" (yāvajjīva) is. Therefore, he says:
"This being the case, the scriptural injunction regarding the Kāmya rites alone would be the occasion [for the performance]."

Alternatively, in the case of the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, since there is the mention of "as long as one lives" (yāvajjīva), they may indeed be rules regarding the performer's duty; but how is it so for the Paśu, Soma, and Cāturmāsya sacrifices?
To this it is said:

even there, the very scriptural injunction containing the suffix -kāna joined with repetition (vīpsā)—such as "in every spring, [one should sacrifice] with the Jyotiṣṭoma," and so forth—must be the cause [for their being duties].
This is not taught as being optional (*kāmya*), because that [optional rite] exists only as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) for as long as one desires; therefore, it cannot be stated in this way.
Furthermore, even if it were the regular (*naiyamika*) performance together with the subsidiary parts, the repetition (*vīpsā*) would still be purposeless.
Furthermore, there is no authority for determining that the spring is limited [to a specific duration].
Therefore, it is understood as "among those who vomit for as long as they live.

Moreover, even the locative case will have the sense of a cause (*nimitta*), just as in the case of *jīvati* and so forth; thus it is said that because there is a restrictive determination of the agent's property in all such instances, the scriptural rule regarding time should be understood as a causal rule (*nimitta-śāstra*).
By this very reasoning, the obligatory nature of the animal sacrifice, the Cāturmāsya, and other rites is established;
for just as a ritual action is perceived in its complete form in one Śākhā,
so too is it found in other Vedas through the mention of certain specific qualities.
The fourth quarter of the second chapter: There should be an option between the two *pṛṣṭha* hymns due to the injunctions found in other recensions;
for it would be redundant [to assume] they are obtained from the archetype if there were identity of the ritual action.
Or rather, because there is no distinction in their connection, form, injunction, and name,
and because there is recognition [of the rite] everywhere through its movement, form, secrecy, and so forth,
the cognition that it is a single action does not depart from the various recensions (śākhās).

By the mention of "studying one's own Veda" (svādhyāya), indeed only a single recensional branch (śākhā) is encompassed; and since there is an option (vikalpa) among those [branches] that have the same purpose, this will occur when the ritual action is one and the same.
Through connection with a single branch, there is the comprehension of the ritual action here.
It is logical that there is a diversity of actions, for a single moment of instruction is not composed; furthermore,
the designation is a product, as it is stated in the Kṛṣṇa, Kāṭhaka, and Ayukta-āmnāya.

Nor indeed are actions divided by that which has a beginning with respect to those that are beginningless; for although the designation [of a text] such as the *Kāṭhaka* is eternal because the genus (*jāti*) is eternal, nevertheless this [designation] is recorded as being based on the act of recitation (*pravacana*).
And actions are not recited, because recitation has sound as its object.
Therefore, even on account of this, there is no division of actions by means of a name; thus, even in the case of unity, [the distinction remains].
Nor is there a difference [in the rite] due to a difference in the number of skull-cups,
because a difference in the associated accessories (hāra) is not admitted.
Therefore, there will be an option regarding the means (sādhana) within a single ritual action.
But surely, it has been stated that there is no option because [the two] are prescribed by their respective originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*); this is not a fault.

Since both are equally strong due to the lack of distinction in being prescribed by their originative injunctions, how then is the unity of that which is produced by multiple sentences understood? We shall explain the clarification of that in the subsequent sūtra.
The repetition [of the example] like that of fire is an indicator of the rule concerning restatement;
or rather, it is for the purpose of excluding the charge of tautology.
Furthermore, because the statement regarding fire has a different purpose as it serves the function of an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) or a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), there is no repetition;

for since there is no distinction in its connection with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), the second mention in the section on the *disīya* sacrifice is intended to exclude other attendants (*parivāra*).
Or it is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); furthermore, that occurs where only as much [as the injunction] is heard,
and where there exists another thing to be enjoined within the same sentence.

Not even one of those [subsidiaries] is included here, because of the hearing of a repeated scriptural injunction (*punar-śruti*) regarding the principal rite, accompanied by its entire set of duties (*itikartavyatā*). For this very reason, the fourth chapter (*caturtha-pāda*), observing the connection with scripture (*śruti-saṃyoga*), considers that the subsidiaries are indeed excluded.
The remainder [of the discussion] is as follows.
Furthermore, this is not a case of repetitive recitation (punar-śruti). Why? Because the various branches [of the Veda] exist simultaneously; therefore, one cannot postulate a repetitive recitation.

For in that case, unlike the study of a single branch [of the Veda] which proceeds sequentially, it is not proper to study one branch after another— except for those branches received through tradition and connected by common recitation— given the immense labor involved.
The fourth quarter [of the second chapter] begins with the second [sūtra].

Even the principal [rites], though they are enjoined for the sake of the sacrificer by means of equal [texts] that do not admit a restriction to the sacrificer, relate to a single person even when they are found in all the Vedic branches.
Since there is a single fruit in that case, there is no combination; for if the fruit were accomplished by any one [rite], it would follow that the others are useless.

Now, if their meaningfulness is due to conceptual construction, then it would be better to postulate that very meaningfulness for the other recensions (*śākhāntara*), which have fixed subjects of exposition; thus, there would be no tautology. Furthermore, the mention of "completion" (*samāpti*) and the observation of the non-connection of the meanings [with the preceding] [would be inexplicable].

Just as from a single Vedic tree many branches are established through the basis of various ritual actions—like the many branches of a single banyan tree—if there were a division of ritual action for each branch, it would be like an incomplete [text] or a break [in the tradition]. In the view that there is a division of ritual action, they would not say that for those whose minds are not one, the entire recitation is completed only for them because it begins to diverge from the very start due to the absence of a single mind; rather, just as there are other flowers and fruits, other Vedas would simply arise from a different mental perspective.
"It is concluded": the *anvārohas* are mantras for ascending the sacrificial ground; regarding them, there are various recensions (*śākhāntara*).

Since they constitute a single ritual action in the form of a collection of injunctions, it is stated that "for those who perform the sacrifice according to the *Samhitā*, it is concluded, but not for us. Considering that even among students there is some variation in what is studied, and observing the similarity [of the rites], it is understood that the established unity [of the ritual] is justified by its conformity.

When options arise among men who have come together for a single purpose, that which is prescribed in proximity to it should be accepted as belonging to the context. While there are options among different recensional branches (*śākhā*), the manner-of-performance (*kathaṃbhāva*) of the seeker—which is enjoined by whatever [text] prescribes the primary act—encompasses only that [specific branch], not the other branches. Therefore, qualities residing in another [branch] are not required by the manner-of-performance; since they are not brought in by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), they do not become auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) and thus are not to be performed. Consequently, those qualities such as the *apatva* (sonship) which are enjoined as being connected by syntactical connection (*vākya-saṃyukta*) possess the capacity for inclusion.
But this does not seem appropriate;
for likewise,
even within each Veda, the specific context teaches the duties of the person.
Nor is that [text] which resides in another Veda invalid; the same should be understood regarding other recensions (śākhā) as well.
These are recognized as ritual duties (karmadharma), and since that very same rite exists in other recensions as well, there is no difference in their status as auxiliary elements (aṅga).

Even though the context (prakaraṇa) may differ, nevertheless, because it is determined that these duties are also grasped by this [text] residing in another recension, they are not distinguished from those grasped within one's own context.

Moreover, since the subject matter is not in any way limited by the specific recension (śākhā) even across all recensions, the effort required is indeed slight; thus, there is no incapacity [to study them]. Furthermore, because the sense of completion is established as being consistent, it does not lead one to postulate a difference [between recensions];
rather, the completion is understood as before, according to what has been known.

Even in the case of unity (*ekatva*), completion (*samāpti*) is stated as the indicative mark (*liṅga*); and just as there is a statement of completion, so too there is a statement of completion even in the case of plurality (*nānātva*). In that regard, because it conforms to the suffix, this justification for the statement [of completion] supports unity alone, since it depends on the commencement due to its being prior.
Alternatively, because the employment of words is preceded by conventional usage (*prasiddhi*), we determine that he has employed [the word] in such a way as we understand completion to be.

And since it is observed that he is employed even when the substance is not yet completed, once the objects to be known from its specific branch have been attained, there is therefore no contradiction.

Alternatively, because it is enjoined regarding the substance, there would be a fixed rule of inseparable concomitance; it would be established by the specific mention [of the branch]. Therefore, it must be a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*).
As for what was said—that there would be no observation of the sweeping of the altar in the case of the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice—[that is not so].
To this we reply: otherwise, however, there is no measurement of the altar and so forth;
rather, according to Bābhravātīka, the state of having a single sacrificial post (*ekayūpatā*) is praised by means of the absence of the eleven posts (*ekādaśinī*).

Alternatively, the repetition may be for the sake of a quality, or it may be for the sake of establishing the distinctness of the terminuses; thus the repetition of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* will serve that purpose.
Or rather, due to the connection with a specific order, the distinctness of the injunctions shall remain fixed within a single [terminus].
Or rather, the distinctness of the injunctions would be established based on the difference in *pratibhā* (intuitive flash).

For if that were the case, the rites prescribed in one's own *śākhā* would not undergo a change in their sequence, nor would they attain a different magnitude; since the matter is already understood through that very [intuition], it would be beyond words. If this is argued, [we reply] no, because the author of the Sūtras has stated this very point at the very beginning.
This is the fourth quarter of the second [chapter] of the Upādhyāya.
Therefore, according to the view that "it is indeed that very same [act]," the action is somehow intended to appear as distinct;
yet there is no other seventh cause, and thus the establishment of difference is exactly as previously stated.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the *Tantraṭīkā* composed by the great Kumārila; and the second chapter is also completed.
May there be auspiciousness!
Now, therefore, follows the definition of the subsidiary (*śeṣa*).

Whatever remains after the duties of the twice-born has been stated— even if it be but a small portion— all of that he began to speak; and thus, from this point onward, is the remainder, which is the debt (ṛṇa), because,
as was stated immediately before, "the remainder is for the sake of others."
In that regard, having first summarized the scope of the *tanmātra* (the specific) starting from the hair-like [subtle elements] and so forth,
one should demonstrate the two types of sentence-meanings (*vākyārtha*) by dividing them into two. For all [meanings],

there exists a state of determination that even those things falling within the scope of other sections— such as the sixfold categories of the employed and un-employed, the motivator and non-motivator, and those concerning the fruit, the action, and the subject of conjunction— are included within the category of "subsidiaries" (*śeṣa*), which constitutes the nature of the various types of subsidiaries.

The instigators (prayojakas) are the performers (prayoktāras), and they are indeed the principals (śeṣins) of the subsidiaries (śeṣas). Sequence (krama) is also a subsidiary, based on the single injunction of performance (ekaprayogavacana). For those purposes which are the means to a single result, whose assistance is established as being like that of a single word, and which are impelled by a single injunction of performance, there must be simultaneous execution (yogapadyānuṣṭhāna).

The sequence, which is subordinate to the efficacy of devotion (*bhakti*), being thus established, is determined by the force of the six means of proof known as textual order (*śruti*), direct statement (*pāṭha*), position (*sthāna*), principal action (*mukhya-pravṛtti*), performance (*krama*),

and the principle that "the person acts for the sake of the ritual act," as stated by Jaimini. Likewise, the relationship between those elements not explicitly mentioned and their governing principals (*śeṣin*) is established through the seventh [means] and others.
The determination of the remaining details— such as the nature, dimensions, and so forth of the Sahā world—

is established by the seventh [section] through the principle of extension (*atideśa*), which proves that "the remaining [details] exist. Thereafter, in the eighth method, there is the investigation of what belongs to whom.

The measure of the application (*prayoga*) is characterized by its own independent sowing (*tantrāvāpa*). This very [measure] is used by way of incidental mention (*prasaṅga*), because it subsists upon the auxiliary members for the sake of others.

The word *atha* (now/then) is employed after having intended one or all of the following meanings: immediate succession (*ānantarya*), reference to what has preceded (*pūrvaprakṛta*), or a specific topic (*adhikāra*).
Since the distinctions previously mentioned have not yet been fully explained, the definition of the "subsidiary" (śeṣa) is now commenced with reference to what was previously introduced.
To the question "Why?", the reason is stated as "for this reason" (ataḥ);
because it is impossible to define the subsidiary without first understanding these distinctions.

Therefore, immediately after this, that [subservience] is stated for the sake of understanding it; for the relationship of the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*) is possible only among distinct entities.
If there were oneness, it could not be taught: who would be the subordinate, and of which principal?
Furthermore, the definition of subservience must be stated immediately after difference.

The consideration of whether the instigator (*prayojaka*) and desire (*kāma*) and so forth are subordinate (*śeṣa*) depends upon this very relationship, which is accepted as that between the two chapters; for it is this alone that was stated by the author of the Sūtras, and no other was mentioned by the author of the Bhāṣya.

The connection between chapters and so forth is based on their subject matter (*artha*), not on the literal form of the text; thus, having first demonstrated the contents of the preceding and upcoming chapters in a concise summary, the connection between the two preceding chapters was stated by the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*) himself.
Here, however, it is established by the Author of the Sūtras (*Sūtrakāra*) himself through the words "Now" (*atha*) and "Therefore" (*ataḥ*), and thus that very connection is explained.
Furthermore, it is stated that "the definition of various rituals has been completed."

Indeed, the classification established in the first chapter— concerning the distinction between means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), mantras, traditional law (*smṛti*), qualities, injunctions of quality (*guṇavidhi*), names (*nāmadheya*), and the determination of doubtful injunctions through the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*)— has been restated in detail because it will be utilized individually in the various sections on differentiation (*bheda*) and so forth. Likewise, from the understanding of the *arthavādas*, sacrifices possessing qualities such as Viṣṇu and others are not [independently] postulated, because the injunctive power (*vidhiśakti*) is impossible for them.
Since the function of mantras is also the illumination of various meanings,
according to the *Tantravārtika*,
the gift of a cow (*godāna*) and the sacrifice of a cow (*goyāga*) do not become distinct [acts] merely through repetition.
Likewise, because the true nature of the relationship between word and meaning is determined through recollection,
and because there is merely an addition [of new elements], the sacrifice becomes distinct; furthermore,
that which is called "denotation" by others is said to have a beginning, being something produced.
If it were the case that a Smṛti could exist simply because the author indicated [the source] by means of the origin of the name— thinking, "This was performed by him"—
then the *Kāṭhaka* ritual would have to be called so because it was indeed performed by Kaṭha.
When there is a connection with something previously unknown, a quality (guṇa) and a name (nāmadheya) are both differentiators.

Therefore, qualities serve the purpose of differentiation in the cognition of [the animal] and [the number] seventeen; for the seventeen animals cannot exist in a sacrifice without a specific quantity.
The first quarter (pāda) of the third chapter:

Since there is accomplishment through the sense of the word "and" (ca), the determination of what is doubtful is established; however, this [word "and"] is not to be taken as having the purpose of expressing a restrictive statement.
Since the elaboration will be employed in exactly the same manner as before,
he will thus establish the systematic arrangement of the properties of the sacrificial butter, medicinal herbs, and so forth, according to the distinctions of action following the previous divisions.
What was stated as a secondary consequence— that the Ṛg, Yajur,
and Sāman [Vedas] would have the status of a source (*jāti*) for the Śruti— will be utilized in this context.
Thus, the two meanings of the word *atha* have been described.
The connection between the two chapters has already been stated; or rather, it is precisely this [connection] that constitutes its meaning.
However, whatever belongs to the speaker or the sentence that possesses a specific qualification (*adhikāra*) does not include the term *jijñāsā*, for that does not define the hearer’s own purpose.
When a burden is first weighed by someone who must carry it, at that time, how could one determine the "carrier" of that burden? Furthermore,
even an instigator is not an instigator unless he is subordinate to the principal object of the action.
Therefore, the consideration of that [subject] following the definition of the remainder (śeṣalakṣaṇa) will be undertaken.
This is the first quarter (pāda) of the third chapter.
[The subject matter is established] by means of the essential nature, the cause, the relationship, the authority for that, and the relative strength of the sources of knowledge.

[Objection: "Surely, just as the remaining [subsidiaries] are to be known, so too must the remainders (the principals) be known by us; both are true. [Reply: It is true that both should be mentioned in the Sūtra, yet both are not. For the second [category] is established through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), since they fall under one [of the two].
Because of the predominance of the principal elements (śeṣin), the definition of the subordinate elements (śeṣa) is stated by means of those principals;
however, that [definition] is not actually applied there, for it would have to be performed [there].
Therefore, in this context, the definition belongs only to the subordinate element, even though it is itself a subordinate [to the principal].
The subordinate element is indeed established by implication through the knowledge of that [principal],

as it is stated in the *Śruti* and other sources; for instance, just as the *nāvala* is not [the principal], so too, because it would contradict the status of the principal, our view holds that the scope of the subordinate remains precisely within the subordinate itself.
In this regard, "What is the *śeṣa*? is the proposition concerning the definition of its essential nature;
"By what reason? refers to that by which it is called *śeṣa*;
and it is proposed that the definition of that very characteristic, which exists within the sphere of the *kārakas*, will now be stated.

The third section establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by presenting that very same authority (*pramāṇa*) and demonstrating its status as a single coherent statement (*ekavākyatva*) through the method of beginning and conclusion; thus, even without the explicit mention of "sentence" (*vākya*), the application of the sentence (*vākyaviniyoga*) is stated on the grounds of "observation of the majority" (*prāyadarśana*). Following this, the application by means of context (*prakaraṇa*), order (*krama*), and name (*samākhyā*) will be explained exactly as formulated in the Sūtras. After that comes the section concerning the relative strength of the authorities (*balābala-adhikaraṇa*). Subsequently, there is the investigation into the conflict or non-conflict between direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and sentence (*vākya*) with respect to context (*prakaraṇa*), continuing until all [authorities] are considered in relation to the injunction for the animal sacrifice (*paśu-vidhi*).

The definition of the *śeṣa* (the subordinate) has been stated as "the *śeṣa* is that which exists for the sake of another" (*ataḥ śeṣaḥ parārthatvāt*). Furthermore, other reasons such as invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) and being dependent (*prayojyatva*) have also been mentioned by those who discuss the *śeṣa*.

In this context, "being for the sake of another" (*pārārthya*) is understood as the means to refute all [other definitions], not some other "remainder" (*śe�ṣa*), because that too is "for the sake of another. Nor do we accept it through any other reason;
rather, the two—the subject (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*)—are grasped precisely through their mutual restriction.
First, by virtue of existing only when that [other thing] exists (*tadbhāvabhāvitva*), whatever does not come into being without something else is the *śeṣa* (subsidiary) of that [latter].

For example, a sprout does not come into being without water and so forth, and a jar [does not come into being] without a lump of clay, a stick, a wheel, and so forth; thus, those [factors] are known as the *śeṣas* of those two [results].
To this it is replied:
for color, touch, and the other [sensory qualities] are always inseparable from consciousness;
yet, because they are of equal status, there is no mutual dependence among them.
Without a master, servants never exist;
likewise, their houses and so forth, as well as the remainder [of their possessions], are not accepted as belonging to them.
In this same way, there is a mutual relationship between the primary and the subsidiary elements, and among the subsidiary elements themselves.
The definition of "subsidiarity" (śeṣatva) as invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) would indeed be overextended;
by this [definition], it would follow that in the cases of Vedic study, the consecration of fire (ādhāna), agriculture, the acquisition of wealth,
and so forth, whatever is used for whatever purpose, that [latter] would be determined to be the subsidiary of the former.
Nor is the master engaged with the servant, or with [objects] such as form and touch as previously illustrated, in such a way that there would be an over-extension [of the definition].
Furthermore, even this definition of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) does not hold.
Why?
Just as the remaining [grains] are intended for that [sacrifice] by means of scattering the husks for the sake of success (*siddhi*),
so too are the oblations employed through the breaking, spilling, and so forth;
its status as a subsidiary (*śeṣatva*) with respect to that [sacrifice] is indicated by way of excess.

When it is argued that "since the injunctions for the subsidiaries (*aṅga-vidhi*) are always subordinate to the injunctions for the primary acts (*pradhāna-vidhi*), and the subsidiaries exceed the primary acts, this very state of exceeding is the correct definition of being a subsidiary (*śeṣatva*)," it is replied:

others, having observed subsequent injunctions following the primary acts specified by the initial injunctions and so forth, determine them to be subsidiaries because they are embraced as the conclusion of the injunction (*vidhyanta*).

The first quarter (pāda) of the third chapter. It has been stated that the author of the Sūtras intends by "subsidiarity" (*śeṣatva*) precisely the characteristic of being enjoined by a complete injunction (*vidhyanta*) capable of fulfilling the requirement for the mode of performance (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*) of a primary rite enjoined by means such as *samid* and others; to this it is replied:

if indeed the injunctions of subsidiaries were traditionally handed down as invariably restricted only to the ends of sentences or contexts (*vākya-prakaraṇa*), then one might rely upon this non-deviating definition.

Those acts such as the cutting of branches and so forth, which are enjoined at the beginning of the primary injunction (*pradhāna*), do not attain the status of being subsidiary (*śeṣa*) to the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) simply because they are enjoined at the start of the injunction. In the case of sentences and contexts (*vākya* and *prakaraṇa*) that begin with subsidiary injunctions, at the time when one must conceive of a purpose for those [subsidiaries] by satisfying their expectancy for "what is to be brought about" (*kiṃbhāva-ākāṅkṣā*), one observes the primary injunction which possesses an expectancy for "how it is to be brought about" (*kathaṃbhāva-ākāṅkṣā*). Since these [subsidiaries] are determined to serve the purpose of accomplishing the assistance required by that [primary], even those [acts] situated at the beginning of the injunction possess subsidiarity. Therefore, it is not the case that only an injunction located at the end of the procedure (*vidhyanta*) can be conceived as the definition of a subsidiary.
For that [auxiliary] does not assist with a distinct purpose from that [primary],
nor is any other cause for subsidiarity observed anywhere in the Veda;
as stated in the Tantravārtika.

Therefore, this definition of "subsidiary" (*śeṣa*) as "that which possesses a characteristic" is untenable; for even when one considers the word *mukhya* (the principal), nothing other than "benefit" (*upakāra*) is perceived.
Thus, benefit alone is to be understood as the defining characteristic of the subsidiary.
This being the case, the status of being a subsidiary (*śeṣatā*) would indeed become confused among all primary rites and subsidiaries, as well as among the subsidiaries themselves.
For just as the subsidiaries benefit the primary rites, so too do the primary rites benefit the subsidiaries by causing them to be performed and by receiving their assistance.
For what reason?
Because even the principal acts become subsidiary to the subsidiaries through their mutual assistance;
and because of this reciprocal benefit, they stand in a relationship of mutual subsidiarity.
Therefore, mutual subsidiarity follows from their mutual assistance. This [assistance] is not characterized merely by one being a subsidiary to another;
in this same way, the mutual contribution of the subsidiaries must also be demonstrated.

Consequently, when there is the performance of a single subsidiary (*aṅga*) within a modification of a single primary (*pradhāna*), it follows that there would be no restrictive rule regarding the performance of all subsidiaries along with the primary,
because nothing whatsoever can be accomplished without the assistance of those [subsidiaries]. (This concludes the first section of the third chapter.)
And once the entire characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is known, it is capable of consuming what is to be consumed;
therein, for those [auxiliaries] whose assistance has been observed, there would be the state of being a subordinate (*śeṣatā*) produced by that [primary].
For in those cases where the state of being a subordinate is not yet understood, no assistance is perceived.
Subservience (*śeṣatva*) cannot be determined as dependent on six [factors].

If it is argued that it will exist through an imagined benefit (*upakāra*), we say no; for before subservience is established, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for imagining such a benefit.

For when it is determined that something is the *śeṣa* (subordinate) of another thing—whether that thing be a result (*phala*) or a means (*sādhana*)—and one asks, "How will this assist that?", those who perceive no visible assistance postulate an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) one. However, as long as the status of being a *śeṣa* itself is not understood, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) could there be a postulation of an invisible [assistance]? Nor can it be argued that because [the relationship] is incidental (*prāsaṅgika*), the assistance is taught by the scripture; rather, having apprehended the assistance through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the status of being a *śeṣa* would be understood.
Thus, even in this view, the entire system falls apart.
Therefore, it is said: "The subsidiary (śeṣa) is that which exists for the sake of another," because its purpose is to serve that other. This is the explanation provided by the Prabhākara school.
However, another thing, even while being beneficial, is not designated as "for that purpose" [in the same way];

for example, the expression "smoke is for the sake of mosquitoes" is used even though it is harmful. Likewise, although the instrument (*prasādhana*) is beneficial, it is not designated as being "for the sake of" the prompter (*prayojaka*).
For no one drinking water from a stream of rice-water determines, "These were brought for my sake";
moreover, it is impossible to conceive of a purpose that is independent of benefit.
Why?

For the *prayāja* and other such rites do not attain their status as being for the sake of another (*tādarthya*) merely by proximity, independent of any benefit (*upakāra*). Therefore, since being for the sake of another is preceded by benefit, that [benefit] alone must be understood as the cause of subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*).
First of all, through direct scriptural statement (śruti), the fact that [the subsidiary] has that [principal] as its purpose is understood from the outset.
Even in other cases, because of its helpfulness, it is preceded by mere requirement (apekṣā);
for it has been stated that in the case of the Prayāja offerings and others, whose status as subsidiaries is already known, there is neither the perception nor the postulation of a helpful effect.

Therefore, when the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices require an auxiliary benefit and the prayāja offerings and others require that which is to be benefited, it is first understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*) that these [latter] serve the purpose of those [former], even while the benefit remains in an unaccomplished state. Since this is otherwise inexplicable, there is an assumption of an auxiliary benefit; however, it is faultless to maintain that subservience (*śeṣatva*) or service to a purpose (*tādarthya*) does not arise from the benefit itself, but rather from its necessary implication.

This being the case, since it is the direct Vedic statements (*śruti*) and so forth that, by way of establishing that [subordinate] purpose, are the applicators (*viniyojaka*) of the subordinate element (*śeṣa*), the definition must be commenced for the sake of distinguishing them. Furthermore,

even though there is a commingling of assistance among the subsidiaries, the primary rites, and so on, the establishment of their non-commingling is achieved through their respective "being-for-that-purpose" (*tādarthya*).

Therefore, it should be understood that the definition of *śeṣatva* (subservience) as "having another as its purpose" (*parārthatva*) alone is faultless; thus, the state of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*) itself is expressed by the result through the word "kāraṇa. One must not, however, fall into the delusion of thinking this is a different definition. But an opponent objects: "Since the meaning is already covered by the very definition stated in that [previous] chapter, there is no need to state it here. To this he replies: "But even in that case, because the other [entity] is indeed helpful (*upakāraka*), there exists some slight trace of 'being for the sake of that' (*tādarthya*). He further objects: "Moreover, since the matter is already established by the definition taught in that chapter, it should not be mentioned here."
Therefore, he says: "In that regard, the state of being for the sake of what was not previously established (apūrvatā) has been excluded.
Regarding this, some explain as follows:
"That is now stated."

The status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) which pervades all objects is indeed established here as the primary subject; it was introduced there for the purpose of refuting the theory of the *apūrva*.

Alternatively, disregarding the previously mentioned definition of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal, and following the previous method, the first quarter of the third chapter now addresses the definition of subordination as "being for the sake of another" (*parārthatva*) by means of other reasons.

Having raised the objection that this contradicts the acceptance of the definition of "benefit" (*upakāra*) in the rule "But those by which a substance is intended to be prepared," he now resolves that contradiction.

Furthermore, the demonstration of "assistance" (upakāra) was stated for the purpose of precluding the postulation of a distinct transcendental result (*apūrva*), and not because it constitutes the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*). Nor is it said that this is the ultimate definition of all subordinate elements; thus, there is no contradiction because their spheres of application are different. Even a quality such as "redness" (*aruṇā*) is a subordinate element by its very nature, due to its capacity to delimit the substance which serves as the means for the action. Now, it may be argued that the status of the word as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) was already stated in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*; true, it was stated, but it was not yet established.

In the *Tantravārtika*, it is stated that since its establishment depends upon the section concerning those desiring heaven (*svargakāmādhikaraṇa*), that [name] merely refutes the status of being a subordinate act (*guṇakarmatva*); furthermore, because the sacrifice is the means toward the fruit, its status as a subordinate element (*śeṣabhāva*) with respect to the person who is the principal (*pradhāna*) is not even mentioned.
Jaimini maintains that ritual actions also [are for the sake of the fruit], because they exist for the purpose of the fruit; this point has already been explained.
For no one acting with deliberation desires in this way: "May heaven obtain itself."
Rather, thinking "it shall be for my enjoyment," even the fruit [of the action] becomes a subordinate element (śeṣa) with respect to the enjoyer;
thus, by means of this section consisting of four sūtras, the entire subject matter of subordination has been established.

As for the refutation of the person's status as a subordinate (*śeṣitva*) at the end of the discussion— namely, that while substances, qualities, and preparatory acts possess subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*), this does not apply to sacrifice, its fruit, or the person— that is irrelevant. Furthermore, the claim that "his subordination toward the ritual act is evident because he is a substance" is both contradictory and redundant, as this has already been stated previously.

Furthermore, it is not logical to mention [the relationship] between the sacrifice and its fruit alongside the refutation of subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*), because their modes of operation are not equal. Therefore, this [objection] is invalid. Moreover, since it was already stated at the very beginning—under the first section of the third chapter—that substances, qualities, and preparatory acts possess subsidiarity independently [of one another], and since it has been established through the Sūtras themselves that the action, the fruit, and the person stand in a state of mutual dependence as primary elements with respect to substances and so forth, this [present argument] is seen to have little fruit, as its meaning has already been expressed.

However, the dual-natured character (*dvayākāratva*) accepted by the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntavādin*) does not apply to the sacrifice, its fruit, and the person; for the sacrifice and the fruit are exclusively the *śeṣin* (the primary), while the person is absolutely the *śeṣa* (the subordinate). Since the negation of that dual-natured character is possible only through the negation of whichever single aspect [of the three] is prohibited, these three are designated as having "equal properties" (*tulyadharman*) on this account.

Jaimini and others have established that even ritual actions (*karman*) possess the nature of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*) precisely in the form of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*), because they accept that subordination is characterized by subservience to another purpose.
[Objection: But if this is so, since the person (*puruṣa*) is a substance (*dravya*), [the opponent] who maintains the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) [in the *Tantravārtika*...]

Having accepted the status of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) once the status of being a principal (*śeṣitva*) has been refuted by the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntavādin*), it need not be stated that "the person [is subordinate] because he exists for the sake of the ritual action," since that very point has already been established.
This is not a fault.

Therefore, since both the sacrifice and the fruit are non-remnants (*aśeṣa*), its status as a subordinate element (*śeṣitva*) has been refuted. Consequently, as soon as the two preceding sūtras have established that the sacrifice and the fruit are both subordinates, it follows that—because the fruit is primary with respect to the sacrifice, while both are equally subordinate—their status as mere subordinates (*śeṣitva*) alone would prevail once their specific forms have dissolved. Thus, in order to restore their status as subordinates, it is stated: "And the person [is subordinate], because he exists for the sake of the ritual action."

Alternatively, considering it improper that subordination (*śeṣatva*) has been accepted on the basis of benefiting another, and intending to demonstrate that for this [agent] as well, subordination is established solely by virtue of being for the sake of another—just as in the case of the fruit and the sacrifice—he says:
"And the person [is subordinate] because he exists for the sake of action, not because he benefits it," and then, "Now, in this regard, the Blessed One... and so forth.
Now, this is not the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the opinion of Bādari.

Rather, having stated the general definition that "the subordinate (*śeṣa*) exists because it is for the sake of another," the subsequent detailed exposition is made by way of demonstrating its specific scope.
In that regard, in the previous commentary, the restriction was made in the prima facie view that subordination applies only to substances, qualities, and purificatory acts.

Now, however, having accepted Bādarāyaṇa’s view as the established conclusion (siddhānta) without refutation, the status of being a subordinate element (śeṣatva) will be described through both its definition and its elaboration;
therefore, by these sūtras, only the relative relationship of the subordinate and the principal is propounded.
But is it not the case that [this is already established] in the first pāda of the third chapter on substances?

Since even the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are primary with respect to their own constituent parts, yet subordinate with respect to the sacrifice, the relationship of being a subsidiary (*śeṣa*) and that which possesses a subsidiary (*śeṣin*) is merely relative.
For instance,
those qualities whose production is to be accomplished are, in relation to them, the possessors of the subsidiary.

Likewise, a preparatory act (*saṃskāra*) such as sweeping or threshing is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to the fire or the rice-grains; it is also a subordinate element to its own instruments, such as the broom, the mortar, and the pestle.
Therefore, the restriction [of the term *śeṣa*] is not established. To this, it is replied:

For substances, qualities, and purificatory acts are necessarily subsidiary (*śeṣa*) with respect to the sacrifice that bears the fruit; although they possess the status of being primary (*śeṣin*) with respect to their own constituent parts, it is said that [this primary status] does not exist with respect to that [sacrifice].

For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya also states that there is "necessarily a state of subsidiarity with respect to the sacrifice. He does not say "there is a fixed state of subsidiarity," because [the subsidiarity] is relative to others. In this context as well, the phrase "with respect to the sacrifice" (*yajiṃ prati*) is understood to carry over.
Thus, in the case of each [element], both subordinacy and predominance are observed.
For instance, the sacrifice— which consists of the substance— is predominant with respect to the person who accomplishes it, but subordinate with respect to the fruit.
And that which is a subordinate element (guṇa) with respect to the result can certainly be described as even more of a subordinate element with respect to the person who is the master of that result.
Likewise, it can be established that for whatever has primacy with respect to the person, its subordination with respect to the result is all the more certain.

Thus, because the fruit (phala) is primary with respect to the sacrifice (yāga), it is also primary with respect to the person who is its means; and because it is subordinate to the person, it is also subordinate to the sacrifice to be performed by him. Likewise, because the person is primary with respect to the fruit, he is also primary with respect to the sacrifice which is its means; and because he is subordinate to the sacrifice, he is also subordinate to the fruit produced by that sacrifice. However, this is not the case for substances (dravya), qualities (guṇa), and purificatory acts (saṃskāra); such is the distinction.

However, it should be understood that this subordinate status (*śeṣatva*) and primary status (*prādhānya*), which have been described even in terms of a traditional succession, is merely an indication of the purpose (*arthalakṣaṇa*) in its essential form as a thing;

it is not for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Otherwise, there would be no distinction between a subsidiary (*aṅga*) and a modified rite (*vikṛti*). Furthermore, if [the relationship were taken] literally, there would be a contradiction with the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the extension (*atideśa*) of both the result (*phala*) and the person (*puruṣa*).
Therefore, it is established that this summary of the subject matter—which consists of the remaining elaborations to be discussed—is of precisely this kind;

however, the masters of the *Tattva* do not accept this. For although there is here a consideration of the operation of various means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it has been stated that while the application (*viniyoga*) based on direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) occurs in this very section (*pāda*), the application based on indicative power (*liṅga*) and so forth will begin from the second section onwards.

The statement beginning with "the properties of the medicinal herbs" (*auṣadhadharmāḥ*) is stated even though it is to be established by this very section (*adhikaraṇa*), according to the intention of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Now, the proponent of the final conclusion raises a doubt on the strength of the Vedic text (*śruti*), asserting that "these [properties] are indeed connected [to the threshing]. However, the opponent, considering the connection with rice and other grains—which is produced by the relationship with other words—to be set aside by the injunction for pure threshing (*śuddhāvaghāta-vidhi*), says:
[End of the first quarter of the third chapter].
Furthermore, a word is not employed [in one sense] while being devoid of its connection to another word;
and in the section concerning sentences (*vākya-adhikaraṇa*), the remedy for the sublation of direct scriptural statement (*śruti-bādha*) has already been stated.
For threshing and other such rites, even when connected with rice and the like, do not cease to be threshing and so forth.
For if they were indeed [independent] in this way, then the scriptural statement would be sublated because it would contradict the Śruti.
In this case, however, since acts such as threshing cannot be performed in isolation, they must necessarily be connected with another element;
for threshing and the like are never performed alone.
But if it were not connected with anything at all, then there would be the consequence of the injunction being purposeless;
therefore, it must be explained in this way:
these ritual items such as threshing and so forth are not enjoined by the Vedic text as independent acts.
The threshing and other such rites are enjoined by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) as connected with the *brīhi* grains and so forth;
and their purpose being the state of being *brīhi* and so on, it is not accepted that they serve any other purpose.
Therefore, because they are specifically connected [to those materials], they would not apply everywhere to all things.

Furthermore, these [substances], such as the *navamāśa* and others, by way of the principle of the *adhikaraṇa*, abandon their status as being directly stated (*śruta*) and are connected as means to the *apūrva*.

And since that [connection] is not understood through the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*), but rather from the sentence (*vākya*) because it pertains to the aspect of being a means to the *apūrva*, he says:
Their connection is by way of purpose (*artha*).

Even if they were to be heard as denoted by isolated words (*kevala-pada*), nevertheless, when the expectation arises as to "where should they be performed?", they must be performed where, being performed, they become purposeful.
And these [rites], when mixed together, are not seen to be purposeful everywhere.

Even if [the acts] were not prompted by the *apūrva*, a connection is only possible through the accomplishment of a visible purpose; or rather, it is by the scripture itself that those acts are understood to be purposeful when performed.
