Since the threshing and other such acts are understood as being for the sake of that which was previously indicated by words such as "rice" (*vrīhi*)—namely, that which is inherent in the same object as the genus denoted by those words—they will not apply to the means of another *apūrva* that has not been so indicated, due to the absence of a connection.

Now, an objection is raised with the thought that there can be no fixed rule based on the observation of those [results], because it is heard that all [results] arise from a single apūrva, and because the specific characteristics and the lack of restriction are not understood, and because the purpose is only obtainable after the injunction (vidhi).
This very point is what we do not understand;
the intention is that it is not necessarily the case that only one apūrva is the motivator, nor even merely apūrva in general.
But that which is enjoined as the universal dharma (*sarvadharmā*) is superior due to its connection with specific causes and because it effects a particular state; he explains his own intention:
for the fruit’s subtle capacity, which exists in a state like a sprout, is called "the unprecedented" (*apūrva*) because it has not arisen previously, as was stated before.
And because that [sacrifice] is determined to be one due to the oneness of its hood (the *phana*),

the status of being its means (*sādhanatva*) is common to all— the clarified butter (*ājya*), the *aupabhṛta*, and the *sānnāyya*. Therefore, it is understood that all properties (*dharma*) prescribed with reference to that [sacrifice] belong to all [of them].

Even though there may be individual intermediate apūrvas for the Āgneya and other sacrifices, nevertheless, because they are fruitless, they lack the power to impel [the performance of subsidiary elements], just like the essential nature of the sacrifice itself. Therefore, it is determined that only the supreme apūrva (paramāpūrva) is the impeller.

Furthermore, even if the subsidiaries were impelled by distinct apūrvas, since they are enjoined with reference only to the means of accomplishing the apūrva within the context (*prakaraṇa*) without being specifically distinguished, and because specifying them individually would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), the injunction applies universally; this is the reason for their being common to all [subsidiaries].
And it has been stated that this is for the sake of establishing identity, due to the connection, the lack of distinction, and the lack of distinction in the context.
That which was previously [stated] as the cause for the connection with dharma—namely, being a means (*sādhana*)—is no different in the other case as well.
As for that which is distinctive, such as *vrīhitva* (the nature of rice), because it serves merely as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), it is not a restrictive factor.
Furthermore, even that which is characterized as being a "performer" (kāraka) is indistinguishable insofar as all [factors] are equally objects to be offered.

Therefore, with the exception of that which is connected to the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), that which is not an object to be offered, and that which is not a means for the *apūrva* of the primary rite (*prakṛta*), all [subsidiaries] must be performed everywhere.
That which is obtained by implication (*arthāt*)—being unenjoined yet obtained through capacity or through a worldly purpose—is restricted by that very observation.

Alternatively, where rituals (dharmas) are obtained by way of a purpose already established elsewhere—and where the purpose is not to be inferred from those very rituals—as is the case in modified sacrifices (vikṛtis), there the principle of "as much as required" (yāvadarthatva) would apply. However, in this case, since they are enjoined in the archetype (prakṛti) through direct instruction, they are prescribed with purposes yet to be determined prior to their specific purposes; thus, [the principle of] "the ritual would not be performed due to the loss of purpose" (arthalopāt akarma syāt) does not apply here.
The Bhāṣya explains [the verse] as follows: "Because the perceived object is absent, or because the object understood from the word is absent.
As for the result, it would occur together with the action; since the meaning of the word is non-existence (*abhāva*), it would follow upon separation.
As it has been stated: "Because there is no assumption of an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), there is no loss of meaning in the other case either."
If, even in the case of clarified butter (*ājya*),

acts such as spreading (*prathana*) were to be performed directly for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*) because there was no other way, or if no visible purpose (*dṛṣṭa*) were to exist at all, then that scriptural injunction (*āmnāna*) would be established as having a visible purpose through some other means; thus, the impossibility of *arthāpatti* (presumption) [as a separate means of knowledge] would follow.
In other cases, however, there is merely physical movement;
and when the performance of an action with a result is possible, a desire for a fruitless performance cannot compel a person to act. This concludes the first quarter of the third chapter.

This results in a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*), because it is accepted that the injunction depends on the result and the result depends on the injunction; the same logic should be applied to the acts of purifying (*utpavana*) and so forth with respect to the clarified butter (*ājya*) and the *sānnāyya* offering.

Likewise, even if a certain purpose has been perceived through direct observation, if it does not contribute toward assistance for the sacrifice or the person, it should not be adopted; however, this is not the case here, for when there is a separation from the visible result, that which arises from its absence [is what must be considered].
Having extracted the meaning of those words, there is likewise a conceptualization of a visible purpose;

for indeed, otherwise these [rites] would be prescribed everywhere, whether they were prompted by the supreme *apūrva* or prompted by every *apūrva*. And in that case, they would be so only if there were no distinct *apūrvas* for the various rites such as the *vrīhi*-grain offering, or if these [rites] lacked an impelling power (*prayojaka-śakti*).
In this regard, the distinction [between the various types of sacrifices] has already been established in the *Apūrva* section.

Although these [subsidiary acts] do not have results directly, they will nevertheless possess the character of being motivators (*prayojaka*) precisely because their own essential nature could not otherwise be established.

Nor are they fruitless; for that which is called "fruitless" becomes non-motivating only if it is absolutely devoid of result, or if it has already attained its own existence independently of them—such as the substances, the sacrifice, and so forth, in their own form.

The intermediate *apūrvas* (unseen potencies), such as those pertaining to the Āgneya and other rites, possess results only through a mediated succession (*pāraṃparyeṇa*), because they serve as constituent factors for the accomplishment of the ultimate *apūrva*.
Furthermore, these are not established prior to the ritual acts (*dharmas*), nor are their means or extent already determined.
Therefore, they are employed solely for the purpose of attaining their own existence.

And that which, when certain factors (dharmas) are being enjoined, brings about a transcendental result (*apūrva*), is the motivator (*prayojaka*) of those factors; it is not merely anything at all. By means of words such as "rice" (*vrīhi*), only the *apūrva* whose accomplishment is its own specific function is brought forward, and nothing else, because of the lack of connection.
This he demonstrates:

since the fruit of the injunction is seen to reside precisely in the rice and other materials mentioned together with actions such as threshing (*avaghāta*), by way of being the means to accomplish its own *apūrva*, therefore there is no transfer [of the injunction] elsewhere.

If, however, there were no *apūrva* (transcendental result) therein, then an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) would have to be postulated by implication; furthermore, even an assistance not presented by words such as "rice" (*vīhi*) would have to be assumed as the motivator. But since that [assistance] exists, because there is no purpose for the *apūrva* of threshing and so forth in its absence, the connection with the *sānnāyya* (offering of milk) and other elements must also be the meaning of the word, either through the mediation of a remote ultimate *apūrva* or through the mediation of the *apūrva* of another ritual act.

In this way, because there is no distinction in the relationship with the apūrva (unseen potency) of the Āgneya and other sacrifices, threshing and so forth would apply to the *sruk* ladles and other implements.
This is not a fault. [End of] the first quarter of the third chapter.

Because they are not perceived as distinct causal factors (*kāraka*), just as the *sānnāyya* and other offerings are not grasped [as part of the same procedure] despite being equally objects to be offered (*pradeya*), because they serve as means for different *apūrvas*; so too, even though there is a connection with a single *apūrva*, the *sruc* and other vessels are not included, because they lack the status of a causal factor in the form of an object to be offered that is inherent in a single purpose.

However, those things which will assist that very same *apūrva* by way of having the same causal status (*samāna-kārakatva*) shall indeed possess the ritual properties (*dharma*). We shall explain all of this in detail in the ninth book (*navama-adhyāya*).
The relationship of origin between the *sphya* and other implements and their functions, such as digging, is established;

in that regard, the statement "these are the sacrificial implements" merely reiterates what is already known. Because of the connection with the word "vai" (indeed), this has the character of a restatement (*anuvāda*). Furthermore, there is no injunctive word here expressive of productive activity (*bhāvanā*) that could either apply or enjoin them.
Furthermore, many more statements would be meaningless in your position;

for there is no purpose whatsoever in their being mere restatements (anuvāda). Moreover, by virtue of their own expressive power, these [statements] are applied specifically to the acts of threshing (*udvapan*) and so forth.

In the sentence concerning the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*), the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) refers figuratively to the constituent parts of the sacrifice by means of indirect indication (*parokṣavṛtti*), and the word "implement" (*āyudha*), which denotes an instrument of hurling, is used metaphorically for the instruments of other ritual actions.
Furthermore, the principle of the seventeen *aratnis* does not apply here;
for in this case, unlike the expression "of the Vājapeya," we do not observe a genitive case after the word "sacrifice" that would denote a mere relationship.

Furthermore, even if they were to descend as subsidiaries because of their lack of purpose [otherwise], the general rules (*sāmānya-śāstra*), being restricted by the specific rules (*viśeṣa-śāstra*) connected with the *ūna* and so forth, would not be connected with other rites.

Therefore, when these items have been brought forward by the sentences concerning the *ūna* and so forth, this phrase "these indeed are ten" restates (*anūdya*) that very nature of theirs which we perceive as being sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*).
As for the objection that there is no motivating factor (*prayojaka*) in the form of a difference in the unseen potency (*apūrva*), [it is answered as follows].
To this we reply:
First, there is indeed a distinction between the *pūrva* (unseen potency) of the *puroḍāśa* and that of the *kapāla* (potsherds) and so forth.

As for the others as well, because they function through means such as the act of turning over (*udvavana*), there is no confusion [of their functions], since the assistance rendered by them does not exist elsewhere.

For example, threshing and other such acts are not performed on the *sruk* ladles and the like, even though they share the same prior connection [to the sacrifice], because they are different types of instruments (*kāraka*).

Now, if it is asked: "Since the words *piṅgākṣī* and *kahāyanī* are also adjectives denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*), there is no substance (*dravya*) in this sentence; how then can they be called adjectives?"—[the answer is that] this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound prescribed in the sense of the possessive suffix *-matup*.
The possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is applied only when there is a relation [expressed as] "it has X";
for one who is not related to cows is not called "possessing cows" (*gomān*).
Therefore, in that case, the relation is first required as the qualifier.
However, because the relational cognition (*pratyaya*) exists therein, it is apprehended.

If that [relational cognition] is apprehended, then since the relational cognition is established by that very [apprehension], there is no expression of the substantive (*viśeṣya*) due to the obstruction of the capacity for expression.
Furthermore, the relational cognition does not arise from the cognition of the substantive.

Prior to the relation, there is an absence of the status of being a qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*), and once [the word] is established as a qualificand, there is no further purpose for the relation; thus, it follows that the relation would simply not be cognized.
Therefore, because it is the first thing to be made known, the relation is the meaning of the suffix.
For this reason also, the relation is the meaning of the suffix.
For it is held that the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) denotes the ground for the application of a word.
When it is said, "Devadatta’s possession of cows" (*gomattva*), both the cows and the relationship are understood.

Thus, when "Devadatta’s possession of cows" is stated, since there is no cognition of the cow itself [as a separate object], it is concluded that the meaning of the abstract suffix consists precisely in the extraction of the relationship.

Furthermore, if the relationship is expressed by the possessive suffix (*matup*), then, according to the principle that "the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together," the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) produced from the nominal stem *gomat* ought to denote the relationship; it cannot do so otherwise.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the relationship is the meaning [of the suffix].
By this, all derivative (yaugika) words—whether formed by primary suffixes (*kṛt*), secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), or compounds (*samāsa*)—are explained.

For in every case, a suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) expresses a relationship, as in *rājapuruṣatvam* (the state of being a king’s man), *āpagavatvam* (the state of being a river), and *pācakatvam* (the state of being a cooker). It is for this very reason that these are called derivative; they function on account of that [underlying] cause.
Therefore, because they have the possessive sense (*matvartha*) as their object, words such as *vaibhītaka* and *ekahāyanī* express a relationship.
Furthermore,
in the expression "one year belongs to her" (*ekaṃ hāyanam asyāḥ*), the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is indicated by means of the genitive case-ending.
Furthermore, because the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) has the meaning of a suffix (*pratyaya*), it possesses predominance here.

The employment of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*) is precisely for the purpose of showing that form [of the genitive], since an inflection (*vibhakti*) alone is never used, and because there is no comprehension of the meaning of a pronoun [when it is absent].
It is well known that the genitive expresses a relationship such as that between owner and owned, or relationships such as a collection, a derivative, or a part.

Even according to the theory of verbal relation (*śrutasambandha*), the expression of the connection would involve a great deal of prolixity; furthermore, the universal (*jāti*) cannot be determined as the meaning of another word [in a compound],
for neither its connection with "tawny eyes" nor its state of being "one-year-old" belongs to that universal.
Although it might be argued that the state of age (*vayovasthā*) is denoted as that which bestows [the capacity for action] at one time,
nevertheless, it is understood that this is merely a quality (*guṇa*) and not a substance (*dravya*).
This is stated [as follows]:
If the relationship were expressed by words such as *ekahāyanī*, then they would not be cited as examples;
however, the relationship is not expressed by these [words].
Why? Because it would involve excessive prolixity (*atigaurava*).
For here, one must consider whether the denotable object is the mere relation itself or a specific instance of it.

If it were merely the relation, then all derivative (yaugika) words would result in having a single common referent, which would lead to their synonymy; furthermore, having denoted that [relation], there would be the excessive burden of denoting the relation once again.
If a relation can be understood through the related term itself,
who would then postulate a further denotative power for the word?
Therefore, the relation must necessarily be one that is implied by the meaning.
As for the claim that "if the relation is not perceived, the qualificand is not perceived," we reply:
for Devadatta is intended to be qualified by the cows.
Cows that are not established on the earth do not serve the purpose [of providing milk];
in that case, what can be said? Is the earth itself also denoted [by the word "cow"]?
Thus says the *Tantravārtika*.
The mere activity of the speaker is the consideration of the relationship;
for he does not intend to speak of one possessing cows when [the object] is not connected with cows.
For in every case, the order of the listener occurs as the reverse of the speaker’s action.

First, the speaker intends a certain qualificand; then, because he is unable to express it without some qualifier, he intends the qualifier; thereafter, he utters the words. The listener, moreover, first hears the word, then the qualifier, then the qualificand, and finally grasps other things for the sake of its logical consistency. Therefore, even if the connection was considered by the speaker beforehand, the listener will nevertheless grasp it only afterwards.
But in this case, it is not even apprehended by the speaker as having previously been established as the substantive (viśeṣya) conjoined with its qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa).
The word "gomat" (possessor of cows) will denote this [person] as "one distinguished by cows";
however, the relationship is not understood in the form expressed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*).
It would have to be stated in some other form, yet no such defining rule (*lakṣaṇa*) exists.
In this regard, the first quarter of the third chapter [begins]:

Should one rely on the denotation of a relationship that is not itself an entity (*asattvabhūta*), or should the related object itself, as qualified by that [relationship], be denoted? Let it be stated:
as for the claim that "once the qualificandum is established, there is no further need for the cognition of a relationship," [that is incorrect].

It is true that [the meaning] does not exist; however, since it is understood as being inseparable (*nāntarīyakatva*) even without that [suffix], what can be done? Furthermore, regarding the claim that this [term] has the sense of possession (*matvartha*) because it is expressed by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), we say this:

in the case of "the state of possessing cows" (*gomattva*), which is the state of one who possesses cows (*gomataḥ*), the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) has as its meaning the cows as a qualifier; and since there is no cognition of absolute difference between them [the cows] and the person, they are not grasped by that [abstract] suffix.
Therefore, just as [the word] *taṇḍin* denotes only that which is connected [to the rice],

so too by means of derivative (*yaugika*) words such as *pādapa*, the referent of the compound is the external object (*anyapadārtha*), because the meaning of the sixth case (genitive) is predominant; thus, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound based on a connection.

To this it is replied: if the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) were indeed the related member ending in the genitive case, then— just as in the expression "the king’s man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), where the king, by virtue of having the genitive suffix,

becomes a qualifier of the man, and the man, by virtue of ending in the nominative, becomes the primary meaning of the compound— likewise, in the case of words such as *citragu* ("possessing brindled cows"), only the cows qualified by Devadatta and others would be understood, and not Devadatta and others qualified by the brindled cows.
Even if the analysis (*vigraha*) were otherwise, nevertheless, because the meaning is seen to be obscured at a later stage, the analysis must be performed in this very way;
and that [obscuration] does not arise from the predominance of either the prior or the subsequent word-meaning,
nor from the determination of the predominance of the substance (*dravya*) which has become the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*).
This is a variegated individual; this [object] is a substance possessing various qualities.
A quality has a single substratum, while action has multiple substrata;

thus, in this case, because the genus (*jāti*) is beginningless, it cannot serve as a qualifier for this [action], which has a single substratum. Therefore, the individual (*vyakti*) is resorted to [as the locus].
For even though entities are infinite, by taking one as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*),

the connection of the word becomes easy to establish and will not be subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*); nor will there be its application to anything other than those characterized by it— thus, there is no deviation.

In every way, even when a series of qualifiers persists at a great distance, the perception of a relationship will be established because there is no difference from the first indicator. Furthermore, the status of being the word-meaning belongs to both the very first and the very last [qualifiers];
however, those situated in between are not denotable because their cognition is established through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Therefore, by means of the qualities "tawny" (*piṅga*) and "eyed" (*akṣi*), their respective individual instances—which consist of qualities and parts—are indicated; by those [instances], the composite substance (*avayavidravya*) is indicated.

This is logical in the case of words such as those ending in a deity-suffix (*devatātaddhita*), because there the addition of a word serves no other purpose than to denote the "referent of another word" (*anyapadārtha*).

However, in cases such as *citragu* ("one who has brindled cows"), since the two words *citra* and *go* denote meanings that are entirely distinct, and since they cannot be brought into grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words like *Devadatta*—either directly or through indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—[the compound must be analyzed differently].
Furthermore, since the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) is understood even prior to the word "Devadatta" and so forth, it cannot be considered the meaning of the sentence.
Nor is it the case that only those two word-meanings apprehended at the time of compounding are related to the referent Devadatta, such that Devadatta would be the meaning of the sentence.
Therefore, one must necessarily accept that the meaning of another word is both denoted [by the compound] and recalled through cognition.
And thus, its predominance will not be contradicted.

Furthermore, since the capacity of a *bahuvrīhi* compound to denote an external referent (*anyapadārtha*) has been observed in such cases as these, even where a [direct] denotation might somehow be possible, it is determined that the status of being the expressed meaning remains due to the non-abandonment of the previously established figurative application (*bhakti*).
Therefore, it is logically established that words such as *piṅgākṣī* denote substances.
As for the claim that "one year" (*ekahāyanyā*) is a word denoting age, that is untenable;
for by that very fact, this meaning alone is determined, and thus a connection with the act of purchase (*kraya*) need not be suspected.
To that end, he says:
Furthermore, a word that has attained the status of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) will not express an object that is unfit for consumption.
This inclusion within the same sentence and the use of the instrumental case ending also produce a firm cognition that [the *cāyanī*] is a qualifier of the purchase alone.
Consequently, because of the authority of the word and yet the contradiction with the actual state of things, a doubt arises as to what is consistent and what is inconsistent.
In this regard, because it is primary, [the author] first introduces the connection with the action in accordance with the word,
since a Vedic word cannot bear too much a burden.
Therein, by the force of the application (*viniyoga*), we shall endeavor to investigate the existence of the object's inherent capacity (*vastu-sāmarthya*).
Therefore, if it can be established by some means or other, then we shall accept that it is indeed included within the purchase (*kraya*).
But if it cannot be established in any way whatsoever, then, having admitted a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), we shall determine this to be a property of the context (*prakaraṇadharma*).
And in this matter, there is no [inconsistency] in the *Tantravārtika*.
The "division" (*bheda*) characterized by the repetition of any one of the [words] beginning with "pratyaya" is what?
What, then, is its nature as a division?
The meaning is: having accepted the division of the sentence of purchase (*krayavākya*) as being characterized by separation (*vibhāga*).
"Splitting the sentence" (*vākyabheda*) means that it divides the sentence into separate parts.
Having accepted such [a division], there is a determination of the property belonging to the context (*prakaraṇadharma*).
What is meant is this: as long as two [independent] sentences are operative, there is no status as a property of the context.

But when those two [the word and the sentence] have their power destroyed by contradiction with the actual state of things and thus become inactive, then there is application according to the context.
What, then, is the prima facie view?
Therefore, this very word is thus divided by the sentence.
That individual who is enjoined as an instrument for the sake of the *apūrva* (the unseen spiritual result) must therefore be colored by all the instruments;
however, that which is prescribed as another factor of action, such as the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and so forth, is different.
The first quarter of the third chapter:
It has been determined that this quality is not a subordinate part (śeṣa) belonging to it, even though it serves all purposes;
and thus, even without a possessive suffix (*matvartha*), these [words] attain grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the substance.
For the meaning to be expressed is not conveyed by the omission of words;
therefore, in that case, both capacities are understood,
and the grammatical treatise does not provide an explanation based on a single moment.
Furthermore, since form and the other [sensory objects] do not arise as momentary entities, they would have to exist without the possessive suffix *matup*.
Just as one says "the fragrance of sandalwood," there would likewise be the usage "the form of a cow" even without an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*).

And just as when "fragrance-ness" (*gandhatva*) is mentioned, the connection with specific instances such as sandalwood is set aside, and the connection with "fragrance-ness" itself occurs for those particulars; [so too would it be here].

In this way, even in the case of "formlessness" (*arūpatva*), there would be no connection with a substance. Furthermore, just as in the case of words like "water" (*apa*), there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between [the word] and a substance such as redness (*aruṇa*). For one who thinks that coreferentiality in the case of "water" and so on occurs through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), for him it would likewise apply to "form" and so on, or to qualities such as redness; for they do not state anything additional at all. By this, the consequence of the elision of the possessive suffix *matup* after "redness" and so on is explained.
Furthermore,
does it not follow that for words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*), the gender and number are determined by their substratum (*āśraya*)?
No, because this would lead to the over-extension (*prasaṅga*) of such rules even to cases like "form" (*rūpa*) or "whiteness" (*śuklatva*).
Moreover,
"that which expresses a quality" (guṇavacana) is not so called merely by denoting a quality; rather, it is that which, having expressed a quality, applies to a substance (dravya).
For the word "utterance" (*vacana*) is not employed in any other sense;
since the very nature of sound (*śabda*) is utterance, the conventional usage is established by the term "group" (*gaṇa*) alone.
For this very reason, there is no separate mention of "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth.
By this, the statement regarding the elision of the *matup* suffix is explained.

Therefore, the word "red" (*aruṇā*) denotes a substance; and since it is possible for that [substance] to express its status as a factor of action (*kāraka*), the unity of the sentence is established.
Consequently, it does not follow that [the quality of redness] applies to all ritual elements (*sarvadharma*).
The phrase "this is unseemly" means that it is unsatisfactory because it contradicts the logic established in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*.

For it has been stated as follows: since the substance, which is invariably related to the universal, is already understood through its very connection with that [universal] once the universal has been denoted first by virtue of being the qualifier, it is impossible to postulate that the substance itself is the direct meaning of the word.
The first quarter (pāda) of the third chapter.
Now, it might be argued that at the time of the production of another quality, the substance itself is indeed different, and thus there would be no deviation [from the rule];
however, for those—such as the Paiṭharas—who maintain that pots and other such things are cooked as mere products of action (*kāryadravya*), according to their view, there is indeed non-difference.
However, there is a deviation even in the case of the Pailukas regarding atoms.
For, as we have described substance, in every such case it is only the qualities that differ, not the essential nature itself;
therefore, this [position] is far removed from the conventional usage of "form" (ākṛti) and is quite clumsy.
As for the objection that this is not so because of the primary cognition (*mukhya-pratyaya*), it is replied as follows:

In the case of "The boy is fire" (*agnir māṇavakaḥ*), because there is an absolute difference between the fire and the boy, everyone knows that the single word, though applied due to similarity, does not denote [the boy] because of the distinctness of the cognition. However, in the case of those words which, being denotative of a genus (*jāti*) or a quality (*guṇa*), cause the substance (*dravya*) to be cognized, there is no distinction between the expressed meaning and the thing being denoted; thus, even when they are perceived, the lack of distinction remains. This [lack of distinction] is somehow removed by skillful investigators through the methods of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
However, for the world, there is only the cognition of a "cow.
Nor is there a contradiction with the world for those investigators who maintain that [the universal] is inexpressible;

for the world, which operates solely on the basis of what is conventionally perceived, does not object when an investigation is carried out by an investigator—remaining indifferent while not making a distinction between the name and the object—in order to establish the generalities, particulars, sublation, and so forth.
Therefore, there is no contradiction.

To the questions, "Why is there not also an elision of the *matup* suffix through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in words such as *rūpin*, and why is the function of the *nañ* suffix explained by the grammatical treatise [only] in certain cases?"—it is replied: in some meanings, the power of the *nañ* suffix is as firmly established (*nirūḍhā*) due to its having been in use since time immemorial as the primary denotative power (*abhidhāna*) itself, as is the case with words like *aśakta*.
In some cases, a name is applied according to its function, as in the case of the *cakravāka* bird being called "chariot-part" (*rathāṅga*).
In other cases, however, it is impossible even to apply one, such as in the case of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
But how is it that here, despite the presence of a specific conjunction, the term "eating" (*jakṣa*) is not applied?
Regarding this, the answer is: "It is like the word 'white' (*avadat*).

Just as for you, although the words *śukla* ("white") and so forth are equally verbal expressions of a quality (*guṇa-śabda*), they denote a substance in which the quality is subordinate (*guṇopasarjana-dravyavacanatva*), whereas words such as *rūpa* ("form") do not; so it is for me as well.
In that regard, this is the reason.
It is said: "The power of primary denotation (*abhidhāna-śakti*) is innate, whereas indication (*lakṣaṇā*) requires a cause beyond the [primary] relationship.
To this it is replied:
this might be so in the case of arbitrary words (*yadṛcchā-śabda*).
In your view, however, the occurrence [of terms] such as "white" in the substance is by way of their inherence in a quality;

since that same [inherence] is not distinguished [from that in qualities] even in the case of color-form and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of their occurring in the substance as well.
Therefore, one must necessarily admit some specific difference in capacity residing in the quality.

Just as some of those words refer primarily to the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), while others have the quality (*guṇa*) as the primary meaning, so too will it be in this case [of the first quarter of the third chapter]. Even though there exists a capacity to convey a perceived object that can be inferred from the result, and even though for us the burden of assuming an unseen power (*adṛṣṭa-śakti*) is equal, the power residing in the meaning (*artha-śakti*) is the one possessed of authority (*pramāṇavatī*), not the power residing in the word (*śabda-śakti*). This is because the function of the words ceases once the mere cognition of the denotable object has occurred, and since the cognition of the meaning remains unfulfilled, it is the power of the meaning that must be postulated.
Therefore, because there is no assumption of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), there is equality between the two [types of] qualifiers;

however, the perception of primacy and non-primacy in substance and quality is inherent. This is always the case when color and other qualities are denoted as primary: in the case of substances, they are expressed as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), whereas in the case of "white" and other qualities, they are expressed as the qualified (*viśeṣya*). Furthermore, because their meaning has been established since beginningless time, these very [qualities] follow through the suffix *matup* in this technical definition (*lakṣaṇā*).
The only distinction here is that even where a thing is a qualifier, [it may still be so expressed].

If the expressive power resides solely in the qualified [substantive], then "white" is a qualifier of the substance; thus, this [word "white"] possesses a twofold nature, whereas [words] such as "fragrance" possess a single nature. And so, for the word "white," there is yet another twofold nature.
In the expression "the whiteness of the cloth" (*paṭasya śuklaḥ*), the quality is initially presented as extracted [from its substrate];
however, in the expression "the white cloth" (*paṭaḥ śuklaḥ*), the substance is expressed through the word for the quality.
But the author of the Bhāṣya, having this very distinction in mind, stated that even a word denoting a quality may possess the gender of the [substantive] itself.

Just as in the case of the words *karuṇā* (compassion) and *buddhi* (intellect), although these two are equal to the word *gandha* (fragrance) and others [in being abstract qualities], they have been cited merely as examples of a distinction. This is what is meant: if even those words which primarily express a quality are somehow joined with gender and number, how much more so those in which the substance (*dravya*) is predominant?

Thus, by this reasoning, the word *aruṇā* is a quality-denoting term (*guṇavacana*). Since a quality-denoting term cannot be syntactically connected with the verb *krīṇāti* (he buys), [the opponent’s position] is set aside; however, the other [proponent] replies again:
"Indeed, it is possible to effect a connection between a quality-denoting term and a substance."

The proponent of the final conclusion (siddhāntavādin), however, states the following in order to demonstrate that because the connection with the action is understood through direct audition (śruti), the connection with the substance—which is indicated by syntactical connection (vākya)—is sublated due to its weakness:

"In this case, since the words *aruṇā* (red) and *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old) denote a quality and a substance respectively, there is first of all no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based on direct audition.
Nor is there a genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī-śruti*). Therefore, because the direct audition of the instrumental case is stronger, there is no connection between the substance and the quality."
Although it may be understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that the word *aruṇa* denotes only a quality,
nevertheless, due to the lack of another way [to reconcile the conflict], its application to the substance is resorted to on the basis of syntactical connection (*vākya*).
In that case as well, the counter-argument is established precisely because there is no other way [to avoid the contradiction].
[Objection: "But surely [the quality] cannot [be the object], because there is no connection with the action.
[Reply: The answer to that is "because it would result in the third case ending being meaningless.
For an unexpressed meaning cannot be understood when there is no other way [to account for the usage].

Nor can it be argued here that, even by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the accusative case-ending possesses the sense of the instrumental—as in the case of the word *sakta*—because the general category of "kāraka" (grammatical participant) is also not desired [as the primary meaning].
Alternatively, he says: having referred to the *kāraka* which is obtained through its substratum of gender and number, the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is being prescribed.

Indeed, there is also this view: that from words denoting qualities (*guṇaśabda*), even in the absence of a *kāraka* status, the accusative and other case-endings occur because they serve as qualifiers of a *kāraka*.
"This is not the reason.

Even if, in some way, the word *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) were suitable for connection with *adravyāya* (for one who has no substance), nevertheless, because there is no connection with both [the substance and the action]—given that the *ekahāyanī* is connected to the action and the *ekam* (one) is connected to the substance according to the principle "as in the case of the *parārtha*"—the connection with the quality (*guṇa*) is set aside by the stronger connection with the purchase (*kraya*).
Furthermore, a genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*), which would indicate a connection with a quality, is not observed here in the same way as the case-ending indicating a connection with the action.
As for those alternatives regarding grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), we shall explain them all in the final section of the sixth book, under the rule *niyamo vaikārye hi*.
In any case, this non-etymological coreferentiality is weak; how so?
But since the meaning of the word is sublated in every respect, what is this proposal? It is said: the word *aruṇā* (red) must necessarily be connected with some possessor of that quality (*guṇin*).

In that case, even when there is a connection with another word, since [the word] has already functioned once, what is the point of veiling it—just as in the expression "kim avaguṇṭhanena" (what is the use of a veil)? Thus, there is a violation of the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) to that extent.
Therefore, let it be connected even with the word expressing a quality (*guṇa*).
This is not the first quarter of the third chapter.

Having accepted that [the substance] exists, there is a contradiction in assuming both an injunction and a restatement (*vidhi-anuvāda*) simultaneously for the root *krīṇāti* (to buy), because it negates the connection with the substance belonging to the sacrifice while simultaneously asserting a connection with substance, quality, and relation.
However, where all [elements] are qualifiers of the action, there is no difficulty due to the performance of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*).

But where the action is enjoined and something [additional] regarding the substance is also enjoined, it is said that there is an absence of restriction, having accepted a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) characterized by the repetition of the suffix.
For a qualification must be something already well-known;

however, since the act of purchasing (*kraya*) in its state of being enjoined is not well-known, it would follow that it could only be connected with the *ekacāyanī* (the single-stalked plant) mentioned within the specific context (*prakaraṇa*).
This will occur in other examples as well, according to similar principles.

For example, in the case of the statement "he measures with ten handfuls," there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the number ten would apply to the handfuls used for other subsidiary offerings as well, not just for the measuring of Soma. Furthermore, the opponent, finding an opening by asserting the acceptance of a difference in form (vairūpya) regarding the *ekacāyanī* bricks, raises an objection:
"But even when something new (*apūrva*) is being enjoined, it will be distinguished from others simply through the context of the subject matter (*prasaṅga*), as it revolves in the mind."
"Not so," is the reply.

For as much as an object is qualified, to that same extent there is a breaking of its natural momentum; therefore, one must accept that once it has been qualified by one thing, it may be qualified by another—asking "what is the use of a veil for that which is already active?
Nor is there any pointlessness, because it possesses meaning within the context.

If it is argued that the connection there is likewise the same, we say no; for there is no contingency of inconsistency (*vairūpya*) in an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), since it does not restate a substance already obtained from another sentence.
This is so even in the case of *soma* by its own nature, as stated in the *Tantravārtika*.

When the purchase (*kraya*) is being enjoined, and the substance (*dravya*) is being restated as a qualifier for that [purchase], a dual form (*vairūpya*) arises. Likewise, the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) cannot be connected to both the purchase and the quality (*guṇa*) due to this dual form.

Furthermore, since there is no mention of the quality consisting of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) within the context (*prakaraṇa*), the principle of "uselessness [of the main act] leading to its subsidiaries" (*ānarthakyāt tadaṅganyāya*) is not applicable; and because that principle is more appropriately applied to the *ekahāyanī* as a subsidiary of the purchase itself, it would follow that the basis for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) lacks foundation, and thus [the opponent's position] should be disregarded.
To this, it is replied:

the phrase "when there is a single purpose" (*arthakatve*) is an indicator for a specific type of sentence; furthermore, the phrase "because of the unity of action" (*aikakarmyāt*) is taught as the reason for that very same point.
Alternatively, the meaning is that where a single sentence is possible because there is unity of the sentence-meaning;

and because of the use of the instrumental case, it is understood through the sentence that both *aruṇā* (the red one) and *ekahāyanī* (the one-year-old cow), though each independently requiring only the action to be accomplished by itself, are connected to the specific act of purchase (*kraya*).
For a factor of action (*kāraka*) is so called because, while performing [something], it performs an action.
Therefore, there is no connection of any *kāraka* with a substance, nor does an injunction operate upon their mutual relationship; rather,
it is the assumption of a connection with the action that we depend upon.
And just as they accept a substance as the means for accomplishing actions, so too do they accept a quality; thus, there is no inconsistency regarding the redness [of the cow].
In this way, as long as a substance is not specifically characterized by its particular quality, [it remains indeterminate].

In that case, since there is no accomplishment of the ritual action (*kriyāsiddhi*) by means of it, the qualities (*guṇas*) are disregarded; therefore, even a substance (*dravya*) is a subsidiary part of the action. And thus, in the rule concerning substances, qualities, and purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*), the mention of "qualities" was made.

[Objection: But surely, because they are inseparable (*nāntarīyakatva*), qualities are performed when a substance is grasped; since there is no separate effort [required for them], it is not proper to expect qualities in the same way as one expects a substance. For instance:

Even when the action (*karman*) has already been performed previously, there is no requirement for the substance (*dravya*). Therefore, if there were a prior expectancy for the substance, it should likewise be understood [as present] even in the case of a quality (*guṇa*), since the purpose would be fulfilled by that much alone; nor is there a lack of engagement for one who is already engaged in such a manner.
For thus it is stated in the first quarter of the third chapter:
"The nature of the qualities is established in this way throughout."
It is not otherwise, because of the lack of activity [in the agent], and because of the favorableness of the injunction;
nor is the means of accomplishment for all [actions] of a single nature,
nor is action— whether consisting solely of motion or inherent in the self— accepted as such in all cases.
Furthermore, not all factors are direct means (*sādhana*) of the principal action;

in that case, while they possess the status of agent (*kartṛtva*), they will elsewhere possess the status of instrument (*karaṇatva*). Thus, from the word *aruṇā* (red), it is understood that the purchase is to be accomplished by the quality of redness delimiting some substance.
Similarly, since it is impossible for a one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) to be a means [to a sacrifice] otherwise, it requires only this much: "I must be defined by some quality.
That quality, in turn, begins to require some substance as its substratum; and the substance also requires some quality.
Because both require each other, their relationship is quickly established.
Furthermore, in this sentence, there is no perception of dependence upon other substances or other qualities;
because there is no reason to bypass what is proximate, it is understood exactly as eightfold.
Moreover:

If a quality, because it cannot otherwise be accounted for (*anyathānupapatti*), brings about a substance not mentioned in the text, then that purchase does not accept a substance such as a one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) which is explicitly mentioned [elsewhere], according to the maxim of "one who eats from a bronze vessel" (*kāṃsyabhojinnyāya*). Or rather, even a primary element would preclude non-restriction; how much more so when it is itself primary? Furthermore, there is no impossibility (*anupapatti*) without the assumption of what is not heard in the text, since the two things already heard are fully satisfied through their mutual connection. And in this way, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) existing within its own sentence will also be established.
And there is no contradiction with scripture here;
as he will state:
"The meaning of the scriptural sentence is not 'no'."
For instance, when purchasing a substance, one indeed considers: "What quality will this possess?
And when acquiring a quality, one likewise considers: "What substance will serve as its substratum?"
Even though those two attain mutual compatibility by virtue of that very act of purchase, they do not stand in a relationship of mutual subservience (aṅgāṅgitva).

As for one who thinks that the quality is understood to be subordinate to the substance because it is the delimiting factor, he should be told: since the quality itself is unable to accomplish the purchase otherwise, the substance, which it takes as its substrate, becomes its subordinate member.

Therefore, it should be understood that only when there is an indispensable mutual assistance between two things that constitute parts of the purchase does that [assistance] result in their being constituent parts (*aṅga*).

As for one who thinks that [the mantra] is to be inserted into the context (*prakaraṇa*), it must be stated by what [means] its quality (*guṇa*) is enjoined. Is it by the injunction of the purchase? [This concludes] the first quarter of the third chapter.

The relationship with the word is not accepted [as existing] at that time, nor is there a conceptual construction (vikalpa), because of the multiplicity of effects; this is said with the intention of referring to the intermediate operation (avāntaravyāpāra).
But the opponent, thinking that only the multiplicity of the primary effects has been stated, says: "But was it not just now stated..."
Furthermore, that which was previously stated—that because it is formless (*amūrta*), it is inactive—is contradicted;
for doubt is raised by all those who stand upon common ground. And since "formlessness" (*amūrtatā*) has been asserted there, it is also contradicted in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

When the two defects have been refuted, [the opponent], failing to see that the status of being the "one-year-old animal" (*ekahāyana*) is established by the nature of the thing itself, objects that there would be a lack of consistency (*vaisṛṣṭāpatti*) because the relationship between the door and the door-keeper is established by the sentence alone.
Thus it is said:
"We do not say that the word *aruṇā* [expresses] the substance. This shows that the connection with the single-cow (*ekahāyanī*) is brought about by the force of the context (*sāmarthya*).
[Objection: "But even so, would there not be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)? To refute this restriction, he says:
The refutation is as follows: "It is like the hundred-fold fine, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, the *abhiṣava*, and the eating.
Now, since the fine (*daṇḍa*) is a consecratory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the one being fined, does it not follow that it must be repeated for each individual Garga, just like eating and so forth?
This, however, is not a valid objection.
The first quarter of the third chapter:
For when the offense is the occasion, the specific number "one hundred" is specified;
thus, the livelihood of kings who commit such offenses is prescribed.
Furthermore, that offense committed against Garga—whether it was committed by a single person or by many—is the cause for the king’s taking of a hundred [coins] from them.

At that time, since the offenders exist in the state of being the source (*apādāna*) [of the fine], and it is understood that "the king must take a hundred from the entire group of Gargas," if the taking were done individually, then once the offense had been expiated by one hundred [coins] paid by a single person, the remainder would constitute an unstated theft of a Brahmin’s property, and an excessive increase in the number would result.
Therefore, the completion of the sentence occurs with reference to the aggregate.

Since the purchase (*kraya*) has primacy—by virtue of its purpose being the acquisition of *soma* as the means for the sacrifice, by the principle of the mention of the accomplished and the to-be-accomplished (*bhūtabhavyasamuccāraṇanyāya*), and by the parsimony of the injunction—and since the substance and the quality are the reverse of the previous reasons, the other [the number] obtains the result of establishing syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*).
In that regard, another [teacher] says: "The singular number is connected [to the object], because of its connection with the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*)."
Thus, according to the principle of syntactical connection (*saṃyoga*), the remaining application of the rule is established:
is the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) for one cup alone, or for all the cups mentioned in the context?
And just as that which is connected with singularity is to be illustrated, so too should that which is connected with duality and plurality be illustrated.
In every case, an action is enjoined with reference to something;
in that regard, there arises the doubt as to whether the number of the object being referred to is intended to be significant or not.
But surely, this kind of inquiry is inappropriate regarding Vedic sentences.
Apart from what is already established by cognition, no other dispute exists.

Because the Vedic sentences are eternal, what is heard therein is not unintended; nor can there be a speaker who might state it otherwise. For it has been stated that for all persons, speech is preceded by [the Veda], since they rely solely upon what is heard.

Nor is there an object cognizable through another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of which the listeners themselves might realize its falsity. Furthermore, the intentions (*vivakṣā*) of speakers, or the specific desires to manifest particular cognitions, are not themselves objects of cognition; therefore, both [the notions] "this was intended" and "this was not intended" are untenable here due to the absence of such a basis.
This is what is being said.

First, oneness has been stated here without doubt, and it is also certain that this [oneness] pertains to the cup (*graha*). However, in this context, there is the capacity of both stem and suffix to express their respective meanings through direct audition (*śruti*), as well as the capacity of case-endings (*vibhakti*) to effect application (*viniyojakatva*).
For wherever one is impelled by that [application], one proceeds in the same manner, whether the object is already expressed or unexpressed, or whether it has been applied or not applied.
For he is not impelled toward performance by either of those two;

therefore, even for that which is enjoined and applied, there exist—relative to the injunction and the performance—the states of being intended or not intended, and being desired to be performed or not desired to be performed.
This is what is said.

If it is asked: "Since the fruit of the desire for non-attachment through the renunciation of grasping is established, how could there be a lack of grasping for what has been heard, given that here [in this context] there might be both the intention to speak and the absence of such intention? [The answer follows: Regarding the welfare of one's own people, just as in the cases of [intentional] omission and non-intention, how could there be no grasping of what was heard?
This is not a fault;

for just as in human compositions it is the person who is the instigator even when a matter has already been stated, so too here, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others function as an injunction (*vidhi*).
The nature of an injunction (*vidhi*) is like that of a person who commands.

Therefore, because it is determined that "only that which is touched by the nature of an injunction must be performed, and nothing else," one must investigate the extent of the contact with the operation of the injunction;
this is what is being stated.

If the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth were to enjoin [an action] either by conforming to our own intention or by the force of the scriptural application (*viniyoga-śruti*), then everything would be enjoined.
However, conforming to their own inherent power (*sva-śakti*), they enjoin only some things and not everything.
For instance:
The cultivation of the purpose, as in the case of what has been heard [from scripture], is enjoined;
because that [purpose] would otherwise be impossible, other causal factors follow by implication.
Consequently, regarding the performance of acts such as cleansing and so forth, a doubt arises as to whether the singularity of the cup and other such attributes must also be observed, or not.
Alternatively, if it is a qualification of the substance, then it is not intended [to be expressed];
or rather,
they convey the meaning of the sentence in accordance with the power of the words.
In that regard, that which is mounted upon their [own] capacity is what they intend to explain;
however, that which is abandoned by them out of partiality (bhakti) will not be explained by them.
Therefore, whatever meaning they desire to explain is what is intended to be expressed (vivakṣita).

Therefore, it may be said that for them, what is unintended is indeed undesirable. Consequently, by presenting the intentionality or lack thereof as residing solely in the speaker, there is no contradiction even in the case of the Veda, because of its being the cause of all things— just as, for example, in the case of great elemental beings, their own selves are conscious.
They manifest some objects and do not manifest others;
and the various modes of their bodily differentiation follow the power of their karma.
These manifestations of the Supreme Selves are seen due to the diversity in the commencement of their primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
In the world of Varuṇa, bodies characterized by transparent limbs are said to be fashioned from water itself, joined with other elemental substances;
whereas in the world of Khara, the bodies consist mostly of fire and are endowed with pure radiance.
Just as [the sun] is nourished by its scattered solar radiance,
so too the Supreme Self, whose body is space, is heard of in the Śruti;
He who is declared to be "Brahman as Space" is eternally worshipped with water.

Furthermore, this scripture known as the Vedas, which is called Śabdabrahman, is entirely presided over by the one Supreme Self. Likewise, those bodies such as the Vedas that are said to exist individually as objects of experience for individual selves are also always permeated by consciousness.
Whatever is accepted through formal injunction and devotion is indeed intended;

however, that which is abandoned by that same [injunction] should be explained as unintended. This applies even to the Veda, which is without beginning or end, and whose scope is the meaning of the Vedas.

In the *Tantravārtika*, it is stated that an explanation may occur even through the primary sense (*mukhyavṛtti*) depending on whether [the literal meaning] is intended or not intended. What, then, is the prima facie position?

Since the Veda consists everywhere of injunctions and prohibitions, whatever is heard therein is understood as being connected to that [injunction]; first, there is the singular number (*ekatva*), for otherwise the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*) qualified by the specific [object] would not be enjoined. Thus, because the injunction of cleansing qualified by the apprehension of the object qualified by singularity would otherwise be untenable, the injunction of singularity itself is established through another *arthāpatti* (presumption). Even when there is a series of such qualifications, the cognition of every injunction occurs through a succession of "conjunction with what is conjoined" (*saṃyukta-saṃyoga*).

Alternatively, even if the suffix denoting an injunction (*vidhi-pratyaya*) does not extend to qualify the substance itself, everything is intended to be enjoined by a single *arthāpatti* (presumption), and there is no contradiction because their objects are distinct. If, however, in both cases the relationship were characterized solely by being for that purpose (*tādarthya*), or if it were a relationship between qualifier and qualified based on a substratum, then they would be understood as having the same object.

However, there is not even a single instance where the oneness [of the cup] and the cup itself stand in the relationship of substrate and superstrate, nor in the manner of qualifier and qualified, because they are accepted as being in the relationship of subordinate (śeṣa) and principal (śeṣin).
Therefore, we shall understand the meaning to be: "One should perform the preparatory rite (saṃmārga-bhāvanā) by means of that oneness which is dependent upon the cup.

Alternatively, when it is determined that the cup is incapable of subsisting for its own sake in the state of oneness, then that [oneness], even while proceeding toward that preparatory rite by virtue of the sentence, does not prevent [the cup from being understood].
Alternatively, let this [number] be for the purpose of the act of taking (*graha*).
And that purpose of being for the act of taking must be demonstrated in whatever manner it is possible.

In that regard, if the cup (*graha*) were to enter into the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) merely by its own form, then oneness would subsequently not be grasped; it would not be included within the productive operation nor would it belong to the productive operation.

Therefore, since it must possess the very nature of a subordinate element (*guṇa*), it presents itself as being co-located with that [substance] preceded by oneness, just like *aruṇa* (the red) and other qualities expressed by separate words; for a qualified injunction is not complete without its qualifiers having been established,
and thus the qualifier enters first, as it is the qualified that distinguishes.

This being the case, when that [substance] has entered into the process of cultivation (bhāvanā) and is touched by its ritual procedure, the cup (graha) becomes established as having arisen from the restriction of substance and quality. Alternatively, because the power of direct scriptural statement (śruti) is stronger, the connection with the substance is declared;
for the substance denoted by the nominal stem (prātipadika) would be proximate due to being expressed within the same word.

And it has been stated that the *kāraka* (grammatical participant), as presented by the case-ending (*vibhakti*), is a single part of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) manifested as having a prior and posterior sequence;

therefore, just like the animal (*paśu*) being taken up [as an object], the number of that which is being pointed out (*uddiśyamāna*) is also intended to be significant. The example "a male animal" (*puṃpaśuḥ*) was cited incidentally. Or rather, since all [the qualities] serve as defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic is indeed non-distinct [from one to the other].
An action prescribed with reference to specific individuals, who are characterized by their own genus and other attributes,
is understood to serve all [such] purposes when it functions as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*).
In that case as well, because the state of being a "cup" (*grahatva*) is unfit for the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*), the cups themselves remain as the objects to be refined (*saṃskārya*).
When that which is the object of perception is purified by its own refinement, it becomes endowed with qualities;
for at that time, when other objects of perception are not being perceived, no deficiency of consciousness is observed in the first quarter of the third chapter.
Moreover, although the path of acceptance is governed by the authority of the *śāstra*,

nevertheless, in the case of its non-performance, the knowledge pertaining to it would be sublated. Therefore, because there is no distinction in the connection with the *apūrva* of the cup (*graha*) and because there is no distinction in the context (*prakaraṇa*), there is cognition [of the mantra] for all [cups].
In that case, the subsequent [word] is accepted even if it is not explicitly heard, provided it is prescribed and employed;
however, even if it is explicitly heard, it would not be accepted if its meaning is disregarded by those two.
Since all [verbal forms] are seen to possess different modes of expression (*vacanavyakti*),

it is investigated which one is prescribed (*vihita*) and which is applied (*viniyukta*), and which is not— by means of a present-tense form that is correct according to the traditional grammatical rules (*smṛti*) regarding verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*).
What indeed is enjoined here by the fifth verbal suffix (the optative)? Is it qualified merely by the meaning of the verbal root— that is, by the act of cleansing—
in its form as established in common worldly usage, characterized by being capable of performance?

Because they share the same purpose, the self is not deliberated upon as distinct from others; nor is there any need here for a formal injunction regarding the *graha* vessels and so forth. Is there an option (*vikalpa*) between the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) and the offering (*agra*), or is there a combination (*samuccaya*)? Or is it a connection (*saṃbandha*) or a collective whole (*samudāya*) that distinguishes the efficient force (*bhāvanā*)?
Having thus established the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the first two,
a similar analysis is performed with the third *saka*. Likewise,
in that case, since the action is predominant, there is a concomitance (*sāhitya*) between the substance and the number.
Having performed such an act once, the agent would become one who has accomplished his task (*kṛtakṛtya*).

In that case as well, is it the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) of the cup itself that is enjoined, or is it the singularity [of the cup] alone? Or rather, is it both [the cup and its singularity] optionally? This is the first quarter of the third chapter.

Is it that a particular number qualified by the cup (graha) is enjoined? Or is the mention [of the cup] intended with reference to the action? Is it understood as being for the cup alone? Or is it enjoined for the cup alone as qualified by oneness?

Or rather, is it a single number qualified by the cup (*graha*) that pertains to the cleansing (*saṃmārga*), such that in whatever manner the number is taken up with respect to the cup, it will bring about that same [number] in the cleansing?
Or is it prescribed in the cleansing? It will bring about that very [number].
Whatever formulation of the statement the proponent shall utter regarding that which is to be enjoined,
the opponent will refute it by means of splitting the sentence;
for when one resorts to the injunction of cleansing while mentioning the cup, [the sentence is split].
Because its power is restricted to that [specific instance], singularity will not be enjoined;
for it is not possible to enjoin it when that [instance] is being grasped, since there is no further scriptural mention.

Indeed, there would have to be two applications (*āvartanīya*): the application of the injunction for the cup (*graha*), and the cup itself would also have to be applied, in order to establish the two relationships;
for these two cannot be established by a single injunction.
The word "graha" (cup), being uttered only once, would incur both the connection with the number and the connection with the sweeping;
yet, being uttered again, it would incur those two [connections] separately, whereas it remains fixed as a single unit within the Vedic corpus.

If this injunction were established by some other means, it would follow that it is not authoritative because it is of human origin. For who would abandon the singular number when performing the ritual of offering oblations and so forth?
If the proponent were to establish that action is the primary element,
then all intended meanings would follow through that very door;
therefore, the mere fact of being explicitly stated in the text is not the cause for accepting it as an injunction.
Therefore, this [quality] is not equal to other qualifiers such as white and so forth.
Among those, first the qualifier of substance is refuted;
in that regard, the effect of a qualifier—namely, the projection of its own form—is indeed possible in all cases where things are being conjoined.

And therefore, since the singular number is obtained through its connection with the status of being a "cup" (graha) and is not prohibited by the singular ending, why should the cleansing not be performed for a second cup and so forth?

Since the nominal stem itself indicates that cleansing is to be performed on one or many cups, the further hearing of the singular number—being impossible as a mere explanatory praise (arthavāda) regarding a subordinate quality—must serve the purpose of exclusion (parisaṃkhyā).
This is not so.
Why?

Because that [distinction] occurs only when there is a plurality of sentences; however, it has been stated here that both the acquisition and the exclusion are effected by a single sentence alone, and that is utterly untenable, for the connection with all cups is established by the nominal stem itself.

For just as there is a difference in the manifestation of speech within a sentence— where one part is the conveyor and another is the recipient— so too does a difference in the manifestation of words necessarily follow here;
moreover:

For its faultlessness is obtained there when it is enjoined; for this [injunction] is resorted to as being established by the excellence of that [result], such as "he takes" and so forth. Thus, from this verb, the possibility of an injunction arises. (Tantravārtika)
Furthermore, regarding the connection with the *abhidhī* (the horse's halter), there is no injunction whatsoever;
nor is there any remoteness of meaning for this [word] with respect to the *raśanā* (rope).
Because of the specific conjunction, both [meanings] are understood simultaneously.
The connection with the name [of the horse] by means of the three words and so forth is not intended; rather,
the mantra "it takes" is completed by these two alone,
so that the mantra clearly reaches the girth quickly.
The apprehension of what is expressed by Vedic words is not so difficult;
for since the aspect of being a means [of knowledge] was previously established, every rule would otherwise be rendered purposeless.
Therefore, the phrase "he does not take" is restated as a reference to that form [of the mantra],
while the phrase "or the horse's halter" is what is enjoined here;
for the direct Vedic statement (śruti) must be inferred by means of both the form [of the words] and the context (prakaraṇa).
The injunction is quickly completed with just those many conditions;
for when one examines what the purpose of this injunction might be,
there is no result other than the turning away [of the animal] from the tethering post named "donkey."

Nor can the mantra— whose Vedic source has not been inferred when it was first encountered in the context of the donkey’s tethering post— be set aside by the subsequent repetition of the word "horse's" rope,
because the direct Vedic statement regarding the horse, being more immediate, establishes the mantra first.

In the Tantravārtika: "When the sacred tradition has been rendered free of expectancy, and likewise when the subject matter of the context [has been satisfied], there is this well-known proverb in the world: 'What was previously carried off by a horse...'"
After that, by what means could the donkey possibly reach it?
Since this mantra would certainly reach the rope even through such an inferred Vedic text, why have you questioned it so urgently?
If the attainment of the horse's halter were merely inferential,
yet one were to treat it as if it were directly perceived through the Vedic text, then that [text] would be purposeless;
for the injunction would apply solely to the horse's halter, just as the suffix [indicates].
It would not be so through an inferential scripture; thus it is handed down in the tradition.

Therefore, because there is no redundancy, the scripture possesses a directly perceptible meaning. Since that [scripture] exists, no other [scripture] is inferred from the mantras, as they are already free of expectancy.
But when the general application is restricted because there is no scriptural injunction [to the contrary],
then the threefold defect does not arise;
and thus, that which was stated here by the author of the Bhāṣya was said without due consideration.
In that case, one should pay no further attention to other syntactical constructions.

Nor can there be an injunction for the mere relationship of oneness, because the injunctive power is exhausted by manifesting the relationship between the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) and the cup (*graha*).

This is just as in a sentence whose purpose is the injunction to ward off damage to the cooked rice (*odana*), where dogs, cats, and so forth—even though mentioned—are not intended as qualifiers because they are not being enjoined.
For dogs, cats, and the like are not excluded from us simply because they do not eat food;
rather, they are excluded even from crows and others due to the commonality of their consumption of impure food.
And so it has been said:
Even a child, when instructed, "Let the food be protected from crows," does not protect it from dogs and the like because the primary concern is injury;
for in this context, every crow and similar creature is intended as the object to be excluded.
However, the non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) regarding the number [of animals] in the case of the "seizing" (*grahaṇa*) is distinct;
an example of this established conclusion (*sthitasiddhānta*) is also heard in the section on the animal sacrifice (*paśu-prakaraṇa*).

In the tenth book, it will be stated that in a sentence intended to enjoin that "the offered portion (*avadāna*) must be made fivefold," the mention of the omentum (*vapā*) is not intended because it would result in a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).

In that regard, an example involving a connection with a laborer, a cat, or the like is appropriate when there is an intention to express mere number; as for the statement heard in common worldly usage, that should be cited as an illustration, just like the expression "the plurality of a *vṛṣala*. (Tantravārtika)
Since plurality is not intended to be expressed, a single injunctive word cannot simultaneously enjoin the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) of cleansing and the connection with the singularity of the cup;
for if the cup does not provide its number to the action, [the injunction fails].
Because it is qualified by the number alone, there is no "qualification of the qualified";

for otherwise, it could not be qualified by that which is itself qualified. Thus, the mental realization (*bhāvanā*), while grasping the cup as qualified by oneness, is unable to grasp the cup qualified by that [oneness] without first grasping the oneness itself;
and we shall refute this point further below.

By means of a specific qualification of the *bhāvanā* through a particular rule (*tantra*) that culminates solely in that qualification, it is not possible to imply another meaning; for that which qualifies the *bhāvanā* does not have "oneness" as its qualifying attribute.
Nor [can it be argued] that what is qualified by the *bhāvanā* [implies another], lest there again be merely the status of being a qualification of the *bhāvanā*. (First Pāda of the Third Adhyāya)

Therefore, because it is not required by the fundamental injunction (*maulika-vidhi*), the inclusion of the qualification "single" (*ekatva*) regarding the substance is not possible; even if we were to grant its possibility, singularity should not be observed at the time of cleansing (*saṃmārjana*), because the injunction of the connection with singularity applies to the cup (*graha*) itself as an independent entity. For the act of purchase (*kraya*), while in the state of being enjoined, does not differentiate the substance that is being connected with a quality—this was made clear in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*.
Even if this singularity were enjoined with respect to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) of cleansing, it could not function either as a subordinate (*guṇa*) or as a primary (*pradhāna*) factor.

Furthermore, the purification (*saṃskāra*) of the substance is not [identical to] the purification of that [substance], because they are distinct; for this [purification] is prescribed by means of the singularity of the cup (*graha*). At the time of performance, one recognizes the very same purification belonging to the cup itself; thus, there would be no cognition based on singularity.
If it is asked, "How then is redness (*aruṇatva*) a quality (*guṇa*)," he says:
For even a quality (*guṇa*) would indeed be non-essential (*anaṅga*).
But surely it is the principal (*pradhāna*) that is the mind;

for a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) does not depend upon another subordinate element. Rather, we shall establish everywhere that it is that which depends upon the benefactor (*upakārin*) which provides benefit.
As for what was said— that because it is formless, it cannot be refined—
even if its refinement occurs by means of an individual instance, that is equally the case for number as well.

Now, if it is argued that the refinement (*saṃskāra*) applies directly to the genus (*jāti*) itself by relying on its corporeality and its non-difference from the substance, that too is no different from the case of [the refinement of] unity.
Or, if a rebuttal is offered on the grounds that the word "cup" (*graha*) denotes the individual (*vyakti*), then the principle established in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* would be contradicted;
for there is no experience of a connection with the individual cups present at the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice occurring at various times and places.

And since nothing other than that [grahatva] is possible, it alone—by virtue of being a particular (viśeṣa)—must be the primary denotable object; nor does there exist anything other than grahatva that is excluded from other substances while simultaneously persisting (anuvṛtta) through each of those [individuals].
Therefore, that alone must be the expressed meaning.
