As for the sweeping performed upon the cup, since it is understood through the determination of its belonging to that [cup] to be the object of the first section of the third chapter,
the repetition [of the word] would have little fruit if the action were limited to just that much, even when connected with singularity.
Consequently, it would follow that [the application] is fruitless; yet there is a distinction because of the single refinement (*saṃskṛti*).

Therefore, since the restriction between substance and quality is established, the purpose of the word *atyaruṇā* (exceedingly red) is indeed the connection with oneness (*ekatva*), and thus its status as something to be refined (*saṃskārya*) is logically justified. This admission—that only a quality must be assisted by a quality heard in the scripture—is a position supported by very weak reasoning.

Qualities that are directly incapable of connection, yet reside in that which is connected to the action, accomplish the action through those [qualities] with which they are themselves unconnected; for there is no distinction between the state of being a quality and the state of being primary residing therein, and thus both are disregarded.
And this much is the cause for the connection:
that which, by benefiting a quality, makes that quality its own;
it will grasp even more firmly that [quality] which resides within the object to be refined.
Just as one who has reached the primary [object] thinks, "Who indeed might grant some favor to me, who am serving the primary?"—
and since this determination of the extent of the primary is itself a great favor,
that very principle applies here; thus, there is no contradiction in the subordinate status of those things which rely upon the primary.

For even in that case, if in a sentence whose primary purpose is to enjoin a *bhāvanā* (efficient force) qualified by substance, deity, and sacrifice, another [element]—namely, a connection with gender and number—is enjoined either with respect to the action or the substance, then it can be said that there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

In this regard, the only difference remaining is that the *graha* (cup) is being pointed out as the object, while the animal (*paśu*) is being taken up as the material; yet nothing is established by this alone.
Otherwise, the distinction between what is intended to be significant and what is not would be established merely by the difference in the relationship between the animal and the cup.

Moreover, even in this very same sentence, when the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) is enjoined with reference to the cup (*graha*), the distinction regarding the *daśāpavitra* (the fringe of the cloth), the singularity, and so forth, is accepted without any contradiction from the perspective of the sentence-meaning; likewise, it will be the same for the singularity of the cup.

If one were to claim a distinction based on its being expressed by a separate word (*padāntara*), then for such a person, there would be no instance anywhere where a distinction exists that could serve as an example, because there is no scope for cases of equal logic.
For [in your view], a quality residing in a separate word is not desired or intended to be significant.
How could that which is mentioned in the same grammatical position as it be unintended?
For otherwise, even without the mention of the "cup" (graha), if the cleansing were performed, the purpose of the scripture would be fulfilled by that alone.
If it is argued that the cup is not enjoined because it is already established [by other means], that is incorrect.

That which is not obtained in the sacrifice is enjoined; this applies equally to the cup (*graha*) as well, for it is possible to say "that which is a cup" just as one can say "that which is a *parīti*.
For instance:

Therefore, because both oneness and the state of being a "cup" (graha) are touched by the injunction through their connection with the qualified object of purification, there exists a relationship of subordinate and principal by virtue of the context. Consequently, oneness is subordinate because it lacks a specific purpose, while the cup is principal because it serves a purpose;

thus, the injunction and non-injunction are logically consistent. Furthermore, these two do not fall within the scope of a single word, nor is a split of the word (padabheda) appropriate with respect to the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya).
Furthermore, an inflectional ending (*vibhakti*) is not a distinct word (*padāntara*), because it is not employed independently and lacks a fixed sequence of preceding and following elements.
If it is argued that it is a word because it conveys meaning (*gamakatva*), this is not so;

for then there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of smoke and the like also being words, and since a single meaning is cognized even in a single verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) etc., there would be the consequence of every such element being a word with respect to its respective meaning.
The word "pada" is a worldly term; it cannot be removed from that which is used by the world and that which is recorded by the traditional authorities (smṛti).
There is a traditional rule stating, "A *pada* is that which ends in a nominal suffix (*sup*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*)," and it is precisely in that context that the word "pada" is employed.
Vārttika:
If it is desired here that the state of being an object (karmatva), which is expressed by a case-ending, is not intended to be significant,
then number also cannot be intended to be significant, because it too is expressed by that same [case-ending].

Furthermore, if the case-ending is abandoned because the number is abandoned, then the abandonment of the status of being an object (*karman*) would also follow, since [the object] possesses a purpose and thus requires refinement (*saṃskāryatva*). If this is argued, we say no; for without a case-ending denoting a grammatical factor (*kāraka*), there can be no connection with the action.
Indeed, a connection with the act of cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) cannot be established for the word *graha* alone, if it is devoid of its case-ending.
If the sweeping were [intended] for all [the cups] because singularity was not intended to be expressed, then this would apply to no one;
for there is no simultaneous application in that manner to the objects denoted by the heard words, just as in the case of the action of the *graha* vessels.

Regarding the argument that "taking up" and "not taking up" are appropriate, like the cooking of a hen, the following response is given: When the wiping (*saṃmārjana*) is enjoined with reference to the unity of the ladle (*graha*), then, because there is no mutual connection between the two things being referred to, there occurs a sentence-split (*vākyabheda*) characterized by the completion of the sentence for each [item] individually; this constitutes one sentence-split according to the first quarter of the third chapter.

Furthermore, when there is a plurality of things to be adopted (*upādeya*), since they serve the purpose of a single most distinguished cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and thus have a single effect, they would naturally form a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*). However, because those things being pointed out (*uddiśyamāna*) are not yet mastered, and because each has the capacity to grasp the action individually, it is the action itself that is mastered and drawn toward them; thus, it is understood that each one is to be performed independently of the others. Therefore, in this case, the cup (*graha*) is to be consecrated independently of its oneness, and oneness is also to be consecrated independently of the cup.

In that regard, if the singularity residing in the cup itself were to be refined, then because it would involve a dependent instrument, the primary status of both [the cup and the offering], which is determined by their independent relationship, would be destroyed.
Alternatively, if it were a singularity residing in another substance, why would it not arise?
For we do not perceive anything called "singularity" within the context of the ritual procedure, as we do with the cup.
It is not the case that one is unable to determine [the specific object] simply because of their great number.
Nor is it the case that this determination does not apply to all of them; for in that case too, there would be the consequence of performing what is enjoined and what is not enjoined.

For when an action is being accomplished by a single subordinate factor (guṇa) conjoined with oneness, it does not require anything else; thus, the purpose of the scripture would be fulfilled by taking up any [object] whatsoever. However, if [oneness] were the primary factor (pradhāna), then only that which is conjoined with oneness would be grasped, and a deficiency (vaiguṇya) would result for that very [action].
For indeed, even when all [the cups] are being consecrated, at the time of performance only one is seen at a time; therefore, it is said that there is no contradiction.
For no one cleanses several cups simultaneously; and thus, even in the case intended [by the proponent], it is exactly the same, so the result of the intended argument is weak.

This is not so; for when each [cup] is grasped individually, there is no possibility of simultaneity once the refinement (*saṃskāra*) has occurred. Furthermore, this is merely an argument *abhyupetyavāda* (an admission for the sake of argument), because an independent unity is not perceived.
Even if that [unity] were intended as residing in another substance, nevertheless, it is not intended with respect to the cup itself; thus, it is established that all [cups] are to be cleansed.
However, if unity were enjoined as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), then it has already been explained in the *Sakṛdadhikaraṇa* that the accusative case does not express a subordinate status at all.

If it is intended that [the mention of] "one" signifies merely the characteristic of a factor (*kāraka*) because its intended meaning has not been abandoned, then that is indeed one fault: namely, the consequence that the cup (*graha*) would also be a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), just like the number "one. And because of that similarity, for the sake of uniformity, it would lead one to understand that the cup is indeed a subordinate quality, just like the number "one. Consequently, since the cup possesses its own purpose, it must be primary; how then can its status as a subordinate quality be asserted at the outset when it does not yet exist?
And how can primacy be desired for a meaning that is possible from a word?

If, on the other hand, having imagined some kind of impossibility for it, one resorts to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then the subsequent imagination of possibility would involve contradiction; thus, even if there were a purpose [for the figurative sense], there would be the undesirable consequence of its being subordinate by virtue of the scriptural text.

Furthermore, because one simultaneously accepts both possibility and impossibility, there is the fault of verbal distortion due to the conflict between primacy and subordination, and the failure to perceive primacy.

For an "object" (artha) is not itself a means of valid cognition; rather, it is the cause for the postulation of the word's capacity. Consequently, since it is caused by multiple postulations, there is indeed a distinction between sentences, even in the case of an object being enjoined or already ascertained from another source.
Since a word does not apply elsewhere when its necessary application is available,

and since the injunction of the predominance of the cup (*graha*) in its necessary sense is obtained through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), who would ever assume it figuratively through a forced interpretation of the meaning?
Therefore, by the inherent power of the word, the predominance of both must be accepted.
The commentary (*bhāṣya*) should also be applied to these very same distinctions of sentences (*vākyabheda*).

Although this genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), by virtue of being a qualifier, seems to present Agni as a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*), nevertheless, because no other relationship is possible, it is understood that the relationship is precisely that of the subsidiary and the principal (*aṅgāṅgisambandha*).

Even there, since Agni possesses a purpose while the removal of grass lacks one, it is understood exactly as follows: just as in the expression "the king’s man" the king is the master of the man, so too Agni is the master of the removal of grass.
It should be explained that even the plural number in the word *tṛṇāni* (grass) is not intended to be significant, as it is in cases such as *bhinne juhoti* ("he offers when [the ladle] is broken").

If, first of all, the locative case were to express the status of the cause (*nimitta*) through options, combinations, or other relations between "brokenness" and "singularity," then, because the sentence would be completed with each term individually, there would be no mutual connection between them.

Alternatively, if singularity were presented as something to be adopted (*upādeya*) while "brokenness" were presented as something not to be adopted, then even though there is no contradiction between being subordinate (*guṇatva*) and primary (*pradhānatva*), there remains a contradiction just as before.
If there were syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), there would be no [need for] the first quarter of the third chapter.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the name "formlessness" (*nārūpatva*) is not intended to be expressed? [Reply: Indeed, the plural number is used when one intends to express multiplicity; however, he thinks that even if something is not intended to be expressed, a non-existent object cannot be spoken of.
In that regard, since the Veda is eternal, the function of persons consists merely in seeking out the meaning as it was uttered; thus, the agent is not to be questioned.
Therefore, it should be understood that the case-ending (vibhakti) exists for the purpose of qualifying the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika).

Furthermore, when the "cup" (graha) is the meaning of the nominal stem, and its connection with an action cannot be established even when sought after, then—given the equal lack of necessity—it is better that this [case-ending] serves as a qualifier of the substance; such is the intention.

Consequently, the sweeping (*saṃmārga*) remains unimpaired even without that [number], and this number—whether belonging to each individual object being swept or to the genus (*jāti*)—must be reconciled. Alternatively, there would be an instability of qualities due to the refinement (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, since the mention of "cup-ness" (*grahatva*) is for the purpose of indicating [the genus] just like "oneness," the sweeping applies to all [cups]. Having thus proposed that the sweeping applies even to equals, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is adopted on the grounds that there is no evidence for it being merely illustrative, and because the connection is established by the syntactical sentence (*vākya*), whereby the sweeping is enjoined as applying solely to the cup after it has been distinguished from others. However, in this case, the matter must be resolved through the removal of the contradiction, just as in the case of threshing (*avaghāta*) and so forth.

It is true that if there were no dispute regarding the section on the cups (*graha*), one might simply assume that [the singular number] is not intended to be expressed due to the nature of the case. However, being terrified by the doubt concerning the unity [of the sacrifice], one considers everything to be unintended.

Alternatively, since there is a distinction between the *apūrva*s (transcendental results) of the *āgneya* and other rites due to the difference in the acts, the restriction of acts such as threshing (*avaghāta*) is logical.

But because the *jyotiṣṭoma* rite is a single act, there is a confusion of functions between the cup (*graha*) and the chalice (*camasa*), as both are means for accomplishing the same single *apūrva*; this is the intended meaning.
The first quarter (pāda) of the third chapter:

"Or rather, there is a fixed rule regarding the meaning because of its connection with the Vedic text; since that [meaning] has the word as its authority, the answer is according to the literal sense."

Since there would be no injunction for cleansing in the absence of a relationship, and because another related entity must necessarily exist, there is no injunction for the cleansing of the vessel alone.

Alternatively, the restriction of speech is prompted by that *apūrva* (transcendental result) which is indicated by the word "cup" (*graha*), because [the injunction] would otherwise be purposeless; thus, it applies to its constituent parts as well.

If it is enjoined that "the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of the Vājapeya is seventeen cubits long," then the word *yūpa* is, in some way or another, a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that [post], and consequently, this measurement applies to the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.
Alternatively, if it is enjoined that "that which belongs to the Vājapeya is seventeen cubits long," the result is the same.

Or, if the formulation is "that which is a sacrificial post is seventeen cubits long," then the word *vājapeya* is either a qualifier in some way or a restatement obtained through the context; in that case, this is a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) for the sacrificial post of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) that is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the Vājapeya.
What follows from this?
Since there is no other way, the function [of the word] must be based on secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) due to its being mentioned in syntactic proximity;
however, the word "sacrificial post" (yūpa) is not perceived as being connected with the upper part of the vessel.
However, there is also this [point] from the first quarter of the third chapter:
the inquiry as to whether the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) might belong directly to the *vājapeya* sacrifice;
but since that is not perceived, it is subsequently understood [to belong otherwise].
Furthermore, it has already been stated that seventeen cubits cannot be directly [predicated] of the sacrifice itself.

Even if it were merely a relative term, it would not be understood as belonging to the Vājapeya unless specifically indicated; however, because the meaning of the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) lacks such a connection, it would be utterly displaced from its context.

Therefore, he will restate its qualification exactly as it was stated above, which is obtained through the context of the section on eligibility (*adhikāra*). For this will be explained [in the sūtra]: "If it is argued that [the subsidiaries] are remote, no; because in that sentence, due to the purpose of that [principal], the ritual duties are enjoined for whatever assists it by virtue of the context, and not exclusively for the direct subsidiaries. Thus, by the force of the context, the duties are prescribed for everything that is beneficial to the principal, not solely for the immediate limbs.

Therefore, since there is no contradiction with any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could it be said that "one performs the oblation by means of stepping forward"? Consequently, it cannot be connected with the *prayāja* offerings.
Consequently, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), as in the prior and subsequent positions regarding the *aruṇā* (red) qualification.
[Objection: But surely, by this very reason, there should be no insistence on other [qualifications] as well; thus, the objection regarding the *aruṇā* is indeed valid. [Reply:
The solution is that since the agent is subordinate to the verbal action (*ākhyāta*), there is no connection with the *homa* (oblation).
There is no connection between the agent who has grasped the *juhū* ladle and the *prayāja* offerings and so forth;
however, in another case, there is no contradiction in the connection with the agent who is grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*) and constitutes the primary [actor].
For a sentence that is expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) would form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*), since it is not completed by what precedes it.
In every respect, the word *abhikrāman* (stepping forward) does not become syntactically complete without another action;
for it does not, in any way, express a connection with a substance.
Therefore, because it forms a single sentence with the previously mentioned *prayāja* offerings, it is understood to be for their purpose.
And it is possible for that [proximity] to assist by means of bringing about the proximity of the agent;

furthermore, the proximity of the *āhavanīya* fire to the *adhvaryu* is required, and just as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings, there is a connection with the substance by virtue of the purpose (*artha*), so there is no fault even though the agent is subordinate.
Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter.

It is also established that actions become the means for accomplishing other actions through their specific forms. As for the statement, "for what was previously incomplete," that is not intended to mean the incompleteness of the sentence; rather, it refers to the incompleteness of the intermediate context (*prakaraṇa*). For the purpose of the previous injunction regarding the nature and qualities of the *prayāja* offerings is doubtful, and because of the intervention [of other elements], there would be a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).

In the section on *middha* (sleep/drowsiness), regarding the integration of actions within a collection of actions, it was raised as a question which of the two—intermediate context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*) or great context (*mahā-prakaraṇa*)—is the regulator [of application], using the *upavīta* (sacred thread) as an illustration. In that regard, the demonstration of the division of the *sāmidhenī* verses is for the purpose of distinguishing whether an intermediate context exists or not.

Now, one might object: "Since there is only the great context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, and because everything is swallowed by that great context, intermediate contexts do not manifest at all.
This is not so.

Neither a transition to another context nor a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) can reach it; and even when the result is seen, [the desire] does not proceed because it remains dependent [on that result].
However, by some visible means, it is indeed turned back.

If that is the case, then because of its superior force due to proximity (*sannikarṣa*), it must necessarily be a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that [context]; so how can there be any suspicion of its application through the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*)?
It is said:
This would indeed be true if it were not separated from that [context] by the *nivid* verses. [This concludes] the first quarter of the third chapter.

There would be no fear of a break in the context (*prakaraṇa*). If that were so, then when that [context] is interrupted, it would be overcome by the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*); thus, because the *sāmidhenī* verses are mentioned on both sides, the context remains established.

The recitation of the *nivid* formulas occurs in a different section; therefore, their status as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of the *sāmidhenī* verses is severed, since the procedure (*prakriyā*) for the *sāmidhenīs* is interrupted by the *nivid*s.
Indeed, that procedure cannot be reconnected with the optional (*kāmya*) ritual injunctions.

If, on the other hand, they were subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) of the *nivids*, then—by the principle of the *godohana* vessel—the context (*prakaraṇa*) would persist for the sake of the optional rites (*kāmya*) even by way of their substratum; and even if the optional rites were themselves subsidiary parts, we might still somehow determine that the context is not sublated by the *nivid*s, through some connection such as the case of the "Pūṣan-mantra. But surely, if the optional rituals are enjoined when the context has been interrupted, then [in the case of the text] "one should attain stability with twenty-one," since no substratum is brought forward by the context, the ritual would remain incomplete due to its inherent expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*).

Alternatively, if the substratum were brought forward by the sentence itself, then, since the action would already be established, the sentence would be split by the act of establishing that connection.

If one were to accept such a split in the sentence or somehow justify it, then in the cases of the *Ṛtuyājāḥ*, the *Ārbhavantiya*, the *Saubhara*, and so forth, the same would apply; the sentence would provide the substratum for the primary context, resulting in the abandonment of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

If, on the other hand, the context were to follow in some way for the sake of providing a substratum, then the *upavīta* (the sacred thread) would likewise be obtained through that very context. Thus, this is a complete dilemma.

In this case, a result cannot logically follow from a quality (*guṇa*) that relies on a disconnected procedure (*vicchinnaprakriyā*), because it is impossible to enjoin multiple meanings without a new ritual action (*apūrva-karman*). Here, the result does not arise from the quality of the twenty-one [pieces of wood] alone; rather, the result arises from the quality of the twenty-one [pieces of wood] as qualified by the [specific] context. Just as in the case of the *āghāra* and other offerings, even here a distinct ritual action is enjoined as qualified by these [details].
And therefore, according to the principle of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, the fruit arises from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
Consequently, one should accomplish stability and other results by means of the recitation of the *anuvacana* qualified by twenty-one [verses].
How so? It is understood that it is like the recitation of the *sāmidhenī* verses, because of the commonality of the word "one should recite" (*anubrūyāt*) and because of the proximity of the number.
And consequently, there is the attainment of numerous other dharmas as well.

Even though, in this case, there is no difference in result whether [the action] is considered a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*) or not a separate ritual act, it has been described in this way so that the scriptural statement may be thus intelligible.
However, this being the case, these subsequent recitations (*anuvacana*) should not be performed at the very beginning, because they are not included within the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
Our position is not refuted by this [objection] in any way,
because the sacred thread (*upavīta*) is established as being for all purposes in the first quarter of the third chapter.
Furthermore, there would be no independent application [of the mantra].
Why?
Because that which is employed prior to the *sāmidhenī* verses, such as the *nigada*, is like the *nivid* formulas; it is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *sāmidhenīs*.
Since they are mentioned as occurring immediately after that [the *sāmidhenī* verses], the injunction "one should recite" (*anubrūyāt*) does not apply to independent acts.

If there were a separate performance [of the *anuvacana*], then—because the term would refer only to the accessory of the *sāmidhenīs*—the status of being an *anuvacana* would be lost in the absence of the other formulaic utterance (*nigada*).
Furthermore, the *sāmidhenīs* must necessarily be counted as twenty-one and so forth; those which illuminate the kindling of the fire are called *sāmidhenīs*.
This is not so.
Why?

Because in all modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), that which is not recited among the archetypal members (*prākṛta-aṅga*) provides no assistance, as its utility has not been established; therefore, it is [supplied] by the archetypal [members].
When a context has been established, that which arrives later becomes subject to the principle of proximity (*saṃnidhi*).
That [proximity] is applied when there is no conflict; however, in the event of a conflict, it is set aside by the context, as in the case of the *diś* mantra and so forth.
Therefore, it is established that the *upavīta* (sacred thread) is for the sake of the entire Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice.
On the grounds of their purposelessness otherwise, they are understood to pertain to the subsidiaries of the Pavamāna offerings.
This being the prima facie view, it is replied:

setting aside the fact that the Pavamāna offerings are understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*) to serve the purpose of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*), their purpose of serving the fires is understood through syntactical connection (*vākya*).

Furthermore, there is a contradiction in that the seventh case-ending (*saptamī*) in one instance denotes the sense of the second case (*dvitīyārtha*), while in another it expresses its own inherent meaning. Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that sacrifices such as the Viśvajit—which have no explicitly stated fruit—would become mere subsidiary rites (*aṅga*). And all of this is untenable.

Furthermore, the Āhavanīya fire is taught as being established even for a fruitless ritual; thus, the name [Āhavanīya] is understood according to the first pāda of the third chapter. Therefore, it must be described in this way: these two sentences are identical in form; one occurs within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Pavamāna oblations, while the other is an isolated statement (*anārabhyavāda*).

In this regard, because it is being produced by the context, the *āhavanīya* fire—requiring refinement—is enjoined as a consecration for the fruitless offerings such as the *pavamāna-havis* and others; however, by means of a statement not connected to a specific context (*anārabhyavāda*), that which already exists in its completed state is enjoined as the locus for all ritual acts. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

What is the point of this? Even without resorting to what is not explicitly heard (*aśruta*), this is indeed established; they say that, like the *sāmidhenī* verses, the kindling of the fire is accomplished through the *nivid* formulas.

Because they are already connected [with other elements], these [rites] do not constitute a constituent part [of the sacrifice] by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*). Their connection with the common [elements] is doubtful; their connection with time and action is contradictory. In the case of a connection with action, there is no sequence; in the case of a connection with time, there is no [such contradiction].
Because there is no mutual connection with the purpose, the relationship between the subsidiary and the principal is not intended;
for there is no connection of the purpose of the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) with the principal [sacrifice],
and the two *āmī* [offerings] at the end of the new moon sacrifice do not have an existing purpose [in that context].
Therefore, this connection [of the subsidiary] with the principal is rightly understood as being for the purpose of time alone, because it is perceived first; for time is indeed difficult to bypass.
At that stage, neither syntactical unity nor equal capability is observed, and the intermediate "how-to" (kathaṃbhāva) is not yet understood.

Nor can it be fulfilled by a subsequent [element] whose purpose has not yet been established, nor likewise by those that follow it, until the primary [element] is reached. If this were the case, then every subordinate element (*guṇa*) situated in the interval would be connected with all the preceding subsidiary parts (*aṅga*),
and the primary [element] itself would never be reached, because the intermediate "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*) would have already been completed.

It is said that in the section concerning *anuṣaṅga* (supplying ellipsis), it was explained that [the word] "goes as far as the end" refers to something characterized by the manner of the principal action (*pradhāna*), having merely stated its connection with another.
But if this were so, would it not follow that all intermediate contexts (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) would be utterly destroyed?
The first quarter of the third chapter is now stated,
because the [preceding] sentences have reached their completion.
For this reason as well, immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) is not a valid means of proof;
because the characteristic of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is observed in each of these individually, but not in all of them together.
Therefore, for that reason too, they do not have mutual purpose.
For it is possible for a deity-dual offering to be produced by means of a single [deity],
just as in the case of the *manotā* hymn, [the dual offering] is joined with Agni; likewise, in the *pātnīvata* offering, Tvaṣṭṛ’s lack of independence has been stated by that same [reasoning].
Likewise, in the *Tantravārtika*, it is stated that "the mother of Ḍittha" is the mother of both Ḍittha and Ḍavittha.

Alternatively, because the meaning is connected with the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and because the gender is connected with the primary object, the mention of a subordinate quality (*guṇa-śruti*) has the purpose of indicating [the principal].
For just as cups (*camasa*) are not indicated by the term "cup" (*graha*) itself, [so too the subordinate is not the primary].

Likewise, the character of being dedicated to Agni (āgneyatva) would not exist as a designation for an offering to two deities; for a cognition that is distributed between two objects is not designated by means of only one.
Therefore, an offering to Agni-and-Soma is not called "dedicated to Agni" (āgneya), nor is an offering to Indra-and-Agni so called.

The term *āgneya* denotes that which has Agni as its deity independently (*nirapekṣa*). Since in a dual-deity offering (*dvidevatya*) Agni is not the deity independently, this secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix does not arise from the word "Agni" occurring in a compound such as *agnīṣoma*; therefore, it does not express that [compound] object's status as a deity.
However, in a case where he [Agni] is the deity independently, it is possible to say "āgneya."
As for the argument that it is "like the *prāśitra*," it is replied:

in this case, the scriptural mention of the quality of being dedicated to Agni (*āgneya*) is for the purpose of restricting the specific location; whereas, since the taking of the *prāśitra* portion would apply everywhere by virtue of the general statement, this specific declaration is intended to prescribe a particular part—the head—for the sake of a specific remedy. Thus, there is a difference between the two cases.
Having observed the Śatapatha Śruti, Kātyāyana has stated here:
"Having divided that sacrificial cake into four parts, he places it upon the sacrificial grass (barhis). To this, it is replied:

The universal necessarily moves toward the particular; and as soon as it has reached it, it is firmly established in that particular. Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter in the *Tantravārttika* composed by the venerable Śrī Bhaṭṭa Kumārila Svāmin.

Because of the connection with the expression of meaning, there should be a status as a subsidiary (śeṣabhāva) in the case of mantras; therefore, there is a connection by way of origin because of the eternal association with the meaning.
Now, the application by means of indicative power (liṅga) is being praised.
Indicative power (liṅga) is the capacity of mantras to convey their respective meanings.
And that [denotation] exists in both the primary (*mukhya*) and the secondary (*gauṇa*) sense in some manner.

Regarding the doubt as to whether its application (*viniyoga*) occurs only in the primary sense or also in the secondary sense, the dull-witted person asks: "What, then, is the primary, and what is the secondary?

However, since the existence of the secondary sense has already been established in the *Siddhi-sūtra*, where its various causes and its function of not abandoning its own meaning were explained, this present investigation should be understood as having preceded that [establishment] by implication (*arthāt*).
And in that context, the word *mukhya*— used in the sense of "as if" (like) according to the rule *śākhādibhyo yaḥ*—
is applicable to all [words] because they are all denotable by words.

In every respect, that which is called a "definition" (lakṣaṇa) functions as a delimiting factor; it is always understood as secondary (gauṇa), having its application dependent on something else. Because of the inherent association of the word and its meaning, this manifestation has been brought about.
However, because it serves as an indicator (*dyotaka*) for another [meaning], its primary status (*mukhyatva*) does not depart, just as earth and so forth do not for words such as "cow" (*go*).

Alternatively, setting aside the status of the prefix as an indicator, an equal status (*tulyakalpatā*) is asserted: since this meaning is always understood from the composite word *māṇavaka-agni*, it follows that when the meaning belongs to the composite as a whole—as in the case of *aśvakarṇa* and similar terms—the individual component is secondary (*gauṇa*).
This is the second quarter of the third chapter.
It is said therein that "conventional usage based on the whole" (samudāyaprasiddhi) occurs where the meanings of the individual parts are obscured and the whole alone is perceived as distinct.

However, it is perceived that the tawny color (*paiṅgalya*) is the distinct denotation of the word *agni* (fire), and the physical form of the boy (*piṇḍasvarūpa*) is the distinct denotation of the word *māṇavaka*. Therefore, since both are denotative of their respective individual objects, they are primary (*mukhya*).
Now, [the author], supporting the view that the meaning of a sentence is derived from its constituent parts, says:

"Because it is understood through two words whose own meanings are followed along, like the word 'blue-lotus' (*nīlotpala*), the sentence-meaning is thus conveyed by the word-meanings; therefore, with respect to the word, it is secondary (*gauṇa*) in the same manner as before. He refutes this.

However, in this case, its primary meaning—firehood—is not present; nor can "tawny-ness" (paiṅgalya) be the denoted meaning for you, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of it being indistinguishable from our own [direct] perception. Therefore, it is not the sentence-meaning. Consequently, since the word applies equally to the movement of the boy and to his tawny-ness, it possesses primacy [in both].

In the Bhāṣya, regarding the phrase "of the boy" (*māṇavakasya*), the genitive case is produced by the distinction from the quality of tawny-brownness (*paiṅgalya*), not by the distinction from the denoter [the word itself].
For the actual nature of the boy is not understood through the word "fire.
Indeed, if they were synonyms, the word "boy" would not be employed [separately].

Now, it might be argued: "That which is well-known" implies that once the function of the qualifying term has been performed, there is both the recourse to and the non-recourse to that [well-known status]; these very states of being poorly or well known show the distinction between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*).
To this, the answer is given:

now [the author] shows the basis for the distinction as the frequency or infrequency of usage residing in the speaker, which is rooted in the difference in the well-known status residing in the hearer.
And as for the argument beginning with "for which there is frequent application," that is refuted;
furthermore, one must show that the word "cow" (go) has applications of weak and strong conventional usage with respect to the earth and so forth.

Satisfaction may indeed sometimes come from *maṇḍakas*, and sometimes from *khaṇḍamodakas*. Yet, in this context, neither the *maṇḍakas* nor the *khaṇḍamodakas* are primary or secondary [in a fixed sense].
Now, he explains the distinction.

Even though there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *māṇavaka*, because it is denoted when similarity exists—according to the principle of the word *aruṇā*—and is not denoted when it does not exist; and because its application is observed elsewhere where there is no similarity, and not observed where there is none; and because it functions as a qualifier, similarity itself must necessarily be conveyed first in the initial cognition. Since that [similarity] is not perceived unless fire is understood, fire is denoted first of all. Consequently, since the remaining [attributes] are understood solely through their connection with that [fire], it is non-denotable, just like the individual instance (*vyakti*).
It has been stated that in such cases as *manti* and so forth, there are certain commonalities of form (*rūpa*) and other factors;

therefore, since the distinction between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*) exists, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) must be commenced. And thus, the nine secondary applications mentioned in the *Tat-siddhi-sūtra* are to be understood.

This being the case, since words such as *pūṣan* would denote Agni and others through a figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*), there would be no displacement [of the mantra]; otherwise, they would have to be moved to wherever Pūṣan and the others are present. Likewise, since words such as *agni* would denote the sun and so forth, if there were no modification, the injunction of the Ṛṣi would be upheld.
To this prima facie view, we reply:
"The mantras are subordinate to the sacrifice because of their connection with the expression of meaning."
Furthermore, for those who have achieved their purpose through the primary [meaning], there is no assumption of a scriptural basis for the secondary [meaning];
moreover, even if it were optional, because it would be non-permanent, it would result in meaninglessness in certain instances.

Because the primary meaning must never be abandoned, this is the meaning of the Sūtra: "Since there is a connection with the expression of meaning in the mantras, they possess the status of being subsidiary (śeṣabhāva) only through that [meaning] which is innate; for their connection would be with that very [innate] meaning alone, because of its constant association due to its non-deviation."
The designation "invocatory formulas for the sacrifice" (yāgānumantraṇa) connects them to the ritual;

therefore, they apply according to their capacity to the deities of that specific rite, because they cannot be enjoined to those [deities] for whom they lack the capacity when there is a consideration of distinctions.

When there is a possibility of the operation of *liṅga* (indicative power) for the application of the word’s meaning, and where a figurative sense (*gauṇatva*) might indeed occur in the case of either a Brāhmaṇa passage or a mantra,
the figurative sense is accepted for the mantras because they do not take the form of an injunction (*anuvāda*).
First of all, it is understood through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) that the *gārhapatya* fire is the object of the primary meaning of the suffix in the second word;
therefore, it must be manifested by the verse addressed to Indra (*aindrī*).
In this regard, if the discrepancy with the actual referent has arisen due to the requirements of the injunction, one must simply accept it as such.
In this case, there must necessarily be either a figurative sense for the Brāhmaṇa or for the Mantra.

Since the Brāhmaṇa prescribes what has not been previously established at all, and since it operates first regarding a matter that lacks any other means of knowledge, a figurative sense is inappropriate for it. However, in the case of the Mantra, because its function is dependent on the object enjoined by the Brāhmaṇa—since it exists for the purpose of illuminating that object—it is indeed proper for it to assume a figurative meaning by setting aside its own primary sense when that would conflict with the injunction.
Nor can Indra [be called] *gārhapatya* because of a connection with the parts of the *gṛhapati*, for it would be so only through the firm cognition of "Agni" based on the word's primary meaning;
even in its figurative application, this function arises only with difficulty.
However, because they are absolutely dissimilar, even a figurative sense is not observed here;
nor is "indra" a technical term [for *i*] like "agni" is for *a*, as in the rule "adeṅ guṇaḥ."
For the relationship between word and meaning cannot be established as having Śiva as its cause;

rather, Indrahood is brought about by his connection with the sacrifice. Or, he is indeed the Lord (Īśvara) because he exercises lordship (indati) over his own effects, in accordance with the etymological sense of the word.
Because it is enjoined as a rule for a specific time and because it is devoted to long-term practice, no mantra is prescribed here;
furthermore, the suffix *śatṛ* occurs in the sense of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*), and that which has already been obtained is merely restated (*anūdyate*).
Furthermore, since the body is already established by virtue of its inherent fitness (*yogyatva*), it is not something to be enjoined;
rather, what is called an "injunction" (*vidhi*) for it is merely a matter of conceit (*abhimāna*).
Likewise, in the context of the lifelong practice (*yāvajjīvaka-abhyāsa*), it has been explained that time and practice serve as mutual causes for the injunction.
Now, as for what was said— that the *hantṛ* alone will perform the *viṣkṛt*— to that it is replied:
or rather, this mantra follows after the [preceding] word.
However, because it is devoted to a threefold repetition, a mantra is not enjoined here.
It is stated that [the mantra] becomes a subsidiary part of the threshing (avaghāta) by virtue of its very form;
for there is the vocative case-ending and the imperative (praiṣa) in the second person singular "iha".

If the mantra were intended for threshing, everything would be rendered useless; and thus, by the indicative mark (liṅga), there will be praise through the word "vāk" (speech) in its definitive form as femininity, which is identical with the object itself.

Otherwise, since the word *kriyā* (action) has an unexpressed feminine gender and is an ambiguous, indistinct gender, it could somehow be conceived as a property of the word (*śabdadharmatā*) by means of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*); therefore, its status as a subordinate element of the invitation (*āhvāna*) is established.
Likewise, regarding rising and dismissal, because this is an extended application (*atideśa*) sūtra, all the meanings of the preceding sūtras must be applied here.
In the preceding discussion, it was stated that [the mantra] serves the purpose of indicating time; now, the distinction is that it also serves the purpose of an injunction.

Furthermore, the reason for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because the focus there was on the threefold repetition, the instruction regarding the mantra was not actually carried out, nor was it so [in the case of the other].
It is established by the statement "Agni is kindled by rising" that the act of rising is what is being manifested.
The second quarter of the third chapter:

And in the *muktavāka*, there is an injunction regarding time because it serves another purpose; since its requirements are fulfilled by the manifestation of the deities and the pouring out [of the offering], there is no need for a relationship of principal and subordinate, and thus it has the purpose of indicating time.

Furthermore, in every case where two things have already achieved their purpose (*kṛtārtha*), the relationship between them will be established as one of temporal sequence; thus, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is understood here in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Moreover, because the mention of the sacrificial grass (*prastara*) having achieved its purpose is intended to be presented as the primary element, it is not possible for it to be a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *sūktavāka*, nor can it be a subordinate part of the deity expressed therein; this is stated for the purpose of establishing that very point—that even the *sūktavāka* itself is a subordinate part of that [act].
Or rather, it is an instruction; for the word *yājyā* cannot be used without cause.

Since the instrumental function of the *sūktavāka* is understood from the direct connection with the action in the statement "he throws the grass-bundle [into the fire] with the *sūktavāka*," that function cannot be discarded, because the case-ending denoting a kāraka is stronger. Thus, the *sūktavāka*, functioning according to the direct Vedic text (*śruti*), will be connected with the ritual act; otherwise, its time [of recitation] would be connected [with the act].
And since it is thus a subordinate element (*aṅga*), the designation *yājyā* will be appropriate on account of its similarity [to other *yājyās*].
"The *sūktavāka* itself is the *yājyā*.
But is its status as a *yājyā* ultimate and real, or is it merely figurative?
And what is the distinction here?
If it possesses the nature of a *yājyā*, it must be characterized by those [features]:
one sacrifices while seated, one sacrifices without pausing,
and one utters the *vaṣaṭ* call over the *yājyā*.
One first employs the *paronuvākyā* with the words beginning [with "may he come," etc.];

then there is mere praise. Therefore, none of these [words] need be attended to. What is the conclusion? It must be so by virtue of the ritual properties (*dharma*). That which is used for sacrifice is a *yājyā*, and since it is sacrificed with the *sūktavāka*, it possesses the nature of a *yājyā*.
In this regard, because it is not feminine due to its being a neuter gender, a feminine suffix would not apply according to the *Tantravārtika*;
this is not a fault.

Since the status of being a *yājyā* (offering verse) is well-established even for those [verses] such as the *samidh-ādi* which are not *ṛc*s, it might be argued: "In the case of the half-verses used as means for *darvihoma* offerings, although they function as instruments of sacrifice, the status of being a *yājyā* is not observed; therefore, this is not an invariable cause. To this we reply: only that in which the word *yājyā* is actually employed is exclusively a *yājyā*. Consequently, since the term is applied there, the *saktavāka* must also possess the relevant characteristics (*dharma*). Nor can its usage be considered figurative, because the primary cause [for such usage] is directly perceived.
Moreover, this term *yājyā* is a general term; it cannot be determined through usage alone to have a distinct scope without a definition.
Therefore, the definition must be stated as follows:
"That object by which one is made to sacrifice by Caitra is the *yājyā*."
If that were the case, the same would apply to the *sūktavāka* as well.
Therefore, since it has been argued that its status as a *yājyā* is strictly primary, we reply:
for in the archetype (*prakṛti*), every entity is defined by its production for the sake of that [purpose].
Furthermore, the status of being a *yājyā* (offering verse) is determined by its being a mantra prescribed for the purpose of designating a deity for the oblation that is being abandoned.
However, the *sūktavāka* was not produced for the purpose of designating the deity of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) that is being abandoned;
rather, its essential nature consists in the naming of deities already worshipped (*iṣṭa*). If it is argued that the indicative power (*liṅga*) is set aside by direct statement (*śruti*), we say no.

Without an application based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), or permission, it lacks the capacity [to function as a *yājyā*], just like the sprinkling of fire (*agni-seka*) and so forth; and we shall explain this further in the subsequent sūtra.
Therefore, it does not possess the status of a *yājyā* by its own nature.
Nor is there any other *yājyā* of such a kind in this context, the performance of whose function would cause it to acquire the characteristics of a *yājyā*.

Furthermore, when the nature of something as a sacrifice has been previously determined, that which is subsequently enjoined as its means is understood to be the *yājyā*. However, in this case, the nature of [the *sūktavāka*] as a sacrifice has not been determined by anyone prior to its connection with the *sūktavāka*; thus, it results in a circular dependency:
it would be a sacrifice because of its connection with a *yājyā*, and it would be a *yājyā* because of its connection with a sacrifice.

Now, it might be argued as follows: even without the designation "yājyā," if it were taken merely as the *sūktavāka* and employed in the sacrifice, then—by virtue of its connection with the deities denoted by that [mantra] and its relation to the principal offering (*praharaṇa*) which possesses the nature of a sacrifice—the status of being a *yājyā* would be obtained. To this, it is replied:
only a word such as "yūpa" (sacrificial post), which has no established meaning elsewhere, acquires its established meaning in this manner.
Furthermore, this term *yājyā*, whether at the time of its origin or at the time of its application, acquires its meaning without depending on a subsequent state.

Moreover, those properties belonging to the *yājyā* have already established their nature in the primary sacrifices; they do not wait for this status of being a *yājyā* which is acquired only with difficulty.

If, however, it were a modified form (*vikṛti*), then its status as a *yājyā* would be determined by its function, just as the status of being a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is attributed to the *paridhi* wood or the *khalevālī* beam.

This is the very nature of things; a definition of *dharma* is not preceded by something that is non-action (*akārya*). For this reason, the *yājyā* verses are not themselves *dharma*. Furthermore, in the statement "the *saktavāka* alone is the *yājyā*," the particle *eva* (alone) indicates a metaphorical application (*upacāra*). This is only possible if there is a metaphorical application of the term *yājyā* to what is not actually a *yājyā*, but not if it were the primary sense of *yājyā*. If it were the primary sense, the particle *eva* would not have been employed in that context; thus, that oblation is the ultimate reality.
Just as the *āghāra* and other offerings attain the status of a *homa* through the pouring of substances,
so too does the *āghāraṇa* (sprinkling) attain the status of a *homa* because it consists of the act of pouring.

Thus, even though the status of being a *yājyā* (offering verse) is prohibited for those who are not entitled to sacrifice (*ayājya*)— as in the case of the statement "one sacrifices with the *ṛc* itself"— it is mentioned here for the sake of praise.
Regarding the point that its purpose is for the deity because of its connection with it—
namely, that since the *sūktavāka* has already fulfilled its function by proclaiming the intended deities, no further application (*viniyoga*) is possible— it is replied to this:
its capacity to serve as a means of manifesting the deity through its own inherent power does not depart from it even when it is applied to the throwing of the grass-bundle (*prastara-praharaṇa*).

Even there, because it would be useless in any other way, this [text] seeks to avoid a great contradiction with the scriptural injunction "by means of the *sūktavāka*," which possesses the capacity to denote the intended deity.

Furthermore, the scripture, being unable to employ that which does not denote the throwing of the grass-bundle (*prastara*) when no such capacity exists—and not creating a new capacity—expects: "How indeed might this [text], while denoting exactly that which it is capable of denoting, accomplish my purpose?"
Everywhere, a mantra attains the status of an auxiliary (*aṅga*) by denoting either an action or its means.
In that regard, first of all, this is the established course: that which is well-known as the form of the principal (*śeṣin*) must be denoted by the mantra.
However, when, due to incapacity, it does not achieve subservience to that purpose, then, by implication, the opposite occurs.
Whatever this [text] expresses, that certainly exists in this action;
otherwise, its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) as heard in scripture would not be tenable.
Therefore, it is established by this scriptural statement (*śruti*), "with the *sūktavāka*."

As for what you assert— that the second quarter of the third chapter establishes the *prastara-praharaṇa* (the throwing of the grass-bundle) by declaring it to be exactly that— so too does the mantra itself declare this very same thing.
By pronouncing the names of the chosen deities with the thought, "Whatever I am doing, I do all that," [the purpose is served].

In that regard, if the chosen deities were merely those connected to the previous sacrifice, then nothing would have been accomplished by the throwing of the grass-bundle (*prastara*). However, if they are indeed its own constituent parts (*aṅga*), then by means of manifesting them, the *sūktavāka* becomes the instrument for the throwing of the *prastara*.

Furthermore, no other utility for these [formulas] is known than by way of their being deities; therefore, they possess the status of deities. Consequently, since the substance of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is designated as an oblation (*havis*) and Agni and the others are designated as deities, this is understood to be a sacrifice (*yajña*). However, because the term *juhoti* applies to the act of taking [the offering], it is determined to be a *homa* due to the addition of the act of throwing [into the fire]. Thus, there is no contradiction between the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and the indicative mark (*liṅga*). And so, even according to the Sūtra, that [formula] serves the purpose of the deity alone.
Why?

Because by those [words], even for this *harati* (the act of throwing), there will indeed be a connection with the meaning of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), due to the contingency that the time [of the offering] is known through the sequence of the mantra-recitation; thus, [the words] such as "If Agni has enjoyed this oblation" and so forth would be used.
Furthermore, the scriptural statement "even before the *sūktavāka*" shows that this particular part [of the mantra] possesses the capacity for the act of throwing.

And although the power of the mantra is common [to all], nevertheless, for the sake of conforming to the Vedic text (śruti), it must be designated as "that which by this [is the oblation]," referring specifically to the grass-bundle (prastara).
Or rather, from the very beginning, the grass-bundle is to be designated by the word "this" (idam), because the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and so forth are not directly perceived [in that context].
If it is argued that the word "ajuṣata" (they enjoyed) is meaningless, we say no.
Since it serves the purpose of praise by means of granting success through what was previously practiced, its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is established.
To the question, "How can the *sūktavāka* or Agni and the others be auxiliaries of a non-primary rite (*apradhānakarman*)?", he recites the subsequent sūtra:
"Because of the instruction for the whole, there is mention of all in both cases."
Living by the context of authority, he deliberates:

should the *sūktavāka* be employed in its entirety for both the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices, or should there be an extraction [of parts] according to the specific deities intended? What is the prima facie view?
"In each single [instance], it is complete.
Why?
Because for that reason, the offering would have been made with the *asūktavāka* alone.

Or rather, as was stated in the section on *stotra* and *śastra*, these [mantras] are excluded from such [rituals] because they are consecratory formulas (*saṃskāra*) belonging to something else; and this was also stated regarding the *anumantraṇa* mantras for Pūṣan and others.
If these were deities belonging exclusively to the act of throwing (*praharaṇa*), then they would be employed in both cases together with the sacrificial cake (*sakata*).

However, since Agni and the other deities are indeed recognized [in the Sūktavāka], there is no reason for their separation. Furthermore, because the Sūktavāka depends upon the manifestation of the intended deities, its extraction (pradaraṇa) is not irrelevant; rather, it is understood to be dependent on them, as it rests upon the deities employed in the primary rites.
And those primary rites are performed according to their respective deities, not without distinction.
Therefore, there is an extraction (apakarṣa).

If the injunction were directed toward the primary acts with respect to the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), then this entire statement would be [applicable] with respect to both; thus concludes the second quarter of the third chapter.
Since the fruit of the sacrifice is connected to each individual inherent [act],
by what means is it understood that the collection [of acts] is for the sake of the fruit?
Just as the word "water" (toya) is accepted to apply both to a single drop and to a collection [of drops].
Because it consists of substances that are conjoined, the term *sūktavāka* is likewise [applied]; therefore, the *sūktavāka* is established as being threefold:
in private study, at the time of the ritual action, and both in the archetypal (*prakṛti*) and the modified (*vikṛti*) rites.
When the deity is excluded from the middle [of the formula], it is understood to apply to the original form (prakṛti) and the collection [of rites],
as well as to the middle of the words "sūrya" and so forth in the modified form (vikṛti),
on account of indicative mark (liṅga), order (krama), and name (samākhyāna); thus, the recitation is connected with the optional (kāmya) rites.
The second quarter of the third chapter:

In whatever order the optional rites dedicated to Indra-Agni and others are recited, do the pairs of *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* mantras—belonging to those same deities and bearing the designation "optional"—set aside that order and serve as indicators (*liṅga*) for the purpose of [indicating] those specific deity-possessing rites? Or rather, by some means, are they applied to those very optional sacrifices (*iṣṭi*) according to their respective order?
Indeed, the multiplicity of examples is intended to establish the scope of the specific qualifications mentioned in the root text.
In this regard, although the indication (liṅga) suggests that [the mantra] applies to all [deities], it is stated in response:
for the indication would establish a connection with a deity,
and there is no purpose in its application to the mere nature of the object itself.
Connection with the sacrifice, or connection with the deity associated with it, cannot be established by this much alone—namely, by means devoid of sentence-context (*vākya-prakaraṇa*) and so forth;
nor is it known in which specific part [of the ritual] the application (*viniyoga*) occurs.
Therefore, the designation (*samākhyā*) must necessarily be relied upon as a basis.

For by that [word "sā"], both the connection with a sacrifice and the specific purpose are established; for it is connected to a sacrifice because one sacrifices *by means of it* (*anayā*), and its specific purpose is also determined because it is intended for the offering of the oblation (*haviḥ*).
Consequently, as to which sacrifice it is connected to, it is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that it belongs to that deity.
But even so, the desired [result] is certainly not established.
How is it not established?
When the designation "the section on optional *yājyā*s" determines that the scope is restricted to optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*) by means of this very name;
moreover—

Even though a name (samākhyā) might establish a connection with the sacrifice in general, it would nevertheless be sublated by the more powerful order (krama). Therefore, this traditional recitation is indeed connected specifically with the optional sacrifices (kāmyeṣṭi). For what purpose, then, were both [name and order] set forth in the sūtra?
He thinks that everything is established merely by the indicative power (liṅga) supported by sequence (krama), or simply by the fact that this is the section on optional (kāmya) *yājyā* verses;
however, he is addressed as follows:

"It is true that in the case of the offerings to Indra-Agni and others, the status of the verses as *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* would be established even by indicative power and sequence alone, since they are not employed elsewhere; but as for those rites dedicated to Agni and others which are enjoined by such texts as 'To Agni, Lord of Vows' (*agnaye vratapataye*), there, by virtue of both position (sthāna) and indicative power, these verses possess the character of *sāmidhenī* verses and *yājyā-anuvākyā* verses in the manifestation of Agni."
Because of the recitation of seventeen [verses], there is a requirement for two ṛks for each of the *sāmidhenī* verses.

In that case, if the designation (*samākhyā*) as "offering verse" (*yājyā*) were not accepted as the means of application, then the application of the indicative power (*liṅga*) and the order (*krama*) would be possible even for the *sāmidhenīs*.
Since there is no reason to bypass the first [verse], the application would consequently fall upon that very one.
But by means of the designation (samākhyā), that [confusion] is removed.
Therefore, one might argue that only that [designation] should suffice, and there is no need for gender (liṅga) and order (krama).
To this it is replied:

If, in this context, only those verses pertaining to that deity which are measured by the *iṣṭi* were to be brought forward, then it would indeed be so; but here, in the sequence of a ritual action dedicated to another deity and already filled with its own appropriate *yājyā* and *anu-vākyā* verses, those *ṛc*s addressed to Agni which occur are—being applied solely on the basis of their name (*samākhyā*)—to be employed for the function of the *yājyā*.
However, such an application is not possible, because they possess different gender markers (*liṅga*) and are thus sublated by the two [verses] possessing the correct gender markers.

Therefore, since there is no application [of the name] when one relies on the order of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), and once the function of the name (*samākhyā*) has ceased, the application by those two [order and position] being established, the employment [of the verses] among the *sāmidhenīs* is accomplished.
He shows that subject matter:

after reciting the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* for the offering to Agni-Varuṇa, the eight verses of the mind (*manas*) are found before the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* of the offerings to Soma-Rudra have arrived.
"These [verses] are to be inserted as *dhāyyās* among the *sāmidhenīs*.
Likewise, the two verses containing the word "broad-footed" (*pṛthupājavatī*) are to be understood in the same way.
There too, because they are recited after the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā*, bypassing the sequence of the *sāmidhenīs*, it is understood that they belong to the subsequent sacrifice.

And if order were not resorted to, then by the mere force of indicative mark (*liṅga*) and name (*samākhyā*), the pair [of verses] dedicated to Indra-Agni would first be applied to the second *aindrāgna* offering, and the second [pair] to the first; however, since order exists, it takes precedence over the name because it establishes the connection with the sacrifice earlier. Thus, the indicative mark, being constrained by that [order], can only imply a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). In this way, an application based on non-order is avoided.
Therefore, it has been correctly indicated.

Regarding the application of the rule for mantras in cases where they are not designated by that [specific] name, because they are taught as being so, in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, first, specific verses such as "O Agni, come for the feast" (*agna āyāhi vītaye*) and others are prescribed as the means for the *stotra*, *śastra*, and so forth; and then, they are again taught in a general sense in such injunctions as "one worships the Āgnīdhra with an *āgneyī* verse.
In this regard, there is a doubt: should verses other than those be taken, or both those and others, or only those? From the text, three positions appear.

However, there is no authoritative evidence for the position that [the term "non-contextual"] refers exclusively to non-contextual [sacrifices]. For, by means of an extensive argumentative sequence, it is established that there is no distinction [between contextual and non-contextual], rather than a determination of only the non-contextual; for by whatever authority the non-contextual would be grasped through the non-distinction of the word *āgneya*, by that very same [authority] the contextual would also be grasped. Furthermore, there is no reason whatsoever by which the contextual [sacrifices] should be excluded. Nor did the author of the Bhāṣya present three distinct positions; rather, at the outset, it was precisely the position of non-distinction that was encompassed by the word "non-contextual" (*aprakṛta*) without the particle "also" (*api*).
By this, the misconception arises that [these suffixes] apply only to what is not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛta*).

However, the authority (*pramāṇa*) for that very point establishes precisely the term "without distinction" (*aviśeṣa*). And so it will be explained further on: "The cognition occurs even with respect to what is not the subject under discussion; they may also take up what is the subject under discussion."
If, however, the third position must necessarily be supported, then this much is the reasoning of the Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*):
[the *puroḍāśa*] is not to be taken because it has lost its potency (*yātayāmatva*) due to being employed for another purpose in the context at hand.
Alternatively, this is a general rule, whereas these [other rules] regarding the *āgneya* cake are specific rules; and general scriptures operate by setting aside the domain of specific rules.
If, however, there were no apprehension of a distinction even in that case, then that too would be taken as an example on the grounds that it is equal to this very [case];
therefore, only those not under discussion (*aprakṛta*) should be accepted.
Alternatively, a cognition of a specific [meaning] has already arisen through words such as "belonging to Agni" (*āgneya*).
Nor do we perceive any other qualifying factor that would restrict the application to the present context, because the context itself, as a grasping agent, lacks the power to qualify.
Furthermore, the worldly context characterized by mere proximity is sublated by the specific cognition produced by the etymological *śruti*; therefore, there is a cognition of all [mantras].
For it is not logical to give instruction on what has already been instructed;
here, "of that which has been instructed" means precisely that.
"Of such a kind" means devoid of qualifications.
Regarding the phrase "of what kind":

the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) maintains that there exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for apprehending a specific distinction even without an explicit qualification, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

However, the opponent, based solely on his own intention, imagines that the proponent's intended justification for apprehending a specific distinction is actually undesirable, and asks: "How [is it so]? If that is its mark, in what way does it serve as its indicator?"
Nor, in this context, is the word *liṅga* employed with the intention of referring to the gender of the deity to be mentioned hereafter;

for [if that were the case], would it mean the force of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*) or the fact of being enjoined by it? Since the consequence of the absence of an injunction (*vidhyabhāva*) is presented when that [force] has been exhausted.

The intention is this: it cannot be recognized as a specific mantra by means of that general indicative mark (*liṅga*) alone, such as "fire" (*agni*), without a clear qualification when all [mantras] are being perceived.

Therefore, if a qualification is desired here, it must be specified by the indicative mark consisting of the statement of its performance, according to the principle of the offering (*nirvāpa*) and the taking up (*ālambha*) in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
That [mark] is excluded from the *daśataya* verses which have become mere subsidiaries; for this very reason, he shows it to be a qualification.
One must understand that "by means of this very mark (liṅga), he performs this [action]"—that is, by means of this mark, whether it be the mark of Agni or the mark of Indra, he performs something.

Since the presence of Agni is indicated by the fact that [the word] is formed with the suffix *ap* (as in *agnyupasthāna*), the injunctive [element] is thereby subsumed as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*); thus, it does not constitute a direct instruction (*upadeśa*). This concludes the second quarter of the third chapter on verbal suffixes.

If, on the other hand, it were taught that "one performs [the rite] with the Āgneyī and so forth," then it would not be specified; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of including every Āgneyī verse without distinction. Therefore, to teach again that which was already taught and merely indicated by that [general term] is without authoritative basis.

Therefore, because the mere mention of deities such as Agni and others—being devoid of an injunction regarding what is to be performed—lacks the capacity [to establish a connection], verses from the *Daśataya* collection must also be taken up.

Now, it was stated [in the previous argument] "by the power of the context" (*prakaraṇa-sāmarthyāt*) with the intention of the Siddhānta view. However, since "indicative mark" (*liṅga*) is stronger than "context," the word *liṅga* here refers to a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) based on etymological derivation through the connection with the deity, and not merely to capacity (*sāmarthya*).

Even in the subsequent section concerning the extensive application (*bahuprayoga*), the word *liṅga* should be explained in exactly the same way as a derivative term expressing direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).

He says, "If there were a contradiction": if we were to take the subject matter at hand as being non-*āgneya*, then a contradiction would arise; however, if we accept the subject matter at hand as *āgneya*, then this [indirect indication] is also accommodated.
Thus, in the section on "that which is sent forth" (*tadūta-adhikaraṇa*), it was stated that there is no contradiction between direct statement (*śruti*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*).
"It is not so.
Even for those [mantras] belonging to the *Daśataya* collection which are obtained through option, it is not proper that they be set aside in accordance with the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Therefore, neither [the general rule nor the specific context] should be favored.

Thinking that there is no contradiction because the universal (sāmānya) is fully present in each individual (vyakti), and thus all the constituent elements of the word are possible even in the specific individual under discussion, he says: "It must be assisted by this [individual] which possesses that mark. Therefore, since the sentence containing the mark has a universal as its object, and since the context provides the required specific detail, sublation (bādha) is not appropriate when there is no conflict with the inherent connection (samavāya).

The other, however, maintains that there is a contradiction because [the word] intends to denote the individual (vyakti) and thereby precludes the application of the *dāśataya* verses. [The opponent replies: "But surely the individual is not the meaning of the word"—this is a rejection of that intention. The other, however, says:
We do not understand this very point: whether the possession of gender-linguistic markers, being a general property, is a constituent factor here or not.

For if it were impossible for words such as "cow" and the like to denote an individual, then, when there is an injunction regarding a universal, the fault would arise that one must either grasp an unspecified individual or grasp the individual under discussion. However, if the word's meaning is indeed the individual qualified by the deity, then, when the specific individual under discussion is grasped, there would be a sublation of only a portion of the cognition produced by the Vedic revelation (śruti). Furthermore, in this case, the individual alone is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), not some so-called "universal. But why does the Commentator now deny the universal as asserted in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*?
We reply: he does not.
Some say that [the word] merely expresses the possibility of its being a constituent part; however, that is incorrect.

For if that were the case, since the individuals would not be explicitly heard, there would be no fault even if they were not included. Therefore, it must be stated that the universal is denied in relation to what is under discussion. Indeed, because this word [“individual,” *vyakti*] is etymological (*yaugika*), it does not attain the status of a generic term (*jāti-śabda*).

Furthermore, no universal (*jāti*) whatsoever is perceived here, because the term "Āgneyī" (pertaining to Agni) is applied solely on the basis of the identity of the deity, even when the verses have various forms and various meters. In the two [verses] "O Agni, come for the feast" (*agna ā yāhi vītaye*) and "I honor Agni, the Hotṛ, the giver of gifts" (*agniṃ hotāraṃ manye dāśvāṃsam*), no universal other than the deity is observed. This [relationship] with the deity does not fail, whereas the universal of the *ṛc* verse fails, since the term is used even for substances, actions, and so forth.
Therefore, he states that the deity alone is common here.
Although the relationship is also common, it was not presented by the author of the Bhāṣya as a subject of expression because it is established by the very nature of the matter.
Furthermore, it is precisely through the commonality of that deity that the defects such as finitude and non-eternality are eliminated.

Furthermore, even when a qualifier has been previously mentioned, it is not contradictory for the suffix to denote the qualificand, because the expressive powers (*śakti*) of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) are distinct. However, in cases where the same word must function for both [the qualifier and the qualificand], there is no denotation of the qualificand, as in the case of words like "cow" (*go*). Nowhere is the word *agni*, which merely denotes a qualifier, ever employed with respect to its qualificands; nor is the word *āgneyī* ever employed with respect to fire (*agni*), such that it would have to be led toward the qualificand.
And if only the qualifier were denoted, then because that alone would be capable of performing the function, the qualified object would not be grasped at all.
