Therefore, it is the qualifiers themselves that are the denotable objects here.
As it has been said regarding the words *piṅga* and *ekahāyanī*:

The second quarter of the third chapter. Consequently, even that which is under discussion [in the primary context] might be adopted in certain cases. [Objection: But was this not already stated? [Reply: It was stated with reference to the first alternative (pakṣa).
But surely you yourself have stated that it is not to be taken up because of defects such as being stale; yet the opponent adopts the middle position and says:

"For if only the original [mantras] were taken, a contradiction would arise because the operation of enjoining and indicating the suffix would have to occur simultaneously; but in our view, there is no necessary rule that only those [original ones] must be used here for the attendance upon the Āgnīdhra and other priests. Rather, by virtue of the specific statement, both those and others may be used, so there is no contradiction."
Thinking, "This [objection] will be seen [later]," he speaks out of an inability to tolerate the subversion of the context (*prakaraṇa*) without cause.
The opponent, however, gives the reply that the strength of the *śruti*—which possesses the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the deity—is indeed superior.

Furthermore, he introduces this to refute the exceedingly confused mode of expression common in the world, namely, the claim that "the context, which is not essentially connected with the indicative mark, must be favored."

In all practical transactions involving means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), people do not engage with objects of cognition (*prameya*) merely to favor the means of cognition; what then is the purpose? If you ask this, the following results: even when there are many [objects], if a single uniform means of cognition has been favored somewhere, then because one's purpose is fulfilled, other distinct objects that are conducive to human goals are not apprehended, even though they exist.

Furthermore, in the case of rites performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*), even for those seeking an abundance of results, there would be no need for repeated performance; therefore, disregarding the favor of the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and acting solely for one's own benefit, one should proceed in each instance—this is the inability to grasp the distinction [between the two].
It should be understood that in the phrase "because it contradicts the cognition of the *liṅga*," the word *liṅga* is used in that very same sense.
Consequently, the Sūtra also effects the application of what is not so designated; thus, it must be explained that it is not for the purpose of restricting what is not so designated.
However, since there is no agreement regarding those [texts] designated by that name, they are not consulted;
rather, this specific ritual application for this mantra is taught.
Furthermore, a specific rule is always intended to depend upon the attainment of a general rule.
Since this connection is established even in worldly usage, it is accepted exactly as it is heard;
thus, the second quarter of the third chapter is not capable of establishing an absolute connection with ritual action.
"Furthermore, the instruction would be purposeless due to the lack of connection with that which possesses a fruit.

[The opponent objects: "Surely, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it would be an auxiliary to the Jyotiṣṭoma; thus, one considers the general connection to be established through other means. [The author replies:
"He shows that even that is not possible unless it is itself enjoined."

If the connection with the *upasthāna* (ritual attendance) related to the Jyotiṣṭoma were intended to be expressed, then it would attain syntactic unity with that [Jyotiṣṭoma]. However, when—without prescribing that [attendance]—the *upasthāna* is merely restated and the mantra is prescribed as being connected to it either by way of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*) or otherwise, then the mantra would apply to the purely worldly and fruitless *upasthāna*, overriding the context (*prakaraṇa*) whose verbal testimony (*śruti*) has not been inferred. For in that case, there would be no cognition of a specific [connection] from the context; whereas in my view, since it is first of all accepted by the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is no application elsewhere, which results in purposefulness and parsimony.

When the connection between the *stobhas*, the fires, and so forth—which are constituent parts of the ritual—and the mantras is being enjoined, the act of "standing near" (*upasthāna*) is also restated; thus, it is more parsimonious.
Even though there is a qualification by the suffix *-matup* (possessive), nevertheless, I would not be released from the requirement to include all of them.
Therefore, it is not impossible for this [word] to be qualified by a verb;
for even when a qualification is provided, there would indeed be every cognition that is free from defects, whether it be worldly or Vedic, as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Everything is relied upon for its own sake, and no fault arises in this regard;

because the meaning is indicated through both its form and its instruction, the removal [of the word] must be performed by the very method stated in the objection, in order to favor the predominance of the direct Vedic revelation (śruti).

And because, as in the case of the *grahaṇa* [offerings], the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is set aside by the capacity [of the word] through its form, or by the context (*prakaraṇa*), or by the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Now, is it not the case that even syntactical unity is itself a type of indicative mark?
True.
Nevertheless, there is weakness due to remoteness from direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
For, by means of the capacity of the words "taking up" (*grahaṇa*) and so forth to imply a direct scriptural statement, the application (*viniyoga*) is performed quickly through inference;
whereas by the other [method], syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) [is established] later.

Therefore, there is a remoteness [of the mantras] because their capacity for the act of eating is established through the medium of the indicative mark (lakṣaṇā), and from that, the inference of the direct Vedic statement (śruti) follows. Consequently, since the act of eating is already fulfilled by the mantra and other elements which are more proximate to it, and since those [mantras] themselves do not apply elsewhere, they are relegated [to a subordinate position]. Now, one might object: "Is the manifestation of things already established by their own nature not purposeless?"

How can they be purposeless? For when even those [subsidiary acts] are not manifested, they cannot be performed at all. That which is obtained through the very meaning [of the primary injunction] is not manifested, because it is accomplished just so without effort. However, all [acts] such as the taking up of the vessels (*graha*) must be accomplished through separate efforts; since these are impermanent, they cannot be performed [automatically]. Therefore, they must necessarily be remembered. Furthermore, even the injunction of the main rite (*bhāvavidhi*) is unable to cause its own object to be performed without enjoining those [subsidiaries]; thus, it enjoins them as well.

Because of the nature of the mantras and because of their specific instruction, as well as the instruction regarding the proper digestion of those two mantras, there is an extraction [of the meaning] precisely because the meaning alone is enjoined; therefore, although it cannot be said here that there is a direct instruction due to the lack of an explicit citation, there is nevertheless no fault. Furthermore, "proper digestion" should be understood as being directly instructed by the traditional injunctions for penance (*prāyaścitta*) in cases of vomiting or purging, for which a separate performance is recognized as being implied by the sense.

The application of those mantras would not extend to the secondary offerings (*anuniṣyādinaḥ*), because of the specification of a particular indicative mark (*liṅga-viśeṣa-nirdeśāt*). Among those governed by the same injunction (*samāna-vidhāneṣu*), the non-*aindra* cups lack mantras;

for the phrase "of that drunk by Indra" (*indrapītasya*) is in grammatical apposition with *soma*, and since it possesses a different indicative mark for the non-*aindra* cups, and because there was no mention [of such mantras] in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the consumption is without a mantra.
Furthermore, when [the cups] are refilled, there is a designation for all [of them], because they are of two distinct types.
Thus, while remaining within the same subject matter as the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he considers the scope of the deliberation (*cintā*).
When the *camasa* cups have been offered and yet contain remnants, the Soma that is poured in again is called "refilled" (*punarabhyunīta*).
He demonstrates, by way of analysis, how those [cups] are refilled and how they become the subject of deliberation regarding the *ūha* (modification).

There are ten cups; among them, four belong to the officiants who perform the duties from the south, beginning with the Brahman. For these, the offering is made twice—once at the *vaṣaṭ* call and once at the subsequent *anu-vaṣaṭ* call. However, the cups belonging to the *hotraka* priests are offered only once, at the *vaṣaṭ* call alone. In all of these, Indra is the deity.
Then, while the Soma in the cups still has a residue remaining, more Soma is drawn into them and offered.
How is this understood? He shows all of that by means of the *preṣa* (directive).

In that regard, during the second *homa*, the *chotrakas* sacrifice to various deities; he shows this precisely through the *yājyās*, such as "O Maitrāvaruṇa, we invoke Mitra and Varuṇa" (*mitrāvaruṇau mitraṃ vayaṃ havāmahe*), and so forth.
In that context, when these *camasas* are brought forward for the purpose of being consumed after they have been offered, then [the *preṣa* says]: "Ho! Ho! (*hī hai*).
The two remaining [portions] are seen:

the first is the remnant of the *homa* dedicated to Indra, and the second is dedicated to deities such as Mitra and Varuṇa. Regarding the mention of one's own [share], a doubt arises: should Indra—even though he has been bypassed by the deity of the *prasthita* offering—be mentioned, and should the subsequent deities, Mitra, Varuṇa, and others, be mentioned in the formula "of that which has been drunk by Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa," or should only Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa [as a group] be mentioned?
Whence arises this doubt?
Is the connection with the deity of the lunar day (parvan) removed by the transition to another deity, or not?
If it is removed, then there is merely an indicative reference (upalakṣaṇa) to Mitra, Varuṇa, and the others.

Now, if it is not excluded, then Indra also must be understood [as the deity]. What is the prima facie view? First, according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), the commencement is indeed for all [deities], because there is no distinction between the two.
For the connection with a deity is established through the scripture; at the very time of taking [the substance], its being for the sake of a deity is initiated by the scripture itself.
And whatever is thus initiated is precisely what is completed, not anything else.

And here, because of the scriptural statement, it is understood that in the case of the *camasa* cups which are subsidiary to the *praśeṣa*, another substance must be taken for the sake of the subsequent deity.
In that case, the remnant is logically established as being indicated by the cup (*camasa*).

And when its status as being for the sake of the deity has not been determined during the time of the drawing [of the liquid], then at the time of the offering, even though it is present, it does not serve the purpose of the deity because it was not previously intended for that purpose. Nor is there any other intention for it at that time, due to the absence of a scriptural injunction.
It is not touched by another intention due to the logical consequence [of contradiction],
because it was already intended at the time of partition;
nor is there another intention at the time of the actual offering.
Furthermore, because that which has already been resolved upon cannot be resolved upon again,
for a single substance is not to be relinquished more than once;
therefore, the resolution does not exist at the time of the actual offering.

Even if the deity were to consume [the offering] perceptibly, nevertheless, like a swan emerging from water onto the bank, it would consume the Soma only after having separated it; for what more could a deity do that benefits merely a portion? Furthermore, it is only the portion subsequently poured out (*punarabhyunnīta*) that is offered to the deity, not the remnant of the previous [offering]. Thus, when the subsequently poured-out portion is being given, the previous remnant is simply set aside and not offered.
However, whatever part of that [previous remnant] remains at the time of consumption, since its connection with Indra has been removed, it should be presented in that very same manner.
Regarding the *pālīvata* cup, however, this [section] is commenced for the purpose of setting aside the previous rule as before.
The remnants of the double-deity cups, beginning with the *aindravāyava*, are deposited in the *āditva* vessel; from there, they again enter the *āgrayaṇa* vessel.
Furthermore, the drawing of the *pātnīvata* cup is heard in the scripture: "One draws the *pātnīvata* from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel using the *upaśu* vessel.

When its remnant is being consumed, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, as before, the recitation of the formula beginning with "of what was drunk by Indra, Vāyu, and the Patnīs" and so forth must be performed.
This concludes the second quarter of the third chapter.
For when the Dvidevatya cups have reached the Āgrayaṇa stage, the dedication to the Patnīvata is enjoined;

even if that dedication were merely for another's sake, its accomplishment through *prasaṅga* (incidental extension) would be unavoidable, much more so when it is indeed explicitly enjoined as something to be dedicated,
since one should mark the cup by drinking from it.

Regarding the view that Tvaṣṭṛ’s status as a deity arises from the mantra-text (māntravarṇika) based on the instruction for the drinking of the *patnīvata* cup by the *patnīvat* [deity], this is the position of the opponent. For in the injunction (*vidhi*), who is the *patnīvat* deity? It is not anyone other than the Great One (Indra). Therefore, he alone is enjoined here; nor does a *taddhita* suffix arise in dependence upon another.
Thus, even that [deityhood derived] from the mantra-text is weak.

Nor is the mantra-text devoid of its status as an auxiliary to the ritual (*karmāṅga*) merely by imagining it to have that deity [Tvaṣṭṛ] as its divinity. For, just as in the case of the wife (*patnī*), its designation is established through direct denotation; thus, the mention of Tvaṣṭṛ would otherwise be inexplicable, since it is explained as being for the purpose of praise (*stutyartha*).
And for this very reason, the meaning of the mantra becomes: "O you who are honored by us, he (Indra), being thus magnified, shall drink the Soma."

Otherwise, as a mere textual reading, what kind of designation of the deity would that be, since it serves only to indicate the deity? Furthermore, even in that case, when there is a mention of conjunction (*sāhitya*), it is merely a figurative assumption (*utprekṣā*), and that [conjunction] is not absolute, for the word "together" (*saha*) is used even in the absence of a connection to a common action.
For example, when it is said that a female donkey carries a load with her ten sons,
the meaning understood there is simply this: even though she has ten sons, she herself is the one who carries it.
Therefore, Tvaṣṭṛ is not understood to be the deity;
consequently, he should not be invoked.
Why?
Every mantra functions in accordance with the meaning of the injunction;
therefore, as in the case of Tvaṣṭṛ, here Agni is praised by means of the thirty [deities].

It is not possible for a mantra—by virtue of being a cause for the recollection of the purpose of the *pātnīvata* injunction—to manifest that Agni is the one being served or that the others are the consumers, when such a thing is not enjoined.

Therefore, because the mantra exists for the sake of another (the ritual act), it cannot be assumed—by overstepping the injunction—to possess the independent capacity to manifest thirty-three [deities].
Its capacity to enjoin, moreover, is utterly lost.
Nor does it merely remind one of the deityhood of thirty [deities], since the mention of thirty-three is intended to manifest the sovereignty of Agni as enjoined.
The second quarter of the third chapter:

For if the substance were being called "give" while still in its unbestowed state, then it would be stated in its primary sense, and that would result in a mere deception. But if, on the other hand, the intent is this—"You alone are the giver and the owner; we are not the owners"—then it is like when someone in the world is told, "You have been invited; you yourself must invite the others. In that case, the sentence becomes coherent.
Furthermore, performing what is enjoined serves a visible purpose;

since the primary meaning of the mantra "mādayasva" (rejoice) is possible, this [mantra] extends to these [deities]. Moreover, Agni’s status as a giver is also for a visible purpose, and thus it is understood to have the sense of defining the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
Furthermore, that which is clearly understood by one who knows the Veda as being independent of anything else should not be sublated by conformity with the mantra.
How, moreover, when it is enjoined as "pātnīvatam," is Agni understood as the deity and not thirty deities? Therefore, here Agni accompanied by Patnīvat is what is intended.
[The word "agnīṣomau"] is not [the deity] because we observe grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "O Agni, accompanied by the wives, thirty-three [gods].
But is there not also coreferentiality with "thirty," as in "the thirty accompanied by the wife"?
True, there is.
Nevertheless, here Agni-Patnīvat is understood;
for by the mention of a derivative suffix (*taddhita*), the specific number of the nominal stem's meaning is manifested.
Since the meaning of the nominal stem cannot otherwise be established there, the analysis (*vigraha*) is made with a word ending in the singular case-ending.
"Patnīvat is its deity"—thus [it is stated].
Furthermore, "triṃśat" (thirty) is always used with a plural ending;
therefore, since the secondary suffix *taddhita* cannot be applied to them, there is an absence of deity-status (*devatātva*).
Just as a subsequent drinker serves as an indicator for the previous vessel, so too,
according to the *Tantravārttika*,
one should not perform this [subsequent] rite with a deity that is not archetypal (*aprākṛta*).
However, the prohibition of *chandas* (metre) follows from the principle of "going everywhere" (*sarvagāmitva*) established [in the preceding discussion]; thus,
there is no modification (*ūha*) according to the deity, but rather, for those [verses] not addressed to Indra, they are simply without a mantra.
For if the repetitions were separate acts, then there would be a relationship of original form and modification; however, this is not the case.
Neither the Soma nor its ritual properties have been enjoined for these by anyone;
rather, in whatever manner one person takes [the draught], so do they all.
As he will state later: "The enumeration of the cups occurs within that very forest of [the Soma] self.
Nor does the Soma become restricted to Indra solely by virtue of the mantra, because direct Vedic revelation (śruti) makes it known as having all deities as its object.

And it is not the case that, just as by the *anārabhyavāda* (general statement) the Āhavanīya fire is for the purpose of all oblations—and thus, because there is no other rite devoid of it, one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) lacks the qualification [for such rites]—so too here the mantra is for the purpose of all Soma. Being recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*), it will manifest [the deity] Indra through its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*). But another [Soma] will be taken up or poured out precisely as it remains unmanifested by that mantra.
Alternatively, due to the absence of distinction, even when everything is being grasped, the application will be determined by mere intention (*saṃkalpa*).
Or else, like the *subrahmaṇyā* formula, it is for the purpose of manifesting Indra as the primary deity. This concludes the second quarter of the third chapter.
It occurs;
the meaning is "for that collection of deities beginning with him.

Alternatively, since the quality of possessing wealth (*vasumattva*) is absent in the word *vidhi*, its mention would be purposeless; therefore, it is stated [in the commentary] as "together with the other deities by virtue of possessing wealth."
Therefore, the Soma sacrifice is governed by the same rules in all cases;

consequently, there is an absence of modification (vikāra). As for the argument that it is a modification because of the prescription of a different metre, namely the Anuṣṭubh, that is explained as a specific prescription (viśiṣṭavidhāna) even though the same rules apply, since the Jagatī metre would otherwise have been expected due to its status as the third pressing (tṛtīyasavana).
Alternatively, since the *saṃsthās* are modifications (*vikāra*), this adaptation (*ūha*) is indeed appropriate; thus, there is simply no [application of the mantra].

Therefore, the mantra for consumption applies only to those [soma cups] dedicated to Indra, just as in the case of the measuring and taking [of the soma]; there is no rule of application by virtue of that [modification]. Thus, for others, the consumption is without a mantra.
Why?
The divinity of Indra is not predicated on the basis of his having drunk [the soma];
therefore, here, a similarity to the Āgneya [offering] is not desired due to a lack of capacity,
just as there is a distinction from another deity in the case of a single [deity].
If it were true that the function of the deity were the defining characteristic of being a "drinker" (pātṛtva) in this context,
then even an offering to Indra-Agni would be included;
however, for us, the deity does not drink.
Rather, it is employed solely as the object of the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*).

Furthermore, in a mixed resolve, the designation of either one [of the two deities] is not possible; for, like a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), a compound does not apply to things that are mutually dependent.

Therefore, just as in the case of the fourfold division of the *Āgneya* offering, because the object has exclusively Indra as its deity, a designation as "having both deities" is simply not possible. Consequently, there is an exclusion of the mantra. And it is precisely by this distinction that this [sūtra] is not redundant.

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) maintains that "drinking" (*pāna*) here is not a qualification of the deity, but rather the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradāna*), and that this status exists even for each [deity] individually.

The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntavādī), however, argues that since primary drinking is impossible [for a deity], what is expressed by this term is precisely the status of being a deity (*devatātva*).
Furthermore, even if primary drinking were possible for a deity, it would still be impossible to say that the substance has been drunk by it.
How indeed can that which resides in the cup be designated as "drunk by Indra"? For it has not been drunk by Indra, since the designation "drunk by Indra" refers to the act [of drinking].
Therefore, because it must necessarily denote an existing property, "drunk by Indra" (*indrapīta*) should be understood as referring to that which has been dedicated to Indra.
Consequently, the mention of "drinking" is merely a figurative designation for the status of being the deity.
Furthermore, the state of having been drunk does not reside in the Soma itself [but rather in the act of dedication]. This concludes the second quarter of the third chapter.
In that case,
it is possible to apply the designation metaphorically, because the expression is justified by the very intention (saṃkalpa) which is itself a property of the self.
For even when only a single part is being offered, this entire substance, being relinquished for the sake of the deity, accomplishes the sacrifice.
The meaning of *pibati* (he drinks) here is like that of *yajati* (he sacrifices) from the root *yaji*, or like *nirvapati* (he offers).
Therefore, because of the efficacy of the cognition "drunk by Indra" (*indrapīta*)— which serves as the means for the sacrifice to Indra— there is the exclusion of the mantra.
Or rather, because it is absent in all [other cases], the qualifier is independent where it can apply to a single meter;
there is no apprehension of that which is dependent, but not in a case where it simply does not exist at all.

According to Maitiśāyana, there is a single mantra for all [cups], because it is a mantra for drinking; since the entitlement to the *savana* (pressing) remains established even after [the soma] has been drunk by Indra, the mantra must be employed without modification even for those cups drunk by Indra—it is not the case that the consumption is to be done without a mantra. Why? Because...
In whichever libation Indra has drunk the Soma that is now being offered,
he who is connected even to its source is designated in this way:
"Salutation to Śrī Rāmacandra."
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.

Having thus described the application by means of indicative mark (*liṅga*) within the section on what is heard (*śruta*), the application by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*) is now introduced.

An illustration of this is the sentence, "The *ṛc* is performed loudly," and so forth; as well as, "If it is performed excessively with respect to the *ṛc*, one should go to the *gārhapatya* fire and offer an oblation with 'bhūḥ svāhā'; if [excessively] with respect to the *yajus*, or if with respect to the *sāman*," and so on.

In this regard, do the words *Ṛc*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman* refer to the classes (*jāti*) of mantras defined as follows—namely, those characterized by the injunctions regarding the properties of loudness and whispering, and the injunctions regarding the oblation connected to the three *Mahāvyāhṛtis* and the three fires, where they are denoted by scriptural texts independent of preceding or following words, and where the status of an *Ṛc* is determined by the arrangement of its quarters according to the sense? Or do they refer to the Vedas in their entirety, consisting of both Mantra and Brāhmaṇa?
Why is there doubt? Because of the contradiction between the opening and the conclusion of the single sentence;
for at the beginning, the "Vedas" are heard.

However, regarding the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*), there are the classes of *ṛk* and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt as to whether the Vedic word at the beginning is intended to indicate the classes that constitute its parts, or whether the classes of *ṛk* and so forth mentioned in the conclusion are intended to indicate the entire collection including the Brāhmaṇas. This doubt between the two consistent interpretations is to be resolved through objection and reply, just as in the case of the statement "the pebbles are anointed.
If that is so, then since this has already been covered by that [previous discussion], it need not be commenced here.
This is not a valid objection; for it was stated that the authority of a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) applies only in cases of doubt.

Here, however, since the words "Ṛk" and so forth occurring within the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) undoubtedly denote specific classes of mantras, the injunctive statement itself is beyond doubt.
Therefore, the following is undertaken: by means of a restrictive interpretation (*vyavaccheda-kalpanā*), one must determine one of the two alternative positions.
What is established?

By the very logic of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding that [topic], because the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) in the injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*) is more powerful, there is an entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the *jāti* (the generic class).
Furthermore, it is not possible in any way to denote the Brāhmaṇa by means of words such as "Ṛk" and so forth.

However, the word "Veda" is capable of referring even to a single part [of it], for it is observed that collective terms can apply to their constituent parts, as in the expression, "The village has arrived. Furthermore, students employ this very term all the more frequently, saying, "We are studying the Veda," or "The Veda is being recited.
Those who are studying the Brāhmaṇa, however, do not speak in such a manner.
Furthermore, certain *ṛc* verses are indeed found in all three Vedas, as are certain *yajus* formulas.

In that case, if being part of a Veda were the basis for the connection with *dharma*, it would not be known which *dharma* should be performed regarding such [common] passages; or else, an improper option (*vikalpa*) would have to be resorted to, because the designations of the different Vedas possess equal force.
However, this fault does not apply to the position that [the term refers to] the genus (*jāti*), for two genera cannot be simultaneously inherent in a single collection of phonemes.

Furthermore, in this way, the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice will be upheld; otherwise, since the Veda would have as its subject matter all *iṣṭis*, animal sacrifices, *ekāhas*, and *ahīnas*, the Dharma following the Veda would transcend the specific context and become universal.
Now, even in the case where the genus is the referent, this is the same, because the genus exists in other contexts just as it does in the Veda.

Now, since there is no reason here to override the context that has been established, this rule would apply equally even to the Vedic side, as one would determine that "the Veda is as much as is contained within the context.
This is not equal [to our position], for if the *jāti* (class) were to be distributed across the entire collection beginning with the *sarva-ṛc* and so forth; [then our view would differ].
It would not be completed within its own constituent parts; therefore, like the Veda, those collections of single sentences— namely the groups of verses (pādas), words, and sections (parvans)—
each of which constitutes a class of Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman, exist for us individually within them.

Just as aggregates such as forests are endowed with a commonality (*sāmānya*), so too is that which is called a "universal" (*jāti*) said to belong to collections of *ṛk*-verses and the like; furthermore, the status of being a word denoting a universal (*jātiśabdatva*) is not postulated for a dual-form word (*dvivacana-pada*).
Just as the genus "sentence-ness" exists, how indeed could the classes of Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman exist?
Just as for derivative words another general property is accepted as their genus,
so too a collection-genus (*samūha-sāmānya*) is desired as a genus distinct from [the individual] class (*jāti*).
"Or [it belongs to] the Veda because it is seen in the majority.
He asks, "What is this 'because it is seen in the majority'? seeing that this is not equal to other instances of being seen in the majority.

For in the case of the rule "also because of the mention of the majority" (prāyavacanāt), it was stated that this refers to a context where there is a majority of primary elements, meaning that the mention occurs where other primary elements are present.

Similarly, in the rule "because of the observation in the context of the subject matter" (viṣaye prāyadarśanāt), it means that its observation occurs where there is a majority of purificatory acts (saṃskāra), such as the *godohana* vessel and others.
However, in this case, one cannot say that the observation of these [metres], the Ṛg-veda and so forth, occurs where other Vedas are present.
For there are no Vedas apart from these [three] among which [the word "Veda"] might be restricted; therefore, there is no occurrence of the term in its primary sense here.

To this, the reply is: when the mind is pervaded by the impressions produced by the cognition of "Veda" due to the predominance of the Veda or the commencement of the Veda, these words are heard. This is demonstrated [in the passage]: "In the beginning, Prajāpati alone was this [universe].

As for the objection that, because it is led by the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), the word "Veda" occurring in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) must refer to a specific part [of the Veda], [that is not so].
To this we reply:
Those explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) which are heard subsequent to the injunction (*vidhi*) possess weakness; however, those which are heard prior to it are stronger because of their primacy.

For in every case, the cause for a word to overstep its own primary meaning is contradiction, and that contradiction is understood to exist when it is observed in actual usage. Thus, in this context, when it is heard that "the three Vedas were created—the Ṛgveda, etc."—there is no utterance of the words *ṛk* and so forth in the sense of [already] existing classes, by the observation of which the word "Veda" could have the meaning of denoting a part (*avayava*).

Therefore, the intellect has already been pervaded by that very literal application of the Vedic text; now, since words such as "deer" (mṛga) and others, while denoting their own primary meanings, cannot be syntactically connected [with the injunction], they are forced to resort to secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). Thus, in the third chapter, third section, even though it occurs within the context of the injunctive statement (vidhyuddeśa), there is weakness [of the Arthavāda], because—as stated in the sūtra "The primary [meaning] prevails, or rather, the former injunction [prevails], as in common worldly usage"—the other [the Arthavāda] is weaker. Now, regarding the sequence [of the injunction and the Arthavāda], the principle "the former is weaker" applies; thus, even if [the knowledge of the object] has arisen from the Arthavāda, the knowledge of the injunctive statement itself is grasped by setting aside the knowledge of the primary Vedic meaning [derived from the Arthavāda].
This is not so;

for when contradictory meanings are heard that reside in separate sentences and are mutually independent, the principle of the relative strength of priority and posteriority applies, because the former has already attained its own nature without being sublated by the latter, whereas the latter cannot come into being without sublating the former. However, this does not apply in a case where there is hearing [of the words] as a single syntactical unity (ekavākyatā) involving mutual dependence.

For in that case, syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) occurs by virtue of mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*); and what has been previously perceived expects a subsequent element as its own attribute or supplement. Consequently, whatever is not supplementary or is inconsistent is not part of that sentence at all, because it is not required. Furthermore, since sublation of the preceding is impossible by means of something non-existent, the preceding possesses greater authority. Indeed, because the injunction (*vidhi*) and the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) share the same subject matter, it must be understood that for exactly as many Vedas as are mentioned in the explanatory passage, for that many alone is something enjoined regarding them.

Furthermore, one considers only this much: "What is to be performed by these [factors]? but not "What will be performed for whom? Therefore, from the very first word, only that which is required is grasped; or rather, only the thing to be enjoined (vidheya) is required, not the object of the injunction itself. Thus, only the high pitch (*uccais*) and so forth are connected, but not the *ṛc* verses and the like. Consequently, because they are not intended [as the primary objects], they do not exist within the scope of the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), and thus they do not sublate the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). On the contrary, since the *arthavāda* itself is understood as having the scope of the injunctive statement, the Veda is determined [to be authoritative].
Therefore, the Ṛgveda and the others do not have the purpose of definition (*lakṣaṇārthatva*).

Furthermore, because the Veda is all-pervasive, it is not possible for it—being joined with the causes and characteristics—to define its own constituent parts; however, the Ṛgveda and the others, by virtue of being regulated, indicate the whole collection. This is just as it is stated elsewhere in the *Tantravārtika* regarding the status of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) as restatements (*anuvāda*).

There is no fault in the occurrence [of the word] at a different moment; likewise, there is no fault even in the *nyāya* (logical method), because in an injunction (*vidhi*) whose subject matter is understood from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the words "Ṛg" and so forth function as mere restatements (*anuvādaka*). Therefore, this mode of expression is as follows: since these Vedas were produced in such a manner, one must perform their recitation with loudness and so forth. Having accepted that very fact which is established by the sense of the text, the words "Ṛg" and so forth are uttered; otherwise, it would indeed be incoherent.
Since the injunction and the explanatory passage do not have different scopes, it follows that the section concerning the Vedas applies;
thus, in the event of a transgression, it should be according to what is heard in the text.
This is a restatement; because of its connection with the Veda, it would not be sublated by the context— or rather, the reading is "it would sublate."

Furthermore, because of the instruction regarding the *dharma* (quality), there is no connection with the substance (*dravya*). In the view that the *dharma* belongs to the genus (*jāti*), since the *Sāman* is mounted upon the *Ṛk*, and because there is no separation between the *Gāyatrī* and the *Sāman*, the *Sāman-dharma* would already be established by the *Ṛk-dharma* alone; thus, the further instruction would be redundant. For indeed, no one who is reciting the *Ṛk*—which serves as the substratum of the *Sāman*—loudly is able to recite the *Sāman* otherwise. However, within the context of the Vedas, one thing is enjoined by the *Ṛgveda* and another by the *Sāmaveda*; thus, the two instructions are meaningful.
If it is argued that the other [text] will also serve the purpose of the *Anṛk-prajāpati-hṛdaya* and so forth, we say no;
for that is not an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Indeed, this instruction regarding the *stotra-sāmans* occurs within the specific context (*prakaraṇa*) of that sacrifice.
Furthermore, because those subordinate applications have a limited scope, their lack of purpose is already easily dispelled.
Therefore, it is established that the Veda has this [study] as its primary qualification.
Regarding qualities, one type of dharma exists by its own nature, while the other exists through the medium of the principal element.

Wherever such a case may occur, it should be understood that there is a sublation of the subordinate rule (*guṇadharma*). When it is necessary to transgress one of two rules, the subordinate rule must be the one transgressed;
for in this way, the principal (*pradhāna*) is performed without deficiency.
And that [activity] is also the effect of the qualities;
for even he (the Pradhāna) proceeds toward action solely for that purpose.
However, if the Pradhāna were to act with deficient qualities due to compliance with its own attributes, then that very purpose for which it proceeded would be frustrated.
Even if a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) becomes defective when its specific quality is not produced, there is no contradiction because that quality was not intended to be performed in that context.

Therefore, since the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) belongs to the Yajurveda, the *sāmans* which are its subsidiaries must be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśutva*). Now, an objection may be raised: since it is understood that only that portion of the *ādhāna* prescribed by the Yajurveda is to be performed in a low voice, this rule would not apply to the singing of the *sāmans*. Furthermore, only the principal act (*pradhāna*) and its other subsidiaries are Yajurvedic; therefore, only those should be performed in a low voice.

This is not so; for it will be stated that "the subsidiaries, however, being prescribed by a rule, are taught along with the primary act," and likewise, "because the injunction has a single tone (ekaśruti) and because they are enjoined simultaneously (aparyāya-vidhāna). This is from the third quarter of the third chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*].

Therefore, because they are encompassed by the injunction for the performance of the primary rite, the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) other than those whose time is explicitly stated must be performed wherever the primary rite itself is; and thus, since the primary rite together with its subsidiaries belongs to the Yajurveda, it must be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).

If that were the case, then since the subsidiaries themselves belong to the Yajurveda, their *upāṃśutva* (whispered recitation) would not arise through the conflict between the qualities of the subsidiary and the primary; furthermore, the *upāṃśutva* belonging to the Sāmaveda is equal to *uccais-tva* (loud recitation) because it resides in the subsidiary. It cannot be said that what exists there [in the subsidiary] belongs to the primary. Nor can it be argued that when that [subsidiary quality] is set aside, the primary quality is thereby set aside, for in that case the primary would not have been performed in a whispered manner. If, however, by some means the quality of the subsidiary is also designated as belonging to the primary, then *uccais-tva* would likewise be a quality of the primary, and thus they would again be of equal strength.
It is said:

if indeed their origin were solely in the Yajurveda, then the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) would be based merely on their own form; however, since these [mantras] originate in the Sāmaveda, they would naturally have to be chanted loudly (*uccais*). Therefore, the whispered nature is caused by contact with the primary act (*pradhāna*), and thus it is a property of the primary act.

[Objection: But surely, because of the injunction "one should perform [the sacrifice] with the Yajurveda along with its subsidiaries" (*sāṅgam kuryāt*), the whispered nature must pertain only to the subsidiary acts, as this restriction implies that there is indeed contact with the form of the subsidiary itself.
No;
for by the very mention of its members, its non-predominance is indicated.
For it is precisely the predominant [factor] that is thus described as having its members as subordinate elements.

Therefore, it is precisely the primary act that belongs to the Yajurveda; however, while the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is indeed its own attribute, it is described as such because it extends toward the subsidiaries.
Yet there is no such direct injunction (*codanā*).

Consequently, this attribute of the primary act would have to be set aside when reaching the subsidiary. For when a primary act distributes its own attribute among the subsidiaries, if that attribute is sublated in a particular instance, the primary act itself becomes defective in that very instance. However, it is not determined in this way that "being loud" (*uccaistva*) is an attribute of the primary act.
For the properties of the subsidiaries do not directly transfer to the primary acts.

[Objection: Even so, the property of the subsidiary would be obtained directly, whereas the property of the primary would be obtained indirectly through the wife of another; thus, in the *Tantravārtika*, an inversion of relative strength and weakness results.

It is true that the quality of the limbs (*aṅga-dharma*) already obtained through direct injunction (*śruti*) is understood more quickly; however, the primary quality (*pradhāna-dharma*), which follows after the subsequent inclusion of the performance-injunction (*prayoga-vacana*), is indeed posterior. In a sequence of priority and posteriority, the former is weaker, and thus it is sublated according to the principle: "as in the case of the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*). [Objection: But by this very logic, would not even the *stotras*, *śastras*, and other limbs belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices of the Yajurveda also obtain the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*)?
[Reply: True, it would so follow; however, by virtue of a specific scriptural statement (*vacana*), there is a substitution of a different accent in all such cases.

How is it that, in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, when various Vedic branches prescribe the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*), and a conflict of Vedic authorities arises, the rule regarding the subordination of the subordinate to the principal (*guṇamukhyavyatikrama-nyāya*) results in the low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*)—the duty of the Yajurvedic primary sacrifice—being applied?

Subsequently, there occurs a specific scriptural injunction (*vācanika*) regarding the pitch: "The portion up to the end of the *yājyābhāga* is in a low tone; the subsequent [portion] is in a medium tone; and the *anuyāja*s and so forth are in the highest tone."

Likewise, regarding the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as the *iṣṭi* and *paśubandha*, although these three original (*prakṛta*) accents would apply by virtue of direct instruction (*pratyakṣopadeśa*), resulting in the application of the accent belonging to the primary Veda (*pradhāna-veda*), it is nevertheless accepted that the accents brought forth by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) alone should be adopted. This is because, according to the maxim "or [the rite] should have its own properties due to the acceptance of that [original]," the *prayogavacana* (the injunction for performance) is weaker as it depends upon the *codaka*. Thus, the adoption of the accents provided by the *codaka* is desired.

Thus, although the archetypal (prakṛta) accent would apply to the Jyotiṣṭoma subsidiaries such as the Dīkṣaṇīyā and others, it is set aside by direct instruction (pratyakṣopadeśa). When that [archetypal accent] is reinstated by the superior force of the extended application (codaka), the following occurs: since the Jyotiṣṭoma belongs to the Yajurveda and because it adopts the archetypal elements whose utility is already established, the rule regarding the "transgression of the subordinate for the sake of the principal" (guṇamukhyavyatikrama-nyāya) leads to the application of the property of low-pitched recitation (upāṃśutva) belonging to those subsidiaries. Consequently, the rule stating, "One should recite the Dīkṣaṇīyā with as much voice as one desires," establishes these accents for the subsidiaries along with the principal rite, precisely by overriding the rule of the transgression of the subordinate for the sake of the principal.

Likewise, since the *jyotiṣṭoma* has its division into pressings (*savana*) prescribed by direct scriptural statement (*vācanika*), and because the determination of low (*mandra*), middle (*madhyama*), and high (*uttama*) intonations is enjoined, all its subsidiaries (*aṅga*)— by way of the primary sacrifice— also obtain those same low, middle, and high intonations identical to those of the archetype (*prakṛti*). Consequently, when the rule "whatever is prior to the *agnīṣomīya* [offering], with that they proceed in a whisper" (*upāṃśu*) applies to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites along with their subsidiaries, these specific tones, though enjoined with reference to the words *dīkṣaṇīyā* and so forth which denote the primaries alone, come to apply only to the primaries.

With whatever degree of voice one desires, with that one should recite at the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice; softly at the *prāyaṇīyā*, and more softly at the *ātithyā*. Since the state of being whispered (*upāṃśu*) there is already established by the preceding general injunction for whispering that pervades everything, this [mention] is merely a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*) intended to praise the specific tones of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and the others.

In the *agniṣomīya* sacrifice, however, there is a restoration of the original (*prākṛta*) accents—beginning with the rule "up to the end of the *yājyābhāga*s in a low tone"—by means of the accentuation belonging to the divisions of the *savana*s; or alternatively, the entire performance along with its subsidiaries (*sāṅga-prayoga*) should be divided into three parts corresponding to the divisions of the *savana*s, and the recitation should be accomplished using low, middle, and high tones respectively.
By this, the specific modes of recitation for the *anūbandhyā*, *avabhṛtha*, *udayanīyā*, and *udavasānīyā* sacrifices are also explained.

When the same accentuation would thus apply even to the *savanīya* offerings and others performed at the time of the Soma-pressing (*mukhya-kāla*), they take their accents according to the respective *savana* (morning, midday, or evening) to which they belong.

If it is argued that, because words such as *ruva* and *naśabda* denote constituent parts of the Soma sacrifice, they would consequently lack their own specific accent— just like the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other subsidiaries— the answer is no; for by the use of the locative case (*saptamī*), one relies merely on their being employed at that particular time, and in the locative, whatever mantra is employed as having that [time] as its locus [retains its accent].
The connection with the *mandra* and other tones depends on the specific parts of that entire [sacrificial rite], such as the *stotra*, *śastra*, and *anuvākyā*;
since these do not exist in the sixth [pressing], those tones beginning with *mandra* are not appropriate for it.
For just as a bird is desired [to be present] even on the flowers and other parts of a tree,
so too is the object that possesses the quality of being contained (ādheya-dharma) prescribed here;
therefore, the various Vedic accents are obtained from the beginning for the hymns (stotra) and so forth.
Since it is sublated by the low tone (*upāṃśu*) due to its status as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) following the primary element (*pradhāna*),
by this [reasoning] all modifications (*vikāra*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma are explained. But where, then, will there now be an occasion for the accentuation belonging to various Vedas (*nānāveda-svara*)?
It is said:

because of that inclusion, it should possess its own specific characteristics; this must be inferred by the force of the context, just as in the case of the rule "the unexpressed [is understood] in the remainder. This is because when a new limb belonging to another Veda is enjoined in a modified sacrifice (vikṛti) that already possesses the original (prakṛta) accents and limbs, [it follows that the new one takes its own properties].
But surely, even in that case, by the principle of the conflict between the subordinate and the principal (guṇamukhyavyatikrama-nyāya), it would simply take on the characteristics of the principal?

If that is the case, then the subject matter would be that new subsidiary (*aṅga*) enjoined for the first time in that very Veda among the remaining subsidiaries which have been obtained according to the archetype (*prakṛti*). But even that [new subsidiary] would not be the subject matter, because it must be applied by means of the primary rite (*pradhāna*), and thus that primary rite itself would be the subject matter. However, that too cannot be the subject matter, because it is already occupied by the archetype. If you argue that the subject matter is therefore that new subsidiary which is obtained through the medium of the primary rite, we say no; for even there, the property (*dharma*) of the primary rite itself exists.

Furthermore, when the sacrificial portions have been divided into three parts and the *khara* (mound) stands as the locus for the ritual duty (*dharma*), even that which is *apūrva* (unprecedented) falls within that portion; therefore, it must necessarily be subject to the archetypal (*prākṛta*) rule regarding the spreading of grass in the sacrificial post-hole (*yūpāvaṭa*).
For this reason as well, there is no [exceptional] scope [for a new rule].
Moreover, the recitation in the context (*prakaraṇa*) would be utterly meaningless; thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter.
It may be so.

Here, the rule "the *yajus* [is recited] in a low voice" (*upāṃśu*) is indeed meaningful in all *darvihomas*. Furthermore, it is also meaningful in the case of the optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) subsidiaries of both the Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda.

For passages such as "softly in the morning pressing" (*mandraṃ prātaḥsavane*)—because they are obligatory (*nitya*)—cannot be connected with the non-obligatory optional and occasional rites, and thus they pertain exclusively to the obligatory subsidiaries.

Therefore, whatever optional (*kāmya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) rite is enjoined by the Ṛgveda or the Sāmaveda, all that must be performed loudly (*uccaiḥ*). Likewise, one should recite [the mantra] over a broken vessel, beginning with "yat cid dhi miśriṣaḥ," and so forth.
In this same way, the low-voiced (*upāṃśu*) character of Yajurvedic rites should also be illustrated.

Furthermore, regarding those subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) occurring after the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing), since there is no mention of the *savana* (pressing) therein, the accentuation follows the respective Veda; thus, the loudness (*uccaistva*) of the *avabhṛtha-sāman* and others is established. Otherwise, their application would be arbitrary.

In the *parisāman* section beginning with the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, the rule "prior to the *agnīṣomīya*" establishes that the *pravarṇya-sāmans* are to be chanted in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), whereas the rule "the *pravargya* [is] loud" establishes their loudness (*uccais*). As for the *āghāra-sāmans*, they are low-voiced precisely because they are prescribed by the primary injunctions of the Yajurveda.
Therefore, Yajurvedic sentences such as "He who, knowing thus, sings the Vāmadevya... serve as the illustrative examples.
Regarding this, some say:
"The statement 'it is not performed' refers merely to the production of its own form (*svarūpa*); it is not an introduction made with the intention of [discussing] the causal factor (*kāraka-hetu*).

But that is not correct; for if that were so, one would be considering only the relative strength or weakness of the power of originative injunction (*utpatti*) versus applicatory injunction (*viniyoga*), rather than considering the conflict between the subordinate (*guṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*).
And in that case, since performance depends upon application (viniyoga), the conclusion would be that [the Sāma Veda] is subordinate to it.
Therefore, others hold that because this injunction exists in some branch of the Sāma Veda as well, it serves as an example.
However, in that case, the result of the repetition in the Yajur Veda would be meager.

Furthermore, if it were to be accepted as a rule from another recension (*śākhāntara*), and if an alternative regarding the accent (*svara*) were to be made in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), this would only hold if such a case were cited; however, since no such example is cited, this is not tenable. Therefore, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is commenced on the grounds that the status of "subordinate" (*guṇa*) and "principal" (*mukhya*) pertains precisely to the origin (*utpatti*) and the application (*viniyoga*): namely, where a matter originated in one Veda is applied in another Veda, in that case, should the ritual property (*dharma*) of the originating Veda be observed? Or [the property of the Veda in which it is applied]? This is the subject of the *Tantravārttika*.

Regarding the question of whether the *dharma* (property) belongs to the originative injunction (*utpatti-veda*) or the applicatory injunction (*viniyoga-veda*), it is argued that since the applicatory injunction is preceded by the originative one, the property belongs to the originative injunction. However, the conclusion is reached that the property belongs to the applicatory injunction.
Why?

Because the originative injunction exists for the sake of that [application], and the [mantra] being applied requires a specific accent; therefore, only that accent which is perceived at the very time of application is what is enjoined, not the accent present at the time of origin, as there is no prescription [of it] at that time.

Alternatively, the word "transgression" (*vyatikrama*) here does not denote sublation (*bādha*) or contradiction (*virodha*); rather, it denotes deviation—that is, occurrence in different places. Thus, it is considered as follows: where both origin (*utpatti*) and application (*viniyoga*) have transgressed—where the origin is in one place and the application in another—which Vedic connection should prevail?
Likewise, when there is a conflict between the connection with the origin and the application, the answer is that the connection with the Veda of the application prevails because of its predominance.
Alternatively, there may be this consideration: where the primary rite (pradhāna) belongs to one Veda and its subsidiary (aṅga) to another, by which Veda should the subsidiary be designated?
Consequently, the conclusion is that it is designated by the same Veda as the primary.

However, under this view, setting aside the rule "or it may follow its own [subsidiary] properties because of being grasped by that," only that which is designated by the same name as the primary (pradhānasamākhyāta) is the one under discussion.
Furthermore, the agent would incur a defect in the case of the *vikṛti* (modified sacrifice).

However, because the force of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) is stronger, the agent is understood from the designation (*samākhyā*) belonging to the subsidiary Veda; consequently, the accent would likewise follow that same [Vedic] source, and thus it is improper to adopt the accent of the primary [sacrifice].
Therefore, this discussion must be considered solely with respect to the origin (*utpatti*) and application (*viniyoga*); this alone is the correct interpretation.
In this way, the example of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) is established.

However, if the "conflict between the primary and the subordinate" (*guṇamukhya-vyatikrama*) is explained as a contradiction between the properties of the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*), then one must consider that there would be a great redundancy with the rule *aṅgaguṇavirodhe ca tādarthyāt*.
Therefore, unlike the case of different Vedic branches (*śākhāntara*), an option (*vikalpa*) based on reasoning is not appropriate here.
The scope of the Veda is such that,
for the sake of merit,
there is at least one [text] that is prescriptive.
But which one among the Jyotiṣṭoma and others is it?
Where there is an abundance of subsidiary elements constituting the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance), its status as that [primary rite] is intended by that very mark.
If something has been determined by its own capacity to be a means of cognition,

whether it be little or much, it does not differ in making that object known. Likewise, when the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) is presented as an inferential mark (*liṅga*), even where it is minimal, it is indeed capable of making [the rite] known, since it would otherwise be inexplicable without the necessity of performance.
Because the *prakaraṇa* (context) and so forth seek the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance), they are not directly connected [to the specific act].
Thus, first of all, the *śruti*, *liṅga*, and *vākya* have been explained through counter-examples as having subjects that are either mixed with or distinct from the primary object of knowledge.

In that regard, since *śruti*—which consists of the expression of injunction and application—and *liṅga*—which consists of the capacity for application—never occur in the use of an isolated word, and because the proximity (*saṃnidhi*) of another word is necessarily present, *vākya* is essentially already included within them; therefore, it was not indicated by being mentioned separately.

Alternatively, because the determination that [the property of being a *mantra*] belongs to the Veda is made precisely through the force of the opening and conclusion—namely, "Or rather, the *veḍha* [is so called] because it is commonly seen"—this very [sūtra] is the rule for the application (*viniyoga*) of a sentence; thus, one should not explain the applicatory power of a sentence merely on the basis of its inclusion within a preceding [section].

As for what was cited by the author of the Bhāṣya regarding "with the red one" (*aruṇayā*), there too, as in the case of the *aindrī*, the third-case hearing (*tṛtīyā-śruti*) itself is the applicator. This concludes the third quarter of the third chapter.

Now, the intention is that once the general connection with the action has been established by direct audition (śruti), the specific connection is made by syntactical connection (vākya); this principle applies equally to the case of the *aindrī* verse as well.

There too, because the word *aindrī* requires only something to be approached (*upasthātavya*) and the word *gārhapatyam* requires only a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), the specific connection is indeed made by syntactical connection alone.
Therefore, since it is possible to demonstrate the inclusion of both within those two, both examples are cited for both direct audition and syntactical connection.
Now, since the inquiry regarding *vacana* (direct statement) is imminent, he demonstrates the nature and the functional capacity (*viniyoga-sāmarthya*) of the other three means of proof as well.
Among these, he introduces *prakaraṇa* (context) by way of one of the following: ignorance, doubt, or misconception regarding its application (*viniyoga*).
As long as it is not stated elsewhere, there remains ignorance [of its application].

Alternatively, there might be a doubt that [the connection] was not stated because there was no occasion for it; or rather, there is no other mode of verbal expression besides hearing a subsequent word, its capacity, the desire to remember it, or the proximity of another word with a suitable meaning.
Therefore, when it is argued that context and the rest are not separate means of proof, it is replied:
"And sequence [is a means of proof] due to the commonality of location."
Just as before, the presentation of order (krama) and name (samākhyā) should also be made by means of ignorance and so forth;

for even without identity of location regarding performance, in whatever extent the primary act is mentioned in the Brāhmaṇa, to that same extent the mantra is mentioned in the Mantra-text. And when there is a requirement for the relationship between the subsidiary and the principal, their proximity arises due to being in the same location, according to the principle of "correspondence" (yathāsaṃkhya) from the third chapter, third section.
Seeking the mantra for the first primary rite, one necessarily examines the entire collection of mantras from the beginning;
consequently, the very first mantra comes to mind first.
Since there is no reason to bypass it, that very mantra is selected.

Likewise, since a mantra requires a principal (śeṣin) for which it is subsidiary, by this very process it must be connected with whichever principal it relates to; and because it thereby becomes satisfied in its expectancy, the second and subsequent mantras must likewise be joined only with their respective second and subsequent principals.

In that regard, since the *anumantraṇa* mantras dedicated to Agni and others possess indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as "Agni," their restricted application is established by those marks. Thus, he cites the mantra "Thou art the inviolable one" (*dabdhir nāmāsi*), which is recited in the sequence of the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice where the indicative mark is not explicitly manifest.

[Objection: But surely, the universal applicability [of the mantra] is understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the syntactical connection (*vākya*); and since that [context] is stronger [than indicative mark], its application would result even elsewhere.
On this point, some say:
"Because of the mention of the *upāṃśuyāja*, both [the sequence and the context] are favored; therefore, that [sequence] is what is mentioned.
However, it can be argued that the sequence itself is indeed what is to be favored, because [if it were not], it would contradict the cognition derived from the context (*prakaraṇa*).

For if the *śeṣa* (the subsidiary) were for the sake of all [principal acts], it would have to be repeated with each principal act (*pratipradhānāvṛtti*), and thus what is understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*) could not be set aside.

This is the response: those other principals, such as the *Āgneya* and others, do not require this [subsidiary], because they are already occupied by other mantras due to their position in the sequence (*krama*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Nor can there be an option (*vikalpa*), because of the inequality arising from the fact that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not equally clear.

If it is argued that this is a combination (*samuccaya*) of rites whose purposes are unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*), we say no. This is because [the offering] has a seen purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) through the inspection of the butter already under discussion. Furthermore, even if there were an unseen purpose, since independent alternatives exist, one would not resort to a combination; rather, having been set aside by the *Āgneya* and other offerings which have already fulfilled their function, it would only return to them as a last resort (*agatyā*). Yet, it does have an alternative: the *Upāṃśuyāja*. Moreover, [The text continues: ...and furthermore... (as per the provided fragment).

The mantra "Dabdhir nāmāsi" (Thou art named Dabdhi) possesses an indistinct indicative mark (*aliṅga*). Nor is it possible for such a context to restrict [the application of] this mantra. However, the word *asi* (thou art), because its referent is the second person (*yuṣmad-artha*), denotes one who is either well-known or present before one, and not anyone else. Since the Upāṃśuyāja is both proximate and present before one, by the power of its denotation, it is understood through the sequence of the text (*krama*) to have the Upāṃśuyāja as its specific object. *Tantravārtika* on the section concerning the context. It is not capable of restricting [the application]. But the word *asi*, because its scope is the meaning of the second person pronoun (*yuṣmad*), denotes that which is well-known or standing face-to-face, and nothing else. And since the Upāṃśuyāja is both proximate and face-to-face, by the capacity of its expression, it is understood through the order [of the ritual] to pertain to the Upāṃśuyāja.
Consequently, since the context is indeed set aside by the indicative mark (*liṅga*), there is no fault.

The sequence of the section concerning the optional *yājyā* verses has already been explained; furthermore, the sequence of the place of performance will apply to the duties of the animal sacrifice (*paśudharma*) because they serve the purpose of the *agnīṣomīya* rite.
Since designations such as *ādhvaryava* pertain to the Veda alone regarding their application, the objection that they are merely worldly is not raised.
In that regard, the Adhvaryu requires only this much: "What must be done by me?
And for him who is thus requiring it, if no specific [instruction] is understood from anywhere, then it will follow that "anything whatsoever" [may be done].
Likewise, regarding the action designated as *ādhvaryava* (the duty of the Adhvaryu), he requires the remainder in exactly this way: "Who will be my performer?"

In this regard, from the very beginning, there arises for each word born of linguistic convention (*śabdaja*) a conceptual construction (*utprekṣā*): "That which is the function of this *adhvaryu* shall be denoted by the word *ādhvaryava*.

Nevertheless, one infers that the agent of this *ādhvaryava* function is named *adhvaryu*; whether it be the modification inferred from the base form, or the base form inferred from the modification. Although the modification is a different word and both of these are independent of one another yet possess an eternal connection, nevertheless, since the eternal connection is the cause for the eternal application of the word, such is the grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) for all etymological (*yaugika*) terms.
For it has been stated that even the application of the word "kingdom" (*rājya*) does not have a beginning in time.

Furthermore, the relationship between cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*) is not contradictory even in the absence of a beginning, just as in the case of words and their meanings. Regarding this, some explain [the following] from the third quarter of the third chapter.

Prior to this application by name (*samākhyā*), there is no relationship between the *adhvaryu* and the *ādhvaryava* [ritual acts]; therefore, it is impossible to understand their etymological connection through the name.

If, however, the name were to function only after the relationship has already been established, then the name would not be the means of application (*viniyojikā*). Consequently, this application must occur through two conventional terms (*rūḍhi*) that are mutually independent and which present themselves due to their similarity of form.
But this is not correct.
For established words do not possess the capacity to bring about [a meaning] based on similarity even when there is a connection with a property (*dharma*);

as for instance, he will later reject the properties of the *Rathantara* in the case of the *Kaṇvarathantara*. How much more so, then, in this case, regarding the relationship between an action and its agent? Or rather, would it be appropriate to cite "pāvaka" (purifier) as an example? Therefore, one must simply accept that [the word] is etymological (*yaugika*).

As for the claim that there is no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) prior to usage, it is true that there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), but it will exist as inferred through the very name (*samākhyā*).

For in their case, the relationship between the action and its agent is established from the very beginning; once that exists, the designation (*samākhyā*) comes into operation. We, however, not perceiving that relationship through any other means of knowledge, perceive it only upon seeing the designation; thus it is known that the designation comes first and the relationship afterwards. In reality, however, the relationship exists from the very beginning, and even though it is unperceived, it causes the designation to function by its mere existence alone. For if this [designation] were something that had a beginning, then there would have to be an initial comprehension of the relationship by the user.
Nor should we be questioned as to why that [connection] does not exist when one relies upon a permanent relationship.

For, once it has been established by the eternally applied designation (*samākhyā*) that there must certainly be some connection, the relationship of subsidiary and principal (*śeṣa-śeṣibhāva*) is subsequently understood through the principle of "presumption from the impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*). Therefore, it is settled that the application (*viniyoga*) occurs solely through a derivative designation (*yaugikī samākhyā*).

For indeed, the single accessory (śeṣa), such as the red cloth and so forth, is connected to the general action by direct statement (śruti), while it is connected to its specific instance, the purchase (kraya), by syntactical connection (vākya), and to the Jyotiṣṭoma [purchase] by context (prakaraṇa). Even though there is a coexistence of direct statement and context, there is no contradiction because they serve as mutual supports. Thus, there is no investigation into the relative strength [of these means of proof], since a general rule cannot exist without a specific instance. Furthermore, if the accessory were used solely for the sake of the mere form of the purchase, it would be purposeless; therefore, both syntactical connection and context are required by direct statement and syntactical connection.
Consequently, one must indeed undertake the consideration of their conflict.
Or rather, it need not be performed.
Why?
Because there is no authoritative basis for its connection, just as in the case of the redness of the dawn.
Inherence (*samavāya*) is not merely coexistence in one place; rather, it is the identity of the object (*viṣayaikatva*).

Here, the connection of the *aruṇa* (red) quality with the action is established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). However, that connection between the action and its factor (*kāraka*), though established by scripture, further becomes the object of the purchase (*kraya*) due to the force of further requirement (*apekṣā*).

Since the purpose is not yet fully achieved by that much, when another requirement arises, the purchase—now connected to the transcendental result (*apūrva*)—serves the purpose of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. Thus, there is a difference in the objects [of the various means], and consequently, there is no contradiction in all of them being applicatory (*viniyojaka*).

Furthermore, in this case, no sublation of the proximate by the remote is observed; for the act of purchasing does not sublate its own connection with the ritual action, nor does performing [the purchase] in the Jyotiṣṭoma sublate its connection with the sacrifice. However, where there is a single subsidiary (śeṣa), and that very same subsidiary is understood through one means of knowledge to serve the purpose of another principal (śeṣin) because it is incompatible with another connection, [then sublation occurs].
The meaning of another [subsidiary] passage is established by the impossibility of its application elsewhere;
and since there is no further requirement for that which has already fulfilled its purpose through a single connection, a second application is impossible.

In this context, *samavāya* (conjunction) is defined as the state of two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) having a common object that is mutually exclusive. Likewise, where there is a single subsidiary (*śeṣin*) and multiple subsidiaries (*śeṣa*), based on an equal degree of assistance—whereby one subsidiary is perceived as a means by one means of valid cognition and another subsidiary by another, yet the subsidiary for whom the assistance has been accomplished does not require any further subsidiary—there too, because they occupy a mutually exclusive common object, there is *samavāya*. And since such a state constitutes a contradiction (*virodha*), contradiction is established by the very mention of *samavāya*.

Furthermore, where there is a clearly evident difference in the subsidiary (*śeṣa*), as in "one should sacrifice with fuel-sticks" (*samidho yajati*) and so forth; or where there is some additional quality belonging to that very same subsidiary, as explained in the case of the red cow (*aruṇā*); likewise, where there is a difference in the principal (*śeṣin*), as in the eight-potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth belonging to the Āgneya and other sacrifices; or where there is an additional quality pertaining to those [principals], as in the case of the various benefits (*upakāra*) of the subsidiaries of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*)—in all such cases, because the subject matter is different, there is no co-inherence (*asamavāya*).

That which is enjoined by direct audition (*śruti*) and that which is [enjoined] by designation (*samākhyā*)—all such means are equal. However, regarding that single primary benefit produced by all the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*), since these means are prescribed without alternation (*aparyāya*), there is only one authority (*pramāṇa*) and one status as a subsidiary (*śeṣatva*). Thus, due to the difference in their operations (*vyāpāra-bheda*), there is no coalescence (*asamavāya*). Likewise, where that very same subsidiary is enjoined for that very same principal (*śeṣin*) by both a proximate and a remote authority, there too, because one [authority] possesses the status of the means of knowledge while the other serves a different purpose, there is no coalescence.
Therefore, the mention of "coalescence" (*samavāya*) refers exclusively to the domain of non-contradiction (*avirodha*).

In that context, although the relative strength and weakness of all six [factors] should be stated together, because speech proceeds sequentially and cannot function simultaneously, there is a deliberation on them one by one.
As for the mention of "the second," it is said "of two each" because it is impossible to state the strength and weakness without its counterpart.
Furthermore, there is another explanation for the word "speech" (*vāc*), namely that it functions toward a single purpose; this is from the *Nyāyavārttika*.

This principle of *bala-abala* (strength and weakness) applies individually to each of the means of knowledge, such as direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and the rest, and not to their collective aggregate.

For those [means] are purposeful through the application of the subordinate (*śeṣa-viniyoga*), and they do not derive their strength from one another. Because it functions with respect to each primary element (*pratipradhāna-vṛttitva*), when a comparative determination (*saṃpradhāraṇā*) must be made for each one, it is impossible to show the non-occurrence of the counter-correlates—namely, the contradiction of the accusative case ending and the sublation by weakness—simultaneously. Therefore, it is stated that the comparison is between two at a time. That is to say, "between two and two."

When a conflict (*vicāra*) is to be conducted between five [conflicting authorities] taken together, if it were performed one by one, then because the sublation of that which is to be sublated by its sublater is easily understood, those things which are sublated by *liṅga* and so forth—which are themselves sublated by *śruti*—would be sublated by the *śruti* itself; thus, they would not be deliberated upon in such a manner [as a group]. Therefore, first of all, the deliberation between *śruti* and *liṅga*, which has not yet been reached, must be undertaken. What is the illustrative example (*udāharaṇa*) here?
