Even there, when some have such a statement—"If he should be a learned *śrotriya*, he may perform the *pravargya*"—then, because the restorative statement (*pratiprasava*), which effects the option, pertains to a specific agent, the option applies only to him; for others, its absence is constant.
Since a restatement of what has already been established would be purposeless if it yielded no more than that same result, its force implies an understanding of excellence (*prakarṣa*).
Just as in the expression "a maiden should be given to one who is handsome," it is understood to mean "to one who is more handsome.
As for the mention of the *anūcāna* (one who has studied the Vedas), because the term "Brāhmaṇa" is connected with the act of reciting, it will serve to exclude the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya.
This very same [rule] applies to the Atirātra sacrifice.

However, because of the prohibition "not at the first sacrifice" (*na prathamayajñe*) and because there is no counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) due to its not being an Agniṣṭoma, it must never be performed [at the first performance]. In other modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), since a "first performance" is impossible, it must always be performed.

[Objection: But even there, because of the extension [of the rule] from the phrase "not at the first sacrifice" (*na prathamayajñe*), and because the nature of the *agniṣṭoma*—which serves as the cause for the counter-exception—is absent, it follows that [the *jyotiṣṭoma*] should indeed be absent during its first performances.
[Reply: This is not so.

Since the word "first" (*prathama*), being unspecified, applies to the very beginning of everything and does not apply elsewhere, therefore [this rule applies] to the first performance of the *jyotiṣṭoma* alone. (This concludes the third section of the third chapter.)
And it is established that this prohibition applies only to the specific subject matter; since it is without distinction, it pertains to all objects.

However, in the case of the *caru* (porridge), it is already implied by the sense [of the rite]; in the case of the *puroḍāśa* (cake), it would not apply because of contradiction; and in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), it would likewise not apply.

If someone were to argue that grinding flour— even if it is merely for worldly purposes— is not an absolute requirement for the preparation of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), the following is said in reply: Since the purpose here is indeed the archetypal (prākṛta) assistance, and since in the archetype grinding was the means to achieve that, the grinding is prescribed for the sacrificial cake by virtue of that which was previously established.
Furthermore, there would be a deficiency in the primary substance; for that [offering] must be accomplished by cutting portions from what possesses the shape of the heart and other organs.

And when [the material] is ground into flour, no portion can be cut from it in that shape. Even if one were to restore that shape, since it would be a mere imitation—as in the case of a clay gavaya—the act of cutting would still result in a deficiency.
Moreover, it is heard in the scripture: "One cuts the portions from the place of production."
Furthermore, from the ground heart and other organs, it would not be known by which specific part of the animal they were cut;
therefore, since grinding is neither prohibited nor naturally required for the *caru*, it is prescribed specifically for that.

Now, one might object: since the reason "for he is toothless" applies without distinction, grinding would apply to both the animal and the *puroḍāśa* as well, and thus the offerings and their remnants would be given after being ground.
Nor will there be [the faults of] preclusion or contradiction.
It is said:

since the offering of the *yavadāna* follows the sequence of presentation, it is not proper to interpose the grinding (*peṣaṇa*) in between; furthermore, it will be stated that the explanatory statement (*hetuvannigada*) serves merely as a commendation (*stuti*).
Therefore, this is the rule for grinding only when it is already established by its own sequence (*svakrama*).

Furthermore, grinding is understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*) in the case of the *puroḍāśa* cake immediately upon its introduction; in the case of the *caru* oblation, it is understood as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) since grinding would otherwise be excluded; and in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), it is understood as an original injunction (*vidhi*) because grinding was absolutely unestablished there.
Furthermore, it is not understood that these many forms belong to a single sentence alone;

since one must necessarily accept a single form among them, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*) and because of its meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), it must be determined that it is indeed a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*).
Thus, it is established that [the rule] has as its object the *caru* offering alone.
How so?
The movement of all things is established through worldly convention;
therein, a particular state of ripening is determined by way of its being a sacrificial oblation (caru).

The purpose stated for the position is weak; such a result has been stated. This much is the misconception: that even though there is no distinction, the purpose is not for the sake of the *puroḍāśa*, but rather for the sake of the animal (*paśu*), and because of the contradiction of the ritual properties (*dharma*).

The third quarter of the third chapter. Furthermore, even in the case of a single deity, would you [hold that] one should grind half [the grain], or [all of it] in its entirety, in a sacrificial oblation (caru) intended for two deities?
In the former case there is a discrepancy in the portions (*pāka-vaiṣamya*), while in the latter there is a confusion of parts (*bhāga-saṃkara*).

But surely all of this is equally applicable to you as well regarding offerings to two deities; for indeed, that [confusion] is accepted when a mixed oblation is offered simultaneously to mixed deities, since there is no contradiction in such a case.
This would be the case regarding those ritual properties (dharma) enjoined by the *apūrva* of the sacrifice; however,
this grinding (*peṣaṇa*) is considered a property of the deity, and since that [property] does not apply to a rite dedicated to two deities (*dvidevatya*),
it simply does not take place.
Furthermore, since this same principle applies even to those oblations offered to two deities (*dvidevatya*), the deity must be regarded as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*).

Since you, however, being unable to assert grinding for an offering to two deities while maintaining your own untenable position, are forced to accept that the deity is the cause (*nimita*) [for the grinding]. This is the *Tantravārtika*.
Furthermore, since the two deities are primary, each should request its own distinct share; therefore, the offering should be performed in that very manner.
To this we reply:
in that case, if one deity's portion were offered to another, a deficiency (vaiguṇya) would occur.

Regarding the word "carum" (the sacrificial pap): since it is intended to be taken as a single entity in its capacity as a material for the sacrifice, there would be the consequence of contradicting the scripture if one were to rely on a division created by separate vessels. Therefore, in no way whatsoever does the grinding (peṣaṇa) apply to a dual-deity offering when it possesses prohibited characteristics; thus, it should not be performed.
Why?
Because if it were to apply to the oblation belonging to Pūṣan, or to that which is a subsidiary part of his sacrifice.

Because it is not explicitly stated, there is no grinding in a sacrifice for two deities; therefore, even though Pūṣan is not here a deity [in the primary sense], since he is included merely by way of association, and because the offering is made with reference to both [deities] equally—as established by the principle that "since the scriptural injunction is equal"—it is understood that this is Pūṣan’s portion. Nevertheless, one might conclude that since nothing is gained by this unscripted act, the grinding should indeed be omitted. Even so, having determined through some skillful means that there is no sublation [of the grinding] due to its being a subordinate factor—whether on account of the simultaneity in the accomplishment of cooking or the singleness of the vessel used for cooking—the grinding must indeed be performed.

To this it is replied: in that case, it is appropriate for the two words *āgneya* and *aindrapīta*, which denote Agni and Indra as capable [of performing the action], to include the deity of the dual-deity cup (*videvatya*). Here, however, because the word *pūṣan* does not participate in a compound, and because the two words *prapiṣṭa-bhāga* retain their semantic capacity even when Pūṣan is dependent [on another], nothing is impaired; thus, the inclusion [of the dual-deity] is justified. Furthermore, since the reason—that "words do not lose their final status when accompanied by another"—is the same, the grinding is logically established.

Because of the explicit statement, there is grinding of all [grains] for that [offering], since it is governed by scripture; for in the case of the *caru*, there is no grinding because of the absence of purpose, and because it is a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), the state of being "not half-ground" (*nemapiṣṭatva*) cannot serve as a reason for the opposite. Therefore, he says: if it were first enjoined that "that which is the *caru* is not half-ground," then, since the scope would be determined in its entirety, the word "Soma-Pūṣan" (*somāpauṣṇa*) would be a partial restatement (*ekadeśānuvāda*) and thus redundant.

Now, if it is argued that the grinding is intended only for the offering to Soma-Pūṣan, even then there would still be grinding of all [the grain], because by the cognition of the offering to the dual deity alone, both the animal-cake (*paśu-puroḍāśa*) and the [other] cakes would be included.
Consequently, as before, the word "cooked rice" (*caru*) would result in being meaningless;
for with respect to that [animal-cake], the grinding would be scripturally enjoined for the offering to Soma-Pūṣan without qualification, since there would be no purpose for such a qualification.
In this view, grinding occurs in the case of the *caru*;

yet its form is not entirely destroyed, nor does there arise a confusion regarding the portion for Uṣas, because the other portion for Uṣas remains distinct. Furthermore, even though it has been ground, it is designated as the portion of Pūṣan, and it would not be confused like the grinding of all [other] portions.

Alternatively, in this view, since the grinding is based on a direct scriptural injunction (*vācanika*), even if it serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), the portion must be taken from that which has indeed been ground.
In that case, this grinding would not be caused by the deity;

therefore, because it would follow that grinding applies universally, the grinding of the *caru* could not be established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). Consequently, the scriptural mention of it would indeed become purposeless. Thus, in a sentence intended to enjoin the connection between the *caru* and the deity, one must necessarily accept that "half is ground" (*nemapiṣṭatvam*) [applies] when there is no [other] fuel (*anindhane*). This concludes the third quarter of the third chapter.
For this is not the property of the deity, nor is it understood as belonging to its portion;
rather, this ritual property (dharma) is recognized as being for the purpose of the sacrifice dedicated to Pūṣan.
Indeed, a portion does not come into existence merely by the act of relinquishing [the offering] for its sake; rather, it comes into being through the act of acceptance.
For the word *bhāga* (portion) is derived in the sense of an object (*karmasādhana*); "portion" means that which is shared or enjoyed (*sevyate*).

And the deity does not enjoy a portion of the oblation, because the status of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) will be refuted in the ninth [book]. Even if it were to enjoy it, its status as the instigator (*prayojakatva*) therein will be precluded at that very point.

Therefore, since it is untenable for this to be a property of the deity as a *bhāga* (share), it must be understood— according to the principle of the first section of the ninth book (*navamādhyāya*) and the principle of the section concerning the deity (*devatādhikaraṇa*)— that this is indeed a property of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) by way of the sacrifice.
However, it should be observed that the Commentator, while intent on refuting its status as a property of the deity, has stated that it is a property of the sacrifice.

In this context, when the opponent has stated "because of the connection with the sentence" and has thus revealed his own intention, [the author] shows by means of the word *bhāga* (portion) that the sacrifice (*yāga*) is what is being denoted, since the primary meaning [of "portion"] is impossible. Because there exists no actual "portion" consisting of the acceptance of another's property, it is the "possessor of the portion"—defined as that which is abandoned for the sake of another—that exists; by this, the sacrifice is indicated. And in the case of a sacrifice dedicated to a single deity, as stated in the *Tantravārtika*, it is qualified by Pūṣan, so the designation "his portion" is appropriate. However, in the case of a sacrifice to two deities, the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is divided and mixed, and it cannot be designated by one [deity] alone.

Just as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) dedicated to Indra-Agni and the cup (*graha*) are not grasped by means of the terms *āgneya* and *indrapīta*, so too, although there is no such fault of compounding (*samāsa*) in the case of the offering to Indra-Pūṣan and others because of the utterance of words such as "the portion of Pūṣan" (*pūṣabhāga*), nevertheless, the very object to be grasped by the word "portion" does not exist; thus, there is no application [of the term].
The fact that it ends in the suffix *-ad* is merely a reason, since it is shown by the illustrative example of the reason, "he who is toothless," that this is a property of the deity.
To this it is replied:
the statement [of the opponent] is supreme;
however, since there is no possibility [of application] in the case of *nemapiṣṭa* and so forth, the statement will indeed come to pass.
A specific injunction is weaker than a general injunction, but such [a general rule] does not exist here;
thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter in the *Tantravārttika* composed by the venerable Śrī Kumārila Svāmin.
[The word] *nivīta* refers to a duty of humans, because the word has that as its primary meaning.

This is precisely the investigation into the contradiction or non-contradiction between that very [text] and the triad beginning with direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), together with the context (*prakaraṇa*).

In this regard, concerning the rule "the *nivīta* [wearing mode] is for humans," these positions arise: Is this a pure duty of humans, or a duty of humans associated with ritual action (*karman*)? Or is it a duty of pure ritual action?

Or is it a duty of that ritual action which has humans as its primary focus within the context, such as the *Anvāhāryapacana* sacrifice and so forth? Or does it find its application in human worship consisting of hospitality toward guests outside of the context?

As for the two positions regarding injunction (*vidhi*) and explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), they are irrelevant to the definition of the "auxiliary" (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) because they fall within the scope of the definition of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), and because they have already been determined among the explanatory passages that resemble injunctions (*vidhivannigada*). Therefore, they need not be introduced here.
As for the introduction made by the author of the *Bhāṣya*, it should be understood as being according to the principle of *kṛtvācintā* (hypothetical consideration).
For the fivefold classification beginning with "the duty of humans" (*manuṣyadharma*) is not tenable without first accepting the status of being an injunction.

Having introduced [the topic] first by treating it as an injunction (*vidhi*), and having subsequently deliberated in accordance with the [apparent] meaning, [the author] will finally conclude by restoring the status of being an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) as it stood previously.

This same principle should be applied, as far as possible, to other sections (*adhikaraṇas*) as well. In this regard, it is first an injunction by the very rule that "it must be an injunction because it conveys something not previously known," for a mere explanatory praise is purposeless; and furthermore, according to the logic of the section concerning the *ahīna* sacrifice and others, it is a duty for humans (*manuṣyadharma*) due to the direct statement of the genitive case.
In the Tantravārtika:
it is understood that those [sacrifices] belong to them as their own property, and not that humans are subordinate members of them,
because there is an absence of an instrumental case-ending which would indicate a subordinate quality.

And since that [status] would be obtained from the sense of the passage itself when [the condition] exists, the mention of "human" (*manuṣya*) would not have been made; yet it has been made. Therefore, we understand from this also that it is a human duty (*manuṣyadharma*).
However, the injunction (*vidhi*) must be considered as something unprecedented (*apūrvavat*).
This is indeed an injunction.
Why?
Because it would be a restatement (anuvāda) of what already exists; that is to say, it would be so only if [the practice] were already established to an absolute degree.
And this [condition] is not absolutely required,
because undistractedness is possible even without it; furthermore, since the binding of the neck is generally not achieved [without it], there is scope for a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*),
as the sentence possesses a remainder (*śeṣavat*).

When two possibilities arise, one must adopt that course of reasoning which does not contradict another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, because of the Vedic recitation in the Yajurveda, there is a sentence connected with the designation (*samākhyā*) "pertaining to the Adhvaryu" regarding the *nivīta* and other such items.

In that case, if this were a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*), then, since there would be a requirement for a specific agent, the designation would become meaningful by restricting it to the Adhvaryu priest. Thus, the designation would fulfill its purpose.
We shall state that the designation "human qualities" (*manuṣyadharma*) is not restrictive; however,
within that context, because there is no contradiction, it first refutes the status of being a ritual duty (*karmadharma*) by means of the superior force of its being a human quality.
For thus, the position indicated as being for ease will be accepted;
for having heard [the text], and having set aside the [arguments of] *prakaraṇasama* (balancing the context), it follows that it is indeed a human duty (*manuṣyadharma*).

To this it is replied: let this position be "for the sake of favoring all," namely "of humans. Thus, the genitive case ending, produced by the distinction from the primary ritual action (*pradhānakarma*), does not refer to the *nīvīta* (the manner of wearing the sacred thread).
Moreover, from the context, it is understood that this refers to the giving of the anvāhārya rice and so forth, and nothing else.
Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is: "If the ritual action of men is to be performed there [in the Pitṛyajña], then it should be offered.
For in these three injunctions, an equal enumeration is observed.
Therefore, it would be as if the human were primary, like the ancestors and gods being primary;
or else, due to the context, it is a mere explanatory passage (arthavāda).
In any case, not even a single one of these positions is free from fault.

In the case of a connection with the context (*prakaraṇa*), there is a sublation of the connection with the syntactical unit (*vākya*); or, in the case of a connection with the *anvācārya* (the one who is being addressed) and so forth, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Furthermore, since it is impossible for the context to serve as a qualifier, a connection with the guests (*atithi*) and others is entirely without foundation.
Since it is not connected by any of the six means of proof beginning with direct statement (*śruti*), it is inferred through its connection with human beings;
however, that is not tenable.
For even in that case, there is the cognition that the sixth case-ending is produced by the exclusion [of others] related to the person who has tied the cloth around his waist;
indeed, case-endings do not arise when the exclusion of an unstated correlate occurs.
Therefore, it follows that the purpose is solely for the sake of humans.
Furthermore, in that case as well, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to assume a distinct subject matter, a separate title, and a different result.

Since there is another possible interpretation, it is not proper to resort to that [assumption]; moreover, there exists the alternative interpretation of being an *arthavāda*, established in the *Audumbara* section.
Beyond this point, the author of the Bhāṣya has not written six sūtras; regarding these, the commentators disagree.
Some say they were possessed by spirits;
others say the manuscript was ancient;
still others say they were disregarded because of their triviality.
Others say it is because [the mantra] is not found in the *Ṛgveda* (*anārṣeyatvāt*).

And thus, the extension (*atideśa*) from the section on the *nivīta*—namely, "and the division of directions is like that"—is appropriate due to its immediate proximity. However, these have been refuted by the authors of other commentaries.
What would be obtained? That all dharmas [would apply].
Why?

For it is heard in the context of the *mṛtāgnihotra* (the Agnihotra for the deceased), which has the ancestors as its deity: "He should cause [the milk] to be milked wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*)."
"For one wearing the sacrificial thread (yajñopavītī) milks for the gods.
If the sacrificial thread is intended for all purposes, then this restatement of the sacrificial thread as if it were obligatory in connection with the ancestral Agnihotra becomes intelligible.
Nor is this a restatement solely of that which pertains to the New and Full Moon sacrifices, because of the great distance [of that context].
And because of the purposelessness of explanatory statements (*arthavāda*) that function as reasons (*hetuvannigada*).

For if a property were to belong to that very same rite while it is in another state, then an explanatory statement functioning as a reason would be appropriate with the desire to avoid that particular state.
However, that which resides in another sacrifice need not be excluded, because it is so remote as to be irrelevant.

Furthermore, the plural form "to the gods" (*devebhyaḥ*) is not appropriate for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, because the deities of those sacrifices— the optional Indra and Mahendra— are singular; however, in the Agnihotra, the plurality is justified by considering the deities of both the evening and morning offerings.
Therefore, because the reference to the *upavīta* (sacred thread) in the context of the *agnihotra* would otherwise be inexplicable, it must be a universal duty (*sarvadharma*).
Or rather, it is not a universal duty.
Why?
Because it is understood from the context that the purpose is the New and Full Moon sacrifices;
as for what was said regarding "the observation of an indicative mark," that has been refuted.
This is the view of that very person regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice;
and when a reference to something proximate is impossible, even a reference to something remote is accepted,
for such a reference depends upon how it is established by other means.
And the plural number is not intended [to be significant].
Alternatively, it will be justified by considering the deities of both the original and the modified forms;
and thus the meaning becomes as follows:

Since this [act] is a duty belonging to another rite associated with the gods, it should therefore not be performed in the *pitrya* Agnihotra; thus, that very example—“he puts on the sacred thread; he thereby creates the mark of a deity”—gives rise to the doubt as to whether this is an injunction (*vidhi*) or a restatement (*anuvāda*).
But how is it that the discussion regarding whether it serves all purposes or specifically the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices proceeded while the status of it being an injunction was still undetermined?

Since this is established by conventional usage and so forth, this subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*) should first be understood according to its underlying meaning. What is the prima facie position? That it is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Why?

For since the rule "one who is constantly provided with water" and "one who is constantly wearing the sacrificial thread" implies that the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) must always be worn, it exists even during a ritual (*kratu*).

Furthermore, this word does not have the form of an injunction; therefore, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*). And in this way, there will be no conflict with the *nivīta* and *prācīnāvīta* modes of wearing the thread. This being the position reached, [the author] says: "Not so."

For there is no fruit whatsoever for a sentence that merely restates what has already been established; furthermore, the mention of the *nivīta* and *prācīnāvīta* will serve a purpose solely as a glorification (*arthavāda*) of the *upavīta* which is being enjoined.

Moreover, since even those [passages] appearing as statements in the present tense (*vartamānāpadeśa*) possess the character of such [glorifications], it has been explained that injunctive power resides in the prescriptive statement (*prayoga-vacana*), the *arthavāda*, and the optative suffix (*pañcamalakāra*). Therefore, this is an injunction.

As for the argument that this is already established by Smṛti alone, the answer to that is the same because it is something previously unknown (*apūrva*): for that [Smṛti rule] prescribes a human duty, whereas this [Vedic injunction] prescribes a novel ritual duty (*kratudharma*).
Therefore, it is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
Or rather, "water-ness" is [the object] because it is something not previously established;
and consequently, this injunction is also indicated by the word because it is something not previously established.
An explanatory restatement (anuvāda) is preceded by what is already established.
Nor is there any attainment of this [prohibition] as being for the sake of the human goal (puruṣārtha) even in the fourth quarter of the third chapter;
nor is it appropriate for it to serve the purpose of praise, because words such as "hi" (for/indeed) are not employed.
Therefore, because it cannot be otherwise [than a prescription], this too is stated as a prescription;
however, this observation of an indicative mark (liṅga) merely serves to illuminate the northward-pointing nature already established by custom, it is not itself a prescription.
Why?
Because of its connection with the word "yat" (that which) and because it lacks both a verb and its specific qualifications, its status as a restatement (*anuvāda*) is clearly established here.
This is so provided that there is some way for it to be applicable; for a restatement must not be disregarded when it has a basis for application.

And such a basis for application exists here, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*): "The blades [of grass] should have their tips pointing eastward or northward, and their points of completion directed toward the east or the north."
Therefore, this is merely a restatement of what is already established for the purpose of establishing that [truth];
and likewise, it is for the purpose of praise.
For this was said in the past, but not at the present time when one is in the state of death.
This very point serves as the answer even to the argument regarding that which is already established (*sthitāt*);
for, just like the particle *hi*, an action expressed by a verb requires attainment from some source or other.

Since such [an attainment] is absent in the present context, must we then postulate a prescriptive force (*vidhitva*) that is not even perceived, or should we rather rely on an attainment existing somewhere else?
In that case, recourse to the *prāpti* (established practice) is required, but not the status of being an injunction (*vidhitva*); therefore, that [recourse] alone is superior.
Furthermore, regarding the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the plural number, it has already been stated that there is indeed another injunction here, so there is no pointlessness;
for the injunction concerns the holding, because it is something not previously established (*apūrvatvāt*).

Every object worthy of honor requires a covering; since such a covering is obtained in some way or another, its specific restriction here regarding the holding [of the ladle] must be a mandatory injunction (vidhi), for there is no prior acquisition (prāpti) of it from any other source.
Since it is impossible to conceal the fuel, it cannot be understood as being situated above [the fire] by virtue of customary practice (*ācāra*);
nor can that which has not been previously established be restated through a statement of reason (*hetu-vat*) or by means of a present-tense description (*vartamāna-apadeśa*).

Therefore, by assuming a restrictive sense (*vyavaccheda-kalpanā*), the status of this as a restatement (*anuvāda*) is set aside, and the sentence is split to resort to its character as an injunction (*vidhi*).
In the ancestral *homa*, the fuel-stick (*samidh*) is to be held below the handle of the offering-ladle (*sruc*);
in the divine (*daiva*) rite, however, it is to be held above. Such is the manner of interpretation stated for these and similar injunctions regarding their status as rules.
Therefore, the notion that it is an injunction arises from its ancient ritual form, which is connected to its purpose;
due to its connection with the division of directions, there is the perception of its similarity to the *nivīta* [wearing of the sacred thread].
The inherent status of directions and so forth as being auxiliary to all ritual actions does not need to be enjoined as something new (apūrva), like the *nivīta* mode of wearing the sacred thread.
In that regard, even when there is a connection with human beings, the result is simply the assumption of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), as stated in the *Tantravārtika*;
it is not the assumption of a result belonging to the action itself.
Furthermore, that [efficacy] is postulated only for worldly activities—the unimpeded completion of which depends on specific requirements—and not for other matters such as heaven and so forth.
Therefore, it appears thus:
whatever action humans perform for their own sake, in that regard, the western and northern directions serve as auxiliary factors.
Whatever requires the cutting of *darbha* grass must be done within that interval; whatever is to be measured must be measured with a full measure.
Whatever task involves oil must all be performed with melted butter (*navanīta*) that has been thoroughly cooked and is designated by the term *niṣpakka-ayuta*.
However, in the case of the *nairṛta* and *raudra* oblations, the states of being burnt and being dependent [on a vessel] are not to be performed.
The undertaking [of this discussion] is because that [the westward-facing rule] must also be established as being equal to the previous one.

In that regard, regarding the statement "the human function belongs to the sound because it is predominant," even without an explicit genitive indication, the term *abhajanta* (they partook) implies a connection with humans, and thus its purpose is for their sake; in the other cases, however, there is indeed a genitive.

Likewise, in the phrase "or by instruction," the attainment [of the westward direction] is stated due to ease, meaning that they operate comfortably with the sun behind them, which results in the attainment of the western direction (*praticī*).
Having performed it thus, because it is accomplished without effort even in the intermediate spaces, forests, and sanctuaries, there is attainment;
and by virtue of both the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the designation (*samākhyā*), it is a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*).
For the sake of favoring all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its application is within the context where humans are the primary agents.

Because the direct statement (*vākya*) sublates both the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the name (*samākhyā*), and because there is the fear of having to postulate a fruit [for the rite], it finds its place in the *Atithyā* and other rites.

Since there is no evidence for a connection with that [Atithyā] either, and since what is possible within the context cannot be displaced (*anutkarṣa*), and because it is a supplement to the preceding injunctions, it is established as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
Thus is achieved the discernment between praise whose subject is correctly heard and understood and praise whose subject is something else.

Therefore, the investigation into the purpose of activity concerns activities themselves; their purpose is determined by the force of the verbal suffixes (ākhyāta) which denote them. Thus, the verbal suffixes must be investigated.
Consequently, since all of this depends upon the determination of the verbal suffix, this inquiry will take place within that context:
"Is the agent denoted by the verbal suffix, or not?"

In this regard, if it is so stated, then because of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—which seeks a purpose—sets aside the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*) understood through context (*prakaraṇa*) and becomes for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). On the other hand, if it is not so stated, then, due to the absence of conflict with the direct scriptural statement, its status as being for the sake of the sacrifice follows from the context.

Now, even if the agent is denoted, because the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) as its primary meaning, the connection of that which is being employed toward it—even if based on direct audition (*śruti*)—is not contradictory due to its conformity with the context; thus, it does not at all sublate the fact that [the act] is for the sake of the sacrifice. For two mutually contradictory connections of equal status would indeed sublate one another, but not those that stand in a relationship of subordinate and principal. For example, in the case of "He cleanses the cup with the fringe of the filter" (*daśāpavitreṇa grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*), there is no such apprehension regarding the cleansing, which has the fringe of the filter as its subordinate element and is being employed toward the cup.
Should it be connected with the *daśāpavitra* or with the cups (*graha*)?
Even so, there is no contradiction whatsoever in an action whose agent is subordinate being employed for the sake of the sacrifice.

However, if the primacy of the agent were expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), then there would be a contradiction with the primacy of the sacrifice as understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Or, if the sacrifice (*kratu*) were also subordinate (*guṇatva*), just like the agent (*kartṛ*), then a contradiction regarding the coexistence of the two subordinates with their respective principal (*śeṣisamavāya*) would be observed; however, neither of those two cases exists here.

Therefore, because the agent is subordinate by virtue of direct statement (*śruti*) and the sacrifice is primary by virtue of context (*prakaraṇa*), there is no contradiction due to their non-coexistence in different domains; and because of that absence of contradiction, there is no sublation (*abādha*).
This is not so; rather,
although these two— base and suffix— are established without distinction,
they are designated as "base" and "suffix" respectively for the sake of grammatical understanding.
For no other rule or other traditional teaching (smaraṇa) is found that serves as an exception to this general principle or traditional teaching;
therefore, just as in the case of words ending in *kṛt* and *dvit* suffixes, the predominance of the meaning of the suffix itself would follow.
Consequently, the subordinate status of the root-meaning, which has been expressed by the word itself, cannot be overridden.
But surely, the universal that has been set forth would be sublated by the specific cognition;
for in this way,
a relation between two things— whether they be primary entities or secondary qualities— is not possible in any case whatsoever.

In this regard, since the status of subordinate and primary must necessarily be postulated, the established rule is determined according to how it is perceived, as stated in the *Ślokavārttika*: "And that perception—

just as elsewhere the meaning of the suffix is observed to have the meaning of the base as its subordinate element— is here self-evident to everyone as having the meaning of the base as subordinate to the meaning of the suffix."
And there is no other factor more powerful than that;
therefore, the objection regarding the agent's primacy does not apply,
for the primacy of the meaning of the verbal root is not [established] in this context.
And the general rule [of grammatical interpretation] will not apply here,
for the king, being a qualifier, is subordinate to the person;
[this concludes] the fourth quarter of the third chapter.
When two things stand in the relation of subordinate and principal, it is that very thing which is intended to be the principal;
however, in cases such as "cook" (*pācaka*), the status of being a principal factor (*kāraka*) is beyond doubt.
Nevertheless, even so, the subservience of actions to [the agent] is not definitively established.
If agency is indeed expressed here primarily,
then its subordinate status is determined by implication;
for agency is established as being instrumental, and that is what is expressed.
However, ownership [of the result] follows after that and is the object of another means of knowledge;
furthermore, agency is attributed even to insentient things such as wood, yet there is no desire for a fruit in those cases. Therefore, this restriction does not hold.

A king, while supporting a man, first assumes the state of being a subordinate (*guṇatva*), and afterwards he partakes in the state of being a master (*svāmitva*). Since the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) regarding the application of an existing entity can be established according to his own preference within two possible meanings, why should we resort to such a cumbersome arrangement based merely on a difference in intention, in consideration of the utility of the action to be expressed?

Therefore, when a word is employed after observing the actual state of affairs—as in the case of "rājapuruṣa" (the king's man)—it is understood that what is intended to be expressed is precisely the status of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) based on the factor of assistance (*upakāra*).

Even in cases where subordination is entirely non-existent for the master, such as with a pregnant slave-girl (*yogarbhadāsī*), it should be regarded as a metaphorical usage because the capacity to provide assistance is possible there as well.
Furthermore, even if the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is obscured, it might still grasp the action.

However, once agency (*kartṛtva*) manifested as residing in the verb (*ākhyāta*), the remaining factors such as number (*saṅkhyā*) and so forth may occur through mere proximity to the substance (*dravya*) which has become subordinate to the factor of action (*kāraka*). But these [factors] are drawn away from that [substance] by the factor of action, which is extremely proximate and primary, and are led toward the action itself. Yet, in this way, there is no stronger means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever by which the fact that the meanings of verbal roots (*dhātvartha*) serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*) is understood, such that their subordination to the agent (*kartṛtva*) would be set aside.
The agency of conscious beings is restricted to matters understood through the scriptures;
this is the fourth quarter of the third chapter.
Furthermore, for them, there can be no injunction without the mental resolve for the fruit.

Therefore, a person who necessarily possesses the status of a performer, out of self-respect, determines: "This action of mine will benefit [the sacrifice] either directly or through a succession. And when a direct benefit is possible, the postulation of an indirect benefit is not permissible. Furthermore, the agent is not incapable of being refined (*saṃskāra*), because he serves a purpose by being the substratum for the fruit of the ritual.
If it is asked, "What is his benefit?"—in any case, it has first been determined in a general sense that there is merely some benefit.
To that extent, the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*) is excluded, and its specific determination may be postulated as desired;
however, that [status] is not useful here, and therefore there is no status of being for the sake of the sacrifice.

And although the aspect of primacy (*prādhānya*) is not expressed by the term "agent" (*kartṛtva*) and is not included therein, it nevertheless connects [with the action] because it is understood precisely through the impossibility of [the agent's status] otherwise.

Just as, for instance, by the word "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), which denotes a specific person, the fact that heaven is the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) will be inferred even though it is not explicitly stated;
so too, the status of ownership (*svāmitva*) will be understood through the very perception of agency on the part of a person acting intentionally out of a desire for the fruit.

In this regard, just as the primacy (*prādhānya*) of the deity intended by the ritual act is understood solely for the purpose of establishing that deity as a means (*sādhana*) of the sacrifice—and not as terminating in the nature of primacy itself—so too here, the subordinate status (*guṇatva*) should be seen as being for the sake of establishing primacy.

Even for one who holds that the agent is the meaning of the suffix, he must necessarily accept [the existence of] *bhāvanā* (efficient force) on the strength of cognition, as stated in the *Tantravārtika*. Therefore, because it is denoted by the same suffix and because of its predominance, it is accepted as being the primary factor in relation to the agent; thus, it does not become subordinate to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
But he, being engaged in the cultivation [of meditation], being unable to perform it otherwise, accepts the very meaning of the verbal root itself.
Nor is it contradictory for it to possess a dual nature, precisely because the objects [of the two aspects] are different.
If one were to assume that it is subordinate solely with respect to the meaning of the verbal root, then there would be a contradiction, as if it were being enjoined only once.
In this case, however, there is no contradiction, because the cultivation (bhāvanā) possesses a subordinate status while the meanings of the verbal roots possess a primary status.
Furthermore, if the word apprehends an entity whose nature consists of both [aspects] in that very manner, what contradiction is there?
Alternatively, one [aspect] is derived from the word and the other from its inherent capacity (sāmarthya); thus, there is no contradiction.
In every respect, since the predominance of the agent necessarily follows, it results that the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha).
Furthermore, this is another distinction:
this is the differentiation between the two types of subordination—namely, that which consists of the word-meaning (śabdārtha) and that which consists of the object-meaning (vastvartha).

In the case of the sentence "Bring the cook and the king’s man," the cook or the king—being related to the bringing of the man—is understood as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) merely by virtue of being the word-meaning (*śabdārtha*); thus, it does not yet attain the status of a "residual" (*śeṣa*). However, in cases such as "He should speak," since there is no mention of the agent's connection with any other action, the subordination of the word-meaning is not even sought; therefore, by process of elimination, the status of being a "residual" is determined solely as the subordination of the actual object (*vastvartha*). Consequently, under the theory of direct denotation (*abhidhānapakṣa*), there exists proof for the fact that the meanings of verbal roots serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārthatva*).

[Objection: If this were so, even though it is not explicitly denoted, that very [bhāvanā] which is conveyed by the same word as the verbal root meaning—being more proximate due to the context—is capable of fulfilling the requirement for the purpose of the verbal root meaning; thus, it would attain a status equal to that of what is explicitly denoted.
[Response: This is not a fault. That word undergoes figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) which is not employed by direct denotation (śruti);
but when it is employed by the meaning of the direct denotation, figurative indication is merely incidental.
From the Vedic revelation "he should increase," it is understood that the person [is the agent];

thus, even the injunction becomes meaningful. Otherwise, it would be purposeless regarding the purpose of the sacrifice; according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), that which is connected to the sacrifice is declared by the traditional scripture.
That cognition which, by virtue of its context and logical connection, is the object of sublation and is always based on the authority of a Vedic revelation as its root—
because it expresses the meaning of such a Smṛti, that [cognition] cannot be a mere restatement (anuvāda).

If, setting aside the context, this [Smṛti] were held to have human purpose as its object, then, being identical in meaning to Smṛti, how could the Śruti— the root— be lost? For here, three types of prima facie arguments (pūrvapakṣas) are accepted by the author of the Bhāṣya.
In the preceding [section], the status of being the root was established; for the other two, however, there is the status of restatement (*anuvādatā*).
Indeed, apart from the person, untruth is not encountered during the *ṛtu* period.
(Third Adhyāya, Fourth Pāda)
If that [prohibition] is established for the person, it is also established for the body;
or rather, there is a rule due to a difference in connection (*saṃyoga*).
Regarding the view that [the action] has the person as its sole purpose, the author of the Bhāṣya describes a different connection.

For in the Smṛti, the restriction to truth is heard for the sake of dharma in the form "one should speak the truth," while the prohibition of falsehood is heard in the form "one should not speak untruth. These two purposes are distinct; moreover, that which is being enjoined cannot be a mere restatement (anuvāda) of what is already established.

Therefore, it is an injunction (vidhi). [Objection: But surely, a person's verbal activity consists only of speaking the truth or speaking untruth. In that case, when truth is restricted, falsehood is necessarily prohibited by implication, and thus it follows that it must indeed be a restatement.
This is not so.
Why?
Because it is only from a different conjunction that there occurs a restatement of a name which is determined to have an absolutely identical meaning.
Furthermore, there is a difference in meaning between injunction and prohibition due to a difference in their results. How so?
Because of the logic of not looking at [the sun] while observing the Prajāpati-vow.
It is understood that the injunction regarding truth is by way of exclusion (paryudāsa);
it is a Smṛti rule for the connection of every person with truth for the sake of accomplishing their own purpose.
This [present case], however, is for the sake of the person connected to the ritual (ṛtu), for the sake of a different result.

For ritual acts (*kratavaḥ*), being dependent upon the injunctions and prohibitions related to themselves, become defective when those are transgressed. However, those injunctions and prohibitions pertaining to the person—just like those pertaining to other rituals—are indifferent to his presence or absence.
Indeed, no notion of "excellence" (*guṇa*) arises regarding them such that a notion of "defect" (*vaiguṇya*) would arise upon their transgression.
Therefore, one who speaks untruth during the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices might go to hell, yet he would still obtain the full fruit of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* itself without any deficiency.
And such is the meaning of the Smṛti; however, when it is heard [in the Śruti] that "this is a duty of the person connected with the context," this is the sense understood:
by which person who has avoided speaking untruth are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices brought to fruition?

For, through the force of the context, having indicated that the quality of being a means to the *apūrva* resides in the person, untruth is prohibited; therefore, upon its transgression, the *apūrva* of the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa itself would not arise due to deficiency (*vaiguṇya*).
But there is no transgression for the person alone;
for at that time, a transgression being postulated cannot be postulated as pertaining to an independent person. Therefore, there is another connection [with the result], and thus it is an injunction.
In this way, regarding the duties of the ritual season (*ṛtudharma*), another connection must be explained based on the specific transgression incurred by the person [if they fail to act].
Therefore, it is not merely a restatement of what is already established.
As for the distinction between being a duty of the ritual season and being a duty pertaining to the person involved therein, we shall explain that further below.

It is not said that [the injunction] is useless now because the injunction is established in both ways; for the opponent [argues], "We accept this as being twofold," as stated previously in the *Tantravārtika*.
For this very reason, we say that it is a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*); in all verbal forms (*ākhyāta*), the agent is certainly not intended as the expressed meaning.
Whatever cognition arises from them, that must arise from another [linguistic] connection.
Since we perceive the number residing in the agent from the suffixes [of the verb],
therefore this much power of the *tiṅ* suffix is understood from its function; just as in some cases, even though it has been expressed, it will not be expressed elsewhere with respect to the object.
In the same way, the number [associated] with this [verb] is also established by the power of the word itself.

For if someone thinks that since the expression of number by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is observed in the case of an action (*karman*), it must therefore exist elsewhere as well, then for him, because it is observed to be expressed by a verbal suffix in some instances, it would have to be expressed in all cases. If, however, that [expression of number] is somehow restricted, then the number will likewise be restricted; thus, this objection is not valid.
Now, this might be argued: "How can a number qualified by an agent be denoted without first denoting the agent? To this it is replied: [as stated] in the *Tantravārttika*.

Since a cognition of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) does not arise when its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) has not been grasped, that quality must be attended to. However, nothing is impaired by the fact that the qualifier is not expressed [by a word], provided that even if the qualifier is unexpressed, it is capable of producing a qualified cognition when made known by some other means. In this case, since the agent, who is made known by the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) itself, possesses the capacity to function as a qualifier, it does not depend on verbal expression.

This is established in all cases involving qualified cognitions (*viśiṣṭapratyaya*), provided they are not [otherwise] taught by another [means]. In that regard, when a qualified cognition has arisen, upon examining what is conveyed by the word and what is obtained by another [means] regarding the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), wherever the qualificand is established from another source, the function of the word lies with the qualifier; and wherever the qualifier is obtained from another source, it lies with the qualificand.

And in all cases, the operation of either one or both of the two components—the qualifier and the qualified—is postulated in the word solely through the force of a specific cognition (*viśiṣṭa-pratyaya*) by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Furthermore, because it consists in the impossibility of being otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*), this [cognition] occurs in a domain that cannot be established by any other means.
Thus, in this case, the oneness that functions as the qualifier and the oneness that functions as the qualified are not obtained from any other source.
By means of which [the universal] could be designated.

For if the agent were able to convey that [universal], then, according to the logic of the *ākṛti* (form), that alone would be the denotable object, while the other [the individual] would be understood as being like an *vyakti* (individual instance).
However, since it is impossible for that [agent] to avoid deviation [from the universal], one must necessarily accept that even oneness is the denotable object.
Consequently, when the expressive power [of the suffix] has shifted there [to the number], the agent—though understood—is rendered expressible even while functioning as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
However, when singularity alone is the qualifier, then that very [number] ending in the nominative case must necessarily be expressed.
And if that [number] is already expressed, the word, its capacity being exhausted, looks toward the agent who is established from another source.
And thus the fourth quarter of the third chapter is established:
that [the agent] is [known] from the efficient force (*bhāvanā*). Therefore, the postulation of a denotative power [in the verb] does not serve as the reason [for the objection].
As for the fact that other factors of action (*kāraka*) are also perceived, whether they are perceived or unperceived, they neither provide nor withhold any assistance.

In every respect, first of all, that agent who is sought after is indeed understood. Even if something else is also understood, how are we contradicted by it, since we are not contradicted by what is unperceived? We do not say this on account of an additional cognition. However, although the instrument and so forth are also perceived, they are not associated with a number distinct from that of the agent due to the power of the word’s expressive capacity; for it is not the case that whatever is perceived must necessarily be grasped. For in all cases, the causes for grasping [an element] are dependence upon perception, semantic fitness, and so forth.
Therefore, in this context, because the number is established for both parties as residing in the agent, [the grammatical operation applies] to the end of the *kāraka* [term].
Because they are neither required nor suitable, even though they are present, they do not attain the status of being related;
nor do they possess a desire for the number expressed by the verbal suffix (tiṅ),
since in all cases [number] is delimited by the number expressed by the nominal suffix (sup).
Furthermore, this number, being perceived in its general form, does not require another related element.
For the distinction between a word and a sentence has already been stated based on the rule of fixed sequence (paurvāparya).
Thus, as soon as the meaning of the verbal root is perceived, it is determined that there will necessarily be some efficient force (bhāvanā) and some agent.
Consequently, when the agent has already been previously apprehended, the number alone, being expressed, undergoes the status of either a qualifier or a qualificand.
This occurs when the agent is first apprehended through the efficient force (*bhāvanā*),
and there is no connection with the number that would necessitate bypassing that [agent].

The operation of cooking (*audana-vyāpāra*) is not primarily denoted by the verbal root, because [if it were], the number belonging to the object—which is already understood as qualified—would have to be expressed; otherwise, since that very [object] would assume the characteristic of an agent, its status as an object would be abandoned in favor of agency. And precisely because it is not an agent, that operation is not *bhāvanā*.
Therefore, even so, there is no presentation of the object in its specific form.

Furthermore, the operation of the person (*puruṣa-vyāpāra*) must necessarily be stated as primary; for otherwise, if it were the operation of another, there would be no injunction (*niyoga*) for this [agent] at all.

Furthermore, agency that is not constructed by the verbal suffix would not manifest even for that which is expressed by another word; consequently, the instrumental case ending in *tvayā* would also not occur. Alternatively, the object—whose own operation is not overwhelmed by the operation [of the agent]—would, because it is not being caused to reach [the agent] (*anāpyamānatvāt*), abandon its status as an object and, through the manifestation of its own operation, assume the status of an agent alone. Thus, by relinquishing its connection with itself, it would be connected solely with the number of the agent.

Therefore, just as in the case of the word *pacati*, even when number is expressed [by the suffix] in forms such as *pacyate*, because it is not suppressed, it would apply to the agent alone and not to the object.
It is replied: in every respect...

In that case, if even when the *nakārīṣu* suffixes are produced by my [Pāṇinian] rules, the number of the agent itself is obtained, then for you as well, there must be an expression of the agent in those instances.
Now, if for you the agent is somehow not expressed there, then for me too there is no expression of its number; thus, there is no fault.
This must necessarily be resolved as follows:

first of all, because it is that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*), the object (*karman*) possesses primacy over all other factors of action (*kāraka*); and furthermore, by virtue of its being the result to be brought about (*bhāvya*), its operation is included within the process of bringing something into being (*bhāvanā*).

In that context, when it is intended to show that prominence [of the object] by means of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) itself, then—even though the agent exists as a form of the word-meaning and is denoted by both the suffix (*niṅ*) and the root (*dhātu*) as a primary factor consisting of a general and particular operation, and even though agency is thereby obtained—since another prominence of the entity is intended to be expressed, the suffix arises in relation to the object (*karman*) or its number.

However, when that [agent], although existing, is not intended to be expressed—either because it is not desired to be mentioned or due to the influence of a particular verbal root—and when the intention arises to emphasize only the form of the word-meaning as the primary factor, then the *sup* (case-ending) is employed to manifest the primacy of the object (*karman*), and the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is produced in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) or its number.

But for the instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth, there is no intention to express primacy either according to the nature of the thing (*vastu-lakṣaṇā*) or according to the nature of the word (*śabda-lakṣaṇā*); therefore, they are always merely external adjuncts (*bāhya-upādeya*) to the word. Some others, however, [hold this view].

When such a capacity of the word is understood—namely, that this [word] is able to express the number of the agent alone, while this [other word] expresses that of the object alone—even if the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is presented by another word, that very number will be taken up by the agent, because it has been expressed as having no other referent. As stated in the *Mantravārttika*:

"For example, the word *śoṇa* (red), while expressing a quality residing in a horse even though the horse itself is not explicitly mentioned by a separate member of the compound, implies the nature of being a horse by its own power."
And this being the case, by this very same logic, it follows that all things such as cows and the like would also be non-denotable.
Furthermore, how can such an extensive power of the word be postulated? [If so,] why does this [word] express only a quality inherent in that [individual]?
What is the point of postulating another power beyond that, since linguistic usage is established by the very first [power] alone?

Furthermore, in such cases as these, the restriction of the relationship [between word and meaning] occurs because they are conveyed by a single word, not by virtue of a separate verbal power (*śabda-śakti*).
Therefore, one must likewise accept this same principle regarding the agent, number, and so forth; thus, the claim that these are "unexpressed" (*anabhidheya*) is abandoned.
In this regard, others think:

"For if horse-ness (*aśvatva*) were not being expressed, how could there arise the cognition of redness as delimited by it? A specific instance of redness is intended by me as a qualifier of horse-ness, and certainly not as a qualifier of something white."
The fourth quarter of the third chapter:
However, this [distinction] is a different quality and species arising from the very nature of things;
for every person, there is a distinct quality belonging to each specific species that is self-evident.

Whether the expression of the mind is by way of its specific distinction or by way of its general nature—now, as for what was said, that even in the case of cows and the like, since the specific universal (*jāti*) is established merely through the expression of the number and other attributes residing therein, it would follow that [the universal] is not denotable; to that we reply: [The text continues: ...therein we say: [the universal is indeed denoted]. Why? Because it is perceived as the object of the cognition "this is a cow" and so forth. For if the universal were not denoted, then the cognition "this is a cow" would have to arise with respect to a substance devoid of the universal, which is impossible. Furthermore, if the universal were not denoted, then the word "cow" would denote a mere individual (*vyakti*), and consequently, there would be no difference between the words "cow," "horse," and so on, because they would all denote the same kind of thing—a mere individual. Moreover, since the universal is the cause of the application of the word, it must necessarily be denoted. Therefore, the universal is indeed denotable. Thus, the objection is refuted.

For if a distinction between oneness and so forth residing in cows and horses were indeed perceived through direct perception—just as [the distinction] between drying and so forth [is perceived]—then it might be postulated in this way.

Furthermore, if—as in the case of the nominal stem *śoṣa*—which, while denoting both quality (*guṇa*) and substance (*dravya*), is determined to denote one or the other due to the impossibility of postulating multiple powers, and is ascertained to express a non-deviating quality because the horse-nature (*aśvatva*) is deviating and thus not a signifier; likewise, since "cow-ness" (*gotva*) and "number" (*saṃkhyā*) are expressed by the same word, the denotative capacity of one of them would have to be ascertained through its non-deviation. But that is not the case; for as far as number is concerned, because it consists everywhere in the act of delimitation (*pariccheda*), no such deviation is observed.
Nor can multiple words be conceived as denoters of both [the genus and the number] simultaneously;

for, based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the nominal stem denotes the genus while the inflection denotes the number. Furthermore, there is no fault in postulating multiple meanings for a single word.
If one were not to postulate a multiplicity of capacities (*śakti*) for that single word, then one or the other would necessarily be rendered meaningless.
Furthermore, there is no invariable concomitance between number and the numbered, such that the mention of one would necessarily imply the other.
For instance, if gender were expressed by the nominal stem itself, it would function as an invariably concomitant property distinct for each class, similar to "whiteness" and so forth.
Thus,

although the feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others do not denote [the gender] as distinct entities because they merely manifest it, and instead bring forth a further power (*śaktyantara*) within the preceding word-form itself, nevertheless, the denotative function (*bhakti*) assigned to that specific word-form prior to the addition of *ṭāp* and so on with respect to the genus (*jāti*) in its state of being a gendered entity cannot be removed afterwards.
Likewise, in cases where masculinity or neuter-ness is manifested through connection with a case-ending (*vibhakti*), the expression of the genus should be understood in exactly the same way.

However, in cases where the gender-cognition arises from the bare nominal stem itself— either before the case-ending has occurred or once it has ceased— such as in *hastī* (elephant), *nā* (man), *devadattaḥ* (Devadatta), *śrīḥ* (fortune), *marittoyaṃ* (sea-water), or *vārī* (water)—

there is nothing contradictory even if one accepts that this is the case. Alternatively, even when the cognition of the meaning occurs without a linguistic division [of gender], everything first apprehends the genus through a division that is internally cognized (*svasaṃvedya*).
Furthermore,
it may well be that gender alone is cognizable through the class (jāti), but the class is not cognizable through gender. Moreover,
since this [gender] is always understood as a subordinate element, it cannot exclude the status of being the primary denotable object from the class, which is perceived as the principal factor.
Furthermore, there is no manifestation of gender through either the word or the sound of terms such as *gopu* (cow-pen) or *gośva* (cow-horse), as there is in the case of a genus (*jāti*).
Therefore, the genus is indeed the primary denotation; it will apply even to those cases where gender does not deviate from it.

Even when deviation occurs and [gender] is understood from another source, it is conceived as one pleases—either that [other factor] alone is the indicator, or the genus assisted by it, or the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself.

Therefore, there is no equality with [the case of] "redness" (*śoṇa*) and so forth. Even in words such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), if number were perceived—like redness—as following after the agent alone, having a form excluded from all other factors (*kāraka*s), then indeed the agent might be understood by means of that [number]; nevertheless, it would still remain unexpressed [by the verbal suffix].

But when, by the reasoning previously stated, no distinction in number is obtained, and it is impossible to postulate infinite distinct universals such as "oneness" and so forth for each individual object, then one must resort to the taking up [of the animal] through the act of bringing (*bhāvanā*) and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) alone. Furthermore, if someone were to bring a horse for the sake of the *śoṇa* (the red one), he himself would not undergo the hardship [of the sacrifice].

Furthermore, since number and the efficient force (bhāvanā) bring about the meanings of verbal roots, they do not themselves exert effort. And the distinction regarding the presentation of the efficient force has already been stated.

Therefore, we understand that because it is possible for the agent—who is not itself denoted—to function as either the qualified or the qualifier, the postulation of a denotative power [for the agent] lacks any basis in valid cognition.

But surely, since the contradiction with scripture has already been shown by the very meaning of the Sūtra, this statement regarding the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) is irrelevant.
How is it irrelevant? Because, according to the previous reasoning, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) must also demonstrate the predominance of the agent (*kartṛ*);
thus, this statement demonstrates that both [the distinction between base and suffix] and that predominance are established by traditional authority (*smṛti*).

Since the base and the suffix express [their meanings] together, and it is recorded in the grammatical tradition (*smṛti*) that the agent and the object are the meanings of the suffix, therefore, because those two are denoted as qualified by the action, there is indeed a contradiction between the direct statement (*śruti*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*).
This is from the fourth quarter of the third chapter.
In that regard, in the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca*, the agent and the object are introduced as being exclusively denotable.

In this context, which [of the two interpretations] is it? Here, one [interpretation] is the observation of a single denotable object (*abhidheya*). The other, however, is that the locative case ending is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), as in a "locative of the other" (*parasaptamī*). But since an agent cannot possibly exist elsewhere within the arrangement of words (*śabdasanniveśa*), [the rule] "because of its lack of purpose, [it applies] to its parts" (*ānarthakyāt tadaṅgeṣu*) is understood to mean that the operation applies to the word itself.
In that case, the meaning is: when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix expressive of the agent is situated after [the verbal root].
In every respect, the meaning of the suffix [expressing] the agent must be conveyed, as stated by the Teacher; therefore, the inference that [the agent] is not denotable is incorrect.
To this it is replied:

in those cases where logic (*nyāya*) and scripture (*āgama*) have the same object, it is appropriate to point out a contradiction with scripture; however, here the object of logic is entirely different—namely, what is the expressed (*vācya*) and what is the implied (*gamya*).
In the view of Grammar (Vyākaraṇa), the matter is entirely different: among those words employed for a single meaning, which is the correct one (*sādhu*) and which is the corrupt form (*apabhraṃśa*)?

It is not logical that something belonging to a different domain should sublate another domain, even if it is weaker; how much less so when the distinction between the expressed (*vācya*) and the implied (*gamyamāna*) is directly perceived by everyone’s own experience?
Therefore, even if the teachers were to say that "the agent is the word-meaning," they would not be worthy of respect if they were speaking outside of their own proper domain.
But they do not speak in that way at all. [Objection:
Has not the Sūtra itself been cited as direct perception? [Reply:
True, but it was not cited merely by way of its own form as a treatise.
What is the use of examining a mere portion of it?
Nor is it possible to distinguish a specific treatise by that much alone.
Why?
The meaning of a treatise is understood in one way through a single portion,
and in another way when it is complete with all its constituent parts;
this is especially so in the case of grammar.

In this regard, for each individual word, the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* is generally operative. Therefore, one must avoid contradiction with the full meaning of the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca*, which is completed by other constituent parts; and here, by this much, the prescription of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*) is fulfilled.
It is a suffix, it follows another [element], and it has an udātta accent on its first syllable.
The *su* and *ti* suffixes are unaccented.
[They are added] after a verbal root (*dhātu*). In that context, the subordinate word (*upapada*) is that which stands in the locative case.
*kudatiṅ* / [A suffix] not similar in form [to another] is optionally [used after a verbal root], except in the feminine;
*laṭ* is used for the present tense.

*kṛt* suffixes [denote] the agent (*kartṛ*). *Laḥ* (the *l*-marked suffixes) [denote] the object (*karman*) and, after intransitive verbs, the state (*bhāva*). [The substitute] *laḥ* [replaces *tiṅ*].
The roots beginning with *ti* [belong to the first class].
That which is marked with an anudātta vowel or the letter *ṅ* takes the *ātmanepada* endings.
From the remaining [roots], the *parasmaipada* endings are used when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed.
When *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are used as upapadas [in the sense of "you" and "I"], the second person and so forth are employed;
for the personal endings (*tiṅ*), there are three triplets called first, middle, and last.
Each of these [triplets] is further divided into singular, dual, and plural.
"The plural is used for many;
the dual and singular are used for two and one, respectively.

Furthermore, all the subsequent rules—whether in the form of technical definitions (*saṃjñā*), interpretive maxims (*paribhāṣā*), or the grammatical teachings concerning elision (*lopa*), augmentation (*āgama*), and the modification of phonemes (*varṇavikāra*)—constitute a single sentence.
And syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) occurs only when there is a relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), and not otherwise.

Furthermore, that [unity] arises either through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) among words ending in the same case-suffix, or through non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) in the form of action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*), or in the form of subordinate and principal elements (*śeṣaśeṣirūpa*).

Therefore, since it is not applicable here [in the case of *la* substitutes], the *la* substitutes occur for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) with respect to other components [of the verbal base], and the singular number (*ekavacana*) applies to a single [referent].

Regarding the rules "the dual for two" and "the plural for many," the relationship between qualifier and qualified is examined; specifically, whether they share the same grammatical locus (sāmānādhikaraṇya) or possess different loci (vaiyadhikaraṇya) is considered in this fourth quarter of the third chapter.

In this regard, it has been established in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* that words such as *dvi* (two) and *bahu* (many) denote number, because it is impossible for them to function with respect to the thing numbered (*saṃkhyeya*) without first denoting the number itself.

Furthermore, in the *Pātañjala-bhāṣya*, having introduced the discussion with the question "In which many [things]? and having pointed out the defects [in alternative views], it is determined that they indeed denote number;
for it is explained: "In the state of plurality (*bahutva*), there is duality and singularity."

When it is asked, "How can an instruction be primarily concerned with a state (bhāva) without the use of an abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya)?", it is explained that this occurs when a quality (guṇa) itself is intended to be expressed as primary.
Likewise, previously it was stated that one quality is enjoined independently,
while another is enjoined as a subordinate part of a substance (dravyāṅgabhāvena), and yet another is extracted from that.
In the case of *hyeka-saṃkhyeya-saṃghāta*, a plurality arises;
[the question] "in which cases? would arise there if there were dependence on number (*saṃkhyeya*).
Likewise, the suffix *tip* would apply even when there is more than one agent.
Furthermore, [the objection] that [the word "all"] would apply to everything including the agent and the like is refuted;

for in the *Tantravārtika*, it is stated that in a technical treatise (*śāstra*), even that which is not denotable by its own primary meaning is accepted as denotable through technical convention (*pāribhāṣika*) on account of the requirements of the subject matter (*kāryavaśena*).
Nor does it follow from that alone that [the same] applies in the world, nor is it our claim in this treatise that action and so forth are simply non-denotable.
Rather, what has been explained here is merely that they possess qualifiers such as "being exclusively denotable" and so on;
therefore, these [words] will function precisely as qualifiers.
Thus, where there is no attainment of the status of being denotable through either scripture (*śāstra*) or logic (*nyāya*), they will be understood as non-denotable.

However, where they would otherwise be unable to comprehend [the meaning] because they are not being denoted while possessing the quality of being qualifiers mentioned in the scripture, they will—having no other recourse—comprehend even the status of being denotable as obtained through logic.
Or else, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), they will be stated in the scripture as well by way of being denotable.

In that regard, since the establishment of the non-distinctness of the basis for the application of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) depends upon the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), it need not necessarily be admitted as the expressed meaning [of the suffix]. However, because the meanings of nominal stems (*prātipadika*)—such as singularity and so forth—are found to deviate when applied to non-agents (*akāraka*) or to other types of agents, and because their capacity to convey one or the other is already known; and furthermore, since there is no other indicator for them apart from the *bhāvanā* and the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), which are themselves unexpressed, there is nothing else to bring them to mind. Consequently, since it is impossible to express a number qualified by an agent without first expressing the agent itself, the agent must also be the expressed meaning [of the suffix].

But surely, since there is no usage of a mere case-ending (*kāraka*) word in isolation, the connection of the number with the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) will necessarily be possible only for those factors of action (*kārakas*) brought forward by the productive energy (*bhāvanā*) expressed by the verbal root (*ākhyāta*).
How is this possible?
