For when, in sentences where the order of words is fixed, a cognition of a *kāraka* is produced by a nominal stem (*subanta*)—such as "the tree" (*vṛkṣam*)—which is sometimes used before the verbal word, that cognition cannot be established without [prior] denotation.

[Objection: But even in that case, since the status of being a *kāraka* is untenable prior to the connection with an action, a *kāraka*-case ending should not arise until the connection with the action has been demonstrated;
and thus, it is established that [the *kāraka*] is preceded by the action.
[Reply: True.

It is thus for the speaker; however, the listener first hears only "tree," and by that [word], neither the action nor its connection [to the tree] has been previously ascertained from any other source. Between two related entities, it must necessarily be admitted that the basis of the cognition of one is independent of the other. Therefore, in this case, if the *kāraka* (participant in an action) is to be understood through the action (*kriyā*), then it must be stated by what the action itself is made known.
Furthermore, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is not expressive of action, because it denotes only the genus (*jāti*) such as "branch-possessing" and the like;
nor is the meaning of the nominal stem an indicator [of action], since it is possible even without an action.
Now, it might be argued that nothing ever exists without action, and therefore some action—such as "exists" or "stands"—will necessarily be implied.

Alternatively, one might argue that since the verb *as* (to be) in the third person singular present tense is understood even when not explicitly uttered—as in the rule "the verb *as* is understood even when not used"—the [action] possesses activity and thus requires a factor of action (*kāraka*), such that it will be possible [for the agent to act]. This is untenable.
Why?

For even when [a verb] such as "he stands" (tiṣṭhati) is employed, although it is intransitive and expresses mere action, only the agent is expressed, and the object and so forth are not necessarily expressed by rule. This is because, if one does not accept that every effect possesses a nature consisting of both existence and non-existence— given that we observe the appearance and disappearance of any given effect— then a single uniformity would have to be maintained.
Its existence must be accepted;

for even if [the cause] exists, there is no contradiction in the non-commencement of the effect due to obstruction, the absence of other causes, or its establishment through something else. Furthermore, since that which is non-existent cannot be obtained even by the gods at the time of the effect, it would follow that the production of the effect is without a cause. This has been stated regarding the permanence of the relationship. Thus, the expressive power (*vācaka-śakti*) postulated for that [relationship] will first operate upon the initial usage.
On the contrary, it will be explained [later] that [the suffixes] will remain indifferent [to the specific agent or object].

Since they have acquired their own nature, even when they are based on direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*), they will proceed with their function by setting aside the cognition derived from inference (*anumāna*).

Therefore, it is established that the meanings of case-endings (*sup*) and so forth also exist; however, in the case of verbal endings (*tiṅ*), because of the necessity of a fixed sequence [of word-constituents], number is understood only after the agent and the object—which are presented by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)—have been established. Thus, at no time does the [suffix] denote a specific *kāraka* (participant in the action). This concludes the fourth quarter of the third chapter.
This is the occasion for postulating a potentiality (*śakti*).
And thus, it is established in the *Tantravārttika* that the agent and the object are always inferable.

For co-referentiality with that [verbal] base is observed in the case of *kṛt*-derived words whose denotative capacity is beyond doubt, such as "Devadatta is a cooker" (*pakta*) or "the rice is cooked" (*pakva*), where they function non-differently from the base.
Furthermore, where there is no expression of agent and object, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not observed, as in the case of words such as "cooking" (*pāka*).
Moreover,
[this is so] because [the word] follows the distinction in number inherent in that which is conveyed by the pronoun *tat*.
In the same way, there would be denotative power; these two are the examples here as well.
And for this reason, it is observed that there is no obstruction of the case-endings of the *kāraka* prescribed by the governing rule of the "unexpressed" (*anabhihita*), as in:
*pacati devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta cooks") and *pacyate odanaḥ* ("the rice is cooked").

For if there were no denotative capacity (*vācakatva*), then the application of case-endings—such as the second case for an unexpressed object (*anabhihite karmaṇi*) and the third case for the agent and the instrument (*kartṛkaraṇayoḥ*)—would not be obstructed by anything, as in the examples "Devadatta cooks" (*pacyate devadattena*) and "he cooks rice" (*pacaty odanam*). Since, however, there is indeed such an obstruction, it is understood that denotative capacity exists; and by virtue of this similarity (*sādharmya*) with the agent and the cooked object, one must demonstrate the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) from other things.

Furthermore, where there is no denotative power (*vācakatva*), there is also no restriction regarding case-endings (*kārakavibhakti*), as in the examples "it is cooked by Devadatta" (*pacyate devadattena*) and "he cooks rice" (*pacaty odanam*).
For this reason also, the word is a communicator (*bodhaka*), because it brings about the cognition of its specific [object],
just as the ear, being the means of perceiving sound, is the communicator of sound.

Furthermore, these two [the agent and the object] are denoted [by the verbal suffix], because they are connected with qualifiers, as in "he cooks beautifully" (*śobhanaḥ pacati*) and "it is cooked beautifully" (*śobhanaḥ pacyate*).
Where there is a connection with a qualifier, denotability is also observed, as in "a beautiful cooker" (*śobhanaḥ paktā*) or "deliciously cooked" (*ramaṇīyaḥ pakkaḥ*).
However, where there is no denotability, a connection with a qualifier is not observed either, as in "he sits beautifully" (*śobhanam āsyate*).

Furthermore, there can be no connection with qualifiers for that which is already being understood, just as fire, once understood from the word "smoke," has no further connection with [specific qualities] such as "blazing" and so forth.
All of this has indeed been demonstrated by the Commentator through the passage beginning with "since the agent is one, the singular number is used," and thus it was not elaborated upon further.
However, the suitability for the number residing in that [agent] is not possible without grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the like.

Therefore, the position that [the word] denotes [the action] alone is logical. To this, it is replied: as for what was stated—that the expressive words such as "cooks" (*pacati*) and so forth [denote the action] because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the agent and the object—[that is now addressed].

In that case, if existence were inferred through the power of denotation (*vācaka-śakti*), then, because all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be untenable due to the sublation by the aforementioned *arthāpatti*, there would be a contradiction with non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). Furthermore, *arthāpatti* is the sole means of valid cognition for all powers, and it has been refuted here as being otherwise possible.
There is also a contradiction with inference (*anumāna-virodha*);
for [the Veda] is not the designator of the agent and the object, as stated in the *Patantra-vārttika*.

The word *tiṅ* and so forth denote meanings that are absolutely inseparable from it; for whatever denotes an object that is absolutely inseparable from something else is not a non-denoter of that thing—just as the word *śiṃśapā* denotes the specific nature of a *śiṃśapā* tree which is necessarily restricted to being a tree. Likewise, the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) are denoted by the *tiṅ* suffix, because it does not abandon its own denotable meaning.
Furthermore, they are cognized through its operation and so forth, just like [the universal] "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*).
In that very word "śiṃśapā," [the meaning] is not denoted by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) because it is a kāraka, just like the instrumental case-ending (*karaṇa*) and so forth.
The verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) word lacks denotative power because it is a verbal suffix, just like [the suffix in] *āsya-te* and so forth.
This too can be said:
"But surely this inference contradicts worldly convention, like [the argument] 'the moon is not the moon'.
This is not a fault.

If we were to deny the status of being the signified (*pratyāyyatva*) or the signifier (*pratyāyakatva*), then we would be speaking in contradiction to the world. However, this is merely a negation of the power (*śakti*) between the signified and the signifier; there is no contradiction with worldly convention by that act.

For the world, which achieves its purpose through the mere production of cognition, pays no heed to the distinction between the four types of objects—the denoted (*abhidheya*), the implied (*gamyamāna*), the illuminated (*dyotya*), and the form (*rūpa*).

If, however, you were to seek to establish merely the state of being signified and signifier as it is commonly recognized in the world, then, because of the acceptance of the cognition of the nourishment of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) as previously stated, you would be proving what is already established.
Furthermore, the contradiction with worldly consensus would fall upon you alone.
Why?
The world does not desire that which is established through something else to be the denotable object;

just as the own-form (*svarūpa*) is not denoted because it is already grasped by the sense of hearing, so too, just as in words such as *pācaka* (cook) there arises a cognition of the form of a substance (*sattva*) due to the predominance of the substance, so it would also be in the case of words ending in nominal and verbal suffixes (*su*- and *tiṅ*-antāḥ).

Furthermore, just as in these very examples—such as "Tell the cook," "Cooked by the cook," and "Give to the cook"—there occurs a connection with other *kārakas*, so too would it follow in cases such as "He cooks rice.

Therefore, even in the view that the *kāraka* is a substance possessing power (*śaktimat*), one must necessarily admit that the mere power (*śaktimātra*) is extracted and expressed by the nominal and verbal suffixes (*sup-tiṅ*).
For when that is the case:

When a substance has its nature brought under control by one manifested power, it cannot at that very same time be understood as being endowed with another power. In the expression "Devadatta cooks," agency is first of all conveyed by the *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) alone; as for the number, that too is conveyed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). What else remains here for which a case-ending (*vibhakti*) would have to arise? But how is it that, when multiple factors of action (*kāraka*) are present together, the *bhāvanā* conveys Devadatta’s status as the agent alone, and not his status as any other factor of action?
Some say it is "by virtue of fitness" (*yogyatāvaśena*).
For Devadatta is fit for being the agent (*kartṛ*) of cooking, but not fit for being the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth;
and it is not possible for that which is not an agent to have a connection with the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

Therefore, [the statement] "it takes up the status of an agent" is not possible in the case of "the pieces of wood cook," for it is well known that those [pieces of wood] are not fit to be agents, but rather instruments (*karaṇa*). Now, if it should be argued: "In this case, there is no agency on the part of the pieces of wood; rather, by the logic already stated, their very status as instruments produces the instrumental case-ending."

Thus, in "the pot cooks," the locative case expresses the state of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*); in "the rice grains cook," the accusative case expresses the state of being an object (*karmatva*); in "he cooks from the granary," the ablative case expresses the state of being a source (*apādānatva*); and in "the Brahmins cook," the dative case expresses the state of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*). This is because, in every instance, fitness (*yogyatva*) is the cause for determining [the specific grammatical relation].
This is untenable, because the cognition of the agent (*kartṛ*) is self-evident to everyone.
He said:

This is not at all a cognition of agency; rather, it is simply the cognition of various factors of action (kārakas). Due to the force of the habitual impression (*vāsanā*) for the well-known status of agency expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), it appears as if it were the agent through a cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). However, for one who observes with precision, there indeed arises for him a discernment of each respective factor of action.
For instance,
even one who at that time determines that a pot or similar object is the agent understands that its activity is nothing other than being a substratum.

In every case where both meanings are possible, it is logical to intend the expression of one or the other form; and it has been established previously that all *kārakas* possess the status of agent (*kartṛtva*) with respect to their own respective operations.
For the diversity of *kārakas* pertaining to the principal action is not precluded by the agency and so forth belonging to the domain of their own operations.
Therefore, it is correct that only that [agency] is intended to be expressed, and not the denotation of the number of another *kāraka*.

This being the case, as for the fact that the number of the object (*karman*) is also sometimes expressed, the reason you have stated applies there, and no other rule exists; thus, the restriction is established. In that case, however, the heading "when not expressed" (*anabhihita*) will be applied as follows: "when the oneness, duality, or plurality of the object has not been expressed," and so forth.
Why?
Because case-endings are prescribed where there is a general term;
non-expression is indeed appropriate there, but not for its qualifier.

Furthermore, there is non-expression (*anabhihitatva*) of both that which has the object (*karman*) and so forth as its expressed meaning, and that which has singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth qualified by those [objects].

This refers to the state where, when the object is unexpressed, the second case (*dvitīyā*) occurs; or, when the object is expressed, the second case occurs for those [numbers] such as singularity that reside therein.
And although the object and so forth are subordinate (*upasarjana*), they nevertheless connect with the qualifier.

For that which is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) in a compound (*samāsa*) cannot be connected with qualifiers; however, in a sentence (*vākya*), such things as "the king of the Kṛṣṇas" or "the man of the king" are seen to be so connected.

In this way, there will be a distinction between the compound and the sentence. Furthermore, since the objects (*karman*) and other factors reside in the sentence, even though they are subordinate members [in a compound], they are capable of attaining the status of being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) under the rule governing unexpressed [factors] (*anabhihitādhikāra*) when they possess the same case-ending. Consequently, in the case of "Devadatta cooks," since the agent is not expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and so forth, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) necessarily applies in order to express its number.
If it is argued that there is no attainment of the meaning already stated, we say no;
for this is not invariably so, as seen in the case of Bhīṣma and others.
For it has been stated that even when an action is performed with a mat as the second participant, the result arises from Bhīṣma and the others.

And if the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) does not arise because its meaning is already expressed, then the number to be expressed by the first case-ending (*prathamā*) is likewise already expressed; thus, it too may well not arise. If you argue that it arises because the use of a bare nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is impossible, we say no; for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the third case-ending arising according to the rule.
Furthermore, this undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) has not been established by logical reasoning (nyāya), but rather by scripture (āgama).
And when there is a contradiction with scripture, logical reasoning is not capable of producing its effect.

Therefore, it is the word itself that is not explicitly stated [in the sūtra] which, through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), is understood as having a specific nature. This concludes the fourth quarter of the third chapter.

In reality, the agent and the object are understood in their specific forms through the connection with number by means of the words *pacati* (he cooks) and *pacyate* (it is cooked); therefore, their respective case-endings (*vibhakti*) are not produced [for them as such]. Other *kārakas* (factors of action), however, are never perceived in such a specific form and thus produce their own case-endings.

And although there is no difference in their status as *kārakas*, it has already been explained how it is that only for the agent and the object does this specific perception and connection with number occur.

As for the objection that there is a deviation [of the rule] under the view that the *lakāra* expresses the *bhāva* (the action/state), because in cases such as "it is not cooked here" (*neha pacyate*) or "it is not eaten here" (*neha bhujyate*), when the intention is to express the mere action (*pacimātra-vivakṣā*), neither the agent nor the object is resorted to, and thus the meaning of the verbal root and the *bhāvanā* are not supported; consequently, [the rule] would lack explanatory power—regarding this it is said:
"That same defect concerning the scope of the word exists equally even under the view that [the *lakāra*] denotes [the agent]."
It is not accepted that the denoter (*vācaka*) is also non-unique (*anekānta*), just like the indicator (*gamaka*);
for if one were to set aside the *lakāra* being uttered and instead grasp its substitutes (*ādeśas*), there would be a contradiction with what is heard (*śrutibādha*).

Even if it were argued that the meanings of the roots, such as "to do" (*karoti*), are expressed by the *lakāra* itself, even so, since they are not directly denoted by it, they could not be determined as such prior to the production of the substitutes.
Furthermore, a contradiction with logic remains as it was before.

Therefore, since some inconsistency must necessarily be postulated, it is better to assume that "denotability" itself is merely conventional (*pāribhāṣika*), because one must rely on a single consistent alternative.
For in no way whatsoever is non-conventional denotability possible in the state of *alā* (the letter *l*).

Therefore, regarding the rule *tena laḥ karmaṇi ca*, since it is an instruction concerning meaning through the medium of substitutes for the sake of both worldly and Vedic usage—as established by the principle of "teaching the meaning"—it must be examined whether, for the purpose of practice within its own grammatical system (*svaśāstra*), the status of being denoted by a *tiṅ* suffix is logically possible in both the world and the Veda. If it can be established through reasoning, then it is proper to assume that purpose; if it cannot be established, then it serves the purpose of the system itself. Since the possibility of its referring to worldly and Vedic usage has already been refuted, it follows by elimination that it refers to the purpose of the system itself. By this, the following is stated:
"In my [grammar], the agent and the object are to be understood as being expressed by the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*).
But what is the purpose of this, since those two are not found to be so expressed in either common usage (*loka*) or the Veda?
Even if there is no purpose there, it does exist within one's own school (*sva-śākhā*).

How indeed could there be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) based on the assumption that those two [the agent and the object] are denoted when the *lakāra* suffixes are employed under the heading of "when not denoted" (*anabhihitādhikāra*)?

Therefore, although they are not denoted in the ultimate sense, nevertheless, because the treatise (*śāstra*) treats them as if they were denoted, the case endings prescribed by the heading "when not denoted" do not appear; thus, the contingency of case endings for the factors of action (*kāraka*) is avoided.
As for the argument that it is due to the denotation of their specific qualities, that is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as seen in the case of words such as *śiṃśapā*.

For the word "śiṃśapā" does not denote tree-ness, earthiness, substantiality, existence, knowability, or cognizability, and yet it denotes the *śiṃśapā* itself, which is a particular instance of those.

Therefore, just as its capacity to denote a particular is not contradicted without first denoting its universal, and just as the capacity of the eye to grasp color is not contradicted even though it does not grasp the universal of impermanence, and just as for you [the Mīmāṃsakas] too, agency—a particular of a substance—is expressed by a verbal suffix (tiṅ) even without denoting the substance itself, so too should the expression of number, which is a particular of that [substance], be understood to occur without the denotation of the [universal] substrate.

Furthermore, as for the claim that because the present process of going (*gamyamāna*) lacks a connection with qualifiers, its expression [as a substance] is due to the observation of such a connection—that too has been refuted by the fact that both possibilities are observed in the *Ākṛti* and *Aruṇā* sections. Moreover, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) in this argument, as seen in the case of "the sweet taste is unctuous, cold, and heavy. For it has been established therein that since the sweet taste is itself a quality (*guṇa*), it cannot logically be connected with other qualities such as coldness and so forth; rather, it is a substance (*dravya*) that is connected. And yet, the word "taste" (*rasa*) does not denote a substance in any way whatsoever.
Similarly, in the case of the statement "the city was plundered by a thousand horsemen," the act of plundering is connected only with those horsemen who are actually being observed;
yet, simply because smoke or the like is not seen in a certain place, or color and so forth are not perceived in a certain object, one cannot thereby postulate its existence everywhere.
Therefore, the agent is not the denotable meaning [of the verbal suffix], according to the Tantravārtika.
And since that [quality] lacks the status of being directly stated by scripture (*śrauta*), the context (*prakaraṇa*) is not set aside.

As for the argument that, under the view that it is a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*), the individual injunction would be purposeless because it is already enjoined by the injunction of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), and therefore it must be for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), we reply:
as long as there is no contact with an injunction, this [quality] has no purpose.

Without that [prohibition], the meaning of the verbal root would not be understood as a subsidiary element (*kratvaṅga*) of the sacrifice; moreover, in the Smṛti, whatever expiation is prescribed for the occasion of speaking untruth must be performed if this is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).

On the other hand, if it is an injunction (*vidhi*), then because it belongs to the Yajurveda, when the sacrifice is ruined due to an error in the Yajurveda, one should offer oblations into the *Anvāhāryapacana* fire with the mantra: "Bhuvaḥ svāhā."
However, because it cannot be determined that the Smṛti has any one specific source [other than the Veda], there would be no determination of the expiation for an error in the Veda.

Even if one accepts the relationship of root and derivative between them, since the meaning of the Veda and its transgression are followed by the Smṛti itself, the expiation must belong to that [Smṛti] alone.
But surely, according to your view as well, since it belongs to the Yajurveda, the expiation for that Veda should apply when it is known to be such?
This is not so;

for since this [prohibition] pertains to the *āhavanīya* fire and other such ritual fires, it depends upon the qualification of one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), whereas the prohibition of untruth, being a duty pertaining to the person alone, remains applicable even to one who has not established the fires.
Therefore, in his case, a Smṛti-based expiation must necessarily be sought.

If that [penance] is required because of the specific occasion, then it is likewise appropriate even for one who has not maintained the sacred fires; thus, there is an absence of Vedic expiatory rites [for such a person].
Furthermore, when any one of the auxiliary sciences (vedāṅga) of the sacrifice is neglected, an occasional rite is prescribed by scripture.

However, in the case of the destruction of that which is not an auxiliary of the sacrifice (*ayajñāṅga*), there would be no occasion for that [penance]. For all the *samidh* offerings and so forth belong to other sacrifices; and the *svobha*, *śakha*, *japa*, and so forth, according to the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*), are purificatory rites for the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*). And since they are performed by the sacrificer (*yājamāna*)—because, like the primary action, they have him as their principal agent—they must be considered the sacrificer's acts by virtue of this section. In that regard, because the *samidh* offerings and so forth consist of the nature of sacrifice, they involve the act of relinquishing the substance (*dravyatyāga-vyāpāra*); thus, like the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other such rites, they are the sacrificer's acts in both ways. And just as before, even when the number of sacrificers increases, the performance is done collectively (*tantra*), so no distinction whatsoever is observed.

However, those [acts] such as the chanting of hymns (*stotra*), the recitation of the *śastra*, and the muttering of prayers (*japa*)—which involve a restriction of the agent and the object as subordinate elements (*guṇabhūta*) and do not pertain to the primary restrictions—would, by overriding the primary designations (*saṃjñā*) such as "Udgātṛ" and so forth, come to have the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) as their performer, just like the cleaning of the teeth and other such acts.

Furthermore, since a commonality of performance (*tantratva*) is impossible when there is an increase in the number of sacrificers due to the principle of the renunciation of common property, these acts would have to be repeated for each individual sacrificer.

Furthermore, even in prohibitions, when the injunctive element is thus determined—namely, that "speaking untruth is something that assists the person engaged in the sacrifice"—then, from this very prohibition qualified by untruth, the following meaning results: "In whatever is spoken by the sacrificer for the sake of self-purification during the recitation of blessings and so forth, one must not practice falsehood either in making an optional determination or in the utterance of the actual words; however, in other cases, as well as for others, there is freedom to speak as one pleases."

However, regarding the prohibition of false speech concerning the ritual (*kratu*) and its constituent elements (*dharma*), whatever falsehood might occur on the part of the sacrificer or the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) during the performance of the rite must not be committed at all, because there is no distinction in their connection to the sacrifice. Therefore, just as the sacrificer, having resolved upon an offering of rice (*vrīhimaya*), must not give an offering of barley (*yavamaya*), so too the Adhvaryu and other priests, having stated "we shall perform the subsequent part," must not subsequently contradict themselves out of a desire for convenience or the like. Furthermore, even if something is said for the sake of a subsequent refinement (*saṃskāra*), that too must be avoided by virtue of its being connected to the purpose of the sacrifice.

But surely, since the person is subordinate to the purpose of the prohibition, the designation "Adhvaryava" would be restrictive; thus, like the carrying of the *praṇītā* waters and so forth, the Adhvaryu alone would undertake the prohibition of falsehood.
True, he would undertake it if the purpose of the prohibition were something to be performed.
However, because this [prohibition] consists in the absence of performance, it does not require a specific agent.

Furthermore, the prohibition is connected with the attainment [of the action] by the Vedic text itself; where that attainment occurs through its own inherent capacity (*svasāmarthya*), it cannot be prevented by a name (*samākhyā*).

Now, one might argue: "If only the injunctive portion, namely 'one should recite' (*vaded*)," is considered, the name will restrict it, and consequently, the prohibition, following that [restriction], will also be restricted.
This is not so.
For it is only when the meaning of the treatise has been fully established and there arises a need for its author that a traditional designation (samākhyā) comes into play.
Moreover, the mere statement "one should speak" is not understood as the full meaning of the treatise;
rather, because of its connection with a prohibition, it stands as a restatement (anuvāda).
Furthermore, it was established in the *Grahādhikaraṇa* that even a qualifier is not applicable to that which is being referred to by way of restatement (*anuvāda*).
How much less so in this case, where the name functions solely to establish a relationship with a specific agent of the ritual act being enjoined?
Therefore, because it is being restated, the oblation is not qualified.

Even the prohibition cannot serve to qualify that [bathing], for bathing is understood to be for the sake of the person by its very nature, since it serves to remove impurity; furthermore, the qualification regarding the sacred site (*tīrtha*) benefits the person—not the sacrifice—by excluding difficult descents and the like through the ease of descent. Moreover, even that traditional injunction (*smaraṇa*) which takes the form of a rule governing the sequence prior to eating and so forth, produces a transcendental result (*adṛṣṭa*) from the restriction of that very purpose, which accrues only to the person. Therefore, being connected with that [result] whose purpose has already been determined, the restriction regarding the sacred site is also understood to be for the sake of the person.
In this regard, first of all, the visible purpose for entering [the water] is indeed evident—namely, the ease of immersion.

Furthermore, even if an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) is postulated because the restriction (*niyama*) consisting in the avoidance of drawing water from other sources and so forth does not accomplish a visible end, there is nevertheless a fruit: for it is said that "one becomes a holy place (*tīrtha*) for one's kinsmen.

Moreover, it is established that when a rite connected to a human goal is derived from a direct statement (*vākya*), the context (*prakaraṇa*) does not prevail over it, as the context is not connected to the person.

Thus, although the agent is not explicitly mentioned by the phrase "if one should say," nevertheless, because the word *jañjabhyamāna* is a *kṛdanta* (a form ending in a *kṛt* suffix), it denotes the agent according to the rule "a *kṛt* suffix [denotes] the agent. Furthermore, because of the principle that "that which is connected with a person [is for his benefit]," it takes up the person as a qualifier of the agent. Consequently, the recitation of the mantra, being connected with that person mentioned within its own sentence, does not attain the status of being grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*); and when there is a connection with a person, that very result [of the mantra's application] indeed exists.
The retention of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths within oneself results in longevity;
therefore, such qualities belong exclusively to the person (*puruṣa*).
Due to the specific context, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) associated with that [person] is like a substance.

The claim that this is merely a quality of the person (*puruṣadharma*) is weak; however, the assertion that because it is a quality of the person alone there is therefore an exaltation (*utkarṣa*) is unacceptable.
Why?
When the non-contradictory nature of the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is being established,
it is not logical to effect a sublation (*bādha*), nor is there a distant scriptural promise of reward (*phalaśruti*).
For just as rice and other grains, when connected with acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), are not yet specified by the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Furthermore, because there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for postulating results such as the absence of fear that are superior to [the primary result], and because [the mantra] possesses purpose by being a means to the sacrifice (*kratu*), the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) is accepted.

Likewise, since there is no postulation of a separate result here, the reciter (*abhyasyamāna*) belonging to the context (*prākaraṇika*) is understood in accordance with proximity (*pratyāsatti*). For when that is possible, no authority is found for postulating another result.

"But has it not been stated that the fruit for these two is already established? True, it has been stated; however, such a fruit is not expressed by the word [in question], because there is an absence of connection with the word *kāma* (desire).
And for this very reason, he says that we do not perceive any injunctive word here.

We shall explain that the prescription of the result is not effected by such a word [as "dadāti"]. Otherwise, however, since the injunctive suffix is indeed present even here in the word "brūyāt," the statement that there is an absence of an injunction would be entirely improper;
for the word "dhatte" cannot be subject to censure simply because it is not injunctive.
Because the portion of the fruit [of the action] is in no way subject to being enjoined.
Therefore, it should be construed exactly as stated.
And by the phrase "in the case of substances, preparatory acts, and rituals," its status as an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) will be declared.
"But the fruit [accrues] when that [action] is primary," and thus, in the case of that which is accompanied by the word "desire" (*kāma*), its purposefulness is directed toward that [fruit].
He says:

"We accept that it is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person. By the utterance of the word "refinement," he accepts that it is a duty (*dharma*) of the person associated with the sacrifice; for an independent [action] is not called a "refinement" because it possesses its own fruit.
Regarding the statement "only those performing the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices [are entitled]," what is the intended meaning?

In any case, since this is understood as a property belonging to one who is being produced, it would exclude worldly persons due to its lack of purpose. This is the fourth quarter of the third chapter.

However, that which is enjoined in connection with the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such sacrifices—being purposeful just like [the observances] belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa—is impossible to exclude; therefore, it becomes a duty for the person connected to every sacrifice (*kratumātra*).
The answer to this contains a hidden intention:
"But there is no purpose served by that [duty] once it has been performed [in one context]."
Why?

Because it has no connection with the *nivīta* just as it has none with the act of hospitality, due to its lack of association with [the injunction] through direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth; likewise, it has no connection with other ritual acts.

Regarding the statement "because the injunction is heard as one" (*vidhestvekaśrutitvāt*) and "because there is no injunction by way of alternation" (*aparyāyavidhānāt*), [the author] will state that there is a single injunction for all the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) by postulating a single purpose for them.

And that [single injunction] will belong to those [auxiliaries] being enjoined by the performance-injunction (*prayogavacana*), since the individual injunctions (*prātyātmikavidhi*) function in alternation. Furthermore, that by which a person is impelled is an injunction (*vidhi*).
Furthermore, since the cultivation (bhāvanā) possesses both auxiliary and primary elements, the person's connection [to them] occurs simultaneously;
therefore, the individual [injunctions] are merely restatements (anuvāda).
To this, it is replied:
These two passages are indeed correct.
How so?
First, the former is not contradicted by the reasoning that "that which is not prescribed [as a primary act] does not become an auxiliary."

For it has been stated that if this [injunction] were not resorted to, then because the mere meaning of the verbal root would be the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it would be purposeless; and being thus purposeless, it would be impossible to conceive of its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*). Therefore, there must first be an injunction (*vidhi*). Now, as for the restatement (*anuvāda*): how is its status as an auxiliary established by the preceding injunction? As long as the application-injunction (*prayoga-vacana*) has not yet brought it [the restatement] into operation, so long does that injunction remain operative. However, once the application-injunction has taken hold, since the person's engagement is accomplished simply through contact with its status as an auxiliary, it becomes a restatement.
Therefore, prior to the assignment of the injunction by the statement of the application, no practical usage is established without the status of an injunction; thus, it is an injunction.

At a later stage, however, since the engagement [of the agent] is already established from that very source, it is a restatement (anuvāda). Thus, both [characterizations] are rightly stated. It would be set aside because of its designation.

Because the context (*prakaraṇa*) is absolutely non-existent, [the number ten] is connected to the sentence; thus, due to contact with the injunction belonging to that [sentence], it is displaced—this is the reading in some manuscripts. In the fourth quarter of the third chapter, the state of having ten attendants (*daśopasattva*), not being grasped by the context, is displaced; therefore, this is not a valid example.

Regarding the *śaṃyu* [formula] as well, because of the "giving over of all" (*sarvaparidāna*), the term "śaṃthau" is an indicator for the Brāhmaṇa passage prohibiting the threatening of Brāhmaṇas and so forth.

In that case, just as before, there are several positions; however, even among those, if one unifies the two types of connection pertaining to the context, only two positions remain: that it is a property of the sacrifice (*kratudharma*) or a pure property of the person (*śuddhapuruṣadharma*).
And by the general principle of the prohibition against speaking untruth, there is a prohibition of threatening (*avagoraṇa*) when it occurs as a means to serve the purpose of the sacrifice.
What is the occasion for its occurrence?

Since the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are to be accomplished by four Brāhmaṇas, when the methods of conciliation, bribery, dissension, and force (*sāma-dāna-bheda-daṇḍa*) might occur for that purpose, it is understood from the text "one should win them over by giving the *anvāhārya* rice" that [threatening] is prohibited.

When they do not desist by that much alone, and when an effort is made such that there occurs the taking or giving [of what was prohibited], and worldly means have become applicable, then this form of punishment—threatening with a staff and so forth—would otherwise result; it is therefore prohibited.

What is stated is that one must not act [in that way], but rather resort to other alternative means distinct from that. When such a situation has arisen, it is declared: "Because of the connection with all [the gods] through the sentence, and because of the granting of boons to all..."
Furthermore, because the fruit is merely conceptualized, this [prohibition] is not governed by the context of the ritual.

For the injunction "one should sacrifice, setting her aside" applies generally to all performance of sacrifices; how then could it be restricted to the specific occasion of conversation? However, since a person possesses independence, the prohibition is meaningful insofar as it precludes conversation at all times.
And if the Smṛti has such a meaning, then the relationship of root and derivative must necessarily be accepted; for no one has stated that it is a mere repetitive restatement (nityānuvāda).
Furthermore, because of the prohibition regarding food, this [Smṛti] is a dharma pertaining to human beings.
Why?
Because a doubtful matter is described by a statement that must be determined through probability;
however, the duty of a man is not doubtful, according to the Smṛti: "She has no food [other than his]."

The purpose of the recitation within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*) is precisely this: namely, that its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that rite might be understood. If even that which is not recited within a context were to be an auxiliary to the ritual act, then the recitation within a context would be rendered meaningless.

Since the Veda itself has made this distinction between what is recited within a context and what is not, it is therefore understood that those recited within a context must certainly be duties pertaining to the person (*puruṣadharma*).
However, because [the former] lacks a material substance (*adravyatva*), it would be a subordinate element (*śeṣa*).
Even if it were indeed a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*), it would still be merely a supplement to the ritual action (*karmaśeṣa*); otherwise, a separate fruit would have to be postulated.
[Objection: But surely the connection with the sacrifice (*kratusambandha*) must also be postulated. [Reply: True, but that postulation is based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇavat*).

Furthermore, when there is a general expectancy for a purpose regarding an action (*karman*), it is the action itself that presents itself; therefore, its connection [to the result] is supported by valid evidence, whereas its connection to heaven is not. This is what is intended:

just as no other thing, apart from sacrifice (*yāga*) or gift (*dāna*), attains the status of a primary action (*pradhānakarman*), and since the nature of a sacrifice and so forth does not exist here due to the absence of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) and the like, it follows that it is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the action by virtue of its inherent nature.

Alternatively, this is heard as an injunction for "retaining" (dhāraṇa), and that [retention] must be performed precisely at the time of its production, as it constitutes a subordinate element of that act.
Furthermore, because a worldly object serves no purpose [in itself], it is not fit for ritual consecration (saṃskāra).
Therefore, this is an injunction regarding the wearing of the garment and the holding of gold, both of which serve as constituent parts of the ritual action.

Alternatively, precisely because of the fault of enjoining multiple meanings, and because it is possible [to avoid this], the injunction of the quality (*guṇa*)—by virtue of the transfer of the injunctive power (*vidhi-śakti*) from the primary act—is established as follows: "Gold is held in the hand" (*hiraṇyaṃ hastena bhavati*), "then he takes it" (*atha gṛhṇāti*), and "having handed over the gold in the hand, they chant with the *ṣoḍaśin*"; thus, the excellence (*suvargatā*) enjoined by such sentences is prescribed. Likewise, in the case of the injunction "he puts on a garment" (*vāsaḥ paridhatte*), the quality of being beautiful (*śobhanatvam*) is prescribed for the garment already enjoined. And this is precisely the basis for the technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) of the authors of the Sūtras, such as "one should understand *hiranya* as that which is born" (*hiranyam iti jātarūpaṃ pratīyāt*).

Otherwise, since the word *hiraṇya* would apply commonly to both silver (*rajata*) and gold (*jātarūpa*), one would have to postulate some other basis for restricting it to one or the other. Furthermore, by the phrase "because it is not a substance" (*adravyatvāt*), no substance is being enjoined here; rather, this is merely an injunction regarding a specific quality of it. Therefore, the meaning is that wherever there is a substance, one must proceed with it according to this [rule]. As for the mention of the deity (*devatā*) made here by the author of the Bhāṣya:

Therefore, that [view] is contrary to the sūtra and improper; for even though recitation (*japa*) and the like belong to the *pradhāna* (the primary rite), the *homās* (oblations) would be restricted by their connection with the *āhavanīya* fire.
And if these *homās* were so restricted, they would occur only among the Vaidikas and not everywhere. Why?

It is always maintained that the subsidiary (aṅga) and the principal (pradhāna) must occupy the same location. However, this commonality of location could not exist for these [subsidiaries] in relation to agriculture and the like. Furthermore, [the text] states:

"Varuṇa indeed seizes him who accepts a horse"; thus, the acceptance of the horse is understood as the occasion (nimitta) for the seizing by sin. Moreover, that seizing by sin is restated here as something already established.
For if it were indeed enjoined, then by the force of this very statement, it might occasionally apply even to Vedic acts;
however, it is not enjoined, because all fruits [of action] are not objects of injunction.
Nor is there an injunction regarding the ritual act itself in that context, because it is impossible for an enjoined ritual act to have sin as its fruit.
And here, the acceptance of a horse is not prohibited, because that is not heard [in the text],
and because it serves merely to establish a connection with the cause.
Therefore, where there is a prohibition due to an absolute connection, there is a fault.
And that prohibition regarding worldly matters is: "He does not give a maned beast, nor does he accept what has two rows of teeth.
Now, is this prohibition also heard as being general?
True; however, we say that it refers specifically to the worldly.
Because it is impossible for the other [type of sacrifice], which is connected with a specific injunction, to be the object of a prohibition;
and therefore, even the iṣṭi mentioned in conjunction with a fault would have to pertain to the worldly domain.

But surely, since the unobserved eclipse being intended as the occasion cannot be qualified by a fault, the mention of the fault—being intended merely as praise for the enjoined iṣṭi—would mean that even a Vedic eclipse could be the occasion.
It is stated: "I do not conceive this as a fault by way of being a qualifier;
rather, its status as a worldly subsidiary is established through its capacity to effect the desired removal of faults."

If, on the grounds that in the Vedic case the sacrifice belongs to the giver, it is stated that even when there is a fault in the recipients—such as being unworthy of receiving gifts—the occasion [for the rite] remains free from defect because the act of officiating at the sacrifice (*yājana*) is itself faultless;

then, in the worldly case as well, when one accepts from Śūdras and others, even if the recipient is faulty, the occasion remains indeed free from defect because the giver is not rendered defective through that [recipient]. Alternatively, if it is held here that the operation of the recipient (*pratigrahītṛ-vyāpāra*) is the occasion and that this is considered to be faulty, then that is equally true in the Vedic case as well.
Now, if it is postulated that in the Vedic case the sacrifice belongs to the giver and in the worldly case to the receiver, then a specific justification for that must also be stated.
Furthermore,
the very same defect that arises from the acceptance of a horse is understood here as well.
The defect of the gift, however, is equal everywhere and is not distinguished by horses;
if the acceptance were not prescribed, how could its procedure be prescribed? Or why would there be a deficiency in the ritual action if that [acceptance] were not performed?
To this we reply:
by the injunction "one who has been chosen as a priest shall give a sacrificial fee" (*dakṣiṇā*), giving is prescribed;
however, their acceptance [of that fee] is established as a necessary concomitant of acquisition, arising simply from greed.
Whatever fault is heard of in the scriptural injunction regarding the ritual act is determined as being something to be expelled.

Furthermore, the fault mentioned here is not known from any source of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to belong to the worldly [act], even though it may be prohibited; for here, "dropsy" (jalodara) is mentioned specifically in the form of receiving a gift from a Varuṇa.
Nor is the worldly acceptance of a gift from Śiva heard of as a cause in any medical compendium (vaidyakasaṃhitā), nor is it established through perception, inference, or other means.
Furthermore, it is not heard in scripture that a lion gives [anything] in a sentence, nor that one accepts [anything] from a lion.

Nor does this sentence have any function toward the cognition of that [prohibition], because it is solely intent upon enjoining a purificatory act (*nirghāta*) by way of restating what already exists.
As for the fault consisting of falling into hell which was postulated based on the prohibitive sentence, that is not relevant here in the *Tantravārtika*.

It is impossible to designate [the victim] by saying, "Varuṇa seizes him"; rather, he is so designated because he seizes (√vṛ) mere evil, and thus Varuṇa seizes him. Consequently, the conventional usage of the term *varuṇagṛhīta* as referring to dropsy (*jalodara*) is abandoned;
however, its etymological derivation remains applicable even to the Vedic sense of sacrifice, since suffering is observed even in that context.

Furthermore, since it is possible that in the act of receiving [a gift], there exists some degree of sinfulness (*ādhamarṇya*) due to the hardship involved in protecting, nourishing, and so forth [the recipient], it is not possible to determine through that [receiving] that the desired [result] has a worldly object.
He speaks thus because the hardship of protecting, nourishing, and so forth is not excluded as being the cause for the activity of the receiver.
Alternatively, it should be understood that this hardship exists even for the giver prior to the transfer of ownership to another.
Furthermore, Dharma itself indeed hears the man dwelling in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
For a man is not concealed by a body consisting of mere sin.
Where the injunction (*vidhi-uddeśa*) is ambiguous, a determination based on the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) is not contradictory.
Since that which is beyond doubt is stronger for you, it must necessarily override the remainder of the sentence.

Therefore, in this case, although Prajāpati is mentioned as the giver in the phrase "Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa," and Varuṇa as the recipient, yet in the subsequent phrase "the deity who is yourself," Prajāpati alone is taken with the same case-ending through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, Varuṇa is his deity because he was previously mentioned as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).

It cannot be the self [of Prajāpati], because it is impossible to conceive both agency and the state of being a recipient—which are contradictory—in a single entity, as it would result in one of the two being figurative.
Nor is Varuṇa the giver to Prajāpati, because that would entail a violation of the grammatical case;
therefore, the meaning is that Prajāpati, having offered the *apūrva*, attained Varuṇa— thus it is stated in the *Tantravārtika*.
Being thus afflicted, his belly became swollen with dropsy.
He perceived this *catuṣkapāla* offering to Varuṇa and offered it; for the reference by the word "he" (*saḥ*) points back to Prajāpati.
Furthermore, the designation of him as the agent in the phrase "he offered it" (*tanniravapat*) is appropriate only for Prajāpati, since Varuṇa stands in the position of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
A sacrifice cannot take place with Varuṇa as the object for one’s own self;
for that which is intended for oneself cannot be considered relinquished.
Therefore, having given the horse to Varuṇa, Prajāpati—being seized by Varuṇa—performed that sacrifice to Varuṇa for his own liberation from Varuṇa’s grasp.
Therefore, it is understood that "the giver" should act in this manner after having given [the gift] even if he is someone other [than the sacrificer]. Furthermore,
because they are constituent parts of the sacrifice, those subsidiary acts share the same agent as the principal rite.

Furthermore, he who is the agent of the primary sacrifice is its master and giver of the horses; this has already been established for the most part by the preceding section—that the sacrifice belongs to the giver. For when it is determined that [the rite] is indeed a subsidiary part of the ritual act of one who accepts the horse, then, according to the principle that the primary acts share the same place, time, and agent, this [subsidiary] must also be performed by whoever is the agent of the main sacrifice. And since the agent of the sacrifice is the giver of the horse—according to the rule that "he who is the agent of the sacrifice is the master in the matter of hiring labor"—therefore, without any doubt, the sacrifice must belong to the giver.
In this regard, its purpose is stated in the Tantravārtika:

since it is capable of providing assistance only when sharing the same agent as the primary rite, and not when having a different agent, the other priests must perform that [subsidiary] for him just as they do for the primary rite; it is not to be performed by the sacrificer himself.

Even though this is established, the subsequent section must be commenced for the purpose of removing the delusion and doubt caused by the contradiction between the opening and the conclusion of the passage.

Furthermore, the power of such an opening and conclusion within the context of that sentence is precisely this: it does not merely enjoin that "one should offer four-pot-sherd cakes to Varuṇa for as many horses as one might receive," but rather, it possesses another opening as well, namely, "Prajāpati led a horse to Varuṇa," and so forth.
And it has been stated that this [merit] brings about the desired result for the donor.
Now, it might be argued: "But was it not also stated that this [merit] is sublated because of the superior force of the scope of the injunction?
This is not so.
Why?
Because it is sublated by the injunction that has already acquired its own nature;
however, in the case of the recipient, the application of the injunction is not yet established.

Even though there exists a relationship of primary and subordinate between injunctions and explanatory passages (arthavādas), there is another distinction between them produced by their respective order of utterance—whether preceding or following.

In all cases, first of all, the primary [cognition]—whether it be "because of an original injunction" (*apūrvacodanā*) or "as in the world"—obtains its status directly through the principle of the section on *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth, because it is a prior cognition that has not yet encountered a counter-agent and remains in a state where no subsequent second cognition arises. However, a subsequent [cognition], arising with respect to an object already occupied by the cognition of the prior [cognition], being in a state of contradiction, is unable to arise in any form other than one that conforms to that [prior cognition]; thus, it undergoes a change [of its own nature].

Therefore, in this case, one cannot disregard the distinction established by the nature of injunction (*vidhi*) and explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) based on their sequential order; for, since the opening and concluding passages would have contradictory meanings if they referred to different recipients [of the gift], there would be no possibility of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) between them.

Furthermore, since both [injunctions] are separate, yet possess the capacity for further injunctions and further inducements (prarocanā) by virtue of their mutual proximity, they are incomplete in meaning due to their mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*). Consequently, because there is the risk of futility (*ānarthakya*), one must necessarily assume a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*). When a common subject matter is thus postulated, it is impossible to abandon the state of being understood as referring to the giver—which was previously determined at a stage where no contradiction had arisen. Therefore, the subsequent cognition of "receiving" (*pratigṛhīta*), which has not yet attained its final status, is determined to refer to the giver through the figurative assumption (*gauṇa*) that it means "accepting" (*gṛhāti*). Moreover:
Furthermore, in this view, there will be consistency with the majority;
otherwise, everything previously stated would become entirely inconsistent.
Thus, by the Taittirīya branch passage cited above, the sacrifice for the giver is established, and that cannot be set aside by another logical argument nor by another scriptural statement.

Even if there were a prohibitive statement, nevertheless, since it would involve a prohibition of what has been enjoined, there would be an option (*vikalpa*), and not the exclusion of the accepted principle. As for that which is an injunction for the recipient: if, by virtue of being a subsidiary part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*), it follows the meaning of the preceding sentence even without a specific introductory context, then by that [injunction] as well, [the act belongs] to the giver alone.

But if, on the other hand, it is independent and depends on the act of receiving, then—since the previous sentence [applies] to the giver—it would apply to both; and because that [act] residing in the recipient lacks the status of being a subsidiary part of the ritual, it would be for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) and would therefore apply even in worldly transactions.

As for the statement "he who would be the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*)," since this refers to the preceding sūtra, it speaks of the recipient alone even in the prior sentence; therefore, because there is no status as a constituent part of the ritual (*karmāṅgatva*) for that [act] performed by him, and because the assumption of results for the person’s benefit is equal for both the other priests and others, since [the act] would thus apply even to worldly [transactions], it must be stated: "By what means of knowledge is it established that it should be understood as occurring in the sacrifice?
Therefore, it is first established by this [sūtra] that it belongs to the recipient.
And this [topic of] "intoxication from drinking" is also an independent injunction (*anāramyavāda*):
"One who vomits *soma* should offer a pap (*caru*) dedicated to Soma-Indra."
In this regard as well, two points of discussion are investigated just as before:

whether the Soma-Indra sacrifice is to be performed when the drinking of worldly *soma*—done for the sake of elixirs (*rasāyana*) and so forth—is impaired by vomiting; or whether it applies to Vedic [drinking], or to both cases.
By the phrase "as in that case" (*tadvat*), the general position is extended here, as is the rule: "But because of the fault, there shall be an *iṣṭi* in the worldly case."

Alternatively, even this pair of topical sections (adhikaraṇa) is extended by way of analogy to the two [previous] topical sections as established conclusions; yet, due to a certain distinction, there is a formulation of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa). In that regard, first of all here, since the presentation of the substance has already been accomplished by means of vomiting, there is never again a need for a counter-argument; thus, the injunction of the sacrifice would be purposeless.

However, in the case of a worldly [remedy], if [the substance] is expelled through vomiting, the absence of the qualities of an elixir (rasāyana) makes an increase in the senses and virility possible.
There is no absolute impossibility, as in the case of *jalodara* (dropsy).
Furthermore, when the *iṣṭi* sacrifice is heard in connection with that [condition], it is understood to be for the purpose of its remediation.
Therefore, it should apply in that case.

If it is argued that there would be a fault in the case of the Vedic, whereas there would be no fault in the case of the worldly because of the purpose, then why is it not said that [the result] occurs in the Vedic precisely through those same factors such as the commonality of being Vedic?

For "vomiting" cannot possibly possess the quality of being Vedic, since it is not enjoined by scripture; therefore, that very same fault which is the reason for its application to the worldly would likewise apply here to the Vedic subject matter.
For instance, the performance ending with the form of complete digestion is prescribed; otherwise, in the event of immediate vomiting, the primary result would not occur as it did before.

In the injunction "He who vomits Soma should offer [this oblation]," because of the connection between the relative pronoun *yaḥ* and the correlative pronoun *saḥ*, a single agent for both the sacrifice and the vomiting is understood.
In that regard, first, the indicative factor (*naimittika*) is beyond doubt because it is performed by the owner; by means of that which is certain, the doubtful act of vomiting is determined.
That [vomiting] also has the owner as its agent, for it is the cause (*nimitta*).
Nor is the cause independent, because the cognition of a cause does not arise from a pure verbal root alone.
That which is connected with the word "yat" (which) indicates its cause;
if it is connected with that [word], then the commonality of the agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) occurring earlier leads to the subsequent cognition of causality.

Now, if they abandon the substance for the sake of the deity and for the sake of hiring the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), then, because of the contradiction of hiring oneself, they must necessarily choose other priests such as the *adhvaryu* and others.

However, because the middle-voice (ātmanepada) ending used in the context of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) indicates that the fires have no connection with any person other than the consecrator himself, one must sacrifice in those fires for one's own sake. Consequently, if they perform [the rites] merely with the intention of assisting the *soma* sacrifice, then—due to the difference in place and time—the act becomes deficient; it is not accepted by that primary rite.
Furthermore, no specific difference of place and so forth is expressly enjoined [in this context], such that one could maintain the absence of deficiency even when such differences exist.
Since the purpose is already accomplished by the vomiting [of the Soma] itself, this very text does not authorize [the act of vomiting] in other locations and so forth.

Or rather, how could a single scripture rely on identity of location and so forth in the case of the sacrificer's vomiting, yet maintain a difference in that regard in the case of the officiating priests' vomiting? Alternatively, they might be employed for their own sake;

even so, since that which is determined to be for the sake of the sacrifice cannot again be for the sake of the person, what is performed for that [personal] purpose would result in nothingness (futility).

If, however, for the sake of establishing this [prohibition], human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) alone were accepted by the scripture, then there would be a remoteness [of the rule] due to the abandonment of the present sacrifice and the postulation of heaven and so forth, which are not immediately present.
This same [objection] applies to ordinary worldly vomiting; thus, it would not apply to the sacrificial context, and that has already been refuted previously.
Therefore, it should apply to vomiting after having eaten at a *Śrāddha*.

Now, even if the vomiting occurs on the part of the Adhvaryu and others, the owner alone would have to relinquish the substance; if that were the case, it would result in that very same [act] having a different agent.

Or, if one attempts to justify that, there would be the assumption of an unmentioned genitive sense and a contradiction of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, if such an assumption were made, it would follow that the vomiting of the owner is not the cause [of the rite].
Alternatively, there would either be a distinction in the purchase (*kraya*) based on both [the owner and the priest] being the substratum, or a distinction based on their heterogeneity (*vairūpya*).

Regarding the rule "he who vomits the Soma" and "the officiant who vomits the Soma," if one accepts either [alternative] as the basis for the *āśrayaṇa* (preparation), it is more appropriate to take the vomiting by the master (*svāmin*), because that accords better with the literal sense of the words.
This is so as long as the rite functions as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*).

However, when it is postulated that the unfitness for obtaining the fruit—produced by a failure in the restrictive disposal (*pratipatti*) of the sacrificial remnant material as introduced by the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*)—is not remedied, then, since the arising of the fruit for the sacrificer is entirely imperceptible (*atyantādṛṣṭa*), one suspects its loss; therefore, it is beyond doubt that the expiatory sacrifice (*pratisamādhāneṣṭi*) must be performed by him alone.

As for the fruit consisting of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) which belongs to the officiating priests, since that is observed to be realized whether vomiting occurs or not, it does not necessitate the performance of the iṣṭi sacrifice, because there is no apprehension [of a failure] requiring a remedial measure.

Even if it is assumed that, by virtue of the restriction regarding the agent of the action under discussion, the act of eating is for the purpose of purifying the eater—and that consequently, when there is an aversion to it, a deficiency arises in the agent because the purification of the substance, which consists in its being consumed, has ceased—nevertheless, since that would lead to the obstacle of a fruitless result for the sacrificer caused by such aversion, and because [the text] is intended to prevent that and employs the demonstrative pronouns "yat" and "tat," the vomiting must pertain specifically to the sacrificer.
By this, the view that [the vomiting] is for the purpose of purifying the *apūrva* (transcendental merit) is also explained away.

For even when one considers that the vomiting of Soma does not constitute either the non-performance of a prescribed act or the performance of a prohibited act—and thus, without relying on the view that the sacrifice serves the purpose of expiating a fault, the rite is regarded as a subsidiary element (aṅga) contingent upon that occasion—nevertheless, since the person is denoted by the word *yat* ("when"), it is determined, according to the principle of the *janman* [birth] passage, that it is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person brought into the context; and even then, its being performed by the sacrificer is established by the very statement "they belong to the sacrificer" (*yājamānās tu*).
Furthermore, because they share the same subject matter, the vomiting of the sacrificer alone is the occasion.

As for the claim that even in the case of the vomiting of the Adhvaryu and others, there is a failure in the disposal of the substance or its destruction due to a defect in the performer's refinement (*saṃskāra*), which thus requires a remedial rite (*samādhi*):
even if such a rite were required, it would not be adopted here because it has not been prescribed.

Furthermore, it has already been stated that regarding all cases—whether they fall under the category of acts for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) or acts for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)—there is no prescription for a rite when the officiating priest vomits.
Therefore, if that pacification is indeed faultless, one should remain silent.
But if it is faulty, then something else prescribed by the authorities must be performed.
Since there is no purpose here in determining any one of the alternative positions such as "kutūhala" and so forth, one need not strive for excessive certainty in this matter.
Furthermore, if the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is the purpose, then the position of one who is undergoing the *jañjabhyamāna* rite must be accepted;
and thus the author of the Sūtras says, "Because it is not for that purpose [of the master]," and because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
He for whom prosperity through the drinking of Soma is desired,
and for whom misfortune is feared due to its deficiency— and since both of these concern the master— it is his sacrifice alone.
There is an offering of the entire oblation, because it is intended for that purpose.

By words such as "on eight potsherds" (*aṣṭākapāla*), the entire substance is understood to be for the sake of the deity; and the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) becomes for the sake of the deity through its casting into the *āhavanīya* fire, according to the injunction "they offer in the *āhavanīya*" and the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "the gods indeed have Agni as their mouth. This being the case, if even a small portion were removed from it, then something else would be done that was not prescribed by the scripture (*śruta*); therefore, there must be the consumption of the whole.

But does this proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) not see the injunction for the remaining rites—the *sviṣṭakṛt*, the *iḍā*, the *prāśitra*, the *śaṃyuvāka*, and the fourfold distribution of portions at the time of consumption? Some say that he indeed does not see it; however, that is hardly plausible, for if it were so, there would never be a prima facie view anywhere.
Therefore, it must be stated that one speaks with this intention while still perceiving [the remainder]:
"While there are remaining substances, [these] would be non-impellers;
for they are sharers of the remainder, whereas in the case of no remainder, they are impellers."

Just as in the case of the statement "he completes the remainder with clarified butter (*ājya*)," the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is employed for what is either additional to or similar to the preceding rite because the previous action has reached its conclusion; and just as in the passage "from that remainder they obtain births distinguished by specific place, caste, and so forth," since the karma whose fruit is heaven is used up without remainder and it is impossible for that which lacks a fruit to have another operation, Gautama Ācārya said "from that remainder" (*tataḥ śeṣeṇa*) when he ought to have said "by something other than that" (*tato 'nyena*). Likewise here too, there will be something other than the principal oblation, whether by way of being distinct from it or by way of being additional to it.

Alternatively, it will be stated under the rule "śeṣāt" [Jaiminisūtra 6.4.1] that this is by virtue of being a subordinate element (*guṇa*). The word *śeṣa* (remainder) denotes that which exists as something more closely associated with the context. Now, nothing of this kind exists for the principal offerings (*pradhānahavis*), whereas all these characteristics are present in other substances; therefore, other materials should be taken.
As he will state:

If it is argued that "because of the specific instruction, there is something else for the purpose," or if, by strictly following the word *śeṣa* (remainder), some part of those very [offerings] is set aside as a remainder—even so, there is indeed another purpose for the investigation; it need not necessarily have the purpose stated for the [first] position (*pakṣa*), as another possibility also exists.

When, because of the contingency of offering the entirety from what is designated as the primary [portion], the remainders are established by virtue of the requirements for the rites pertaining to the remainder, then just as the primary [offering] is the motivator (*prayojaka*) of that oblation, so too are the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other such rites.
Even in the cases of loss, defect, or theft of the portion cut for that purpose, another sacrificial substance (havis) must be produced, just as in the case of the primary offering itself.

However, when the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other such rites take as their recipients only that remnant which is implied by the injunction for the primary offering, then—since those rites depend on a substance already employed elsewhere and thus lack independent causal efficiency (*aprayojakatva*)—it follows that they need not be performed even upon loss, defect, or theft.

Therefore, although there is no practical necessity for the non-total offering (*asarvapradāna*) in either of the two views, this investigation is meaningful [as it clarifies the underlying principles].
However, there would be a remainder because of the non-exhaustion [of the offering].
If it were the case that "the cake on eight potsherds is for Agni" and so forth, then the offering of the whole would indeed be determined.

But here, on the contrary, it is heard that only a portion is to be offered after extracting something from that sacrificial cake and so forth: "He cuts twice from the oblation; he cuts twice from the middle and from the front; the portion to be cut is the size of a thumb-joint."
For, by considering such statements as "they offer the *dyavadāna*," it is understood that only a certain portion is to be offered; therefore, something must be left over.
Or rather, [the leftovers] serve as a means, because they are for that purpose.

If these sentences were not to find their place without subverting the complete offering understood from the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), or if they were more closely related to the primary act (*pradhāna*), then they would indeed subvert it. However, these are sentences concerning preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*), and thus they are established without contradiction.

For it is indeed possible to offer the oblation without remainder by repeatedly performing the ritual preparation with portions (avadāna) that are the size of a thumb-joint, extending forward from the middle of the [animal] and reaching toward the quarters.
Therefore, by the force of all these statements, this is the meaning of the scripture:
when one offers the oblation without remainder, that alone is the proper means; thus, no *homa* whatsoever is prohibited.
Therefore, the offering of everything must be performed.

As for the objection that the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) as it was heard cannot be executed simultaneously because it would result in the simultaneous performance of the great portions (*mahāvadāna*) and the oblations (*homa*),
[the answer is] as in the case of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, according to the *Tantravārtika*.

The oblation (homa) must be performed with the entire eight-potherd cake (aṣṭākapāla), because it is for that purpose, because it is for the sake of the deity, because it is for the sake of the sacrifice, and because it is for the sake of the transcendental result (apūrva).
There can be no possibility of fulfilling the meaning of the originative injunction (utpattivākya) through an oblation consisting of only a single part.
Alternatively, because the consecration (*saṃskāra*) pertains to the substance (*dravya*),
and because the ritual action (*karman*) has already been performed, it would occur only once; however, this is not the case, because the substance is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to the action.
The repeated breaking [of the vessel] and the offering of its parts should be practiced.
Why?
Because although the breaking is a subordinate element here, it should nevertheless be repeated.

However, because the *homa* (oblation) is the primary element, it does not undergo repetition; for the connection between the *āgneya* injunction and the *homa* is inferential (*ānumānika*), and that [injunction] applies to the commonality of all parts of the *puroḍāśa*. As long as that [injunction] has not been fully accomplished, the *avadāna* (cutting of portions) remains in existence. Indeed, by the statement "he offers the [portion] into the fire" (*juhoti*), a separate connection is postulated [for the specific portion]. Once that [separate connection] is established, the inferential one no longer applies.

Therefore, the general status of being dedicated to Agni (*āgneyatva*) that has been established is restricted—just as the number seventeen [is restricted] by the injunction regarding the *avadāna* (cutting-off)—to the specific context of the *avadāna* portions within the ritual section.

In this regard, the meaning understood is: "One makes the *avadāna* portion dedicated to Agni. Consequently, since other parts have not been enjoined, there is no occasion for an oblation (*homa*) of them.
Furthermore:

Nor is it necessarily intended that the entire oblation (*havis*) is for Agni by means of its offering; for when two portions (*avadāna*) are taken, the possibility of the whole being for Agni arises. Indeed, the number seventeen (*sāptadaśya*) of the *sāmidhenī* verses was stated as a general injunction (*anāramyavāda*), not as an attribute of specific sacrifices.

However, its connection with the sacrifice would have to be inferred through that [connection], and it is not logical to assume an inferential connection when a direct one exists; thus, the application (upasaṃhāra) is justified.
But the connection of the eight-potherd cake (aṣṭākapāla) with the deity is not obscure, because it is explicitly stated by the Taddhita suffix.
For that [connection] would indeed be merely inferential for the two portions (avadāna).
