Furthermore, in the originative injunction, the connection of the ritual action with the *aṣṭākapāla* (the cake baked on eight potsherds) is heard;
however, in the subsequent injunction of production, it is connected with the *hāvadāna* (the two portions).
To this, you might say:

The connection of the sacrificial action with the *aṣṭākapāla* cake is inferential, whereas that with the *jyavadāna* (the cut-off portion) is perceptual; therefore, when [the latter] exists, the postulation of an inferential [connection for the former] is not possible.
This is not so stated.
For if this were the case, the sentence "he offers the *jyavadāna*" would have to be accepted as the very originative injunction (*utpattivākya*).

For if the statement regarding the eight-pot-sherd cake were not subsumed under the statement regarding the oblation (*juhoti*), then the origination of the ritual act would be effected by this [statement] alone.

Consequently, since that [cake] is for the sake of what is enjoined in the *Āgneya* statement, there would result a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) such as "one should offer" and "of that [cake]. This is the fourth quarter of the third chapter.

Furthermore, it has been stated that without inference, neither the requirement for other sentences nor the connection between the sentences concerning the Āgneya and other sacrifices can be established.

Therefore, even though the connection is inferential, because the sentences cannot otherwise fulfill their own purpose, it must first be inferred; once the connection is established, its status cannot be altered even by a hundred direct perceptions.
Moreover, the relationship of general and particular is not possible here, because the conventional usage of "general" and "particular" does not apply to parts and the whole.
For by the injunction regarding the eight-potherd [cake], the entire *puroḍāśa* is indeed directly taught;
thus, even by the injunction regarding the cutting of portions (*avadāna*), it possesses equal force.
Now, an objection may be raised: "But surely, the application of the word *puroḍāśa* in its general sense to include parts other than the cut-off portions would be weak."
It is said:
for if the *puroḍāśa* were enjoined by means of its etymological sense (*avayavārtha*), then it would function as a general term; however, it is enjoined directly.
For when people renounce material goods to give to a deity, they do not do so out of a sense of abundance.
In that context, whatever exceeds the actual requirements of the purpose remains unmanifested, like other goods kept within the house;
nor is there any injunction here for a distinct act of renunciation regarding such surplus.
For this [offering] is implied by the very injunction that establishes the connection with the deity through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
And that presumption is established only to the extent that the act of giving to the deity would otherwise be impossible; it does not extend further.
Indeed, there is no inconsistency in the case of the abandonment of the remaining substance and so forth.

Furthermore, it is accepted that the injunction for completion applies everywhere; therefore, by that [injunction], only as much of the sacrificial procedure as constitutes a constituent part of the completion of the sacrifice is implied, not the other constituent parts.

Consequently, just as rice or barley grains remaining in the mind beyond the four handfuls do not lose their status as one's own property because they were not offered at the time of the pouring-out (*nirvāpa*), so too here, that [loss of ownership] would not apply to the other constituent parts.

Now, it might be argued that at the time of the pouring-out, a substance whose internal divisions—such as the *apūrva*—have not yet arisen must be relinquished by force, even if its abandonment was not intended.

For at that time, it is not known from which specific grains the sacrificial portion (*avadāna*) will be produced and from which it will not; since no distinction is understood, one might occasionally offer a portion from those very grains that were not intended to be relinquished.

In that case, there would follow the undesirable consequence of non-offering of those grains already relinquished and offering of those not relinquished, resulting in a failure to perform the rite as prescribed.

Therefore, this is not so [in the case of] the relinquishing of all [grains]. For when a transaction has been carried out by means of a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*), [the specific application is determined].
Therefore, that is the occasion for the specific scripture from the very beginning.

For if the casting of the oblation were denoted by the injunction for the Āgneya and other sacrifices themselves, then, because it would be impossible to exclude it by means of the injunction for the portions (avadāna), the casting of the whole [of the substance] would result. And in that case, the casting would be enjoined by the Āgneya injunction itself only when there is no distinction between sacrifice (yāga) and oblation (homa).

The distinction between these two, however, is established by the logic of the *Śabdāntara* (Differentiation by Different Words) section. We shall support for you exactly what the author of the Sūtras states in the aphorism: "Because it is heard as being uttered by that [word], *juhoti* should include the act of pouring (*āsecanādhika*). Just as a sacrifice (*yāga*) is merely the renunciation of one's own ownership with reference to a deity, whereas *juhoti* is the casting into [the fire] of a substance whose ownership has been renounced and which is dedicated to a deity.
Regarding that, as for those objections—such as that because [the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and *jyotiṣṭoma*] are not *ahomas*, the *āhavanīya* fire would not be required—we shall address them right there.

Furthermore, since there is a distinction between the two, by the injunction "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (*āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālaḥ*), only that much is enjoined by the word which is necessary for the cake to possess the character of being "for Agni.

And its character of being "for Agni" does not arise except through the mere renunciation of ownership and the dedication to the deity; it does not even require the act of throwing [the offering into the fire]. If there were no other sentence [to provide that], then the ritual action would be of such a nature.

In the *Aṣṭakapāda-tantravārtika*, it is stated that after properly preparing the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and placing it in the prescribed region according to the Vedic injunctions, one should form the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) with reference to the deity, thinking, "This is not mine. Furthermore,
for the sake of maintaining that resolve, one must never again establish ownership over that substance.
For if one were to bind [the animal] at that time, one would destroy the prior intention and speak a falsehood.
For one who already knows from the very beginning, "I shall again establish my ownership over this," it would not even be possible for him to form the intention, "This is mine; this is for the deity.
Therefore, having determined, "Let whatever happens to this [animal] after the renunciation dedicated to the deity happen," no further action need be performed by anyone.

When that [procedure] has been established, there are other scriptural statements such as: "He spreads the under-layer," "He cuts off twice from the oblation," "He pours the butter over it," and "He offers the fourfold portion. By these, it is first determined that what is to be offered as the oblation must be given.
And all of these proceed by taking hold of the substance belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*), not by grasping a previously unknown substance. For instance:

In the injunction "he offers with four portions" (*caturavattaṃ juhoti*), since the act of offering (*homa*) itself is not previously established, the substance is not enjoined with reference to that offering. Furthermore, the "four-portioned" (*caturavatta*) element, having been established by the preceding sentence, remains in need of a purpose. Therefore, what can be enjoined by this [injunction] is merely the casting-in (*prakṣepa*) of that [substance]; thus, an injunction of an offering qualified by the four-portioned [substance] is not tenable.

Furthermore, since even the oblation (*homa*), which consists of three parts, must extend until its completion, when the casting [of the offering] is enjoined as occurring at the very end of all [parts], one must consider whether two entirely new elements—namely, the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) and the designation of a deity (*devatoddeśa*)—should be postulated through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), or whether one should simply rely on those two elements as already established from some other source. In this regard, by the principle of non-co-referentiality (*vyadhikaraṇanyāya*), since simplicity (*lāghava*) prevails and complexity (*gaurava*) lacks authoritative basis, one adopts precisely those eight-pot-sherd offerings (*aṣṭākapālādi*) for which the two elements of relinquishment and designation are already understood.
Nor does this contradict their inherent status as means of accomplishing the sacrifice (*yāgasādhanatva*).

Even for the fire-sacrifices (*agniyāga*) that are about to be performed, [the rule] applies to that sacrifice (as per the *ka-pā* reading), because it does not obstruct their status as means of accomplishment. For a contradiction would exist only through a connection with another deity or through a connection with an action contrary to the sacrifice; however, such a thing does not exist here.

Therefore, this is the meaning: one should sacrifice with the eight-potsherd cake situated anywhere in a particular place, and one should offer its two portions (*avadāna*) by placing them anywhere. According to the statement, "He places the oblations on the altar (*vedi*) upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)," the sacrifice is performed with the *puroḍāśa* situated there.

And according to the statement, "He offers [the oblation] into the *āhavanīya* fire," the offering of the portions is made there. Now, it must be considered whether that *homa* (offering) is a distinct act from the preceding sacrifice and thus constitutes a separate procedure (*itikartavyatā*), or whether it is merely another part of that very same sacrifice, having arisen as a different form through a modification of its components.
In that very case, we say there is the production of a different form.
For if it were a different action, a different substance and a different deity would result, as in the case of the *nāriṣṭha* oblations and others;
however, according to the reasoning already stated, that same sacrifice, becoming more intensified, attains the status of a *juhoti*.
Nor does the mere fact of its being a specific instance of *yajati* (to sacrifice) imply that the root *hu* (to offer) necessarily involves the destruction of the form of the substance;
for while a particular may indeed exist within a general category,
no particular can possibly exist without a general category.

And therefore, just as when it is said, "Bring a tree," the subsequent mention of "a *śiṃśapā*" is not contradictory because there is no conflict, so too, when it is said, "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), one should understand that there is no contradiction with the act of offering (*juhoti*). This very form of the sacrifice is accomplished by the entire sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*); having been brought to the state of an offering through the *hāvadāna*, it is then offered; and by means of the remainder, its general form is established. Furthermore, even within a single moment, the form of the sacrifice is fully realized.

For as soon as the *avadāna* (cut-off portion) is cast into the *āhavanīya* fire, the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) regarding the deity for the entire sacrificial object is produced by means of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses; therefore, one must not fall into the error of thinking that because the *avadāna* held in the *sruva*-ladle is offered through the calls of *āśravaṇa* and *pratyāśravaṇa*, it alone is what is resolved upon for the deity and not the rest. Following the meaning of the Veda, the learned Adhvaryu and Yajamāna should duly perform the relinquishment of the whole and the dedication to the deity; for the Adhvaryu must perform the casting of the *avadāna* as a supplementary act.
Nor should it be thought that the sacrifice becomes unsightly or defective by this much;
for, by the force of the scriptural statement, it is precisely such [a form] that is understood to be beautiful.
Just as when one foot of a certain person is placed in front, no difference in his appearance occurs because of that.

Likewise, in the case of the *avaḍāna* (offering) portion, even when an additional part is added, there is no contradiction because the status of being a means for the sacrifice—prescribed by the original injunction—is accomplished through the entire eight-pot-sherd (*aṣṭākapāla*) cake.
Therefore, this separation should be understood as merely verbal (*jhākāra*).
Alternatively, that which is the sacrifice therein possesses primacy, whereas the act of throwing [the offering] is merely a subordinate limb (*aṅga*).
For thus:
in the sentence expressing the result, the connection of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) alone is clearly heard;
because it is recited in proximity to that, the root *hu* (to offer oblations) is understood as being subordinate to it.
Because it serves no further purpose, the remnant should not be offered from a single portion, since the remnant is subordinate to the primary act.

It is therefore considered how the rites pertaining to the remnant, such as the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and others, should be performed once the remnant of the oblation has been disposed of by being cast into the *āhavanīya* fire.
Regarding this, one who considers the rite to be for a specific purpose (*arthakarma*) says "from a single [portion]."

Even though they serve a purposeful function, if these substances were produced solely for that purpose, then—just as in the case of the animal-offerings (paśvavadāna)—the connection of all of them would be established through a single sacrifice intended for the possibility of all; however, that is not the case because they are not the primary motivators (aprayojaka). Therefore, the accomplishment is achieved by a single vessel for the pouring of husks (tuṣopavāpa), and this is also due to their being consecrated (saṃskṛta).

Furthermore, that consecration which is observed for the primary substances alone succeeds in its remaining effects accomplished by a single substance, and thus does not require another substance; moreover, the word "once" (sakṛt) intends a single cutting-off (avadāna). Otherwise, even if all [the parts] were cut off, since the performance would still be accomplished as a single act, the term [“once”] would be redundant.

Alternatively, if the remaining rites were to be performed for all [the deceased] from that point onward, they would have to be performed as purificatory rites; however, these are not purificatory rites.
Why?
Because they have already been purified by other purificatory rites.
If it is argued that this too will be without contradiction, then in that case as well, this is the meaning of the Sūtra:
because the sequence of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) has been transcended.

As long as a substance has not yet accomplished its purpose, it requires consecration (*saṃskāra*); however, once the primary act (*pradhāna*) has been completed, the purpose of the consecrations has already been served, and thus there is no further occasion for them.

Alternatively, since there is no distinction among all [the acts] regarding their causal nature and because consecration exists for that very purpose, these are indeed acts of consecration (*saṃskārakarma*), according to the principle that "those by which a substance is intended to be prepared are acts of consecration."

For at the time of your production, there are cognitions such as "that which is connected," and these are required by all [the substances] without distinction because they have achieved their purpose;

even though these [cognitions] do not employ the substances, nevertheless, since they are employed by the substances themselves, their universal scope is established. Furthermore, when the primary [substance] has been disposed of, and it is asked, "What shall be the disposal of these things that still belong to it? a restriction of the disposal can be prescribed. This is also because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga).

The repetition of the term "sviṣṭakṛt" in the phrase *sakṛt-kṛt* (performed once) is intelligible only if there is a desire for the offering to be made from all [the portions], or if one adopts the view that it is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) performed upon the entire offering; it is not otherwise possible.

These sūtras serve a specific purpose: even if, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the entire substance were offered away due to the requirement of the subsequent rites for the remnants (*śeṣakārya*), what then would be the purpose of this investigation? It is precisely this [purpose] that is being established.
In this regard, the point previously stated by us should be applied to your own Sūtra:
according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) are not the motivators for the subsequent rites (*śeṣakāryāṇi*), they should be performed only once.

However, because the removal [of the portions] is done by force, and since it is said that "when it has been done once for the primary acts, it is as if done for all," the consecration having been accomplished, it need not be performed from any other [portion] either.

In the Siddhānta, however, because there is no difference in the fact that all the sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) are equally the motivators (*prayojaka*), [the text] indicates the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the purpose—just as in the section on the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa*)—by means of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga-darśana*). Regarding the phrase "if from one, then according to desire" (*ekasmāccedyāthākāmya*): since there is no distinction, it is "according to desire" (*yāthākāmya*). When the feminine suffix *strī* is intended for this very term through grammatical coreferentiality (*buddhi-sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ṣigaurādibhyaśca*. Then, by the rule *halastaddhitasya*, the *yaK* suffix and its vowel are elided, resulting in *yāthākāmī*. (Tantravārtika)
Because it precedes the primary [rite],
the subsidiary rite— which is enjoined as a necessary duty on account of the remainder— occurs first for the initial [rite] in accordance with the order of the textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).
And since there is no contradiction at that time, it is performed.

Once the action is completed, the injunction ceases its operation and no longer serves as a cause; thus, due to this contradiction, it is not the reason [for the distribution]. Furthermore, since there is no mention of eating, the word "giving" refers to the purchase.
In the fourfold division of the *puroḍāśa* cake, the instruction is heard in the form: "This is for the Brahman," and so forth.
And how does that [gift] come to be designated as belonging to those [deities] such as Brahmā, if it is given to them? For by that, the gift is prescribed.

Now, is that [gift] enjoined for the purpose of hiring (*parikraya*) so that the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) may dispose of it as they wish, or is it for the purpose of the ritual disposal (*pratipatti*) of the remainder of what was consumed?
He says: it is for the purpose of hiring.

For here, unlike the case of "the five, including the sacrificer, eat the *iḍā*," neither the predominance of the substance nor its consumption is heard [as the primary purpose]. Therefore, since substances are subsidiary to the ritual action, and because they are given to those engaged in the action, even in the absence of an explicit scriptural statement regarding purchase (*parikraya*), it serves the purpose of purchase—just like the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). This is also supported by the praise: "This indeed is the sacrificial fee for the New and Full Moon sacrifices. The sacrificial fee inspires the priests with enthusiasm, and this is the very nature of purchase.
Or rather, the purpose is consumption, because of the equality regarding the substance;
nor is this division for the sake of purchase.
Why?
For in all cases, a purchase is accomplished by means of one's own property. When [the substance] has been relinquished for the sake of the deity, ownership no longer belongs to anyone.

It has been stated that [the deities], such as Brahmā and others, do not in any way provide a visible benefit to the portions [of the sacrifice]; this is because a visible purpose is required for the bartering of the substance.
By the phrase "by means of portions that benefit Brahmā and the others," it follows all the more clearly that this constitutes a purchase (*parikraya*).
Furthermore, they are not necessarily benefited by the act of consumption alone, since their benefit can also be established through such acts as bringing them home;
and [the author] will state everywhere that the purpose of consumption is the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the substance.
Because the cessation [of faults] is not stated to be through vows and the like;
for it is through the refinement of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*) that one would be turned away by vows.
Therefore, it should be stated as follows:

While it is true that there is an understanding of [the portions] as shares, nevertheless, at the time when the purpose of the restriction regarding the primary agent (kartṛ) is required, since the seen [purpose] is weaker than the unseen, an unseen refinement (saṃskāra) in the form of capacity belonging to the agents is postulated.
And among all [purposes], the refinement of the agent—namely, eating—is the most internal.
Furthermore, even after bringing [the portion] to the house, as long as the eating is not performed, it provides no benefit because it is not yet put to use.
Therefore, even if one must go very far, one must ultimately conclude with the act of consumption.

Since there is no reason for you to bypass the first [option], and because it is necessarily to be performed by completing the consumption that was commenced through the opening of the mouth according to the principle of fitness (*yogyatā*), it is understood that the consumption must be carried out using only the *brahma* and other [specific portions].
Furthermore, for the remainder (*śeṣa*) which stands in need of disposal (*chapaṇa*), it is determined by fitness that its disposal is effected solely through the act of consumption.

The praise of giving as "the sacrificial fee" (dakṣiṇā) arises from the specific instruction; it occurs either with reference to the incidental benefit [of the priests] or because of the formal similarity in the designation "for the Brahman priest," and so forth.
Therefore, it is established that this teaching has a meaningful purpose.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the *Tantravārttika*, composed by the venerable Śrī Bhaṭṭa Kumārila Svāmin.
[The fifth quarter of the third chapter in the *Tantravārttika*.]
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
An exception is now made to the overly broad rule that "the [oblation] is from the clarified butter because of its connection with everything, or because there is no distinction in the cause."
He first recalls that very prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa):
"And thus, the restatement (anuvāda) 'from all the oblations' is appropriate,
because its scope is the entirety of the oblations."

Regarding the reason and the ancient precedent: the reason that was cited for the portion cut off for the Sviṣṭakṛt is equally applicable to the clarified butter (ājya). Since this [Agni] carries the oblation to the gods, a share for him has been requested;
and he must necessarily carry the clarified butter as well to the deities of the Upāṃśuyāja.
And for this reason, it must also have a portion from that [other substance].
Because of the word *samavatta* (cut-off) being used in the singular,
"in one," the meaning is "in some [specific] ritual act."

Alternatively, according to your view, when the *viṣṭakṛt* portion is being cut from a single oblation (*havis*), the word *samavatta* (the "collected portion") would not be applicable [to that case], as it denotes what is being cut along with another [portion]; for [otherwise] there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This [objection] does not exist in manuscript G. In our position, however, since clarified butter (*ājya*) is also cut there, it will be logically consistent. Where, then, is this heard? That is now stated: [The relevant scriptural passage is: "He cuts the *samavatta* from the *upastṛta* [clarified butter] and the *abhighārita* [clarified butter]. Here, the term *samavatta* refers to the clarified butter that has been spread under (*upastṛta*) and poured over (*abhighārita*). Since the clarified butter is indeed cut there, the word *samavatta* is appropriate. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *samavatta* is used in the sense of "that which has been collected together" (*saṃhṛta*). And since the clarified butter is also included within that collection, the word *samavatta* applies to it as well. Therefore, there is no fault. Consequently, the *viṣṭakṛt* offering is established as being made from all the sacrificial materials (*sarvadravya*). The *āditya-prāyaṇīya* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) in milk is prescribed as one sacrifice; however, it is stated again in that very same context: "Having filled this *caru* with clarified butter (*ājya*), the four deities beginning with Pathyā [Svastī] are to be sacrificed to. Since these [four] share the commonality of the substance (*dravya-sāmānya*), all four sacrifices are modifications (*vikāra*) of the *upāṃśuyāja*, while the *āditya-caru* is a modification of the *āgneya*. In that regard, it is heard in the scripture: "He makes an offering (*samavadyati*) for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Therefore, if the *caru* were a single entity, by extension (*atideśa*), the rule would simply be: "He cuts off the portion from the *sāmnāyya* for the Sviṣṭakṛt."

But when the *viṣṭakṛt* is offered from the *ājya* used for the *upāṃśuyāja*, then the term *samavatta* (the combined portion) becomes justified with respect to the portions taken from both the *caru* and the *ājya*. Therefore, there are indeed remnant-rites (*śeṣakārya*) regarding the *ājya*; this is also because the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the *sviṣṭakṛt* is observed in the case of the *ājya*.

It is understood from the word "again" (*prati*) in the statement, "Having taken portions repeatedly from the *dhruvā*, one pours [clarified butter] over them; having taken the portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt*, one does not pour over it," that the portions are indeed taken from the *dhruvā* itself, both because of the explicit term and because this serves a visible purpose.

Furthermore, even that which is offered to the *sviṣṭakṛt* is taken from the *dhruvā* alone; for it is on account of that [portion] being taken for its sake that the pouring over of the *dhruvā* is prohibited.
Indeed, by the explanatory statement, "There is no offering beyond that," it is shown that the previous pourings were for the sake of the *sviṣṭakṛt*.
And consequently, based on that commonality, the same status would apply to the others; thus, all remaining rites (śeṣa-kāryas) ought to be performed.
However, because they are not "remaining" [in this context], it would not be so. Since all [the offerings] have been made, there is no state of being "remaining";
for when a principal substance remains, the remaining rites are performed, but in the case of the Upāṃśuyāja, there is no such remainder. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.5.10)
The remainder of the sacrificial oblation exists because of the taking of all;
if it is asked how there is the taking of all,
he explains that with the following sūtra.
Because it is common to all, there can be no remnant in the *dhruvā* vessel; for in the *dhruvā*, there exists no remnant of the *upāṃśuyāja*.

This is because the *dhruvā* is produced as unconnected [to any specific rite], because it is taken for the purpose of all functions involving clarified butter (*ājya*), and because of the scriptural statement: "All this is indeed taken for the sake of the sacrifice."

However, because the Taittirīyas enumerate the sequence of certain actions such as spreading [the grass] and pouring [the butter], and because the *upāṃśuyāja* is also mentioned therein, it is understood from the sentence "spreading [the grass] over those many [portions] together, pouring [the butter] over them, and sacrificing with the clarified butter" that this applies to all of them. And this is the established rule regarding common activities, such as sitting in an assembly, making offerings, staying in a guest-house, eating, and so forth.
When one part has been removed from a portion belonging to a single person, that much alone remains for him;

however, when what remains is determined to belong to those sharing an equal portion, it is not considered a "remnant" (pūrvaśeṣa) of the former, and thus, because its purpose has not yet been fulfilled, it does not require a disposal (*pratipatti*).
But when the portions have been distributed as appropriate by all those sharing the equal portion, then there arises a requirement for disposal consistent with its common ownership (*sādhāraṇya*).

Thus, when the portion for the *upāṃśuyāja* has been set aside, no remnant of it remains, because the remainder is subsequently taken up by acts such as the spreading of the under-layer (*upastaraṇa*) and the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*), and thus its purpose is not yet fulfilled.

Furthermore, the ritual functions performed with remnants (*śeṣakāryāṇi*) are intended for the disposal of what has already served its purpose; they do not employ a substance that has not itself already fulfilled its function.
Therefore, there is no remnant in the *dhruvā* vessel.
However, that which remains common after the completion of all the primary rites has another disposal prescribed for it, known as the *samiṣṭayajus*.

If, on the other hand, this too were determined to be a primary act (arthakarma) like the *upastaraṇa* and so forth, then there would be no remnant at all. But, with reference to the Taittirīya passage, since the *samiṣṭayajus* is connected with something else at its origin and is enjoined by the verb *juhoti* (to offer), it is not a sacrifice; thus it can be determined to be a disposal (*pratipatti*).
Furthermore, because it exists as a complete residue, it sets aside other subsequent acts involving the remnant.
Therefore, there is no residue in the *dhruvā* vessel at all.
However, because it has been offered into the *juhū*, and because that [offering] is connected with the *homa*, one might think:
"That which was taken into the *juhū* for the sake of the exclusive *upāṃśuyāja* will have a residue, just as there is a residue of *soma* in the cups and vessels."
That is untenable.
Why?
Because that entire [substance] is connected with the oblation by the injunction, "He offers it as a fourfold portion."
For this has been stated: that which is heard for the purpose of an accessory (upadhāna) must not be employed elsewhere; it is not heard in another context.
Therefore, a remnant in the *juhū* ladle is not tenable.
If it is argued that it is like the *camasa* cups—

Now, as for what was said—that even though there is a connection with the oblation (*homa*), there will be a remnant just as in the case of the *camasa* cups—that must be refuted. It is not so, because it would contradict the injunction and because of the preparation of the sacrificial material (*havis*). This is not equal to the case of *soma*; for in that case, once the mere preparation of the sacrificial material has been performed in the *graha* and *camasa* vessels, there is no total oblation. We shall explain this in the section where we state that "in the case of *soma*, there is no scriptural statement [to the contrary]."
By thus avoiding the contradiction with the injunction that will be stated later, it will not be a case of offering the entire [soma];
for [the text] says, "because a remnant has been offered" (śeṣāvattatvāt).

Furthermore, the observation of other purposes for the function of the remnant—such as "O Agni, offer the soma," "he performs the anuvaṣaṭkāra," and so forth—and the designation of the cups (*camasa*) such as "he consumes the Āśvina cup" and so forth, are not contradicted by this [interpretation]. This constitutes a complete resolution of all [objections].

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction. Alternatively, since no injunction is contradicted when the oblation is not performed in its entirety, the oblation is not performed in full because there is no contradiction;
however, in this case, a contradiction would arise, and this very absence of contradiction is the reason [for the performance]. Such is the interpretation of the Sūtra.

However, just as the Commentator previously introduced the sūtra *camasavaditi cet* without citing the cup (*camasa*), so too should the refutation be stated by assuming that very sūtra of objection (*paricodanāsūtra*) to demonstrate the non-absolute nature of the connection with the oblation (*homasaṃyoga*).

In that case, because the remainder [of the rite] is established by another scriptural statement, it would exist even in the absence of such a statement; thus, since the specific reason is not subject to deviation, the conclusion follows.

Alternatively, by replacing the word *tu* with *ca* in the phrase "because it has been cut off (*avattatvāt*), [the remnant] is in the *juhū*," those who explain this as a counter-argument from the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) should provide the *camasa* as an illustrative example; or else, the sūtra of restatement (*anubhāṣaṇa*) should be stated.
This is what is meant:
because it has been cut off, let the remnant be in the *juhū*, just like the *camasa*.
The response to that is "because of its connection with the oblation," which has already been explained.
Since the qualification refers to what has already arisen, the statement "of all" (*sarva*) applies when it exists;
as for the restatement "who [desires] all," which depends on the attainment [of results], we consider that it is a restatement of exactly that kind of "allness" (*sarvatva*) which we perceive here.

Furthermore, since there is no usage of the term "all" (*sarva*) in its absolute sense, the word "all" is understood here as being relative to those who are qualified; thus, there is no contradiction.

Therefore, according to the *Tantravārtika*, it is understood that "from all" refers to those for whom there is a qualification for the performance of the ritual act due to the absence of a remainder, or those for whom the remainder of the context exists because it is present—namely, from all such persons, distinguished by their specific class (*jāti*).

Just as before, because the act of "cutting" (*samavadyati*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), when the *ājya* (clarified butter) or the *caru* (cooked rice) is being cut according to the circumstances, the cutting of that portion belonging to Soma—which was not even intended—is nonetheless effected by force.
Thus, with respect to these two mixed substances and classes, the word "mixed" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) is a restatement;
the final [word] is for the sake of avoiding a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

As for the final reason—that the statement regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*)—this is indeed consistent even with our position, because it serves a purposeful function.
From the words "one should cut off [the portion] for the *sviṣṭakṛt*," it is understood that the cutting off occurs from that [cake], and that it is done in whatever manner is possible.

Furthermore, the cutting off for the *sviṣṭakṛt* is from the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and other such items, while the spreading of the base-butter (*upastaraṇa*) and the sprinkling of butter (*abhighāraṇa*) are taken from the *dhruvā* vessel.
The word *dhauva* (the sacrificial butter in the *dhruvā* vessel) is not connected exclusively with the *avadāna* (the portioning out of the offering) by means of the dative case-ending.

For that [butter] indeed requires re-sprinkling (*pratyabhighāraṇa*) even when there is a portioning out of other substances intended for the deities, because it serves the purpose of the under-sprinkling (*upastaraṇa*) and the over-sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*). Therefore, since the use of the *dhauva* butter exists both before and after the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the meaning of "filling up again" (*pratipūrayitvā*) is not that nothing further is to be done after each portion has been taken; for this filling up would not be a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the previously taken portion, as that would lead to the undesirable consequence of it serving a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*).

The pouring out (*āreka*), however, is for the sake of the subsequent rite and is directly perceived; therefore, even without being for the sake of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is justified as having the purpose of defining its limit.

In the *sākaṃprasthāyya* sacrifice, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* portion are likewise [treated]; thus, "the purpose also [occurs] according to possibility" (as found in the Ka, Ga, and Pu manuscripts).

The phrase "of its part which is permeated" (*tadavayavasyānusyūtasya*) and the word "not intended" (*acikīrṣitam*) do not appear in the Ka and Ga manuscripts. Regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* and *iḍā* portions: at the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*), these are invariably cut from the *sānnāyya*; likewise, the *sākaṃprasthāyya* is a modification (*vikāra*) of that. Since there is a doubt based on this similarity—that here too [the offering] must be cut from it—the present rule of extension (*atideśa*) is made.
However, because it is not a remnant (*aśeṣatvāt*), it would not be so; for it is not a remnant due to being offered entirely.

For in this way, the text—"all the oblation, as it proceeds for the purpose of the *homa*, together with the two jars"—prescribes that the entire milk-offering (*doha*) which has not been set aside is to be offered together with the two jars; thus, it ordains the offering of the whole without remainder, so that nothing can be left over.
And in the case of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, the rule "as in the cups" (*grahēṣu tadvat*) likewise applies.

In the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice, there are the *surā-grahas* and the *payas-grahas*, beginning with those for the Aśvins and others, which have been prescribed. Since these consist merely of separate preparations (*pṛthak-prakalpana*), there arises a specific doubt that—unlike the *camasa* cups—there is no requirement for a complete offering (*sarva-homa*) of them. However, by means of extended application (*atideśa*), it is declared that even in this case, there is a connection between the taking [of the vessels] for the purpose of offering and the offering itself, according to how they were received and how they were obtained. Thus: "The officiating priests take up the cups as they were received; they offer the *payas-grahas* in the northern fire, and the *surā-grahas* in the southern fire.
And so there is the statement regarding the remnants.
Furthermore, the prohibition—which is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that which is not otherwise exhausted—is expressed as "he does not offer the whole";

whereas "he leaves a remnant" (*ucchiṇatti*) is the injunction (*vidhi*), and its restatement is the prohibition. By means of the attainment of the non-exhaustive offering, it demonstrates the cessation of the purpose of the remnant. And since there exists another disposal (*pratipatti*) or another purposeful act (*arthakarma*) for the scripturally prescribed remnant, for that reason also, the *viṣṭakṛt* and *iḍā* offerings should not be performed.

Since the substance is one, the ritual acts being distinct, they should be performed for each individual act, according to the Tantravārtika. Now, regarding the remaining subsidiary rites, their specific details are considered.

In that context, there are six distinct substances and deities postulated through six nominative case-endings (*caturthyanta*) that are mutually independent. Because no other deity can be present in a sacrifice already occupied by another deity, these constitute six separate acts distinguished by their qualifying attributes (*guṇa*). Among these, for some the sacrificial oblations (*haviḥ*) are indeed different, while for others there is only one cake (*puroḍāśa*), the size of a chariot wheel; this is not the case for all.
When this is accepted, the inquiry arises: is there a division of the subsidiary rites (*śeṣakārya*) due to the difference in acts, or are they unified because of the oneness of the substance?

But surely this matter will be settled in the eleventh book [of the Mīmāṃsāsūtra], where it is explained that "the single-naturedness of purificatory acts (saṃskāra) regarding a single substance" has already been established; therefore, it need not be deliberated upon here. It is replied: [The response follows: ... [as per the original Sanskrit context] ... [the point is that while the general principle may be established elsewhere, its specific application and exceptions require further analysis in this particular context].
This substance to be prepared undergoes the ritual action along with its divisions;
and because it serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the primary acts (*pradhāna*), there is no single unified performance (*tantratā*).

This would be the case whether one adopts the view that the action is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the rite itself, or the view that it is a refinement of the animal being sacrificed. In either instance, there would be a distinction based on those divisions.

This, however, is the remaining portion of the ritual procedure (*saṃskāra*); and that remainder is common to all [the principal offerings]. It is taken from the southern and northern halves [of the sacrificial cake], not from the location of the primary cutting (*pradhānāvadāna*), because that was not enjoined in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Consequently, it is possible to maintain that no specific distinction is being grasped.

For even if they were to take the northern half with reference to a single principal offering, nevertheless, by the fulfillment of the purpose as enjoined in that manner, the other principal offerings would also have their purpose accomplished.
Therefore, it is a tantra;
however, that which is to be performed according to its capacity is useful when applied to another performance through the fourfold method.
But in the case of the Aindravāyava cup, there should be a consumption for each ritual act because of the specific scriptural injunction.
Some say that after performing a general investigation into the consumption [of the soma], this specific investigation ought to have been performed;
however, that which is done first is because it presents itself more quickly by way of an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding section.

Since the principle is that "when the substance is one, as in the previous case, the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled once [the act] has been performed," the consumption would [otherwise] occur only once. But by virtue of the explicit statement—"He consumes the portion belonging to Indra and Vāyu twice"—there is a double consumption.

If there were other such topics for which a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established by reasoning and a final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached through scriptural statement, that might be appropriate; however, this is not the case here. For that [method] is employed where what has been established by reasoning is sublated by a scriptural statement; since such sublation is absent here, it will be of no benefit to the other principles of reasoning.
And since this has already been demonstrated here by the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*), this investigation would yield little fruit.
Therefore, it should not be described in this manner; rather, as stated in the *Tantravārtika*:
"In the *Sarvapṛṣṭhā* sacrifice, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and *iḍā* offerings must be performed for each ritual act (*karman*) separately, because of the difference in the principal acts (*pradhāna*)."

For instance, [the opponent] states as if it were established that the differentiation of the principal act (*pradhāna*) is the cause for the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *aindravāyava* cup, citing: "He consumes the *aindravāyava* twice; he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call for this one twice. Therefore, when the reply has been given—that the consumption of the remnant is based on the *vaṣaṭ* call—one must state the refutation by means of the Sūtra after restating the example: "But in the case of the *aindravāyava*, although a single consumption would have been expected, there is a double consumption due to a specific scriptural injunction (*vacana*), and not because of a differentiation of the principal act, since the reason was already rejected in the section concerning the reason (*hetvadhikaraṇa*)."

This being the case, since the general discussion regarding the consumption of Soma is merely recalled by way of the remainder of the preceding section, there will be no violation of the sequential order. Regarding Soma, because there is no scriptural statement [to the contrary], the consumption does not exist; however, in the case of the Aindravāyava cup, consumption would indeed occur because of the specific injunction. But as for the Soma contained in other cups and in the *camasa* vessels, there is a doubt.

Regarding the question of whether there is a portion [to be consumed] or not—even in such cases as "he consumes the Āśvina cup from all sides," and so forth—the same principle as that of the Aindravāyava would apply.

However, in this matter, it must be investigated in every respect: is it that when the consumption is already established, only a qualification is enjoined by the statement, or is this an injunction of a qualified whole?

And what is the distinction here? If it is based on the explicit statement (*vacana*), then it must be performed exactly as stated; but if it is based on some other reason, then even a sign (*liṅga*) residing in only one part will, according to the *sthālīpulāka* maxim, indicate the whole.

In this matter, three positions are possible: (1) since the observations of other purposes depend on [the existence of] remnants and there is no injunction [for eating], there is no eating at all; or (2) due to the absence of remnants, one should eat as much as the text permits, making the observations of other purposes the basis for the injunction; or (3) there is eating even based on the name (*samākhyā*), the *vaṣaṭ* call, the oblation (*homa*), and the pressing (*abhiṣava*). What is the prima facie view? Because of the connection with the entire oblation—just like the *ājya*, *sākaṃprasthāyya*, and *saunāmaṇī* offerings—there is no remnant at all; how then could there be eating?

Nor is there attainment through the original nature (*prakṛti*), nor is there a direct scriptural injunction (*pratyakṣopadeśa*); even that which appears to be an injunction is incapable [of establishing the rule] because it is intended for another purpose.
Therefore, [the conclusion is] "there is no *bhakṣa*.
This might be so on account of seeing [other] purposes.
But these are direct injunctions; because there is no basis for a mountain-like restriction [of scope], they must follow the specific instruction.

If these were merely observations of other purposes, then their application might extend elsewhere; however, these are indeed injunctions, and therefore this consumption (bhakṣa) occurs only according to the instruction and not elsewhere.
In the case of the cups (camasa), it is due to the designation (samākhyāna), since the connection is based on that [designation].

"We accept this according to the instruction," it is said; however, that instruction must be followed as distinguished by differences such as designation (*samākhyā*) and so forth, and not restricted merely to what is explicitly heard in the text. In the case of the cups (*camasa*), although no direct instruction (*pratyakṣopadeśa*) found within the Brāhmaṇa is perceived, it is nevertheless inferred from the designation contained in the *praisha* (direction). For the direction to bring the substance, qualified as "the Hotṛ’s cup" and so on, would in no way be possible if the Hotṛ and others did not consume the Soma from them.
How so?

Regarding the word *camasa*, derived from the root *cam* (to eat) with the *uṇādi* suffix *asan* used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), when the time for the command (*praiṣa*) arrives and a connection to past, future, or present is required, the future tense is inferred because neither the past nor the present is observed.
For otherwise, the performance of the command "Let the *camasa* of the *hotṛ* go forth" would not be possible.
Therefore, the *hotṛ* and others must consume [the soma].

"The cups containing the remnants of Soma have been sent forth"—from this very statement, as explained in the *Tantravārtika*, it is understood that the quality of being "consumable" (*bhakṣyatva*) belongs specifically to those [remnants] due to their proximity. For the cup is offered with its remnant remaining, according to the scriptural injunction: "He offers a small portion."

Furthermore, no other substance such as boiled rice (odana) is perceived, by the drinking of which the status of being a *camasa* (cup) would be justified; nor would that [substance] constitute an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the ritual action (*karma*),
in which case the scriptural injunction (*raṇa*) would be contradicted.

Furthermore, the *praiṣa* (direction) would have to be displaced, and the designation (*samākhyā*) "Soma-cup" would be sublated if rice-porridge (*odana*) and the like were eaten. Moreover, if the vessel were defiled by such remnants, a subsequent oblation could not be performed with that same vessel. For you, who rely on indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the sake of purification, since the substance whose status as the *hotṛ*-cup and so forth was previously determined has been destroyed, it no longer possesses that designation; thus, there would be a sublation of the injunction for an oblation performed by means of that which is designated [as such]. By this, the proposal to take up another cup is refuted.
And in producing that [juice], there would be a transgression of the scriptural number of cups;
nor can it be offered by one who has not rinsed [the mouth],
for the force of the scriptural statement applies even without violating established custom, as it finds its scope in the drinking of Soma.
If it is argued that all this is the same even in the case of one who consumes Soma, we reply: it is not so; for there is a scriptural text stating, "They do not become impure by means of Soma.
Therefore, the Soma must be made to be consumed by the cup-holders (camasins).
The commentary also should be interpreted according to this very sequence, and not exactly as it is written.

Because the intermediate birth is defiled by being separated from another birth, it therefore prohibits the non-Brahmin from consuming the Soma. Furthermore, if the consumption of Soma were not established for the one performing the sacrifice by the designation (*samākhyā*) "of the sacrificer" (*prayajamānasya*), then the mention of the prohibition—"if he should desire to consume the Soma" and "not [the non-Brahmin] the Soma"—in the injunction regarding the *phalacamas* would be inexplicable. Therefore, there is indeed Soma-consumption for those who hold the cups (*camasins*).
"One [should eat] from the Udgātṛ's cup because of its connection with the Vedic text.
Now, without yet discussing the eating following the *vaṣaṭ*-call, the oblation, and the pressing, he first follows up on the specific eating based on the name (*samākhyā*) as it arises incidentally.

In that very same injunction, it is heard: "Of the Udgātṛs" (*prodgātṛṇām*). Regarding this, there is a doubt: does only the single Udgātṛ eat, or all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), or those who perform the chant (*stotrakārin*), or rather all four members of the Chandoma group?
However, some maintain that there is identity between the second and fourth positions;
for in both sūtras the word "all" (sarva) is employed, and because of the proximity of the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇā), it refers exclusively to the Chāndogas.
Whence arises this doubt?
For here there is a clear contradiction between the meanings of the base and the suffix;
in that case, they remember that one should follow the base *udgātṛ* and apply the suffix *aṇ*, rather than following the suffix and effecting its elision by treating it as the agent.
Therefore, this [term] is not to be understood as derived from the word *udgātṛ*.
And since he will state that it is caused by the act of choosing (*varaṇa*), this explanation is incorrect.
To this, it is replied:
Therefore, the *udgātṛ* here is only secondary (*gauṇa*), because the primary *udgātṛ* is impossible;
this [term] is applied by metaphorical transference (*parāvṛtti*) to the Brāhmaṇas and others, just as [the term "king"] is used for ministers and so forth.

Just as in the case of the statement "one sacrifices the *sviṣṭakṛt* with the limbs," it is not the case that the limbs are restated and the state of being three is enjoined; rather, the meaning of the compound already established previously is what is to be enjoined—so too here, because the complete word is joined with another word, and because there is no capacity for extracting a single part, it is impossible to restate [it] as "that which is the portion of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer."

For it is not logical for the word *prāk* (first) to be compounded with *samanvāgata* (endowed), because when there is a state of mutual expectancy (*sāpekṣatva*), a compound is not possible. [Objection:

But surely a compound occurs even when the principal member is expectant; thus, even if there is a connection with the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer, the compound will be valid. [Reply: This would be so if *bhakṣa* alone were expectant; however, in this case, *prāthamya* (primacy) is also expectant, as it is connected with the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer.

For primacy is not the cause for the consumption; rather, it is the status of being the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer. Therefore, the connection would have to be understood as "the first [consumption] belongs to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer," and from that, a clear inconsistency would arise. Furthermore, if it were restated as "the consumption of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer," there would be the fault of a qualified restatement (*viśiṣṭānuvāda*), because the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer is not implied by the mere act of consumption.

Moreover, since the status of being a *vaṣaṭ*-utterer is not restricted to this specific action alone (as it occurs in other actions as well), if either one were restated, then primacy would have to be enjoined for all consumptions and for all the activities of every *vaṣaṭ*-utterer.

And since that [prior state] is impossible to achieve, this is therefore an injunction for a first consumption (*prathama-bhakṣa*) characterized by priority, which is a new, unprecedented (*apūrva*) act, performed by the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ* call (*vaṣaṭkartṛ*).
Because there is a mutual restriction between these two, they have an entirely identical scope; thus, to whatever extent the *vaṣaṭ* call occurs, to that same extent there is the first consumption.
But how can the utterer of the *vaṣaṭ* call be adopted as a causal condition (*nimitta*), and how is a restriction possible for that which is not being adopted?
It is said:
First of all, the restriction [regarding the agent] must in every respect be based on a single action;
otherwise, no distinction would be perceived between what is appropriated and what is not appropriated.
The price and the cost of delivery must be paid.
Other noble-minded individuals should collect certain portions, and for each of those portions, the price and the cost of delivery must be paid.

For, by the designation "Hotṛ," everything previously belonged to the Hotṛ because of the statement that the sacrifice belongs to the Hotṛ; by your statement, however, the portion beginning with the *yājyā* has been made to belong to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), while the *vaṣaṭkāra* and so forth remain with the Hotṛ as before.

If, however, it were explained as "removing [the portion] from the sacrificer," then, since the portion for the *yājyā* would have already been assigned to him and then removed, there would be no possibility of obtaining the *vaṣaṭkāra* and so forth; consequently, the removal itself would be impossible.

Therefore, because the phrase "in place of the sacrificer's *yājyā*" indicates the removal of only the *yājyā* portion, and because the *vaṣaṭkāra* is entirely distinct from the *yājyā*—and furthermore, because there is no relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgin*) between them—the Hotṛ should utter the *vaṣaṭkāra* and consume [the portion] after [the offering] has been performed by the sacrificer.
For the consumption is caused by the *vaṣaṭkāra*, not by the *yājyā*; thus, [the portion] is not removed.

Or, because of the arrival of the cause for the sacrificer: if only this much were heard, namely that "the yājyā belongs to the yajamāna," then the consumption [of the portion] might perhaps not be removed from him; however, here it is heard thus: "having sat down himself, he sacrifices.
And by means of the *vaṣaṭ*-call, the sacrifice is performed for the purpose of offering the oblation, not by the *yājyā* alone.

Likewise, in the injunction "one should sacrifice with the invitatory verse" (invānam yajati), the [sacrificer] must recite the invitatory verse starting from the yājyā until the meaning of the sacrifice is completed.
And this is possible only if the yājyā and the vaṣaṭkāra have a single agent, not otherwise.
Therefore, wherever there is a yājyā, there must also be the vaṣaṭkāra and the consumption [of the offering], even without [explicit] mention.
It is understood that [the *pravara*] is brought to a state of unity and subordination;
because it has already commenced, there is no removal of the *pravara*.
As for the point regarding "like the *pravara*," that is addressed in the *Tantravārttika*:
The *pravara* has not been bypassed, yet it is recited at the time of the *yājyā*. However, because eating is yet to occur, the assumption of its proximity (*upanaya*) would have to be postulated;
furthermore, the sense of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyārtha*) would have to be postulated, which would result in the sublation of the sense of the accusative case (*dvitīyārtha*).
Furthermore, there would be a total sublation of the Soma [offerings] if one were to assume an extraction (*niṣkarṣa*) of the sacrifice.

If the act of eating (*bhakṣa*) were enjoined as something entirely new (*apūrva*), then it could not serve as a subordinate auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*); for this would involve the assumption of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) and would entail a remoteness in both the application (*prakaraṇa*) and the syntactical connection (*viniyoga*), resulting in an unconnected benefit.
Likewise, by the accusative case in the phrase "he should give that" (*taṃ prayacchet*), its status as a thing to be refined (*saṃskārya*) is clearly understood.

Otherwise, the word "by that" (*tena*) would [refer to the action] itself; therefore, it refers to the *saṃskāra* (consecration). And this is the nature of a *saṃskāra*: that it depends upon a substance that has been employed or is being mentioned in the ritual procedure (*tantra*).

In that case as well, since it is impossible for what has already been consumed to be used again, it is understood that [the fruit-cup] is intended solely for the purpose of a consecratory rite (*saṃskāra*).

Therefore, the *phalacamas* can only be enjoined as approaching a consumption that serves as a consecration; if it is to serve some purpose, then it is consecrated by the act of eating, and not otherwise. And that [cup], seeking to be employed, attains its utility for the sacrifice through the context (*prakaraṇa*) and other such factors.

In that case as well, since the portion of the sacrificer (*yajamānabhakṣa*) does not attain the status of being something to be consecrated unless it is employed, it is necessarily connected by implication with only that much of the sacrificial share; therefore, it is connected specifically with the single *camasa* of the sacrificer. For it is not the case that its status as the sacrificer’s portion is untenable when not employed in other *grahas* or *camasas*; thus, even the Soma will be favored [by this rule]. Alternatively, this word "portion" (*bhakṣa*), being uttered in connection with the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, refers only to the Soma-portion under discussion.
And since that [Soma] is known as a consecration for the remnants of the substances used in the sacrifice, it is capable of consecrating the *phalacamas* in exactly the same way.

However, it is not possible to assume that this [consecration] now has some other purpose; nor is there any reason—such as a different word (*śabdāntara*) or the like—for it to be a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*).

Furthermore, by the phrase "if he should desire to consume the Soma," it is understood that it is connected specifically with the consumption of Soma mentioned in its own sentence; otherwise, the mention of that [desire] would be entirely useless.

Furthermore, the restatement "not Soma" would not be appropriate. If this were enjoined as a distinct act of consumption that serves as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), then, because it would lack the same function [as the original], it could not exclude the Soma; and if the Soma were not excluded, there could be no restatement of a prohibition. Nor could it be a mandatory injunction, as that would entail a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) and the undesirable consequence of postulating multiple unseen merits (*adṛṣṭa*). Moreover, the sentence would become incoherent.
If one intended to effect the refinement of the Soma by means of eating, then one would either have to perform the eating of the fruit-cup as a remote auxiliary or refine the fruit-cup itself.

When this meaning is grasped—that by which means one who desires to prepare the Soma as it truly is, should likewise prepare the fruit-cup (phalacamasa) in that same manner—then, by implication (arthāpatti), a non-connection with both the sacrificer’s cup and the sacrifice is established. Therefore, it is proven that this [fruit-cup] is a modification of the Soma;
such is this construction of exclusion (vyavadhāraṇakalpanā).

Just as in the case of the *Aśvapratigraheṣṭi*, where based on the Vedic text "as many horses as one might receive," it is determined and established that "one should cause [the recipient] to receive [them]," so too, based on the text "one should offer the sacrificial portion (*bhakṣa*)," it is inferred that "one should offer the means for the sacrifice.
By this, passages such as "one should press the *pūtīka* plants" are explained.
[This applies] from the point of the oblation (*homa*).
The injunction regarding the young *darbha* grass-blades, following upon the mention of the *homa*, is intelligible only if it is a modification of the sacrifice;

and because of the simultaneity with the *camasa* cups, the syntactic unity with the drawing out (*unnayana*)— which is the means of the sacrifice whose nature is doubtful— is intelligible only in this case of equality [of the *darbha* blades with the *camasa* cups], and not otherwise.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark;
it has been explained that the restatement of the prohibition of Soma is an indicative mark,
on account of the commonality among those who have entered [the sacrificial ground].

In the *daśapeya* sacrifice, a hundred Brāhmaṇas consume the Soma; it is prescribed that they should approach each of the ten cups in groups of ten. Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether the cup belonging to the Kṣatriya (*rājanya*) should be consumed by those same ten Brāhmaṇas, or by Kṣatriyas. What, then, is the cause of this doubt? Some say it is due to a difference in the interpretation of the sentence structure. For if the injunction "ten for each one" were the primary rule, then [the consumption would follow that specific pattern]. However, in the *Tantravārtika*, it is stated that they are of equal caste.

If ten groups of ten [persons] are prescribed for all the waters, the statement "one hundred Brāhmaṇas" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already obtained, and thus it becomes a mere praise (*stuṭi*), like the expression "the village of Brāhmaṇas"; in that case, there would be ten Kṣatriyas.

However, if "one hundred Brāhmaṇas" is the injunction (*vidhi*) and "ten each for one [cup]" is the restatement, then since a figurative sense (*gauṇatva*) is impossible in an injunction, the consumption must be performed by Brāhmaṇas alone in every instance; thus, there are ten Brāhmaṇas.

What, then, is the prima facie conclusion? By the force of the injunction [that they] "should enter," and by the force of the restatement that they "do not eat," when the injunction "ten each for one" exists, and there arises the expectation as to who those ten are, it is understood—due to the inherent nature of numbers to apply to things of the same class—that in the Brāhmaṇa cups there are Brāhmaṇas, and in the Rājanya cup there are ten Rājanyas.

And having raised the objection regarding the number ten on the grounds of "commonality" (*sāmānyāt*), once the treatise has ceased its operation, when those individuals are being selected for the purpose of filling that number, only those among them for which there is some indicative mark should be taken; for a commonality exists as a signifier for those of the same class, but not for those included within a different class.

Alternatively, "on account of similarity" means that because of the similarity of the subject matter (*viṣaya-sāmānya*), there is a unity of purpose; for when *kṣatriyatva* (the status of being a Kṣatriya) and *daśatva* (the number ten) are employed in relation to the *phalacamasam*, and there is a mutual restriction between them, it is understood that wherever there is the quality of being a Kṣatriya, there is the number ten. Thus, by force of logic, ten Kṣatriyas are determined. Alternatively, "on account of similarity" means that what performs the same function and belongs to the same class serves as the sublater of what is similar.

In that case, if the status of being a *rājanya* (king) is obtained from the injunction for the *Rājasūya*, and singularity is obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*), then the number ten being enjoined there sublates that singularity because it is common to all and is based on extension (*atideśa*), but not because it is a different function (*kārya*) than the genus (*jāti*). Consequently, the sacrificer’s cup (*yajamānacamasa*), its genus remaining unremoved, must be joined with the number ten; thus, there are ten *rājanyas*. But surely, when ten is enjoined, since there is a qualified reference (*viśiṣṭānuvāda*) stating "they move toward each cup one by one," there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
This is not a fault.
The word "camasam" (the cup) is cited in the accusative case; by that much alone, its status as something to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*) is understood.

Since there is no other consecration for the cups except consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*), it is that very act which is indicated by the term "approaching" (*anuprasarpaṇa*). And since consumption is established as occurring individually [for each person], that too is restated. Therefore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Or rather, because the word is the same, the Kṣatriyas should not consume [it]; for what reason?
Because the injunction is understood here as being connected with a hundred Brāhmaṇas.

Otherwise, that assumption [of the sacrifice] would be figurative and purposeless for you, whether in the view of the extension of the meaning of the word (*padārtha*) or in the view of the extension of the ritual procedure (*śāstra*), because of their difference; however, we shall explain in the tenth book that it is the operation belonging to the sacrifice that is extended, and since it is partless, it is extended all at once.

And by this [extended application], for the sake of the self-same purpose, the *apūrvas* (unseen potencies) of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are grasped simultaneously; by those [potencies] the *prayāja*s and so forth are grasped, and by the *prayāja*s and so forth their own respective scriptures are grasped. Thus, because the extended application (*atideśa*)—in the form "as in the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*)—is a single entity that is undifferentiated across all subsidiaries, its operation occurs everywhere or it does not operate at all, but not in only some parts.

It has been stated in the section on strength and weakness (*balābalādhikaraṇa*) that even by means of *śara* grass, the *kuśa* grasses, having already been obtained [by extension], are simply set aside.

In that case, if the extended application (*atideśa*) regarding the use of *khadira* wood and so forth is abandoned because it follows from the absence of a specific injunction (*anārabhyavāda*), then for that very reason it would also apply to other auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), resulting in the undesirable consequence of the cessation of everything. And this has already been stated. On the other hand, if the extended application regarding those [elements] is established as authoritative in accordance with certain original (*prākṛta*) elements, then the attainment of *khadira* wood and so forth would likewise be undifferentiated, and thus the fault of "double-stating" (*dviruktatva*) clearly ensues. Furthermore, because they depend on the activity pertaining to the sacrifice, we shall establish everywhere that modifications (*vikṛti*) first adopt the original elements, even bypassing what is recited in their own specific context (*svaprakaraṇa*).

Since that [extension] also does not begin until the application of the extended rule (atideśa) has been reached, the initial application of the *sruva* and other implements in the archetypal sacrifices (*prakṛti*) must necessarily be expected.

Furthermore, to the extent that the *sruva* and others do not apply, so too do the *khādiratva* (the quality of being made of khadira wood) and so forth; thus, it is not possible for these to be the subject matter of a direct injunction (*upadeśa*).
Nor is their connection with the sacrifice clearly evident.

That [application] must also be inferred through the principle of "otherwise it would be impossible" (*anyathānupapatti*) as involving the taking up of the *sruva* ladle and other implements. Furthermore, one who maintains that [the rule] applies to all [rites] must first admit its connection with the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*). Once its lack of purpose (*ānarthakya*) has been removed by that [archetypal connection], a connection with the modified rite (*vikṛti*) lacks any basis of proof.

For the connection with the sacrifice is more strongly supported by a transfer-rule (*atideśa*) for those [injunctions] whose connection with the sacrifice is indeed direct; such are the *anārabhyavāda* (uncontextual) statements like "This Prajāpati, the seventeenfold, is attached to the sacrifice," and so forth. Therefore, it is established that the use of *khadira* wood and the like is for the sake of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
However, according to the *Tantravārtika*, due to the specific context (*prakaraṇa*), there would be a contradiction in the case of the ectype (*vikṛti*).
This is an instance of an exception (*apavāda*).

Here, by means of the preceding section itself, it removes the specific doubt that the non-contextual statement (*anārabhyavāda*) regarding the seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses might be optional (*vikalpa*) with respect to the fifteen *sāmidhenīs* prescribed by the context (*prakaraṇa*), since it serves the purpose of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
But how can an option be asserted for that which is of unequal strength with a specific injunction belonging to the context?
He said:
In that case, there is indeed a specific negation of the general,
where the relationship with the particular is perceived through direct perception.

If the nature of the *sāmidhenī* verses were the sole factor [for their application], the number [of verses] would be purposeless; therefore, one must necessarily accept a connection based on their being means for the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the sacrifice.
Furthermore, as we shall explain in the ninth book (*navama adhyāya*), it is not possible to indicate that they are means for the sacrificial *apūrva* without the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Consequently, because the favor of the context is a specific qualification, the fifteen-fold number—which is proximate to the means of knowledge for the connection with the *apūrva*—is stronger.

For even an injunction first enjoins a person toward that which possesses a purpose; and since the fifteen-fold number (*pañcadaśya*) is perceived more quickly as possessing a purpose than the seventeen-fold number (*saptadaśya*), they possess unequal strength due to the disparity in the timing of their injunctions. This concludes the sixth quarter of the third chapter.
Furthermore, a person proceeds to act in order to perform the sacrifice (*kratu*) without defect, not for the sake of the *sāmidhenī* verses themselves.

Moreover, we do not find any means of knowledge such as direct statement (*śruti*) or the like to establish that the seventeen-fold number is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice, whereas the context (*prakaraṇa*) establishes the fifteen-fold number.

Therefore, this number fifteen (pañcadaśya) is determined by both syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*) to belong to both the *sāmidhenī* verses and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

However, the number seventeen (*sāptadaśya*) belongs solely for the sake of the *sāmidhenīs*; since it would otherwise be purposeless, its connection to the sacrifice is now inferred, just as in the case of the *khādiratva* (the quality of being made of khadira wood). Yet, if it were to accept that connection, it could not do so while already occupied by another number.

In your case, there is non-deficiency of the *sāmidhenī* verses in both ways; furthermore, by means of the fifteen-fold number (*pāñcadaśya*), there is no contradiction even with respect to the subordinate element (*aṅga*), just as in the maxim of "eating from a bronze vessel" (*kāṃsyabhoji*). How much more so, then, when the non-contradiction of the quality belonging to the subordinate element (*yavāṅgaguṇa*) is clearly evident?

Therefore, having stated the established conclusion—that the *sāptadaśya* (the number seventeen) was displaced by the *pāñcadaśya* (the number fifteen), which is emboldened by its support from the *kratu* (the sacrifice), such that even when the *sāptadaśya* is reached through a strained extended application (*atideśa*), it is set aside by the directly taught (*aupadeśika*) *sāptadaśya* because the latter has already occupied those [vikṛtis] first, and thus the *sāptadaśya* is determined to apply exclusively to the *prakṛti* (the archetype)—it is now replied:
"The directly taught *sāptadaśya* is not stronger in the *vikṛtis*;
for that [number seventeen], being an *anārabhyavidhi* (a rule not occurring in the context of a specific rite), has become a subordinate element of the *sāmidhenī* verses."
Just as that which is obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*) is stronger than the primary form (*prakṛti*),

so too is that known through extended application (*atideśa*); for even in the modifications (*vikṛti*) of the sacrificial acts, the fifteen-fold number (*pāñcadaśya*) pervades the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) by virtue of extended application.

The Sūtrakāra also stated that the seventeen-fold nature (*sāptadaśya*), which is prescribed as a subsidiary of the *sāmidhenī* verses, is not adopted in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) because it is contradictory;
he said this with the intention of expressing only this much: that such a rule does not exist in the primary model sacrifice (*prakṛti*).
Although, for us, the context is weaker than the syntactical statement,
nevertheless, because its subject matter is different, it serves as the applicator within the sacrifice;
and this very fact— that it is specific to the sacrifice— is its distinction.
When the *sāmidhenī* verses are established as being equal or as subordinate elements (*śeṣa*) by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*),

the contingent rule (*naimittika*) regarding the number seventeen (*sāptadaśya*)— which is enjoined on account of specific causes such as the sacrificer being a Vaiśya— is restricted to the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*) because of a specific connection with its modifications (*vikāra*).

It might be argued that those two [the *sāmidhenīs*] alone are the sublaters of the *pañcadaśya* (fifteen-fold nature); for that [the *pañcadaśya*] could not establish its own existence without sublatting [the others].
Therefore, it is indeed heard [as an injunction] in all the *madhu* sacrifices and in all ritual performances.

There are other ritual applications (prayoga) performed by Brahmins and Kṣatriyas in which the requirement of seventeen [priests] is not sublated, and through which the self obtains its own nature; in these,
the numbers counted by one are not counted again by another in a single place.
Indeed, the capacity to sublate an eternal injunction cannot be established even through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti),
for every eternal injunction is prescribed while its contradiction has not yet arisen; however, a conditional injunction contradicts it because its scope is pervaded by that [eternal rule].
Furthermore, in the case of a general application (*prayoga-sāmānya*), everything is prescribed as permanent;
however, in the case of a specific occasional rite (*naimittika-viśeṣa*), it is even more like oil [in its consistency].
But for optional (*kāmya*) and occasional rites, the purpose is that which is conveyed by the sentence itself.

Therefore, because they are more quickly applied, the obligatory [rites] are stronger than the occasional ones; for by means of the Vedic injunction (*śruti*) alone, the agent is immediately impelled toward the human goal (*puruṣārtha*),
whereas in the case of the occasional rite, being remote, he is impelled only after a long time.
