The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) presented here is not at all the same as that in the previous section; for there is indeed a distinction between the obligatory (nitya) and the optional (kāmya) within this context. If, according to your view, the obligatory were to be set aside by the optional due to the desire for its fruit, [it would lead to an inconsistency].
For one who perceives the honey, a fall occurs due to delusion;
for such is the nature of the substratum as the sacrifice is revealed to be— namely,
that it is understood to be pervaded by constant requirements such as the use of *khadira* wood and so forth.
For by that [injunction], one indeed grasps its own purpose, but never a desired [result];
because there is a requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), that which is merely connected [to the rite] is not grasped.
(Third Adhyāya, Sixth Pāda)
Even its own meaning is not found to be established in its primary sense;
therefore, the principle of the preceding section applies even to the occasional rites (*naimittika*).
Because there is no connection [with the primary purpose], there is no sublation; rather, its connection is distinguished [as being specific].

Furthermore, because the application [of the rule] is understood as being qualified by the agent, there is no sublation between those two which have unequal objects— namely, that which is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and that which is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
It is not logical [to claim sublation], for there is no contradiction between those two, as they operate within different spheres.
Just as the cup (*camasa*) is for the sake of the sacrifice and does not accomplish [any other] purpose such as that of an animal,
so too the *godohana* vessel, being for another purpose, is not a means for accomplishing the sacrifice;
for the formulation of the injunction differs when it is prescribed with reference to a specific result.

Since another [act] is intended for the purpose of leading forward [the fire], there is no possibility of this [leading forward] being [the primary act]; therefore, because it implies a word expressing desire, there is no injunction for its leading forward.
Due to the lack of an injunction and the absence of being a subordinate element, there is no sublation of other subordinate elements.
Therefore, in the case of a desirable quality (*kāmyaguṇa*), the practice of leading forward (*praṇayana*) must be performed; as stated in the *Tantravārtika*:

"Just as in the case of a cup dedicated to Indra and Vāyu, because Mitra and others are not possible [as deities], there would be no deficiency for these two, and there would be the fruit of the sacrifice."

For a ritual act intended for the sake of the sacrifice does not, by abandoning its own means, accept [an auxiliary] established by the means of another; rather, it is that very act which, for the sake of accomplishing its own purpose, employs the auxiliary.
An auxiliary that is devoid of activity will certainly not accomplish anything at all.
And that [action], consisting of the leading forward [of the Soma], is given to him by virtue of the context;
and since there exists another cup (camasa) already established therein as a subordinate element,
no injunction for it is heard here that would not merely set aside that [other cup].

And when an action consisting of leading [the fire] is undertaken for the sake of a desired result (kāmya), there would be a defect in its performance, just as there is in the case of a prohibited act joined [with another].

For even though the optional accessory (guṇa) has a different ultimate purpose, because its intermediate effect is one and the same, it is capable of determining the falsity of the cognition of other contradictory accessories.
For instance:
"Indeed, it is the optional accessory that accomplishes the success of the sacrifice;
and sacrifices, having already achieved their purpose, do not then take up their own accessory."

Since the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) of the water intended for mixing with the oblation (*havis*) is already established, one who desires a specific result (*kāmya-guṇa*) should employ that very act; it does not necessitate a different ritual action (*kriyāntara*).
Therefore, even though the repetition of the carrying forward (*praṇayanābhyāsa*) serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), it is not [independently] enjoined.

Therefore, because it would otherwise be fruitless, there is a sublation [of the former] by the application [of the latter]. For, while the *camasa* (wooden cup) is used repeatedly, the *godohana* (milk-pail) is used only once; thus, the latter, having established its own status through the sublation of the previously obtained [usage], prevails. This is not the case for the *godohana*, as it has its own scope according to the *Tantravārttika*. Furthermore, the former is remote from the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), whereas the *godohana* is proximate to that goal; and the entire activity of the scriptures is directed toward the human goal.

And that distinction which arises from being for the sake of that [subordinate] or not for the sake of that will not be considered a *tantra* (common application), because it is stated that "the purpose is not altered.

For this distinction is weak: that which is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) must be set aside by that which is for the sake of the sacrifice and is prescribed as a specific rule, but not by that which serves another purpose.
Therefore, due to the proximity of both, there is a restriction (*niyama*) resulting from the mutual sublation of their respective capacities.

Furthermore, since the act of fetching water (*praṇayana*) has already been established as accomplished through its application elsewhere, its capacity to bring about its own specific means would be lost; likewise, the capacity of the *godohana* vessel to be conceived as a distinct act of fetching water would be obstructed.

The scriptural status of the *camasa* belongs only to those instances other than the performance for one desiring cattle; therefore, the *godohana* is a modification (*vikārin*) of that [the *camasa*].

However, as to how the *camasa* itself will indeed be used in the modified rite (*vikṛti*), this will be explained in the eighth book under the principle: "Or rather, there is exclusion because of the difference in the ritual acts."
Therefore, this [text] is a modifier (vikāraka) only with respect to the primary context (prakṛti).

Since the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) serves the purpose of the Pavamāna offerings due to its context, first of all, the fact that it is an independent statement (anārabhyavāda) is established by way of introducing the topic of independent statements; for, by means of the context, it would otherwise follow that the agnyādheya serves the purpose of the Pavamāna offerings.

However, because of the specific context (*prakaraṇa*), it serves the purpose of the pure fire; or rather, as stated in the rule "the consecration belongs to that which is connected [to the rite], like the material," since it is a consecration of the fire for the sake of the *iṣṭi*, its purpose is determined to be the fire for the *iṣṭi*—as this avoids contradiction with the weight of the direct statement (*śruti*), the syntactical connection (*vākya*), and the context (*prakaraṇa*). Furthermore, if it were for the sake of the pure fire alone, it would be purposeless; therefore, by way of that [fire], the capacity to include the laying of the fire (*agnyādhāna*) is established. Consequently, the general designation refers to the purpose of the *iṣṭi*. Moreover, precisely because of the context, it should be understood as pertaining specifically to the *pavamāneṣṭis*.
Or rather, [the establishment of the fires] is not for their sake, because they have that as their purpose.

If the establishment (*ādhāna*) were a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), then it would be understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*) to be for the sake of the *iṣṭi*s; however, due to the syntactical connection (*vākya-saṃyoga*), since the fire is indicated by the accusative case, this [establishment] is for the purpose of purifying the fire. This being so, if the fires were for the sake of the *pavamāneṣṭi*s, then the establishment would also be for their sake through them.

But it has been stated that those [iṣṭi*s], being fruitless in themselves, are for the sake of the fire; and therefore, by the very principle "and because qualities are for the sake of others," there is no mutual subordination. For the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) in the accusative case is not set aside by the context.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark,
the text "he makes it new again" shows that [the action] has the purpose of consecrating the fire;
it is for the sake of its original form, just like other unattached statements (*anārabhyavāda*).

Once it is established that the statement regarding the *anāramyavāda* (independent injunction) is not for the sake of the archetype (*prakṛti*)—just as the use of *khadira* wood and so forth [is not restricted to the archetype] because it enters the archetype through the *agnihotra*—then, according to the Sūtra, the following understanding arises: "Since the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) has its own specific time, it serves all purposes. For if the establishment were performed at the time of the archetype, it would then serve the purpose of the archetype; however, when it is performed at its own time, such as spring and so forth, it is understood to serve all purposes because no specific distinction is perceived.
And likewise, the commonality of its performance will be stated in the eleventh [book]: "Because the substance is produced at one time, the performance should be for the sake of all.
If it were for the sake of the archetype (*prakṛti*), this would be for the sake of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices.

And in that case, because it must follow the authority of the primary rites, it would have to be performed both at the full moon and the new moon; and if that were so, one would establish the sacred fires (*ādadhīta*) at the spring full moon and the new moon—so says the *Tantravārtika*.
Therefore, these statements would be meaningless; hence, [the conclusion is] that it serves all purposes.
But this is not correct.

For there is no evidence whatsoever for a connection of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) with either the archetype (*prakṛti*) or the ectype (*vikṛti*). Since the context (*prakaraṇa*) exists, that which has not already become for the sake of the *pavamāneṣṭi*s will not, even in the absence of the six means of proof beginning with direct statement (*śruti*), serve the purpose of any other ritual action. Whence could such a thing follow?
If this were the case, would this not have already been resolved by the previous section?

True, it would have been resolved if the Pavamāna-iṣṭis, like the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and others, were themselves fruitless. However, because those [latter] possess fruits, the principle that "accessories exist for the sake of another" does not apply; thus, it is possible to assume their status as auxiliary parts of the rite through the medium of the fire-offering (agnihotra). Since the subordinate act is fruitless and its purpose must necessarily be determined, it attains the status of being for the sake of the primary rite through the fire-offering, just as the use of *khadira* wood [serves the purpose of the sacrifice].
For fires situated within the context of ritual application (*prayoga*) are indeed capable of bringing about ritual acts.

Just as, in the case of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites, it is postulated that they transcend the mere nature of the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) and so forth, and that the quality of being made of *khadira* wood and so forth transcends the mere nature of the *sruva*-ladles and so forth—because these are prompted by the unseen potency of the ritual (*karmāpūrva*)—so too must it be postulated for the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) that it transcends the mere nature of the fire. If the fire-installation were prompted solely by the mere nature of the fire, then rituals would be accomplished even by a fire that has not been installed;
and yet, it is not with such fires that a person has need, but rather with those fires possessed of specific qualities.
Therefore, since a connection with desire is necessarily present, its status as the primary meaning [of the word] has been set forth on the basis of its inherent power.

As for its being fixed to its own specific time, that is for the sake of commonality in performance—like the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)—which is obtained through both direct injunction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*); thus, it does not imply that it serves all purposes.
Furthermore, the mention of "spring" and so forth will be meaningful as referring to a domain where [the timing] is otherwise not established.
For the *avāhana* (invocation) intended for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices does not obtain the status of having spring as its time, because its performance is prescribed every half-month;
nor does the *avāhana* intended for the Agnihotra and other *darvihomas* obtain the time of the full moon and new moon.
Furthermore, since commonality of performance cannot be established without a statement regarding its own specific time, it is not purposeless; for this very reason, he explains it in this way.

The establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) is not an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of any specific ritual action; rather, because of its connection with the accusative case, it is for the sake of the fires themselves. As for those fires, they will serve all purposes by virtue of the rule "but those fires, because they have their own time," and thus it is said that through them, [the *ādhāna*] serves all purposes.

The phrase "because it has its own time" (svakālatvāt) also means "because it is enjoined independently" (svātantryāmnānāt). As for the argument that it is like other independent injunctions (anārabhyavāda), it is replied: once their status as auxiliary elements (aṅgatva) is established, only then is the purpose of those [injunctions] investigated.

But there is no means of valid knowledge whatsoever for its being a constituent part of the ritual action. For, in the context of the initiations (*dīkṣā*), the *agnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice] is mentioned near the purchase of the Soma; and although, by the force of that statement, its performance will take place near the animal-ritual details (*paśudharma*), it is nevertheless not occupied by the *prakaraṇa* (context), because all constituent parts do not exceed the location of their origin.

Even for the *savanīya* offerings, the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) pertains to the time of the Soma-pressing (*sutyākāla*), whereas the mention of the Upavasatha day is merely a statement regarding a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).
Furthermore, there is no such context (*prakaraṇa*) [for the *savanīya* offerings].

However, because the *anubandhya* animal sacrifice is performed at a great distance—at the conclusion of the Soma sacrifice—it is [separated] from that immediate context. Therefore, by the unobstructed context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, established through syntactical connection (*vākya*) and direct mention (*saṃyoga*), the position (*sthāna*) of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice—which would otherwise serve a remote purpose—is set aside, and it is concluded that these [animal sacrifices] are for the sake of the Jyotiṣṭoma. Since that [Jyotiṣṭoma] has Soma as its substance, there is no utility for the characteristics of the animal sacrifice; thus, due to this lack of purpose (*ānarthakya*), they descend into those [subordinate acts] themselves. And because there is no distinction among them, they descend into all three [animal sacrifices].
Even though it is a constituent part of that [sacrifice], because of the absence of suitability (*yogyatva*), there is no application to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites;
and even though suitability exists, because of the absence of a general connection (*sāmānyasambandha*), it does not apply to the animal sacrifices that are its subsidiaries.
Therefore, when it is argued that the injunction applies equally to all three, the following is stated in reply:
This might be so if there were no distinction in the context by way of the Jyotiṣṭoma;

however, there is indeed a distinction. Because the Savanīya animals are produced on the day preceding the Soma-pressing (aupavastrya), as in the injunctions, "At the Agniṣṭoma, one should sacrifice a goat dedicated to Agni; at the Ukthya, a second one dedicated to Indra and Agni," and so forth, the Savanīyas are produced in close proximity to the ritual details of the animal sacrifices. Therefore, they serve exclusively for the purpose of the Savanīya offerings.
Furthermore,
how can this be stated as contrary to the section on *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth?

For it was not accepted there that the gambling and other such acts belong to the *rājasūya* by virtue of context (*prakaraṇa*), while they belong to the *abhiṣecanīya* by virtue of position (*sthāna*).

Similarly, [in the case of] the *aindrī* verse, it would follow from direct statement (*śruti*) that it is for the sake of the Gārhapatya fire, while from indicative power (*liṅga*) it would be for the sake of Indra.

It is logical for you that when [the purpose] has been determined by the stronger means of proof, namely context (*prakaraṇa*), the weaker means of proof do not arise, and thus no combination (*samuccaya*) is resorted to. For here, nothing remains unestablished for the subordinate element (*śeṣa*) without further assumption; nor is there anything for the principal elements (*śeṣin*), such as Indra and Agni, since their recollection is established even through other means.

Furthermore, even though the requirements [of the ritual] are satisfied by the connection with the *savanīya* offerings, since the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice cannot exist without the *paśudharma* (animal-ritual duties), another [set of duties] must necessarily be postulated; for there is no disagreement regarding both [the necessity of these duties and their source].
Moreover, at that time, this [animal sacrifice] could not have the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as its archetype (*prakṛti*).

For that which is the archetype (*prakṛti*) of the animal sacrifices becomes the model for the modifications (*vikāra*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices; the others, however, being modifications of that [archetype] due to the commonality of having a living being as their substance, one might ask: does the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice receive its details from the Savanīya through an extended application (*atideśa*) arising from the transfer of similarity (*sārūpya*), or rather by some trace of direct instruction (*upadeśa*)? Since it is included within the scope of direct instruction, its application according to the sequence of the ritual is more appropriate; for extended application is only postulated when the sixfold modes of direct instruction have ceased to apply.

Therefore, just as elsewhere the operation pertaining to the sacrifice serves both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*) through direct injunction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*), so too here it serves both purposes by virtue of position (*sthāna*) and context (*prakaraṇa*). However, since there is no direct injunction for the *anūbandhyā* cow anywhere, its application will occur solely through extended application (*atideśa*). Consequently, the Sūtra is not subject to criticism.
As for the statement "on the next day, according to some," there, the prior mention is for the purpose of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).

As for what was said—that by virtue of their position (*sthāna*), they are for the sake of the *agnīṣomīya*—we accept that. However, we do not tolerate the claim that by virtue of context (*prakaraṇa*), they are for the sake of the *savanīya*; why?
Because on the day of the preparatory fast (*upavasatha*), which is for the sake of the subordinate elements (*guṇa*), there is a repeated mention (*punaḥśruti*) of the *savanīya*.

The origin and the procedure for these [offerings] follow after the drawing of the Āśvina cup. By this very statement—"They proceed with the sacrifice after it has been bound with the omentum"—since the primary act is not displaced, and because the subsidiaries must occur in the same location as the primary, even though acts such as the *upākaraṇa* (dedication) would otherwise have no fixed time, the immediate sequence following the drawing of the Āśvina cup is prescribed. Therefore, that very mention is for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*); otherwise, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), due to the prescription of both the time for the binding and the dedication, and the prescription of the sacrifice itself as connected to a specific material and deity.
[Objection: But surely the encircling (parivyāṇa), which is already obtained through extended application (atideśa), is merely restated when the sacrifice is enjoined at that very same time.

[Reply: True, it is obtained by extended application, but it is not performed at this point; for its benefit is accomplished by that which was performed at the time of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, since that serves as common to all the sacrificial posts (yūpa).
[Objection: If that is so, then since it is already obtained and exists by virtue of being common, it cannot be restated, because there is no recognition (pratyabhijñāna) of it.
That which is obtained through its name is restated as something already established; it is recognized as such by means of the substance.

Furthermore, there can be no restatement of what was performed on the previous day as being present at a time subsequent to the drawing of the Āśvina cup, for at that time one does not perform the encircling (parivyayati).
Nor can there be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what was previously performed by means of such a word as *paryagnikṛta*, because it is delimited by two limits defined by preceding and succeeding times.
If that were so, then let it be a restatement of what is obtained from this [text]: "Having taken the Āśvina cup, having gone out, he encircles the sacrificial post.
That too is not possible, precisely because of the absence of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).

Since this non-archetypal (*aprākṛta*) encircling of the *savanīya* animal is heard as being for the sake of this pure [rope], and since the archetypal encircling is dependent upon the girth-rope (*raśanā*), if the act were performed with any material whatsoever—such as grass (*darbha*) and so on—the restatement of its being "threefold" (*trivṛt*) would not be applicable. In that case, because multiple matters would be enjoined simultaneously, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). And at that point, the text of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) is as follows:

For otherwise, something would have to be enjoined regarding the binding [of the sacrificial post], namely that the substance which is mentioned as being connected [to it] and the time would be enjoined; and the time for the *upākaraṇa* (dedication) and the ritual act qualified by the substance and deity would also be enjoined.
Therefore, because this [text] serves the purpose of enjoining a subordinate element (*guṇa*), there exists the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *savanīya* offerings on the previous day.
[Objection: No, because it is only a part [of the whole].

For when the recitation of the Savanīya offerings together with their ancillaries occurred previously, then, since the performance of everything was established at that very time, by virtue of the scriptural injunction (*vacana*), there would be a displacement (*utkarṣa*) only of the offering of the omentum (*vapāpracāra*) and so forth, and not of the preliminary rites (*upākaraṇa*) and the like; or rather, as stated in the rule "or [displacement] from that point onward due to connection," only those ritual acts which occur after the offering of the omentum, or those which are concomitant with it, undergo displacement, but not the preceding acts such as the *upākaraṇa*. Furthermore, regarding those ancillaries whose timing is unknown, it will be stated that they take the time of the primary sacrifice;
however, the animal-offering ancillaries do not attain the time of the primary sacrifice because their own specific time has already been determined.

Therefore, excellence must be established by means of a sentence that is not itself subordinate or through a non-excellent locus; consequently, if there were a sentence of quality, the sentence would be split due to the prescription of multiple meanings.
There is no such fault in the originative sentence; therefore, this [sentence] is for the purpose of origination.
However, the author of the Bhāṣya has not demonstrated here the presence of multiple objects to be prescribed within a single sentence.

In this very way, however, the sentence-split (*vākya-bheda*) has been stated regarding the purpose of the qualities. But here, the sentence-split can be avoided by the injunction of merely postponing the *upākaraṇa* (the ritual act of bringing near) which was obtained on the previous day. In that regard, some explain it as follows: Just as it was said that there is a multiplicity of purposes when both the connection with the Jyotiṣṭoma and its specific detail are enjoined in the case of "with an Āgneyī verse, [one approaches] the Āgnīdhra fire," so too here, there would be a multiplicity of purposes because both the postponement of the *upākaraṇa*—which had not been postponed during the offering of the omentum (*vapāpracāra*)—and its specific detail would have to be performed.

But this is not similar to the *āgneyī* passage. For in that case, when an injunction is intent upon a specific relationship and requires the attainment of a general relationship from elsewhere, the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the general relationship in other instances—given that it exists in certain *āgneyī* verses—is set aside by its presence there. However, for one who would postulate such an injunction not accepted by the Veda, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) occurs; but here, no such counter-argument exists.

For, having observed the attainment of excellence in a general sense, an implication (arthāpatti) might be postulated for one who intends a specific [application]. Even in that case, as stated in the Tantravārtika, if there were not a general attainment acting as a counter-position to sublate the implication, the authority of the mere Āgneyī [verse] would not have been set aside.
Even when [the time] is already established, the injunction of multiple meanings conveyed by a single word has been demonstrated in your own system through examples such as *śoṇa*.

Therefore, although by the phrase "having taken the Āśvina cup" both this [cup] and the sequence following the Āśvina cup might be enjoined, nevertheless—due to the requirement that an injunctive word follow a single term—it is not possible for each of these to be taught individually; how much less so here, since when one thing is enjoined, the other is established by implication?

For this very reason, the Commentator, while stating the refutation of multiple injunctions, declared: "And when there are multiple objects that are not mutually related, it is impossible for them to be enjoined. For he [the author of the injunction] knows that when one among a set of related objects is enjoined, the others follow without any further effort. Therefore, when one object is enjoined, even if a thousand other objects are implied by the force of the meaning (*arthāt*), no contradiction or burden upon the injunction is observed; thus it is accepted.
However, the only means of refuting that [position] is the fact that it can be established otherwise.

And in this case, there is no such alternative view whereby this injunction, without establishing a connection with the Sutyā and the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), would enjoin [the act] immediately after the drawing of the Āśvina cup; therefore, there is no fault.
Nor indeed is there such a fault for one who maintains that the injunction prescribes an action qualified by multiple substances and deities.
Furthermore, another connection with the specific time of the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) during the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma would have to be assumed.

Moreover, in all cases of displacement (*utkarṣa*) or non-displacement (*apakarṣa*), there exists the fault of multiple injunctions in the form of general and particular rules; thus, since it is impossible for this to be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) regarding an already established action, it follows that it must be an injunction of a distinct ritual act (*karmāntaravidhi*).

This is just as in the case of "He is consecrated in relation to the *māhendra* stotra," where the injunction of the time of the *māhendra* stotra at the midday pressing (*mādhyandinasavana*) for the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice involves multiple purposes; the same logic should be applied to such passages as "They perform the fore-offerings (*prayāja*) while the animal stands."
Furthermore, when a single object is being performed or enjoined, another object arises in two ways:
some is accomplished through a separate effort, while some is produced as a byproduct of that [primary effort].
This is as in the sixth section of the third chapter concerning the injunction regarding eating, which relates to the taking up [of the cup].
[The two factors are] compassion and satisfaction.

In that regard, when something is to be accomplished through a further effort, and it is determined that the performance of what is enjoined is not possible without performing that [further act], then another power of the injunction, obtainable through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), is postulated.
And whatever [cognition] there is, and however much of it, constitutes the scriptural understanding.

However, that which is produced as a byproduct (*anuniṣpādi*), even if it is much, is accomplished for the person and for the sacrifice without any other separate operation; therefore, no effort is required for it.

Furthermore, when the immediate sequence following the drawing of the *āśvina* cup is being enjoined or performed, there is no need to operate separately with regard to its connection with the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*) or the morning extraction (*prātaḥsavana*).
Thus, nothing here enjoins a general displacement (*utkarṣa*).

If, when the immediate sequence following the *āśvina* cup-taking is prescribed merely by hearing [the text], it were to entail—by virtue of being included therein—the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), specific parts of the day, moments (*muhūrta*), minutes (*nāḍikā*), instants (*kṣaṇa*), lava-measures, time-units, substances, existence, and so forth, what could be done?

Furthermore, even in the case of the command "bring a *śiṃśapā* tree," there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) due to the implication of "tree-ness," "substance-ness," "existence," and so on.

Therefore, since the *upākaraṇa* (initial rite) was already established for the previous day, the prescription of the mere interval of time following the *āśvina* cup-taking as its new timing involves no fault.
Others, however, argue that there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to the displacement (*utkarṣa*) of both the encircling (*parivyāṇa*) and the bringing near (*upākaraṇa*).

But even that is easily refuted, because the displacement of the bringing near is established simply by the displacement of the encircling alone, according to the principle "that which begins with it" (*tadādi vā*) or "due to the connection" (*abhisaṃbandhāt*).
In this regard, a ritual element (*dharma*) that is displaced from its original context causes the displacement of what is connected to it, but not something entirely new (*apūrva*).

That is incorrect, because by describing the displacement (apakarṣa) of even the non-original acts such as the gambling (videvana) and so forth—on the grounds that "for the predecessors [the rule] applies from the specified place"—and because of the explanation that the term "not previously mentioned" (apūrvam) has a specific scope;
or else, there is no syntactical split (avākyabheda) because it is a restatement of the intermediate winding (parivyāṇa) obtained from the sentence "He [takes] the Āśvina cup.
If it is argued that a restatement of the threefold nature (trivṛttva) is not possible there because the means (sādhana) is not specified, that is also incorrect.

For in this way, even the proponent of the final doctrine (siddhāntavādin), when challenged by the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin), will himself state the refutation; that shall be his "future commentary" (bhaviṣyan-tantravārtika).

Now, it might be argued that while for that [other case] the injunction of a previously unestablished action (*apūrva-karma*) allows for the injunction of multiple factors, this is not so for the present case; however, there is no such distinction. Where multiple qualifiers are employed as adjuncts to a single action, the injunction of them through that medium is easily obtained; this is the principle of the injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa-vidhāna*). On the other hand, where an action qualified by its own qualifiers is enjoined, and another action already obtained from a different sentence serves as its qualifier, the injunctive suffix must necessarily recur. For a sacrifice being enjoined as qualified by a deity and so forth is capable of implying only its own qualifiers, but not the qualifiers of an *parivyāṇa* (encircling) that is not itself being enjoined.
Therefore, this same point should be explained even regarding the rules for unprecedented rituals (*apūrva-karma-vidhi*):
which of these two is the qualifier of that [sacrifice], and which is the qualifier of the other?
Consequently, since this applies to both sides, it should not be raised as an objection against only one.
In that case, the proponent of the final conclusion (siddhāntavādin) must necessarily state the following rebuttal: that the term "girdle" (raśanā) is common to both types of encircling.
For it will be stated later: "And the girdle [is for the post], because of the observation of an indicative mark.
Whichever encircling there is of this sacrificial post, for each of those, this [girdle] is understood by means of the direct statement (vākya).
Thus, because it is a restatement of what has already been established, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Alternatively, since it is already established from the previous day that one performs the *upākaraṇa* after having encircled the sacrificial post (*parivyāya*), the text merely restates this sequence of the *upākaraṇa* following the encircling, and then enjoins the sequence of following the drawing of the *āśvina* cup.
And it is better to resort to an interpretation involving a slight displacement [of the action] than to accept a syntactical split.
Therefore, it is described in this way: necessarily, among the *savanīya* offerings, the production must be established by one [text] and the quality (*guṇa*) by the other.
In that regard, there is no reason for the former to be the sentence of production. [Objection:

But is there not likewise none for the latter? [Reply: Even if that is so, since neither option nor conjunction is possible, and one or the other must be accepted on account of some specific distinction, that specific distinction is now stated.

This very point was established previously: that a quality which is to be adopted (*upādeya*) can be enjoined by means of a restatement of something whose sequence is concealed, but not one that is not to be adopted; for the latter forcibly brings about the status of a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*), just as in the case of the *homa* in the *Kuṇḍapāyinām ayana*.

Therefore, in this case, the performance of the *vapā* (omentum) could be enjoined by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the *savanīya* [animal] standing at the time of the next day; however, since there is recognition of the *savanīya* belonging to that specific place through the explicit mention of the "morning pressing" (*prātaḥsavana*), and since the mention on the following day has its purpose already determined, there is no connection as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) with the *āśvinagraha*. Consequently, because the connection is for the sake of time (*kāla*), that [mention] cannot be something to be taken up (*anupādeya*). Thus, since an injunction is untenable by way of a primary action (*karman*), the action must necessarily be enjoined by way of time.

Even if there were an injunction [of the Āśvin cup] as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) with respect to the [Agniṣṭoma], nevertheless, because the principal (*aṅgin*) is not something to be enjoined (*anupādeya*), this alone is the correct mode of expression. Consequently, since an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is untenable, by the principle of "another context" (*prakaraṇāntara*), and because there is no obstruction by another originative injunction (*utpattividhi*), when the origin is being determined, it must be a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).
Thus, its status as an originative injunction is established in view of that specific time.

Therefore, for the other [the Āśvin cup], its status as an injunction of a quality is established by elimination (*pariśeṣa*), for there is indeed no cause for differentiating it [from a quality-injunction].

For this very reason, it has been deliberated whether or not there is a postponement (*utkarṣa*) of the offering of the omentum (*vapā*). For if there were a postponement of the offering of the omentum, the time for the preceding [rite] would be understood as being applied to the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) because of its recognition;
as it is said: "But when in proximity, there is no division."

Furthermore, when the action is being prescribed at the proper time, the operation of the suffix will pertain to a proximate object; however, since the time for the offering of the omentum (*vapāpracāra*) is qualified by an action other than the act of producing the *savanīya* [animal], a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) would be difficult to establish, resulting in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
In our view, however, there is unity of sentence (*ekavākyatva*), as has already been stated.

And thus, even for the *parivyāṇa* (encircling), its status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*) will be restated here; otherwise, it would not be mentioned, as it would be attained only by a much more remote sequence of enumeration (*gaṇakrama*). Therefore, this alone is the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*). But how, then, in this view, is the author of the Bhāṣya’s presentation of the "splitting of the sentence" (*vākyabheda*) to be explained?
It is said:
This very distinction in action is what is designated as "sentence-split" (vākyabheda).
However, unity of sentence (ekavākyatva) is understood even when there is a difference in meaning, provided there is a connection;
for instance, when the Soma has perished and there is a requirement for a substitute, the Putīka plants are enjoined, not because of a requirement for a means of sacrifice.

Therefore, this is indeed a restrictive rule (*niyama*) which states that when it is impossible to perform all the properties (*dharma*) pertaining to *soma*, one should produce those partial properties found in the *pūtīka* plant.
For it will be stated later that "in some cases, an injunction is for the purpose of restriction," and "that [restriction] is constant because of the desire to perform that [action]."

Therefore, there is no defect here at all; rather, [the mention of *pūtīka*] is for the purpose of indicating the properties of Soma. Consequently, even that which is based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is not different from the previous case.
Thus, the very same purpose for the deliberation applies here as well.
Therefore, since the basis [of the ritual] remains and its cognition does not depart, one must proceed with the optional rites for specific qualities (*guṇakāma*).
Others say: "Since those desiring specific qualities (guṇakāma) depend upon the entirety of the individual components, they do not proceed here [in the case of a deficiency].

For since a compulsory rite (nitya-karman), which by its very nature must be commenced and brought to completion, must necessarily be finished, it is logical that even if some part is deficient, there is permission for it to remain non-defective (avaiguṇya). However, just as there is no commencement of optional rites (kāmya) by means of substitutes, so too one should not proceed with those desiring specific qualities. But if, while some ritual procedure for a quality-desire has been commenced, the substance is lost—as stated in the Tantravārtika—"

Since that [sacrifice] must necessarily be completed, its completion—whether by means of a substitute or by the original procedure—is equivalent; thus, the purpose [of the discussion] lies precisely in the modification (*ūha*) or non-modification (*anūha*). As for the terminuses (*saṃsthā*), they are governed by the same injunction because there is no distinction in their context.

The *Jyotiṣṭoma* is determined to have four terminuses, consisting of multiple repetitions of the cup-offering (*graha*) and the bowl-offering (*camasa*); however, the essential form of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* is woven through all these terminuses.

Just as Devadatta’s identity as Devadatta does not depart even when there are differences in his states—such as standing, sitting, walking, or lying down—so too, the essential nature of the Jyotiṣṭoma does not depart despite the arising and passing away of its various terminuses (*saṃsthā*). Furthermore, because the terminuses are mutually contradictory, they do not coexist; however, the form of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself persists everywhere without contradiction.
And that Jyotiṣṭoma is enjoined for the sake of a fruit, as in the injunction: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma."
Similarly, for the *saṃsthās* such as the *ukthya* and others, there are injunctions regarding results, such as "one desiring cattle should take up the *ukthya*.

With reference to this very *jyotiṣṭoma* of such a kind, the ritual duties (*dharmas*) such as the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the *gavāmayana* are taught; these are now questioned: are they enjoined with reference to the *jyotiṣṭoma* in all its *saṃsthās*, or only with reference to the *agniṣṭoma* *saṃsthā* alone?

However, this formulation is not tenable, for at the time of the connection with the duties, no particular *saṃsthā* is heard in scripture as a qualifying attribute of the *jyotiṣṭoma* which is being pointed out.

Even if they were somehow heard [in the text], nevertheless, because they function as qualifiers of that which is being indicated (*uddiśyamāna*), they would not be included. Furthermore, the Jyotiṣṭoma does not possess the status of a "grasper" (*grāhaka*) with respect to the inclusion of the Ukthya and other elements; for it is precisely the Ukthya and others that become possessed of the *itikartavyatā* (procedural details) by virtue of their being the means to the result. Since the Jyotiṣṭoma exists as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) by serving as their substrate, it is understood to be unfit for the reception of these ritual properties (*dharma*).

As for the phrase "one desiring heaven [should sacrifice] with the Jyotiṣṭoma," there is a division of this [sentence]—so reads the manuscript from Ka. This concludes the sixth quarter of the third chapter.

Since the connection of the *jyotiṣṭoma* with its ritual properties (*dharma*) is indistinguishable across all its terminuses (*saṃsthā*), it is incorrect to say that it belongs to the *agniṣṭoma* terminus alone; therefore, it must be stated thus:
"Does this measurement of properties belong to the *jyotiṣṭoma* itself, or to the terminuses such as the *ukthya* and others?
And that [point] is to be supported in this way, as has been stated in the text.

Although these [rites] are grasped by means of their specific forms (saṃsthās), nevertheless, because those forms themselves are not of the nature of action, the Jyotiṣṭoma alone serves as their substrate; thus, it is said that [the rule] "begins with" applies to all forms.
Does this mean it refers to that which serves as the substrate and possesses a fruit, or does it refer only to that which possesses a fruit?

And when it is for the sake of the Jyotiṣṭoma alone, then, because it is not common to others and by process of elimination, it arises only for the Agniṣṭoma form; therefore, the designation belongs to that specific form.

For although the Jyotiṣṭoma also possesses the capacity to receive [ritual details] in the Ukthya and other forms, nevertheless that capacity is not manifested; for it remains doubtful whether the ritual details received by the Ukthya and others accrue to this [Jyotiṣṭoma] because it serves as their door (dvāra), or because they are the means to its own specific results. Furthermore, since the Agniṣṭoma-saṃsthā is its inherent limb (nijamaṅga), one may say that when it receives [details] while established in that form, it receives them all.

Therefore, the commonality of ritual details has been correctly set forth; and since both the direct injunction (upadeśa) and the extended application (atideśa) are admitted in both views, the term "vidhāna" (injunction) is employed.

What is established? That the prescription of the ritual details (*dharma*) for the terminuses (*saṃsthā*) is common to the Jyotiṣṭoma. Why? Because there is no distinction in the context (*prakaraṇa*). For the Jyotiṣṭoma, being possessed of a fruit, gives rise to the requirement of "how" (*kathaṃbhāva*); thus, it takes up those [details] recited in its proximity through that continuity, and not merely by virtue of being the Jyotiṣṭoma. And this applies equally to the Ukthya and the others. Since all of these are undifferentiated with respect to these ritual details, and since extended application (*atideśa*) occurs only when direct instruction (*upadeśa*) is impossible, therefore the direct instruction itself is common. Furthermore, the designation is equal.
By prescribing the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the remnant, [the text] mentions it as being connected to the context of the sacrifice (*kratuprakaraṇa*), just like the *tulyavat* (equal) conclusion.
As stated in the *Tantravārtika*: "If it is an *agniṣṭoma*, he offers;

if it is an *ukthya*, he anoints the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) with that very remnant; if it is an *atirātra*, having muttered this very *homayajuṣ* formula, 'O Agni, [protect] the mortal in battles,' he should proceed to the *havirdhāna*. From this, it is understood that the entire rule regarding the subsidiary parts (*aṅgavidhi*) is common (*sādhāraṇa*) to all.

What you have stated is as unreasonable as the *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* inference; for if something mentioned in a particular context were connected with the *saṃsthās* by virtue of the sentence alone, then why should it not also be connected even with that which is unrelated? Indeed, in cases such as "of the twelve-day sacrifice" (*dvādaśāhīnasya*) and so forth, it is not suspected that the subsidiary properties (*śeṣadharma*) are intended for the purpose of the *ahīna*.

Having set forth the statement "because of the mention of the words," he explains it as follows: For if that which is prescribed generally were to belong only to the Agniṣṭoma form, then its status as an auxiliary would be established even without the inclusion of that [word]; thus, he would not have mentioned the Agniṣṭoma. Since, however, he does mention it, we conclude that surely it cannot be obtained for the Agniṣṭoma unless it is specified. And this cannot be obtained if the context (prakaraṇa) is common to the various forms (saṃsthās) as well. On the other hand, if the position were that the context belongs solely to the Jyotiṣṭoma, then the repetition [of the word] would be redundant.

Similarly, if the Ukthya and other rites also possess a *prakaraṇa* (contextual setting), then it is appropriate to mention them with the word "if" (*yadi*) for the purpose of determining one or the other; however, if they are not part of the context, there would be a connection [to the main rite] even without the word "if," as in the case of the phrase "of the twelve-day sacrifice" (*dvādaśāhīnasya*). Indeed, such a statement—namely, "If it is the Jyotiṣṭoma, then this; if it is the Dvādaśāha, then that"—is not logical for one who remains within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma alone.
For that statement depends upon many things being present; therefore, for this reason as well, the context is the same.
This is another indicative mark:

"In the Agniṣṭoma, one should sacrifice a goat dedicated to Agni; in the Ukthya, a bull dedicated to Indra-Agni; in the Ṣoḍaśin, a wild ox dedicated to Indra; and in the third [Atirātra], a hornless goat."

If they are of equal status (*samānavidhāna*), then because each preceding one is perceived in scripture as being [the basis for] each succeeding one, the second and third observations are established as being performed.

However, under the view that they are modifications (*vikāra*), since the *āgneya* sacrifice would be set aside by the *aindrāgna* and others which are directly heard in scripture, there would be only one [form] everywhere.
But even if they are directly heard in scripture, because one sacrificial form (*saṃsthā*) cannot coexist with another sacrificial form, [this is so]. This is the sixth section of the third chapter.
In the absence of a specific indicative mark (*nirnimitta*), each preceding [sacrifice] cannot be attained.

For that which is completed at the *agniṣṭoma* stotra is indeed the *agniṣṭoma*, and not merely that much; likewise, that which is completed in the *ukthya* and subsequent [stages] is not completed in the preceding one. Therefore, the contingency of applying [the result] based on the observation of the second [stage] is equal in both positions.
It is true that they are equal in their status as *saṃsthās* (terminuses), but they are combined (*samuccaya*) insofar as they are the causes for the *stotra*.
Thus the author of the Bhāṣya says: "For there are two causes therein—the Agniṣṭoma-stotra and the Ukthya-stotra"—he states this as an established fact.

But how is it that, when the mention of the Agniṣṭoma and so forth is equally common to both the *saṃsthā* and the *stotra*, only the status of being the cause for the *stotra* is accepted, and not the status of being the cause for the *saṃsthā*?
For since these [stomas] possess a purpose by virtue of their being results, they attain the status of a cause (*nimitta*) without any difficulty.
Regarding this, some say:

even though the word is common [to all], one resorts to the stoma as the cause in order to favor the great scope of the scripture; or else, because the *saṃsthā* (sacrificial session) is thus qualified by the stoma, and since it is possible for that which has already been previously perceived as the qualifier to serve as the cause, it is not proper to assume a later-occurring qualification as the cause.
Or rather, according to the principle of the *ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, the word is primary with respect to the stotras and figurative with respect to the *saṃsthās*;
and when direct denotation (*śruti*) is impossible, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) must be resorted to.
Moreover, the stotra is also capable of being understood as the occasioning cause (*nimitta*) due to its mention in the locative case.
Furthermore, even for acts such as piercing that are otherwise fruitless, their status as a *nimitta* (occasioning condition) is accepted by virtue of the power of the scriptural statement.
Alternatively, according to the principle "in cases of doubt, [the decision is made] from the remainder of the sentence" (*saṃdigdheṣu vākyaśeṣāt*), there is recourse to the *stotra* (hymn).

Or, even though the *saṃsthās* (termini of the sacrifice) possess primary importance, the *stotra* is adopted through the remainder of the sentence by means of a restrictive interpretation (*vyavaccheda-kalpanā*).
For it is heard thus:
"One should sacrifice a goat dedicated to Agni (āgneya) at the Agniṣṭoma, for the Agniṣṭoma belongs to Agni.

In which [type of] Agniṣṭoma is this one dedicated to Agni? For while the deity Agni exists as a participant in the praise (*stuti*) of the *stotra*, he does not exist as a participant in the *saṃsthā* (the formal conclusion of the rite).
For that [non-existence] consists in the abandonment of activity and is thus of the nature of non-being; and there is no function for a deity with respect to non-being.

As stated in the *Tantravārttika*: "Even when the sacrifice is repeated, the deity belongs only to that [sacrifice], thereby effecting its *āgneyatva* (the state of being dedicated to Agni), not that of the completion (*saṃsthā*)."
Nor is that very [deity] the *saṃsthā* (the completion),
because the verb *tiṣṭhati* preceded by the prefix *sam-* denotes indifference at a time subsequent to that [action]. Furthermore, a designation belonging to one deity cannot apply to another.
The same should be shown for the Ukthya and Ṣoḍaśin as well;
moreover, in the phrase "the Ukthyas dedicated to Indra and Agni," there is a clear reference to the *stotra* (hymns),
for by this term "Ukthyas" the *saṃsthā* (ritual terminuses) are certainly not meant.
Therefore, since the hymns serve as the occasion for the ritual, their combination is logical.

Now, one might object: even under the view that they are modifications (*vikāra*), because the animal sacrifices have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), it is impossible for them to take on each other's functions; thus, their combination is indeed justified.
For it is not the case that everything which is merely inferential is sublated by what is directly perceived.

When there is a conflict, there is indeed sublation, and conflict occurs when two things occupy the same scope. For all the animal sacrifices, being applicable everywhere, the later ones do not occur in the earlier *saṃsthās* because of the absence of their cause; however, by means of a perceptible cause, each preceding sacrifice is established in the subsequent one through the force of the sentence (*vākya*). In this regard, should one assume a single function based on the name (*samākhyā*) and then resort to either sublation or option, or should one assume a plurality of functions in accordance with the combination (*samuccaya*) obtained from the sentence? Since the sentence is more powerful, there must be a combination.

Just as in the case of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings, although there is identity of name (*samākhyā*), there is a difference in function due to the syntactical connection (*vākya*) and their combination (*samuccaya*); so too, in the case of extended application (*atideśa*), there is identity of function through the name, yet a difference in function through the extended application itself— and thus there is no contradiction.

Therefore, since the designation (samākhyā) contained within the instructional text (upadeśa) is indeed more powerful, one should accept the burning [of the head] by resorting to the unity of the body as established by that [designation]. Furthermore, because there is a requirement for connection with the characteristics of the original form (prakṛti-liṅga-saṃyoga) in the case of a modification (vikāra), it is understood to be a case of functional transference (kāryāpatti).
However, in the view that they share the same rule (samāna-vidhi-pakṣa), no connection with the characteristics of the original form exists, and thus functional transference would not be determined.
Some say:

"If they were of equal injunction (*samānavidhi*), a difference in rituals would be determined by the conjunctions of substance and deity which are mutually independent; however, in the case of a modification (*vikāra*), a mere accessory (*guṇa*) is enjoined by way of restating a sacrifice already obtained through extension (*atideśa*), and therefore there would be only one sacrifice, not a second and so forth. But this injunction of an accessory regarding the *aindrāgna* [offering] is possible; it is not [possible] for Indra and Sarasvatī, because enjoining multiple substances and deities would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), and thus there is certainly a distinct ritual (*karmāntara*)."

Therefore, it must be established in this way: when this other subsidiary (karmāntara) is being enjoined, does it attain the status of being a means for a distinct transcendental result (*apūrva*), or does it accomplish the very same transcendental result as the original *savanīya* offering? Since the application [of the subsidiary] is possible through the mere connection with the previously established transcendental result, it is not proper to assume a new transcendental result and determine that it is a means for that.

Likewise, even the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) does not, at the time it requires a means of accomplishment, abandon the *savanīya* sacrifice directly enjoined by scripture to take up another *savanīya*. For in all cases of requirement, when the primary element is unavailable, one takes what has been previously established; thus, the operation belonging to the sacrifice, having its connection already fixed with the original *apūrva*, cannot enter into a connection with a different *apūrva*. If it is asked, "How can another *savanīya* sacrifice, whose capacity is not yet established, accomplish the original *apūrva*?"—the answer is that there is no fault, just as in the other alternative where a different *apūrva* accomplishes the operation belonging to the sacrifice.
What, then, is the distinction between these two?
It is said:
when they reside in the operation pertaining to the sacrifice.

The archetypal (prakṛti) apūrvas are not displaced at that time; rather, it is the modified (vaikṛta) savanīya apūrva that is established, and it is into that [modified] portion that [the new element] falls. However, when a ritual action is displaced by means of an apūrva, one then perceives another existing action—one connected with the characteristic marks of the savanīya archetype—and thereby rejects the archetypal one. Furthermore, since the assumption of an apūrva occurs within the archetype, four distinct apūrvas are postulated corresponding to the four savanīya offerings being enjoined.
For it is not known therein which specific apūrva is more firmly established such that it could have a connection with a different means of accomplishment.

For at the time of reflecting upon the ritual action (*karma*), only the forms of the actions themselves are perceived; even the postulation of an *apūrva* (unseen potency) occurs simultaneously, so no distinction is known [between them]. However, in the view that [the *apūrva*] is a modification (*vikāra*), it is known that the primordial (*prākṛta*) form is postulated earlier. Thus, since one of the two actions must necessarily be abandoned, the more remote primordial form would have to be discarded, which results in the undesirable consequence of sublation (*bādhaprasaṅga*).

But surely, under the view that these are modifications (*vikāra*), the subsequent sacrificial terminuses (*saṃsthā*) would be modifications of the *agniṣṭoma* terminus alone, and not of one another; thus, because the original *āgneya* [offering] which has been established would be sublated by the subsequent ones, there would be no observation of a second [instance] anywhere. Why, then, is it said that "the observation of a third does not obtain"? This is not a fault, for if he were to say that there is non-observation due to the sublation of the subsequent [offerings] such as the *aindrāgna* and others once they have been established, that would be without proof; however, what he says here is merely that there is no observation.

And that [sublation] is indeed logical because of the sublation of the Āgneya sacrifice and because it is not obtained in the two middle ones; for that very reason, the Āgneya would be sublated by it. Thus he says: "The former is not [sublated] by the latter. Therefore, they are prescribed as equal. But in the case of a connection with a specific desire (*kāmasaṃyoga*), there are modifications (*vikāra*), because of the equality of the obligatory (*nitya*) rite.

The *ukthya* and other such [sacrificial forms] are specific terminations (*samāpti-viśeṣa*) that, being enjoined as means to a result, require a substrate consisting of a completion. They take their place by modifying the original Agniṣṭoma Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice’s own Agniṣṭoma-termination; thus, they are designated by the term "modification" (*vikāra*). Now, it might be argued: "If the status of the *ukthya* and others as terminations were already established, then there would be a requirement for a substrate possessing those terminations. However, prior to their connection with the Jyotiṣṭoma, their status as terminations was not established. [This is answered in the *Tantravārtika*:]...
The term "completion" (*samāpti*) is applied because its accomplishment depends upon both the beginning and the middle.

Now, if there were first a connection with that [result], then, once it is determined to be for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) at the outset, there would be no connection with a result; and since it would thus be equal to the obligatory (*nitya*) rite, the consequence would be that it is subject to modification (*avikāra*).
Furthermore:
And when the injunction regarding the result is clearly stated in relation to the act of drawing [the cup] and so forth,
how can the connection of the results with the ritual forms (saṃsthās) be determined?
But surely, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the statement "one should draw the ukthya," it would apply to the acts of drawing and so forth themselves.
This is not so.
Because of its connection with the Ukthya-stotra, it is the completion itself that is denoted by the word "Ukthya"; through that connection, the cup (graha) is figuratively designated as such.

Furthermore, when a primary sense is possible, a figurative one should not be accepted; for the use of terms like "Ukthya" is always observed in grammatical coordination with the word "sacrifice" (yajña).
"One should sacrifice with the Ukthya, for the Ukthya is the sacrifice.
Likewise, "one sacrifices with the Ṣoḍaśin; the Ṣoḍaśin is the sacrifice.

Indeed, there is no sacrifice named "Ṣoḍaśin" [as a distinct entity]; rather, that term is appropriate as a designation for the final completion that is not separate from the end [of the rite], and not as a designation for the cup (graha) or the hymn (stotra).

Furthermore, the term *ṣoḍaśī* is masculine and denotes completion; thus, it is appropriate [as the name] for the sixth section (*pāda*) of the third chapter. Since the neuter form denotes a hymn (*stotra*), as for the occasional use of the masculine form in reference to a hymn—such as "the twenty-first *ṣoḍaśī*"—it should be understood as being used figuratively (*gauṇa*).

In this supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), the masculine term *ṣoḍaśī* is understood; thus, it denotes a *saṃsthā* (a completed ritual form). In the phrase "for one desiring offspring, [one should perform] the Atirātra," the fact that it denotes a *saṃsthā* is perfectly clear, for no other action is mentioned there. Furthermore, the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is heard as subordinate to the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) and would have to be made the primary element with great difficulty. Therefore, the completion (*samāpti*) which follows after the night is what is connected with the fruit.

Furthermore, if there were a connection between the *graha* (cup) and the *stotra* (hymn) with respect to the result, then—since those two are actions (*kriyā*)—they would have no requirement for a substratum (*āśraya*), and thus their employment would necessarily follow as being entirely independent. Moreover, the purpose of their mention within the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the employment of terms such as *ukthya* and so forth would remain unintelligible.
Therefore, for this reason also, the *samsthās* (terminuses) possess results.
As for how they can be considered "terminuses" prior to their connection with a specific sacrifice (*kratu*), some say as follows: [text continues]

Since it is recorded that "there are seven Soma-sacrifices—the Agniṣṭoma, Atirātra, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśin, Atirātra, Vājapeya, and Aptoryāma"—and since it is established that [the term] refers to the completion of the Soma sacrifice, the Jyotiṣṭoma is established as the substratum by virtue of the context, as no other rites are required when only the Soma sacrifice in general is intended.

Others, however, hold that in certain specific repetitions of the *agniṣṭoma*, another sacrifice is known to arise—one which receives the designation of an *ukthya* and so forth and is connected with a fruit; in that case, because the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is more authoritative, the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*), which is obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*), is set aside.
As for the relationship between the substratum and the dependent (*āśrayāśrayi-sambandha*), it is accepted because it is consistent [with the other evidence].

Furthermore, another view holds that something denoted by terms such as *ukthya* and so forth is connected with the fruit from the very beginning; however, when there is a requirement for that [connection], it is understood through another scriptural statement (*vacana*) that it occurs at the conclusion of the *jyotiṣṭoma*. Alternatively, this is merely a specific modification (*vyāsaviśeṣa*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma* which, being enjoined for the sake of a fruit while entering into the end of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, causes the sacrifice to be completed either by that [modification] or in that [state]; thus it is designated by the term "conclusion" (*saṃsthā*). Others, however, think differently.

The term *saṃsthā* (completion) refers to the cessation of activity immediately following the final repetition; it is not, however, logical for this [cessation] to be the means of attaining a result, since its nature is non-action (*akriyātmaka*). Therefore, it is the repetition characterized by that [cessation] which is enjoined. Others, however, say:
"Since there is no excessive burden on the verbal injunction, even a non-entity (*abhāva*), when being enjoined, is not at all contradicted as being a means of attaining a result."
Just as in the statement "one who does not perform the enjoined rite," non-performance—which is non-existent—serves as the cause of sin;
or alternatively, there exists indeed a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) in the form of adopting an attitude of indifference, and thus there is no contradiction.

Furthermore, in this context, how a result arises from a subordinate factor (*guṇa*), and how a desired subordinate factor modifies the meaning of an obligatory (*nitya*) rite, should be understood by drawing upon the *Indriyakāmādhikaraṇa* and the *Godohanādhikaraṇa*.
He demonstrates this:
"In such cases, the accomplishment of the fruit arises from the qualities alone.
For it is heard thus:

"One desiring cattle should take the Ukthya cup, not one desiring the Jyotiṣṭoma, nor one merely desiring the taking of the Ukthya"—by this [statement], the author refutes its being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*). For if it were for the sake of the sacrifice, even without the connection of the word "desiring" (*kāma*), it would be understood that this must be performed simply because it is beneficial to the sacrifice. Furthermore, if the mere nature of taking the Ukthya were what was intended to be performed, then by implication this injunction would belong to one desiring the taking of the Ukthya, since his prayer would be: "How may the very nature of taking the Ukthya be accomplished? However, that too is untenable because of the mention of "one desiring cattle."

Therefore, because it is optional (*kāmya*), there exists a status as a modification (*vikāratva*) according to the analogy of the *godohana* vessel; in that regard, when there is an expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*), the procedure belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma is extended (*atidiśyate*) [to it].

But what is the mode here by which the procedure is grasped? If it were by way of proximity (*sannidhāna*), then it would be accepted that there is a common injunction (*samānavidhāna*), for proximity is not the cause of extension, since it will be stated later that extension arises from similarity (*sādṛśya*). If, on the other hand, it is by way of being something to be performed (*kāryitva*), even in that case, the existence of another cause has been refuted.

Furthermore, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are not properties of the *saṃsthās* (concluding forms), such that they would apply when one *saṃsthā* is replaced by another; for the *ukthya* and other forms do not function as the purpose (*kārya*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, which is why they are undertaken in its stead. By this, the position of "extended application" (*atideśapakṣa*) is refuted. For one who thinks that the properties will exist through extended application, there is no basis for such extension, namely, similarity (*sārūpya*). Although there is a commonality with the *agniṣṭoma* *saṃsthā*, there is no similarity whatsoever between the *jyotiṣṭoma* and the *ukthya* and others; thus, it lacks the status of being the archetype (*prakṛti*).

For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya, having stated only "because of proximity" (*sannidhānāt*), remained silent; therefore, that which ought to have been said by him is now being expressed.
It has already been established previously that this is an extension (*atideśa*).
Furthermore, similarity alone is not the sole cause for an extension.

If this [status of being for the sake of the obligatory] is asserted as belonging to the obligatory even without logical justification, why is it not said that it belongs to the optional alone? This would be far more illogical.
If you desire that it applies solely to the obligatory even without any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then, alas, let it apply solely to the optional by my will as well!

Now, if this [position] is not accepted because it lacks authoritative proof (*apramāṇaka*), then let it be desired that there be a commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) like that of authoritative means of knowledge.

In this regard, the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), unable to tolerate such hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), and intending to assist the position of commonality, first refutes by logic the position of mere optional rites (*kāmya*) even though it is without proof:
"In every case where there is a desire for a quality, that occurs only when the action is being accomplished, and not otherwise."

If indeed a subordinate element (*guṇa*) were capable of independently grasping the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), then this [consequence] would follow. But how could it be so? It could only be so if the instrument (*karaṇa*) were connected with the procedure, and if the subordinate elements themselves were the qualifiers of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*). First of all, it has already been stated that the instrument is not connected with the procedure.

And regarding the seventh, ninth, and first [sections], he will explain how one should meditate (*bhāvayet*), in response to the expectation [of that method]; it is not the case that there is no instrument (*karaṇa*) or no "how.

However, in that meditation where the meanings of verbal roots (*dhātvartha*) serve as the instrument, they—being independent of any other entity—subsequently obtain a connection with the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) which is obtained through the principle of the "red one-year-old cow" (*aruṇaikahāyanī*).

Furthermore, in that [bhāvanā] where the qualities (guṇas) function as instruments, since their status as instruments is untenable through the specific meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) alone, another verbal root-meaning existing as the object to be accomplished (sādhya) must be expected. For the production of a mere general activity (vyāpārasāmānya) by means of qualities is not possible; nor does a quality attain the status of being a general instrument without accomplishing a specific action. Therefore, in whichever bhāvanā a quality situated therein adopts its procedure (itikartavyatā), the verbal root-meaning is seen to be the first to be established within it.
And consequently, he first established a rule regarding the host of gods together with him.

If that [substance] were not capable of being grasped as part of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), then it would not be grasped; however, because it possesses a fruit and because it is a qualification of the *bhāvanā* which serves as the gateway to the procedure, it is in no way not grasped. In this regard, all four factors prompt its prior grasping. First, the *bhāvanā* cannot grasp the procedure without the specific meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and so forth. Furthermore, a quality (*guṇa*) cannot independently grasp it without bringing about the meaning of the verbal root, because it lacks a *bhāvanā* independent of that [root], and because the mere sense of "acting" (*karoti-artha*)—being devoid of qualifications—is neither something to be performed nor an activity (*vyāpāra*). Therefore, [the quality] takes recourse [to the root-meaning].

Similarly, the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance), while proceeding toward the subordinate quality (*guṇa*), cannot proceed by overstepping the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*); thus, it first falls upon that [root-meaning]. And since the meaning of the verbal root itself requires the *itikartavyatā*, why would it—being capable of grasping this [manner of performance] which has set out for the sake of the subordinate quality—abandon it?

Therefore, when the Ukthya and other sacrifices—impelled toward their own results and understood to have the Jyotiṣṭoma as their substratum—are in need of a procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites, being brought forward by the context (*prakaraṇa*), necessarily fall into the mouth of the Jyotiṣṭoma due to the absence of any other path. For the Ukthya and others, being of the nature of a completion (*samāpti*), are not capable of grasping those rites by bypassing it; nor does the Jyotiṣṭoma ever disregard those things that have fallen into its own mouth. As it is said: "That which does not exist for the sake of the goal [to be accomplished] is not connected with the means."

That specific mode of performance (*itikartavyatā*) is enjoined in this way: "One should act so that by means of this [act] there is the accomplishment of the fruit, [namely] the realization of the *ukthya* and other [sacrifices]"; the meaning is, "one should act in such a manner that it becomes an effective means.
Consequently, due to its contact with the root *kṛ* (to do), it is connected only with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).

This being the case, there is no such method by which, setting aside the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the *ukthya* and others could be made effective by means of this mode of performance.
The meaning is: "when the action is not being accomplished," that is, when it is not being performed.

As for those who connect [the phrase] "by that which is not being accomplished" with "by the Ukthya and so forth," for them there would be a lack of coherence due to the abandonment of the specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*) previously introduced; furthermore, there would be redundancy with the phrase "when the action is being accomplished. Therefore, even one who desires a procedure for the means (*sādhaka*), as stated in the *Guṇatantra-vārttika*, must accept that this [procedure] belongs to the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), which is the meaning of the verbal root.
Thus, having stated the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), he now applies it to the specific case under discussion, stating: "and the Jyotiṣṭoma is the object to be accomplished" (*sādhya*).
Therefore, it cannot first of all have the status of being solely for the sake of a desired result (*kāmyārtha*).
Now, as to why it does not have a common [status], the second position is presented on the grounds of its superior strength (*balavattva*).
The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntavādin) says: "Because they are recorded as if they were permanent.

For a connection through a single ritual procedure (tantra) is possible only when there is uniformity (ekarūpya) in all respects; however, there is no such uniformity between the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and its various terminuses (saṃsthās) with respect to their constituent elements (dharmas).

For the constituent elements (*dharmas*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* are traditionally taught as if they were permanent, due to the absence of any connection with specific causal motives (*kāraṇanimitta*). Thus, whenever there is a *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites must be performed. Furthermore, even when the *Jyotiṣṭoma* exists, the *Ukthya* and other terminuses (*saṃsthās*) do not occur without a specific motive such as the desire for cattle; and when one terminus is being employed, another terminus necessarily cannot occur simultaneously. However, it is never the case that the *Jyotiṣṭoma* itself is absent from these [terminuses], because it inheres in each of them in its entirety, like a genus (*jāti*).
Therefore, these [details] are connected with the Jyotiṣṭoma as they are recited in the scripture, not with the occasional (anitya) terminuses (saṃsthā).

Now, even though these terminuses are occasional, since the single Jyotiṣṭoma is eternal (nitya), the scriptural injunction of the details—which is formulated as if for something eternal—will not be contradicted by being for the sake of the occasional; rather, that eternal injunction will fulfill its purpose with respect to that [eternal sacrifice].
But if, on the contrary, another occasional connection is postulated even while acknowledging that [eternal one], what of ours is sublated?

That which presents itself as permanent for the sake of what is actually permanent is contradicted; it is not of such a nature. This is not so. If this were the case, the principle of "body" (*tantra*) would first be abandoned, because it would fall under the definition of being non-contributory (*aprayojaka*).
