For when the recitation is performed for the sake of what is permanent, it cannot exist without that purpose; and once that purpose is established and the requirement is satisfied, any subsequent connection with other elements occurs only by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*), and thus there is no commonality of subject matter (*sāmānaviṣya*).

Otherwise, there would be this rule regarding the ritual procedure (*dharma-vidhi*): "One should always perform these rituals in the Jyotiṣṭoma, and also occasionally when there is a desire for cattle and so forth. And that is contradictory for a single injunction. [Objection: But surely these two are injunctions inferred from their respective contexts (*prakaraṇa*); one of them will enjoin them as permanent (*nitya*), and the other as non-permanent (*anitya*). [Reply: True, there is no contradiction because of the difference between the two *prayoga-vacana*s (injunctions of performance). However, the *prayoga-vacana*s themselves are contradicted because they must conform to a performance-injunction that is either permanent or non-permanent.
Therefore, by one who desires not to obstruct their eternity, the apprehender must necessarily be accepted as being that very same [self].
Consequently, because there is no deviation [from this fact], it is logical that [the sacrifice] has the Jyotiṣṭoma as its sole purpose.

Now, one might object: "Since even the *agniṣṭoma* termination is optional (*kāmya*), and since all terminations are thus non-obligatory (*anitya*), and there is no form of the *jyotiṣṭoma* other than these that is obligatory (*nitya*), then—because the *jyotiṣṭoma* is enjoined as obligatory—all the ritual properties (*dharma*) must be brought in equally through its medium; therefore, because it cannot be determined where an obligatory performance exists, the properties will necessarily apply only to the optional cases according to the logic of alternative options (*vikalpa*). To this, he says: "That [property] belongs to the obligatory [form], because of its equality. This means: Since the *jyotiṣṭoma* itself is established as obligatory by the injunction "One should sacrifice with the *jyotiṣṭoma*," and since the various terminations are merely specific forms of that same obligatory rite, they share the status of being obligatory. Therefore, the properties are brought in equally for all terminations, and there is no lack of determination regarding the obligatory performance. Consequently, the rule of alternatives does not apply here. Thus, the properties belong to the obligatory form.

For the injunctions regarding what serves the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*) and what serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) are indeed equal; for, having considered both, according to the principle "but when one [act] has both [purposes], there is a separation of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), the connection with desire applies only to that which is constant up to the *agniṣṭoma*, whereas the other is non-constant because its connection is solely with desire—this is the distinction.

Therefore, although this [agniṣṭoma] is non-eternal (anitya) by virtue of its performance, nevertheless, because the Jyotiṣṭoma is eternal and because this [agniṣṭoma] is eternal insofar as it is attained in relation to that [Jyotiṣṭoma], and because it obtains the subsequent portion of the properties grasped by that [Jyotiṣṭoma], there is thus the designation of the properties as belonging to the Agniṣṭoma. Alternatively, even though attainment occurs in the Ukthya and other forms as well, the distinction is that the attainment which occurs through the portion of the Jyotiṣṭoma is by way of direct instruction (upadeśa), whereas that which occurs through the portion of the Ukthya is of the nature of extended application (atideśa).
Furthermore, because of the explicit scriptural statement, there is a combination [of the two];
for a qualified injunction (viśiṣṭavidhi) does not entail an excessive burden.
"Then for this [text] also," according to the Kha manuscript;
from the *Tantravārtika*:
"And because of the prohibition of the previous indicative marks."

Furthermore, regarding the performance of sacrifices, when a subsequent injunction restates the absence of a prior element, it is subject to option (*vikalpa*) under the theory of modification (*vikārapakṣa*).

This is because the prior element, though obtained through the general rule (*codaka*), is superseded by the subsequent one. For if there were equal status in the injunction (*sāmānavidhya*), since the occasion is directly present, the occasional rite (*naimittika*) would necessarily have to be performed, resulting in a combination (*samuccaya*); thus, your proposed prohibition, if accepted as a separate injunction, would split the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
For in this case, a distinct injunction for the second and third days is not possible;
because there would be a contradiction between an injunction and a prohibition, and because an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is impossible.

Here, in all instances concerning the *savanīya* animal sacrifice, the reasoning stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) must be countered by the arguments of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). For if the occasion were the completion of the rite (*saṃsthā*), then even though the rule would be uniform (*sāmānavidhya*), the observation of its non-occurrence would be logical due to the absence of that specific occasion.

Even in the Siddhānta, since there is a possibility of their combination because they serve an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha), it should be understood that the designation "instrument of the sacrifice" (kratukaraṇa-samākhyā) is an indicative mark (liṅga) from the archetype (prakṛti). However, some say: "Just as in the case of the disposal of the remnants of the *pracaraṇī* oblation, when the oblation is disposed of by means of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), its non-existence [in the modification] is established despite the commonality of the injunction (*sāmānavidhya*). To this it must be replied: "But when it is enjoined as an independent act by means of a direct statement (*vākya*), how can its status as a disposal (*pratipatti*)—which was not under discussion—be understood?"

And even though the offering is accomplished by means of the oblation, as long as the purpose of the term "smearing the enclosing-sticks" (paridhyañjana) is fulfilled and something is expressed by the direct Vedic statement (śruti), that much indeed remains possible; therefore, according to the reasoning already stated, this mention of non-existence is merely an observation.

The designation of one thing [as another] is due to a specific quality; however, the connection with the word "if" (yadi) regarding that which is not the primary subject matter is not tenable, as in the case of the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) and others.
The *nokthya* and other rites do not possess equality with other rites that are not part of the original context (*aprakṛta*).

For although these [rites]— due to the contradiction of being joined with both the permanent and the non-permanent— are not the cause for grasping the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) according to the sixth section of the third chapter, nevertheless, because they are proximate, they receive the designation of the word "if" (*yadi*).

Alternatively, through the string of qualities belonging to the subject at hand, it is possible for the qualities of even those things under discussion to be treated as if they were the primary subjects themselves.

Furthermore, the mention of the *agniṣṭoma*, which is already established by the context, is a restatement of what is constant (*nityānuvāda*). Or else, since its purpose is to establish that [the *agniṣṭoma*] is the occasion for the hymns (*stotra*), it is indeed meaningful; thus there is no fault.
"What is the purpose [of this]?
Some say it is exactly like the *phalacamasa* (the fruit-cup).

But this must be said: while it is true that this is the purpose, it does not apply to all ritual elements (*dharma*). For as many accessory-desires (*guṇakāma*) as there are in the measurements of the *sadas* and so forth—even when there is an extension (*atideśa*), that very basis (*āśraya*) which is directly taught (*aupadeśika*) remains; thus they are not destroyed, unlike [the case] of other modifications (*vikṛti*)."

For in other modified forms (*vikṛti*), because the *Jyotiṣṭoma*—which serves as the substrate—is absent, the desires for specific qualities (*guṇakāma*) do not occur according to their literal scriptural injunctions, and thus they are not established.

However, in the case of the terminuses (*saṃsthā*), although the fruit of a subsidiary (*aṅga*) is not extended by analogy, nevertheless, since a person desiring to act is personally motivated, when there is the possibility of a substrate as heard in the text during the employment of a quality, there is no inconsistency regarding the desires for those qualities.

Therefore, the purpose [of this discussion] is that whatever non-archetypal elements—such as the *mukthya* cups, the *stotras*, and the *śastras*—are occasioned by the *saṃsthās* like the *mukthya* and so forth, and which might otherwise be obtained through the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rules for other cups, *stotras*, and *śastras* for the sake of certain desired qualities (*guṇakāma*), those do not apply here. Furthermore, if they were governed by the same injunction (*samānavidhāna*), then according to the principle "but in the case of the manifest forms of Soma" (*vyaktāsu tu somasya*), all *saṃsthās* would be established as optional alternatives in those modifications (*vikāra*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma; however, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), only the *agniṣṭoma* *saṃsthā* proceeds. Thus, it is established that the acquisition of those specific rules occurs only where there is an explicit injunction (*codanā*) for particular features such as the *ukthya* and so forth. This is the proven purpose.
Thus ends the sixth quarter of the third chapter in the *Tantra-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Kumārila. In the *Tantravārtika*:
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
[The rule] "that which is not connected [to a specific rite] belongs to the primary [rite] due to the distinction of context" [is established].

This topic is also introduced under the heading of the rules for common and uncommon [elements], by way of the conflict or non-conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*).

Regarding the altar (*vedi*) situated within the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), as well as its properties such as digging, and likewise the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and its properties such as cutting—what is their purpose?

Although, through an unqualified statement such as "he cuts the sacrificial grass on the altar" or "he digs the altar," there arises the notion that [these acts] serve both the subsidiary and the principal rites—just as "he places the oblations on the altar" and "he places the oblations on the sacrificial grass"—nevertheless, since these acts would apply even to ordinary sacrificial grass used for covering a house if they were independent, and this would lead to their purposelessness, one must necessarily accept a connection characterized by being a means to the *apūrva* (unseen potency). Furthermore, since that status of being a means to the *apūrva* is not perceived through the power of the sentence itself, it must be obtained from the context (*prakaraṇa*).

And thus, by the specific qualification "belonging to that [context] of the principal matter alone" (*tatprakaraṇam*), it is understood that the properties belong to the principal matter itself. Furthermore, although the context (*prakaraṇa*) does not possess the power to specify, it has been stated that its function as a cause for establishing a specification lies in its role as a grasper (*grāhaka*), since it does not enjoin anything without such a qualifier. As for the phrase "unconnected" (*asaṃyukta*), even though there is a connection between the oblation (*havis*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) through syntactical connection (*vākya*), this refers to the absence of a connection with a meaning that would contradict the context. For it is considered possible to integrate the words "oblation" and "sacrificial grass" within the context, unlike the *Ahīna* sacrifice, which is entirely unrelated.

Or rather, it applies to all [the subsidiaries], because subsidiariness does not depend on that [specific context]; for it has already been stated that there is no distinction in their connection with the sentence.
As for the claim that the context (*prakaraṇa*) is the specific factor that assigns [subsidiaries], he replies to that: "because it does not depend on that."
The meaning is that context (*prakaraṇa*) does not serve as a determinative factor here.

But how is it that the established status of context as a means of application (*viniyojaka*) is set aside? Or how can subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*)—characterized by utility (*upakāra*), which is distinct from the definition based on direct statement (*tādarthya*) and involves many defects—be asserted?
It is said in reply: context has no such power of application regarding matters of this kind; for it has been stated that "that which is not connected [by other means] is [determined] by context."

As for the claim that there is no contradiction—how can it be said there is none when, because the oblations (*havis*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) are primary, their connection with the ritual duties (*dharma*) applies to each individually, and even the fact that they serve as auxiliaries (*aṅga*), though known, is set aside in accordance with the context (*prakaraṇa*)? But the opponent, having understood the context to be free of contradiction once the over-extension of the syntactical connection (*vākya*) has been refuted by a certain reason, now puts forward this argument: "It would follow [by implication] even for worldly things, and consequently, [the Vedic injunction] would be rendered purposeless. To him, this very response must be stated: [The response: That is not so; for the application of the auxiliary character (*aṅgatva*) is restricted solely to those things which are connected with the sacrifice through the context. Since worldly things are not connected with the sacrifice, the application of the auxiliary character does not extend to them. Therefore, there is no such contingency of purposelessness. Furthermore, since the context is established as being without conflict, the restriction of the auxiliary character to the specific items within that context remains uncontradicted. Thus, the objection is refuted.

A sentence that proceeds by its own inherent force (*svarasapravṛtta*) should cease to apply from the very point where its meaninglessness becomes clearly manifest; however, the auxiliaries (*aṅga*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) do not possess meaninglessness like worldly things, and therefore they will remain applicable, nor does this lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

With this very intention, it is said: "For that [auxiliary] is characterized by its contribution (*upakāra*); its being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) is designated by means of the fruit. For when something is postulated as a purpose, it should be understood as serving a useful function only if it is capable of accomplishing the required contribution that was sought after. Therefore, it must be postulated as being for that specific purpose.

As for the fact that the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) stated "because of the context" (*prakaraṇāt*) in order to preclude over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), that should be disregarded for now as an overly hasty remark, since it results in the impossibility of introducing the subsequent objection (*paricodanā*).
[Tantravārtika:
"If it is argued that [the connection] exists even from afar..."]

For if the exclusion of ritual properties (*dharma*) from the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) used in worldly activities were due to its uselessness there, then it would follow that those properties should apply to the sacrificial grass used for other rites where such uselessness does not exist. If, however, there is some reason for that exclusion which applies equally to the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), then in the case of the *saurya* sacrifice and others, the properties would still exist by way of extension (*atideśa*). Thus, because it lacks both acquisition through direct injunction (*upadeśa*) and acquisition through extension (*atideśa*), the *Mṛgaśīrṣa-pitṛyajña* serves as the illustrative example.
For this [argument] will remain unprecedented and bodiless;
therefore, there is the consequence of an absolutely undesirable conclusion.
For that statement does not [establish] that meaning.

This might be so if this sentence were independent; however, since it is a sentence belonging to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with them. Therefore, the meaning is that this defect applies only to that sacrificial grass (*barhis*) which is included within the end of that single sentence, and not to that which belongs to a separate sentence.
Furthermore, the sacrificial grass of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is not included within the sentence of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*; therefore, it is not connected [to the defect].

Now, if it is intended that [the mantra] forms a single syntactical unit with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, then, since it cannot be obtained by any other means apart from their context (*prakaraṇa*), and since that context belongs only to the principal acts themselves, it would follow that there is no connection for the subsidiaries.
This is not a fault.

In any case, acts such as cutting and digging cannot be connected directly with either the subsidiary or the principal; they will go where the altar (*vedi*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) are. And the altar and the sacrificial grass are connected with the placing of the oblation (*havis*).

And that *āsādana* (placing down) which is grasped by the injunction for the performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* is indeed connected [to the main sacrifice]; likewise, the placing down of the subsidiary oblation (*aṅga-havis*) is included therein, because the primary [sacrifice] and its subsidiaries constitute a single performance (*eka-prayoga*).

Now, one might object: just as the *prayāja* offerings and others, despite being grasped by the same injunction for performance, do not attain mutual subsidiarity—according to the seventh pāda of the third chapter [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra], "and because qualities are for the sake of another"—likewise, the subsidiary oblation does not attain a connection with the [main] oblation.
This is not so.

For just as the placing of the principal oblation is connected as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice, so too the placing of the subsidiary oblations is connected as a subsidiary to those subsidiaries.

And if it were assumed that "he places upon the sacrificial grass whatever oblation is for the sake of the Darśapūrṇamāsa," then [the rule] would apply only to that [principal oblation]. But this is not the case; rather, out of fear of its becoming purposeless (*anarthakya*), when its own form is being transgressed, why should the transgression be made in this way—[should it be] "that which is for the sake of the Darśapūrṇamāsa" or "that which assists the Darśapūrṇamāsa"?

If "being for that purpose" (*tādarthya*) were taken [as the sole criterion], an excessive restriction would be imposed upon the scope of the word *vākya*. However, if one adopts the criterion of "being helpful to that," there is a much wider range of application.
And how this [wider application] occurs must be accepted as following from that [criterion].

It is understood that even without being for the sake of that [the whole], each constituent part (aṅga) assists it; and it is joined with that [whole] merely to that extent, not because of being "for the sake of that" (tādarthya). For that which remains in something that does not assist does not assist, nor does it assist if it is not for the sake of that. And thus, he will state that "being for another's purpose" is a commonality of purpose. Even without being for the sake of that, since the assistance of the curd and milk is seen in the Abhyuditeṣṭi sacrifice, there is the attainment of the dharma of the primary [sacrifice].

Therefore, from this very context, a single syntactical unity is inferred: that which, if not performed, would cause the *apūrva* of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) to fail, must necessarily be performed. Furthermore, even with defective auxiliary oblations (*aṅga-havis*), the primary *apūrva* is not accomplished.
Consequently, it is logical that the performance of the auxiliaries is prompted solely by the primary *apūrva*.
This is also because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

And if such a [procedure] pertains to both the subsidiary and the principal acts, then the statement "he sprinkles the oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja*" pertains to both the subsidiary and the principal acts.

In that case, this sequence—which is established by logic—is stated as an accomplished fact within the sequential injunctions; thus, the explanatory passage (*hetuvannigada*) is appropriate because it serves a purpose, as in: "He indeed sprinkles from the *dhruvā* vessel; for from that, the two initial *ājyabhāga* offerings are drawn. (Tantravārtika on Abhighāra).
If the sacrificial portions (*ājyabhāga*) were also to be sprinkled with clarified butter (*abhighāraṇīya*), then it should have been stated in that way;
otherwise, there would be sprinkling solely for the sake of the *upāṃśuyāja* in the *bhuvā* [ladle].
In that case, there would be no sprinkling in the first [ladle], and thus the reason—"for from those [two], the two *ājyabhāgas* [arise]"—would not be consistent.

Therefore, it is "for the sake of all. Regarding the connection with the result, however, by the principle established in the section [sūtra] stating, "But those belonging to the sacrificer are for the sake of the principal because that is the principal, like the action," it has been proven that certain acts belong to the sacrificer. Now, do these acts serve both the subsidiary and the principal rites through the sacrificer's aspect as *kartṛ* (agent), or do they serve only the principal rite through his aspect as *bhoktṛ* (beneficiary)?

What is established by the preceding section? That [the subsidiaries] apply to all purposes; for when the sacrificer is present for the sake of all [purposes], they are able to assist everyone, and there is no cause for their exclusion. This being the prima facie view, it is replied: By the very same reason that these [subsidiaries] are determined to belong to the owner, by that same reason their application to the purpose of the primary sacrifice is also clear.

For if there were a mutual relationship (*graha-gāha-bhāva*) between them, either the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) would be a subsidiary part of the altar (*vedi*), or the altar would be a subsidiary part of the post; yet not even one of these is tenable. This is because both are already self-sufficient (*nirākāṅkṣatvāt*), it would involve the assumption of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa-kalpanāt*), and it would entail a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda-prasaṅgāt*).

To begin with, the sacrificial post engaged in the animal sacrifice has no requirement toward the altar. Nor does the altar—engaged in supporting the sacrificer, the oblation, and its implements—have any requirement for the post, which is related to only a thousandth part [of the entire ritual]. Furthermore, a visible benefit (*dṛṣṭopakāritva*) cannot be conceived for either of them in this context.
Furthermore, in your view, this [injunction] regarding the exterior of the sacrificial altar (*bahirvedī*) cannot be either an injunction (*vidhi*) or a restatement (*anuvāda*).
However, in our view, since it is impossible to indicate a specific location without both [the altar and the exterior], this must necessarily be enjoined.
How so? [As stated in the] *Tantravārtika*: "Of the whole... (*samastasya*... [and so forth].

When the measurement [of the sacrificial post] is obtained as being either inside or outside the altar, it is restricted by the rule "half [is] inside the altar. Since there is again the possibility of non-restriction regarding the second half, one would have to enjoin "the other half is outside the altar" as well.
Consequently, because of the multiple meanings, a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) would result, as well as the laborious necessity of supplying the verb "measures" (*minoti*) twice.
Furthermore, one would have to assume that what is merely optional is being restated as if it were mandatory, which is purposeless.

But surely, once the connection with the interior of the altar (*antarvedi*) has been enjoined, since there is no further injunction, the other half will naturally occur outside the altar (*bahirvedi*).

This would indeed be the case if measuring the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) were invariably subject to the contingency of being either entirely inside the altar or entirely outside it. For if the contingency of the whole [post] being inside the altar existed, then by the force of the restatement (*punarvacana*), there would be an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*), and the measurement of the other half outside would be understood; or if the contingency of the whole being entirely outside existed, then that which is not so enjoined would necessarily be determined to be inside. However, neither of these two contingencies exists.

Therefore, this restriction of "half" means "half within the *antarvedi*," and not that "only half is within the *antarvedi*. If that were the case, since the interior would be unrestricted, one might at times measure even inside [the altar], and thus the location outside would not be fixed.
[Objection: But if one measures the whole [altar] within the *antarvedi*, then one should simply do so by the injunction "half within the *antarvedi*" itself.

Why does one not do so? [Response: Because what is enjoined is merely that "that which is half must be measured within"; nothing else is prohibited. Therefore, a single specific location characterized by both [factors] is expressed; thus, there is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

Regarding the statement "he brings the *sāmidhenī* verses after that," because of the mention of the two *havir-nayas*, the *sadasya* must indeed be chosen separately; however, the *brahmā* is not denoted by the term *sadasya*.

Furthermore, he is not called an *ṛtvij* (priest), because there is no rule for his selection during the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtuyajana*), because he has no connection with a share of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and because he is not mentioned in the injunctions concerning the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).

Just as the *camasādhvaryus* are not designated as *ṛtvij*s because, despite there being both the act of selection (*varaṇa*) and a connection with the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtuyajana*), the two requisite causes are absent;

whereas for the masters (*svāmin*), although there is no selection, all other factors are present, and thus it is logical that they possess the status of *ṛtvij*. As for the argument that even the *sadasya* performs the sacrifice through oversight and so forth—

This [designation] is derived solely from the force of the statement itself; there is no distinct entity dependent upon it by virtue of which its designation could occur, nor is there any such entity as "inspection" (pratyavekṣaṇa) by which a specific agent for it could be established through any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Therefore, since the Sadasya exists, it is correctly stated that "the master is the seventeenth.

As for that which was said by the author of the Bhāṣya regarding the refutation of the Sadasya, that should be disregarded as an overly hasty remark intended to refute the status of the [Sadasya] as an officiating priest (ṛtvij).

"Because they are employed for all purposes, and because the fires [are established] at their own time; thus, having established the difference between the agents, he now formulates the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument regarding application by designation (samākhyā-viniyoga): 'In that regard, those are for all purposes. It is not known whether this belongs to the seventh section of the third chapter on ritual action.

[The opponent’s view is: "It is intended for one’s own purpose and for human goals (*puruṣārtha*), whereas [the other] is intended for the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and for all purposes (*sarvārtha*). Furthermore, regarding that [latter], are those things connected with the sentence for all purposes, or are they for all purposes even when not so connected? If, first of all, the intention is that they are also for human goals, that is incorrect because choosing (*varaṇa*) and supporting (*bharaṇa*) are for the purpose of the sacrifice due to their being mentioned in the context (*prakaraṇa*);
for it has been said:"
Furthermore, due to the distinction of context, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of that which is connected to it occurs in cases such as "like a substance" (*dravyavat*);

likewise, in the eleventh [book], he will state: "Or rather, it should belong to the Vedic [rites] because of the specific instruction. Therefore, for this reason, it is not the case that [the *agnihotra*] serves all purposes.

Nor is there any room for the introduction of other [rites] mentioned in the scriptures—such as "he does not distribute them before the Adhvaryu" and so forth—into those [passages] that are already connected [to specific rites].
However, those actions which are unconnected (asaṃyukta) may be performed by any agent according to their capacity, wherever they are recited in the Veda; thus they serve all purposes.
This is because they are employed [for all], for indeed all such actions are capable of being employed for them.

Likewise, those [fires] should also be understood as performing all tasks, for everything is a human function (*puruṣakārya*). Whatever action can be accomplished by men through their own capacity prior to any specific scriptural injunction, that alone is appropriate; it is not so because of an intention toward the "human purpose" (*puruṣārtha*).

As for the Āhavanīya and other fires, their being for the sake of all purposes is entirely irrelevant here, nor is it mentioned as a secondary application (*prasaṅga*), because the reason—that they exist at their own time—is also ineffective.
Furthermore, there is no consideration of the opponent's position or of the reason for that position.

If "all-purpose-ness" (*sarvārthatva*) is asserted with respect to worldly activities, then—having stated that "the sacrificial hall (*vihāra*) would accomplish the purpose of worldly people because of its sovereignty"—it has already been determined in the *Nirdeśa* that it would belong to Vedic [activities] as well; therefore, this need not be further deliberated upon. As for the claim that the fire-altar prescribed by the Veda is all-purposeful for both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*), that too, having cited the example "they praise while placing the fire nearby," is a matter of doubt: it would be for worldly purposes because it serves all aims, and not for Vedic purposes because of the specific mention of the aim.
Since it has been determined that the production of the other Viṣṇu-fires should likewise occur, this matter is not to be further deliberated;
for this is merely a statement of the established conclusion (siddhānta), as there is no expression of a refutation.
Therefore, it is described as follows.

This universal applicability (*sarvārthatva*) of the fires is not the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) set forth here in the *Tantravārtika*; rather, this is stated as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) itself through a distinct formulation of the sūtra, with its prima facie position inferred by means of the logic set forth in another section of the sūtras. Furthermore, this universal applicability is not in relation to the functions of the fire (*agnikārya*), but rather in relation to the archetypal and ectype sacrifices (*prakṛti-vikṛti*). Therefore, following the principle of the detached injunction (*anārabhyavāda*), the prima facie and final positions should be formulated just as in the case of the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*): namely, whether the *āhavanīya* and other such fires serve the purpose of the archetype alone, or whether they serve all purposes.

In that regard, as for the meaning of their original nature (*prakṛti*), it is argued that "the unconsecrated injunctions (*anārabhyavāda*) apply to the archetype (*prakṛti*), because they would otherwise be stated twice. This being the position reached, it is replied: "The fires (*agni*) serve all purposes; they should belong to both the archetype and the ectype (*vikṛti*). Why? Because they have their own time (*svakālatva*); the meaning is that they possess independent origination."
This has been described as being for the sake of all [rites] because the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) has its own specific time; however,
this status of being for the sake of all is not applicable to every case,
for in those instances where the means (*dvāra*) is dependent on another, it depends upon the attainment of that [other].
Such states of being are by no means independent;

for it is heard in scripture that "they offer in the Āhavanīya," and not that "if they were to sacrifice. Therefore, one must necessarily wait for the injunction regarding the Āhavanīya until [the point when] "he offers the fourfold portion," "that which he offers the cups (grahas)," and "that which he offers the chalices (camasas)" are obtained through connection by way of extension (atideśa).
Consequently, this [offering] occurs together with the Āhavanīya precisely by virtue of such extension.

Or rather, there would be this certainty: "Because it is recited in its primary form (prakṛti). To begin with, the word *hotṛ* is not based on the office of the Hotṛ; this is understood because, just as in the case of the word *rājan*, there is no traditional rule (smaraṇa) for the elision of the suffix or the restoration of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-pratyāpatti*).

Nor can the word *hotṛ* be inferred from the word *hautra*, any more than the word *rājya* can be inferred from the word *rājan*; for, just as in that case the protection of the subjects ordained by Manu and others is understood as the duty of a Kṣatriya and thus becomes the meaning of the suffix, so too here there is no well-known duty of a Hotṛ—such as the recitation of the *sāmidhenī* verses—that would serve as the basis for this designation. This being the case, it is not determined that the designation itself is the factor that assigns the function. How then, if the etymological derivation of the parts exists, can there be a functional assignment?
This has been stated as being based merely on the similarity of words (*śabdasārūpya*).
However, this was not [properly] stated.

For if the *hautra* were not derived in this way from the priest's function (*hotuḥ karma hautram*), then, since the similarity of words and the designation (*samākhyā*) would be established even without a connection between the agent and the action, there would be no presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) that could lead one to infer a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). This is because, as the *Sannavārtika* states: "Indeed, [the relationship] does not exist."
There is some connection between *śālā* and *mālā* by virtue of their commonality alone;
and so he will say later: "For there is no connection whatsoever with the *rathantara* in the case of the *kaṇvarathantara*."
Furthermore, as for the claim that the word "kingdom" (rājya) is applied because of a connection with the king's actions,
that is incorrect, because it would entail the consequence that the connection has a beginning in time.

This is merely an illusion; for when the eternal relationship between the two eternally existing entities—the word and its meaning—is being understood as permanent, then at the time of comprehending grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), even though the word *rājya* is explained after having explained the word *rājan*, and is said to be derivative (*yaugika*) and based on that [relationship], it does not acquire a beginning (*ādimatva*) because its basis is eternal. In the same way, since the increase (*vṛddhi*) is seen in the form *aulauvam* from the word *auḍa*, it is understood that this is an explanation [of the word] as "this belongs to him" (*tasyedam*) following the suffix *ka*. But by what means is that specific action of his understood? We shall infer such a statement from the observation of the traditional designation (*samākhyā*).

[Objection: But does this not result in a circular argument, since the statement of the name depends on that [connection], and the establishment of the name occurs through that connection? [Reply: This is not a fault.
First of all, the name is perceived as a direct cognition (*pratyakṣa*). As for the question of by what cause it was applied, one seeks the cause precisely in its prior application.
Since no such [prior application] exists [in the present moment], there must certainly be a Vedic revelation (*śruti*) to that effect.

Just as it has been explained that "this is how the office of the Hotṛ-priest must be performed" applies to all the indicative marks (*liṅga*) and so forth—namely, that "this is the case"—therefore, there is no mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) here.
[Objection: But surely this is already established by the very section [sūtra] stating, "And the name is likewise, because its purpose is that [same thing]. [Response:
True, it is established; however, in that [section], the presence or absence of contradiction was not investigated.

In this case, however, having raised the objection of contradiction due to the possibility of [the mantra] serving all purposes because of its general fitness (*yogyatva*), [the author] either refutes it or restates it with the intention of explaining what follows; thus, there is no tautology.

By means of the designation of instruction (*upadeśa-samākhyāna*), even the specific designation (*nirdeśa-viśeṣa-samākhyā*) becomes sublated because it functions more rapidly, just like a specific scriptural statement (*viśeṣa-śruti*).
The observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) is indeed an indicative mark for application (*viniyoga*) through general designation (*sāmānyasamākhyā*); however,
in the case of specific designation (*viśeṣasamākhyā*), something else must be observed.

The recitation of the *praiṣas* belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa because of direct instruction (*upadeśa*). Since direct instruction overrides conventional designation (*samākhyā*), there is an inquiry as to whether it applies to the whole or to a part [of the ritual]. This is stated within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice itself.
Therefore, it was stated "in the case of the Agni-Soma [animal sacrifice]" for the purpose of illustration, namely that the Maitrāvaruṇa shall both direct (*praiṣya*) and recite after (*anu-āha*).
In this regard, there is the designation (*samākhyāna*) of all directions as belonging to the Adhvaryu, and the designation of all recitations as belonging to the Hotṛ.
Now, does this instruction set aside the two designations with respect to the entire subject matter, or only in certain instances?

What is established? Since the Maitrāvaruṇa is mentioned with reference to the recitation of the *praiṣas* and the *anuvacanas*, and because it is impossible to intend a conjunction (*sāhitya*) between two things being so indicated when that is not expressed by the word itself; and since the heard particle *ca* expresses only a simple conjunction (*samuccaya*) or a mere mention (*anvācaya*), and not mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) or a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), as these latter are always understood through a compound;
and since the characteristic of *anvācaya* is not applicable here because both [actions] are equal, there must be a simple conjunction (*samuccaya*).

And since that [quality] is indeed possible even when all [the rites] are being performed individually, there would be a cognition of it for all [of them] due to the general statement; or rather, the qualification of the *puronuvākyā* [would apply] because of its proximity to the *praiṣa*.
Thus, it would not apply to all *praiṣas* and *anuvācanas*.
Where, then, does it apply? To the *puro'nuvākyā*.
The *anuvākyās* end with the *preṣa*, and this statement was made with reference to those *puronuvākyās*;
therefore, it refers to the Maitrāvaruṇa.
This is from the Tantravārtika on the Vākya section.
Since those [formulas] are recited by the Hotṛ alone in that manner, they would apply to him exclusively.

As for the word "yajati" (he sacrifices) at the end of those formulas, it applies to the Adhvaryu in the subsidiaries based on the *iṣṭi* sacrifice through extended application (*atideśa*); however, in the Soma sacrifices, because the direction (*preṣa*) pertains to another, that [application to the Adhvaryu] is set aside. Thus, according to the principle "from whom a distinction [of function] arises," it would belong to the Maitrāvaruṇa alone; or else, since the one who gives the direction is the agent in both cases, the status of being the one directed (*preṣyatva*) is assigned to the Maitrāvaruṇa by the logic to be explained later, and thus it would apply to the Hotṛ alone.

Likewise, because of the scriptural injunction of another direction (praisha), namely "Adhvaryo preṣya," the word "Ājya" is displaced and falls to the Pratiprasthātṛ; however, since the remaining directions and recitations have their specific performers already determined and are thus complete in themselves, it is not possible for them to be governed by the rule concerning the Maitrāvaruṇa.

Furthermore, because the *puro’nuvākyās* pertain to both parts [of the sacrifice] and constitute a single unitary act, it is impossible for them to have multiple performers; thus, since the duties of the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu would otherwise conflict, and because they are proximate and mutually expectant, the injunction for the Maitrāvaruṇa is appropriate. In this way, the word "ca" (and) is justified as having the sense of "pre-eminence" (*prakṛṣṭārtha*) due to its association with the proximity of the *praśas* (directions). Nor is it possible that the directions such as "praṣya" and so forth refer to himself as their own object.
Moreover, the Hotṛ is observed to be present during the *prātaranuvāka*.

Regarding the *camasa* cups, because of the specific designation "cup-priest" (*camasādhvaryu*), whatever duties pertaining to the cups— such as drawing [the soma], placing them down, offering them, and so forth— that generally fall to the *adhvaryu* by virtue of his general title, all of that must be performed by the cup-priests due to their specific designation;
or rather, the *adhvaryu* himself may perform it, because that is the logical conclusion.

A specific designation indeed sets aside a general designation when it functions independently of the latter; however, the designation "camasādhvaryu" (cup-attendant) establishes the function of an *adhvaryu* with respect to the cups.
Therefore, if the *adhvaryu* himself were not to offer the oblations, then those [cup-attendants] would not become *camasādhvaryus* by virtue of offering them.
They might perhaps acquire that status even without offering, but not otherwise.

If, however, he were to offer the oblation, then at some point, due to being otherwise occupied and thus unable to do so, those who are offering would become like him; therefore, the Adhvaryu offers. Furthermore, because another person is seen in connection with the *camasa* (cup), and because there is no other purpose for one who utters the *vaṣaṭ* call, the text speaks of the *camasādhvaryu* as the one who brings [the cup] for the sake of eating. Since it is impossible for the one who has not offered to eat, the very person who offers hands it over for the purpose of eating. And since the *camasādhvaryus* are occupied by virtue of their role as *grahītṛ*s (seizers), the text indicates that the person who gives it is an Adhvaryu other than them.
If they were unable to understand them,

they would do so from the instruction of the Veda, as before; and in the case of a discrepancy between the subordinate and the principal, it has been explained under the principle that "because the purpose is for that [the principal], the connection with the Veda is by way of the principal," just as the subsidiaries receive the designation of the primary Veda.
Therefore, in the Śyena sacrifice, all constituent elements obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) must be performed by the *udgātṛ* priests.

Because of that specific mention, it would follow that its own ritual duty (*svadharma*) applies; this is due to the force of the qualification (*adhikāra*), as has been stated and will be further explained regarding the "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) subsidiary parts.

For instance, because it occurs at a later time, the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance) is weaker than the *codaka*; and since the primary designation (*pradhāna-samākhyā*) is dependent upon the *prayogavacana*, it is weak even though it is directly perceived (*pratyakṣatva*).

As long as the subsidiaries (aṅgas) are obtained through extended application (atideśa), for what purpose does [the name] restrict the agent? But when they have been obtained, since their connection with an agent is already established, there is no expectation [for another]; so what will the name accomplish?
Nor is there here a sublation of what has been obtained, because the name is remote due to the necessity of postulating a direct Vedic statement (śruti).

For it has been stated that sublation of what has been obtained occurs in the case of means of knowledge whose basis is already established, but not in the case of those whose basis is yet to be postulated.

Therefore, by virtue of the mention of the archetypal (prakṛta) elements and the capacity for their application, it must have multiple performers, just like the Jyotiṣṭoma. Even though in the archetype itself the multiple performers are established by name (samākhyā) alone, nevertheless, because the relationship [of the new elements] is already established, here there is an equality with direct scriptural statement (śruti). As for whatever non-archetypal element is introduced, its performer will be determined by the name of the primary rite; showing this, he says: "The subsidiary is unmanifest" (avyaktaḥ śeṣaḥ).
Because its state is not yet established, this connection with a performer is "unmanifest," and it must be other than that which is already established.
However, its subject matter is not clearly perceived.

For instance, regarding the *kaṇṭakavinodana* and other such texts: if they are recited in the very same Veda that is designated as the "Principal" (*pradhāna*), then their connection with the author is established by that designation alone, and not through the medium of the Principal. But if they are recited in another Veda, then even though they are directly perceived [in that context], the specific designation (of the other Veda) must prevail over it because it is more powerful.

Now, if even here the principle of non-transgression by way of the subordinate is relied upon, then, because the *stotra* and *śastra* and so forth are designated as belonging to the Adhvaryu in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma, it would follow that the Adhvaryu must be their performer.

Nor is there a remedy here such as "in the morning pressing, [the voice is] low" (*mandraṃ prātaḥsavana*), and so on; therefore, the designation is not set aside in the subsidiaries by the primary act.

Rather, being already assigned its purpose through its innate connection with a specific performer, it is taken up by the primary act; nor is it appropriate for the designation of the Adhvaryu and others to apply to the subsidiaries by way of the primary act.

For the primary acts are not connected with designations such as "Adhvaryava" and so forth, because [those designations] function with respect to subordinate elements (guṇabhūta). And how could it be that what does not function with respect to the primary acts would nevertheless descend to the subsidiary parts (aṅga) by means of association? From where is this [conclusion] derived?
The designation "Ṛgveda" and so forth is not contradictory with respect to both the primary rites and their subsidiaries;

thus, the designation "it is performed by this" applies there as well. Furthermore, because it is to be enjoined by the injunction for the performance of the primary rite, that designation is appropriate for the subsidiaries. Moreover, the designation such as "Adhvaryava" (pertaining to the Adhvaryu) based on the order of recitation must exist exactly according to that recitation.
And nothing is impaired here by the principle of the non-transference of qualities and benefits (*guṇasukha-avyatikrama-nyāya*), which has not been accepted [by us].
Furthermore, acts such as the removal of thorns should be understood as arising only from the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*) and its subsidiaries (*veda*).

And it is possible to say that the unmanifest (*avyakta*) remains in its own nature; for the name (*samākhyā*) is not necessarily favored by descending directly from the primary sacrifice alone—whether there is direct favor or no favor at all—because there is no contradiction since its purpose is fulfilled in other subsidiaries. Thus, it is established that the name is the allocator (*viniyoktrī*) with respect to those things distinct from the archetypal (*prākṛta*) ones.
The seventh quarter of the third chapter of the *Tantravārtika*.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. The hiring of the master [is performed] by the sacrificer, because the ritual act is for his sake.

This point is also investigated as a refutation of the [proposed] designation: Is that which is to be performed by those persons designated as *adhvaryu* and so forth to be done by them because of the scriptural injunction regarding their hiring (*parikraya*), or rather by the master (*svāmin*)?
However, once this [question] is established, it should be understood that "another [may perform it] because of the scriptural injunction regarding hiring."

Thus, it might be argued that a master should employ worldly means just as debtors purchase others with their own property for the sake of securing a livelihood; to this, it is replied: you may resort to worldly means only where no Vedic alternative exists. When the giving of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is available according to the Veda, why resort to worldly means?

Since these [functions] are prescribed with reference to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), they apply to all of them according to the principle of repetition for each principal act (pratipradhānāvṛttinyāya); therefore, they cannot be set aside by mere designation (samākhyā). Consequently, there can be no fixed restriction here; likewise, desire [is determined] through its connection with the purpose.

Since the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*)—by virtue of its being in grammatical apposition with the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) suffix—and because the middle voice found in the context of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) establishes that the result belongs to the agent without interruption, it is established from elsewhere that this applies to the primary agent. Consequently, regarding those desires for subsidiary results (*guṇakāma*) heard in connection with specific measurements of the sacrificial hall (*sadas*) and so forth, where the text says "he should measure" (*minuyāt*), the common agency (*samānakartṛtva*) would lead one to conclude, via the name (*samākhyā*) of the ritual, that these belong to the Adhvaryu priest. However, since the connection of the fruit with the entire performance is understood to pertain to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) by means of the middle voice attached to the primary act, and since the phrase "if the sacrificer should desire" is determined by the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is understood that the ownership of the result belongs to him.

And thus, the *parasmaipada* ending is justified as referring to the activity of the Adhvaryu priest; otherwise, since the root *ḍumiñ* (meaning "to scatter") is marked with the *ñi* indicatory letter, the *ātmanepada* would occur when there is an intention to express that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent.

And by this scriptural statement, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) understood from the sentence is set aside; thus there is no fault. On the contrary, in accordance with the sacrificer’s prayer—"O Adhvaryu, may this desire of mine, that the sacrificer obtain rain"—coreferentiality with respect to that [desire] is not contradictory. By the word "tathā" (so), it is extended from the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*) that [the rule] is not restricted by the name (*samākhyā*). [The sūtra states: "It would belong to the others because of designation; it would belong to the others elsewhere because of a specific statement. Since such a specific statement is absent here, it is said "because of designation" (*vyapadeśāt*). It would belong to the others [the Adhvaryus] because of their designation, as in other cases where there is a specific statement. But here, in the absence of such a statement, it is designated [as belonging to the sacrificer].

Because of the inclusion of the word "or" (vā), because the self is mentioned as distinct from the sacrificer, and because the fourth case-ending clearly indicates a blessing for the sake of another, it can be understood that the connection with the fruit belongs to two agents: "either for himself or for the sacrificer.

And likewise, the mantras used in the *ākramaṇa* rite—namely, the benedictory mantras (*āśī-mantra*) not connected to a specific action—are restricted by their name (*samākhyā*), since no production of fruit arises from them; for mantras are not injunctive, and there is no other possible ground for postulating a fruit [for them].

As for the prayer (*āśāsana*), since it is not distinct from that of the *adhvaryu* priest insofar as it generates extreme enthusiasm in the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the conclusion reached [by some] is that it belongs to the sacrificer; thus it is stated: "They belong to the sacrificer. For they pray for the attainment of the fruit of the sacrifice because there is no other fruit [for them].

And that prayer must be made by the sacrificer, because—unlike the case of a dancer—the obtaining of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is already accomplished otherwise, and because it is not to be prayed for by Agni, as it is obtained from the sacrificer.
Now, he (the sacrificer) requested that very thing for his own sake, saying, "Grant me long life," thus referring to himself;
therefore, these [mantras] should be employed by the sacrificer alone for the purpose of inspiring him with zeal toward the attainment of the primary fruit.
This is also because they are seen [to be used] in the case of separation [from the object].

And in the case of the *āśīman* [formula] during the *pravasadyajña* (sacrifice performed while traveling) and the *agnihotra* of one who is away from home, the *Vārtika* shows that it serves the purpose of maintaining the fires for the sake of the one who has gone abroad; it does not apply to a priest who is away from home, because priesthood is impossible for one who is absent due to the lack of connection with the ritual action, whereas for the sacrificer it is possible through the renunciation of the sacrificial materials (*dravyatyāga*).
Therefore, by analogy with that, the same applies to the other cases.

Regarding those [formulas] recited in both [sections], since the dual recitation must have a purpose, and because they are read generally in the *Adhvaryava* section—beginning with the *jyagrahaṇa* formulas—and then specifically again in the *Yājamāna* section, the question arises: are both [the Adhvaryu and the Yajamāna] the performers, either alternatively or by combination, or is it one or the other?
In this regard, when the possibility of both performing them or of an alternative has arisen, [the author] says "both."

But surely, due to the specific designation (*viśeṣa-samākhyā*), there would be only the status of being for the sacrificer alone (*kevala-yājamānatva*). In that regard, we maintain that the specific designation is stronger where there is a single recitation; however, in cases where [mantras] are recited separately both in a general and a specific context, if the specific designation were accepted, then the general reading would indeed be rendered purposeless. And when they refer to the same subject, the general is set aside by the specific. Even though there is no difference in the mantra itself, the subject matter differs due to the difference in the recitation; for one must assume a specific purpose for the difference in the recitation.

And nothing else is possible besides those two being employed; therefore, both [the injunction and the mantra] are required. Now, one might argue: "Of these two readings, one must be for the purpose of making known the essential nature [of the action], while the other must be for the purpose of its application (*viniyoga*). Even so, since mantras serve to manifest the sequence [of actions], and since the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary acts (*pradhāna*) share a common agent, it is logical that the application of a mantra—once it is understood as something to be employed—should occur precisely where the performance of the act, such as the taking of the clarified butter (*ājyagrahaṇa*), is enjoined by the very same agent designated by the name [of the ritual]. And it is only there that the agent has a requirement for a specific performer, not elsewhere.

Since the mere designation of form is accomplished simply by the study [of the texts], even without the application of action at the time [of performance], and since acts such as the taking of the clarified butter (*ājya*) are indisputably the duty of the Adhvaryu priest,
it follows that these are not to be performed by the sacrificer.
To this, it is replied:

Even in the case of the *yajamāna* (the sacrificer), since the form [of the action] is established as something to be employed even in the absence of an explicit purpose—because it is determined to be that which is to be performed—the requirement for an agent certainly exists; thus, the status of the sacrificer as the agent is established.
But what is the "state of being employed" (*prayojyatva*) of those [actions] that are being employed?
It is said:

Just as the ritual acts (*padārtha*) must be performed by the *adhvaryu*, so too must they be supervised by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) for the sake of avoiding negligence. In some cases, these [acts] are not recorded in the mantras; there, supervision is carried out by other means. But here, it is done by means of the mantras—this is their purposeful utility (*arthavattā*). Furthermore, recitation occurs once [the act] is known, for one who is ignorant is not authorized [to perform it]. Where it is heard in the scripture that "he causes the sacrificer to recite," even an ignorant person can be made to recite it word by word; thus, there is no fixed rule. Alternatively, one who is learned may recite it himself.

In this regard, it might be argued that the activity of the instructor would be rendered useless; therefore, it follows that only one who is unlearned should be made to recite. To this, it is replied: "For there is no one ordained as unlearned.

If the study of the Veda were governed by injunctions based on specific desires (*kāma-śruti*), then it might be taught even at the time of ritual performance. However, since it is enjoined as an independent rule (*anārabhya-vidhi*)—namely, "The Veda is to be studied"—it must be undertaken [at the outset].

This being the case, since there would be no room for presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), it follows that all ritual acts (*karmāṇi*) grasp [the mantra] like fire and do not employ instruction; nor does the Veda become "learned" [merely by such instruction]. Therefore, those mantras which have been recited prior to the ritual act attain the status of being auxiliary (*aṅga*) to it. Thus, there is no entitlement (*adhikāra*) for one who is ignorant [of them]. Furthermore, even in that case, the operation of the prompter (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*)—like a directive (*praiṣa*)—is purposeful; for even when one has the capacity, one should not speak if one is not prompted.
And that state of being a prompter occurs either when the task is handed over in parts, or when one is told, "Speak! (or "Recite!").

Regarding the question, "By knowing how much [of the Veda] may one perform actions as desired?", the Vaiśeṣikas and others, in the *Svatantravārtika*, state that there is no entitlement [to perform rites] even with respect to a portion of the scripture not yet mastered. To provide a clear determination of this, he asks: "By knowing how much? Since learning [the Veda] assists [one in performing rites] through the direct production of capacity, he says, "by knowing however much."

Although the entire Veda is encompassed by the injunction for the study of one's own recitation (svādhyāya), nevertheless, for one performing the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Mantra and Brāhmaṇa portions pertaining to the Jyotiṣṭoma are of no use whatsoever; yet even this non-utility does not exclude [the sacrificer] from eligibility, because his fitness is already established by the very performance of the Iṣṭi. Therefore, for one who performs that sacrifice, his svādhyāya extends only so far.

As for the fact that this [Veda] is recited in its entirety, since obligatory (nitya), optional (kāmya), and occasional (naimittika) rites may be performed at any time as circumstances arise, it is not known which one will be performed when. Consequently, if at some point a desire for the fruit of a rite not yet recited, or a specific occasion (naimitta) for it, arises, he is frustrated because he is unable to perform it due to the lack of that [text]. Furthermore, while studying, there is an impossibility of observing the vows and restrictive rules (vrata-niyama) required for study; and since the Veda has no further expectancy once its requirements are satisfied by the performance of specific ritual acts, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of deficiency (vaiguṇya) if such [unstudied portions] were not grasped.

Furthermore, because of the non-acceptance of [Vedic] revelation regarding sensual desires, the Veda—purified by the injunctions of the *anārabhyavāda* (independent statements)—is required by all; therefore, the entire Veda must necessarily be studied during the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*). However, if someone is incapable and does not study the whole, but somehow acquires only the *Agnihotra*, *Darśa*, and *Pūrṇamāsa* rites, he is not thereby disqualified from [the knowledge of] reality.
This being the case, external knowledge is indeed far removed [from the goal];
as for the knowledge of the Self, without it there is no activity at all, and thus it must be accepted for the sake of all ritual action.

However, because of the designation "pertaining to the sacrificer" (*yājamāna*), actions such as placing the fire-pan on the hearth (*ukhādhiśrayaṇa*) and threshing (*avahanana*)—which are recited in both the *Yājamāna* and the *Ādhvaryava* sections among the twelve ritual acts belonging to the sacrificer—must be performed by the sacrificer. This is because it is impossible for them to be performed by both, given that they possess mantras specifically prescribed [for the sacrificer]. Thus, due to the designation "pertaining to the sacrificer," these acts belong to the sphere of the sacrificer. Alternatively, the *Adhvaryu* priest should perform them, for the designation is governed by the principle that [the priest] exists for the sake of that [sacrifice].

Because there is no power to bring about lordship (*indratva*) over those [rites] that have not yet arisen, and because there is an absence of any word that would obstruct them, their origin does not belong to the sacrificer alone; rather, it belongs to the Adhvaryu.

Since the requirement for an agent exists therein, and the hiring (*parikraya*) is understood to be for that purpose, once the agent is established, there is no need for an expectation at the time of the recitation of the *indra* [formula]; thus, the sacrificer’s status as the agent is untenable. In that case, if the sacrificer has no connection with the essential nature [of the act], how could the state of being *indra* (*indratā*) be performed by the sacrificer?

Furthermore, that [designation] is not possible for acts being performed by another agent, for the designation "Indatā" (the state of being the performer) consists in immediate performance; and one person is not capable of performing immediately what has been performed by another. Nor can the very nature of the act itself—though it belongs to the sacrificer—be altered merely to conform to immediate performance. Therefore, according to the principle of the conflict between a subsidiary and its quality (*aṅgaguṇavirodha*), even that [act] belongs to the Adhvaryu alone. However, the sacrificer will perform it [thinking], "May he perform it for me"; thus the designation remains meaningful. In case of a conflict, the performer [is determined] due to a specific connection; the other [is assigned] to those from whom a distinction arises.

Regarding the two mantras, "parivīrasi" (the preparatory mantra) and "yuvā suvāsāḥ" (the subsequent mantra recited while the action is being performed), there arises a doubt: since both are employed simultaneously by the Adhvaryu and the Hotṛ in the Kuṇḍapāyināmayana sacrifice, and because they cannot both be performed by a single agent due to the impossibility of simultaneous action, which one of the two should be adopted? In this regard, the initial conclusion is that there is no fixed rule. Alternatively, it might be argued that the Hotṛ's mantra is established by the *Tantravārtika* because, as the Adhvaryu's duty is prescribed for himself, the Hotṛ's function remains appropriate without abandoning its own inherent characteristics. To this, the following is stated in reply: [The established view: Because the Adhvaryu’s duty is specifically ordained for himself, and because the Hotṛ’s duty would otherwise be abandoned, the Hotṛ’s mantra is indeed appropriate; thus, the [Hotṛ’s] mantra is to be accepted. (Note: This passage discusses the principle of *sva-dharma-tyāga*—the abandonment of one's own specific duty—and the preference for the Hotṛ’s role over the Adhvaryu’s in cases of conflict, based on the authority of the *Tantravārtika*.)
In this conflict, the instrumental case (*karaṇa*) should be employed; why? Because of a specific relationship of inherence (*samavāya-viśeṣa*). Regarding this, some say:
"The specific relationship of inherence is the proximity to the primary [element].

Since the external factor (*bahiraṅga*)—being of the nature of an indirect auxiliary (*dhārādupakāraka*)—is a restatement of what is being performed, whereas the instrumental factor (*karaṇa*) is internal (*antaraṅga*).

If the agent were to transfer [the performance] to the subsidiaries by means of the primary [rite], then proximity (*sannikarṣa*) and remoteness (*viprakarṣa*) would be relevant; however, he is indicated without distinction for both the primaries and the subsidiaries by means of the name (*samākhyā*) and the extended injunction (*codaka*). There is no principle of conflict between a subsidiary and a quality, because there is no difference in the subsidiariness of both. Nor is the status of being a remote benefactor (*ārādupakāritva*) residing in another action weakened by virtue of [the subsidiary's] being a direct contributor (*sannipātin*).

And this [injunction] is not at all devoid of utility, because it produces a visible mental impression (*saṃskāra*) through the uninterrupted mindfulness of the performance of the *parivyāṇa* (encircling). Therefore, by virtue of its being directly perceived (*pratyakṣatvena*), it becomes a specific instance of that inherent relation (*samavāya*) which is otherwise known inferentially through other connections.
How so?

For the syntactical formulation here is as follows: the *adhvaryu* and others, whose functions are established by direct audition (*śruti*), are enjoined with respect to the rituals indicated by the words "adhvaryu" and so forth.

In this regard, the connection of the *hotṛ* with the *hotrā* (the office of the Hotṛ) is inferential, whereas the connection of the *adhvaryu* with the *ādhvaryava* (the office of the Adhvaryu) is perceptual.

As for the claim that the *hotṛ*, without relinquishing his own specific duty, becomes connected to the *ādhvaryava* function—that might be possible if his status as a *hotṛ* were established solely by the performance of that [specific] act, or if the *adhvaryu* were enjoined in relation to the *hautra* (the office of the Hotṛ), or if there were an injunction for the *ādhvaryava* function directed toward the *hotṛ*. But none of that is the case.
To begin with, the *hotṛ* is determined solely by his fitness; and even though the action is occasioned by [the office], thousands of other factors will serve as its indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Nor is there an injunction here regarding the *adhvaryu* with respect to the *hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ priest); for since the two words "Hotṛ" (*hotṛ*) and "Adhvaryu" (*adhvaryu*) denote two entirely distinct persons, they lack primary grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Consequently, one of the two must necessarily be understood through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Since the assumption of figurative indication is prompted by a conflict [between the literal and the required sense], we do not perceive any grounds for such an assumption in the word "Hotṛ," which is uttered first. Therefore, following the principle that "the primary [meaning] prevails because it is enjoined as something new (*apūrva*"), one should accept that word in its own primary sense; thus, the word "Adhvaryu" is determined to have the function of indicating the ritual action [of the Adhvaryu].

Even there, the Hotṛ priest is enjoined with reference to that [sacrifice]; for he serves a purpose as a constituent of the ritual (*kratvartha*), whereas the agent is not similarly the primary factor in such cases. Consequently, when the subordinate Hotṛ is introduced, he is connected only with those properties that do not conflict with the primary element.

If, however, the *ādhvaryava* (the duties of the Adhvaryu) were enjoined for the Hotṛ, then that [duty] would proceed without conflict with his own ritual actions, and he would not omit any part of the *hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ), because it would otherwise follow that the *ādhvaryava* would become a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of an agent other than its original one. Since such a connection does not exist, another position has been adopted. Therefore, it is established that the connection with the *ādhvaryava* alone is directly perceived and is primary.
On this point, they raise an objection: "In this case, the connection of either mantra with the Hotṛ need not be set aside."
Why?
Because a contradiction between two mental states would occur only if they were applied at the same time;
however, one [the instrument] exists prior to the action, while the other exists subsequent to it.
Thus ends the third chapter of the Mīmāṃsā-vārttika composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Kumārila.
And this Tantravārtika is completed.
May there be auspiciousness!
